16192-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Germany's seizure of a Chinese port leads the December 9, 1897 Great Round World, and the children's paper presents it bluntly as robbery. Some German missionaries had been killed in China, and Germany took a port in revenge. The paper says the deed seems, to simple folks who are not diplomats, a plain, everyday case of theft. Missionaries, the paper reminds readers, are holy and devoted men who carry the Gospel to far countries at great risk.

The number then recalls missionary sufferings in early American annals, setting the China news in a longer story of faith and danger. Young readers could judge empires and missions in plain language. The issue preserves a schoolroom view of the Kiaochow crisis and its moral framing.
2699-pages-from-an-old-volume-of-life-a-:
Oliver Wendell Holmes gathers essays in this old volume of life, opening with Bread and the Newspaper in September 1861. This, he says, is the new Panem et Circenses: the Roman crowd demanded bread and shows, and Americans demand bread and news.

My Hunt After the Captain, The Inevitable Trial, Cinders from Ashes, and The Pulpit and the Pew follow, mixing memoir, war, and religion. Holmes writes as a man looking back over a long life, with wit intact. The essays offer a sage's scrapbook, and a view of America through one brilliant Boston mind.
27681-the-last-of-the-mohicans-a-narrati:
James Fenimore Cooper's The Last of the Mohicans, a narrative of 1757, appears here illustrated by N. C. Wyeth, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York, copyrighted in 1919 and printed in 1933. Its epigraph asks readers not to mislike the speaker for his sun-shadowed complexion.

Illustrations show Uncas slaying a deer, the battle at Glens Falls, and the fight in the forest, where only the struggle between Le Renard Subtil and Le Gros Serpent remains. The meeting of the generals follows, with Montcalm baring his head and letting his spotless plume fall nearly to the earth in courtesy. Cooper's frontier tale of 1757 remains his most famous novel.
6161-copyright-renewals-1957: The hosted file for the 1957 copyright renewals holds no renewal lists at all, and this note says so plainly. It states that the file was kept empty years ago as a placeholder, while the real 1957 data went into two other files instead. Readers seeking renewals for that year must look elsewhere, since this record offers no entries of its own.
940-the-last-of-the-mohicans-a-narrative:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this narrative of 1757, in the French and Indian War, about Hawkeye, the scout, and his Mohican friends Chingachgook and Uncas. They guide two sisters, Cora and Alice Munro, through the forests of New York, pursued by the Huron chief Magua and his warriors.

Cooper fills the tale with ambushes, sieges, and flights by canoe and trail, and with the clash of empires on a wild frontier. The Last of the Mohicans, Uncas, gives the book its title and its tragedy. The novel remains the classic American frontier romance, and a founding work of American fiction.
arxiv-2412-01457:
Martin Lemoine and Frank Rieger ask how wild flow near black holes could speed protons to make the small grains IceCube spots. Views hint that the crowns of near Seyfert star groups give off such grains at TeV scale through acts of light with core grains. The team models chance speed up in those crowns in close points: move in push space, loss, and drift.

They test three tales. One is pure wild flow speed up. One is first speed up and then shear speed up. The third is speed up held in check by the grains as they damp the wild flow. All three can fit the proton range read from data. But the first two need the proton strength set by hand. The third case hits the seen flow in a plain way, and the team marks it as the tale that most please.
arxiv-2412-06957:
Miller and a large team used the Webb space scope in twenty twenty-four to measure how fast young galaxies grew in the first billion years. They read near one thousand galaxies in a lens field with rich light data. Shape fits in six bands gave size at both blue and red light.

Low-mass galaxies grew fast, near doubling in size from the far end to the near end of their range. That pace is faster than plain scale rules from past work would give. Shape spread and the slope of size with mass stayed the same in time. Strong acts in small systems in that era may drive the fast growth.
arxiv-2412-09357:
Amit Kumar, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, models the light curves of eleven burst stars that had shed their outer coats. He asks if a fast-spinning, highly magnetic dead core could drive their glow.

He fits each curve with a code that seeks the best match, with the dead core as the power source. The model remade all eleven curves well. It set bounds on the core's first spin rate and field strength, the burst's energy, and the size of the star that blew up. Two super-bright cases had the lowest field and spin values, while one fast, broad case had the highest. Most bursts held huge energy, which hints jets may have driven them.
arxiv-2412-10057:
Salvatore Muratore, Danilo Triggiani, and Vincenzo Tamma show a quantum way to beat a classic limit in imaging. Their twenty twenty-four paper concerns two light sources too close to tell apart by standard optics, a bound known as Rayleigh's criterion. Their trick uses pairs of photons that interfere.

One photon comes from a reference, the other from one of the two sources. Their interference makes a beat pattern that encodes the gap between the sources. By sampling the sideways momenta of the photons, the team reaches near the ultimate quantum precision for the gap, with few samples and no extra optics. Uses in microscopy and astronomy are in view.
arxiv-2412-10857:
Ali Nasr-Esfahani, Mehdi Bekrani, and Roozbeh Rajabi recognize Persian digits in noise in two thousand twenty four. Spoken digit systems falter when real world noise intrudes. Phonetically similar Persian numbers are easy to confuse. Their hybrid model mixes residual CNNs with bidirectional GRUs.

Word units replace phoneme units for speaker independent recognition. Mel frequency features feed the network after augmentation. Test accuracy reached about ninety six percent in their runs. Noisy condition gains beat phoneme based LSTM models by far. The margin over a cepstrum plus MLP baseline was clear too.
arxiv-2412-12457:
Aitzhan and Ambrose proved in twenty twenty-four that a wave equation for long water crests starts well with near-repeat start shapes. The shapes repeat with a twist, not in lock step. Stock proofs lean on plain repeat grids and fall short for such twist data.

They built the needed function-space facts for twist-repeat shapes first. An energy method then gives short-time sound starts for the equation. Guard laws still hold for such shapes, they show. Those laws no longer cap the main norms, so long-time claims stay open for now.
arxiv-2412-14357:
Prem Talwai and David Simchi-Levi rebuilt regression for spaces where functions have no point values in a 2024 paper. Dirichlet spaces, from fractals to rough domains, contain only equivalence classes of functions defined almost everywhere. Classic ridge regression, which judges a function at each data point, is not even well-defined there. Their fix replaces point values with local averages around small obstacles centered at the data points, renormalizing the loss into something meaningful.

The renormalized problem admits a representer theorem: the optimal fit is built from equilibrium potentials, truncated Green functions cut at a data-chosen threshold. The estimator achieves optimal rates, with a self-tuning bound exposing how the space's analysis, shapes, and probability interact.
arxiv-2412-15457:
Kristóf Bérczi and three co-authors study a conjecture in combinatorics in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The story starts with the Ryser-Brualdi-Stein conjecture on Latin squares. Later authors broadened it to common bases of two matroids. In a special graph case, the claim is called the Rainbow Arborescence Conjecture. It says that a graph built from many spanning trees holds one tree that takes exactly one arc from each.

Simple counterexamples cap the size in the general matroid case, yet none is known for the tree case. The authors prove several partial results toward the conjecture. Their work sharpens what is known about rainbow structures in graphs. It will interest readers in combinatorics and discrete math who follow transversal problems.
arxiv-2412-18457:
Richard Evan Schwartz wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on representations of the modular group, a classic symmetry group of fractions and lattices. The representations land in the isometry group of a symmetric space built from three-by-three matrices.

Schwartz focuses on one connected piece of this representation space, known as the Barbot component. He shows it has a simple shape, a plane times a half-line. Its boundary recovers a known family called Pappus representations. Its interior extends a known family of Anosov representations, which behave like well-ordered hyperbolic actions. The members act as symmetry groups of geodesic patterns that echo the Farey triangulation of the disk. Two shearing moves generate the Anosov family from the boundary one, and two foliations by rays encode that structure.
arxiv-2501-00057:
Witold Wydmanski and colleagues adapt image-trained vision transformers to work on tables of numbers, the most common data form in biology, industry, and finance. Deep learning has transformed text and image work, yet small tabular data sets still favor older ensemble methods, and training a fresh network for each small table is wasteful. Writing with a twenty twenty-five arXiv release, the team projects each table row into patch-like tokens. A pretrained vision transformer can accept those tokens. The team then runs the borrowed image encoder unchanged on them.

On several small data sets with under a thousand rows, the borrowed model beat both classic ensembles and recent purpose-built deep models. No new architecture had to be designed for tables. The authors present the result as a widening of transfer learning: skills learned from pictures can carry to spreadsheets.
arxiv-2501-00357:
Lv and Zhang wrote a combinatorics paper, published in twenty twenty-four, on mesh patterns in permutations. A permutation is an ordering of numbers, and a mesh pattern adds shading rules to a pattern within it. They study how often the patterns one-two-three and three-two-one appear together.

The authors prove twenty of twenty-two possible joint equidistributions for symmetric shadings. An equidistribution means two different patterns occur the same number of times. They prove all thirty-six such results for a second shading type. Their results connect these counts to known number sequences. Those include Stirling numbers and harmonic numbers, plus counts of special sequences studied by Lin and Yan.
arxiv-2501-02657:
Oday Hazaimah proposes a faster solver for variational inclusion problems that borrows tricks from spectral methods, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Gradient descent handles convex problems well but stalls at local minima once the landscape turns non-convex.

His method pairs a spectral step, which uses eigenvalue information to pick better search directions, with a nonmonotone line search. Nonmonotone means the method may temporarily climb uphill. That freedom helps it escape shallow local minima instead of settling there. The spectral conditions adapt the direction as the search proceeds. The author argues the resulting spectral subgradient algorithm keeps global convergence while moving faster. Variational inclusions cover a wide family of equilibrium and optimization problems. A solver that is both quick and hard to trap could serve many of them.
arxiv-2501-03757:
Khanday and four colleagues build a system that turns brain signals into speech in twenty twenty-five. Sensors placed inside the skull record brain waves from people as they hear or say words. For people who cannot speak, such a system could restore a voice. The team focused on a fast band of brain waves tied to speech.

Their network mixes two designs: one that spots local patterns and one that tracks order over time. It rebuilds the sound wave chart of speech from the brain signals. The rebuilt charts matched the true ones well, though scores varied by person. The authors see promise for tools that help people with severe speech loss.
arxiv-2501-05157:
Marius Constantin Chirita Mihaila and Martin Kozák correct microscope blur with light itself rather than magnets. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Ultrafast electron microscopes suffer spherical aberration near the beam crossover. The authors use ponderomotive forces, the push light gives free electrons. Shadow images of thin silicon nitride films reveal the distortion. Simulations test whether shaped light can cancel it.

A gradient descent search shapes the correcting beam. Zernike polynomials parameterize the light pattern. Modified Gaussian and Laguerre-Gaussian forms emerge as winners. The compensated clear angle reaches a useful width. No physical corrector hardware is needed. Electron microscopy gains a programmable, light-based fix.
arxiv-2501-05457:
Riza Ozcelik and Francesca Grisoni wrote a critical study of how new drugs are made by computer models. Their work, tied to a twenty twenty-five paper on the traps in this field, asks a plain question. How should we judge the molecules that a model dreams up?

The pair trained language-style models for chemistry and looked at close to one billion designs. They found that the size of the set of designs can skew the score and make one model look better than it is. Some common scores, like how new or how alike the designs are, can also mislead. They propose new scores and rules for fair tests.
arxiv-2501-06857:
Daxin Liu and Vaishak Belle define a counterfactual notion of cause inside the situation calculus, in a two thousand twenty-five artificial intelligence paper. The situation calculus is a first-order logic for reasoning about actions and change over time.

The popular Halpern-Pearl account defines actual causality counterfactually but has limited expressiveness. A richer achievement-cause notion exists for action histories, yet without a counterfactual basis. The authors supply one and show it generalizes naturally to achievement cause. They compare their account with both predecessors and flag subtleties for disjunctive effects, a recurring trouble spot in defining actual causes. The result bridges logical action theory and causal reasoning.
arxiv-2501-07557:
Niccolò Di Marco, Edoardo Loru, Alessandro Galeazzi, Matteo Cinelli, and Walter Quattrociocchi wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It turns music into networks to measure how complex compositions are, and how that complexity has shifted over nearly four centuries.

The team drew on about twenty thousand MIDI files across six broad genres. Each piece became a weighted network of notes, whose structure they could score. Classical and jazz pieces showed the richest structure and the most varied melodies. Newer genres scored lower. Over time, though, every genre drifted toward simpler patterns, with even classical and jazz nearing modern levels. The authors link the slide to digital tools and streaming platforms, which reward catchy simplicity and spread new genres fast.
arxiv-2501-10757:
Drexel and a team of colleagues worked in twenty twenty-five on aligning dark-field chest X-rays taken at different breathing states. Dark-field imaging can reveal fine lung structure and may help diagnose lung disease. Past studies looked only at the state after breathing in.

To compare images, the lungs must first be lined up, a step called registration. The authors discuss fitting methods for this task and test their framework on scans from a study of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. They used full breath-in and breath-out scans from the same patients. Their maps of local signal change show the approach works in principle. They suggest dynamic lung checks may gain from registered dark-field images beside standard X-rays.
arxiv-2501-13357:
Saleh Sakib Ahmed and six co-authors generate water index maps from radar images in two thousand twenty-five. The NDWI index spots water bodies from optical satellite views. Clouds block those views and stall the method. Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds and at night.

Their light weight deep model takes radar as input and outputs the index. Accuracy and area scores ran high on their test set. Regression of the index values gave a fair fit as well. The mask task under it scored in a mid range. They call it a first robust fix for cloud bound water checks.
arxiv-2501-16057:
Luisa Ferrari and Massimo Ventrucci made prior setting easier in a family of Bayesian models in a 2025 paper. Latent Gaussian models are flexible and fast, but their variance knobs lack intuitive meaning, so choosing sensible prior beliefs for them frustrates practitioners. A recent idea reparametrizes the model by how total variance splits among effects, letting users state beliefs about shares instead of raw variances.

Existing share-based priors handled fixed and random effects separately. The authors give a standardization procedure that covers both together, widening the approach to a broader model class that includes spatial random fields in common use. Simulations and a survival analysis example show the practical payoff of priors users can actually reason about.
arxiv-2501-17457:
Swagata Ghosh wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It asks whether the light Higgs boson hinted at by collider experiments is a neutral particle or a charged one. The hints point to a mass near ninety-five gigaelectronvolts, and the question is posed inside the Georgi-Machacek model of particle physics.

That model extends the Standard Model with a crowd of extra Higgs bosons: six charged, plus neutral ones of even and odd parity. Experiments also carry hints of a light charged Higgs, lighter than the top quark. Ghosh weighs theory limits against the Higgs signal strengths measured at the Large Hadron Collider. The answer tilts neutral: accepting the light neutral Higgs rules against the other eight light Higgs states in the model. It also forces a key model parameter, the triplet vacuum value, above a fairly high floor.
arxiv-2501-17957:
Hocine Boumrar, Hand Zenia, and Mahdi Hamidi derived a new formula in twenty twenty-five for how energy carriers pass through interfaces, split by their vibration or spin pattern. Transmission functions govern heat and charge flow at the nanoscale, central to computing and energy devices. Older formulas for splitting transmission by mode could give unphysical answers.

Their individual Caroli formula fixes the source of those failures. They show several splittings are mathematically possible, but only one route yields physically meaningful results, and they critique the arbitrary choices behind the rest. A simple model system confirms the formula's accuracy. Though built for phonon heat carriers, it applies to electrons and other particles, and to spin and orbital patterns as well. The method sharpens design tools for thermoelectric devices.
arxiv-2501-19157:
Vaibhav Kumar and Marwa Chafii design beams for a system that must sense and communicate at once, without letting the sensed target listen in. Integrated sensing and communication is slated as a basic sixth-generation service. The catch is structural: the target of sensing sits inside the information-bearing signal, receiver in hand. Reconfigurable surfaces can harden the physical layer, but passive surfaces suffer multiplicative fading.

The paper maximizes beampattern gain under reception quality floors for users and leakage ceilings at the eavesdropping target, for both passive and active surfaces. A successive convex approximation method updates every variable at once each round, unlike alternating schemes. Simulations show clear superiority over a penalty-based alternating benchmark for the passive case. Active surfaces deliver notably higher beampattern gain in turn, at their known energy cost.
arxiv-2502-01557:
Benoit Dherin, Benny Avelin, and colleagues study how the order of operations inside training steps shapes learning in a 2025 study. Training neural networks is expensive and prone to instability, and tuning learning rate schedules to calm it eats time and compute. Working at a constant learning rate strips the problem to its essentials, letting theory speak about why updates sometimes diverge.

Composition of iterations, applying the same map in different orders and groupings, turns out to influence both convergence and stability. Practical guidance follows for building optimizers that behave predictably, instead of relying on schedule folklore discovered by trial and error.
arxiv-2502-04557:
Meiyu Zhong, Noel Teku, and Ravi Tandon speed up how language models write text. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, builds on a trick called speculative decoding. A small model drafts words fast, and a big model checks them in bulk. Those bulk checks still slow things down.

Their system, SPRINTER, trains a small checker to guess which draft words the big model would accept. The big model is then called only when a word looks wrong. Math in the paper shows how much time this saves. Tests on many data sets show the words stay good while waits and costs fall.
arxiv-2502-04957:
Lucy Evans and ten co-authors use ALMA telescope data to show methanol ice leaves dust by both heat and non heat paths in a planet forming disk round the star HD 100546. Methanol and formaldehyde are linked organic molecules on the path to prebiotic compounds. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Many lines of both molecules were read in the inner disk and in a far dust ring. Spin heat gauges ran higher for methanol in both zones and fell with distance for both species. Inner values fit heat driven release from ice. Outer values point to non heat release, so the two zones hold distinct chemical settings.
arxiv-2502-10957:
Haoming Chen and eight co-authors forecast convective clouds from satellite images with a diffusion model designed to stay sharp and physical. Nowcasting matters most where ground radar is scarce, including many developing regions. Video prediction models tend to blur exactly the storm structures forecasters care about.

Their system, SATcast, stacks a cascade of diffusion stages and takes two kinds of input: recent satellite observations and physical fields predicted by the FuXi weather model. Across multiple metrics it beat conventional methods, and ablations credited both the multimodal inputs and the cascade design. Skill held up as far as twenty-four hours ahead, an unusually long horizon for cloud nowcasting. The authors pitch it for operational use.
arxiv-2502-11157:
Zhong, Li, Xu, Wen, and Xu present Dyve in twenty twenty-five, a checker for step by step reasoning in language models. A model can reach a wrong answer if one step in its chain is flawed. Dyve aims to spot such flaws as the chain unfolds. It mixes fast checks for easy steps with deep checks for hard steps.

The design draws on the idea of fast and slow thought in human minds. To train the checker, the team blends two ways to score steps and filters out noisy labels. Tests on a process benchmark and on the MATH data set show clear gains. Dyve beat prior checkers and raised scores when used to pick the best of many answers.
arxiv-2502-14857:
Kada Williams answers a question in combinatorics, in a 2025 preprint, about how three sets can overlap. The sets live on the corners of a high-dimensional cube and are upward closed, meaning membership spreads upward. A classic result, the Harris-Kleitman inequality, governs pairs of such systems. For two systems, the share of points in exactly one of them is largest when they are independent. Kahn asked whether a matching bound holds for three systems of equal size.

The hoped-for bound said the share of points in exactly one of the three sets stays at most four ninths. Williams shows that this is false. A counterexample beats the bound, so three-way overlap behaves in ways the pair result does not predict. The paper is short and pointed: it closes a natural guess by construction. Results like this guide how correlation inequalities can and cannot be extended.
arxiv-2502-16257:
Apurba Das developed the cohomology theory of Nijenhuis Lie algebras in 2025. A Lie algebra equipped with a Nijenhuis operator. A special linear map with a compatibility trait, appears across geometry and math physics. Cohomology is the standard tool that measures deformations of such forms. But the version tailored to the Nijenhuis setting had to be built.

Das defines that cohomology with coefficients in a suitable version and shows it controls simultaneous deformations of the algebra and its operator. The paper also defines homotopy versions of these operators on two-term higher algebras and links them, in some cases, to third cohomology classes. A second part extends everything to Nijenhuis Lie bialgebras. It introduces matched pairs and Manin triples and proves they match the bialgebra notion. It ends with an admissible form of the classic Yang-Baxter equation.
arxiv-2503-01457:
Raphaël Mouravieff, Benjamin Piwowarski, and Sylvain Lamprier analyze how transformers should read tables so they can answer questions about them, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The naive approach flattens a table into a stream of words, which erases the links between rows, columns, and cells and scales badly on big tables.

Earlier fixes added special tokens, structured embeddings, or sparse attention. The authors run a broad comparison of tabular encoding techniques. Their analysis singles out attention sparsity as the key to preserving a table's structure. They then design new sparse attention masks built for tables. The masks cut computation while keeping the structural information the answers depend on. Performance improves as a result. Table question answering is a everyday business need, from spreadsheets to databases. How a model sees the grid decides how well it can reason over it.
arxiv-2503-04857:
Abhisek Ganguly, Alessandro Gabbana, Vybhav Rao, Sauro Succi, and Santosh Ansumali borrow from statistical mechanics to keep function learning honest. Fitting an interpolator resembles minimizing a physical system's energy. Their regularization adds corrections that pin down the low-order moments of the data distribution. Those constraints shrink the gap between the discrete data and its continuum shadow.

Cleaner moment matching opens friendlier energy landscapes for the optimizer to descend. Accuracy improves on both interpolation and regression tasks, even in high-dimensional spaces. No empirical tuning knobs are needed, a relief with noisy data. The method's local nature also beats radial basis function interpolators on compute and memory for large data sets. Physics here is not decoration: the moment constraints do measurable work.
arxiv-2503-05757:
Prasenjit Dey, Srujana Merugu, and Sivaramakrishnan Kaveri fight language model hallucinations by fusing several models and listening to each one's self-doubt. Ensembles are an old trick, but they usually ignore how sure each member is. Recent work shows models can partly grade their own reliability. The catch is unevenness: different models shine in different situations. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's framework weights members by accuracy and self-assessment skill, then combines their answers on factoid questions.

Across several public benchmarks, the fusion beat leading hallucination fixes by a clear margin in factual accuracy. It also narrowed or reversed the gap to a top proprietary model. No representation surgery or retraining is needed. The recipe is deliberately simple: measure uncertainty, then vote accordingly.
arxiv-2503-08157:
Zhanjie Zhang and eight colleagues present U-StyDiT, an artistic style transfer method built on diffusion transformers. The goal is repainting very high-quality content images in a learned artistic style. Earlier reconstruction-based and disentanglement-based methods leave artifacts and disharmonious patterns at that quality level.

A multi-view style modulator reads the style image from local and global perspectives to condition generation. A dedicated block learns content and style conditions simultaneously for cleaner disentanglement. The team also built Aes4M, a dataset of four million style images across ten categories, attacking the data bottleneck directly. Experiments show higher-quality stylized images than state-of-the-art methods, which the authors call a first for transformer-based diffusion.
arxiv-2503-08457:
Zeng presents a math paper from twenty twenty-five on a higher Riemann-Hilbert correspondence for layered spaces. Regular foliations split a space into leaf-like layers. The paper builds a functor translating leafwise algebraic data into transport data. Iterated integrals and holonomy formulas from prior work drive the construction. On each small star-shaped patch, an explicit local inverse exists. Integration proves faithful on the objects compared. When the space is compact, local matches glue into a global equivalence.

Descent tools on both sides power that gluing step. Compact proper submersions give a clean class of examples. The author asserts no claims for singular layers or broader settings. The result extends a classic correspondence into higher structures.
arxiv-2503-09057:
Luís Bettencourt, Brandon Grandison, and Jordan Kemp re set fitness in growth of life forms as a type of stats guess work. The stock sense, kin birth win next to peers, has flaws. They are loops in sense, clash, and calls for what comes next. In its place they set fitness through a Bayes chance score. Each type holds a model that calls its world in chance terms.

When growth is made a mean through past worlds, choice links to facts in chance terms. Types with more good world models grow more. Long run moves lift the shared facts that lie in the space from group form to world stats. The team shows the way with task switch, growth games, and groups split in parts. In each case they work out phase charts and rules of the Hamilton type for when joint acts come forth.
arxiv-2503-10957:
Albada and Sonola wrote in twenty twenty-five about guessing stock moves from social media posts. Prices jump around and do not follow a steady pattern, which makes prediction hard. Earlier teams mixed price records with text from posts to do better. Some used complex nets, attention methods, and extra data sources. Albada and Sonola test a simpler route built on BERTweet, a language model trained on Twitter text.

Their transformer model reads posts and predicts the direction of a stock move. On the StockNet data set, it matched strong past results. It also set a new best score on one strict measure of agreement, without extra side data. The work shows a focused text model can hold its own in this noisy task.
arxiv-2503-11257:
Sergio Dorado-Alfaro and five colleagues simulate how ionic liquids dissolve and dissociate in epoxide and carbonate media, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The context is turning carbon dioxide into cyclic carbonates by reacting it with epoxides. Halide-based ionic liquids are candidate catalysts for that reaction. Which ions perform best, and why, is still debated.

Molecular dynamics simulations test force fields for the solvents and several ionic liquid combinations. Liquids built on the smaller cation proved insoluble in the medium. Those built on the larger cation diffused through it. For the soluble cases, the team studied interactions between key atoms. Cation-anion association followed the catalytic activity trend, with iodide the least associated halide. A radial distribution measure correlated with the experimental behavior. The cation-anion dissociation constant emerges as a key descriptor for catalyst design.
arxiv-2503-11557:
Jing Bi and ten co-authors present VERIFY, a benchmark for visual reasoning fidelity in two thousand twenty-five. Past multimodal tests stress recognition more than true reasoning. VERIFY strips text context so models must reason from sight. Each problem ships with a human marked reasoning path.

That pairing grades the decision process, not just the answer. New metrics score fidelity of the visual reasoning itself. Top multimodal models show sharp limits under that lens. Imbalances in how they reason stand out in the results. The team calls for balance between perception and reasoning.
arxiv-2503-12457:
Thelasingha and co-authors set conditions for motion replanning in robot teams that share news only when chances arise. Mixed teams face disturbances, model errors, and shifting tasks that can void set paths. Uneven sharing also means agents hold unequal knowledge of each other's plans.

The paper gives conditions for keeping the team in sync and plans feasible under such spotty links. It also ties task success to how much disturbance the iterative scheme can absorb and repair. Planning repeats in rounds, with quantified recoverability setting the bounds. A drone and ground vehicle task assignment test backed the theory in practice.
arxiv-2503-14757:
Marcelo Sanchez, Gil Triginer, Ignacio Sarasua, Lara Raad, and Coloma Ballester set a benchmark for filling image holes at high resolution on edge devices. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that top inpainting tools fail at high resolution and need beefy hardware. Phones and tablets are left out. Their RETHINED baseline pairs two light parts to fix that.

A small convolutional network first restores the scene's structure. A patch replacement step then lays in fine texture at any resolution. The pair runs within a real-time budget on a wide range of mobile gear. Quality matches heavy rivals while running far faster, by the team's count. A new ultra-high-resolution data set with free-form masks ships with the work. The study gives edge inpainting its first shared yardstick.
arxiv-2503-17757:
Hao Xu probes Lorentz violation with an Unruh-DeWitt detector in two thousand twenty five. Some quantum gravity work hints that Lorentz symmetry may break at the Planck scale. Changed dispersion relations encode that break, and a detector based probe can read them sorted by momentum.

His math lets the probe speed up with no fixed guess for the rules in place first. He checks thin shells of momentum one at a time, in a narrow band around a base point. A Taylor series near that point yields coefficients that encode how fast the rules change there. Those coefficients rebuild the full profile of the rules, shell by shell, like a scan. Large breaks wreck the thermal spectrum, while small breaks show up as phase shifts in it.
arxiv-2503-19157:
Mingzhen Huang and a large team present HOIGPT, a system that both reads and makes 3D scenes of hands grasping objects. Their twenty twenty-five paper unifies two tasks: writing a caption for a hand-object interaction, and building such a scene from text, an object, or a partial sequence.

The core is a language model trained on tokens for both words and motion. A new tokenizer, built as a split-hand-and-object autoencoder, turns motion into tokens the model can handle, with physics kept in mind. A motion-aware model then works both ways, text to scene and scene to text. Tests set new best scores on both caption and generation benchmarks.
arxiv-2503-19557:
Sawdayee and five co-authors introduced LoRA-MDM in twenty twenty-five, a light way to stylize computer-generated human motion. Text-to-motion models create three-dimensional actions from words but miss fine styles, such as moving like a chicken. Style examples are scarce, and pushing each output toward a reference often degrades quality.

Their key idea is to adapt the model's prior, its built-in sense of plausible motion, rather than each motion separately. A low-rank adaptation, trained on just a few style samples, shifts that prior in a meaningful direction. The styled prior then serves many text prompts, even for actions absent from the samples. Keeping the distribution's shape also allows style blending and motion editing. Tests showed a good balance of text fidelity and style consistency.
arxiv-2503-22657:
Anowar Shajib and six co-authors set out dolphin, a fully hands-free pipeline that models strong lenses made by galaxies, steered by smart tools. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Strong lensing probes how galaxies are built, what dark matter is, and how the cosmos grew. For most such work, the mass that bends the light must be modeled. The norm is to fit the image pixel by pixel. But that work eats expert time, in loops of trial and tweak. The pipeline runs that fit on its own. It cuts the expert hours a lens study needs, and can treat the vast lens sets new surveys will bring.
arxiv-2503-23057:
Tomáš Kaiser and four co-authors colored square tilings of projective spaces. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, starts from a known fact: each non two part square tiling of the projective plane needs four colors. A past team stretched the shape notion to high spans and proved a floor that grows with span. A rival team set a new kind, normal quadrangulations, and proved four colors for some with a shape side rule. They asked if that rule is needed at all.

The new work takes up that ask for normal tilings. The color count is read against the side rule. Readers in combinatorics get the next step in a three way pull on how few colors such tilings can take.
arxiv-2503-23357:
Lyuye Zhang and co-authors wrote this software security paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how open-source projects really fix vulnerabilities. Official advice leans on patches and version bumps, but maintainers in the wild reach for a far wider kit.

The team studied more than twenty-one thousand GitHub issues and built a family tree of forty-four remediation tactics. Community-born moves, like swapping in another library or routing around the flaw, made up much of the record. Forty-four percent of the tactics lack support in current tools. The study also logs which fixes get accepted and why others get refused. More than half of the entries in the standard CVE database carry no fix advice at all. The authors note that GitHub threads already hold an actionable answer in most cases.
arxiv-2504-00357:
Keiya Ichikawa and Kenji Yasunaga prove a limit, in a 2025 preprint, on a class of quantum error-detecting codes. Pauli manipulation detection codes are built to catch any Pauli error with high chance. Users face a trade-off between how much data the code carries and how surely it catches errors. No firm bound was known. The authors derive the first one, covering codes over alphabets of any size.

The bound says the rate must fall short of one by a term tied to the log of the inverse error chance, scaled by the code length. In plain terms, demanding a tinier miss chance forces a real rate cost. Bounds like this fence in what code designers can hope for, and future constructions can be measured against it.
arxiv-2504-00457:
Qin and four co-authors presented a method in twenty twenty-five for turning a single picture into a three-dimensional object in a fraction of a second. Models that imagine an object from many angles hold rich knowledge, but running them is slow and they do not directly output usable 3D files.

Their approach, DD3G, distills that multi-view knowledge into a compact generator built on gaussian splatting, a fast way to render fuzzy 3D scenes. The student generator learns to follow the teacher model's path from noise to image, aligned in a shared space. A two-stage decoder first finds patterns, then builds detail step by step. Training drew on one hundred twenty thousand high-quality images with transparency. The generator produces a 3D object in about six hundredths of a second. Tests on standard datasets showed strong quality for the speed.
arxiv-2504-05257:
Utsav Dewan generalizes a recent line of analysis results in this two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. Earlier work by Carlen, Jauslin, Lieb, and Loss studied functions satisfying a convolution inequality and proved such functions must be non-negative with a bounded integral. Nakamura and Sawano extended the result to repeated convolutions. Dewan replaces the single repeated term with a genuine polynomial in the convolution powers.

He proves that real integrable solutions must still be non-negative, with an integral bounded by a quantity read off from the polynomial's derivative. An analogue holds on Riemannian symmetric spaces of non-compact type as well. The arguments use Fourier and complex analysis. As an application, he obtains an a priori estimate for an integro-differential equation tied to the ground state energy of the Bose gas.
arxiv-2504-07557:
Gaspard Merten, Gilles Dejaegere, and Mahmoud Sakr published a computer science paper in 2025 on using language models to analyze ship traffic data. Ships broadcast position signals that build huge movement records. Analysts want to question those records in plain language. The authors tested how well large language models handle that job.

They designed a careful set of test queries first. Then they tried four ways of connecting models to the data. One route let the model query a spatial database. Others fed raw, compressed, or meaning-labeled movement tracks. Each route showed different strengths and weaknesses. The paper guides practitioners on picking a method for their analysis goals.
arxiv-2504-08157:
Soonpil Kang, Francis Giraldo, and Seth Camp present a study from twenty twenty-five on a fast storm model that runs on graphics chips. Their case is a tropical cyclone that grows in strength at a swift rate. They port a known air model to graphics chips with a directive based code style. Heat seen in real gauge data drives the storm in the runs.

The team lays out how the main parts of the code were moved to the chips. The ported code yields high grade runs of a real storm shape. Speed tests show the runs use energy well. The code scales well in both strong and weak test modes. Such speed aids storm science where fine detail is a must.
arxiv-2504-09357:
Doe, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, proposed a unified theory of school choice. In school choice systems, districts rank students by priority and assign them to schools. Policymakers must balance honoring those priorities against giving students schools they prefer.

Doe notes that priorities blend many policy goals, and some are firmer than others. His model splits priority into two types. Between-group priority ranks whole groups and must be respected. Within-group priority orders students inside a group to use seats well. His solution, the unified core, joins both types. A two-stage algorithm he introduces carries it out and extends two classic methods, Deferred Acceptance and Top Trading Cycles.
arxiv-2504-11957:
Hui-Hui Qin, Shao-Shuai Zhao, and Shao-Ming Fei ask how much plain, unlinked material a quantum state can absorb before its deep links break. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The links at stake join three or more parts at once. Such many-party entanglement powers quantum tools but can be fragile.

The team coins measures based on the ranks that describe how a state splits across its parts. From the smallest such rank they build a test for when the entanglement survives any mix with plain states. A matching test covers the weaker property of inseparability. They also count how many plain states can be mixed in before the state turns separable. A finer version of the ranks handles the three-party case. The results give clean rules for judging robust quantum states.
arxiv-2504-12057:
Victoria Ginga, Bin Shen, Ece Uykur, Nico Giordano, Philipp Gegenwart, and Alexander Tsirlin map the magnetism of the mineral brochantite under pressure. Their paper from twenty twenty-five joins high-pressure X-ray work on single crystals with heat gauges and density-based sums. The goal is the microscopic magnetic model and how squeezing shifts it. Brochantite layers hold copper ions in chains.

Inside each layer, longer copper gaps and wider bond angles forge antiferromagnetic chains. Cross links between second neighbors add a ferromagnetic push, while weaker opposed links frustrate the order and trim its onset point. Pressure keeps the crystal's symmetry but stiffens the main coupling. The growth is driven mostly by the cross links. The authors tie coupling strength in such minerals to chain spacing and layer buckling.
arxiv-2504-14957:
Chuhan Lu, Minglong Qin, Fang Song, Penghui Yao, and Mingnan Zhao wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It shows that a row of parallel Kac's walk steps forms a pseudorandom unitary family with strong security.

Pseudorandom unitaries act like true random ones to any bounded test, and are a base tool in quantum crypto. A prior build, the PFC construction, was lately shown secure by a path recording proof. The authors prove the same for their walk-based build, settling a guess from their own past work. Their version also stands up to foes that can run the unitaries backward. The result gives a second route to the same strong tool.
arxiv-2504-16257:
Alejandro Mus and five co-authors reconstruct both a hidden source and the fog hiding it, in radio images of the Galactic Center. Interstellar scattering scrambles the view toward the center, breaking the usual link between image and measured visibilities. Untangling source from screen is one of radio imaging's hardest inverse problems.

Their strategy uses multiobjective optimization with evolutionary algorithms to explore the landscape of joint solutions. In simulations the method recovered the scattering screen and the source together across a wide range of cases. It even tracked a moving screen at high frequency and rebuilt a ring structure from scattered lower-frequency data. Success here opens a path toward event-horizon-scale imaging through the murk.
arxiv-2504-17757:
Sara Maggio and Yoann Sohnle derive canonical differential equations for Feynman integrals in two thousand twenty-five. The integrals have a Calabi-Yau geometry at their core and span many scales. A past method found canonical forms for simpler cases. The pair extend it to this harder class.

They first redo the sunrise integral with all masses distinct. They then give first time forms for two banana integrals with two distinct masses. The forms have a clean pole shape in the small parameter. Picard-Fuchs operators on the integrals ground the build. Appendices explain in steps why the extension works.
arxiv-2504-17857:
AJ Miller, Fangzhou Yu, Michael Brauckmann, and Farbod Farshidian report on training a reinforcement learning policy for the Spot robot, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Spot is Boston Dynamics' quadruped robot. Their work is cast as the first public end-to-end learning pipeline on Spot with code released for all to use.

Rules trained in simulation often stumble on real hardware. The team gauges that sim-to-real gap with two scores for how far apart two data sets sit: Wasserstein distance and maximum mean discrepancy. They set the data from the real robot and from runs side by side, head-on. Those scores drive an evolution strategy that tunes unknown simulation parameters. The tuned simulator then gives rise to better rules for the robot. Low-level motor access came through the Spot RL Researcher Development Kit. The training ran in Nvidia IsaacLab.
arxiv-2504-18157:
Suntae Hwang, Seonghyeon Kang, Kyungsu Kim, Semin Ahn, and Kyogu Lee extract drum one shots in two thousand twenty-five. Drum one shot samples anchor sound design and electronic music. Pulling clean ones out of full mixes is the new task here. They name it Drum One-Shot Extraction.

A dataset, RMOD, pairs random mixes with their source one shots. The DOSE model uses neural codec language models end to end. It skips the classic source separation stage entirely. A new onset loss sharpens the first transient of each hit. Scores beat a separation based baseline on quality gauges.
arxiv-2504-21157:
Brian Lacki, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, promotes a borrowed tool for catching extremely fast flickers in starlight. Rapid optical transients are hard to detect because they produce so few photons.

The tool is the normalized autocorrelation function, called g-two in quantum optics. Chaotic fast variability leaves a bump in the function at short time lags, and no periodicity is required. Lacki computes expected signal-to-noise ratios including shot noise and atmospheric scintillation. Example applications include a flickering artificial lantern near a host star, optical microbursts from the Crab pulsar, and frequent irregular transits by cometary bodies. Sub-millisecond variability is the prime target.
arxiv-2504-21857:
E. Petrova and co-workers caught a fast transverse wave rippling through a solar fibril in a 2025 paper. Fibrils, thin dark threads in the Sun's chromosphere, carry magnetohydrodynamic waves that may ferry energy upward into the corona. Most stated oscillations are slow; the team hunted a high-rate one using watching from August 2018 taken with a prototype hyperspectral imager on the Swedish one-meter Solar Telescope. An instrument resolving space, time, and spectrum at once.

They found an oscillation with a period of about fifteen seconds and a sway of some forty kilometers, elliptically polarized by Doppler readings. Its energy flux, a few hundred to a couple thousand watts per square meter. Falls short of balancing the chromosphere's radiative losses, so this wave alone does not heat the layer.
arxiv-2505-00657:
Ann-Kristin Malz and John Veitch tackle glitches in gravitational wave data in two thousand twenty-five. Glitches are short bursts of non-Gaussian noise in the detectors. They can bias the traits read off from real signals. Past fixes strip glitches first or model them with plain wavelets.

The pair train a flow model on known glitches from a public catalog. That gives an informed prior for the glitch shape. The model then sits inside the main inference, run with a known toolkit. Signal and glitch traits are fit at the same time. Tests on real glitches show less bias and cleaner source traits.
arxiv-2505-01757:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and Mohammad Pirani design distributed estimators that keep working when sensors or links fail, using graph theory as the design tool. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets sensor networks, vehicle fleets, and cloud systems. The pitch is a single time-scale protocol: no slow inner consensus loop, yet weaker connectivity demands than rival single-rate designs. Speed and frugality arrive together.

Resilience is built into the definitions. Network notions of q-node and q-link connectivity capture survival after losing that many sensors or links. Proper graph design then proves Schur stability under exactly those losses. Biased readings from attacked sensors need not be dropped at the cost of observability. Estimation theory gains a failure-proofing recipe.
arxiv-2505-01957:
Mert Yakup Baykan, Vijayamanikandan Vijayarangan, Dong-hyuk Shin, and Hong Im speed up combustion simulation in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Stiff reacting systems, like fuel mixes as they ignite, cost much to integrate, as their chemistry runs on split timescales. An autoencoder and neural ordinary differential equation model can squeeze the state and evolve it at low cost, as a reduced-order model. The team adds a loss term built from gradients of the latent variables.

Training data came from the Cantera solver. It covered ignition of hydrogen-air and ammonia-hydrogen mixes at constant pressure, across ranges of temperature and fuel ratio. Models trained with the latent gradient loss did far better past the training range, beating the mapping loss there. The study shows that putting time derivatives in the loss counts. A latent space can call dynamics at high fidelity, for a part of the cost.
arxiv-2505-02957:
De Monte, Huser, Papastathopoulos, and Richards wrote in twenty twenty-five on extreme events. Their tool is generative modeling with normalizing flows. Extreme weather rarely strikes one variable at a time. Joint tail pattern in many directions is hard to project. A geometric approach tells of extremes through shapes on a sphere. Normalizing flows add flexible learning on that sphere. Their method links model parameters to those geometric shapes.

Designs range from flexible to spare under one scheme. The generative side gives fast probability estimates for complex risk regions. Monte Carlo integration handles arbitrary event shapes efficiently. Tests in up to ten dimensions backed the method. Uses covered low and high wind speed extremes. Results matter for wind turbine power planning and risk. The wind data also showed interesting dependence structure.
arxiv-2505-06757:
Greenfeld and Tao prove three variants of the periodic tiling conjecture in twenty twenty-five. The conjecture says a tiling of a group by a fixed tile set can always be made periodic. It holds for some groups and fails for others. Their variants loosen the rules in set ways.

One swaps plain tiles for bounded whole number weights against a zero target. A second, on the plane grid, allows a periodic whole number target. The third, hardest, keeps true tiles and settles multi tilings on the grid. Decidability for some tiling questions follows. The paper extends the map of when order must appear.
arxiv-2505-07657: Maltsev takes up Novikov's problem for level lines of repeating patterns with mirror symmetry in twenty twenty-five. The patterns are quasiperiodic: they echo with two base rhythms that do not align. Level lines are curves where the pattern holds one fixed value, and for some patterns they run open across the plane. For patterns with the symmetry of a two sided polygon, he shows open lines can occur at just one energy level. That single level trait brings these patterns close to random ones.
arxiv-2505-09857:
Spencer Lee and Daniel Appelö introduce a method for quantum optimal control in two thousand twenty-five. Control tasks need the slope of a cost with respect to pulse shapes. Their method gets exact slopes while the forward model runs at high order. The solver is a Hermite Runge-Kutta scheme for the core quantum equations.

The method is the first of its kind for this pairing. It is built into a free software package in the Julia language. Tests on real style problems show large speed gains over a rival package. The gain reached hundreds of times in some cases. The work helps users design gate pulses with less wait and no slope error.
arxiv-2505-09957:
Hayato Uchimura, Takahiro Kudoh, and Yusuke Tsukamoto calculate the largest dust grains a young star's outflow can lift and fling beyond its disk. This ashfall process redistributes solid material during protostar evolution. How big a grain escapes depends on the outflow's strength and the system around it.

Using an analytical magnetohydrodynamic outflow model, the authors derive an empirical formula for the maximum grain size. It grows in direct proportion to the mass ejection rate and shrinks with disk size, stellar mass, and grain density. For realistic ejection rates, grains from a tenth of a millimeter to a millimeter can be carried well outside the disk. That range matches recent observations linking outflow strength to dust opacity signatures.
arxiv-2505-14257:
Jianfei Zhao, Feng Zhang, Xin Sun, and Chong Feng tackle false claims, or hallucinations, in large vision-language models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In such models, image facts flow into word-based states step by step. Yet the model's focus does not rest on those states as much as the flow would call for.

That gap weakens image sense and feeds false claims. The team finds the focus heads that do rest on core states, then spreads their edge across the model in two stages. Tests on three caption sets and five models show a clear drop in false claims. A trade-off with detail shows up, and users can tune how careful the model should be.
arxiv-2505-15757:
Daniel Hajto, Waleed El-Geresy, Deniz Gunduz, and Gyorgy Cserey tackled memristor state measurement in twenty twenty-five. Memristors are resistors with memory. They are candidate building blocks for storage, neural accelerators, and neuromorphic chips. To use them well, you need to know their state inside. That state cannot be read in a direct way from the terminals.

The authors focus on self-directed channel memristors. They set out a general model of their state, drawn from physics. They then show how to pin down that state from measured voltage-current pairs. Their estimation method is aware of measurement noise by design. It is built on minimum variance principles. The work is foundational. It gives a sound way to say what state a device is in. That step must come first for trustworthy memory and computing uses.
arxiv-2505-15957:
Chih-Kai Yang, Neo Ho, and Hung-yi Lee survey how large audio-language models are evaluated, and sort the tests into a clean taxonomy. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that these models add hearing to language models and claim broad skill. Benchmarks have sprouted fast but lie scattered, with no shared frame. The survey claims a first for this niche.

Four classes organize the field. One covers basic sound awareness and processing. One covers knowledge and reasoning over audio. One covers dialogue skill, and one covers fairness, safety, and trust. Each class gets a detailed tour of its tests. Gaps and strain points are flagged along the way. The team will post and maintain the paper list. The aim is a map that evaluators can share.
arxiv-2505-16457:
Hasegawa, Le Gall, and Modanese proved in twenty twenty-five the widest gap yet between quantum chat with and without shared linked pairs. In some tasks two sides must swap bits to solve a joint task. With shared pairs some tasks need no swap at all, while without them they need a swap that grows with task size.

Their tasks repeat a paired game where a quantum plan wins in full but no plain plan does. That gives the top gap that can be shown for this kind. The result breaks a quantum form of a known claim on such swaps. It is the first bound of its kind at zero top cost.
arxiv-2505-16557:
Junchi Yao, Di Wang, and five co-authors test whether travel planning agents can be fooled by fraud. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at systems where several language model agents plan trips together. Such systems lean on review sites and social media. Those sources can hold fake reviews and false claims, which may cost users money.

The team builds a test world called WandaPlan with planted fake content. They probe three fraud styles, from single false claims to group plots that grow over rounds. Current systems chase speed and miss the lies. Adding a special anti-fraud agent helps a lot. The test world can grade other planning systems too.
arxiv-2505-18957:
Alexander Altland and four colleagues investigate a special class of quantum states just above the ground state of chaotic systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. They call it the universality class of the first levels. Most synthetic random matrix models realize this class. Among microscopically defined systems, only low-dimensional gravity is known to do so.

The states stand out for exceptional rigidity against external perturbations. That rigidity is quantified by quantum state fidelity. The authors examine the structures through random matrix theory and string theory lenses. Their discussion highlights why these levels matter for low-dimensional holographic principles. Understanding them may clarify how a handful of states above a ground state can behave so stiffly. The paper connects abstract spectral theory with the physics of quantum gravity models.
arxiv-2505-19957:
Cunha and Lehum wrote this theoretical physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on gravity at extreme energies. They work inside Agravity, a version of quantum gravity built to stay well-behaved at very high energy.

The pair compute how quarks and gluons scatter off each other through graviton exchange when the energy far exceeds the Planck scale. They cover four scattering setups and work out the rates for each. All the rates fall off in the same gentle way at high energy, as a sound theory should. They also check a worry raised by extra ghost-like modes in such theories: whether the math stays positive and sane. It does, once the finite mass of quarks is kept in the sums. The authors read this as support for Agravity as a workable extension of Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2505-22457:
Haonan Wang and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on teaching video models to reason about time. Language models learn to reason by predicting the next word; the authors ask what the video version of that task should be.

Their answer is next-event prediction. A video is split into past and future parts. The model watches the past and must write a summary of what happens next, which forces it to think ahead in time. To train at scale, they built a set of thirty-three thousand clips cut automatically from real-world footage. A new test, FutureBench, grades how sensibly models predict unseen futures. Tuning strategies around the new task were compared head to head. The authors report that next-event training builds temporal reasoning more cleanly than question answering or captioning.
arxiv-2506-05057:
Moshe Ofer, Orel Zamler, and Amos Azaria set out TALL, a trainable build that lifts large language models in tongues with scant training data. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such models shine in rich tongues but lag in poor ones. TALL joins a large model to two translation models that work both ways. Text in a poor tongue is turned into a rich form. The large model's strength can then be used, while traits of the first tongue are kept by match layers and custom parts. Tests on Hebrew beat plain use, naive translation, and fine-tuning. Most parts stay frozen; just light adapters train.
arxiv-2506-08257:
Lukas Lao Beyer, Tianhong Li, Xinlei Chen, Sertac Karaman, and Kaiming He wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It shows that a highly compressed image tokenizer, which squeezes a picture into as few as thirty-two tokens, can edit and even create images with no trained generator at all.

Normal tokenizers lay tokens out on a grid; the one-dimensional kind packs the whole image into a short string. The authors found that crude tricks in that packed space, like copying tokens from one image into another, cleanly transfer looks and meaning. Building on that, they craft new images by nudging tokens at test time toward goals such as matching a photo or fitting a text prompt. The pipeline handles filling gaps and text-guided edits, and produces varied, realistic results.
arxiv-2506-13957:
Narsimlu Kemsaram and co-workers floated objects on sound and moved them jointly in a 2025 paper. Ants carry loads jointly with no central controller. The team borrowed that trick for sound-based robots: devices using phased very high sound sound units to create localized pressure fields that float small objects in mid-air, no contact at all. Their system sorts touch-free transport into uncoordinated free-standing carrying and coordinated forward-facing teamwork. Mirroring the living strategies, with synchronization and control handled onboard the robots.

Tests validated the pieces: floating stability gauged with a mic. Transport speed tracked by a motion capture system, and clock synchronization checked on an oscilloscope. Both free-standing and joint airborne transport proved feasible. Touch-free handling matters where touch dirties or damages the cargo, from tiny circuits to cell cell groups.
arxiv-2506-15457:
Steven Amelotte and Benjamin Briggs link the shape of some spaces in topology to the algebra of the ideals that define them. Moment-angle complexes turn simplicial complexes into spaces whose homology mirrors an Ext-module of the Stanley-Reisner ideal that matches. Past work found these spaces to be wedges of spheres when terms of linearity held.

The team show the Hurewicz image in homology holds the linear strand of the ideal. That gets back the past matches and sharpens them. Next they treat moment-angle manifolds from Gorenstein ideals with almost linear resolutions. For a broad new class of simplicial complexes, those manifolds are formal. Their rational homotopy type is that of connected sums of sphere products. Side results in algebra extend a known characterization of Koszul modules.
arxiv-2506-17457:
Dong Xiao, Guangyao Chen, Peixi Peng, Yangru Huang, Yifan Zhao, Yongxing Dai, and Yonghong Tian wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a fast anomaly detector for self-driving cars, where spotting trouble a blink late can mean a crash.

Their network joins two feeds: event streams from event cameras, which catch fast change, and still images from RGB cameras, which hold spatial detail. A graph neural network reads the event stream as it flows, while a convolutional network reads the images, and the two merge. Tests on benchmark sets beat prior methods on both accuracy and response time. The system answers in milliseconds, fast enough for live driving.
arxiv-2506-19257:
Yinan Xia and five co-authors present MSR-Align in two thousand twenty-five. MSR-Align is a data set for safe reasoning in vision language models. Such models reason well across image and text, but that skill opens new risks. Harmful mixed prompts can coax out unsafe acts.

Past safety data lack fine, policy based reasons for mixed inputs. MSR-Align gives reasons tied to set safety policies in both modes. Its build stresses variety, policy roots, and strict quality checks by strong judges. Fine tuning on it cut jailbreak success a lot. General reasoning skill held or rose at the same time. The set is public.
arxiv-2506-19557:
Lu, Si, and Zhang calculated measurement reach for the tau lepton in this physics paper from twenty twenty-five. The tau's electric and magnetic dipole moments test the Standard Model with great sensitivity. A nonzero electric moment would be a clear sign of new physics. Electron-positron colliders are the natural place to hunt for these values.

The study weighs observables built from the full motion of tau decay products. It compares planned and running machines at several energies. At a future collider tuned to the Z pole, sensitivity to the electric moment could reach a very fine level. A running flavor factory could pin the magnetic moment's parts to about one part in one hundred thousand. The authors map where each machine wins.
arxiv-2506-21457:
Claudio Cacciapuoti, Andrea Posilicano, and Hamidreza Saberbaghi wrote this mathematical physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a tiny three-body quantum system. One light particle moves in a line with two heavy ones, and all contact forces act only at zero range.

The authors study the energy levels that sit below the free range when the light particle is pulled toward the heavy pair. As the mass ratio shrinks, they pin down how each bound level behaves. The levels approach a fixed limit with a correction that follows the extrema or zeros of the Airy function. Which of the two applies depends on whether the heavy pair act as bosons or fermions. They also show the free range starts exactly where expected. The paper gives a rare exact picture of a classic approximation at work.
arxiv-2506-22257:
The Euclid Collaboration, with Guidi and co-authors, prepares models for the Euclid space mission's map of the universe. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with correlation functions, which count how galaxies cluster at each separation. The two-point version pairs galaxies, and the three-point version triples them, each adding shape detail about the cosmic web.

The work models the full shape of both functions in real space, not just their peaks. Such models let the mission turn raw galaxy counts into measures of dark matter, dark energy, and gravity. As a preparation paper, it sets the methods that later Euclid data releases will use.
arxiv-2506-22457:
Iulia Orvas and four co-authors present a new way to pull a baby's heart signal out of a mother's belly recording. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Watching a fetus at home calls for soft, dry cloth electrodes that a mother can wear with ease. Such sensors pick up much noise and motion, which blurs the faint fetal signal.

The team built a test data set that mimics real home recordings, noise and all. Their method, a network called Complex UNet, cleans the signal in a smarter way than past tools. It works on both the size and the timing parts of the signal's spectrum. In tests on both fake and real data, it beat older methods at tracing the fetal heartbeat. The work points toward safe, round-the-clock checks on babies before birth.
arxiv-2506-23957:
Zinuo You and colleagues stabilize shaky video by rebuilding the scene in three dimensions, locally and consistently over time, then re-rendering it. Two-dimensional stabilizers warp frames and crop edges; they distort geometry and generalize poorly. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's method starts from estimated camera poses. A reconstruction model predicts Gaussian splatting primitives for each stretch of video. At test time the model is fine-tuned with photometric supervision that respects scene motion, plus cross-frame regularization for consistency. A scene extrapolation module fills the borders, avoiding the crop.

Tests used a repurposed data set enriched with three-dimensional ground truth. The method matched or beat leading two-dimensional and hybrid approaches on standard metrics and on new geometry consistency measures. A user study agreed the output looks better. Stabilization becomes a rendering problem with a memory.
arxiv-2507-00257:
Salaorni and a large team release a benchmark suite that puts reinforcement learning through realistic, messy tasks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Learning agents have beaten humans in tidy simulations, but real deployments bring huge state spaces, shifting conditions, and partial views. Standard benchmarks mostly ignore those hardships.

Their suite, Gym4ReaL, packs tasks designed to expose agents to practical complications. Early experiments find standard algorithms still competitive against rule-based baselines in these settings. That result, the authors argue, should motivate new methods that squeeze more from learning when the world refuses to sit still. The suite is offered as shared ground for measuring progress toward real-world agents.
arxiv-2507-07757:
Keerthana Chand, Tobias Fritsch, and three co-authors measure warping in 3D-printed parts with a deep learning method. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, compares printed shapes against their design files. Shrinkage and bending mar printed parts for cars, medicine, and aerospace. X-ray tomography captures the true shape in fine detail.

Volume correlation should map each point's drift, but no ground truth exists. Their network processes the huge scans in small patches. A new score counts mismatched voxels between design and scan. Standard overlap scores back it up. Precise drift maps could certify printed parts faster.
arxiv-2507-08557:
Yuxuan Jiang, Zehua Chen, Zeqian Ju, Chang Li, Weibei Dou, and Jun Zhu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents FreeAudio, a training-free way to make long audio clips from text with exact timing for each sound.

Past text-to-audio tools blur when a prompt says when each sound must start and stop. A language model first plans neat, non-overlapping time slots and rewrites each slot's text. Attention tricks then pin each sound to its slot, a latent blend keeps the joins smooth, and a reference guide holds the whole clip in one style. Tests put its timing work at the top of training-free methods, near trained leaders.
arxiv-2507-09357: Maram Almahariq studies approximate ideals in descriptive relator spaces in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is an approximate commutative ring with unity. Building on a past notion of approximate prime ideals, she defines new classes. These are the approximate primary, semi-primary, and one-absorbing primary ideals. Theorems spell out their special traits. One key result: the radical of a one-absorbing primary ideal is prime. Chains among the classes are also proved, from prime down through the rest.
arxiv-2507-09757:
Chunyan Li, Wenkai Yu, and Qi Wang improve physics-informed neural networks, which solve equations by training a network to respect the physics at sampled points. Where points are placed decides accuracy, and the usual strategy chases the largest equation errors. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team instead guides sampling by the local rate of energy dissipation, a quantity with physical meaning in the phase-change model they study. Points are refreshed in both the interior and the boundary as training proceeds, following where energy is actually being spent.

On a standard phase field problem in disk and ellipse domains, the guided sampler cut error up to sixfold against the leading residual-based method, while costing less compute. It also handled moving, time-dependent boundary rules. The authors say matching the sampler to the physics, not just the residuals, is the key step.
arxiv-2507-14357:
Wisne and Chandrasekhar wrote in twenty twenty-five about tuning Josephson junctions with supercurrent instead of magnetic flux. Josephson coupling energy sets the operating frequency of superconducting qubits. Tuning is usually done by threading flux through a loop of two junctions. Loops expose qubits to magnetic noise from the environment. Their device biases a junction with supercurrent from a separate lead pair. That bias adjusts the coupling energy without any flux loop.

The multiterminal design keeps the tuning fully non-dissipative. No resistive elements are needed in the control path. Qubits built this way should suffer far less flux noise. Frequency-tunable qubits are central to superconducting quantum processors. Removing a major noise channel could improve their coherence and control. The paper demonstrates the tuning principle in a working device.
arxiv-2507-15757:
Yassine Hamdi and Deniz Gündüz analyze remote channel synthesis, a problem in information theory about recreating a statistical link at a distance. An encoder sees only a noisy partial version of a source sequence. It must help a decoder produce output that stands in a target statistical relationship to the unseen source.

The terminals share a noiseless link and possibly a limited supply of common randomness. The authors give a single-letter formula for the best possible compression and randomness rates. They also show that when common randomness is scarce, standard synthesis schemes usually fall short. Coordinating the observed data and the output directly often beats forcing them toward independence.
arxiv-2507-17957:
A team led by Khan built a module to sharpen image masks when a model moves to a new domain, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The task is semantic segmentation with no labels in the target field. A model trained on fake scenes must work on real ones. Past ways juggle fine local detail and broad context poor, so masks err in hard zones. Their module refines high detail features with sense hints from low detail outputs.

It also folds in high tone parts that mark edges and thin shapes. A balance step weighs local and global reads as the scene asks. Readers in vision get a plug in that lifts mask truth at borders, where domain shift hurts most.
arxiv-2507-22057:
Chaofei Qi, Zhitai Liu, and Jianbin Qiu present MetaLab, in a 2025 preprint, a method for recognizing images from one example per class. Few-shot recognition matters where labeled images are scarce, but it lags far behind ordinary recognition. MetaLab runs two networks that teach each other. One, LabNet, restates images in the CIELab color space and pulls out grouped features. The other builds graphs from lightness and from color, and lets the two graphs trade what they learn. Color space choice is the core bet: CIELab matches human vision better than raw red-green-blue.

The team tested on twelve benchmark sets: coarse, fine-grained, and cross-domain. With one sample per class, MetaLab stayed accurate and steady across all of them. The authors report scores near the human ceiling on their tests. They present the method as an answer where new classes arrive with almost no examples.
arxiv-2507-23557:
Alin Bostan, Valentin Féray, and Paul Thévenin sum products of Catalan numbers over all trees of a given shape class. Their paper from twenty twenty-five finds a tidy answer for a wild-looking family. Each sum turns out to be a polynomial in one over pi, with rational weights. The proof builds the sums rather than merely claiming them. An algorithm falls out that computes any such sum outright.

Wider lifted sums join the story on the way. Those are polynomials in the complete elliptic integrals of both kinds. Their degrees stay under half the tree's vertex count. The work is driven by meandric systems, non-crossing loop patterns in the plane at large size. Tree sums feed the counts of those systems. The paper serves enumerative combinatorics with a rare closed form.
arxiv-2508-02257:
Yuepeng Guan, Mamiya Kawaguchi, Shinya Matsuzaki, and Akio Tomiya map the phase structure of strong interaction matter in a 2025 theoretical physics study. The Columbia plot charts how the chiral phase transition, where quark masses effectively melt away, changes character with quark masses. Their tool is a three-flavor linear sigma model handled with a formalism named for Cornwall, Jackiw, and Tomboulis.

The textbook version of that formalism breaks chiral symmetry artificially, violating bedrock identities. A symmetry-improved version repairs those violations, and the authors redraw the plot under the repaired rules. The corrected map guides lattice simulations and heavy-ion experiments.
arxiv-2508-04057:
Wang Chen and five co-authors made retrieval for language models both leaner and safer. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems fetch facts for each query. That wastes work on plain queries the model can solve from its own weights. Worse, thin queries can pull in junk documents. Their frame, PAIRS, asks first if a fetch is needed at all.

It runs two paths: one draft from the model's own knowledge, and one check path that weighs fetch worth. Pick of sources then adapts to the query's strength. No training is needed. Readers who build fact backed chat get fewer, better fetches at less cost.
arxiv-2508-04357:
Fernández-Nieto and seven co-authors turned teacher know-how into pictures in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Universities lose expertise when staff turn over, and writing workflows down eats expert time. Pattern mining can extract expert routines from system logs automatically. The catch is turning those patterns into forms novices can use.
