Their approach, Visual Process Representations, blends mining with storytelling design. One hundred sixty teachers rated four versions, from plain text lists to enriched pictorial styles. Richer visuals improved task performance, usability, and engagement. Memory of the process and task speed, though, barely moved. The authors see promise for onboarding novice educators at scale.
arxiv-2508-08957:
Wang and five colleagues present QAMRO, a training method for rating generated audio in twenty twenty-five. Systems that make speech, music, or sound from text need quality scores. Human judgement is subjective, so simple score regression misses relative differences. QAMRO instead ranks outputs with margins that adapt to quality gaps.

The method blends regression goals from several viewpoints. It builds on pretrained audio text models such as CLAP. Training used only the official AudioMOS Challenge twenty twenty-five data set. The framework beat strong baselines on alignment with human ratings. Gains held across all rated dimensions. The authors aim for evaluation that matches how people actually hear quality differences.
arxiv-2508-09057:
Zeyu Huang and colleagues built a test set in 2025 for AI agents that use phones on a person's behalf. Phone agents can tap through apps to finish tasks, but older tests feel neat and fake next to real requests. From user surveys the team named five kinds of real demand, from vague wishes to tasks that span several apps, and even harmful orders an agent should refuse.

Their bilingual set holds hundreds of tasks across well over a hundred apps. A helper module that asks clarifying questions and flags risk lifted success a lot, with the biggest gains on harmful and back-and-forth tasks. Gaps to real-world use remain clear.
arxiv-2508-11657:
Yuanhao Li and co-authors hardened a brain reading method against noise in 2025. Sparse Bayesian learning is a strong tool for reading intentions from high-dimensional brain recordings. But its usual likelihood functions assume tidy Gaussian or Bernoulli noise, while real neural signals are messier. When the noise model is wrong, reading accuracy and clarity both suffer.

The team rebuilt the method around minimum error entropy, a learning rule known for shrugging off non-Gaussian noise, regulating the model settings with that loss inside a broadened Bayesian form. Their method, tested on two real brain reading tasks, one regression and one classification, beat current methods on results. It also made results the authors describe as more physiologically clear, a key quality when a decoder's output should tell neuroscientists something true about the brain.
arxiv-2508-13857:
Carlos Cabezas and a large team of co-authors report finding, in a 2025 preprint, a new carbon molecule in a cold cloud in space. The molecule is phenalene, a ring-shaped compound with three fused rings. It belongs to a family called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, long suspected to be common in space. The team found it in the cloud TMC-1 during a radio survey of spectral lines.

Despite the molecule's weak signal strength, the survey picked up hundreds of its rotational lines. The pattern of those lines matched values worked out from quantum chemistry. To be sure, the team then made the molecule in a lab and measured its spectrum there. The lab result backed the match. They also estimate how much phenalene the cloud holds. The find adds one more firm piece to the puzzle of which ring molecules exist between the stars.
arxiv-2508-15357:
Haji Gul, Abul Ghani Naim, and Ajaz Ahmad Bhat present a study from twenty twenty-five on how to rank models that fill gaps in knowledge graphs. Such graphs store facts as links between things, and they often miss links. Fill methods guess the gaps. Scores to grade them clash: a model may top one data set and trail on the next, or win on one gauge and lose on the next.

Their frame, KG-EDAS, fuses all gauges and data sets into one score for each model. The score rates how far a model sits from the mean pack. Tests on two known graph data sets give one clean ranking. The authors say the fused view makes model picks more fair and clear.
arxiv-2508-17357: Daniel López Garcia and Fabricio Valencia extend Hamiltonian geometry to a setting built on cosymplectic groupoids with a zero shift. They introduce zero-shifted cosymplectic structures on differentiable stacks and build the matching moment map theory for Hamiltonian actions of that kind. A reduction procedure follows from the theory. The authors also establish a version of the Kirwan convexity theorem in this setting and give examples involving Morse-Bott Lie groupoid morphisms.
arxiv-2508-20857:
Xiangyun Meng and Martin Stynes present a study from twenty twenty-five on a hard math problem with a tiny factor that makes the answer change fast near the edges of a square. Such sharp edge layers break plain grid methods. They solve the fourth order problem with flat Morley elements on a Shishkin mesh, a grid packed tight near the edges.

In a norm fit for this problem, they prove a clear rate at which the error shrinks as the grid grows fine. In the worst case, where the tiny factor matches the grid scale, the rate beats an older proof for a rival element. Tests with numbers back the claim that the rate is sharp. The work aids codes that must stay exact when edge layers are thin.
arxiv-2508-21657:
Zhang and a team of colleagues proposed a new network for computer-generated holograms in twenty twenty-five. Holography builds three-dimensional images from light patterns, but computing them is a hard, unstable puzzle. End-to-end networks treat the physics as a black box, and standard networks see only small local patches at a time.

Their deep unfolding network splits the solving process into two modules. One preserves signal bandwidth and allows wider working distances than common spectrum methods. The other cleans the phase pattern using complex-valued attention that can stretch and adapt, capturing global structure. Quality scores passed thirty-five decibels on the standard scale. Tests on simulated and real data gave top results, the authors report, with clearer physical meaning than black-box rivals.
arxiv-2509-00157:
Mohamed M. Anber and Erich Poppitz study super Yang-Mills theory on a four-dimensional torus in 2025 with a small gaugino mass and a vacuum angle. Yang-Mills theory governs strong-force-like fields, and its supersymmetric form pairs each particle with a partner. Twisted boundary conditions on the torus create instantons, which are localized field events with fractional charge.

A detuning parameter measures how far the torus sits from a perfectly self-dual shape. The team computes scalar and pseudo-scalar condensates, the vacuum values of key fields, to leading order in a small ratio. Summing over all twisted sectors proves crucial to match the correct results at large size. In the massless limit, known strong-coupling facts are recovered.
arxiv-2509-00457:
Salah Eddine Bekhouche, Abdellah Zakaria Sellam, Hichem Telli, Cosimo Distante, and Abdenour Hadid present an efficient encoder-based system in 2025 for Islamic inheritance reasoning. Islamic inheritance law requires precise identification of heirs and calculation of shares, a demanding task for AI. Their system solves multiple-choice inheritance questions with a specialized Arabic text encoder.

Attentive Relevance Scoring ranks answer options by semantic relevance to the question. No generative reasoning is used, which enables fast, on-device inference. Arabic encoders such as MARBERT, ArabicBERT, and AraBERT are compared with large API models on the QIAS 2025 data set. The MARBERT system reaches near seventy percent accuracy, below the best large model but with strong gains in speed, privacy, and deployability.
arxiv-2509-00557:
M M Chernyshov and one co-author, P N Vabishchevich, solve two-dimensional boundary value problems, tasks where a quantity and its boundary values are given, on merged meshes. Their mesh mixes Delaunay triangulations, grids that link points into triangles, with Voronoi diagrams, partitions where each cell holds points closest to one generator.

Chernyshov and Vabishchevich place nodes at both triangle vertices and Voronoi generators, giving cells that are orthodiagonal quadrilaterals, four-sided cells whose diagonals cross at right angles. On such meshes, scalar and vector functions, and gradient and divergence operators, measures of slope and outflow, approximate cleanly. They show the method on a steady diffusion-reaction problem in an anisotropic medium, one whose properties vary with direction.
arxiv-2509-00757:
Xiufeng Huang leads a team of five authors on watermarking 3D Gaussian Splatting models. Splatting renders three-dimensional scenes from many soft blobs. It has grown popular very fast. Copyright protection for such models is now a clear need. Current methods fine-tune the model for each new message. That process is slow and costly.

The team proposes MarkSplatter as a general solution. It embeds a message in a single forward pass. A module called GaussianBridge converts loose Gaussians into Splatter Image format. That format allows direct neural processing of the model. A heatmap strategy preserves visual quality during embedding. A dense segmentation method then recovers the message. Recovery stays reliable even when marked objects are tiny in a view.
arxiv-2509-01057:
Yi-Ning Weng and Hsuan-Wei Lee propose Q-learning-driven adaptive rewiring for cooperation in networks. Cooperation in multi-agent systems is a basic problem in statistical physics. Small learning rules can drive large collective shifts there. Their method builds on adaptive rewiring work in the literature. It joins temporal difference learning with network restructuring.

Agents optimize both strategies and social ties from past interactions. Neighbor-specific Q-learning lets agents manage partnerships with care. Cooperator clusters form, set apart from defective regions in space. Tests use power-law networks that mirror real connectivity patterns. Three regimes appear across rewiring constraint levels. A permissive regime enables rapid cluster formation. A middle regime depends sensitively on dilemma strength. A patient regime optimizes structure only gradually.
arxiv-2509-01257:
Devices at the edge of a wireless network must decide fast whether to run a task locally or send it to a shared server. Andrea Fox, Francesco De Pellegrini, and Eitan Altman propose a decentralized learning framework for that offloading choice. Each agent acts on its own, with limited sight of the whole system and little talk between agents.

Each agent solves a constrained decision problem, and coordination happens through a shared constraint vector updated only now and then. That vector stops agents from overloading shared servers while keeping communication light. Using safe reinforcement learning, agents learn policies that serve both local and global goals. The team proves guarantees under mild assumptions and shows gains over centralized and independent baselines, most clearly in large-scale settings.
arxiv-2509-01357:
Heavy neutral leptons are proposed particles that could explain why neutrinos have mass, and finding them means measuring their mass peak with care. Marzieh Bahmani, with four co-authors, presents methods to reconstruct that peak when such a particle decays to a lepton and a rho meson, which then splits into pions. Only the lepton and the charged pion from the decay point are used.

Two methods add known mass constraints, from the rho meson itself or from a parent W boson at colliders. Both suit experiments that can track displaced vertices, decay points set apart from the collision. Simulations show the rho-mass method gives promising resolution in both beam-dump and collider settings. The W-mass method, limited to collider production, did even better, sharpening searches for sterile neutrinos.
arxiv-2509-01457:
A new product spreads when people copy peers and when their views turn warm. But unhappy users may drop it and later return. Martina Alutto, with four co-authors, builds a group-based model of this spread. It links take-up with how views form on a layered social network. One layer carries exposure to the new product. Another carries the social talk that shapes views.

The team studies the model's resting points and their stability. From that, they derive exact terms for take-up to persist. They then add a control method that looks ahead and adapts its steps. Three policy types are compared. One sways views, one pays users to adopt, and one cuts unhappiness by improving the product. Tests favor the forward-looking, adaptive approach.
arxiv-2509-01657:
Robots learn skills from demonstrations, and when only a few examples fit a new task, fetching more from large prior data sets can help. Amber Xie, Rahul Chand, Dorsa Sadigh, and Joey Hejna study that retrieval step for few-shot imitation learning. Standard retrieval picks prior points nearest to the target data in a latent space, a rule the team shows equals the limit of a kernel density estimate.

That lens exposes two flaws: nearest neighbor estimates vary wildly and invite noise, and the rule ignores how the prior data itself is distributed. Their method, Importance Weighted Retrieval, estimates importance weights, the ratio between target and prior distributions, to guide selection. Xie and the co-authors argue the weighted rule retrieves data that serves the target task better, strengthening few-shot learning for robots in new settings.
arxiv-2509-02157:
Yingjie Zhu leads fifteen co-authors in tracing active region upflows at the Sun corona boundary and their links downward. Upflows with strong blueshift at active region edges may seed the slow solar wind. Two upflow regions flank one decaying active region with different magnetic settings. Observations combine a Japanese solar telescope line with high resolution imaging from Solar Orbiter.

The eastern site sits over moss with small dynamic fibrils, while the west hosts fan like loops. A neon line is blueshifted in the east but redshifted in the west. Field extrapolations reveal a pseudostreamer topology connecting both sites. The pattern supports pressure imbalances from coronal reconnection driving steady upflows. Lower atmosphere flows below the eastern site respond passively to that drive.
arxiv-2509-02257:
Ying Li and three co-authors wrote a 2025 particle physics paper. It studies a rare change in heavy baryons. A Lambda-b baryon turns into a Lambda-c baryon. A lepton and an antineutrino come out with it. The team checks the electron, muon, and tau forms of this decay.

The team uses perturbative QCD. That method works out strong-force effects step by step. First they compute six shape factors at low momentum transfer. Then they extend the factors across the full range. They use a model-free expansion for that step, plus lattice results. From the factors they get decay rates and angle-based measures. One key ratio tests lepton flavor universality, the idea that lepton types act alike. Their value lands a bit above the newest data. That gives labs a clear target to check.
arxiv-2509-02557:
Dilek Söylemez and Mehmet Ünver wrote a 2025 paper on approximation theory. It extends the Korovkin theorem. That classic result says a scheme checked on a few test functions will converge for all of them. Their version works in general spaces. It uses a statistical notion of convergence.

The key lemma says one thing. Any sequence that converges in the power-series statistical sense holds a classically convergent subsequence. That subsequence lives on a set of density one. The authors then study generalised linear operators. Those operators may lack positivity, a trait older theorems required. A Korovkin-type theorem for periodic functions follows. Examples and corollaries round out the paper. It widens approximation guarantees to rougher settings.
arxiv-2509-02757:
Feng Chen, Wen O. Wang, Jia-Xin Zhang, Leon Balents, and D. N. Sheng present a 2025 condensed matter paper reporting strong evidence for topological chiral superconductivity in a triangular lattice model. Moiré materials, made by stacking patterned layers, motivate the mix of strong interactions and large magnetic flux.

Two large numerical methods, density matrix renormalisation and quantum Monte Carlo, study the lightly doped Hofstadter-Hubbard model. Both point to a robust superconducting phase whose pairing correlations decay as a power law, with a quantised spin Chern number marking its topological character. The phase appears at very weak interaction and strengthens at intermediate strength across wide doping ranges. The authors also discuss how the normal state differs between interaction regimes, informing the hunt for exotic superconductors.
arxiv-2509-02857: Charles L. Fefferman, Jacob Shapiro, and Michael I. Weinstein presented a 2025 mathematical physics paper on a magnetic double well. A double well is an energy landscape with two low pockets, like two valleys side by side. Quantum particles can often tunnel, meaning leak through the barrier, between such pockets. The authors present a case, recently announced before this write-up, where that tunneling between the two wells drops to zero when a magnetic field shapes the system.
arxiv-2509-02957:
Navya Sri Kelam and 3 co-authors tested a 2025 system for spotting mitotic figures in pathology slides. Mitotic figures are cells caught in the act of dividing, and counting them helps grade cancers. They are rare, varied in shape, and hard to keep consistent across labs and stains.

The team trained two versions of the YOLO detector, one that guesses locations with preset boxes and one that works without them. Color and texture tweaks during training helped the models cope with stain differences. Each model had strengths: one was more precise, the other found more true cases. Joining their outputs into an ensemble gave the best overall balance in internal tests. The combined system also placed near the top on an early public leaderboard.
arxiv-2509-03757:
A 2025 research paper by Wei Cai and one co-author examines ARDO, a deep learning method for solving partial differential equations of elliptic and parabolic type. Such equations describe steady and slowly evolving systems, from heat flow to diffusion. Neural network solvers often need derivatives of the network's own output, which adds cost and fragility.

ARDO uses a weak adversarial formulation, where the equation is tested against many probe functions instead of enforced point by point. Its twist moves a random difference operator, which approximates change through random probes, onto the test function rather than the solution. The solution network then needs no derivatives at all during training. That derivative-free property suits Fokker-Planck type equations especially well. Those equations track how probability distributions evolve, and they appear across physics, finance, and biology.
arxiv-2509-03857:
Kishor Datta Gupta and five co-authors' 2025 research paper focuses on monitoring large generative AI systems with knowledge graphs. Generative models raise reliability worries: invented facts, semantic drift over time, and hidden biases. Because the models act as black boxes, checks usually lean on subjective human judgment, which scales poorly and lacks transparency.

Their method builds two knowledge graphs in parallel. One is deterministic, assembled by explicit rules, ready ontologies, domain dictionaries, and structured extraction from text. The other is generated by a language model from live news streams, keeping data fresh and hard to game by memorising benchmarks. Set graph metrics quantify how the two structures deviate, in class and property usage. An automated framework tracks those deviations, setting anomaly thresholds from past distributions. Large departures get flagged promptly, catching semantic anomalies and hallucinations as they emerge. The design aims for proactive monitoring at scale.
arxiv-2509-04057:
Naser Ahmadiniaz and three co-authors examine a clash between quantum computing and its environment in a 2025 physics paper. Adiabatic quantum computing changes a system very slowly so it can settle into an answer. Quantum annealing uses a similar slow change to solve hard problems. Both rely on smooth jumps between energy levels at narrow crossing points, like lanes merging on a road.

Surrounding noise constantly measures the system, the authors show, and that watching freezes change under the quantum Zeno effect. For a slow version of Grover's search method, the freeze badly limits any speed gain. Gentler state changes or echo tricks that undo noise might ease the problem, they suggest.
arxiv-2509-04257:
Madhav Sinha and three co-authors place every topological defect line of certain toy universes onto a lattice in a 2025 physics paper. Conformal field theories, or CFTs, describe scale-free systems such as certain magnets at critical points. Defect lines are seams whose physics stays unchanged under reshaping, labeled here by Kac labels. Most seams become truly topological only in the smooth continuum limit, though one family is exact already on the lattice.

Integrable lattice models called RSOS models supply the construction, using rows of tiles with tweaked parameters. The authors map which parameter ranges realize each defect and compute their eigenvalues exactly. Merging defects matches stacking operations in the algebraic machinery. Numerical checks across several minimal theories confirm the formulas.
arxiv-2509-04657:
Reword a database question and a strong model may suddenly answer it wrong. Mohammadtaher Safarzadeh, lead author with two co-authors, study that brittleness in a 2025 evaluation paper on natural language to SQL systems. Their framework turns SQL back into natural language to create equivalent, differently worded queries.

Because the new queries stay aligned with the original schema and intent, the test isolates wording alone. On paraphrased Spider queries, large models lose substantial execution accuracy, and smaller models suffer most. The authors argue benchmarks should measure this linguistic robustness directly, since real users phrase questions in many ways.
arxiv-2509-05057:
Space radiation has slowly damaged the Hubble Space Telescope's main survey camera over more than two decades. Richard Massey, lead author with ten co-authors, track that damage across two solar cycles in a 2025 paper. Solar protons and cosmic rays create defects in the silicon of its imaging sensors, and the damage rate varies with the solar cycle.

The defects trap photoelectrons and release them later, leaving spurious trails in images. The authors present an updated open-source correction algorithm that models that capture and release. Calibrated on hot pixels, it removes nearly all charge transfer trailing, even in the worst recent data.
arxiv-2509-05157:
A dynamic graph that keeps changing still needs its smallest cuts available on demand. Monika Henzinger, lead author with three co-authors, build a data structure for that task in a 2025 algorithms paper. The structure maintains a sparsifier, a smaller multigraph preserving all non-trivial minimum cuts, for a fully dynamic undirected graph.

Simple dynamic forest tools allow fast construction of the sparsifier from scratch at query time. Different versions trade worst-case, amortised, and adversary assumptions for speed. Applications include reporting a cactus representation of all minimum cuts efficiently. The authors present the design as a flexible tool for dynamic graph algorithms.
arxiv-2509-05457:
Stars that rotate almost unbelievably slowly are examined spectroscopically by Gautier Mathys and four co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Ap stars, a chemically unusual class, have rotation periods spanning a huge range, and why some spin so slowly remains unknown.

The team took new spectra of candidate super-slowly rotating Ap stars picked out by a space telescope survey. For most of the sample, the measured line broadening is low enough to imply very long periods. Nearly all proved magnetic, with first field detections for several, and some showed lines split by magnetism. A few turned out to be double stars with moving spectral lines, adding fresh facts about this extreme group.
arxiv-2509-05657:
Language models are taught to design neural networks across task domains by Yuxuan Hu and nine co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Architecture search is usually tuned per domain with heavy prompt craft, limiting how far language model approaches scale.

Their framework encodes any architecture as a universal string of numbers, letting one representation travel across domains. The search problem becomes ranking: the model learns to pick strong candidates from a pool, trained on examples built by a pruning-based sampling of the design space. Experiments cover image classification networks and adapter settings for segmentation and generation. Performance stayed competitive in and out of domain.
arxiv-2509-05757:
Language models built in curved space are surveyed by Sarang Patil and four co-authors in a 2025 review paper. Much real data, from protein networks to syntax trees, has a hidden tree-like hierarchy that flat Euclidean representations fit poorly, while hyperbolic geometry models trees naturally.

The survey organises hyperbolic language models into four families: models using maps between flat and curved space, fine-tuned hyperbolic models, fully hyperbolic models, and hyperbolic state-space models. Each family's main techniques are explained in context. Applications and future directions are also mapped. A public repository collects the key papers, models, datasets, and code, making the fast-growing area easier to enter.
arxiv-2509-05957:
Tiny flickers inside a pulsar's radio beam, called microstructure, are hunted inside interpulses for the first time in a 2025 paper led by Wei Li with fourteen co-authors. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth; some show a second, interpulse beam. The team used China's FAST telescope, the world's largest single-dish radio instrument, on four such pulsars.

Autocorrelation and Fourier analyses measured the flickers' timescales and quasi-periods in both the main pulse and the interpulse. Microstructure inside an interpulse was detected successfully for the first time. In one pulsar the two beams' microstructure matched within errors, while in another the interpulse flickers ran smaller. The study also reconfirmed a known link between microstructure period and the star's rotation period across neutron star populations.
arxiv-2509-06157:
Which factory should pack which meal kit order? Thi Minh Thu Nguyen and two co-authors formalize that daily puzzle as the Box Allocation Problem in a 2025 paper, set in the United Kingdom's large meal kit market. Assigning orders across plants should minimize day-to-day recipe variation while respecting capacity and eligibility limits over a fifteen-day horizon.

Cast as a mixed-integer linear program, the problem is attacked with the CBC branch-and-cut solver and with heuristics including tabu search and targeted pairwise swaps. On instances up to one hundred thousand orders, CBC consistently finds optimal solutions in under two minutes, even as capacities and orders fluctuate. Steadier recipes improve ingredient forecasting and cut food waste, and the authors offer the first full framework for this allocation problem.
arxiv-2509-06257:
Weighing a patient who cannot move, by playing music through their bed, is the system MelodyBedScale in a 2025 paper led by Yuyan Wu with seven co-authors. Weight drives drug dosing, defibrillation energy, and fluid decisions in emergencies, yet scales and tapes fail for immobilized patients. A body on a bed changes how the bed vibrates, and that transfer function carries the weight signal.

The team composes soft, natural music rich in the weight-sensitive frequency bands and plays it through a bed-mounted speaker, reading vibrations from sensors on both sides. A physics-informed neural network, its activations shaped by theory, learns the weight-vibration map from little data. On wooden and steel beds with eleven participants, error stayed near a kilogram and a half.
arxiv-2509-06457:
A machine learning weather model trained for days ahead can also forecast seasons, test Bobby Antonio and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. GenCast, a leading probabilistic model, is run with sea surface temperatures persisted from climatology or forced from observations, extending it far beyond its training horizon. El Niño and La Niña precipitation patterns emerge largely correctly, with the forced variant repairing several errors.

Against the European seasonal system SEAS5, GenCast trails in the tropics for temperature and pressure but wins in some higher-latitude and mountainous regions, correlating better with the observed North Atlantic Oscillation. Its persisted variant is overconfident, while the forced one calibrates well. The authors see promise for learned models in the full seasonal problem.
arxiv-2509-07157:
Data-heavy cloud workloads are the target of Crossword, a 2025 consensus protocol from Guanzhou Hu and 3 co-authors. Consensus protocols let many machines agree on the same data even when messages vary in size. Large payloads can clog the network at random moments, and older protocols assign fixed roles that cannot adapt when traffic changes.

Crossword codes each data item with erasure coding, which splits data into shards that can rebuild the whole from a subset. It then shifts how shards are assigned and how many machines must agree, based on live workload and network state. A lazy gossip scheme handles leader failure with little cost. In tests it matched the best older protocols in calm settings and beat them by up to 2.3 times under changing loads. A trial inside CockroachDB lifted total throughput as well.
arxiv-2509-07357:
Repetitive stretches of DNA cause false matches in genome searches and errors in variant calling. Heng Li and Brian Li introduce longdust in a 2025 research paper. Longdust is an algorithm that finds low-complexity sequences, regions built from short repeating patterns. Older tools either lacked a clear mathematical definition of complexity or ran slowly on long context windows.

Longdust defines complexity by modeling counts of short DNA words called k-mers. Users set the word length, window size, and a complexity threshold. The tool catches long repeats, including centromeric satellite DNA and tandem repeats with fairly long motifs. Tests on real data show strong performance and good agreement with existing methods. The code is freely available, so genome pipelines can add it as a cleaning step.
arxiv-2509-07457:
Shakhzod Yuldoshkhujaev and 4 co-authors map a decade of advanced persistent threats in a 2025 study. An advanced persistent threat, or APT, is a covert, long-term cyberattack, often state-sponsored, that targets key sectors and can hide for years. Reports from investigators worldwide document these campaigns, but the dossiers are scattered and rarely reviewed as a whole over time.

The team systematically analyzes six reliable sources, three of technical reports and three of threat actors, covering 1,509 dossiers and over 24,000 pages from 2014 to 2023. They identify 603 unique APT groups worldwide. A hybrid search method joins rule-based retrieval with language-model search to mine the archive efficiently. The longitudinal analysis connects key insights and global trends across the decade. The macro view is meant to help defenders see patterns that single-case studies miss.
arxiv-2509-07957:
Two-armed robots learn tasks from human videos in a 2025 paper by Shunlei Li and 3 co-authors. Copying low-level motion trajectories fails when objects, layouts, or robot arms change. Their framework, GF-VLA, instead aims at task-level reasoning, understanding what a demonstration is trying to achieve before acting.

An information-theoretic step picks out the important cues, mainly hand-object and object-object interactions, from colour-and-depth video. Those cues are organised into graph structures that a vision-language-action system can reason over. The dual-arm robot then plans its own movements for the same goal. Reasoning about goals rather than replaying motions should transfer skills to new kitchens, benches, and assemblies where exact repetition is impossible.
arxiv-2509-08057:
Assumed background cosmology can quietly shift survey results, warns a 2025 DESI collaboration paper led by R. Gsponer and colleagues. Full-shape fits to the galaxy power spectrum measure cosmic structure, but the analysis pipeline starts from a fiducial cosmology, a reference universe. The authors test whether that starting choice biases the final answers.

Mock catalogues from the AbacusSummit simulations, built on the Planck 2018 cosmology, are reanalysed under five alternative reference cosmologies. Variations cover matter density, thawing dark energy, extra neutrino species, lower clustering strength, and a dynamic dark energy fit. Quantifying these systematic shifts protects DESI's headline claims about dark energy from an avoidable, self-inflicted error.
arxiv-2509-08357:
Children practise inhibition control in a recycling-themed sorting game while eye tracking reads their attention, in a 2025 educational technology paper by Abdul Rehman and 4 co-authors. The ReStroop game adapts the classic Stroop conflict: respond to one feature while suppressing a tempting wrong one. Gaze data turns gameplay into assessment evidence.

A unified framework processes raw gaze through fixation detection, using two complementary methods, then evaluates performance across areas of interest and plans personalised interventions. Teachers gain assessment detail that scores alone cannot provide, such as where a child's eyes went before a mistake. Personalised inhibition training matters because self-control predicts school success, and games can deliver the practice at scale.
arxiv-2509-08557:
How does a chain of magnets behave when its total magnetization is held fixed? Ivan Balog and 1 co-author study that question for the one-dimensional Ising model in a 2025 paper. They focus on the scaling limit near absolute zero.

In momentum space, the correlation function shows surprising swings as magnetization changes. The swings repeat with a period tied to momentum, and the authors link them to domain walls, the borders between magnetized regions. That pattern differs sharply from behavior in a steady magnetic field. It also helps explain recent computer simulations of the two-dimensional model.
arxiv-2509-08957:
Gayana Jayasinghe and 3 co-authors establish logarithmic wave decay for short range wavespeed perturbations in a 2025 paper. Wave equations with varying speed model sound or light in uneven media. Local energy should decay over time, but the rate depends on the perturbation.

The speed differs from a constant by a short range term with mild smoothness in the radial direction, in dimensions two and higher. A key step is continuity of the weighted resolvent, a tool for solving the equation at fixed frequency. Low frequencies use a series expansion, while other frequencies use a Carleman estimate, a weighted inequality. Together they give logarithmic local energy decay, with special care at low frequency in two dimensions.
arxiv-2509-09057:
Yici Zhong and 1 co-author explain radio pulses from long period sources in white dwarf pairs in a 2025 paper. Two such sources are tied to white dwarf and M dwarf binaries. Their pulses track the orbit period, which hints that the pair's interplay drives the radio waves.

Kinetic plasma simulations test the electron cyclotron maser process, also seen at Jupiter. In its nonlinear range, that process makes coherent pulses under the right plasma states. The pulses come out partly linearly polarized, in line with the seen spectra. Exact traits hinge on plasma mix. The work sets up full nonlinear models of radio waves from such pairs.
arxiv-2509-09257:
Anti-de Sitter space, the negatively curved universe beloved of theorists, needs its quantum fields expanded in the right waves. Ugo Moschella presents a new plane-wave expansion in a 2025 research paper written alone. The expansion applies to the Wightman functions of scalar fields in that space. Wightman functions are the basic correlation objects of quantum field theory.

From the expansion, Moschella derives a new integral form for the Feynman propagator. That representation clarifies how Euclidean and Lorentzian Feynman diagrams relate in concrete examples. The expansion also yields fresh formulas for the Bessel and Legendre functions, the special functions that permeate mathematical physics. Two examples are worked out in the paper. Better tools here matter because anti-de Sitter space underlies the holographic duality. That duality connects gravity with quantum fields, a central idea in theoretical physics.
arxiv-2509-09457:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang's 2025 number theory paper studies integral bases for pure number fields, fields built by adjoining one root of a simple polynomial. Fixing the degree at three or more, he encodes each basis by its shape in a standard coordinate set. The central question is how much local information fixes that shape, and how the pattern repeats as the defining value varies.

Nguyen-Dang proves a sharp local-to-global rule: at each prime power dividing the degree, the local shape depends only on the defining value modulo one higher power, and no coarser precision suffices. Globally the shape repeats with a minimal period he computes exactly, giving a firm tool for later work on these fields.
arxiv-2509-09557:
Michael Vaz and 1 co-author compute how the empty-space electromagnetic field at two moving points relates to itself in a 2025 physics paper. Fresh experiments on quantum vacuum fluctuations have revived interest in such correlations. Any useful model must blend zero-point jitter with ordinary thermal radiation, and motion changes what a travelling probe actually registers over time.

After a short history and a time-domain look at electric field links, the authors give exact and approximate formulas in frequency space. One case follows two points flying apart on parallel paths at steady speeds. Another places them opposite each other on one circle, swept around at fixed angular rate. Self-correlations and links with spatial derivatives are also worked out and discussed.
arxiv-2509-09757:
Caner Tanış introduces a new lifetime distribution in this solo 2025 statistics paper. The model, built by a record-based transformation of the log-logistic distribution, is meant for data on how long things last, such as parts or devices. Tanış works out its basic properties, including its quantile and hazard functions, its moments, and how it orders against other distributions.

Seven different estimation methods are compared, from maximum likelihood to several least squares and distance-based approaches. A Monte Carlo simulation checks how well each estimator performs. The distribution is then fitted to two real data sets, on petroleum rock and on reactor pump failures. The author reports it matched the data better than rival models.
arxiv-2509-09957:
Seungyeop Han and 5 co-authors use Markov chains to plan spare satellites for giant constellations in a 2025 aerospace paper. A mega constellation cannot afford grounded service while replacements crawl upward, so operators park spares in holding orbits and shuttle them into working planes as failures strike. Judging such a two-storey stock system over the long run is the paper's first job.

Failures and restocking in each storey become separate Markov chains, joined by a fixed-point loop until their steady states agree. That joint picture captures the random interplay honestly, without the flattening shortcuts older studies needed. A genetic algorithm then searches design choices on top of the fast analysis. A realistic case study closes the paper, showing the machinery guiding real architecture decisions.
arxiv-2509-10057:
Jakub Mojsiejuk and 2 co-authors use reinforcement learning to control a spintronic device in this 2025 paper. A spin torque oscillator is a tiny magnetic device that vibrates at a set frequency, and locking it onto a target frequency by hand is fiddly. The team simulated the oscillator with the standard macrospin equation for magnetic motion, then trained learning agents inside that simulation.

Two kinds of agents learned to reach the target frequency within a fixed number of steps. The authors then varied the task and found simple changes that improved both how fast the agents converged and how much energy the synchronization used. The result is a step toward automatic tuning of spintronic parts for future electronics.
arxiv-2509-10557:
Atefeh Irani and 5 co-authors present HiLWS, a framework for cleaning up medical video data, in this 2025 paper. Videos of hand movements can help assess conditions such as Parkinson's disease outside the clinic. Home recordings, though, are messy: poor image quality, tasks done wrong, noisy labels, and a shift away from clinic conditions all corrupt the data.

HiLWS works in two cascaded stages. First, weak supervision merges expert annotations into probabilistic labels, which train machine learning models. Then the models' predictions, joined with expert input, pass through a second round of weak supervision. The pipeline also filters bad clips, sharpens pose tracking, and cuts out the task segments, sending the most doubtful cases back to experts.
arxiv-2509-10657:
Splitting a network's traffic into a few simple lanes is the problem here. George Pennington and seven co-authors tackle it in this 2025 quantum computing paper. Formally, a graph is decomposed into a weighted sum of matchings. The fewer matchings, the better. The task arises in peer-to-peer energy exchange and similar allocation problems. Classical algorithms strain at it, even at small sizes.

Their hybrid algorithm is called E-FCFW. It extends a classical Frank-Wolfe method. A matching sampler, run on a quantum optimizer called QAOA, does the sampling. Benchmarks cover complete, bipartite, and heavy-hex graphs. Runs used simulators and IBM's Kingston quantum hardware, with up to one hundred eleven qubits. On small graphs, the quantum version gave sparser decompositions, again and again. On hundred-node graphs, it gave lower error. One caveat stands out. At the largest scale, hardware noise badly hurt results, compared with simulation.
arxiv-2509-10857:
Unmixing a signal into its pure components, online, is the task here. Hugues Kouakou and six co-authors take it up in this 2025 paper. Simplex-structured factorization appears across machine learning and remote sensing. The standard minimum-volume algorithms work well offline. They choke on memory and computation when data stream in, one observation at a time.

Their approach wraps any existing offline algorithm in a sequential shell. The trick is restraint. The solution updates only when a check says the new observation is informative. The check runs against the optimization constraints and the underlying geometry. Everything else is discarded. Storage and processing stay lean. On synthetic and real datasets, the online version matched the offline method's accuracy. It cut computational cost significantly at the same time. A mature offline literature thus gains a bridge to streaming applications.
arxiv-2509-11057:
Hridoy Sankar Dutta and Biswadeep Khan introduce YTCommentVerse, a giant corpus of YouTube comments, in this 2025 paper. Public social media data sets rarely combine many languages, clear topic labels, and rich metadata for video platforms. Their corpus holds more than 32 million comments drawn from about 178,000 videos, posted by over 20 million distinct users.

The comments span fifteen content categories, from music and news to education and entertainment, and more than fifty languages. Each record carries video and comment identifiers, channel details, upvote counts, and the category label. The authors offer the set for studying sentiment, toxicity, and engagement across cultures and topics, and note it fills a real gap for video platform research.
arxiv-2509-11357:
Yahav Bechavod, Jiuyao Lu, and Aaron Roth merge two demands that usually pull apart. This 2025 theory paper treats forecasts that many agents act on. Each agent wants low regret. Each also wants its long-run limits, like budgets, kept over time.

The authors show one shared forecast can serve all agents. Each agent acts by a simple rule based on that forecast. Regret then grows only like the square root of the rounds played. Total breach of the limits stays bounded by a fixed amount. The claims extend to context-defined slices of rounds. They hold within each slice, not just on average. Each agent is checked against act sets tailored to that slice.
arxiv-2509-11657:
Anh Duc Nguyen and three co-authors speed up a class of optimization algorithms in this 2025 paper. Their target is difference-of-convex programs, problems whose objective splits into the difference of two convex functions, with a nonsmooth twist, a structure that appears across machine learning and signal processing.

Their algorithm, DCA-PAGE, marries the difference-of-convex algorithm with a probabilistic gradient estimator that reuses past stochastic gradients to cut variance. In the finite-sum setting it lowers the gradient computation cost compared with the previous best stochastic variance-reduced methods, improving the exponent in the problem-size term. Unlike those rivals, it also extends to online settings where data arrive as a stream, with a similar optimal cost. A refined analysis using a gap function recovers comparable guarantees under milder assumptions.
arxiv-2509-12157:
Twenty-eight long looks by the Chandra X-ray Observatory anchor a 2025 study of N132D, a supernova remnant in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Xi Long and seventeen co-authors measure how fast its forward shock is expanding, using a baseline of about fourteen and a half years.

In the bright southern rim the shock moves at roughly sixteen hundred kilometers per second. Two features in a blowout region in the northeast move more than twice as fast, though their gas reads cooler than that speed would suggest. One-dimensional models fit both regions with an age near twenty-five hundred years, matching older optical estimates.
arxiv-2509-12257:
Martina Alutto and 4 co-authors study an epidemic model where people's behavior feeds back into spread, in a 2025 paper. Their SIR model divides a population into susceptible, infected, and recovered groups. Unlike fixed-rate versions, the infection rate adapts dynamically based on how many people are susceptible and infected.

The team finds an invariant of motion, a quantity that stays constant, and uses analysis to characterize the peak level of infection. They then ask how to keep infections below a healthcare capacity limit at the lowest economic cost. Their feasible strategy applies only the minimal restrictions needed to meet that limit. They characterize the cost of that strategy, giving a clear framework for balancing health protection and economic burden.
arxiv-2509-12457:
A wireless controller wakes a subset of channels each round. It wants three things at once. It wants high total reward. It wants a fair floor for every channel. And it wants rewards that arrive regularly, not in bursts. Xiaoyi Wu and one co-author design an algorithm for that triple demand in 2025. The model is the combinatorial multi-armed bandit.

Their score for each arm blends three signals. One is a virtual queue tracking fairness violations. One is a clock counting rounds since the arm last paid off. One is an optimism bonus. That bonus balances exploring against exploiting. Clever Lyapunov arguments prove zero cumulative fairness violation. Strong regret bounds come with them. Simulations on two real datasets confirm the theory.
arxiv-2509-12657:
Siri Vennela Geddam and 3 co-authors analyze resource allocation in space-air-ground joined networks in a 2025 paper. Such networks coordinate low-earth orbit satellites, aerial base stations on uncrewed vehicles, and terrestrial infrastructure to give seamless connectivity. Uses range from smart transport and healthcare to smart cities and disaster response.

The paper reviews resource management systems and tests methods including alternating optimization, damped iterative water filling, and genetic methods. MATLAB model runs across many trials benchmarked the methods for robust, fair, and low-latency allocation. The authors also analyze user association methods, how devices choose between terrestrial and aerial base stations during emergencies and overloads. Their comparative assessment offers guidance for building resilient joined networks.
arxiv-2509-13157:
Guillermo Toyos-Marfurt and Petr Kuznetsov pin down in 2025 the space-time trade for shared memory with capped cells. Full-data protocols share all knowledge each round but need unbounded cells. Capped cells can match that power at the cost of extra rounds.

Exact links tie rounds to process count, round count, and bits per cell. A state-shape study yields must-hold bounds. A capped protocol tuned to the bit budget is given. For more than two processes, rounds must grow with a factorial term and a bit-gap term. The tuned protocol is best for one model and near best for snapshot models.
arxiv-2509-13257:
Sriram Narayanan, Sajad Ahmadi and two co-authors fuse density functions into predictive control in 2025 for safe nonlinear steering. MPC-CDF uses the dual navigation form. Density tracks how long paths occupy zones, a physical read on safety and risk.

Discrete-time proofs give both convergence and safety. Controllers are built from the occupancy view. A unicycle case compares against barrier methods. An underwater craft then steers past complex obstacles at the set safety level. Occupancy thinking gives safety a direct dial inside the planner, not a bolt-on check added after plans form.
arxiv-2509-13357:
Yongchao Huang and Hassan Raza fuse fuzzy semantic traits into a transformer in 2025 for controllable generation. Each token gains a side vector of readable traits: role cues, edges, sentiment sign and strength. Values are graded via smooth membership functions.

Sentence trait matrices join the model via a gated adapter. Training adds next-token loss, trait rebuild loss, and a spread rule for adjective classes. On a two-clause fake corpus with held-out adjectives, perplexity improves. Polarity and punctuation can be dialed by users with precision. Overhead stays small and embeddings stay tied.
arxiv-2509-13557:
Zesong Jiang and six co-authors present MACO in a 2025 hardware design paper, an open-source framework that uses several cooperating language model agents to design coarse-grained reconfigurable arrays. These chips rearrange their computing units for each task, but finding a good layout means searching a huge space of linked hardware and software choices by hand.

MACO splits the design loop into four stages covering co-design, error correction, best-design selection, and evaluation with feedback. Tricks such as decaying exploration and rule-based error fixing speed the search. Against strong baselines it cut power use by about a quarter, raised performance by about a fifth, and searched several times faster. A full physical chip design flow validated the results.
arxiv-2509-13657:
Aidos Issadykov and five co-authors revisit radiative decays of charmonium in a 2025 particle physics paper. Charmonium states are bound states of a charm quark and antiquark, and their decays that emit a photon test how well quark models describe these particles.

Working in the covariant confined quark model, the team first shows every calculated amplitude respects gauge invariance, a basic consistency check. They then fit the model's parameters, including the charm quark mass and a meson size, to three measured decay channels. With the fit fixed, they predict branching fractions for several unmeasured or less precise channels involving the h_c and chi states, and the predictions agree well with available experimental data.
arxiv-2509-13757:
Opanasenko and Vitolo extend the geometry of the WDVV equations in a 2025 mathematics paper. These equations were born in field theory. In low dimensions, they can be rewritten as commuting systems of conservation laws. Two compatible structures appear in that rewriting. Whether the picture survives in higher dimensions was unclear.

The authors work in any dimension, with any scalar product. They show suitable subsets of the equations can be read as linear line families. The families sit inside Plücker embeddings, a classical geometry language. That reading recasts the subsets as a family of such systems. The authors also reduce the equations to an orthonomic, passive form in dimensions up to five. The systems commute there. They guess the passive property holds in every dimension.
arxiv-2509-14457:
Lisa-Yao Gan and three co-authors analyse metadata fields for natural language search on open data portals in 2025. Portals give public access to government and research data sets. Their search boxes still lean on keywords and a narrow field set, frustrating plain language queries.

Incomplete or uneven metadata make the gap worse, especially for users who lack domain terms. The authors run a controlled ablation study with simulated natural queries over real data sets. Removing or adding fields shows which metadata actually drive retrieval success. They also test whether language models can bridge natural phrasing and structured fields. Results guide portal owners on which fields to complete first and where model help pays off most.
arxiv-2509-14557:
YoungChul Yoon and four co-authors build a contextual choice frame in 2025 on Gaussian mixture models. Contextual choice uses side facts to guess unknown values before a choice is made. When outcomes cluster in more than one mode, simple fitted forms break down.

Free form models flex to fit modes, but they suffer in high dimensions. Gaussian mixtures give a middle path: more than one mode, with maths that stay tractable. Flow based spread to new cases, robust forms and multistage forms are all built in the frame. Choices such as stock levels or care plans often face just this clustered doubt. A model that honours modes can dodge averaging two likely futures into one poor choice.
arxiv-2509-14757:
Damianos Iosifidis, writing alone in 2025, builds a math framework for a tiny test body that can spin, stretch, and shear as it moves through curved space. The space is far more general than the one used in standard gravity theory. It allows twist and stretch of space itself, not just curve.

He starts from a broad action principle built from speed, a material frame, and the shape of the background space. By varying the path and the frame, he derives rules for how the body's momentum and spin-like charge change as it moves. The new rules extend classic results for spinning bodies by adding stretch and shear effects. A conserved quantity also falls out of the work.
arxiv-2509-15257:
Silpa Sreelatha and four co-authors make text-to-image tools that stay true, fair, and safe at once in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models draw rich images, yet some prompts trigger biased or unsafe output. Past fixes tend to buy fairness or safety by spending image quality and faith to the prompt.

Their method, RespoDiff, reshapes the squeezed middle layer of the model, where meaning is packed tight. Two small learned modules share that layer. One enforces fair and safe concepts. The other guards faith to the plain prompt. A fresh score-matching goal keeps the two in step. The authors report wins over past methods with the prompt's meaning intact. The work frames safe drawing as a problem of inner form, not of output filters.
arxiv-2509-15357:
Yu Chang, Jiahao Chen, Anzhe Cheng, and Paul Bogdan give text-to-image users region-level control over SDXL generations in a 2025 computer vision paper. As prompts grow structured and multi-object, diffusion models mix attributes between objects, break spatial relations, or drop requested items entirely, and standard quality metrics barely notice. Their MaskAttn-SDXL module plugs into the existing pipeline without retraining it.

The module injects token-conditioned spatial gating into cross-attention scores before the softmax step. Gating sparsifies which image locations each text token may influence, tying words to their intended regions. Attribute leakage between neighboring objects falls because tokens can no longer attend everywhere at once. The approach aims at compositional reliability: every requested entity present, wearing its own attributes, in its stated place.
arxiv-2509-16057:
Spaces with a rare kind of symmetry, tied to the Spin(7) group, can have rough points where the shape is not smooth. Viktor F. Majewski builds a method to smooth such orbifold spaces into proper manifolds with the same symmetry and no torsion. Rough zones are swapped for smooth fibred patches, and local data are encoded with systems drawn from orbifold theory.

A key test checks whether local smooth pieces glue into global forms on the fixed space. When a certain obstruction vanishes, the glued shape can be deformed into a true smooth structure. The result extends a classic theorem and yields new families of such spaces.
arxiv-2509-16157:
In crypto markets where traders swap tokens through pooled funds, some actors add funds for a single swap and pull them out at once to grab fees. Bruno Llacer Trotti and four co-authors give the first formal, trade-level model of this just-in-time tactic for focused-range pools. They map how prices move and fees split, then solve for the best tactic such an actor can use.

Fitted to real pools, actual actors fall well short of the best tactic, mostly since they ignore price impact. Clever use of the tactic cuts trader costs but can cut passive funders' profits a lot per trade.
arxiv-2509-16457:
Crowd simulations driven by language agents can drift far from how real people act, a gap the authors call behavior-realism. Yunzhe Wang and three co-authors frame the fix as matching distributions: behavior flows from a person and their setting, so agent personas should be tuned until group behavior matches expert benchmarks. Their optimizer rewrites personas step by step toward that match.

In an active shooter drill simulation, divergence from the benchmark fell by most of its value versus no steering. Tuned personas also carried to new, related scenes. More faithful drills could sharpen training for rare, high-stakes events.
arxiv-2509-16557:
Muhammad Hamza, Danish Hamid, and Muhammad Tahir Akram build a way to tell who is who from hand motion in a 2025 paper. Their setting is video shot from the user's own view, as in smart glasses. The system watches how hands grasp and move objects. Such clues could support help tools in cockpits, repair work, and surgery.

Their system, named I2S, works in stages and reads three-dimensional hand pose. It links object use to the person doing it, with no extra sensors on the body. Tests show strong scores with a tiny model. It runs fast enough for live use on a device. That mix suits security tasks where quick checks matter.
arxiv-2509-16857:
Xingyu Xiang and co-authors speed long-context language model serving in a 2025 systems paper. Servers reuse cached data for shared text prefixes, which saves work. Fetching that cache across machines can clog limited network links, though. Their system, ShadowServe, fetches cache without getting in the way of live work.

A smart network card handles the fetching. A chunked pipeline spreads work across the card's small processors. A low-copy memory scheme eases pressure on the card. Tests show much lower delay per output token than prior systems. Time to first token also fell. Higher throughput means cheaper serving for long chats.
arxiv-2509-17057:
Masaki Murooka and co-authors release a unified framework for robot manipulation learning in a 2025 paper. Imitation learning teaches robots from human demonstrations. Research code for it is often scattered across data collection, training, and rollout tools. Their open framework, RoboManipBaselines, covers that whole pipeline in one place.

It works across both simulated and real robots. Teams can collect data, train a policy, and test it under one roof. The authors report results showing it forms a useful research base. A shared, open pipeline should make results easier to compare and reproduce across labs working on robot hands and arms.
arxiv-2509-17157:
Anu Sreedevi and four co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper about dark magnetic patches that emerge on the surface of the Sun. These paired regions show the Sun's inner magnetic field reaching the surface. New software can find and track them on its own, but it often spots a region only after the region has already emerged.

The team adds a module to the AutoTAB tracker that walks each new region back in time to its birth. Of about twelve thousand regions, the module traced just over three thousand to their start. Two groups stood out: regions whose flux grew as expected, and regions with no clear growth, most likely missed at birth. The second group shows no clean tilt pattern, so the authors warn that mixing it into tilt studies can hide real trends.
arxiv-2509-17357:
Yunzhao Liu, Qiang Xu, and Y. Charlie Hu built a system that serves large language models on mixed GPU clusters. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a common setup: firms own GPUs of several ages, and the newest cards sit beside older ones. Splitting the prompt phase from the reply phase across cards sounds clean, but raw splits often mismatch card strength and workload.

Their system, Cronus, splits each prompt phase itself. The weaker card runs the first slice of the prompt work, while the stronger card overlaps the rest with replies to earlier requests. Tests across many pairings of high-end and low-end cards show clear gains in throughput over full splits. Long waits for first tokens and between tokens also fell sharply next to standard parallel setups. Cronus suits on-premise clusters that cannot simply buy uniform hardware.
arxiv-2509-17457:
Paweł Jakub Borsukiewicz, Jordan Samhi, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé map which parts of a face drive recognition systems. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that face recognition is widespread and raises sharp privacy risks. Most defenses use one generic trick for every face, yet each face has its own traits, which limits how well those defenses work and how discreet they stay.

Their technique, LEAM, scores which facial areas matter most for a given person. It is an explainability tool, not an attack: it aims to show how the systems work, which could guide later privacy research. Joined with a face parser, LEAM was run on a thousand people across nine trained recognition models. Layers inside one model differ in where they look. Across models, though, the same person tends to light up the same regions, far more than distinct people do.
arxiv-2509-17657:
Ian Kemp, Steven J Tingay, Stuart Midgley, and Daniel Mitchell report on commercial supercomputing for radio astronomy. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a market shift. Commercial high-performance systems now outgun the machines Australian radio astronomy relies on. One even exceeds what the Square Kilometre Array's science processors are expected to need.

The authors surveyed scientists and providers with commercial HPC experience in astronomy and kindred data-heavy fields, through semi-structured interviews. They add lessons from two earlier case studies with very different data and processing demands. A thematic analysis pulls the key messages out of the interviews. Commercial systems offer real advantages in access and scale, the study finds, alongside new risks in cost and control. The paper gives observatories a grounded brief for deciding what to rent, what to own, and what to keep in-house.
arxiv-2509-17957:
David Hyland and Mahault Albarracin argue that mental bias can be a sane reply to the cost of change. Their 2025 paper notes that folk defend dear beliefs, bend facts to fit a tale, and pick what facts to seek. Such habits break the neat rules for how beliefs should update.

Their frame treats each belief update as a choice with a price. The price of a new belief is scored by how far it sits from the old one, weighed against its use. Sim runs of the plain model mimic known habits, such as favouring facts that agree with us. Split views in a group also emerge.
arxiv-2509-18057:
Ansh Nagda, Prabhakar Raghavan, and Abhradeep Thakurta use an AI code agent to push hard limits in complexity theory. Their 2025 paper asks if AI tools can help prove new bounds on how well hard tasks can be approximated. The agent, AlphaEvolve, mutates code to search for fresh constructions.

With its help, the team sharpens bounds for graph cut tasks on random regular graphs. New hard cases for two cut variants rest on gadgets the agent found. A route task, the travelling salesman problem, also gets a stronger hard bound. Some results still trail the best known, and the paper says so plainly.
arxiv-2509-18457:
Forecasting blood sugar is hard, and a model must keep learning as new patient groups arrive. Ebrahim Farahmand and 11 co-authors present GluMind, a transformer model for long-term glucose forecasts across varied populations. Their 2025 paper joins sugar data with signals like activity, stress, and heart rate. Two attention designs run side by side to read those mixed signals.

One design links the sugar stream with the other body signals, even when they sample at different rates. The other reads patterns across long time spans. A knowledge retention module fights the loss of old skills when new data arrives, a known flaw called catastrophic forgetting. Tests used a fresh data set covering healthy people, prediabetes, and type 2 diabetes. GluMind beat top rival models on both error measures used. Its gains held as new patient cohorts were added.
arxiv-2509-18657:
A histogram sums data into bars, and a matching curve should keep the total area of those bars. Aiswarya T and Srijanani Anurag Prasad build such curves with fractal methods in this 2025 paper. Classic fractal interpolation gives smooth, continuous curves that pass through set points. Histopolation is different: the curve must preserve area, not height at points.

Their construction uses an iterated function system built on a generalized contraction idea. The result is a bounded curve that can be integrated, though it need not be continuous. Unlike older versions, their scaling factors may exceed one, which widens the shapes available. They derive the conditions under which the curve truly solves the histopolation problem. The paper extends the theory of fractal functions to a nonlinear setting. It is a proof-driven contribution aimed at approximation theory.
arxiv-2509-18757:
Teaching robots by demonstration needs lots of examples, and handheld grippers make collecting them cheap and portable. Omar Rayyan, John Abanes, Mahmoud Hafez, Anthony Tzes, and Fares Abu-Dakka present MV-UMI, a multi-view upgrade to that idea, in this 2025 paper. Wrist cameras alone miss the wider scene. That gap also widens the shift between human demos and robot use.

MV-UMI adds a third-person camera beside the gripper's own view. The extra angle captures scene context that a wrist view cannot. Tests, including an ablation study, show clear gains on sub-tasks that need broad scene understanding. Success there rose by about 47 percent across three tasks. The gains came without losing the cross-robot portability that makes handheld collection attractive. The authors pitch the system as a scalable way to gather richer demonstrations.
arxiv-2509-19057:
Turning free text from medical papers into tidy graph data is the goal of a system built by Olawumi Olasunkanmi and five co-authors. Biomedical knowledge graphs support drug discovery and clinical tools, but they stay incomplete. Large language models can pull relations out of abstracts, yet their raw outputs use loose wording that graphs cannot take. Their system, RELATE, fixes that in three stages.

First it readies a standard ontology, the Biolink Model, with embeddings for each approved relation type. Next it retrieves close matches for each extracted relation, helped by a biomedical language tool called SapBERT. A language model then reranks the matches, with special care for negated claims. On a standard benchmark the system matched the exact relation about half the time and placed the right answer in its top ten nearly always. On thousands of project abstracts it correctly rejected almost all junk links.
arxiv-2509-19357:
Many algebra students assume an inverse operation always returns the positive root, a mistake Meliksah Yorulmazlar names the inverse function fallacy. The sign of a root is fixed by the function's domain, a detail students overlook. Yorulmazlar proposes the Inverse Function Point method, which anchors the sign choice to one domain-based reference point, making the decision systematic rather than guessed. The paper reports a classroom study at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.

Of 69 STEM students, only nineteen percent solved a sign-determination problem correctly on the first try. The author re-tested forty of those who missed it, after teaching the method. Accuracy in that group rose to eighty percent. The jump suggests the fallacy is a gap in assumed knowledge, not ability. Simple, intuitive procedures, the author argues, can repair fragile fundamentals.
arxiv-2509-19557:
Matching records that name the same product or firm is a quiet backbone of data work. Iris Kamsteeg and five co-authors test how much trust to place in a language model's confidence when it makes those matches. They compare raw confidence from a tuned RoBERTa model against three fixes: temperature scaling, random dropout sampling, and ensembles. Four public data sets cover products, papers, music, and firms.

The tuned model proved a bit overconfident across the sets. A simple temperature tweak cut the confidence error by up to about a quarter. The authors report exact error scores per set so others can judge the gains. Calibrated confidence matters when matches feed billing, catalogs, or research records. A model that knows when it is unsure is easier to deploy with human checks.
arxiv-2509-19957:
Retinal implants give blind users a field of bright spots called phosphenes, a crude sketch of the world. Eleftherios Papadopoulos and Yagmur Güçlütürk ask users what such a sketch should draw. Interviews with visually impaired people yielded design principles. A gaze-controlled system then segments scenes with the Segment Anything Model, highlighting what the user looks at.

In a simulated phosphene display, participants identified objects under three conditions: the new system, plain edge detection, and normal vision. The segmentation approach beat edge detection clearly. User guidance shaped the algorithm from the start rather than grading it at the end. Prosthetic vision research often optimizes images sighted engineers find clear. This study lets the intended users steer.
arxiv-2509-20157:
Ahmad Mohamadnejad wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on gravitational waves from the early universe. It studies scale-invariant models, theories whose basic laws contain no built-in mass scale. At high temperature, the vacuum state of such a model can decay through a first-order phase transition. That decay would fill space with a background hum of gravitational waves.

Mohamadnejad builds the effective potential step by step, adding quantum and thermal corrections. He computes the key transition values, including its strength and duration. The decay turns out to be dominated by sphaleron transitions rather than quantum tunneling. He then computes the full wave spectrum from bubble collisions, sound waves, and turbulence. A broad scan finds two regimes: one audible to pulsar timing arrays, the other aimed at the future LISA space mission.
arxiv-2509-20257:
Carlos Cabezas-Moreno, Yingxiang Hu, and Mohammad Ivaki settle a conjectured inequality in a 2025 arXiv paper on convex geometry. The classical Blaschke-Santalo inequality bounds the volume product of a convex body and its polar dual. A capillary version extends the question to hypersurfaces that meet a boundary at a fixed contact angle. The extension had remained a conjecture.

The authors prove the capillary inequality for a wide class of surfaces. The class covers unconditional, strictly convex capillary hypersurfaces whose contact angle is acute, below a right angle. For obtuse contact angles, the story flips. There, they show the capillary volume product has no finite upper bound at all. The pair of results draws a sharp line at the right angle between the two regimes.
arxiv-2509-20557:
Machine translation for Sinitic languages lacks the error-labeled data that quality research needs. Hannah Liu and fourteen co-authors fill that gap with SiniticMTError, a dataset described in a 2025 arXiv paper. It annotates machine-translated examples from English into Mandarin, Cantonese, and Wu Chinese. A Mandarin-to-Hokkien part comes from a non-parallel source.

Each example carries the error span, the error type, and a severity judgment. Native speakers produced the annotations through pilot rounds and iterative feedback, and the authors analyze the patterns that emerged. The dataset supports training models that detect their own translation errors, estimate quality, and evaluate low-resource languages. Baseline tests with leading language models showed weak precision on error detection. That shortfall, the authors argue, is exactly why such a resource was needed.
arxiv-2509-20957:
Language models become far more useful when they can call external tools, but training data for that skill is mostly English. Asim Ersoy and three co-authors study tool calling for Arabic in a 2025 paper. They ask what kind of data Arabic tool calling actually needs.

Three questions guide the study. Does in-language Arabic data beat cross-lingual transfer from English? How does general instruction tuning affect tool-calling skill? Does fine-tuning on a few high-priority tools pay off? The authors run extensive experiments with base and tuned variants of an open model. Their answers inform how to extend tool use to other under-resourced languages, where simply reusing English data may not suffice.
arxiv-2509-21057:
Watermarking a language model's output at the level of whole sentences resists paraphrase attacks, but earlier methods distorted the text. Jiahao Huo and seven co-authors present PMark in a 2025 paper accepted as an ICLR 2026 poster. Their goal is semantic-level watermarking that is robust and distortion-free.

The theory rests on proxy functions, which map each sentence to a single number. PMark estimates the median of that proxy for the next sentence by sampling, while respecting channel constraints during generation. Reject-sampling methods warp the output distribution; PMark is designed to avoid that. Robustness gains strong theoretical backing in their framework. Invisible, provable marks on generated text matter for tracing AI content at scale.
arxiv-2509-21257:
Seyed Amir Kasaei and Mohammad Hossein Rohban wrote a 2025 paper on hallucination in text to image models. In language models, hallucination means content from prior bias rather than from the input. For image models, past scores check if prompt items appear. They miss what the model adds beyond the prompt. The authors argue that those additions should count as hallucination too.

They define hallucination for image models as bias driven deviation from the prompt. They sort it into three types: attribute, relation, and object hallucination. This framing sets an upper bound for evaluation. It also brings hidden biases to the surface. The paper offers a base for richer tests of image models beyond simple prompt alignment.
arxiv-2509-21457:
Bubbles in a cooling liquid grow and merge over time in a pattern called coarsening. Parameshwaran A and Bhaskar Sen Gupta study that process with molecular dynamics in a 2025 paper. A hot Lennard-Jones fluid is quenched below its critical temperature. Vapor bubbles nucleate inside the dense liquid. Large scale simulations track the structural evolution in detail.

Correlation functions and the structure factor both show dynamic scaling and sharp interfaces. The characteristic length grows as a power law in time. Finite size scaling gives an exponent near one. That value shows coarsening is dominated by viscous hydrodynamic interactions. Classical diffusion limited ripening, described by Lifshitz Slyozov Wagner theory, does not govern here. The results give atomistic evidence for the viscous growth law.
arxiv-2509-21557:
Citations can be written while a model generates an answer, or attached after drafting. Yash Saxena and 3 co-authors compare those two attribution paradigms in a 2025 paper. High stakes domains like health, law, and finance need human verifiable sources. Making time citation produces answer and citations in one pass. Post hoc citation adds or verifies citations after the answer exists.

Scoring spans zero shot to advanced lookup augmented methods across four attribution data sets. A steady trade off appears between coverage and citation correctness. Lookup quality is the main driver of attribution quality in both paradigms. The authors give evidence based recommendations weighing trade offs by use case. Trustworthy attribution, they argue, depends more on lookup than on citation timing.
arxiv-2509-21857:
Chinmoy Nath Saha and four co-authors report a powerful new electronic switch in this 2025 device paper. The device is a vertical trench diode made from beta-phase gallium oxide, a material prized for handling high voltages. Its fins are narrower than a micron, and a layered insulating stack helps spread the electric field, an effect called RESURF, while a field plate guards the edges.

Both fin widths tested gave strong forward performance, with low resistance and a huge ratio between on and off current. A self-aligned printing and etch-back process exposed the fin tops for contacts, avoiding hard alignment steps at such small scales. The diode held off more than two thousand volts before breaking down, with very low leakage. Simulations traced the limit to the insulating layer at the trench corner, and showed the design keeps the junction field low.
arxiv-2509-22357:
Last-mile delivery can cut its emissions if customers help with the last step. Valentina Bonomi and 3 co-authors build a two-level routing model that plans depot sites, truck routes, and pick-up choices at once. The model counts how customers travel, what mix of vehicles firms run, and how much each leg pollutes.

The team solved the model for real-world based cases under four plans. A case study with a large Portuguese delivery firm showed clear trade-offs. Plans that cut distance alone could raise emissions a lot. Plans that cut emissions used customer travel well and kept service fast. A joint view of cost and emissions gave balanced options.
arxiv-2509-22657:
