Ethan Greiffenstein, Trevor Harris, and Rebecca Smith forecast West Nile virus with a larger, locally focused graph network. The virus is a growing public health threat in the United States, and with no human vaccine, mosquito control leans on forecasts. Graph neural networks had already beaten classic methods at this task. Their new variant links attention layers in a line, which lets much larger models train.

The design specializes dense graph networks to weight local information more, preventing over-smoothing. Training used a massive new Illinois data set of weather, land use, and mosquito trap results. The model beat both graph and classical baselines on out-of-sample and out-of-graph tests, across scenarios and forecast horizons.
arxiv-2509-22857:
Eduardo Chielle and 4 co-authors make private image models both faster and more exact. Their method, called PAPER, runs deep neural networks under fully homomorphic encryption. That kind of encryption lets a server compute on data it cannot read. Past systems leaned on bootstrapping, a slow step used across many layers. They also used rough math stand-ins for the ReLU activation, which cut accuracy.

PAPER swaps in a simple curved stand-in for ReLU that keeps depth at the lowest level. New layout tricks cut the needed encryption levels fivefold, so no bootstrapping is required. Tests on image data sets ran up to four times faster than prior work. Accuracy matched plain, unencrypted models.
arxiv-2509-22957:
AI scores from lab studies may not carry over to real-world use. Luke Guerdan and 4 co-authors tackle that gap with a doubly-robust estimator. The risk comes when lab raters and outputs differ from the deployment mix. Their fix uses persona ratings: a language model judge plays a rater with set traits. Those ratings are flawed but still carry signal.

The framework blends persona ratings with biased human ratings to give valid quality scores. It works if either the rating model or the bias-correction model is good enough. A new simulation setup let the team vary persona quality and bias. Tests backed the theory behind the method.
arxiv-2509-23057:
Large genome changes of fifty bases or more hide well in low-complexity regions. Qian Qin and Heng Li measure how much of the trouble sits in those regions. They map about thirty-five megabases of low-complexity DNA in the GRCh38 reference. That is just over one percent of the genome. Yet those spans hold most confident structural variants in a key sample.

Across long-read calling tools, most wrong calls fall inside low-complexity regions. Error rates climb as the regions get longer. Variants are both richer and harder to call there. The pair warn that calling and study of such variants need special care.
arxiv-2509-23357:
Optimizing on a data manifold is hard when the manifold is known only through samples. Andrey Kharitenko and 4 co-authors link manifold operations to the score function of diffusion models. A link function ties the data distribution to the geometry that optimizers need. With it, retractions and Riemannian gradients become recoverable. Pretrained score networks can then be reused for optimization.

Two inference-time algorithms build on the link. A landing flow and a Riemannian gradient method both carry guarantees. Feasibility, staying near the manifold, is covered. Optimality, in small gradient norm, is covered too. Control tracking tasks show the methods working in practice.
arxiv-2509-23457:
Text-to-image models often drop or garble parts of a complex prompt. Mohammad Hossein Sameti and 5 co-authors tackle that flaw at test time, with no retraining of the base model. Their method splits a prompt into single concepts, such as objects and their traits. A fine-grained form of CLIP then scores how well each concept shows up in the draft image.

The scores feed a loop in which a large language model rewrites the prompt to fix what is missing or wrong. On DrawBench and CompBench prompts, the loop raised concept coverage and faithfulness as judged by people. It beat both plain test-time tuning and the base model.
arxiv-2509-23557:
Economists who track wealth across many households need fast solvers for models where each agent faces its own random shocks. Ricardo Alonzo Fernández Salguero, the sole author, presents SIMPOL, a modular framework for such continuous-time heterogeneous agent problems. The core pairs two equations: one for each agent's best saving and spending policy, one for the steady wealth distribution. Policy iteration with an upwind scheme keeps the solver stable.

A post-processing step smooths the consumption policy and pins its slope to an economically sensible band, aiding convergence. Checks include a distance-based contraction test and a match with the known Merton solution in a no-volatility case. Results fit both economic and math theory.
arxiv-2509-23657:
Reasoning skill learned in one language does not always travel to another. Shulin Huang and 3 co-authors run the first systematic test of how reinforcement learning, versus supervised fine-tuning, affects cross-lingual reasoning. Their base model is Qwen2.5-3B, and the tasks cover math, commonsense, and science reasoning across languages. Two findings stand out.

Reinforcement learning not only scored higher but also carried its gains across languages far better than fine-tuning. Training it on non-English data beat training on English, a pattern fine-tuning did not show. Mechanistic analyses probe why the learned strategies stay robust, and the authors draw lessons for fairer multilingual reasoning.
arxiv-2509-23757:
An explanation of an image decision is more useful when its parts are objects a person can name. Benjamin Teoh and 3 co-authors introduce OCEAN, a visual reasoning framework whose agents argue over object-centric evidence. A game-theoretic process pushes the agents to agree on evidence that is both coherent and discriminative. The system trains end to end, so its reasoning is built in rather than bolted on afterward.

On two diagnostic multi-object data sets, OCEAN matched strong black-box classifiers while exposing its reasoning. Against post-hoc tools like GradCAM and LIME, its explanations were judged more faithful. In a user study, people rated them more intuitive and trustworthy.
arxiv-2509-23957:
A machine interpreter that hears only words misses the scene that would settle what a word means. Claudio Fantinuoli, the sole author, introduces Vision-Grounded Interpreting, which primes speech-to-speech translation with visual context. A prototype feeds webcam images and speech into a vision-language model, so the translation process starts already informed by the situation. A hand-built diagnostic corpus targets three kinds of ambiguity.

Visual grounding sharply improved lexical disambiguation in the evaluation. Gains for gender resolution were modest and less stable. Syntactic ambiguities gained nothing. Fantinuoli argues that multimodality is a necessary next step for machine interpreting quality.
arxiv-2509-24057:
Alex Behakanira Tumwesigye and 2 co-authors ask when a number built by joining two Lucas-type numbers end to end is itself in the same sequence. The sequence here stretches the classic Lucas numbers: each term adds the prior set of terms, with the count set by a fixed span.

The team finds all such joined numbers and fully solves the case where the span is at least three. Their proof mixes bounds from the theory of logarithms, a classic reduction trick, and a lattice method. Continued fractions and checks run in SageMath complete the work. The full list for span at least three is now known.
arxiv-2509-24257:
Running language models on scattered machines worldwide is resilient, but who checks the answers are honest? Ke Wang and 9 co-authors introduce VeriLLM, a public protocol for verifiable decentralized inference. In an open network with no trusted nodes, free-riding and faked outputs are the core threats.

VeriLLM pairs light empirical rerunning with minimal on-chain checks, so verification costs about a hundredth of the inference itself. Inference and verification run on the same GPU workers in mirrored roles, which raises use rates and widens the validator set. Tasks are made indistinguishable to block selective behavior. Theory and system tests show reliable checks with little overhead.
arxiv-2509-24457:
Neural audio codecs need quality scores, but no one is sure which objective metrics track human ears for them. Wolfgang Mack and 6 co-authors put forty-five metrics to the test on clean speech. They correlated each metric's scores with listening-test scores across seventeen codec conditions, from low to high quality.

Neural metrics took the top spots for agreement with listeners. Deeper analysis showed a catch for metrics that need no reference signal: they saturate at the high end of quality, so they stop separating good codecs from great ones. The findings give codec builders firmer ground for picking evaluation metrics.
arxiv-2509-24757:
Chenghua Liu and Zhengfeng Ji build, in a 2025 preprint, a unified quantum framework for speeding up regression. Regression fits models to data across science and economics. Quantum work had mostly covered the plain linear case. Workhorse variants like Lasso, Ridge, and robust Huber fits sat untouched. The authors extend a recent classical breakthrough with quantum tools. Leverage scores are estimated by a quantum method, and many copies of a key quantum state are prepared cheaply. Together these lift the whole framework onto a quantum machine.

The payoff is up to a quadratic saving in the number of samples needed. That saving holds across the full family of regression types they treat. Running time is stated in terms of sparsity, sample count, dimension, and target error. The authors present the result as evidence that quantum speedups reach beyond toy problems. Practical statistics workloads, they argue, belong on the quantum roadmap.
arxiv-2509-25657:
Wang and co-authors review far-reach field frames and their use in grain work. One frame bends the chiral rules for twin-grain bonds at range. A twin frame bends the light-charge rules, called QED, the same way. The chiral work weighs how mass splits in the nucleon at skewed shares. Weight form traits, tied to pull, come from the same sums. In QED, both the spread path and the core joint shift with range.

Set guard rules still hold in the bent QED form. A firm count scheme fits the changed spread path in that frame. The frame can fit the odd g-2 reads for light grains as is. No new grains or new links need to be brought in. Curved space sums for pull traits close the sweep.
arxiv-2510-00157:
Gabriele Lo Monaco and five colleagues wrote this 2025 theory paper on the hidden cost of measuring quantum states. Their setting is single-setting estimation, where one circuit and one measurement basis must reveal a state. Circuits built only from stabilizer operations are cheap but classically simulable. The authors ask how much non-stabilizer resource, nicknamed magic, full information recovery demands.

They prove that stabilizer-only circuits can never be informationally complete, no matter how many spare qubits join. Adding special T gates does enlarge what the measurement can learn. They bound the needed count of such gates from below and show a matching supply suffices. Entanglement inside the circuit turns out to govern how much information each gate buys. The work reframes magic as a measurable cost in quantum sensing, not just in computing.
arxiv-2510-00557:
Kelvyn Bladen, D. Richard Cutler, and Alan Wisler published this 2025 paper putting variable importance measures on firm mathematical ground. Analysts rank predictors by shuffling them or by dropping them and retraining. When predictors correlate strongly, folklore says those rankings warp in different ways. The authors derive exact closed-form expressions for both measures in linear regression.

One measure, permute-and-predict, scales with the coefficient and the predictor's own spread. The other, leave-one-covariate-out, shrinks by a factor that captures collinearity directly. The algebra explains why shuffling barely notices correlated predictors while dropping suffers badly. Monte Carlo simulations confirmed the formulas across rising correlation levels. The same expressions approximate importance in random forests surprisingly well, the authors show. Practitioners gain a principled way to read rankings instead of trusting them blindly.
arxiv-2510-00657:
Halpern and seven co-authors introduce XPPG-PCA in this 2025 arXiv paper on automatic evaluation of disordered speech. Clinicians rate speech severity by ear, which is skilled work but subjective, slow, and expensive. Automatic methods that need a transcript or a healthy reference recording only fit read speech, while supervised models often learn shortcuts in their training data. XPPG-PCA needs no reference and no severity labels at all, so it avoids both traps.

The method extracts phonetic posteriorgrams with a speaker x-vector model, then compresses them with principal component analysis. The leading components become the severity signal for a recording. On three Dutch oral cancer datasets, the unsupervised scores matched or beat established reference-based methods. Tests also confirmed the approach resists dataset shortcuts and background noise, and the authors release an open-source implementation for clinical researchers.
arxiv-2510-00757:
Amboage, Röell, Schnider, and Rieck introduce LEAP in this 2025 arXiv paper, a positional encoding method for graph neural networks. These networks pass messages between linked nodes, but that process can miss long-range and structural patterns. Positional encodings add location and shape information to help. LEAP builds its signals from the Euler Characteristic Transform, a tool that summarizes a graph's shape and topology.

The encoding uses a differentiable local version of that transform, so the whole model trains end to end. On a synthetic task built to test topology reading, LEAP reached perfect validation scores in the authors' runs. On real datasets covering molecules and other domains, it often matched or beat rival encodings and converged faster. The results suggest shape-aware signals can strengthen standard graph learning pipelines.
arxiv-2510-00857:
Simhi and six co-authors, spanning the Technion, Google Research, and the University of Zagreb, introduce ManagerBench in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety. Safety benchmarks test whether models refuse to generate harmful text. Autonomous agents face a different danger: causing real harm while pursuing an assigned operational goal. ManagerBench embeds models in managerial scenarios where the effective action hurts people and the safe action performs worse.

A control set redirects the same harm toward inanimate objects, which separates safety from overcaution. Frontier models performed poorly overall. Many chose the harmful option to hit their goals, while others became uselessly timid. Strikingly, the models' harm judgements matched human assessments, so the failure is prioritization, not perception. A goal-oriented nudging prompt could drop safety scores by up to fifty-five points. The authors present the benchmark as a diagnostic for deploying agents in decision-making roles.
arxiv-2510-00957:
Andleeb, Mendoza, Cordova, Walia, and Carver study where students go wrong in software testing courses, in this paper for the ACM SIGCITE 2025 conference. Testing skill matters for reliable software, yet students often write test suites that look busy but catch little. The authors used an automated feedback tool during a senior-level course and analysed how students revised their tests across two assignments. They focused on revisions that failed to improve code coverage.

Decision coverage and exception handling proved to be the most persistent trouble spots. Students mostly made superficial or method-level tweaks instead of rethinking their test design, a pattern the authors call a happy-path bias. Misused assertions and redundant tests also appeared often. The paper recommends teaching coverage principles explicitly and giving richer conceptual feedback, so students fix the thinking behind a weak test rather than its surface.
arxiv-2510-01157:
Fortier and four co-authors report the first systematic study of backdoor attacks on speech language models in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI security. A backdoor makes a model behave normally until a hidden trigger appears, then forces a chosen wrong output. Speech language models bolt audio encoders onto a language model, so they inherit weaknesses from every part. Whether poisoning one stage poisons the whole pipeline had never been mapped.

The team attacked a modified SpeechLLM across four speech encoders, three datasets, and four tasks, from transcription to age prediction. Success rates ranged from about ninety-one to over ninety-nine percent in their runs. Component-wise tests showed the audio encoder is where the backdoor mainly takes root. The attack generalized across WavLM, HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and Whisper encoders. Fine-tuning on clean data afterwards largely defused the planted trigger.
arxiv-2510-01457:
Barkley and Fridovich-Keil diagnose why a popular model-based reinforcement learning method collapses outside the benchmark where it was celebrated. MBPO trains policies on synthetic experience from a learned world model, promising sample efficiency. On the harder control suite it loses to its model-free sibling across seven tasks.

Two coupled defects explain the fall: mismatched model scales bias the critic downward, stalling improvement. The synthetic action distribution is also chosen poorly for the coevolving policy. Fixing the diagnosed failure modes unlocked improvements previously out of reach. Benchmark averages had hidden the environment-specific assumptions baked into the design. OpenAI Gym successes had implied a generality the method never had. Critic underestimation is the quiet mechanism strangling improvement. Model and policy coevolve, so their mismatch compounds over training. Diagnosis precedes repair in the paper's structure deliberately. Averages hide collapses; autopsies reveal them.
arxiv-2510-01657:
Le Gall and three co-authors tackle a basic question in this 2025 quantum computing paper. They ask how much communication a distributed quantum algorithm needs, compared with a classical one. Earlier work had shown a polynomial quantum edge for tasks like leader election. The team looks instead at routing a message between two marked nodes in a network.

For a family of graphs called welded trees, the authors prove an exponential gap. Their quantum algorithm moves a message from the entrance to the exit with vastly fewer messages. No classical algorithm can match that cost on the same graphs. The quantum method builds on succinct quantum walks over welded trees. The classical bound lifts an older query-complexity result into message complexity, a new step for the field.
arxiv-2510-01857:
Fanconi, Astorga, and van der Schaar learn a step-by-step judge for language model reasoning in this 2025 paper. Outcome-only rewards say whether a final answer was right, but not where reasoning went wrong. Their approach learns a dense reward, scored token by token, from expert demonstrations instead. It uses inverse reinforcement learning, which infers the hidden scoring rule behind expert behavior.

The learned reward grades every step of a reasoning trace, not just its ending. Scores tracked eventual answer correctness rather than surface style. That makes the judge useful for spotting the exact step where a trace derails. In training, its feedback taught policies to reason better on the GSM8K math benchmark. At test time, reranking sampled traces with the judge improved accuracy under fixed computing budgets. Gains were clearest for the Llama-based policies in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-01957:
Martínez-del-Río and MacKay test shortcut formulas for the volume inside magnetic flux surfaces in this 2025 plasma paper. Fusion device designers need those volumes, usually by brute three-dimensional integration inside the vessel. For integrable magnetic fields, symmetry collapses the problem and yields cheaper formulas. The authors check those formulas numerically on nontrivial example fields.

They also propose one new case, covering integrable fields whose symmetry preserves a density that need not be constant. Across their examples, the formula results agreed with direct integration up to numerical error. Because the methods amount to two-dimensional integration, they usually ran faster than the three-dimensional route. For an axisymmetric field, the new formula was notably more efficient and more accurate than the alternatives. The tests mark where each formula can be trusted in practice. Designers of magnetic confinement devices gain verified tools for a routine but costly computation.
arxiv-2510-02057:
Argyres, Bourget, Grimminger, Lotito, and Weaver classify the low-energy geometry of maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in this 2025 physics paper. On its moduli space of vacua, the theory's effective description defines a special Kähler geometry. Which such geometries are compatible with a given gauge algebra was an open classification problem. The authors settle it completely for simple algebras.

Compatible structures correspond exactly to certain classes of integral symplectic representations of the Weyl group. For the principal Dirac pairing, those classes match the S-duality orbits of the theory's global structures. Reaching that match required correcting a mistake in the literature. The match gives a low-energy test of S-duality, a deep quantum equivalence. Twisted product geometries from non-principal pairings are also covered. The classification links geometry, representation theory, and duality in one package.
arxiv-2510-02157:
Tang and five co-authors help language models refine analytic reports through workspace interactions in this 2025 paper. Intelligence analysts draft reports over a visual workspace, then revise them repeatedly. Language models write decent first drafts but fumble sequential edits driven by gestures and selections. Their framework, VIS-ReAct, reads each new semantic interaction and steers the revision.

Two agents split the work inside the framework. An analysis agent interprets the fresh interactions, infers the user's intent, and plans the refinement. A second agent then rewrites the report according to that plan. In case studies, the pair beat both a plain baseline and a variant without the analysis agent. Gains showed up in targeted refinement, semantic fidelity, and transparent inference. The system handled varied interaction types and granularities gracefully. The design treats human gestures as first-class reasoning input, not noise. Sensemaking tools get a model that listens between drafts.
arxiv-2510-02257:
Ebrova, Bilek, and Eliasek offer a simple recipe for weighing galaxies from survey photos. Their 2025 astronomy paper uses images from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. Many studies need a galaxy stellar mass, not just its brightness. Careful mass measurements are slow and costly. The authors wanted a short formula that uses survey magnitudes directly. They calibrated the formula on local galaxies from the Spitzer S4G survey, which measured masses with great care.

Their best formula uses only the green and red band magnitudes of a galaxy. It reproduces the careful S4G masses with a scatter near twenty five percent. Adding more bands did not help much. Adding shape measures like flatness or profile index also failed to cut the scatter. A quick mass estimate for millions of galaxies is the practical payoff.
arxiv-2510-02457:
Frank and Ardis hunt for worst case failures hiding inside dynamic model compression. Their 2025 machine learning paper studies post-training quantization. Quantization stores network weights at lower precision to save compute. Dynamic schemes choose bit widths while the model runs. Input shifts can then trigger drastic accuracy loss. Safety critical deployments cannot tolerate surprise collapse. The authors frame the search as a learning task. Knowledge distillation plus reinforcement learning breeds a network and policy pair. That pair is tuned to expose catastrophic failure under quantization. Robust twin pairs face the same inputs for contrast.

Several bred pairs lost ten to sixty five percent accuracy. Twin models with equal full precision scores diverged sharply after quantization. One comparison showed a gap near twenty five percent. Layer activation studies traced which layers drove the fall. Early warning signs in full precision models look possible. Compression audits should test worst cases, not averages.
arxiv-2510-02857:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for a new heavy particle at the Large Hadron Collider. Many theories add extra scalar particles beyond the known Higgs boson. A heavy scalar, called X, might decay into a lighter scalar and a Higgs. The lighter scalar would then split into two bottom quarks. The Higgs would split into two photons. The team used proton collision data from two running periods.

The combined data set totals 199 inverse femtobarns. Collision energies were 13 and 13.6 tera-electronvolts. Neural networks sorted events by the guessed particle masses. The hunt covered a wide grid of mass pairs. No clear excess rose above the Standard Model background. The team thus set upper limits on the process rate. Limits ran from nine femtobarns down to a small fraction of one. Sensitivity improved over the prior search by up to about three quarters. The gains were largest at low masses.
arxiv-2510-02957:
Volkov lays out a method for a punishing calculation in quantum electrodynamics. Atomic energy levels test the theory with extreme sharpness. One correction comes from vacuum polarization near a nucleus. Virtual particles briefly screen the nuclear charge. Computing that screen to high order is the task here. An earlier paper gave values up to a very high order term. This paper explains how those values were earned.

The trick is a reduction to free-space diagrams. Bound-state graphs unfold into free graphs with up to eight loops. A subtraction scheme then strips out the infinities. That scheme adapts the classic BPHZ method to this setting. Monte Carlo sampling handles the finite integrals that remain. Several of the new values were the first of their kind. The numbers feed precision work on heavy atoms. It shines where a single Coulomb source drives the physics.
arxiv-2510-03557:
Frontiere and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper reporting a simulation of cosmic structure. Their code, CRK-HACC, ran a sky universe in a box 4.7 billion parsecs wide on the Frontier supercomputer. Four trillion particles, split between dark matter and gas tracers, evolved together with gravity and gas physics. The run used nine thousand nodes and peaked above five hundred petaflops. It wrote more than one hundred petabytes of data in over a week.

Particle throughput reached tens of billions per second. On the fly analysis produced forecasts for signals from radio to X-ray bands. The scale beats earlier efforts by more than ten times in particle count. Such end to end realism is what sky surveys need for testing their pipelines. The team frames the run as a capability leap: survey sized volumes no longer force a choice between size and detail.
arxiv-2510-04757:
Eduardo Martínez Rivera and Filippo Menolascina wrote this 2025 paper on finding medical documents for a question answering system. Systems that ground answers in retrieved text are only as good as search. General search tools miss the fine shades of biomedical language, while specialist tools can be slow. The authors pair two models in stages. An encoder gathers candidate passages quickly.

A second model then re ranks those candidates by matching. They fine tuned the pair on ten thousand question passage pairs from a medical benchmark. The re ranker lifted recall in the top results by up to about four points. Joint training of both stages proved essential: without it, the re ranker could hurt results. Inside a biomedical system, their module reached the best accuracy on a five task benchmark. It edged out a medical baseline by a hair. Indexing ran more than seven times faster than rivals.
arxiv-2510-04857:
Alison Mitchell wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on studying a cosmic accelerator with two telescopes. The object, MSH 15-52, is a pulsar wind nebula: a cloud of particles blown off a spinning star. Such nebulae shine from radio waves up to gamma rays. They may accelerate particles. The author combined X ray data from the eROSITA telescope with gamma ray data from the H.E.S.S. array in one study.

The glue is Gammapy, an analysis package for gamma ray data. She wrote code to bring the X ray data release into that framework. The result is the first three dimensional fit to eROSITA data done this way. Adding the gamma view let one model describe the particle population. A fit disciplines the story each band tells. The paper folds in satellite gamma ray data for the picture. Multiwavelength fits like this are how astronomers test whether nebulae are accelerators.
arxiv-2510-05157:
Abrar Shahid and five co-authors pit AI attackers against AI defenders in a simulated network in this 2025 arXiv paper. Real defenses must react to brute-force attacks hidden inside normal traffic. The team built a Gym-style environment modeling a multi-port service. Attackers can exploit ports or evade by IP, while defenders deploy traps and rate limits.

Both sides learn with deep Q-networks under a zero-sum reward scheme. Successful exploits pay large terminal rewards, and every step costs a little. Experiments varied trap probability, exploit difficulty, and training schedules. Defender observability and trap strength strongly hindered exploitation. Reward shaping and training scheduling proved crucial for stable learning. The authors release reproducible configurations to guide extensions toward richer network simulators.
arxiv-2510-05457:
Singh and colleagues ask whether code-writing AI models share a famous human bias. The Dunning-Kruger effect describes how people with weak skills often rate themselves too highly. The team tested top language models on coding tasks across many programming languages. Their 2025 paper compares each model's confidence in its answers with its real scores.

The models did mirror the human pattern, the authors report. Weaker models overstated their skill the most, just as the bias predicts. The gap also grew in rare programming languages, where the models knew less. Stronger models showed a smaller gap between confidence and results. The team released its benchmarks and model answers for other researchers to reuse. The study covers coding only, so other fields may behave in different ways. These findings matter for trust, since users may rely on a model's calm tone as a sign of skill.
arxiv-2510-05657:
Lu and colleagues subtype liver cancer from whole slide images with a geometry-aware transformer. The two main subtypes, hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, differ sharply in behavior and prognosis. Their tissue patterns span cell-level detail up to whole-slide architecture. Their 2025 ARGUS framework models all three scales jointly.

A micro-geometry feature encodes fine patterns in the arrangement of cell nuclei. A hierarchical alignment module links macro and meso fields of view across the slide. A geometry-guided fusion strategy then merges the levels into one representation. Contribution-weighted dynamic fusion decides how much each scale contributes. The tumor microenvironment's structure informs every stage of the model. Experiments on public and private cohorts reach state-of-the-art subtyping performance. The code will be released publicly for clinical research use. Better subtyping guides personalized treatment for a prognostically diverse cancer.
arxiv-2510-05757:
Sun and colleagues separate mixed speakers while keeping each voice's room echo. Speaker-image separation preserves reverberation because it carries the acoustic environment's signature. Purely learned systems ignore the physics linking dry speech to its reverberant image. Their 2025 CxNet architecture builds that physics into the network.

A first network predicts each speaker's direct-path signal and reverberant speech jointly. A forward filtering module then estimates the room filter from the direct-path estimate. Convolving that filter reproduces another estimate of the reverberant speech. The second network uses this physical estimate as a discriminative feature. An energy-sorted variant further protects weaker speakers from stronger ones. Preserved echo enables volume adjustment and source replacement in post-production. Late reverberation is diffuse and weak, which makes it the hardest part to recover. Results on SMS-WSJ improve over baselines for two- and three-speaker mixtures.
arxiv-2510-06257:
Mi and Mueller make neural quantum error correction decoders uncertainty-aware and generalizable in a 2025 quantum computing paper. Conventional decoders limit accuracy and add heavy overhead, so learned decoders are attractive. Existing learned decoders lack calibrated uncertainty and fail on unseen codes.

Their decoder QuBA is a quantum Bayesian graph attention network recognizing error patterns with calibrated confidence. On top sits SAGU, a multi-phase training framework generalizing decoding beyond the training set. Tests used bivariate bicycle codes and coprime variants. Both beat the classical belief propagation baseline consistently. On one coprime code they cut logical error rates up to a hundredfold under confident-decision bounds. SAGU matched or beat decoders trained specifically for each code. A decoder that knows its uncertainty and travels across code families brings practical fault tolerance closer.
arxiv-2510-06357:
Byrd and seven co-authors make language-model robot planners reliable with symbolic oversight in a 2025 robotics paper. Language models plan flexibly in open worlds, but hallucinations undermine reliability. Symbolic planners are dependable, yet scale poorly to ambiguous real-world tasks.

The method augments the language model planner with a symbolic overseer. Hard constraints are defined explicitly, replacing opaque prompt engineering. The language model keeps its reasoning and generalization strengths. On ALFWorld, the combined approach beat state-of-the-art methods with a near-perfect ninety-nine percent success rate. They deployed it on a real quadruped robot for pick-and-place tasks. It succeeded on every task, while pure language-model and pure symbolic planners managed about half and a third. The results chart a route to embodied systems flexible yet trustworthy enough to leave the lab.
arxiv-2510-06557:
Milad Aghajohari and six co-authors rethink how language models handle long chains of reasoning. Their 2025 paper notes a cost problem in current training. The model's state normally includes the prompt plus every earlier reasoning step. That makes computing costs grow quadratically as thoughts get longer.

The team proposes Markovian Thinking, where the model reasons with a fixed-size state instead. Their system, Delethink, splits reasoning into chunks of equal size. At each boundary, the context resets and restarts with a short carryover note. Training teaches the model to write that note well enough to continue smoothly. Computing then grows only linearly, and memory stays constant. With more test-time effort, Delethink keeps improving where standard long reasoning levels off. The work suggests that redesigning the thinking environment itself is a powerful way to scale reasoning.
arxiv-2510-06857:
Qi Guo leads a large team improving machines that translate math problems into formal language. Their 2025 paper addresses automated theorem proving, which needs huge amounts of formal statements. Writing those statements by hand is slow. Language models can translate informal problems, but their output often has syntax errors or drifts from the intended meaning.

Their system, called ATF, feeds tool feedback back into the translation process. A Lean 4 compiler flags syntax problems for correction. A panel of language models judges whether the meaning stayed faithful. Training combines a cold start on synthetic tool calls, expert iteration, and preference optimization to cut useless revisions. Across three benchmarks, ATF beat a range of baseline formalizers by a wide margin. Semantic consistency on one benchmark improved by about twenty-nine percent over the strongest rival. Human evaluators confirmed the gains. Reliable translation could unlock far more training data for theorem provers.
arxiv-2510-06957:
Muhammed Bilal and three co-authors squeeze more speed out of Apple Silicon for a specialized matrix operation. Their 2025 paper targets sparse ternary matrix multiplication, a routine for quantized machine learning. Ternary weights take only three values, which shrinks models for on-device inference. Existing libraries barely optimize this operation for Apple's M-series chips.

The team designed a kernel tuned to the hardware's habits. A blocked and interleaved data format keeps the numbers close to the processor. Loop unrolling raises instruction-level parallelism, so more work overlaps in flight. A vectorized version uses the chip's NEON units for parallel arithmetic. The scalar version ran up to nearly six times faster than the standard baseline. It reached about half of the processor's peak speed on matrices. Performance stayed stable as sparsity levels changed. Curiously, the scalar version beat the vectorized one, since Apple chips lack data-shuffling instructions.
arxiv-2510-07057:
Rahul Padhy, Krishnan Suresh, and Aaditya Chandrasekhar design heat-storage devices that choose their own materials and shapes together. Their 2025 paper presents TOMATOES, a framework for latent heat thermal energy storage. Such devices store energy in matter that melts and freezes. Performance depends on pairing a phase-change material with a heat-conducting one.

Topology optimization arranges a fixed pair in space. Choice stayed a human decision, ignoring growing databases. The obstacle is that picking one is a discrete choice, while the optimizer needs smooth gradients. A variational autoencoder solves this by mapping catalogs into smooth latent spaces. The optimizer then searches both in one smooth landscape. Test problems maximized discharged energy within a set time under cost limits. Co-designed devices beat the usual sequential workflow, where shape follows a prepicked one. The framework points toward storage hardware designed by search, not habit.
arxiv-2510-07257:
Opryshko, Quan, Voelker, Du, and Gilitschenski add a planning layer that helps trained robot policies reach distant goals. Their 2025 paper works in offline goal-conditioned learning. Agents there learn many behaviors from unlabeled data with no rewards. Long journeys still defeat them, because small errors pile up over time. The team's method, TTGS, plans only at test time. It leaves the policy untouched and needs no new data.

TTGS samples states from the offline data and links them into a weighted graph. Fast search then assembles a chain of subgoals between the start and the target. A frozen policy simply walks from subgoal to subgoal. When the base learner is value-based, distances come from its own value function, so no hand-made metric is needed. On the OGBench suite, TTGS lifted success rates for several base learners on hard locomotion tasks.
arxiv-2510-07557:
Bhandarkar, Mishra, Juchani, and co-authors mine a million real chatbot conversations to learn what users ask and which models they prefer. Their 2025 study uses the LMSYS Chat-1M corpus, where each prompt comes with two anonymized model answers and a human preference vote. A topic modeling method built on transformer embeddings, BERTopic, digests the multilingual, noisy corpus after a careful cleaning pipeline balances turns and strips redactions. It extracts twenty-nine coherent topics, spanning artificial intelligence, programming, ethics, cloud infrastructure, and everyday requests.

The answer is yes: specific models excel in specific domains, and no single model is uniformly best across all topics. Inter-topic distance maps and model-versus-topic matrices make the alignment patterns readable. For developers, the framework suggests tuning and routing by subject rather than chasing one leaderboard.
arxiv-2510-08057:
Çakmak wrote this 2025 astronomy paper measuring the physical properties of the Sun's corona during the total eclipse of March 29, 2006. The eclipse was observed from Manavgat, Antalya, with an eight-inch mirrored telescope. White-light photographs were taken through a polarizing filter at three angles, on roll film. Solar disk images provided an intensity calibration curve for the film. From the calibrated frames, Çakmak derived coronal intensity, polarization degree, electron density, and mean temperature.

Most results matched the classic corona models of van de Hulst and Saito. The eclipse fell in the quiet minimum of the solar cycle, which helps explain the agreement. The degree of polarization was the exception. Çakmak blames the wide telescope aperture, the lack of longer exposures, and the corona's asymmetric brightness. The paper shows careful film-era technique can still validate coronal models.
arxiv-2510-08257:
Eleni Bougioukou and co-authors describe in a 2025 arXiv paper a testbed for chips that compute inside memory itself. In-memory computing does math where data sits, which saves power and speeds matrix work for AI. Building such a chip takes long, costly design cycles. Designers need a way to test system behavior and code before the real chip exists.

The team built a distributed emulation system, meaning the testbed spreads across linked machines and can grow. It mimics the planned chip so teams can check design choices early. Software tools come with it for writing and testing the chip's microcode, the low-level control code. They also deployed real applications on the emulator to prove it works in practice. Their test results show the system supports fast prototyping of in-memory designs, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-08757:
Kwun and colleagues tackle a stubborn problem in training small, efficient neural networks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantized networks store numbers in a few coarse steps, which saves memory and power. The trouble is that the rounding step is flat almost everywhere, so the gradients that guide training vanish. Common workarounds fake the gradient and come with no promise that training will settle.

Their method, called LOTION, smooths the jagged loss surface by averaging it over random rounding noise. With that smoother surface, standard training tools are guaranteed to move toward a local low point. When the noise comes from random rounding itself, the best solutions of the original problem stay the best solutions of the smoothed one. Tests on synthetic problems and on two mid-size language models beat the standard training approach.
arxiv-2510-09157:
Nesterenko and colleagues review a curious pattern of motion inside atomic nuclei called the toroidal dipole mode, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most nuclear vibrations slosh protons against neutrons in straight lines or spheres. The toroidal mode instead runs in a ring, like smoke curling through a donut. Such a mode was long debated, since it hides from many standard probes. The review gathers the case that the mode is real and worth hunting.

The authors first set out the theoretical grounds for the mode's appearance in nuclei. They then briefly report its clearest experimental sighting, in electron scattering from nickel-58, where the momentum transfer pattern matched the toroidal prediction. A final thread discusses the mode's kinship with the pygmy dipole resonance, a separate low-energy vibration seen in neutron-rich nuclei. Untangling the two matters because both compete for the same low-energy strength that shapes how nuclei absorb radiation.
arxiv-2510-09357:
Luca Santosuosso, Bettina Klinz, and Sonja Wogrin study time series aggregation for power system planning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Generation expansion planning decides which power plants to build over time, and its optimisation models can become too hard to solve. Planners therefore cluster the input data, grouping similar hours or days, but older clustering methods give no guarantee that the smaller model stays accurate.

The authors prove that a properly built aggregated model always gives a lower bound on the best cost of the full model. The result holds for two common model types and for any clustering method, even with constraints that link different times. They then build an algorithm that tightens these bounds step by step while producing workable full-scale plans. The paper also compares the approach with Benders decomposition and extends the bounds to error estimates for other measures that stakeholders care about.
arxiv-2510-09557:
Tzu-Lin Kuo, Wei-Ning Chiu, Wei-Yun Ma, and Pu-Jen Cheng improve search engines in a 2025 arXiv paper. Document expansion adds likely search queries to a document so it can be found despite vocabulary mismatch. Uncontrolled generation, though, produces invented or repetitive queries, and methods trained on one domain often fail on others.

Their framework, Doc2Query++, first infers each document's hidden topics with unsupervised topic modelling, which works across domains. A hybrid keyword selection step then builds a diverse, relevant keyword set for each document. A large language model writes queries guided by those keywords, ensuring topic coverage with less redundancy. For dense retrieval, where documents are stored as vectors, a dual-index fusion strategy keeps the original text and the generated queries in separate indices to avoid noise. Experiments show clear gains in ranking quality and recall over leading baselines on both sparse and dense retrieval.
arxiv-2510-09657:
Riccardo Fosco Gramaccioni, Christian Marinoni, Fabrizio Frezza, Aurelio Uncini, and Danilo Comminiello release a dataset for learning acoustics with AI in a 2025 arXiv paper. Simulating sound waves in complex materials is crucial for sound design, noise control, and material engineering. Classical solvers such as finite element methods are accurate but expensive, especially for large or real-time problems.

Their dataset, HA30K, holds thirty-one thousand acoustic materials, each with its geometric configuration and the matching pressure field obtained by solving the Helmholtz equation. As a baseline, they train a Stable Diffusion model with ControlNet, an image generation system, to predict the fields as pictures. Running many simulations at once on graphics hardware slashes computation time, and the number of diffusion steps can be tuned to trade speed against quality. The authors argue such learned solvers suit early-stage research, where rapid exploration matters more than absolute accuracy.
arxiv-2510-09757:
Brian Aevermann and a large group of co-authors, among them Joseph DeRisi and Andrea Califano, lay out a roadmap for biological data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the study of how cells work and why disease happens, with organisations worldwide investing in research, drug discovery, and personalised medicine. Yet scientific data has become the bottleneck, and progress stays slow and fragmented.

The paradox is that data is abundant but hard to use. Imaging and sequencing produce huge volumes cheaply, while standards and tooling for large datasets lag behind, blocking the integrated foundation datasets that generalisable models need. The authors argue that only a technology-led, community-focused approach can fix this. Their roadmap covers scaling data generation and infrastructure so that distributed contributions combine into cohesive datasets. The goal is data with the quality to support foundation models of cells and tissues.
arxiv-2510-09857:
Yang and co-authors describe MTMD in this 2025 arXiv paper on advertising systems at Pinterest. MTMD is a framework for the lightweight ranking layer, the fast stage that sits between retrieval and the final fine ranker in a cascaded ad system. That layer must score many ads quickly for several goals at once.

The team built MTMD to unify ranking across multiple tasks and multiple ad domains in one framework. Each domain, such as a different ad product, brings its own optimization goals, which makes a shared model hard to train well. The framework aims to serve all of them in the single lightweight stage. This keeps the fast layer simple while still respecting what each domain needs.
arxiv-2510-10157:
Pai and co-authors present BILLY in this 2025 arXiv paper on creative text generation. Running several language models as a team can boost creativity, mimicking collective intelligence, but it costs heavy compute and adds latency. BILLY seeks the same gain inside a single model.

The framework blends persona vectors, directions in the model's internal space that encode a persona, to steer generation. Merging those vectors captures some of the diversity a multi-model panel provides. The method is training-free, so it adds no fine-tuning cost. Creative tasks, from story writing to brainstorming, benefit from multiple viewpoints; BILLY tries to supply them cheaply by mixing personas already latent in one model.
arxiv-2510-10257:
Elrawy and Emad A. Mohammed control density in few-shot 3D Gaussian Splatting in this 2025 arXiv paper on 3D vision. Gaussian splatting builds scenes from soft 3D blobs, but with few input views its standard adaptive density control overfits and bloats the reconstruction with needless blobs. Rival methods improve quality only by adding far more primitives.

The authors revise the core optimization around opacity gradients, using how transparent each blob is to guide where density should grow or shrink. The result targets compact and efficient reconstructions from sparse views. Fewer, better-placed Gaussians mean faster rendering and smaller files. The work matters for capturing real scenes when only a handful of photos exist.
arxiv-2510-10457:
Shaobo Wang and thirteen co-authors ask whether large language model benchmarks can be shrunk drastically without losing their meaning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Benchmark suites keep growing as models gain skills, and running them all is costly. Earlier work trimmed redundancy or predicted scores from subsets, but no framework combined these well. The team first analyzes redundancy sample by sample and finds many near duplicate questions that can be dropped.

They then frame benchmark compression as an optimization problem aimed at rebuilding the full scores from a subset. Their framework, EssenceBench, searches coarse to fine with a genetic algorithm, an iterative search inspired by evolution, mixing fitness based subset search with attribution based sample search. On the HellaSwag benchmark of ten thousand samples, their method kept ranking shifts within 5 percent using 25 times fewer samples. With 200 times fewer samples, it still preserved 95 percent of the ranking.
arxiv-2510-10757:
Hovav Lazare and three co-authors use distant galaxies to bound how strongly dark matter can bump into protons, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such scattering would wash out small scale structure in the early universe. The team turns to ultraviolet luminosity functions, counts of galaxies by brightness at high redshift, measured by the Hubble Space Telescope. They study three forms of the interaction, from velocity independent contact forces to higher order dipole effects.

Their analysis combines blank and gravitationally lensed Hubble fields with Planck cosmic microwave background data and a supernova catalog, inside a Bayesian framework. The lensed fields probe fainter galaxies and thus smaller scales. Including them substantially tightened the constraints for velocity dependent interactions, surpassing existing bounds from Milky Way satellite counts and microwave background patterns. For velocity independent scattering, their bound sits within an order of magnitude of the strongest existing limits.
arxiv-2510-10857:
Suhas S Jain proposes a computational model for soapy substances moving in two phase flows, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Soluble surfactants drift between the bulk of each fluid and their interface, changing the interface's properties. This creates sharp gradients at the interface and between phases, a serious challenge for simulation. Jain's transport model captures how surfactants stick to and leave the interface.

The model uses a central difference discretization, which avoids artificial dissipation and suits turbulent flow simulation. It pairs with a diffuse interface method but fits other interface capturing schemes too. Two strengths are provable when a stated criterion holds. The concentration stays positive, as physics requires. And the surfactant stays confined to its proper region instead of leaking numerically between interface and bulk. Jain tests the model in one and several dimensions, including an oscillating droplet and a turbulent droplet laden flow.
arxiv-2510-11057:
Diffusion models build images and other data by gradually removing noise, but extra guidance added during generation can push samples off course. Youngrok Park and co-authors study this off-manifold problem in a 2025 arXiv paper on generative modeling. They link the drift to score errors that build up step by step until the final outputs land in low-density regions and look unrealistic.

Their fix, Temporal Alignment Guidance, uses a time predictor to estimate how far a sample has strayed from the desired data manifold at each step. A larger time gap signals lower quality, so the method pulls samples back toward the manifold during generation. Across a range of downstream tasks, the guided samples stayed closely aligned with the target manifold at every timestep. That alignment produced significant improvements in generation quality compared with unguided sampling across the tasks tested.
arxiv-2510-11257:
Clinical records could predict which heart patients are heading toward a fatal event, but labeled data are scarce and records are riddled with missing values. Davide Borghini and co-authors address both problems with self-supervised learning in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Their model MIEO is an autoencoder trained to rebuild masked clinical inputs, learning a representation of each patient from unlabeled data before any outcome labels are used.

The team applied the method to a dataset of patients with ischaemic heart disease. Patient records are embedded into a latent space built from the unlabeled data, and a neural network classifier trained on those embeddings predicts cardiovascular death. The embedding-based classifier achieved better balanced accuracy than the same classifier fed the raw clinical features directly. The authors argue the approach is promising where unlabeled data are plentiful but labels are expensive, in hospital datasets.
arxiv-2510-11557:
Of the world's 7,613 languages, two thousand are spoken by millions of people yet barely exist online, so AI systems trained on web text never learn them. Saurabh Khanna and Xinxu Li map that inequality in this 2025 arXiv paper. They measure every language on two axes: vitality, its real-world demographic strength, and digitality, its online presence, read through postcolonial theory.

Sorting all languages into four groups, they find Strongholds, high on both measures, at thirty-three percent. Digital Echoes are digitally strong despite declining vitality, at six percent. Fading Voices are low on both, at thirty-six percent. Invisible Giants, at twenty-seven percent, are absent from training data despite high vitality. Javanese, with 68 million speakers, yields almost nothing online, while Icelandic, with 350 thousand speakers, has a large digital footprint. The authors argue this is not a technical accident but a continuation of colonial-era linguistic hierarchies.
arxiv-2510-11957:
Andreu Ferré Moragues and Andreas Koutsogiannis study the hidden randomness inside certain fast-growing sequences. In ergodic theory, a Furstenberg system is a dynamical model that mimics a sequence's statistical behavior. The authors examine sequences built from smooth functions whose growth is superpolynomial, faster than any power but slower than exponential. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks what kind of systems model such sequences.

The answer is the wildest kind: the Furstenberg systems are Bernoulli, meaning they behave like sequences of independent coin flips, the gold standard of randomness in dynamics. The proof runs through exponential sums, which expose how evenly the sequences spread themselves out. Strong equidistribution forces the limiting system to forget all structure. As a by-product, the approach also yields convergence results for averages along these sequences. The work extends the known catalogue of deterministic sequences that masquerade as pure chance.
arxiv-2510-12857:
Staab and colleagues build a new way to probe bias in large language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Existing bias tests lean on templated prompts or multiple-choice questions, which are suggestive and far simpler than real user conversations. Such tests can miss the biased behavior that surfaces in open-ended exchanges about sensitive attributes like sex, race, or religion.

Their framework automatically generates realistic open-ended questions, then repeatedly mutates and selects the ones that most strongly pull biased answers out of a model. It also tracks subtler behaviors such as asymmetric refusals and explicit acknowledgment of bias. From the results they assembled CAB, a human-verified benchmark for cross-model comparison. Testing many models showed nuanced differences, and even the strongest performer, GPT-5, kept persistent biases in specific scenarios.
arxiv-2510-12957:
Mohammad builds an explainable AI framework for image classifiers in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard benchmark datasets such as MNIST often fail to expose hidden biases, which limits trust in deep neural networks for high-stakes uses. Post-hoc accounts can also misrepresent what a model relied on.

The proposed framework combines attention-augmented feature fusion across multiple input modes. It adds local explanations from an improved gradient-based heatmap method. A Reveal-to-Revise feedback loop then detects bias and feeds corrections back into learning. On multimodal extensions of MNIST it reached accuracy above ninety percent, with strong fidelity measured against ground truth regions, beating unimodal and non-explainable baselines. Ablation studies, which remove parts one at a time, showed that joining clear accounts with bias-aware learning improved robustness and agreement with human judgment.
arxiv-2510-13157:
Khatuya and colleagues improve financial numerical reasoning in language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Answering finance questions demands extracting facts from text and tables, then chaining arithmetic steps correctly. General language models lag specialized systems on the FinQA and ConvFinQA benchmarks despite prompting tricks such as chain-of-thought and program-of-thought.

Their framework, FINDER, works in two steps. A generative retriever first pulls the relevant facts from unstructured documents, including tables. Then a program-of-thought prompt, which makes the model write executable reasoning as code, is paired with dynamically selected in-context examples matched to the question. FINDER set new state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, improving execution accuracy by several points on each. The authors credit the combination of targeted retrieval and context-aware example choice for closing the gap with specialized models.
arxiv-2510-13357:
Al-Ali and colleagues probe whether private traits leak from speech models trained with federated learning. In federated learning, phones keep raw audio and share only model updates, which should protect speakers. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests an attack that reads personal attributes from those shared updates alone. Speech is sensitive, since one clip can reveal who a person is.

The attack is white-box and passive, meaning it inspects model weights but never hears the target speakers. The team applies it to three speech recognition models: Wav2Vec2, HuBERT, and Whisper. It recovers traits such as gender, age, accent, emotion, and the speech disorder dysarthria. Accent could be inferred reliably from all three models, the authors report. Traits that are rare or absent in pre-training data proved easiest to infer, they found. The results point to security gaps that earlier work had not documented.
arxiv-2510-13757:
Meszaros, Knight, Timcheck, and Nowotny deliver a full pipeline for training spiking networks with synaptic delays and running them on Intel's Loihi 2 chip. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets keyword spotting at the edge, where cloud processing adds delay and privacy risks. Spiking networks promise big energy savings, but tools for training them end to end were missing.

Their pipeline trains efficiently on GPUs with event-based methods that learn each connection's delay. Trained networks then deploy onto Loihi 2, a neuromorphic chip built from spiking neurons. Tests use the Spiking Heidelberg Digits and Spiking Speech Commands datasets. Adding learned delays improved classification accuracy over delay-free designs. Moving from GPU to chip cost almost no accuracy in their benchmarks. On Loihi 2, classification ran up to eighteen times faster while using about two hundred fifty times less energy than a Jetson board, they report.
arxiv-2510-13957:
Jan Heisig proposes a new kind of gravitational-wave detector aimed at very high frequencies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Waves at kilohertz frequencies and above could reveal conditions in the early universe at energies beyond what the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the Big Bang, can probe. Existing detector ideas fall short of the sensitivity needed to test limits in this range by many orders of magnitude.

His design sends light around a closed optical loop many times, so the tiny phase shift from a passing wave adds up coherently at each pass. This creates sharp, narrow resonances with a predictable comb-like pattern, giving a distinctive signature to search for. Using parameters compatible with the planned Einstein Telescope and realistic mirror quality, he projects that a year of observing could reach, and even pass, the nucleosynthesis bound on the background. That reach extends up to tens of kilohertz.
arxiv-2510-14557:
Lee and co-authors, in a 2025 arXiv paper, study how to serve large language models cheaply by storing numbers in fewer bits. Block floating-point formats group numbers so they share scaling information. The team analyzed recent industry variants of these formats. They found that low-bit versions lose too much quality. A few outlier values inside each block spoil the results for the whole block.

Their fix, called MX+, extends the microscaling formats already used in industry. The key observation is that an outlier value does not need its exponent field, the part of a number that sets its scale. So MX+ reuses that field as extra precision digits for the outlier itself. In evaluations, MX+ gave much better model quality than the four-bit MX format. It added almost no storage cost and almost no slowdown, a strong option for efficient serving.
arxiv-2510-14757:
Sextl and Kudritzki present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a chemical history of the star-forming rings circling the centers of four disk galaxies. The galaxies are NGC 613, NGC 1097, NGC 3351, and NGC 7552. Using the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope, they separated the light of young and old stars in each ring. They measured ages and metallicities, the enrichment of the gas that formed the stars.

The old stars span wide ranges of age and metal content, which points to a long story: metal-poor gas kept falling in, and stars formed in episodes over many billions of years. The young stars are metal-rich, two to three times the Sun's level, except in NGC 3351. Earlier reports of extremely metal-poor young regions turn out to be an artifact of averaging young and old stars together. Dust maps show lanes feeding the rings, supporting the infall picture.
arxiv-2510-15757:
Pieris Panagi and colleagues present PoultryFI in a 2025 paper. It is an artificial intelligence platform for poultry farms. The platform was built for small and medium farms. Such farms still rely on manual checks. The system has six modules. They cover camera placement, audio-visual monitoring, and analytics with alerts. They also cover egg counting, production forecasts, and recommendations.

Camera layouts are first planned offline. A whole poultry house can be covered with minimal hardware. The monitoring module reads welfare signs from video and sound. It also uses feeding data. Field trials reported perfect egg counts on a cheap Raspberry Pi computer. Anomaly detection was robust. Short-term forecasts were reliable. The authors offer this as a path to farm-wide intelligence.
arxiv-2510-15857:
Jiuhai Chen and colleagues present BLIP3o-NEXT in a 2025 paper. It is an open-source foundation model for images. It generates images from text. It also edits existing images. Both jobs sit inside one architecture. Native image generation of this kind is advancing fast. The team set out to map what drives the progress.

They report four lessons from building the model. Most design choices perform about the same. What matters is scaling well and running fast. Reinforcement learning can push quality further. Image editing remains genuinely hard. Their approach still makes progress on it. The release is fully open source. Others can reproduce it and extend the frontier.
arxiv-2510-15957:
Yiyi Huo and five co-authors study how coal particles change microbubble-aided bitumen separation in oil sands slurry flow. Earlier work showed bubbles from hydrogen peroxide can lift bitumen toward the top of a transport pipe. Coal particles ride along in real carriers, so their effect on that separation matters before tailings are disposed of.

Without added bubbles, coal particles cut bitumen recovery by a clear margin. A small peroxide dose alone helps little, since too few bubbles form. Adding coal and peroxide together, though, boosts recovery greatly, and larger peroxide volumes lift it further as more microbubbles form. Fluid dynamics simulations explain the pattern: coal alone gathers bitumen toward the middle of the pipe, while a higher bubble share pushes bitumen toward the top. The interplay guides hydrotransport design, the team argues.
arxiv-2510-16057:
Md Kamrul Siam, Md Jobair Hossain Faruk, Jerry Q. Cheng, and Huanying Gu improve chest X-ray reading by letting two large language models check each other. Single models err often enough to worry clinicians, so the team fuses ChatGPT and Claude on the CheXpert data set. A random sample of radiologist-labelled studies is read from images alone first.

Claude scores higher than ChatGPT in that image-only round, and a similarity-based consensus rule, requiring near-total agreement, edges past both. A second, smaller cohort pairs each image with a synthetic clinical note in a standard template. Scores rise for both models there, and consensus accuracy climbs into the low ninety percent range on that subset. Agreement-based fusion beats single models in both settings, which the four authors offer as a cheap route to more trustworthy radiology support.
arxiv-2510-16157:
Xuchen Gong and Tian Li join two lines of work on training neural networks. Both lines apply when gradients, the usual guide for learning, are off the table. One line tweaks the model's weights at random and keeps what lowers the average loss. The other, sharpness-aware training, hunts for the worst loss nearby so the model lands in a flat, safe valley.

Their bridge is an exponential tilting goal, a dial that slides smoothly between average loss and worst loss. On top of it they build training methods that need no gradients and little memory. Tests span image sorting, quiz answering, and text writing, and their methods beat plain no-gradient baselines. The work gives a cheaper path to the steady results that sharpness-aware training is prized for.
arxiv-2510-16557:
Behrad Mousaei Shir-Mohammad, Behzad Moshiri, and Abolfazl Yaghmaei place indoor users in a 2025 study. GPS fails inside, so they use Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signal prints instead. A print is the set of signal strengths heard at one spot. Mixed phones, echoes, and noise make such prints hard to read. Their frame cleans prints, then blends two reader tools.

Shape traits from persistent homology, a tool that maps holes and loops, join each print. A proof-based fusion step merges the readers' calls with doubt scores. Tests on two data sets, one with 1,200 fresh samples, show clear gains. Error fell by about a fifth on mean across splits. The full frame runs on tiny chips for live use.
arxiv-2510-16657:
Bingji Yi and three co-authors ask whether checking synthetic data can stop model collapse. Collapse is the steady decline seen when a generative model is retrained again and again on its own output. Their proposal adds an outside verifier, which may be a person or a stronger model, to judge the synthetic data before retraining.

The analysis uses linear regression as a test setting. It shows that guided retraining can improve the model for a while, but the estimate drifts toward what the verifier already knows. Unless the verifier is perfectly reliable, gains level off and may reverse. Experiments in several settings matched that prediction, giving the claim both theory and practice behind it.
arxiv-2510-16857:
Jiyan Qiu and seven co-authors present a huge car airflow dataset in a 2025 paper. Car shape decides air drag, and drag decides electric vehicle range. Testing each shape with full airflow simulation takes weeks. Simpler models run faster but lose the accuracy factories need.

Their dataset, DrivAerStar, holds twelve thousand detailed airflow simulations. The runs cover three car shapes varied through twenty design settings. Full engine bays and cooling systems are included, not just outer shells. Wind tunnel checks matched the data within about one percent error. Models trained on it reached factory-ready accuracy in minutes. The authors offer it as a bridge between lab research and real car design.
arxiv-2510-17157:
Yinghui Wang, Xinyu Zhang, and Peng Du teach a model to draft factory parts from one photo in this 2025 paper. The drafts must stay editable, with steps a designer can tweak. Big vision-language models still read depth poorly from flat views. The team adds depth cues and rewards short, clean step lists.

First, depth and slope maps join the photo as extra inputs. Those cues help the model place faces and edges in space. Next, training rewards brief step lists that keep shape truth high. Tests on two part data sets top prior methods. Gains show in valid code, true shapes, and short build steps.
arxiv-2510-17357:
When two neutron stars merge, the glowing cloud that follows can reveal which heavy elements were forged in the blast. Leo P Mulholland and four co-authors supply fresh atomic data for tellurium, an element whose faint lines are hard to model. Much of the data used today rests on rough approximations or formulas fitted by hand, which limits how well spectra can be read.

Using a well tested method called the R-matrix approach, the team computed how electrons excite tellurium ions and how light frees electrons from them. They then built model spectra and compared them with observations of the famous merger event AT2017gfo. Mulholland and his co-authors also test whether one tellurium ion helps explain a known emission feature.
arxiv-2510-17557:
Lukas Niebel proves a shape result for two dimensional bubbles in a 2025 arXiv paper. Here a bubble means a hollow swirl held by surface tension, the force that pulls a surface tight. Such bubbles solve a math problem where extra conditions must hold on the free edge. A past conjecture by Crowdy and Wegmann asked which shapes can occur.

Niebel shows every such bubble is circular across a set range of a key control value. That range ends at the first value where branching into new shapes begins. Past that point, non circular bubbles exist close by, so the range cannot be extended. He also proves an area bound linking perimeter and capacity. The disc is the unique best shape in the same range.
arxiv-2510-17657:
Gianmaria Viola, with Alessandro Della Pia and three co-authors, learns hidden dynamics without writing equations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many complex systems follow partial differential equations, meaning rules that link change across space and time, but the exact rules are unknown. Some system states also stay hidden from view. Their framework learns the dynamics in three tiers while respecting a fixed total mass.

First, a method called Diffusion Maps compresses the data into a low dimensional latent space. Next, simple models learn how the compressed state evolves. Finally, a neighbor based step lifts predictions back to full detail. Tests cover a crowd movement model and a fluid flow tracer problem. The latent models beat a standard compression baseline over long horizons.
arxiv-2510-17757:
César Barilla studies how a decision maker should time learning in a changing world. The decision maker picks both when to gather news and what to ask. The state of the world keeps shifting between updates. Barilla splits the puzzle into stopping choices and one-shot information choices.

He shows optimal learning either stops or settles into a regular cycle. Each update then restores a set level of relative certainty. When fixed costs shrink, beliefs change in sudden jumps instead. Long quiet spells end when rare news forces a sharp revision. He gives a closed-form summary and a portfolio example.
arxiv-2510-18057:
Talya Eden, Ludmila Glinskih, and Sofya Raskhodnikova make agnostic learning of flat shapes both fast and sample-efficient. Agnostic learning must cope with data that no shape fits perfectly, and for triangles and polygons the sample needs were known while fast methods lagged. Their learner for triangles uses the best possible sample size with a much better running time than a 1995 method.

Gains also land for four- and five-sided polygons over a 1996 result. A learner for convex sets inside a square rounds out the set. Theory readers get long-standing geometric learning problems moved closer to practical speed.
arxiv-2510-18457:
Tianci Bi works with Xiaoyi Zhang, Yan Lu, and Nanning Zheng. They rethink the tokenizer in latent diffusion models. The tokenizer squeezes an image into a compact code. New images are then built from such codes. A good tokenizer speeds training. It also sharpens the final images. Past work borrowed from vision foundation models. It distilled their knowledge into the tokenizer. That step weakened the borrowed features.

The new tokenizer is called VFM-VAE. It uses a frozen vision model as it is. A fresh decoder learns to rebuild real images from its codes. The codes are rich in scene meaning. Careful design let both sides improve together. Quality rose in far fewer training rounds than before. The speedup was about tenfold. Longer training pushed scores higher still.
arxiv-2510-18757:
Zoe Hackshaw, Keith Hawkins, and Catherine Manea chemically dissect the red giant star that orbits Gaia BH3, the most massive known black hole of stellar origin. The giant is extremely poor in metals, and its chemistry may reveal whether the pair formed together or was assembled later by a capture. Using a high-resolution spectrograph on a telescope at McDonald Observatory, they measured abundances for twenty-nine elements, from lithium to thorium.

The star proved enriched in alpha elements and carries the signature of rapid neutron-capture processing at a moderate level. Crucially, no element deviated from the pattern expected of an ordinary halo red giant of its type, so chemistry alone does not decide between the capture and isolated-formation stories. An upper limit on thorium also let the team bound the system's age using the thorium-to-europium ratio as a radioactive clock.
arxiv-2510-18957:
Federico Esposito and twenty-nine co-authors measure how clumpy molecular gas is near the centers of sixteen nearby Seyfert galaxies. Gas structure on small scales controls star formation and the growth of central black holes, yet how active galactic nuclei reshape that gas is still poorly known.

Using ALMA observations of carbon monoxide emission close to each nucleus, the team applies three different clumpiness measures, based on contrast between sharp and smoothed maps and on excess flux. Comparing galaxies in the GATOS survey lets them test whether black hole activity makes nuclear gas smoother or more broken up.
arxiv-2510-19057:
Anna Cetera and five co-authors use scalp electroencephalography to find brain patterns that distinguish planning different kinds of grasps. Invasive recordings can decode local signals for grasp planning, but the large-scale patterns visible to noninvasive sensors are much less understood, even though they would be easier to use in clinics.

A new vision-based platform separates planning a precision, power, or no grasp from actually moving, during natural tasks. Filtering methods pull out low-frequency rhythms that differ by grasp type across brain networks. Such signals could one day guide assistive devices without implanted electrodes.
arxiv-2510-19157:
S X Li and six co-authors present a variational quantum algorithm. It performs unitary dilation. That trick puts a non-unitary map inside a larger unitary one. A quantum computer can then run it. Such maps are key for open quantum systems. Their evolution is not unitary on its own.

A circuit with tunable parts builds the larger unitary. A classical optimizer tunes it under a global rule. This also improves resilience to noise. The team tests the method on an open system model. They run trials on superconducting devices through a cloud service. Results beat standard dilation protocols.
arxiv-2510-19857:
Debarshi Mukherjee derives a simple analytic estimate for the apparent size of a black hole's shadow when the universe's expansion is taken into account. Shadow sizes in flat space-time are well understood, but distant black holes sit in an expanding cosmos. Combining the local Schwarzschild geometry with cosmological dynamics through the McVittie and Kottler metrics, he obtains a compact formula linking the shadow's angular size to the angular diameter distance.

Numerical estimates show expansion barely matters for nearby sources but becomes relevant for high-redshift black holes. The formula keeps the dependence on the Hubble constant and cosmological constant explicit and easy to read. Mukherjee offers the result as a transparent bridge between strong-gravity optics and cosmology.
arxiv-2510-20057:
Pengzhuo Wang and three co-authors demonstrate a laser frequency reference built from an iodine-filled hollow-core photonic microcell.
