A green laser at five hundred thirty-two nanometers is locked to a specific transition of molecular iodine inside the sealed fiber cell. Its stability is compared directly with the same transition in a free-space iodine cell.

Noise analysis showed the system was limited by stray beams interfering with the main beam and spoiling the error signal. The team identified three kinds of such interference and designed a suppression method for each one. After those fixes, stability improved by more than tenfold and reached the best level yet reported for this kind of fiber reference.
arxiv-2510-20457:
Louis Mozart Kamdem Teyou and six co-authors give EBR, a neural judge for facts in knowledge bases cast in a rich logic. Such bases store facts as axioms, and rule-based judges can break when facts clash or hold slips. Their judge leans on learned codes to guess what a strict judge would say. That guess work makes it tough in the face of bad data.

EBR needs the facts of just base terms and has-a links to get or guess the full fact set of any term in the logic. Tests next to top strict judges show it stands firm when facts are lost or wrong. Past judges fail in those states, the team finds. The step aims at real-world bases.
arxiv-2510-20557:
Ekaterina Konopleva, Gleb Fedorov, and Oleg Astafiev plan a quantum sim of a grown zig-zag model with polarization transmons. Such sims of topo models are much worked on, and multi-trait meta-atoms are a fresh path, probed most in the classic sphere so far. Their transmons hold twin dipole orbits and allow long cross-polar links in the zig-zag chain.

Phase shifts of the grown model are mapped by counts and by sums, with topo marks to sort the phases. In-gap trapped states show up, both plain and Tamm edge kinds. With lined meta-atoms, wave models show the plan tracks the target model with care. The work opens a path to tests of topo quantum group acts not reached in the past.
arxiv-2510-20857:
Phat Tran, Enbai Kuang, and Fred Xu test a light tool for brain bleeding. Bleeding inside the skull after a head injury can kill quickly. Head injury causes about sixty-four thousand deaths each year in the United States. CT and MRI scans work, but they cost much and need large setups. Many poor or remote places lack access to them.

The team uses ultrasound tissue pulsatility imaging, called TPI. TPI is portable and tracks tiny tissue moves with each heartbeat. Records came from head injury patients with CT confirmed labels. The team cleaned the signals and cut down their size. One method kept parts that held ninety-five percent of the variation. They tried many classifier types across three data forms. Group methods did best after that size cut. They reached ninety-eight percent accuracy in the tests. Such tools could help in emergency, rural, and military care.
arxiv-2510-20957:
Josh McGiff leads nine co-authors on Irish-BLiMP, the first fine grained benchmark of linguistic skill in Irish, an endangered language. The set holds just over a thousand minimal pairs spanning eleven grammar features, built and reviewed by fluent speakers from grammar literature.

Humans and large language models are scored on the same syntactic judgments. Fluent humans beat every model on every feature, by a wide average margin, showing how far models lag in a low resource language. The benchmark gives Irish a measuring stick for future tools and a template for testing other under served languages.
arxiv-2510-21157:
Frank Garvan and Avi Mukhopadhyay return to mock theta functions, curious series that Ramanujan introduced in his final letter to G. H. Hardy. Earlier work by Watson derived transformation formulas for two third order examples, and Zwegers later tied the functions to real analytic modular forms.

Instead of the older routes, they derive the same transformations from Lerch sums, a different family of series. Proving that the new and old results agree requires fresh identities for q-series, which are series built from powers of a variable named q. As a byproduct, their argument gives a new proof of the theorem Zwegers established in 2000.
arxiv-2510-21457:
Daan Caljon, Jente Van Belle, and Wouter Verbeke estimate how a treatment's effect varies across a network when people influence each other. In such settings an outcome depends on neighbors' treatments too, and most causal machine learning tools demand a preset recipe summarizing that spillover, a guess that is often wrong.

Their neural method, HINet, avoids the preset recipe. A graph neural network learns, alongside outcome prediction, a summary of each node's neighborhood that captures the spillover that actually matters. An adversarial training step balances the learned summaries across treatment groups. The authors add a theory bound on errors over whole populations and two scores for judging counterfactual networks. Across synthetic and partly synthetic data, HINet stays steady under many spillover patterns, while preset-recipe rivals falter when their recipe misses.
arxiv-2510-21657:
Zehua Liu and Tilo Burghardt teach cameras to name wildlife in trail photos where a few common species swamp millions of images and rare ones barely appear. In the North America Camera Trap Images corpus, one head class alone takes over half of the 3.7 million pictures. So ordinary training learns the frequent animals and neglects the tail.

Building on an existing wildlife model, they systematically test long-tail training methods: losses designed for imbalance and regularizers that respect it, plus the scheduling choices around them. Their best setup scores about ninety-nine point four percent top-one accuracy on their test split, well above a ninety-five point five percent baseline. Also leads on a reduced-bias test built from another data set, where night shots, occlusion, and motion blur shift the domain. Honest failure cases remain for the rarest classes under heavy shift.
arxiv-2510-21857:
Anthony Zhang, Mahmut Gokmen, Dennis Hein, Rongjun Ge, Wenjun Xia, Ge Wang, and Jin Chen work on cleaning up low-dose CT scans, where cutting radiation leaves images grainy. A recent generative family based on Poisson flow can denoise well, but its consistency-style version could only be trained by copying a teacher model, which narrowed where it could be used.

The team introduces a training method that builds such a model from scratch. Changes to the noise schedule and the noise distribution help the model adapt and produce cleaner samples. On low-dose scan denoising, the directly trained model improved standard quality scores and matched the effectiveness of established consistency models. The authors note that tuning and wider tasks still need study, but the route is now open.
arxiv-2510-22057:
James Thiering, Tarun Sethupat Radha Krishna, Dylan Zelkin, and Ashis Kumer Biswas build a system that reads student engagement in online classes. It is trained not to cheat with protected traits. Judging involvement through a webcam feed is harder than in a physical room. A model that secretly keys on gender would be unfair and misleading.

Their multi-task model uses several transfer learning strategies. A regularization step forces its features to stay independent of sensitive attributes. Engagement predictions cannot lean on them. The link between predictions and the sensitive grouping fell sharply from its starting level. The system still read engagement effectively. The authors argue the design serves ethics and clarity together. A model that cannot use a shortcut must show its real reasons.
arxiv-2510-22657:
Automated systems can leak private state information when an attacker probes their sensors or controls. Xiaoyan Li and Christoforos N Hadjicostis study such state attacks in 2025 for discrete event systems, which move between states in steps and can be modeled as finite state automata.

An attacker with a limited number of probes learns whether the current state lies in certain subsets. The question is whether anonymity or opacity, two privacy properties, can always be broken. Li and Hadjicostis characterize when violations can be forced and design attack strategies that guarantee reaching a violating situation. The work clarifies how bounded probing threatens system privacy.
arxiv-2510-22757:
Good decisions should hold up when data distributions shift. Jiaqi Wen and Jianyi Yang study robust optimization in 2025. Their frame guards against a set of nearby distributions. That set is called an ambiguity set. A good set stays close to the nominal data. It must also cover many adverse cases.

Their set is built with a diffusion model. Diffusion models can reach cases beyond the nominal support. Yet they stay consistent with the nominal law. The team then solves the inner worst case step. They prove the method settles at a stationary point. Tests show stronger out of distribution performance in a prediction task.
arxiv-2510-22857:
A whole room can become a stage for a shared story. Naisha Agarwal, Judith Amores, and Andrew D Wilson present Storycaster in 2025. It is a generative AI cave system. Cave systems project images onto room walls. Unlike headsets, users keep spatial awareness.

Live camera feeds guide the wall projections. Physical items can turn into virtual counterparts. A narrator agent leads the session. Users co-create stories by voice commands. Each scene gains ambient audio, dialogue, and imagery. Thirteen participants joined the study. They found it immersive and engaging. The narrator and audio had most impact. Latency and image resolution need work.
arxiv-2510-23057:
Oskar Natan and Jun Miura present Seq-DeepIPC, a sequential model that takes a legged robot from sensing to control in one chain. The model fuses color, depth, and satellite position data over time. It jointly predicts scene segmentation and depth, giving richer spatial features for planning than either output alone.

A lightweight encoder keeps compute low enough for edge devices on the robot. Heading estimation is simplified by dropping a noisy inertial sensor from that step. Tests in real settings show the integrated design can guide legged robots through complex ground while running on modest hardware.
arxiv-2510-23257:
Qing-Hong Cao, Jian-Nan Ding, Yandong Liu, and Jin-Long Yuan probe CP violation in electroweak interactions at a future high-energy muon collider. CP violation, a matter-antimatter asymmetry, is studied here through vector boson fusion that makes W and Higgs bosons. They work within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory.

Four dimension-six CP-odd operators are targeted with CP-odd observables and asymmetries. Detailed simulations include parton showering, hadronization, and detector effects, and yield exclusion sensitivities from binned data. The study shows what a muon collider could reveal about new sources of CP violation beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-23457:
Saleh Darzi and five co-authors address a core weakness of 5G networks: base stations are not robustly authenticated during initial bootstrapping. Fake base stations, spoofed broadcasts, and manipulation of system information blocks follow from that gap. Forged blocks are a root of trust, enabling fake alerts, tracking, and false roaming.

Existing fixes carry high overhead, rely on centralized trust, and lack accountability or long-term breach resilience. The authors argue for distributed trust, verifiable forgery detection, and audit logging, and study feasibility. Their analysis charts how 5G access could stay trustworthy even when some base stations fall.
arxiv-2510-23657:
Saklain Niam and three co-authors build the first machine learning framework for predicting how cold plasma treatment will change seed sprouting. Cold plasma is an eco-friendly way to boost germination, but results swing with seed type, plasma settings, and surroundings, making outcomes hard to foresee. The team gathered traits of seeds and plasma parameters for soybean, barley, sunflower, radish, and tomato.

Among the models tested, Extra Trees predicted best, explaining about ninety-two percent of the variation in germination uplift. The analysis found a hormetic pattern: little effect at low voltage or short exposure, the strongest sprouting in a middle band, and harm when voltage or exposure ran too high. Discharge power mattered most, with rates peaking at high power and brief exposure. Radish and soybean were modeled most reliably, sunflower least. The framework ships inside an MLflow tool to guide precision farming choices.
arxiv-2510-23857:
Madelyn Broome and three co-authors present Wind-AE, an open-source code that models how high-energy starlight boils atmospheres off close-in exoplanets. X-ray and extreme ultraviolet light heats and ionizes the air of short-period planets, driving winds that escape to space. This photoevaporation shapes how planets evolve and explains patterns in the observed population, yet the loss rates cannot be measured directly.

The code solves a steady one-dimensional Parker wind with many photon frequencies and several chemical species, building on an earlier model. Two effects fight: adding hard X-rays raises the loss rate, while metals lower it. For a typical hot Jupiter they roughly cancel, leaving a hotter, faster, more gradually ionized wind. The team also maps where the wind launches. For puffy low-gravity planets that radius sits far above the surface, and ignoring it underestimates how fast they evaporate.
arxiv-2510-24057:
Qirong Zhu and four co-authors present a virtual reality system to help new guide dog trainers learn their work. Guide dogs help blind people move around on their own, but few skilled trainers are available. Training is hard because the trainer must watch the dog closely and give clear commands, mostly with the right hand.

The system, called PanoHaptic, gives a full view around the trainer and lets the user feel cues through the harness hand. It records and studies right hand motions across scenes and stages of training. The aim is to let beginners learn from a trainer's point of view, which flat video cannot offer.
arxiv-2510-24157:
M. Obradovic and N. Tuneski survey uses of Grunsky coefficients to bound key quantities for univalent functions, which are analytic functions that never take the same value twice. For the general class of such functions, no simple analytic description exists, so sharp bounds are hard to obtain by direct means. The Grunsky method offers another route.

The survey collects estimates, some of them sharp, for the size of the third and fourth logarithmic coefficients and for Hankel determinants of the second and third order. It also covers coefficients of the inverse function and differences between coefficients. The paper gathers scattered results into one reference for work on univalent functions.
arxiv-2510-24257:
Ziqi Ma and two co-authors present HMAMP, a method for teaching robots manipulation skills in a human like style. Robots that work near people should handle objects and tools much as humans do, for natural and intuitive interaction. Their approach learns from adversarial motion priors, which capture both the motion patterns of manipulation and the goal of the task.

An adversarial network is trained with a mix of real world data and simulation data produced by the agent itself. The discriminator judges whether motions look human and task directed, training a policy that generates realistic manipulation behavior. The method aims to give robots task oriented skills that resemble human movement rather than stiff machine motions.
arxiv-2510-24357:
Christopher W. Churchill presents the first paper of a two part series modeling how the circumgalactic medium around galaxies absorbs quasar light, working alone. The circumgalactic medium is the gas halo surrounding a galaxy, and quasar sight lines through it produce absorption profiles that encode its structure and motion. Churchill builds a mathematical model to synthesize those profiles from idealized setups.

Paper I develops the spatial geometries of several galaxy and halo structures and fills them with three dimensional velocity fields. For any viewing angle and impact parameter, he derives formulas for the perceived angles and the line of sight velocity along the sight line. These structures set up the profile synthesis completed in the second paper.
arxiv-2510-24857:
Federico Semenzato, Nicola Bellomo, Alvise Raccanelli, and Chiara M F Mingarelli flag a bias in maps of the space time hum caught by pulsar clocks. Each pulsar's time slips hold hum power from all sky scales at once. But with few pulsars to watch, maps can be rebuilt just at large scales.

That mismatch lets small scale power leak into the large scale map, the team shows with math. The leak pumps the read power up by at least ten fold across a wide scale range. Since this bias has not been counted yet, claims of a shaped hum may be too high. The work sets a fix list for map makers as true finds near.
arxiv-2510-25057:
Robin Maisch, Larissa Schmid, Timur Saglam, and Nils Niehues guard code cheat checks in class from a new trick: reshaping code so it runs the same but looks new. School check tools stand up to plain masks, yet fall when code form is swapped in set ways by hand or by AI. Their frame adds a graph view to top check tools.

Code is turned into a graph of its traits, then graph moves undo the reshape tricks in a set way. Tests used real class work, masked by both rule based and AI based attacks. Finds rose a lot with the new frame on top. The frame can grow to more reshape types as they show.
arxiv-2510-25157:
Gautam A Viruthagiri, Arnuv Tandon, Gerald G Fuller, and Vinny Chandran Suja read tear film depth from light wave marks with a vision transformer, in real time. Such marks can gauge a thin film with no touch, of use in eye care. But the flip from marks to depth is an ill set task, blurred by phase loops and noise.

Old ways are slow, noise prone, or need a hand expert, which blocks live clinic use. Their net was trained on a mix of fake and real tear data that fits the body. It uses long range space links to sort phase doubt in one pass. Depth maps stay in step over time, from films caught in live and loose eyes.
arxiv-2510-25257:
Zijun Liao, Yian Zhao, Xin Shan, Yu Yan, Chang Liu, Lei Lu, Xiangyang Ji, and Jie Chen are the eight authors. They boost real time object spot nets with help from big vision base models, at low cost. Fast spot nets are lean by design, which caps how rich their traits can be. Big base models hold rich traits, but are too heavy to run live in the car or phone.

Their frame teaches the lean net from the big one in training, so the big one is not run at test time. A deep inject part feeds high traits into the lean net's deep layers. A slope led tune step shifts how much of that feed lands, by the task at hand. The plan fits more than one base model.
arxiv-2510-25457:
Jun-Long Zhao, Li Yu, Ming Yang, and Chui-Ping Yang study quantum Fisher information. Their 2025 paper links it with quantum coherence. Quantum metrology concerns precise setting estimation using quantum readings. Fisher information indicates estimation precision in that field. Quantum coherence is an major quantum feature. multi-part systems are the focus of their work.

They present a concept called General Quantum Coherence. Eigenenergies are the allowed energy values of a system. General coherence captures high-dimensional quantum state nature better. It addresses shortcomings in current coherence reading methods. They observe a stringent square relationship involving coherence. That relationship connects general coherence and Fisher information tightly. The finding gives guidance for improving estimation precision. Better coherence measures may guide metrology design choices. Setting estimation is central to quantum sensing uses.
arxiv-2510-26157:
Hyuntae Park, Yeachan Kim, and SangKeun Lee improve how models link a molecule to its written description. Such links help chemists search and reason with chemical information, but existing models miss subtle differences because they align the whole molecule with the whole text. Their framework, MolBridge, adds fine grained alignment signals between molecular substructures, recognizable parts of a molecule, and the chemical phrases that describe them.

Park and the team train with substructure aware contrastive learning, which pulls matched pairs together and pushes others apart, plus a self refinement step that filters noisy alignment signals. Results across a wide range of molecular benchmarks beat prior state of the art methods in their tests, which highlights the value of part level alignment.
arxiv-2510-26557:
Nina Herrmann, with four co-authors, shrinks boosted decision trees so they can run on tiny devices. Boosted trees are a strong, common learning method, but their ensembles can be too big for the small computers used in the internet of things. The team wants models that keep their accuracy while using far less memory.

Herrmann and her co-authors reward the training process for reusing features and thresholds, which lets the final ensemble store less. A changed memory layout helps as well. In tests, their models matched the performance of LightGBM models while taking four to sixteen times less room. Such small models let devices work on their own, with little power and no constant link, for tasks like remote monitoring and edge analytics.
arxiv-2510-26957:
Qiao Wang and Joseph George test whether public images can predict how much water homes use in Hubballi-Dharwad, India. Door-to-door surveys measure water use well but cost much time and money in fast-growing cities. The pair instead use satellite tiles, Google Street View pictures split into parts, and simple map data such as night light and population density.

Street View parts plus the map data reach accuracy close to survey-based models for sorted water-use classes. The method works best at the high and low ends, while middle groups blur because their street views look alike. The findings suggest open images plus light map data can stand in for costly surveys in city planning work.
arxiv-2510-27057:
Martin Ottens, Kai-Steffen Hielscher, and Reinhard German present TheaterQ, a Linux tool for replaying changing network conditions. Standard emulators hold delay and bandwidth fixed, which poorly matches real links that shift over time. TheaterQ instead reads trace files, meaning timelines of recorded network traits, and applies them inside the kernel traffic control layer without user-space help.

The tool handles delay, bandwidth, loss, duplication, and reordering, and can update traits as fast as a microsecond. Multiple instances can stay synchronized for complex test setups. Evaluations show accuracy and speed comparable to existing tools, with far more flexibility for time-varying cases. Released as open source, it supports developers testing modern communication protocols under realistic, moving conditions.
arxiv-2510-27257:
Mengshi Qi leads five co-authors in a schedule that synergizes tensor and pipeline parallelism for training large models. Hybrid parallelism splits model tensors across devices while also pipelining stages, and it dominates large language model training. Tensor splitting adds heavy collective communication, while pipelining leaves idle bubbles at stage boundaries, and prior work attacked each problem separately.

The new schedule splits forward and backward passes into fine-grained units and braids them into one composite sequence. That structure nearly eliminates tensor-related bubbles, and the pipeline schedule is then tuned to shrink pipeline bubbles too. Experiments improve training throughput by up to about twelve percent for language models and sixteen percent for multimodal ones over existing schedules. Source code is released.
arxiv-2511-00157:
Miguel Escudero, Clara Garcia-Perez, and Maksym Ovchynnikov revisit limits on axion-like particles, light hypothetical particles that interact mostly with light. They focus on short-lived, fairly light cases and ask what the early universe allows. Their evidence comes from the making of light elements and from the cosmic microwave background, the faint glow left from the young universe.

The limits shift with the unknown reheating temperature, which sets how hot the early universe was. The team also adds rare decays into light hadrons, particles made of quarks, and this widens the ruled-out region. Some allowed regions could ease small tensions in current measurements of light elements.
arxiv-2511-00357:
Niklas Wölki and five co-authors bring cloud detection aboard small satellites that see the Earth in thermal light only. CubeSats often carry a single thermal band and little labeled data, so standard cloud masks fail. For the FOREST-2 CubeSat, the team starts from a model pretrained on a public Landsat-7 cloud dataset, then fine-tunes it jointly with a small set of mission images.

The model pairs a UNet with a light MobileNet encoder, sized for weak onboard hardware. Fine-tuning lifted accuracy over mission-only training baselines. Converted to a fast inference engine, it segmented a full image in under five seconds on a Jetson Nano chip. The result shows public data plus transfer learning can deliver real-time cloud masking in orbit.
arxiv-2511-00657:
Eshaan Tanwar and five co-authors ask a pointed question of multilingual language models: what do you know about my nation? Standard benchmarks span many languages but lean Western in content, leaving regional knowledge untested. Their XNationQA benchmark holds nearly fifty thousand questions on the geography, culture, and history of nine countries, presented in seven languages, built to probe cultural literacy directly.

Eight standard multilingual models were benchmarked, scored with two new transference metrics that track knowledge moving between languages. Access to cultural facts varied sharply by language. Models often knew more about a culture in English than in that culture's own dominant language, and skill in Western languages did not mean literacy about Western countries. Knowledge transfer across languages proved limited, above all in open-source models.
arxiv-2511-01657:
Athira Kalavampara Raghunadhan and five colleagues ask how best to measure the links of a quantum network. In quantum network tomography, the links are noisy channels distributing entangled Werner states, and the measurement scheme chosen at the nodes decides how precisely the link parameters can be estimated.

Three schemes are compared: local Z-basis measurements, joint Bell-state measurements, and measurements assisted by pre-shared entanglement. For each, the authors derive the outcome distributions and closed-form quantum Fisher information, then judge precision by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound. Entanglement assistance wins outright; joint measurements balance precision against complexity; the simplest local scheme, though noisier overall, beats joint measurements for a single link under heavy noise. A four-node star network test compares joint-only and hybrid layouts.
arxiv-2511-01757:
Shamse Tasnim Cynthia and Banani Roy fix a search problem inside Galaxy, the workflow platform that bioinformaticians use to build and share multi-step analyses. Galaxy hosts hundreds of reusable workflows, but its keyword search misses relevant ones whenever the user's words differ from the workflow's, a common failure for long or vague requests.

Their system retrieves in two stages. Dense vector search with modern embedding models gathers candidates. Then instruction-tuned language models, GPT-4o and Mistral-7B, rerank them by how well they fit the task. To evaluate fairly, the authors built a benchmark of Galaxy workflows labeled with topics from BERTopic and realistic task queries synthesized by language models. The two-stage approach significantly improved top-ranked accuracy and relevance in the first systematic study of Galaxy retrieval, and a prototype already runs inside Galaxy.
arxiv-2511-02557:
Yao-Bei Liu and Jing-Wei Lian scope out what a future electron-positron collider could learn about heavy neutrinos, hypothetical particles predicted by many extensions of the Standard Model. Their machine is the Compact Linear Collider running at three tera-electron-volts, and the targets are Majorana neutrinos heavier than about one tera-electron-volt. Such a particle would decay in recognisable ways, and the authors study two in detector-level simulation.

In one channel the neutrino decays to a charged lepton and a W boson that merges into a single fat jet. In the other it decays to a light neutrino and a Higgs boson that appears as a tagged fat jet plus missing energy. From the simulations they draw exclusion and discovery limits for the neutrino's mass and its mixing with usual neutrinos. The collider's sensitivity to the mixing improves on hadron collider reaches by a hundredfold.
arxiv-2511-02657:
Phones and sensors can train a shared model together, but a few bad actors can poison the result. Lihan Xu and five colleagues study that threat, called Byzantine attack, in a 2025 federated learning paper. Their algorithm, Byrd-NAFL, adds Nesterov momentum at the central server to harden training while keeping each device simple.

Each worker just sends a rough gradient and holds no state, which suits devices that drop in and out. The authors prove the method settles in finite time for any momentum level below one, with no need for the gathered gradient to be unbiased. Tests on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Sentiment140 show faster training and higher accuracy than rival methods under many attacks.
arxiv-2511-02957:
Mohsin Mahmud Topu, Mahfuz Ahmed Anik, Azmine Toushik Wasi, and Md Manjurul Ahsan pair a digital twin with a graph neural network to watch road surfaces decay. Road networks fail in tangled, non-linear ways, and classic pavement systems mostly react after damage shows. Their 2025 framework models each road segment as a node and its links as edges, while drones, sensors, and LiDAR feed the twin live data.

The network learns decay patterns from that graph and forecasts distress, so crews can act early. On a realistic test set it beat baseline regressors, though its fit score stayed modest. A dashboard and a reinforcement learning module let managers simulate and adapt maintenance plans. The authors frame the loop as a base for smarter, greener pavement care.
arxiv-2511-03057:
Dev Pradeepkumar Nayak, Ali Tarokh, and Muhammad Saif Ullah Khalid compare two ways to move a robotic fish's tail. One drives it with a motor. The other lets it swing passively like a hinged fin. Fish swim superbly with body and tail working together, but whether a passive tail helps or hurts was unsettled. Their 2025 simulations use fluid-structure interaction at two flow speeds, varying joint stiffness, damping, and inertia.

Active tails made more thrust overall. At the lower speed, passive tails won on power use, and they stayed competitive in a few high-speed cases too. Wide swings helped only at high tail-beat frequency; wide swings from lighter, looser joints hurt. A steady tradeoff appeared: thrust and power pulled against each other. Small swimmers may gain from passive tails, larger ones from active control.
arxiv-2511-03157:
Yi Zhou, Chunyu Luo, Zhengren Wang, and Zhang-Hua Fu hunt the largest dense subgraph that also stays compact, with diameter at most two. Dense subgraph models like quasi-cliques find tight communities in networks. But the densest piece can be scattered or barely connected. Their 2025 paper demands both density, defined by a flexible edge-count rule, and short diameter, then solves the combined problem exactly.

Their branch-and-bound method first splits the graph into n smaller pieces under special orderings. It then searches each piece with a new sorting-based upper bound to prune dead ends. On 139 real-world graphs under two density rules, the method beat a mixed-integer solver and a plain branch-and-bound, solving nearly twice as many cases to proven optimality within an hour.
arxiv-2511-03957:
Yangyang Cheng, Zhenyu Li, Wanting Sun, and Guanghui Wang advance the Chen-Lih-Wu conjecture on equitable graph colouring, where colour classes must differ in size by at most one. Meyer's earlier conjecture and the strengthened Chen-Lih-Wu version list very few connected graphs that resist equitable colouring at the degree bound.

A refined Kierstead-Kostochka version replaces the degree bound with an Ore-type condition on edge endpoints. For any fixed positive constant and all large enough graphs, both conjectures hold whenever the colour count grows at least proportionally with graph size, the team prove. Their proof also yields a polynomial-time algorithm that decides equitable colourability in that regime.
arxiv-2511-04057:
Anastasia Bednyakova is the lead author among eight authors building a transformer model that predicts nonlinear pulse evolution inside erbium-doped fibre amplifiers when experimental data are scarce. Direct learning from measurements alone would starve the model, so training happens in two stages.

Pretraining uses a synthetic dataset from numerical simulations of amplifier dynamics. Fine-tuning then adapts the model with a small set of real measurements. The combined approach reproduces fine spectral structure seen in experiments across several regimes, including modulational instability and propagation of high-order solitons. Transfer learning of this kind lets simulation carry most of the training burden for optical systems.
arxiv-2511-04157:
Asma Yamani, Malak Baslyman, and Moataz Ahmed compare how twenty-three large language models rank responsible artificial intelligence values against two human groups, a United States representative sample and artificial intelligence practitioners. Models increasingly help with requirements, design, and evaluation in software work, so their value leanings carry practical weight.

Four tasks covered selecting key values, rating importance in context, resolving trade-offs, and prioritising requirements that embody values. Models aligned closer to practitioners than to the public sample, stressing fairness, privacy, transparency, safety, and accountability. Yet stated values in early tasks clashed with requirement choices later, a faithfulness gap. Human oversight in requirements work remains essential, the authors warn.
arxiv-2511-04357:
Maelic Neau, Zoe Falomir, Paulo E Santos, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, and Cedric Buche present GraSP-VLA, a neuro-symbolic framework that lets robot policies plan over long horizons. Vision-language-action models imitate skills end to end but lack high-level symbolic planning, while symbolic action learning generalizes and scales poorly on its own, leaving long tasks stranded between the two.

A continuous scene graph turns human demonstrations into a symbolic representation, from which new planning domains are generated at inference time. That symbolic layer orchestrates low-level vision-language-action policies, chaining more actions in a row than imitation alone manages. Modelling results and real-world robot experiments show the representation can indeed coordinate extended task sequences effectively.
arxiv-2511-04457:
Jaime Gonzalez-Hodar and two colleagues tackle ranking and selection when no new data can be gathered. Managers must pick the best option while the input distributions stay uncertain. Their procedure, NIOU-C, builds a confidence set that holds the true optimum with a chosen probability.

An ambiguity set of input distributions comes from empirical likelihood methods. Each solution's mean performance is then written as a linear functional of those inputs. Worst-case pairwise gaps inside the set mark which solutions cannot be told from the best. The authors also give sample size rules for the method to stay valid.
arxiv-2511-04657:
Jasper Kranias and three colleagues analyze photodetection of squeezed light with Whittaker-Shannon tools. Their decomposition describes squeezed light in time-localized pieces, even in the continuous-wave limit. Squeezing strength can then be counted by photon pairs present at a moment.

Worked examples show the payoff across three classic setups. They compute quadrature variance for homodyne detection and coincidence rates in the continuous limit. The Hong-Ou-Mandel effect for strongly squeezed light is also treated. One finding stands out: pair correlation effects peak at weak squeezing, while variance dips lowest at strong squeezing.
arxiv-2511-04857:
Rosanne Di Stefano and two colleagues extend common envelope modeling from pairs to triple stars. Many stars live in triples, where unstable mass transfer can wrap the system in shared gas. Predicting the orbits that emerge afterward is the hard part.

Their SCATTER formalism computes post-envelope separations for all the stars involved. It also judges whether the envelope forces mergers now or makes them inevitable later. The outcomes feed straight into big questions in astrophysics. Gravitational-wave mergers and Type Ia supernovae both trace back to such multiple-star interactions, so triple-aware models fill a real gap.
arxiv-2511-04957:
Bruno Fava studies how to train and test a predictive model on the same data set without fooling oneself. Split-sample work avoids bias by using one part to fit and one part to judge, but each part is then small and scores swing by split.

Fava averages across many splits, which uses more data for training and the whole set for testing, with steadier results. He proves a central limit theorem for the averaged estimator, which handles the links made when points recur across splits. The theorem gives a firm base for sound error bars.
arxiv-2511-05057:
Yuanxiang Huangfu, Chaochao Wang, and Weilei Wang present Role-SynthCLIP, a way to make synthetic image-text pairs with richer meaning. CLIP models learn from such pairs, but past synthetic sets add bulk while their captions stay shallow and alike.

Role-SynthCLIP asks a large multimodal model to write captions from set roles, such as a layout analyst or a reader of scene context. Each role sees the image in a fresh way, so captions vary more and match fine detail better. The result is training data with broader sense and tighter image-text fit.
arxiv-2511-05157:
T. Fastnedge and co-authors model a branched channel filter meant to catch microplastic fibers shed by clothes in wash cycles. Such fibers make up a large share of primary microplastics in the sea, and plain dead-end filters clog fast.

Their ricochet idea copies how manta rays feed. Some fluid slips through side branches while fibers bounce off walls back into the main flow, then reach the end filter. Using a multi-scale frame for a simple branch layout under fast flow, they work out how well such a filter can sort fibers with less clogging.
arxiv-2511-05257:
Quentin Peres shows how an SU(n) structure can pass to a quotient space when a torus acts on a Kähler manifold in a Hamiltonian, holomorphic way. The source space starts with a larger SU structure, and the quotient is the space left after the symmetry is divided out.

The transfer works if a set of special one-forms, called twist forms, exists on the source. Peres then applies the result to projective spaces, to cones over Fano Kähler-Einstein manifolds, and to toric bundles. A final part studies the case of three complex dimensions in depth.
arxiv-2511-05357:
Mikhail Tsukerman and co-authors use a conditional diffusion model to design scattering structures straight from a target pattern, with no slow loop of trial and error. The task is inverse: given how a surface should scatter waves, find a shape that does it.

Their 1D U-Net, guided by feature-wise modulation, maps a wanted angular pattern to a small dielectric sphere array. Trained on eleven thousand simulated surfaces, it gives many valid designs for one target, which suits a task with many right answers. Test errors beat the baselines they compare.
arxiv-2511-05457:
Merin Joseph and co-authors give a flexible code form of strong segregation theory for two-dimensional ABC star terpolymers, plastics whose three arms meet at one core point. In the strong segregation limit, the arms split into sharp zones whose shapes set the material's traits.

Their method computes free energies for common two-dimensional forms and builds phase diagrams with speed. Star branch points sit in core zones, modeled as cylinders, and the frame covers forms with one or many core types. Fast phase maps help chemists pick mixes that yield a wanted nano pattern.
arxiv-2511-05657:
Arnau Bas i Beneito, Svjetlana Fajfer, and Alexey Petrov look for baryon number violation in a new place: oscillations between lambda baryons and their antimatter twins. The known case is the neutron flipping into an antineutron. A lambda contains a strange quark, so its oscillation involves a different set of six-quark operators.

Working in an effective theory, the authors classify the operators that can drive such changes and study models that produce them. In those models lambda oscillations can occur directly, while neutron oscillations appear only in higher-order loops. Using limits from neutron searches and dinucleon decays, they bound the lambda mixing. The channel probes fresh parameter space, though beating current indirect bounds looks hard.
arxiv-2511-05757:
Hassan Iqbal and co-authors present a control framework that adapts to new machines without retraining. Their system pairs two parts. A function encoder neural model learns how a whole family of nonlinear systems evolves, so it can describe a new system on first sight. A differentiable predictive controller then learns control policies offline, by self-teaching.

Classical predictive control solves a costly optimization online at every step. Here the policy is learned across system settings in advance, so deployment is fast. The authors test the method on a range of nonlinear systems under varied parameters. They report strong efficiency, accuracy, and online adaptability, and pitch it as a general tool for fast adaptive control.
arxiv-2511-06357:
Nassim Athmouni computes exactly where the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff series stops converging in a family of non-associative algebras. That series combines two exponentials into one and appears across physics and numerical methods. The setting is special Banach-Malcev algebras of shifts, meaning algebras that fit inside an alternative algebra with a working size measure.

Under a simple bound on how large commutators can grow, Athmouni proves the series converges absolutely inside an explicit radius set by that bound and the series coefficients. A Catalan-number majorization produces the constant, which is sharp in the exponential-weight model. Concrete values are worked out for five shift algebra families, including the split-octonionic case, and the radius also controls integrator stability.
arxiv-2511-06457:
Shaoxiang Wang and co-authors erase unwanted objects from full three-hundred-sixty-degree scenes captured as Gaussian splats. Filling holes in a single forward-facing view is now routine, but panoramic scenes add three headaches. They must find the target object in three dimensions, untangle heavy overlaps, and keep every viewing angle consistent afterward.

Their framework, Inpaint360GS, lifts two-dimensional segmentation into the three-dimensional field to mark objects precisely. Virtual camera views supply context that guides the fill, so removed regions complete plausibly and coherently. A new dataset with known object-free ground truth supports fair testing, an ingredient the field lacked. Experiments show the method beating existing baselines with state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2511-06657:
Eunseok Hwang, Heamin Ko, Myung-Ki Cheoun, and Dukjae Jang rebuild the energy window used to compute laser-driven fusion rates. Lasers blasting a target create plasma far from equilibrium, so the ions' energies are not Maxwellian. Analysts still often borrow the thermal Gamow window, a habit this work shows can mislead yield estimates.

For ions accelerated by target normal sheath acceleration, the authors couple a self-similar plasma expansion model to a closed-form rate calculation. The effective reaction window and fusion reactivity come out systematically different from thermal predictions. The framework gives experimenters a quantitative basis for reading fusion yields and for designing laser-driven nuclear reaction setups.
arxiv-2511-06857:
Fanding Li and eight co-authors work on medical image segmentation where experts truly disagree, such as outlining tumors in scans. A good system should produce several plausible outlines, both accurate and diverse. Their method, Ambiguity-aware Truncated Flow Matching, redesigns how the system generates its answers to separate those two goals instead of trading them off.

A data-hierarchical scheme improves accuracy at the distribution level and diversity at the sample level. A Gaussian truncation representation replaces sampling approximations with an explicit distribution, raising fidelity, and a segmentation flow matching step keeps the varied predictions plausible. On the LIDC and ISIC3 data sets the method beat leading alternatives, improving key scores by up to about twelve percent while running more efficiently.
arxiv-2511-06957:
Markus Penz, Michael F Herbst, Trygve Helgaker, and Andre Laestadius write a review of a mathematical tool, Moreau-Yosida regularization, and its many roles inside density-functional theory. Density-functional theory computes how a substance behaves from electron density rather than the full wavefunction, and the regularization smooths its central functionals. That smoothing both reformulates the theory and gives the Kohn-Sham approach, its workhorse computational scheme, a mathematically well-defined foundation.

The regularization also appears in density-potential inversion schemes, which recover potentials from target densities. Through the choice of topology on the spaces of densities and potentials, it connects to classic field theories. The review collects these uses in one place, maps how they relate, and outlines where the tool could develop next, offering experts a unified view of a tool scattered across the literature.
arxiv-2511-07857:
Wei Wang proves a universal fitting result once for many network designs. Deep designs keep multiplying, and each new one usually needs its own proof that it can approximate any sensible function. Split proofs waste effort and hide what the designs share.

A general method supplies a common foundation across fully connected networks, convolutional networks, Transformers, and more. New designs can inherit the result by checking shared conditions rather than starting over. Unified theory helps researchers see which parts grant expressive power. That clarity can steer design toward features that matter.
arxiv-2511-07957:
Cunshi Wang, Zuke Feng, and Difan Yi teach a CubeSat to spot gamma-ray bursts on board. The Cosmic X-ray Polarization Detector prototypes technology for a larger polarization mission, and its wide field of view floods it with background. Real-time burst identification must separate cosmic flashes from that noise with tiny computing power.

A language-model-based identifier, trained on Geant4-simulated spectra mixing background and burst events, does the sorting in orbit. Catching bursts live lets the satellite react and alert others while the flash lasts. Small satellites doing their own event triage multiply the value of wide-field sky monitors.
arxiv-2511-08257:
Angelo Passariello and co-authors add random energy backscatter to hybrid turbulence simulations inside a compressible flow solver. Hybrid methods blend mean and eddy resolving methods, but a grey area appears where neither account fully controls the flow. Careful treatment of the convective terms is needed to keep dissipation and dispersion acceptable without rewriting the current mean solver.

A blending strategy mixes non lossy and strongly lossy discretizations to improve stability. Calibration uses decaying isotropic homogeneous turbulence, a classic test case. The method then reduces the grey area in a mixing coflow test: an airfoil wake at zero angle of attack meeting a flat plate turbulent boundary layer.
arxiv-2511-08457:
Qian Wang, Suhaib Ardah, Tom Reddyhoff, and Daniele Dini build a computational setup for friction at soft lubricated interfaces where surface roughness spans many scales. Soft contacts couple thin film fluid flow with nonlinear solid deformation, and classic half space models miss parts of that interaction. Their modular setup combines Persson statistical roughness theory with a deterministic conjugate gradient Fourier method for surface response.

A reduced stiffness method rigorously models how pressure deforms the surface, replacing the weaker classic assumptions. Optimal solvers keep realistic configurations tractable, from direct solid contact to full fluid separation. Tests on rough elastomer glass interfaces validate the simulated transition between those regimes, showing how roughness and material softness jointly drive frictional conduct.
arxiv-2511-08557:
Fernanda Alves Caixeta and Keti Tenenblat study a special family of surfaces in Euclidean space called Laguerre isotropic hypersurfaces. For these surfaces the Laguerre form vanishes and the eigenvalues of the Laguerre tensor stay constant, conditions that sharply restrict the shapes allowed.

The main result is a rigidity theorem covering the surfaces that are parametrized by their lines of curvature. When a surface is both isotropic and isoparametric in this sense, the authors show the constant eigenvalue must be zero. They also give conditions that any example with a positive eigenvalue must satisfy. A function built from the radii of curvature turns out to have a firm upper bound.
arxiv-2511-08657:
Rakesh Saini and three co-authors fix a frustrating choice in quantum optimization: the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm needs its circuit depth set in advance, with little guidance on what value works. Their variant grows the depth on its own, starting shallow and deepening only as convergence criteria demand.

Learned parameters pass from each shallower circuit to the next deeper one, so work is reused rather than restarted. On one hundred instances of the Constrained Shortest Path Problem, at ten and sixteen qubits, the dynamic method beats fixed-depth runs on approximation quality and success probability. It also uses far fewer two-qubit gate evaluations, since standard runs at high depth needed more than twice the gate count for similar results.
arxiv-2511-08757:
Alex Rose proves finite-field versions of Bourgain's projection theorem, a result about how sets look when projected onto lines and planes. Projection theorems sit at the meeting point of geometry and combinatorics, and moving them to finite fields changes the tools available and the statements that can hold.

The new results live in higher dimensions and cover a range of parameters where earlier bounds were weaker. In particular, Rose improves the exceptional set estimate due to Chen in every dimension and codimension within that range. Exceptional sets collect the directions where a projection behaves worse than expected, so shrinking their possible size strengthens the whole theorem. The paper is a technical contribution to finite-field incidence geometry, written for specialists in harmonic analysis and additive combinatorics.
arxiv-2511-08857:
Cleverson Andrade Goulart, Gleb Oshanin, and Mauricio Porto Pato follow what happens to a random matrix ensemble when a small dose of non-Hermiticity pushes its eigenvalues off the real line. The ensemble is an unstable cousin of the beta-Laguerre ensemble, a workhorse of random matrix theory with a tunable repulsion parameter.

Breaking the symmetry drives eigenvalues into the complex plane as conjugate pairs, and the authors derive analytic formulas for the curves those pairs trace. The pairs organize into a balloon-like structure, trailed by a finite line of eigenvalues that stay real. Large matrix-size asymptotics are worked out, and numerical simulations back the theory. The beta-Hermite case under symmetry breaking was already understood; this study closes the matching Laguerre gap for PT-symmetric style models.
arxiv-2511-09057:
The PAN Team and fourteen co-authors introduce PAN, a world model meant to simulate how worlds evolve on their own and under an agent's actions. With it, the agent can plan by rehearsing futures internally. Video tools and game simulators have advanced quickly, but general, open-domain, action-driven prediction over long horizons remains unsolved.

PAN rests on the Generative Latent Prediction architecture. Stateful latent encodings of world states and an encoder-decoder loop keep information flowing. A mixed reasoning backbone combines a language model with diffusion. A rebuild objective, whose fidelity can be damped, trades fine detail against semantic salience. Against several existing systems, PAN shows advantages in action-conditioned runs, long-range foresight, and planning by rehearsal. The authors argue those abilities, not video quality alone, should define how world models are judged.
arxiv-2511-09857:
Xiaokang Wang proves structure theorems for two related kinds of geometric spaces: locally conformally flat orbifolds with positive Yamabe invariant, and ALE manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature. The two families connect through conformal blow-up and compactification, so results can move between them. Orbifolds allow mild singularities, while ALE spaces flatten out at infinity in a controlled way.

Wang shows such orbifolds admit a manifold cover, and that the map of fundamental groups induced by an ALE end is always injective. These facts yield classifications in low dimensions and settle a moduli question: one named football orbifold cannot arise as a Gromov-Hausdorff limit. The paper also proves a positive mass theorem for these ends and solves the orbifold Yamabe problem in the locally conformally flat case.
arxiv-2511-10057:
Makoto Kawashima, writing alone, builds new Padé approximants for a product that past work had not handled head-on: a binomial term times powers of a log term. A Padé approximant fits a function with a ratio of two polynomials, and clean forms were known for each factor on its own. Products of this kind show up in proofs about which numbers can be linked by simple ratios.

The main result gives new bounds on how well such linked forms can be cut off from zero, for many index pairs at once. The bounds hold with algebraic weights in both the plain complex case and the p-adic case. Kawashima also shows that Padé fits of a single polylog are, in general, perfect.
arxiv-2511-10457:
Kiamehr Rezaee, Jose Camacho-Collados, and Mohammad Taher Pilehvar test how well large language models keep track of changing states. State tracking means following several entities as their properties change step by step, a skill many reasoning tasks quietly depend on. To isolate that skill, the team built a benchmark from three precisely defined tracking tasks.

Recent models such as GPT-4 and Llama3 tracked state fairly well, especially when allowed to reason step by step in a chain of thought. Older models understood the tasks and solved the early steps, but their tracking broke down as sequences grew longer. The results separate genuine tracking ability from general task understanding and show where current models still lose the thread.
arxiv-2511-10857:
Seyedeh Mobina Noorani, Shangde Gao, Changjie Chen, and Karla Saldana Ochoa build a planning support system that redraws the map for disaster preparation. Census tracts and zip codes rarely match what a community actually needs during a hazard, and they cannot flex as conditions change, so the authors generate demand-oriented regions instead.

The platform pairs agentic AI with a spatially constrained self-organizing map that has adaptive geographic filtering and region-growing refinement. The agents suggest input features, guide the spatial constraints, and support interactive exploration, while a human stays in the loop for transparency. A case study on flood risk in Jacksonville, Florida shows users generating and evaluating alternative regionalizations interactively. The authors argue the combination offers both computational rigor and user-driven judgment.
arxiv-2511-10957:
Allana Tavares Bastos, Tiago Alves Schieber, and their colleagues offer a new clue for spotting fraud in public buying. Their case is Brazil's public health system, where firms bid to supply medical goods and some may collude in secret. Standard checks can miss the joint patterns that such collusion leaves in the bid network.

Their measure, named for Heron, scores how far a small part of the network strays from the whole shape. On more than eight years of bid data it flagged collusive patterns, and tests with fake data backed the result. The authors stress it should aid, not replace, legal and economic review.
arxiv-2511-11057:
Kotaro Kimura and Tomohiro I revisit r-enum, a method that lists key repeated patterns inside a text string while using only compact memory. The method works from a compressed form of the string and lists repeats such as maximal repeats. Its cost grows with text length plus the number of patterns found, which suits very large strings.

The authors first cut a slow term in the running time down to a clean linear bound. They then extend the method to rarer repeat types and to a count of varied contexts for each maximal repeat. A new net count, for repeats not covered by others, can also be listed in linear time and compact space.
arxiv-2511-11157:
Francis Bloch, Bhaskar Dutta, and Marcin Dziubiński study how a planner can pick one agent when the trait that matters is known to the agents but hidden from the planner. Agents are linked as friends, enemies, or neutrals, and each most wants to be picked, then a friend, then a neutral, and least of all an enemy. The planner needs a rule that makes honest reports the best strategy.

The authors give conditions for an efficient, honesty-proof rule when the planner knows the friendship network. Without that knowledge, no such rule exists, so they compare two second-best rules. For balanced networks, where friendships and enmities fit a clean pattern, they give sharp results.
arxiv-2511-11357:
Haixin Li, Yanke Li, and Diego Paez-Granados introduce KarmaTS, an interactive platform for building causal simulations of multivariate time series. Access to real physiological data is often restricted, so synthetic series with known causal structure are valuable for testing discovery methods. KarmaTS lets users construct lag-indexed causal graph models that can actually be run as simulations.

Expert knowledge and algorithmic proposals combine in a human-in-the-loop workflow to form a structural causal process. That process supports simulation and interventions, even under user-set distribution shifts. Mixed variable types, same-time and lagged links, and edge functions from templates to neural networks make the platform a flexible testbed.
arxiv-2511-11857:
Taimur Khan, Ramoza Ahsan, and Mohib Hameed propose a three-stage framework for automated narrative analysis of movie scripts, tackling a long-standing natural language challenge: stories carry meaning at many levels at once. Their stages move from sentiment arcs, through structure learning, to concept detection.

Dictionary-based sentiment analysis with a custom lexicon built from the LabMT story lab tools traces how a plot's emotional tone rises and falls, with attention to the characters involved. Higher and lower level concepts conveyed by the narrative are extracted on top of that structure. At modern data volumes, manual story analysis cannot scale, so frameworks that recover plot shape and theme computationally serve media researchers and archives.
arxiv-2511-11957:
Rory Barnes and seven co-authors publish version 1.1 of the FILLET protocol, a community plan for running identical experiments through many different energy balance climate models of exoplanets. Energy balance models are fast, simplified climate tools, but each code carries private assumptions that can quietly drive its answers.

Standard experiments, Earth-like planets at varied tilt, starlight, and carbon dioxide levels, let the community separate genuine model differences from setup noise and produce ensemble averages instead of single-model claims. The update widens the original protocol's reach. For a field hunting habitable worlds with simple models, shared benchmarks are how results become trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-12057:
Ashwin Gerard Colaco and five co-authors propose GenIE, a system that brings physics simulators inside a database instead of treating them as a separate first step. Today analysts must run a simulation by hand, export the results, and load them before any query can start. That slow chain blocks quick, iterative exploration.

GenIE, built as an extension to PostgreSQL, calls simulators on demand with settings drawn from the user query. It can skip data the query does not need, reuse data already made, and refine results step by step at interactive speed. Use cases cover wildfire smoke spread and hurricane wind, surge and flood risk.
arxiv-2511-12157:
Jonathan Chirinos-Rodríguez, Cédric Févotte and Emmanuel Soubies study sparse recovery problems where a signal is found by penalizing the number of nonzero entries. Exact continuous relaxations can keep the true global solutions while removing some false local ones. Their focus is a family built with Bregman distances.

The authors give conditions under which a critical point stands alone in sparsity, meaning any other critical point uses strictly more nonzero entries. They also study when the solution that shares the true support is the unique global minimizer. Their analysis rests on a new property they call Bregman restricted strong convexity, and they apply the results to sparse Gaussian cases among others.
arxiv-2511-12257:
Elhadji Cisse Faye and three co-authors build a Bayesian sampling method for Poisson inverse problems, where noisy counts must be turned back into an underlying signal. Poisson likelihoods pose hard issues: sharp gradients and a need to keep values positive. Standard Euclidean geometry fits the problem poorly.

Their framework uses data augmentation with splitting variables derived from a Bregman divergence based on Burg entropy. The augmented posterior then has conditional distributions with natural conjugacy that respect the geometry of the variables. Most Gibbs steps can be done in closed form. For the step tied to the prior, they use a geometry-aware Langevin sampler that runs on a mirror space.
arxiv-2511-12557:
Kamlesh Bora and five co-authors simulate structured upflows rising from plumes in coronal holes on the Sun, a possible source of the solar wind. Small jet-like events at plume roots may drive those outflows, but their magnetic origin is unclear. The team runs three-dimensional radiative simulations spanning from below the visible surface up into the low corona.

They synthesize iron emission that can be compared with observations and track plasma flows, heat structure and magnetic topology together. A sharp transition appears at the boundary of like-polarity flux patches, from cool downflows below to hot upflows above. The upflows run along a filamentary network of quasi-separatrix layers, and the average mass flux exceeds observed solar wind loss rates.
arxiv-2511-12757:
Nicholas Karris, Luke Durell, Javier Flores, and Tegan Emerson rethink how to blend between two text prompts in Stable Diffusion. The CLIP embeddings that guide image generation have a symmetry: shuffling the rows of the embedding matrix changes nothing. That suggests embeddings are better viewed as point clouds than as fixed grids. Under that view, moving from one prompt to another is an optimal transport problem, and the shortest path between the two clouds should give the most natural transition between the two images.

Experiments support the idea. Images interpolated along the transport path looked smoother and more coherent than those from standard interpolation methods. The authors argue the point-cloud picture better matches the true geometry of embedding space and puts it to work. For artists, the method promises intermediate frames that pass through plausible images instead of muddy blends.
arxiv-2511-12957: Joseph T. A. Peterson, Manoranjan Majji, and John L. Junkins recast orbital motion using closed-form Kepler answers written in projective coordinates. From those answers they define eight orbit elements and derive the rules that govern them for two-body motion with arbitrary perturbations. The elements stay free of singularities except in straight-line motion, where angular momentum vanishes. The classic case of a satellite perturbed by Earth's oblateness, the J2 effect, is worked out in the new variables and used to check the formulation numerically.
arxiv-2511-13157:
Yi Pan and Bo-Chao Liu work out which excited states of the lambda hyperon drive a particular photon-producing reaction. When a negative kaon strikes a proton and a photon and a sigma hyperon emerge, the intermediate steps pass through lambda resonances, and different resonances dominate at different energies. Using an effective Lagrangian in an isobar model, with s-channel hyperon exchanges, t-channel kaon exchanges, u-channel proton and Delta exchanges. With a contact term included, the authors fit the available data.

Their answer is layered. The Lambda(1600) resonance is crucial at lower energies. At higher energies the fit improves significantly with either the Lambda(1670) or the Lambda(1690), but current data cannot tell which of the two is responsible. The authors prescribe the remedy: measurements at higher beam energies and of the sigma polarization.
arxiv-2511-13657:
Nitish Kumar Chandra, Eneet Kaur, and Kaushik P. Seshadreesan compare three architectures for fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing by their entanglement costs. Modular quantum hardware must link small nodes with shared entanglement to run protected computations. The three designs differ in how they share measurements: through GHZ states, through nonlocal gates at code patch edges, or through operations between whole code blocks.

Using the planar surface code and the toric code as test cases, they track how the needed Bell pairs and generation attempts grow with code distance in each design. The scaling picture helps builders judge which architecture fits near-term hardware limits and scarce network resources best.
arxiv-2511-13857:
Muhammed Can Keles, Bedrettin Cetinkaya, Sinan Kalkan, and Emre Akbas improve how computers find human body joints in images. Standard training uses a loss that treats every pixel error the same, which can blur the peak that marks a joint, and it does not match the score used to judge results. The authors propose ranking-based losses instead.

Models trained with the new losses, which they call RSPose, tie confidence scores more tightly to how well each joint is placed. That link improves selection between rival detections and raises final accuracy. On the COCO test set RSPose set a new best mark with a large vision transformer, and it also lifted a coordinate-based method by a clear margin.
arxiv-2511-14257:
Bannanje Ananthamoorthy, Debbijoy Bhattacharya, and P. Sreekumar ask whether active galactic nuclei can boost, rather than suppress, star formation at a galaxy's edges. Evidence on feedback in non-jetted galaxies is thin. Using ultraviolet images from AstroSat's UVIT and GALEX, they studied the outskirts of six barred spiral galaxies hosting active nuclei and four similar galaxies without them.

Star-forming knots in the active hosts showed higher star formation rate density, fading more slowly with radius than in the comparison galaxies. Ultraviolet dimming by dust was also stronger and flatter in the active hosts. The authors suggest radiation pressure or wind-driven feedback from even faint nuclei may be enhancing outskirt star formation.
arxiv-2511-14357:
Hoang Chuong Nguyen, Wei Mao, Jose M. Alvarez, and one co-author sharpen 3D Gaussian splatting by borrowing detail from the original photos. Splatting renders new views quickly, but its low-degree color model misses fine texture and view-dependent shine. Global textures wash out in complex scenes, while per-primitive textures cost too much storage.

Their image-based variant computes each pixel as a base splatting color plus a learned residual inferred from neighboring training images. That design ties colors to the actual surface and restores high-frequency detail and specular effects. On standard novel-view benchmarks the method clearly beat earlier splatting approaches while adding no storage overhead, since the source images already exist in the pipeline.
arxiv-2511-14657:
Ilario Bonacina, Maria Luisa Bonet, Sam Buss, and Massimo Lauria build a structured family of proof systems for MaxSAT, the optimization version of the satisfiability problem. In SAT, redundancy rules let solvers add clauses that do not change the answer but make proofs far more powerful. Similar rules have recently been adapted to MaxSAT by several groups.

The authors define MaxSAT versions of known systems such as SPR, PR, and SR, ordered into a clear hierarchy. Every rule can be checked in polynomial time, unlike some earlier work, and the rules stay simple enough that lower bounds may be within reach. The framework sharpens the study of how hard MaxSAT proofs must be.
arxiv-2511-14857:
Garv Chauhan and Cecilia Lunardini show that dying stars could leave a glowing echo that reveals new particles. When a massive star collapses, its hot core may create heavy particles beyond the Standard Model. Those particles can decay in the outer layers and produce positrons, which then slow down and meet electrons.

Each meeting can release gamma rays at a fixed energy, forming a delayed echo after the blast. For axion-like particles, the authors use old satellite data from Supernova 1987A to set limits on how strongly such particles link to light. They also forecast what planned telescopes could see from a future nearby supernova.
arxiv-2511-15257:
Hiep Hong Trinh, Federico Ciccozzi, and three co-authors present M, a toolchain and language for compiling one system model into many specialized forms. Engineers of software-driven physical systems need simulations, deployment code, and verification models, each in its own formalism. Deriving each by hand from the master model invites drift and error.

A model compiler should generate all targets from one source, the way a program compiler emits code, yet most modeling tools lock onto a single target. M is designed for reusable compilation across heterogeneous targets, so a change to the source model flows into every derived form. The work targets the model-driven engineering of complex distributed and physical systems.
arxiv-2511-15357:
Yinan Yu, Falk Dippel, and five co-authors build a heart failure mortality predictor that shows clinicians the price of being wrong, not just the odds. Models are usually delivered as bare risk scores, leaving the trade-offs among quality of life, treatment cost, and error cost invisible. The cost-aware framework here wraps the model in a decision support system for choosing which patients get home care.

Trained on records of tens of thousands of patients, the model forecasts one-year mortality. Clinical impact projection curves then map predictions onto cost dimensions patients and providers actually feel. Four language model agents draft patient-specific explanations of those trade-offs. The design treats a prediction as the start of a decision conversation, not its end.
arxiv-2511-15457:
Ziheng Su and Huifu Xu revisit when a Bayesian Nash equilibrium exists, is unique, and stays stable. In such an equilibrium, each player acts on private information, called a type, and no one gains by changing strategy alone. Earlier work proved existence and uniqueness separately, using different tools and extra conditions on how players respond to each other.

Su and Xu prove existence and uniqueness together with a single fixed-point theorem under moderate conditions. They require players best responses to behave in a continuous and monotone way. They also show the equilibrium changes in a stable way when the shared distribution of types is perturbed, which supports using such models with real data.
arxiv-2511-15657:
Lucas Kotz and four co-authors systematically explore how parametrization choices affect pion parton distributions extracted from global data. Parton distributions describe momentum carried by quarks and gluons inside hadrons. Flexible forms are needed, but form choice can bias uncertainty estimates. Their Fantômas tool automates generation of polynomial parametrizations using Bézier curves inside a fitting program.

Applied to the charged pion, the analysis reveals strong correlation between sea quark and gluon distributions. Solutions with vanishing gluon and a large quark sea remain allowed by current data. That degeneracy shows true uncertainties are larger than single parametrization fits suggest. The automated tool lets analysts sample many functional forms. Better uncertainty accounting is vital for hadron structure physics.
arxiv-2511-15757:
Kareem Shehada and six co-authors rethink automated repair for the Linux kernel with a benchmark and pipeline called RGym. Language models have transformed program repair for user applications, but kernel debugging is harder. Monolithic structure, concurrency, and hardware interaction set kernel work apart. Prior kernel efforts reported low success or needed costly cloud pipelines.

RGym is a lightweight evaluation framework that runs on local commodity hardware. Its repair pipeline uses call stacks and blamed commits for localization instead of unrealistic oracles. Tests run on a filtered, verified set of kernel faults. The design aims for realistic, affordable evaluation. Better kernel repair tools could cut maintainer burden for critical infrastructure software.
arxiv-2511-16757:
Wei-Cheng Tseng and five co-authors run the first principled study of audio-language pretraining as a route to general-purpose audio representations. Whether pairing audio with text can yield one encoder good at speech, music, and environmental sound was unsettled, with corpus scale, caption coverage, and objective choice all murky.

They first assemble CaptionStew, a dataset of more than ten million audio captions aggregated across domains and captioning styles. Then they compare contrastive and captioning objectives across tasks and scales. Audio-language pretraining does produce competitive, transferable representations, with a clear trade-off: contrastive learning is more data efficient, while captioning scales better. Supervised initialization, a common habit, helped less as scale grew. The study charts a viable path toward general audio encoders.
arxiv-2511-16857:
Vineet Bhat and eight co-authors present BOP-ASK, a large dataset and benchmark for object-interaction reasoning in vision-language models. Current spatial benchmarks test coarse relations like left of or behind, while real applications need precise three-dimensional localization, physical compatibility, affordances, and multi-step planning around objects.

The generation pipeline harvests six-dimensional object poses from established pose estimation datasets and derives fine-grained annotations: grasp poses, referred object poses, path planning trajectories, and depth and object-to-object relations. The result spans over a hundred fifty thousand images and thirty-three million question-answer pairs across six tasks. Models trained on BOP-ASK beat baselines and showed emergent skills such as precise grasp pose estimation and trajectory planning in clutter. A companion out-of-distribution benchmark tests generalization beyond the source images.
arxiv-2511-17857:
Krista Schoonover and three co-authors study how ordered melts of block copolymers, plastics made of linked blocks that separate into tiny repeating domains, relax and resist stretching over long times. Most prior work covers short and medium times, not the near equilibrium response.

Using a field theory that gives equilibrium properties, they compute stiffness in different directions for layered, columnar, spherical, and gyroid patterns. They compare two block architectures and map how stiffness changes with design choices. Columnar phases bend far more stiffly than layered ones, a fact that matters for making durable thermoplastics.
arxiv-2511-18057:
Ahmed Gamal Eldin proposes that understanding works like a release of constraints across the whole body, not as computation in the brain alone. Standard models treat body signals as noise that corrupts neural work, but Eldin cites earlier results where removing those signals cut prediction sharply. Here he studies brain recordings from ten subjects doing a target recognition task, with hundreds of trials.

He reports patterns he reads as coupled resonance between brain and body, with causal influence running strongly both ways and peaking at the same early moment. A time-sliced entropy analysis is described in three phases, from constraint build-up to a sudden expansion he calls a transition. The paper presents a bold, testable framing; readers should note some reported effects sit near standard significance borders.
arxiv-2511-18457:
Duncan Stothers, Ben Stothers, Emily Schaeffer, and Kishore Mulpuri set a scan first policy for infant hip checks that saves X-ray use. A loose hip joint in babies, if missed, can harm gait for life. Ultrasound can screen most cases, yet X-rays give firmer measures. A policy that asks for X-ray only when the scan is unclear spares dose.

The team pre-train image encoders on large log sets of scans and films with no labels, then fit small heads for key hip measures. A calibrated rule, with a finite sample coverage pledge, decides when the scan alone is safe and when to defer to X-ray. Scan measure error stays modest in held out tests. Film based heads also track well. The flow aims to cut dose with no loss in catch rate.
arxiv-2511-18557:
Yacouba Diarra and six co-authors report hard lessons from building speech technology for Bambara, a West African language with few digital resources. Low-resource work lacks a base of shared experience, so the team documents its full pipeline. They collected over six hundred hours of spontaneous Bambara speech in the field, built a semi-automated transcription process for it, and trained several compact monolingual models on the result.

Both automatic and human judges scored the model output, and the authors stress how much the human checks mattered. Practical advice on collection protocols, annotation, and model design runs through the paper. The data set, extra evaluation sets, models, and code are all released in public, giving the next low-resource team a running start.
arxiv-2511-19157:
Weitao Liu introduces a new Kalman filter designed to estimate a system's state reliably when both the process driving the system and the measurements of it contain unmodeled noise and outliers. Classic filters assume clean noise statistics, so stray values can badly distort the estimate, a risk in tracking and control.
