The team instead uses administrative records for more than 2.7 million Chilean students from 2021 to 2024.

Machine learning sorted the students into seven archetypes, and the authors built an Educational Space charting each student by academic performance and family background. Students with equal ability followed sharply different paths depending on their origins. High-achieving, low-income students tended to stay at regional institutions, while wealthy peers moved freely across the country. Enrollment, career choice, and migration all bent along social lines. The framework scales to any country with similar records.
arxiv-2512-16657:
J. R. Silva, C. Antunis, and B. S. Santos ask how the memory of a surrounding bath shapes light moving through a single waveguide. A bath with memory does not forget at once, and its past states can feed back into the system, unlike the memory-free case.

The authors compare three memory shapes: Lorentzian, Gaussian, and uniform. For each they track how much light passes, when the guide turns clear, and how the system settles over long times. A score based on information flowing back in lets them rank how far each bath sits from the memory-free limit. The memory shape clearly shifts the passing bands and can boost or damp the memory effects.
arxiv-2512-17057:
Lyes Smaili and Soulaimane Berkane build smooth safety filters for nonlinear control systems that can only sense nearby, a common limit for drones and robots. Classic barrier-function filters assume the safety function is known everywhere and often switch harshly when limits engage.

Two designs answer that. One adds a smooth perception gate that scales barrier limits by sensing range, giving a closed-form controller with forward-invariance proof. The other swaps the hard barrier rule for a differentiable penalty, an unconstrained optimization filter in the same spirit. Both yield existence, uniqueness, and safety of closed-loop paths. Tests show far smoother, sturdier tracking for drones and ground robots than classic filters.
arxiv-2512-17257:
Iason Kyriakopoulos and Yannis Theodoridis compare ways to forecast how much power electric cars will draw from chargers. Grid managers need those forecasts, since a surge of charging at the wrong hour can strain the local network. Past studies often tested one method at one scale, which leaves planners guessing about the rest.

The pair test five forecasting models, from classic statistics to deep learning, on four public real-world data sets. They check short views of minutes, mid views of hours, and long views of days. They also zoom from a single station out to whole cities. Reporting each data set on its own, the study gives a broad map of which method wins at which scale.
arxiv-2512-17557:
The CMS Collaboration measures the spin links inside pairs of top quarks and antiquarks made in proton collisions at 13 TeV. The data were recorded from 2016 to 2018 and amount to 138 inverse femtobarns, with each pair rebuilt from an electron or muon plus jets.

The team reports the spin correlation coefficients in the beam basis. Joined with earlier results in the helicity basis, those numbers split the pair's quantum state into Bell states and spin eigenstates across several regions of the data. The same numbers yield the state's purity, its von Neumann entropy, and its entanglement. Every result agrees with standard model predictions, which makes top pairs a clean test bed for quantum behavior at the highest energies a lab can reach.
arxiv-2512-17657:
Ramaneswaran Selvakumar and four co-authors teach a speech recognizer to guess names it has never heard. Voice assistants stumble exactly there: a contact called Xochitl or a street name outside the training data comes out garbled. Given a candidate list, such as the user's contacts, the model should lean toward list words when the sound is close.

Their trick makes the model predict several tokens ahead at once, not just the next sound. Peeking ahead lets it score whole candidate names against the coming audio before committing. No extra name encoder or attention layer is bolted on, so the design stays lean. On the LibriSpeech benchmark, errors on named entities fell by up to 50.34 percent relative to the plain baseline.
arxiv-2512-17857:
Stéphane Lavignac and three coauthors hunt for heavy neutral leptons, ghost like particles also called sterile neutrinos, at the Large Hadron Collider. Such particles might explain why known neutrinos have mass. The team looks for pairs made in the decays of higgsinos, in a model with supersymmetry.

Their signal is a vertex that appears away from the collision point, a sign of a particle that traveled before decaying. Using ATLAS search tools and Run 2 data, they rule out masses from 20 to 230 GeV for a range of mixing strengths. The high luminosity upgrade could push the reach to 295 GeV and test even weaker mixing.
arxiv-2512-18957:
Debamita Ghosh, George K. Atia, and Yue Wang make reinforcement learning robust when the world shifts between training and deployment. Distributionally robust RL optimizes against the worst dynamics inside an uncertainty set, but earlier methods needed a simulator, big offline datasets, or tiny tabular worlds. Their algorithm, posted to arXiv in December 2025, learns purely by interacting, with general function approximation and no prior data.

A dual-driven fitted robust Bellman procedure estimates both the value function and the worst-case backup at once. The regret guarantees are organized by a new complexity measure, the robust Bellman-Eluder dimension, spanning a broad family of phi-divergence uncertainty sets. Crucially, the bounds are sublinear and do not grow with the size of the state or action spaces. Autonomous systems that must survive distribution shift, from robots to network controllers, need exactly this kind of scalable guarantee.
arxiv-2512-19057:
Guy Schacht, Ziyad Sheebaelhamd, Riccardo De Santi, and Mojmír Mutný cut the cost of teaching AI systems what a user likes. Preference learning needs many human judgments, and each judgment takes time and money. Their idea borrows from optimal experimental design, the study of which questions teach the most.

They frame query choice as maximizing information about the hidden reward model behind a user's taste. The framing yields a convex problem and an algorithm, ED-PBRL, with theory behind it and structured queries such as images or text. In a test that styled a text-to-image model to one user's taste, it needed fewer queries than random choice.
arxiv-2512-19257: Willem de Graaf, Alexander Elashvili, and Mamuka Jibladze classify sets of four spinors in ten dimensions, up to symmetry. The group Spin(10) and the group SL(4) act together on a tensor product of a half-spin module and the natural four-dimensional module. Using Vinberg's theory of theta-groups and the computer algebra system GAP4, the authors work out the list of orbits of that action. The result is a complete census of how such four-tuples of spinors can sit, which algebraic geometers use when sorting related classification problems.
arxiv-2512-19457:
Ho Yun recasts entropic optimal transport between Gaussian laws as a clean spectral operation. Optimal transport matches two distributions at least cost, and the entropic version smooths the match. On Hilbert spaces, with possibly degenerate Gaussians, the structure of the solution had stayed murky.

Using proper alignment and the Schur complement, Yun shows the optimal coupling simply shrinks the spectrum of the correlation operator by one universal scalar rule. That turns the usual iterative Sinkhorn loop into direct algebra: one decomposition prices every smoothing level at once. As smoothing vanishes, the limit selects the most diffusive among tied optimal couplings.
arxiv-2512-19757:
Alexander Marsteller heads a thirteen-author team with first results from a new experiment. The setup, called T2ApIR, sits at the Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe. It was built to measure the traits of tritium and its sibling forms of hydrogen. Checked data on tritium are oddly scarce. Yet fusion fuel work, cooling plants, and neutrino hunts all rest on them.

The cold apparatus can study all six hydrogen isotopologues. It handles their mixes in gas, liquid, and solid form. It also tracks how they change phase. Mixes with noble gases like xenon and neon can be studied too. Windows let light in for three kinds of optical checks. Gauges track heat and pressure at the same time. The paper describes the setup in its start-up phase.
arxiv-2512-19957:
Luciano Araujo Dourado Filho and three co-authors entered the PlantCLEF 2025 challenge. In it, one high-resolution photo of a vegetation plot can hold many plant species at once. Their method never trains on such plots head on. It first builds class prototypes. It clusters features from single-species training images to do so. Then it teaches a narrow segmentation transformer to rebuild those prototypes from plot images.

The transformer's patch layer is a frozen DINOv2 model. It was pretrained to classify single species. The attention scores it yields mark where each species likely sits. Those marks guide the final call on the plot. The system placed fifth on the private leaderboard. It sat close behind the winning entry. The code is public.
arxiv-2512-20157:
Sofian Chaybouti leads a nine-author team distilling two vision giants into one student family. Multi-teacher distillation promises unified visual representations. Yet its learning dynamics and data efficiency were unmapped. SigLino distills SigLIP2 and DINOv3 at once, into dense and mixture-of-experts students. The paper's payload is four findings on what makes such training cheap and strong.

A new loss keeps each teacher's geometry while it transfers knowledge. Token-balanced batching steadies learning across image resolutions. Clustering the training data, a trick from self-supervised work, beats random sampling on efficiency. The learned features transfer well into grounding vision-language models. The team releases a corpus of two hundred million images, OpenLVD200M. Five distilled checkpoints come with it.
arxiv-2512-20257:
Daniele Cardullo, Simone Teglia, and Irene Amerini built LADLE-MM, a detector for misinformation carried in image-text pairs. Existing detectors tend to be computationally heavy and hungry for annotated training data. LADLE-MM instead uses two single-modality branches plus a third branch that enriches both with embeddings from the BLIP vision-language model.

On the DGM4 benchmark, the detector stays competitive on binary and multi-label tasks while using far fewer trainable parameters than previous leaders. It performs best exactly in the limited-annotation setting it was designed for, where no grounding annotations are available. On the VERITE dataset it beats heavier state-of-the-art systems that rely on large vision-language models. Careful design, the results suggest, can substitute for brute scale.
arxiv-2512-20357:
R F dos Santos and S J J M F Kokkelmans make a standard quantum approximation dramatically cheaper. The Magnus expansion approximates how a driven quantum system evolves over short times by an effective static description. Higher-order terms capture more accuracy, but existing methods for computing them are expensive.

Their method uses the Lie algebra structure of the problem to cut the cost down to the size of the control function alone. The result is a polynomial expression for the expansion that evaluates orders of magnitude faster than previous techniques. The setting covers Hamiltonians with a constant drift plus a controllable term, common in practice. As a showcase, they design control pulses for a five-qubit phase gate on neutral Rydberg atoms.
arxiv-2512-20457:
Marco Aruta, Francesco Improta, Vadim Malvone, and Aniello Murano make strategic reasoning more human. Formal models of multi-agent systems usually assume agents use arbitrarily complex strategies, act for free, and see a crisp world. Real people use short rules, pay costs for actions, and perceive facts fuzzily.

Their logic, HumanATLF, builds on natural strategies written as concise guarded rules. Each action now carries a real-valued cost drawn from a budget that never refills, and facts and goals hold to degrees between zero and one. The authors pin down the complexity of model checking in several regimes. They implement the methods in an open tool, VITAMIN, and test them on an adversarial drone rescue scenario.
arxiv-2512-20557:
Shengchao Zhou and co-authors teach vision-language models to reason about a world that moves. Models ace static understanding yet stumble when object geometry and relationships evolve through time, largely because scalable four-dimensional training data barely exist. Their DSR Suite attacks the gap on three fronts: data, benchmark, and model.

An automated pipeline mines ordinary videos with modern vision foundation models, extracting camera poses, point clouds, masks, orientations, and three-dimensional trajectories. Those cues generate question-answer pairs for training and a human-refined benchmark for evaluation. A lightweight geometry selection module then feeds a vision-language model only the geometry tokens a question needs. Plugged into Qwen2.5-VL, the combination lifts dynamic spatial reasoning sharply while general video accuracy holds steady.
arxiv-2512-20657:
Martin Sterchi, Nathan Brack, and Lorenz Hilfiker ask who started the rumour and want it settled firmly. Source detection means finding the origin node of an epidemic spreading over a contact network, a problem set down by Shah and Zaman in 2010 with their rumor centrality measure. Graph neural networks have been proposed again and again, but sloppy, mismatched tests left their true standing unclear.

The authors first review the GNN papers in order, then reproduce four typical designs and race them against classic and multilayer-perceptron benchmarks under controlled conditions. They probe how detection holds up over time, training-set scaling, and response to timing and parameter uncertainty. The GNNs win by far across networks, a verdict the initially doubtful authors report plainly. All code and data are public for reproduction.
arxiv-2512-20757:
Gül Sena Altıntaş and six co-authors isolate a quiet design choice inside every language model: the tokenizer that chops text into pieces. Tokenizers differ widely, yet their effect is hard to measure because models usually differ in many other ways too. TokSuite removes those confounds.

The team trained fourteen models that are identical in architecture, data, budget, and starting point, differing only in tokenizer. They also built a robustness benchmark covering English, Chinese, Farsi, Italian, and Turkish, with real-world text disturbances checked by native speakers. Comparing the models reveals clear strengths and weaknesses among popular tokenizers. The suite gives future tokenizer designers a fair testing ground.
arxiv-2512-20957:
Zhaoxi Zhang, Yunfang Wu, and ten co-authors strip a coding agent down to one tool and show it beats crowded toolkits. Finding the files and functions behind a bug report in a huge repository is the task. Their agent, RepoNavigator, can do exactly one thing: jump to the definition of a symbol the code invokes, following the same path execution itself takes.

Trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning from a base model, with no distillation from closed systems, the agent learns to navigate by structure rather than by search tricks. Its seven-billion-parameter version outperforms fourteen-billion baselines, the mid-size version beats thirty-two-billion rivals, and the largest surpasses closed models such as GPT-5 on most metrics. One well-chosen, execution-aware tool can carry repository-level localization.
arxiv-2512-21357:
Roughly seventy known exoplanets sit at temperatures where liquid water could exist, and about fifty of them circle M-dwarfs, small stars prone to violent flares. Rebecca Szabó and colleagues ask whether such worlds can stay habitable under repeated ultraviolet and X-ray blasts. These nearby systems offer the best ratios for detailed follow-up, and Gaia and PLATO should soon add many more.

Rather than study the few dozen known hosts one by one, the authors call for a comprehensive survey of flaring exoplanet hosts and their activity, scaled for the hundreds of cases coming. They argue the proposed Wide Field Survey telescope fits that job. The answer decides whether the most common habitable-zone planets in the galaxy are plausible homes for complex life.
arxiv-2512-21457:
Faeq Abed, Asmaa AlMellah, and Gaber Faisel assess how well a future collider could spot a hidden sector of particles. Their study concerns FCC-ee, the electron-positron stage of the proposed Future Circular Collider. A Higgs boson decays into a pair of long-lived scalar particles, candidates connected to dark matter models.

The team simulates Higgs production alongside a Z boson at a collision energy of two hundred forty giga-electronvolts, using standard event generators and a detector simulation. The long-lived scalars travel some distance before decaying into bottom quark pairs, leaving displaced vertices. Their selection requires a reconstructed Z boson plus at least two displaced vertices, which suppresses ordinary backgrounds while keeping the signal. The analysis finds sensitivity to scalar decay lengths from about a millimeter to ten meters, showing FCC-ee could probe Higgs decays that present-day colliders would miss.
arxiv-2512-21657:
Angshul Majumdar studies the coalition structure generation problem: splitting a set of agents into groups so the welfare of all groups is as large as possible. The problem is a classic in multi-agent systems and economics, and exact solvers are slow because the number of possible groupings explodes.

Majumdar compares three algorithmic styles by their anytime behavior, meaning how good their answers are when stopped early. Dynamic programming and mixed-integer programming are exact but, he proves, need exponential time before reaching high-quality solutions in settings. Sparse relaxation methods, based on greedy or absolute-value penalties, behave oppositely under a random model where coalition values have sparse synergy. With high probability they recover structures whose welfare is arbitrarily close to optimal, in polynomial time. The result is a separation: for quick, near-optimal answers, sparse relaxations win, though exact methods remain best if allowed to finish.
arxiv-2512-21857:
Haodong Lei, Pan Zhou, and their co-authors speed up visual autoregressive image models, which generate an image token by token and can need around two thousand sequential steps. Speculative decoding accelerates text models by drafting several tokens and verifying them together, organized as a draft tree. Applied naively to images, it underperforms because prediction difficulty varies across an image.

The proposed method, ADT-Tree, makes the draft tree adaptive. Easy regions get deeper trees; hard regions get wider ones. It initializes the tree from horizontal adjacency information, then adjusts depth and width by bisection, guided by the acceptance rates of neighboring tokens and earlier rounds. On MS-COCO and PartiPrompts, the method achieved speedups slightly above threefold, and it composes with relaxed sampling for more. A face and a blank sky should not be drafted the same way.
arxiv-2512-22057:
The Royer law estimates alpha-decay half-lives with twelve parity-dependent parameters and drifts systematically near shell closures. Kai Ren, Pengfei Ma, Minghui Hu, and Junlong Tian revise it into a unified formula. A shell-correction term, an odd-even pairing indicator, and an orbital angular momentum term cut the free parameters to four.

Across five hundred fifty experimental data points, the root-mean-square deviation falls from about zero point five two to about zero point two eight, a near halving of error with two-thirds fewer parameters. The refined formula is then used to predict alpha-decay half-lives for superheavy nuclei, where measurements are scarce and reliable systematics guide experiments.
arxiv-2512-22157:
Nikolaj Maack Bielefeld proves reassuring traits of the zonal method, a classic technique for computing radiant heat exchange inside enclosures using Hottel's exchange factors. Engineers worry whether the method's balances always have a sensible answer, mainly when exchange factors come from Monte Carlo ray tracing and break the usual reciprocity symmetry. Bielefeld rewrites the balances in power variables as one linear system.

He proves the solution exists, is unique, and is never negative whenever at least one prescribed-temperature element absorbs radiation, and that energy is conserved exactly. Only mild conditions on the exchange factor matrix are needed. Both key traits follow from one discrete minimum principle and were machine-checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant. Textbook and published test cases confirm the formulation.
arxiv-2512-22257:
Dingyi Rong and six co-authors introduce LiveProteinBench, a benchmark for testing language models on protein science without the answers leaking into training data. Older benchmarks reuse stale test sets and skip multimodal questions. This one contains twelve tasks on protein property and function prediction, and its test proteins were all validated after the start of 2025, so no tested model could have memorized them.

Benchmarking general and biology-specialized models, the team found large proprietary models led in zero-shot accuracy, beating open and domain-specific rivals by over twenty percent. Adding structural images often failed to help and sometimes hurt, exposing weak multimodal fusion. Performance also tracked inference-time compute more than parameter count, underlining the value of chain-of-thought reasoning for protein questions.
arxiv-2512-22457:
Chansong Lim and four co-authors build a demo system that fills in railroad accident paperwork from news reports, in real time. After a highway-rail grade crossing incident, local railway committees need quick situational awareness, but official Federal Railroad Administration investigations take days to weeks. The system's target is the FRA's Form 57, the standard incident data form, which is visually irregular and semantically dense, while news text is noisy.

The pipeline first converts Form 57 into a JSON schema using a vision language model with sample aggregation. Grouped question answering then follows the form layout's intent, reducing ambiguity while extracting answers from articles. For evaluation, the team aligned scraped news with official FRA records and annotated what information was retrievable, then compared retrieval accuracy and coverage against alternatives.
arxiv-2512-22757:
Zheng Qiu, Chih-Yuan Chiu, and Glen Chou tackle a robotics problem: a robot watching demonstrations must infer the hidden constraint that shaped them, such as a region the demonstrator was avoiding. In high dimensions, random demonstrations waste effort because most reveal little about the constraint. Their active constraint learning algorithm instead asks for the demonstrations it expects to be most informative.

The method fits a Gaussian process model of the unknown constraint to the demonstrations seen so far. It then uses that model's uncertainty to pick start and goal states likely to teach it something new. Fresh demonstrations from those states are added and the loop repeats. In simulations and on real hardware with nonlinear dynamics and nonlinear constraints, the approach infers constraints more accurately than a random-sampling baseline while using sparse, well-chosen examples.
arxiv-2512-23057:
Corwin Cheung, Marcos Johnson-Noya, Michael Xiang, Dominic Chang, and Alfredo Guevara build the first physics-informed neural network surrogates for relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, the equations of magnetized plasma moving near light speed. Such flows power jets and accretion events, but solving the equations is expensive, so a neural surrogate that respects the physics is worth having. Their workflow mixes physics-driven training with data.

Instead of training on the equations' standard form, the networks work with Jacobians and wave characteristics written in primitive variables, the physical values themselves. The divergence-free condition on the magnetic field is added to the trainable system, avoiding separate cleaning steps. Using a new version of the MUON optimizer, a baseline network trained on early-time snapshots pushes the dynamics forward in one and two spatial dimensions. A second, residual-guided stage then reduces the remaining equation errors.
arxiv-2512-23357:
Michael Ackermann, Sean Reiter, and Lloyd Trefethen compute the best rational approximations to analytic functions on the unit disk, comparing two classic ways of judging best. One norm, L2, cares about average squared error over the disk; the other, L infinity, cares about the worst error anywhere. Rational functions, ratios of polynomials, can hug functions with poles or sharp features far better than polynomials can, but best rational fits are notoriously hard to compute.

Although theory for these problems reaches back decades, the authors believe this is the first computational study putting the two side by side. For the L2 problem they use a new barycentric formulation of the TF-IRKA algorithm, a modern rational approximation workhorse from Trefethen's group. The computed examples let readers see how the two optima differ in pole placement and error shape, turning an abstract approximation theory question into pictures and numbers.
arxiv-2512-23557:
Toqeer Ali Syed, Mishal Ateeq Almutairi, and Mahmoud Abdel Moaty defend networks of cooperating AI agents against prompt injection. An attack in which hidden instructions smuggled in text, images, or metadata make an agent misbehave. In multi-agent systems built with tools such as LangChain, a poisoned message can spread from agent to agent and corrupt the shared state.

Their framework sanitizes every incoming prompt and checks every model output before it reaches the next agent. Separate sanitizer agents handle text and images, a validator screens outputs, and a provenance ledger tracks each message's source, modality, and trust level across the network. In their experiments, detection of multimodal injections improved sharply, trust leaked far less between agents, and execution stayed stable.
arxiv-2512-23657:
Igor Sergeev settles the depth question for a special family of arithmetic circuits that compute prefix operations. In these, each output combines all inputs up to its position. Optimal prefix circuits use the fewest possible operations, but their outputs can only be fanned out to a limited number of successors when fanout is capped, which forces extra depth.

Sergeev proves that, for fanout bounded by a constant k, the minimal depth of an optimal prefix circuit on N inputs grows like the logarithm of N. That growth uses a base set by a specific polynomial's unique positive root, up to an additive constant. The formula was previously known only for the extreme cases of fanout two and unlimited fanout. His short note, published in English and Russian versions, fills in every intermediate case.
arxiv-2512-23957:
Kihoon Seong, Hao Shen, and Philippe Sosoe study the sine-Gordon measure. The setting is a Gibbs measure from mathematical physics. Configuration space splits into infinitely many classes. An integer topological degree labels each class. One puzzle stands out. The action has no minimizer in classes of degree two or more. Yet the measure still behaves in an orderly way there.

The authors prove concentration around the multi-soliton manifold. The result holds in a joint limit of low temperature and infinite volume. Fluctuations near the manifold look like an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Soliton collisions turn out to be unlikely events. Typical states keep their solitons well separated. The centers of the solitons also follow a clean law. They match the ordered statistics of independent uniform variables. Each single center thus follows a Beta distribution.
arxiv-2512-24157:
Xinzhang Liu and a large team report on training TeleChat3-MoE. The series is the latest in the TeleChat line of language models. The design is a mixture of experts. Sizes run from about a hundred billion parameters to over a trillion. Training ran end to end on Ascend processor clusters. That hardware differs from the usual graphics chips.

The report focuses on infrastructure more than on the models. One theme is numerical accuracy. The team verified it operator by operator and end to end. Checks spanned hardware platforms and parallelism choices. A stack of speed techniques follows. They include interleaved pipeline scheduling. Long-sequence training gets attention-aware data scheduling. Expert parallelism uses overlapped communication. A planning framework picks parallelism layouts from estimates and integer programming. Throughput gains and near-linear scaling are claimed across thousands of devices.
arxiv-2512-24357:
Dibyendu Das studies the symmetry groups of associative algebras up to R-equivalence. The algebra is finite-dimensional over an arbitrary field, with identity. Its group of symmetries is an affine algebraic group. The paper asks how rational that group is. R-equivalence is a birational sorting tool for such groups.

The main study concerns the identity component of the symmetry group. The field is assumed perfect. The paper asks when that component is R-trivial. It also asks what the property says about the algebra itself. Work of this kind links the geometry of symmetry groups to algebraic structure. It continues Das's program on symmetry groups of algebras. Readers in algebraic groups and ring theory share the audience.
arxiv-2512-24557:
Daiki Kawasaki and Ippei Danshita study collective excitations in a spin-1 XY model. The model adds a quadratic Zeeman term and long-range interactions. The interaction decays algebraically with distance. Two modes concern them: the Nambu-Goldstone mode and the Higgs mode. Their arena is the ferromagnetic ordered phase near a quantum phase transition.

Finite-temperature Green's function methods supply the theory. The Higgs mode's damping rate is the key target. For dipolar-style decay, the two-dimensional results surprise. The Higgs mode's energy grows linearly with momentum. The Goldstone mode instead follows a square-root law. Long-range interaction strongly suppresses Higgs damping. That makes the mode easier to see. The authors propose how to excite and probe it in Rydberg-atom experiments. Such platforms naturally carry the dipolar interaction used here.
arxiv-2601-00157:
Sean Lourette leads ten coauthors toward a diamond clock that ignores temperature swings. Solid state spins promise small, tough frequency references that pack many emitters into one device. Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond are a natural pick. Their electron splitting, though, shifts a lot with temperature. That drift has blocked their use as a stable clock signal.

The team pairs that splitting with a second one from the nitrogen nucleus inside the same center. An eight phase pulse scheme interleaves both readings and suppresses pulse errors. Over ten days at room temperature, the combined clock beat a plain version by large factors. It also held very low fractional instability against a rubidium clock. Checking other error sources showed temperature no longer dominates. The result points to compact solid state clocks and sensors.
arxiv-2601-00457:
Hyunjun Kim reports a negative result about a popular trick for mixture-of-experts models. These models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks, and a geometric penalty called orthogonality loss is meant to push the specialists apart so they diversify. Kim applied that penalty and measured what actually changed in weights and in activations.

Across seven penalty strengths, weight overlap did not fall and sometimes grew sharply, while activation overlap stayed high no matter what. Effects on language modeling quality were small and inconsistent across three text datasets, and weight and activation measures barely correlated. Kim concludes that weight-space penalties neither reach their geometric goal nor reliably help, so they are a poor tool for expert diversity.
arxiv-2601-00657:
Z. Neishabouri and two co-authors study rare decays of a heavy particle in a 2026 paper. The particle is the Omega-b, a baryon made of heavy and strange quarks. It can decay into an Omega-c baryon plus a light meson, a two-part outcome. The team use a simple frame that splits the decay into parts. They treat each of the three routes the decay can take, one by one.

The three routes go by the names tree, colour-suppressed, and penguin, from their shapes in diagrams. For each route, the team work out how strong the decay should be. They then add the routes to get decay rates and branch shares. The authors set their sums next to those from other groups. The sums give test labs a clear set of marks to check as data grows.
arxiv-2601-00957:
Christine T Cheng and Chelsea Ann Lambert wrote a 2026 primer on a classic graph result. It concerns graphs that are fixed by their degree lists. A graph is a web of points and links. Its degree list says how many links each point has. A unigraph is a web pinned down by that list alone. In 2000, Regina Tyshkevich showed how every web splits into basic blocks. She also listed all basic unigraphs.

The primer retells her results in plain terms for new readers. It then shows how the split makes hard counts fast. Many graph values for unigraphs can be read off in time that grows only with the web's size. The authors also built a free toolkit on the web. The toolkit runs the splits and counts from the paper. Such tools turn a deep theorem into daily practice. The paper is a bridge for students and coders alike.
arxiv-2601-01257:
Gaetane Tchana, Damaris Fotso, Antonio Hendricks, and Christophe Bobda introduce SENA, a method for stitching photos into panoramas without the warped look that plagues hard scenes. Standard stitching assumes the scene is flat. With two cameras and real depth, that flat assumption bends straight lines and bulges shapes.

SENA warps images with affine maps instead, first globally, then locally, with a smooth final deformation that keeps shapes, parallel lines, and proportions intact. It finds regions where the two views agree best, using the consistency of matched features, and cuts the seam there with strict one-to-one matching. That design removes ghosting and doubled objects by construction. On tough test sets, SENA matches leading methods on alignment while clearly beating them on shape preservation and visual realism. The work suits dual-camera phones and other setups where scenes have real depth.
arxiv-2601-01357:
Ke Xiao and four co-authors introduce FlamePilot, an AI agent that runs combustion simulations largely on its own. Combustion modeling mixes deep literature knowledge with demanding simulation codes, a combination that general AI assistants handle poorly. FlamePilot is built to read papers, set up simulations in the OpenFOAM and DeepFlame codes, run them, and fix its own mistakes.

The agent works through small, reliable tools rather than one monolithic prompt, and it extracts setup details from scientific articles to guide each run. On a public benchmark, it reached a perfect score for producing runnable setups and a success rate well above the best prior agent. In a case study on a low-oxygen regime, it turned a paper into a working simulation and ran a parameter study to convergence. The authors frame it as a copilot that handles workflow so scientists can think.
arxiv-2601-01557:
Nikko John Leo Lobos tests whether a black hole that breaks a basic symmetry of physics would leave signs we can already see. The setting adds a steady background field, from Kalb and Ramond, that favors some directions over others. Lobos studies a round, still black hole inside that background and scales it by its real, observed mass.

Heat and disorder for the hole match standard relativity, with the usual area law intact. But the extra parameter shrinks the hole's shadow and raises its ringing tone after a merger. Using telescope images of the Milky Way's center hole, Lobos caps that parameter at a low value, opening a way to probe tiny effects.
arxiv-2601-01657:
Floating offshore wind turbines need ever taller towers as rotors grow, but wind and waves acting together wear those towers out through metal fatigue. João Alves Ribeiro, Francisco Pimenta, Bruno Alves Ribeiro, Sérgio Tavares, and Faez Ahmed present FLOAT, a design framework meant to make fatigue-aware tower design far cheaper to compute.

FLOAT combines a fast fatigue estimator, a sampling method that cuts the number of wind and wave cases to simulate, and refined modeling run on high-performance computers. Applied to a standard 22 megawatt floating turbine, it produced a redesigned tower whose estimated fatigue life rose from nine months to twenty-five years while avoiding harmful vibration. The work shows how heavy simulation campaigns can shrink enough to guide real design.
arxiv-2601-01757:
Biclustering groups rows and columns of a data table at the same time, a natural fit for gene data where samples and genes both form patterns. Jiakun Jiang, Dewei Xiang, Chenliang Gu, Wei Liu, and Binhuan Wang argue that existing biclustering methods lose accuracy on today's large, noisy, high-dimensional datasets.

Their method, SpaCoBi, uses a convex optimization framework, which avoids the instability of non-convex searches, and penalizes noise directly during clustering. A stability-based rule chooses the tuning level that balances cluster quality against sparsity. In simulations and on mouse olfactory bulb data, SpaCoBi clearly outperformed leading alternatives. The authors present it as a robust option for the large omics datasets now common in biology.
arxiv-2601-01957:
Vision-language models sometimes describe objects that are not in the picture, a failure called object hallucination that comes in category, attribute, and relation forms. Tianbo Wang and six co-authors attack the problem by editing the model's internal activations, steering them toward factual semantics rather than language habits.

Their method, AFTER, first builds steering guidance enriched with factual text, then adapts the edit to each query with a learned offset estimator. Across three widely used vision-language models and standard hallucination benchmarks, the approach cut hallucination by up to about sixteen percent over baseline on the AMBER benchmark. Cheap activation editing guided by facts is a practical route to more trustworthy image description.
arxiv-2601-02257:
Joel Daniel Andersson, Palak Jain, and Satchit Sivakumar work on counting distinct items in a data stream while protecting privacy. Items can be added and removed at any time, and many updates can arrive at once. The count must be released again and again, not just once, under differential privacy, which limits what the output reveals about any single item.

Earlier methods turned the counting task into counting changes in a second stream, but one change in the input could cause many changes there. The authors study the sensitivity of that second stream and use matrix factorization methods for the counting matrix to cut the error. The same idea improves degree histograms and triangle counts in graphs, under a slightly relaxed privacy rule for the last case.
arxiv-2601-02357: Trey Brosnan presents DARC, a generative model that creates a drum accompaniment while obeying a rhythm the user supplies. Earlier stem to stem tools can listen to the other instruments but give little rhythm control, while rhythm transfer tools take a tapped or beatboxed pattern but ignore musical context. DARC conditions on both at once. It is built by parameter efficient fine tuning of STAGE, a leading drum stem generator, so the base model keeps its musical sense while new rhythm control is added.
arxiv-2601-02657:
Amir Khosravanizadeh, Pierre Sens, and Farshid Mohammad-Rafiee simulate how a cell membrane wraps around an elastic particle, a step at the heart of uptake processes such as phagocytosis and receptor mediated endocytosis. How easily a particle deforms affects whether wrapping completes. Most earlier studies also ignored a basic fact of cell anatomy, that the membrane is tied to a supporting cytoskeleton beneath it.

Their two dimensional simulations add a substrate that mimics that cortical support and vary the particle's flexibility and the membrane particle adhesion together. Whether flexibility helps or hinders wrapping depends on the adhesion strength. One pattern never reverses, the membrane protrusions that reach around the target always extend farther for stiffer targets. Since protrusion growth is an essential step in phagocytosis, the authors suggest immune cells may effectively select targets partly by stiffness.
arxiv-2601-02857:
Chunzheng Wang and fourteen co-authors tackle a safety problem for humanoid robots: falls, and the harm rigid metal and plastic bodies can do when they hit people or surroundings. Their answer is a soft and rigid co-design built around non-Newtonian fluids, materials that stay soft during normal contact but stiffen sharply on impact. Simulations guide where the protective material goes and how thick it should be.

Fitted to a life-size humanoid weighing forty-two kilograms, the protectors sharply cut peak impact forces. The robot survived repeated falls without hardware damage, including drops from three meters and tumbles down long staircases. By joining responsive materials, structural design, and learned fall control, the work points toward humanoid robots that can work safely around people.
arxiv-2601-03157:
Zhan Wu, Tristan Aurégan, and Luc Deike study how bubbles multiply when a large air cavity is torn apart by turbulence, and how surfactants change the outcome. A breaking cavity stretches into filaments and sheds bubbles across a wide range of sizes, at rates set by turbulence and surface tension. In their experiments, adding surfactant or salt sometimes produced five times as many bubbles.

For bubbles larger than the Hinze scale, where turbulence and surface tension balance, the size distribution stayed the same for every solution tested. Below that scale, surfactants and salt increased bubble counts and steepened the distribution. The effect appeared only for surfactants that adsorb fast enough. They must adsorb faster than turbulence creates new surface. That timing condition explains the fast and slow surfactants of the title.
arxiv-2601-03257:
Grégoire Pierra and Alexander Papadopoulos measure the expansion rate of the universe from gravitational waves, with special attention to the heaviest black holes. The fourth gravitational-wave catalog from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration lists two hundred eighteen candidate mergers, a rich source set for standard siren cosmology. The authors test a new parametric model of the full mass spectrum of merging binaries, designed to reveal what heavy black holes do to the measurement.

Using one hundred forty-two mergers with low false alarm rates, they infer the Hubble constant jointly with the population parameters, by both spectral and dark siren methods. The two approaches give values around seventy-nine and eighty-three kilometers per second per megaparsec respectively, with wide uncertainties. The study shows how population modeling choices, especially at the heavy end, shift cosmological conclusions.
arxiv-2601-03757:
Nguyen Cong Luong and nine co-authors survey incentive mechanisms for managing resources in satellite networks. Satellites move fast, cover huge areas, and face long signal delays plus tight energy, communication, and computing budgets. Traditional allocation methods rely on rigid performance metrics and ignore how human users actually behave and what they value.

Incentive mechanisms, drawn from game theory and auction theory, add an economic lens: they design payments and rules so sensible users gain by cooperating. That can improve scale, flexibility, and fairness in allocation. The survey covers communication resource allocation, computation offloading, and related problems across the satellite writings. For operators of growing fleets, aligning user incentives with system goals may matter as much as raw engineering.
arxiv-2601-03957:
Paul Guillot and three co-authors present, to their knowledge, the first online method for robust covariance estimation and outlier detection on streaming data. Covariance matrices summarize how variables move together, and outliers can badly bias them. Worse, outliers mask each other, hiding in the very distortion they cause. Existing robust methods were designed for fixed datasets processed all at once, not for points arriving one by one.

The new method estimates the geometric median and variance simultaneously as data streams in. Each incoming point gets a Mahalanobis distance, a scale-aware measure of strangeness, before being judged an outlier or not. Robust estimates of center and spread are what keep the masking effect in check during that live decision. Streaming robust statistics serve fraud monitoring, sensor networks, and any system that cannot wait to clean its data.
arxiv-2601-04157:
Adar Avsian, Christopher Richardson, Anirudh Sundar, and Larry Heck improve language models with just a few written explanations of past mistakes. Models err, and the same errors recur on related questions. Expert explanations can fix the pattern, but collecting many is costly where experts are scarce.

Their method, FLEx, clusters model errors by embedding to pick representative cases, checks that each paired explanation truly repairs its error, then sums the lessons into a short prompt prefix. That prefix is added at run time, with no change to model weights. On CounterBench, GSM8K, and ReasonIF, FLEx beats chain-of-thought prompting throughout. The four authors report it removes a large share of the errors that chain-of-thought leaves behind, up to the great majority on the sets tried.
arxiv-2601-04257:
Sunny Shu, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag predict speaker traits such as gender and age across languages from short posts. Language change, domain shift, and lopsided data across languages make the task hard. Their method extends reinforced multiple instance learning with adversarial domain training.

Instance selection by reinforcement learning picks the most telling examples, while domain adversarial training pushes the shared encoder toward features that ignore language identity. Tests use a five-language Twitter corpus in a few-shot setting and a forty-language speech-derived corpus in a zero-shot setting. Macro F1 improves over both standard and reinforced baselines across many settings and seeds, with the largest gains for gender. The three authors find adversarial training drives most of the gain, aiding transfer from English to scarcer languages.
arxiv-2601-04757:
Cristian Riveros, Benjamin Scheidt, and Nicole Schweikardt index a database by its symmetries rather than its values, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ordinary indexes sort entries or hash them. This one compresses a relational database into an auxiliary structure whose size reflects how many structurally distinct roles its tuples play, as measured by a relational color refinement procedure. For graphs, that count is the minimal equitable partition — tiny for trees and constant for regular graphs.

Against that index, an important query class becomes cheap. For any free-connex acyclic conjunctive query, the authors prove the answers can be counted, or enumerated with constant delay, after preprocessing linear in the small auxiliary database rather than the full one. Even a database with no symmetries at all keeps the index linear, so nothing is lost — and where structure exists, query evaluation can run in time strictly below the database size.
arxiv-2601-04857:
Zhiwei Liu's second entry in this block, written with 7 co-authors, introduces MisSpans, a benchmark for finding false spans inside news text in a 2026 paper. Most benchmarks label whole claims true or false, yet true and false details often sit inside a single sentence. Coarse labels also hide which exact segment misleads and whether it was distorted or invented outright.

MisSpans is a multi-domain, human-annotated collection pairing real and fake news stories. It supports fine-grained detection and analysis at span level. Finer labels give better explanations for readers and moderators, and they let researchers measure whether a detector truly pinpoints falsehood rather than guessing at a whole article's tone or source.
arxiv-2601-05057:
Kartik Ramkrishnan and 3 co-authors warn that chip guards can clash with each other in a 2026 paper. Chips have been hit by a run of deep-level hacks that abuse how the chip acts at small scales. Each hack has drawn its own guard. The clash: one guard may change a chip part that a next guard counts on for its own safety. The team name that clash a guard clash of the deep kind, in short a clash where one guard voids the base claim of a next.

Their two-step plan screens for such clashes at the start, as guards are first joined. Step one builds a joined design in a set form. Step two checks the base claims of each guard for breaks. Such checks count for more as chips pile guard on guard: a chip is as safe as the whole stack, not its best patch.
arxiv-2601-05557:
Vinesha Peiris and Nadezda Sukhorukova test, in a 2026 paper, whether difference-of-convex programming can train neural networks under a uniform loss. Most network training minimizes average squared error. Uniform, or minimax, approximation instead controls the worst-case error, which is harder because the objective is nonsmooth.

A difference-of-convex method splits a difficult function into two convex parts that are easier to handle. Earlier work showed the approach works as an optimizer for neural networks. Here the authors apply it to minimax approximation and run numerical experiments. They compare its performance against AdaMax, a commonly used method for this task, and report the difference-of-convex approach is also efficient in the uniform-loss setting.
arxiv-2601-06257:
Deep focus has a brain signature, and Sobhana Jahan and 3 co-authors map it in a 2026 paper. Sustained attention involves strong gamma brain waves plus coordinated eye behavior. Few computational studies combine these signals or pinpoint which regions drive deep cognitive attention.

Their Gamma2Patterns framework joins gamma and alpha band EEG recordings with eye-tracking data from the SEED-IV dataset. Features cover spectral power, burst timing, and fixation, saccade, and pupil signals across 62 electrodes. Frontopolar, temporal, anterior frontal, and parieto-occipital regions showed the strongest gamma activity in high-focus states. Eye signals pointed to overlapping frontal areas. Gamma power and burst duration marked deep focus better than alpha power alone, giving a foundation for attention decoding.
arxiv-2601-06457:
Why is the third generation of particles so much heavier than the first two? Duong Van Loi and 4 co-authors propose a gauge symmetry answer in a 2026 particle physics paper. Their extension of the Standard Model adds a doubled right-handed U(1) symmetry, designed following a flipping principle.

All left-handed fermions stay neutral, while third-generation right-handed fermions carry charges distinct from the lighter generations. Heavy third-generation masses then arise directly at tree level, while first and second generation masses appear only through one-loop radiation. Neutrino masses mix tree-level and two-loop seesaw mechanisms, reproducing the observed atmospheric and solar splittings at different orders. A leftover parity symmetry stabilizes a scalar dark matter candidate matching the observed relic abundance. The paper maps collider prospects for the new bosons.
arxiv-2601-06757:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Zheyuan Liu and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers MTMCS-Bench. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as assistants that interact through text and images. Making it crucial to evaluate contextual safety when risk depends on both the visual scene and the evolving dialogue.

Existing contextual safety benchmarks are mostly single-turn and often miss how malicious intent can emerge gradually or. The same scene can support both benign and exploitative goals. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07057:
Research by Valeriy Bardakov and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with idempotents and powers of ideals in quandle rings. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. This article addresses two central problems in the theory of quandle rings. First, motivated by Conjecture 3.10 in Internat.

2350011: for a semi-latin quandle X X. Every nonzero idempotent in the integral quandle ring ℤ [ X ] Z[X] necessarily corresponds to an element of X X. The authors investigate idempotents in quandle rings of semi-latin quandles. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07457:
Elettra Piacentino and eight colleagues examine how atomic oxygen changes benzene ice, in a 2026 astrochemistry preprint. Benzene is a simple ring-shaped aromatic molecule. Small aromatics and their altered forms appear at many stages of star and planet formation. Oxygen-bearing versions, likely including phenol, were found in the coma of comet 67P.

That comet finding raises a basic question: how do such molecules form in cold space? The authors study functionalization, the adding of new chemical groups, when atomic oxygen meets benzene ice. Ice chemistry in cold clouds and disks is a leading route to complex molecules. Readers get a focused look at one reaction path that may link simple rings to the chemistry found around comets.
arxiv-2601-07557:
Enes Kutay İşgörür, Osman Cevheroğlu, and Arkadaş Özakın build a simple quantum system that shows two kinds of behavior. Their model couples one discrete state to an endless ladder of evenly spaced states. The coupling strength follows a Lorentzian profile, a bell-shaped curve. Such models help explain how atoms and molecules exchange energy with their surroundings. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

With weak or strong coupling, the system can swing between Rabi oscillations and decay with revivals. Rabi oscillations are steady back-and-forth exchanges of energy. Decay-revival dynamics fade and then partly return. One model that interpolates between both regimes gives physicists a clean test case. It can clarify when a bound state survives inside a near-continuum of states.
arxiv-2601-08157: Kewang Chen wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on one-dimensional isentropic gas dynamics, in the form of a Cauchy problem with broad pressure laws. Chen proves that weak entropy solutions exist for all time. One hard spot is the vacuum, where the gas thins to none and the strict wave-like trait of the system fades. To pass that spot, Chen sets out a fix he calls Synchronized Dual Translation. The pressure law in view has an exponent that tends to a value greater than one.
arxiv-2601-08557: Sushant Gautam and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a tool that spots false claims in video answers. Models that watch video and reply in words are called Video-VLMs. They state false claims, called hallucinations, often and with high trust. Past gauges of doubt do not line up well with when a reply is right. The tool, called VideoHEDGE, grows a gauge built for still images into one for video. It groups claims by sense and tests if small twists change the reply.
arxiv-2601-09857:
Dylan Borchert, Semhar Michael, and Christopher Saunders estimate a normal distribution whose edges are unknown. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats parameter estimation for the truncated normal with unknown bounds. Truncated distributions model data that only appears inside a window.

Estimators for known truncation regions are well studied. Work on unknown bounds exists mainly for known parent distributions. The harder joint case is the paper's ground. Fits like these arise in wage data, sensor ranges, and trial windows. In all of them, the cutoffs themselves must be learned from the sample at hand.
arxiv-2601-10257:
Nan Li, Bo Kang, and Tijl De Bie pull apart two ways tongue can shift a model's moral calls. A model may judge a hard case in one tongue and a next tongue. The calls may not match. Two forces could be at play. One is the tongue of the case. One is the tongue of the thought.

Past tests match the two by fate. An English case gets English thought. The team built a test that splits them. A case in one tongue can pair with thought in a next. That split shows which force drives the shift. The work aids fair tests of models in many tongues.
arxiv-2601-10657:
Minghao Yan and a large team of co-authors present PACEvolve, a scaffold for evolution driven by language models. Large language models now act as operators in evolutionary search, proposing varied candidates and keeping the best. Yet the scaffolds that manage this process are mostly ad hoc. Current systems lack a steady way to run the search itself.

PACEvolve aims at long runs that stay consistent and track progress over time. A good scaffold decides what to keep, what to vary, and when to stop. Without one, search quality swings with each prompt trick. The work speaks to teams that use language models to design code, molecules, or plans over many rounds of trial.
arxiv-2601-10757:
Kenichi Takemura studies circulant matrices built from primitive roots over finite fields. A circulant matrix repeats the same pattern in each row, shifted by one. Primitive roots are special generators in finite field arithmetic. Takemura links the two by reducing exponential sums to Jacobi sums, classic objects in number theory.

The results tie character theory to matrix structure in explicit form. They show how circulant layouts encode arithmetic facts in a highly symmetric shape. They also expose rank duality, a pairing between the ranks of related matrices. Such links help both algebraists and engineers, since circulant matrices show up in coding, signal work, and fast transforms.
arxiv-2601-11357:
Steffen Knoblauch and six coauthors rate how buildings hold up in heat. Their 2026 preprint joins drone views with street-level images. Climate change is raising heat exposure for city dwellers. The risk bites hardest in dense centers of the Global South.

Cheap build materials make the heat risk worse there. Surfaces with high thermal mass soak heat and shed it slowly. Yet ways to rate such traits at scale are scarce. The team uses a vision transformer with global context. It reads both the aerial and the street imagery at once. Coupled views can flag the walls, roofs, and shades that count. Scalable ratings help cities target aid where heat hits most.
arxiv-2601-11457:
Joshua Roy Palathinkal and four coauthors compare indoor neutral-host networks. Their 2026 preprint uses real-world deployments for the test. Indoor coverage is often weak in dense built areas. Thick walls cause heavy penetration loss for signals.

Outdoor macro cells also face an uplink power cap. Phones can only send so hard back to the tower. That gap makes uplink speeds lag far behind downlink. Neutral-host networks share spectrum and infrastructure among carriers. The team compares such setups as built in the real world. Operators must split spectrum across low and mid bands. The study shows how sharing plays out in practice.
arxiv-2601-11557:
Seyed Moein Abtahi, Majid Fekri, Tara Khani, and Akramul Azim rethink vector search. Their 2026 preprint runs from HNSW to information-theoretic binarization. Semantic search and RAG systems lean on approximate nearest neighbors. Most keep vectors in memory at full float precision.

That stack is HNSW plus float32 plus cosine similarity. Its operational cost keeps climbing with data scale. Latency, throughput, and accuracy trade off against each other. Past cost cuts include storage disaggregation and lossy quantization. Each cut sacrifices performance or accuracy in the end. Binarization guided by information theory is the proposed path. One-bit vectors could slash memory while holding accuracy.
arxiv-2601-11657:
Jack Beerman, Shobhan Roy, H. Udaykumar, and Stephen Baek argue size is not the fix. Their 2026 preprint uses deformable convolutions for physics-aware learning. Such learning predicts complex physical systems at high speed. Standard CNN designs struggle with highly nonlinear flows.

Scaling model size is the usual answer in broad AI. For physics modeling, that path yields diminishing returns. Bigger nets cost more yet add little accuracy here. Deformable convolutions bend their sampling grids to the data. That bend can track curved shocks and swirling flows. The team tests if shape-shifting filters beat raw scale. The claim speaks to fast surrogates for fluid physics.
arxiv-2601-11757:
Walter Moreira and Joe Stubbs report a bid to put a famed maths data base into a strict proof tool. The data base is the OEIS, a web list of whole number sequences and linked theorems. It is cited in more than 12,000 works and is a core source in pure maths.

Their project, named Sequencelib in the work, states OEIS maths in Lean. Lean checks each proof step by machine. A checked form would let users trust and reuse those results in new proofs. The work sets out the plan and the form of the new library.
arxiv-2601-11957: Bingxuan Li, Jeonghwan Kim, Cheng Qian, and their co-authors present a self-evolving aide for time management. The aide, named PEARL in the work, learns by reinforcement learning. It aims to grow its skill at plans and schedules as it works. Time plans shift with new tasks and delays, so a fixed rule set soon fails. An aide that learns from results could adapt its advice to each user. The work is a joint effort from the University of Illinois and Eightfold.
arxiv-2601-12057:
V. Smaldore studies a family of graphs tied to polar spaces and to Ramanujan graphs. Ramanujan graphs are strong expanders. They keep the second eigenvalue of their link matrix as small as can be. A recent work built small codes from a near-Ramanujan family.

Smaldore calls such graphs Ramanujan, since known strict builds rest on the Ramanujan conjecture in number theory. His polar graphs give a new build route. Good expanders help networks, codes, and derandomized algorithms. The work links graph maths to finite geometry.  The graphs are strongly regular, a strict form class.
arxiv-2601-12157:
Paolo Bordignon studies congruences for meromorphic modular forms via p-adic cohomology. The congruences link Fourier coefficients of the forms to Frobenius eigenvalues of elliptic curves tied to their poles. Such links are deep and hard to prove by plain means.

He builds a p-adic frame for them. The frame reads the congruences through rigid cohomology of modular curves. It also uses the crystalline structure of the linked curves. The work joins two strong tools to one problem in number theory.  The frame may serve more forms than the cases shown.
arxiv-2601-12257:
Fadlullah Raji and John Murray Bruce rebuild hidden scenes from soft shadows, a form of imaging round corners. Normal imaging needs a line of sight. That line may be unsafe, blocked, or not there at all in key cases.

Non-line-of-sight imaging rebuilds a scene from indirect data. Their method, called Soft Shadow Diffusion in the work, is led by physics and learns in 3D. Shadow data are faint, so a physics guide helps a lot. The work targets search, defence, and medical uses.  Soft shadows are a faint but rich data source.
arxiv-2601-12357:
Hailong Jin and Huiying Li work on semantic correspondence, the task of matching points that mean the same thing in two images. Recent gains in this task have come from large pre trained models. Those models have a catch, though. They need high resolution input images to do their best work.

High resolution images cost a lot of compute, and that cost adds up fast. Jin and Li put forward a method called SimpleMatch as a fix. The name frames it as a simple and strong baseline for the task. A baseline like this gives the field a clear bar to beat. It also hints that good matching may not need the heaviest tools on hand.
arxiv-2601-12457:
Semchankau A. S. and Shkredov I. D. take a first step toward a structure theory for set addition with two operations. Sets in a ring can be combined by addition and by multiplication at once. Most past theory treats one operation at a time. The pair ask what can be said when both act together on sets inside a finite field.

They prove a series of inverse results for such sets. Inverse results work backward: if a set of sums stays small, the set itself must have a rigid form. Their bounds tie the size of power sum sets to the size of the base set and the field. Results like these are core tools in additive combinatorics. They help explain when arithmetic structure must appear.
arxiv-2601-12657:
Yin Wu and four co authors use multi agent reinforcement learning to harden microgrids against extreme weather. Power cuts from severe weather events grow more frequent each year. Microgrids can island from the main grid and keep local power flowing. Good energy management systems already coordinate distributed energy resources to boost resilience.

The hard part is the uncertainty of load demand during extreme weather. Demand can swing in ways that calm day models miss. Multi agent learning lets each resource act as an agent with a shared goal. Agents learn policies that adapt as conditions shift. The work was published in an expert systems journal under an open license. It targets grids that must ride out storms without going dark.
arxiv-2601-12957:
Hanne Kekkonen and Andreas Tataris select regularization strength automatically in Bayesian inversion. Inverse problems infer hidden causes from noisy data, and priors keep solutions sane. Random tree Besov priors are both expressive and computationally feasible, a rare pairing. One key challenge is picking the regularization parameter that balances fit and prior.

The team develop a data driven algorithm for that choice under these priors. Automatic selection removes a hand tuned knob that can bias results. Besov priors suit functions with edges and local spikes, like images. Tree structure adds adaptivity across scales. The work serves imaging and other inverse problems in science.
arxiv-2601-13157:
Hang Zou, Bohao Wang, and co-authors ask if vision language models can read radio waves as pictures. Such models join sight and text in one brain. Radio work, by old habit, builds a fresh net for each task, such as naming the mode of a signal.

The team turns wave forms into images and feeds them to such a model. They find that the model can learn to name modes from the pics, with no past radio skill. They also stress a clear read of why the model picks a mode. For radio teams, the path hints at one broad tool in place of many narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-13257:
Giulia Manco, for the ATLAS team, sums up marks of jet rich crashes at the Large Hadron Collider. Jets are tight sprays of bits made when quarks and gluons fly out of a crash. Some crashes make many jets at once. Others make a vector boson, such as a W or Z, plus jets.

Such events give a sharp test ground for quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. That force is hard to sum at high energy, so lab marks count. The sum covers how ATLAS counts such events and what the counts say. For force theory staff, the marks are a check that no model can skip.
arxiv-2601-14157:
Bruno Sienkiewicz, Łukasz Neumann, and Mateusz Modrzejewski build a dataset for explaining music AI in 2026. Concept-based interpretability methods like TCAV need clean concept examples. They require well-separated positive and negative examples for each concept. Existing music datasets lack this structure, with sparse, noisy, or ill-defined tags.

Their ConceptCaps holds twenty-one thousand music-caption-tags triplets. Explicit labels come from a two hundred attribute taxonomy. Clean concept data lets researchers test what a music model has learned. Explanations of model taste could build trust in recommendation tools. The set is built for tests, not for play lists. Its clean tags let teams probe one trait at a time.
arxiv-2601-14257:
Om Sharan Salafia leads a team of nine authors on this 2026 study of a record gamma-ray burst. The burst is GRB 221009A, the brightest one seen to date. Its afterglow was tracked in fine detail at TeV energies by the LHAASO observatory. The burst is also the most energetic one known.

One odd trait is a line in its spectrum at MeV energies. The team offers a self-consistent account of that line. Their title says the account also points to a dense circum-stellar medium, gas packed close around the star that burst. Readers get a case where one odd signal helps map the space near the source.
arxiv-2601-14357:
Alice P. Curtin and eight co-authors report on one astronomy meeting in this 2026 paper. The meeting is FRB 2025, a conference on fast radio bursts. The FRB field has grown fast, and its conferences have grown with it. Such meetings matter for meeting peers and starting joint work. Many stay out of reach, though.

Travel funds, flexible schedules, and sheer distance shut many researchers out. The team describes one attempt to run an inclusive and accessible hybrid conference. Hybrid means people could join in person or online. Readers get a case study of what the team tried, framed for others who plan science meetings.
arxiv-2601-14457:
Martin Burger, Ariane Fazeny, Gilles Mordant, and Jan-Frederik Pietschmann study transport distances on networks in this 2026 math paper. The networks are metric graphs that represent gas networks. Their tool is the p-Wasserstein distance, a measure of the cost of moving mass from one distribution to another. They start from the dynamic formulation of that distance.

The authors review extensions of the distance to networks. Some versions allow mass to be stored on the vertices, and some do not. They then examine the static Wasserstein distance on a three-dimensional network domain. That domain converges to a metric graph, a 3D to 1D limit. Readers get a careful bridge between pipe-flow models and graph models.
arxiv-2601-14957:
Harry Mead, Bruno Lacerda, Jakob Foerster, and Nick Hawes work on training agents in worlds that design themselves. Their 2026 arXiv paper sits in unsupervised environment design. The goal is curricula that make reinforcement learning agents generalize and cope with new tasks.

Building a good curriculum is still hard. A few settings in a world's design space can sharply raise the skill a policy needs. Methods in this field lean on a regret estimate to pick the next task. The authors work on making that regret estimate closer to the truth.
arxiv-2601-15157:
Laura Monk proves that a typical curved surface is hard to split in two. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with hyperbolic surfaces, shapes with constant negative curvature. The key gauge is the spectral gap, the first nonzero eigenvalue of the Laplace operator.

A large gap means the surface is well connected. Such a surface has a small diameter and mixes fast. Monk shows that typical hyperbolic surfaces have an optimal spectral gap. In other words, the generic surface is about as hard to cut apart as the theory of such surfaces allows.
arxiv-2601-15757:
Yimin Zhu and a large team make hyperspectral image classification easier to read in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hyperspectral images record many wavelength bands per pixel. Deep models classify them well, but their feature mixing is opaque. Users cannot see how a decision was reached. The team presents a white-box framework called ES-mHC. It is aware of the electromagnetic spectrum by design.

The framework models interactions among spectrum groupings directly. It uses structured, directional matrices for those interactions. The residual stream carries information between groupings in a traceable way. Interpretability is the headline gain. Analysts in remote sensing need to defend their maps. A model that shows its spectral reasoning earns more trust than a black box.
arxiv-2601-15857:
Giovanni Ceccio, Jiri Vacik, Yuto Kondo, and co-authors study hybrid thin films in a 2026 arXiv paper. The films mix cobalt with C60 fullerene molecules. Such organic-metal hybrids draw interest for electronics and magnetism. The study tracks how the film surface changes. Various external stimuli supply energy to the system. The team watches the morphological and structural evolution that follows.

How a film's surface reshapes under stimuli decides its uses. A film that reorganizes may switch properties on demand. One that degrades sets limits on handling and operation. Detailed surface studies guide both hopes. The work sits in materials science, where thin hybrid layers are building blocks for sensors and devices. Knowing their response to energy input is basic design knowledge.
arxiv-2601-15957:
Courtney Carreira and a large team catalog galaxy shapes from JWST images in a 2026 arXiv paper. The catalog belongs to JADES Data Release 5. It covers sources in the GOODS-N and GOODS-S fields seen by NIRCam. For each source, the team reports morphological parameters and their uncertainties. Morphology describes a galaxy's shape and structure. Those numbers feed studies of how galaxies formed and changed.

The team models each galaxy's brightness profile with a single Sérsic component. Bayesian inference yields the structural parameters. Uncertainties come with them, which honest catalogs require. A single-component fit is a simplification, but it scales to huge samples. Data releases like this are infrastructure. Hundreds of later papers will build on these measured shapes.
arxiv-2601-16057:
James Agostino and a large team weigh the gas near the hearts of two merging star systems. Their 2026 preprint uses sharp CO views of the GOALS set. The two rich mergers hold much mass in their first tens of parsecs. If all that mass were a black hole, it would look too big. That clash with known black hole to host links drives the study.

The team weighs the cool gas from the CO light. Gas mass can then be split from black hole mass in the core. A clean split tests if the black holes are in truth too big. It also shows how much fuel sits near the core. The work aids the study of mergers and their core growth.
arxiv-2601-16157:
Sanjeev Verma shows why summed acts oft level off in spread systems. His 2026 preprint deals with sums that grow then reach a cap. Past work oft ties the cap to case facts. Those facts span clash counts, wave match or set fade laws. Each case then needs its own tale of the cap.

Verma shows the cap can come from plain local ease alone. Local ease means each spot drifts back at a set rate. No case tale is then needed for the cap. A plain root for the cap eases work in many fields. It warns teams not to add need less case parts.
arxiv-2601-16357:
Allyson Bieryla and coauthors report a giant world on a long, bent path round its star. Their 2026 preprint sets out TOI-6692 b. The world is of Jupiter size and takes a span of days to loop its star. Its path is bent, with a curve mark near the mid range. It was first seen as one pass in TESS views.

Citizen groups, the Visual Survey Group and Planet Hunters, flagged that lone pass. More work then pinned the long loop and bent path. A lone pass world is hard to pin, so proof took care. Such long loop giants test tales of how worlds move. The work adds a rare case to that set.
arxiv-2601-16557:
Pierre Colmez and Wiesława Nizioł survey p-adic Hodge theory for analytic forms. Their 2026 preprint sums a field born with Tate in 1967. Tate set a claim of a Hodge like split for p-adic sums. Those sums live on firm analytic forms in the p-adic world. Fontaine then honed that claim in key ways through his work.

The survey traces how the claim grew to a full theory. It maps main proofs, tools and open ends in one place. Such maps let new teams enter a deep field with speed. They also show which claims still lack full proof. The work is a guide note, not a new proof.
arxiv-2601-17257:
Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Samar Hadou, and Alejandro Ribeiro rethink how transformers are trained. They treat training as constrained optimization. Each layer must lower the goal value as data flows through. That rule makes the network act like a descent method. Standard training, by contrast, just cuts mean loss with no layer rule.

Their scheme uses a primal-dual method to enforce the layer rules. The payoff is models whose inner steps drop the loss in a steady way. Such models are easier to read and to trust. Each layer has a clear job tied to the goal. The work links deep learning to classic optimization in a tight, useful way.
arxiv-2601-17457:
David Delepine and A. Yebra extend a classic neutrino result. The Dirac-Majorana confusion theorem says the two neutrino types look alike at high energy. Their split shrinks with the square of mass over energy. That makes them near-impossible to tell apart in many tests. The authors add new physics vector interactions to the frame. They also add CP-violating phases.

With those terms, the old suppression may shift. The generalized theorem maps where tells can survive. Neutrino type is a deep open question in physics. Any window that splits the two types draws wide interest. This work tells experimenters where to look. It also warns where the old blind spot still holds.
arxiv-2601-17557:
Aref Farhadipour and five co-authors describe a system for the WildSpoof 2026 challenge. The task joins two checks at once. One check verifies who is speaking. The other checks if the audio is real or spoofed. Their system is called spoofing-aware speaker verification. It runs as a cascade, one stage after the next.

A key part uses wavelet prompt tuning on a speech model. A multi-model ensemble adds more votes. Joint checks matter as voice fakes grow sharp. A system that trusts a good fake fails both tasks. The challenge setting tests real-world fraud risk. Call centers and banks face that risk daily. The design shows one path to meet it.
arxiv-2601-18057: Christian Koke studies Laplacians on graphs whose clusters grow ever more tightly linked. His 2026 preprint follows graphs on a shared node set where edge weights inside set clusters tend to infinity. As the links inside a cluster grow, the graph Laplacians converge, in the resolvent sense, to an effective graph Laplacian. The note gives a clean limit picture for graphs with tight groups.
arxiv-2601-18157:
Aniket Rege and co-authors build agents that can understand very long videos. Their 2026 preprint starts from a shift in daily tech. Always-on assistants, worn in devices like smart glasses, are becoming real. They face a nonstop, day-long stream of first-person video. Understanding that stream is a step past reading short, isolated clips. The meaning of a moment may depend on hours of prior context.
