An agentic design lets the system plan what to re-check and recall. Memory and search over the stream become core skills. Such understanding serves memory aids, work logs, and safety tools. The work targets a form of video that barely existed a few years ago.
arxiv-2601-18357:
Vishnu Varma and Bernhard Müller study how computer models of exploding stars change when the detail of the grid is changed. Their work looks at a star that does not spin and has about thirteen times the mass of the Sun. The models also test how strong the starting magnetic field should be.

The team tracks three things across the runs. First comes the moment when the stalled shock wave starts to move out again. Next comes the shape and the strength of the blast that follows. Last comes what is left behind at the core once the star has blown apart. Work like this helps show which parts of a model can be trusted. It also shows which parts shift when the grid gets finer or coarser.
arxiv-2601-18457:
Fake Lin and seven colleagues tackle a clash at the heart of smart shops that use language models to pick goods. Old shop tools learn from what users clicked and bought in the past. That past gives rich signs of taste. Language models, in turn, learn word by word. The two ways of learning do not line up in a neat way.

Their plan aligns the two at the level of single words and word parts. Shop signs are fed in so the model can use them as it picks each next word. A tight fit should give picks that feel both apt and in line with what like users chose. The work aims at shop tools that learn taste from text and from clicks at once. Such tools could serve each user a list that fits them more.
arxiv-2601-18557:
Tony Feng, Zhiwei Yun, and Wei Zhang study a kind of stack that charts bundles on a curve in a deep field of maths. The stacks are built from a trick that mixes a curve with a twist of its own past. They have grown key in the study of how counts and waves meet. The pair of authors and their mate set out new classes that live on those stacks, built from the stack's own form.

They then prove a claim that ties the size of those classes to the slopes of deep wave scores at a key point. The claim is a kin of a famed rule that ties shape counts to size counts. Such ties let staff work out hard counts by a shift to a twin field. The work is a deep brick in a long build.
arxiv-2601-18957:
Karlo Lelas and Dario Jukić solve classic mechanics problems by a fresh route: splitting total energy into factors. They use complex numbers to factor the energy of systems whose potential energy stays positive. From that one start, they reach exact answers for several well known problems.

The list covers the simple harmonic oscillator and a projectile thrown straight up. It also covers motion under a repulsive inverse cube force and a damped oscillator with linear drag. A single energy trick that solves all four gives students and teachers a new lens on old textbook ground.
arxiv-2601-19557:
Riccardo Giubilato and five colleagues release a dataset recorded on a volcanic island. The island is Vulcano, part of the Aeolian Islands near Sicily, Italy. Its rough, natural terrain looks more like another planet than a city street. That makes it a good test ground for robots that must find their way in wild places.

The dataset supports SLAM, the task of mapping a place while tracking your own position in it. It also supports place recognition, spotting that you have been somewhere before. Recordings combine camera images with LiDAR scans, so methods can use both sight and laser depth. Teams can test their algorithms on the same hard sequences and compare scores. Such shared data helps planetary robotics move forward.
arxiv-2601-19857:
Matheus R. de Jesus, Eduardo O. C. Hoefel, and Renato M. Angelo connect graph structure to quantum symmetry. Graph states are a central tool for describing entanglement among many particles. They are built by applying controlled-Z interactions along the edges of a graph. In their standard form they encode symmetric exchange properties.

The authors prove a precise correspondence between a graph's topology and the exchange symmetry of its state. They show exactly when a graph state is fully symmetric under swapping particles. Symmetry decides how states behave in quantum protocols and error correction. A clean graph criterion makes symmetric states easier to design and recognise. The work sharpens the dictionary between combinatorics and quantum information.
arxiv-2601-19957:
Ira Wolfson introduces a deterministic algorithm for a core quantity in Bayesian statistics. The Bayesian evidence measures how well a model explains data, averaged over its parameters. In high dimensions, computing it by sampling becomes far too slow. Sampling also runs step by step, so parallel hardware helps little.

SunBURST replaces global exploration with mode-centric integration. It locates the modes, the peaks of the posterior, and integrates around them with a Laplace approximation. The algorithm is built to run natively on graphics processors, which supply the parallelism sampling lacks. Deterministic output means the same answer every run, easing verification. Faster evidence would sharpen model comparison in fields from astronomy to medicine. The gain is speed with no loss of trust. Each run gives the same score. That is rare for this kind of task. The peaks are found first, then summed. No dice are rolled at any step.
arxiv-2601-20057:
Toby Meadows works on the foundations of mathematics, asking what countable set theory can and cannot do. The theory he studies assumes every set is countable, a stark restriction of standard set theory. One desirable feature of a foundation is eliminating imaginaries: giving concrete representatives for objects defined only up to equivalence. Many theories can do this for arbitrary definable equivalence relations.

Meadows shows this countable theory cannot. Some definable equivalence relations have no representatives the theory can provide. That failure marks a real limit on the theory as a foundation. Foundations research maps which conveniences each axiom system buys. The result tells logicians a popular simplification costs more than it seemed.
arxiv-2601-20257:
Jinren Ding and five colleagues improve decision transformers for automated bidding in online advertising. These models plan bids by learning from sequences of states, actions, and returns. The authors name two limits: the model weakly links state, action, and return-to-go sequences, and it learns from good and bad behavior alike without distinction.

Their design adds a cross-learning module and a constraint-aware loss, reflected in the name C2. Better bidding models matter because ad auctions spend large budgets in real time. A model that reads its own past returns more clearly could bid with less waste.
arxiv-2601-20657:
Valerij G. Kiselev and Jing-Rebecca Li ask what the FEXI method actually measures in neurons. FEXI, filtered exchange imaging, estimates how water exchanges between tissue compartments in brain gray matter, a key quantity for reading diffusion MRI. Reported exchange times are broadly dispersed, spread over about two orders of magnitude.

The authors solve the Bloch-Torrey equation numerically inside digital neurons taken from the NeuroMorpho.org archive. Realistic cell shapes show what the measurement truly responds to. Resolving the spread matters because exchange time is used as a marker of cell structure and health.
arxiv-2601-20957:
Arihant Tiwari, Rachana, M. Vivek, and Suvendu Rakshit hunt for oddballs among a special class of galaxies. Their 2026 paper analyzes narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies from SDSS DR17. The sample holds more than twenty-two thousand such galaxies. Their redshifts run from a tenth to nearly one. The team seeks sources that are spectroscopically anomalous. Odd spectra can flag rare physics or data problems.

The anomalies were detected by the SQuAD algorithm. It combines principal component analysis with hierarchical k-means clustering. That pairing compresses each spectrum and groups the results. Sources far from every group stand out as anomalous. Studying them can reveal extreme black hole behavior. It can also clean catalogs used by many other studies. The paper gives the community a vetted list of strange cases.
arxiv-2601-21257:
Shangbin Feng and more than twenty co-authors build a shared home for research on language models that work together. Instead of one big model, several models can team up, split tasks, and cover each other's gaps. Past work on this idea is scattered across groups with no common way to compare results.

Their platform, MoCo, gathers tasks, tools, and measures in one place. Researchers can test how models combine and check claims against the same yardstick. That shared base should make results easier to trust and repeat. It also shows where teamwork helps and where a single strong model still wins.
arxiv-2601-21357:
Joshua Hang Sai Ip, Georgios Makrygiorgos, and Ali Mesbah improve a workhorse method for tuning costly black-box functions. Bayesian optimization picks each new test point by expected improvement over the best so far. That rule is popular but greedy, and it can stall at points that are not truly optimal.

The authors add gradient size into the choice rule. Points where the slope is still large carry information the classic rule ignores. Their version should keep searching where the function is still changing fast. That helps when each test is expensive, as in lab experiments or engineering design, where wasted trials cost real money.
arxiv-2601-21457:
Tomer Adar, Yahel Hotam, and Amit Levi study how to count the edges in a graph the team cannot see directly. The graph can only be probed through limited questions. Some questions test whether a set of nodes has no edges inside it, while others ask a node's degree or its neighbors.

Mixing both kinds of questions turns out to beat either kind alone. The authors prove the mixed model gives strictly faster edge estimation. Better counting with fewer probes matters for huge networks that can only be sampled, such as web graphs and social platforms.
arxiv-2601-21957:
Cheng Cui and co-authors present an upgraded model for reading documents in the wild. PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 is a vision-language model with just under a billion parameters, tuned for many document tasks at once. The team reports it sets a new best accuracy on the OmniDocBench benchmark for document parsing.

Real documents arrive scanned, skewed, warped, photographed off screens, and badly lit. To test robustness against those physical distortions, the authors propose a new benchmark built around five such real-world conditions. Their 2026 preprint argues the enhanced model holds up under that abuse. Reliable parsing of imperfect documents is the unglamorous core of digitizing archives, invoices, and forms at scale.
arxiv-2601-22057:
Archer Wang, Emile Anand, Yilun Du, and Marin Soljacic teach diffusion models to take data apart and put it back together in new ways. Splitting complex data into factorized parts can reveal reusable components. Recombining those parts then creates new samples that never existed.

In images, the factors might capture background, lighting, and object traits. In robotics, they might capture separate elements of a scene or motion. The team's 2026 preprint studies diffusion models that learn such factorized latent spaces without supervision at the level of individual factors, guided by a discriminator. Unsupervised decomposition matters because labeled factors are rare, while the ability to recombine is the heart of creative generation.
arxiv-2601-22257:
Eva Silverstein, Daniel Kunin, and Vasudev Shyam found spare spin in how a transformer model pays heed to words. In their 2026 preprint they note that the heed step holds twist room that never changes the output. They add a simple fix that picks a set path in that room.

The fix uses small shifts, picked per batch and not learned, for two parts of the step. The team state two gains that tests then backed up. Their work aims to make training both leaner and easier to read. It gives model builders a cheap new dial to try.
arxiv-2601-22357:
Julien Delavande, Regis Pierrard, and Sasha Luccioni put a price, in energy, on saying thanks to a chatbot. Their 2026 preprint uses real chat traces and fine measures of power draw. Short, polite notes feel free to the user, yet each one still makes a large model run.

The team track how input length, reply length, and model size drive the cost. Even tiny asks add up when they occur at vast scale. Their work gives users and firms a clear sense of that hidden bill. It may shape kinder, leaner chat habits. It also aids green design.
arxiv-2601-22457:
The ATLAS team at CERN report on a long-running program of virtual visits to their giant particle detector. Since 2010, the program has offered live, guided tours of the detector and its control room to audiences around the world. Their 2026 preprint sums up what those visits have done for science outreach.

Remote classes and public groups can question working physicists in real time, from any continent. The team weigh how such access breaks down walls between frontier science and the public. Virtual visits cost little and travel anywhere with a network link. The report offers a model other big labs can copy.
arxiv-2601-22557:
Ke Du, William Mansky, Paolo Giarrusso, and Gregory Malecha give recursive mutexes a firm spec in separation logic. A mutex is a lock that guards shared state; a recursive one can be re-taken by its holder. Their 2026 preprint notes that plain mutex specs are well known in this logic.

They build the same two spec styles for the recursive kind: guarding an invariant, and atomically flipping lock state. Sound specs let proofs of lock-heavy code go through. Such code runs through servers and apps in C++ and Java. The work closes a known gap. The result is small, exact, and meant to last.
arxiv-2601-23157:
Paulius Rauba and three co-authors apply the least-privilege principle to language model services. In security, least privilege means granting only the minimum access a request needs. Deployed models rarely follow it: one endpoint serves every user and every request at full power.

That gap persists not because limits would be useless, but because they are hard to build. The authors argue deployments would gain much from cutting needless capability exposure. Least-privilege design could shrink the damage from misuse and prompt attacks. A single open endpoint is the anti-pattern named here, exposing full capability to every request regardless of need.
arxiv-2602-00357: Chenyang Yuan and Xiaoyuan Cheng study planning with language and generative models for reward guided wireless network design. The authors first benchmark general purpose language models as agentic optimizers for access point planning, finding strong wireless knowledge but dependence on external verifiers, high computational costs, and limited scalability. They then study generative inference models steered by a unified reward function capturing core deployment objectives across diverse floorplans.
arxiv-2602-00957: Waqar Muhammad Ashraf and colleagues test how to revive a failed plant model when live data drifts from training data. Their case tracks flue gas pressure gaps across an air preheater in a 660 MW thermal plant, which mimics batch runs. Three transfer fixes update the failed feedforward net: ensemble, all-layers, and last-layer transfer. Ensemble transfer gives the best scores for 5-day batches, while all-layers transfer suits models trained on 8-day batches. Compute needs vary, so this guides teams adapting failed models to drift.
arxiv-2602-01157: Mohammed Osman Gani and co-authors test deep time-series nets on wild power prices in Australia's grid. Price spikes, sub-zero dips, and fast regime flips make power calls hard, and past work rarely tracks day shifts. Their plan tests top deep nets head-on for day-ahead and two-day-ahead calls on jumpy data. New deep time nets often lose to plain deep baselines, and all wilt at extreme and sub-zero prices. Day splits show errors peaking at dusk ramps and midday sub-zero spells.
arxiv-2602-01257: Yunchuan Ma and co-authors boost point-marked action spotting in video with refined text cues. Past plans lean on sight traits alone and waste sense tucked in text notes. Their TRA plan first drafts frame notes with a pretrained mixed-media model, then refines them with point marks and fixed pretrained models. A second module maps sight and text traits into one sense space, trained to match by point-based contrast. On five tests, TRA lifts strong point-marked baselines, reaching 58.5% mean score on THUMOS'14.
arxiv-2602-01957: Xiaoxin Zhou and colleagues study CI in open source Android projects, where fast reliable updates face strain. Existing work focuses on general software, leaving mobile dynamics like store visibility and user engagement unknown. The team compares adopters and others, maps adoption with activity and bug metrics, and assesses pre post changes and user results. CI adopters run larger and busier projects, with faster regular releases, focused in integration and reliability intensive areas. Adoption brings stronger Play Store engagement, with more downloads and reviews but no rating drop, supporting steady delivery.
arxiv-2602-02157: Egor Serov and others make neural managed differential rules cheaper by smoothing the driving path rather than interpolating it exactly. Standard splines inject high-rate wiggles that force adaptive solvers into tiny steps and many function evaluations. The team uses kernel and Gaussian process smoothing to control path regularity straight. A focus-based multi-view extension then recovers detail lost to smoothing by querying several trajectories at once. In tests, the Gaussian process variant matches leading score with fewer evaluations and faster inference than spline rivals.
arxiv-2602-02257: Hannah Markwig and Angelina Zheng study trigonal curves in tropical shape, where trigonality lacks a unique translation from standard shape. Classically, trigonal curves always embed into Hirzebruch surfaces. The authors focus on trigonality as existence of a degree-three morphism to a line, and relate it to embeddings dual to a Hirzebruch polygon. For tropical curves of genus three and four, they compare obstructions for embeddings against obstructions for the degree-three morphism. Finally, they exhibit cases where a non-smooth embedding unfolds to reflect traits of the morphism.
arxiv-2602-02357:
Victor H. Alencar reframes black hole evaporation as a jump between shapes of spacetime in a 2026 arXiv paper. He studies the electromagnetic field near the event horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole, the simplest black hole that does not rotate. His method uses Euclidean path integrals, a standard tool that turns quantum sums into geometry problems.

Alencar finds the horizon wrapped in a finite cloud of photons at the Hawking temperature. That quantum atmosphere adds to the entropy and makes the heat capacity positive, which points to stability. Counting holes in the geometry, he shows evaporation tunnels from one topological type to flat spacetime. A boundary term dominates the transition, much as instantons dominate in gauge theory. The picture supports the Parikh-Wilczek view of Hawking radiation.
arxiv-2602-02457:
Naiming Liu and 2 co-authors frame AI tutoring as coaching how to learn, not just delivering explanations, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Metacognitive tutoring prompts learners to plan, monitor, debug, and evaluate their own thinking. A good coach also knows when to step back, a judgment that depends on the learner's signals and trajectory.

Their framework, MetaCLASS, selects among eleven interpretable coaching moves aligned with self-regulated learning. It first plans a teaching trajectory from learner profiles, then generates dialogue that follows the plan. The process produced a validated dataset of over a thousand conversations with turn-level labels. Benchmarking nine language models at predicting the next move, the best reached only about forty-three percent accuracy. Models intervened compulsively, almost never choosing silence when silence was right. Content tutoring skill, the authors conclude, does not transfer to coaching skill.
arxiv-2602-02657:
Zuzanna Kocjan and 1 co-author trace the rhythm by which interstellar gas cycles into stars and back, across whole galactic environments, in a 2026 study. Star formation laws link gas depletion time, the star-forming gas fraction, and gas surface density on kiloparsec scales. Their analytical framework connects those large-scale relations to the fast local cycle of individual star-forming regions.

Idealized disk simulations, from dwarfs to a gas-rich starburst, supply the measurements. Star-forming regions assemble on roughly the disk's vertical turbulent crossing time, a few to a few tens of millions of years, shrinking where gas is denser. Local depletion takes far longer, hundreds of millions to billions of years, and also shortens at higher density. Individual star-forming gas parcels live under a million years. Galaxy-scale star formation laws, the authors show, emerge directly from turbulence, dynamics, and these local clocks.
arxiv-2602-02857:
Robots that work beside people must guess what others are thinking, and Kevin Alcedo and 2 co-authors address that problem in 2026. Exact models of nested beliefs are too slow to compute. Hand-built models also break in open settings. The authors aim for a learned, structured alternative.

Their system splits a social task into local dynamics, social influence, and outside factors. A neuro-symbolic world model stores those parts as a network. A special operator then shifts the robot's beliefs into another agent's viewpoint. Early tests use a grid navigation task with social elements. The setup lets the robot plan while accounting for another agent's mental state.
arxiv-2602-03057:
A heat engine that runs on spin rather than a second heat bath is designed by André R. R. Carvalho and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. The proposed engine uses trapped ions. It operates between an energy reservoir and a spin reservoir, departing from the conventional design that needs two thermal energy reservoirs to convert heat into useful work repeatedly.

In the work stage, heat becomes optical work through a two-photon Raman transition between nearly degenerate spin states. Internal spin states are then reset by information erasure using the spin reservoir. That reset costs angular momentum, not energy. The design is a first step toward demonstrating such engines. It points toward harnessing quantum coherence in other conserved quantities through similar machines.
arxiv-2602-03757:
A control system that always runs on schedule leaks its own timetable, and attackers can read it. Arkaprava Sain and 2 co-authors defend real-time cyber-physical systems against such timing-based attacks in a 2026 paper. Prior defenses randomize or isolate schedules but ignore what the changes do to control quality and real-time promises.

Their scheduling-based defense adds bounded, structured timing perturbations to control tasks. The method weighs worst-case execution behavior and the effect of delays on control performance together, keeping the system inside predefined safety and performance limits. Tests over typical workloads and control scenarios show exposure to timing inference drops sharply. Predictable execution and acceptable control quality survive the perturbation.
arxiv-2602-03957:
How a mortality model is validated changes whether it looks useful. Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim and 3 co-authors test prediction of under-five deaths in Bangladesh across four national survey rounds. Their 2026 study compares validation designs, including training on older surveys and testing on the newest.

Random splits flattered the model; temporal validation gave lower, more honest scores. At a fixed screening capacity, the temporally tested model still caught a substantial share of deaths. Workload estimates swung widely across designs, more than across model types. The lesson for public health: validate against the future, or the promised benefit may be an artifact.
arxiv-2602-05057:
Quantum key distribution promises encryption keys whose security rests on physics rather than hard math problems. Patrick Andriolo and 5 co-authors review recent security proofs for these systems in this 2026 article, written for a special issue marking a century of quantum mechanics. The catch they address is imperfection: real devices never match the idealized models used in early proofs.

That mismatch is where attacks live, since an eavesdropper can exploit gaps between the assumed and actual hardware. The review gathers recent analytical and numerical methods that fold imperfections into the proofs and restore guarantees under realistic conditions. The authors frame these tools as versatile, covering a wide range of eavesdropping strategies. At 55 pages with new examples and references, the article serves as a map of where practical QKD security now stands.
arxiv-2602-05457:
Some optimization problems have endless lists of variables or constraints, and solving them exactly can be out of reach. Rafael Correa, Abderrahim Hantoute, and Marco López study when a relaxed version of such a problem gives the same best value as the original. Their setting is infinite convex programming, where the goal and constraints follow convex rules but the problem has no finite size.

The authors show that Slater-type conditions, which require a point that meets the constraints with room to spare, together with continuity conditions, close the gap between the problem and its biconjugate relaxation. Their proofs use calculus rules for combining functions built from sums and pointwise suprema. They then apply the results within duality theory, where relaxed problems pair with dual problems. For readers in optimization theory, the paper pins down when a common shortcut is safe to use.
arxiv-2602-06257:
People game the systems that judge them, reshaping their features to win a loan or a job offer. Chase Hutton and 2 co-authors study online strategic classification, where a learner faces such gaming round after round. Randomized algorithms might help the learner, but they have been little studied in this setting.

The pair of settings split into a realizable case, where a perfect rule exists, and a harder agnostic case. The authors give sharper mistake and regret bounds for both, tied to the complexity of the rule class and the size of the manipulation network. In the realizable case, they extend a lower bound once known only for fixed-rule learners to all learners, closing a gap.
arxiv-2602-06357:
A firm pricing a new product could ask a language model to invent a crowd of fake customers and read off what they would pay. Jackie Baek and 3 co-authors study that strategy, which they call LLM-SAA: build a distribution from model output, then optimize the decision under it. The question is whether such invented data supports good decisions.

They test three classic problems: assortment choice, pricing, and the newsvendor stocking problem. The model-made distributions proved practically useful, especially when real data were scarce. Judging them by plain distance measures, like the Wasserstein distance, could mislead, since a distribution can sit far away yet still induce near-right decisions. Decision-aware metrics are the better yardstick.
arxiv-2602-06457:
Bilevel optimization, where one problem sits inside another, shows up across machine learning, from tuning to meta-learning. Tingkai Jia and 2 co-authors improve the online, non-convex version, where the problem shifts over time and performance is scored by local regret. Whether earlier regret bounds were the best possible was unclear.

For the standard local regret, their algorithm uses an adaptive iteration plan and reaches the optimal bound with modest inner work. A fully single-loop variant adds only a gradient-variation term. For the window-averaged version, a new window-based analysis captures steady environmental change and again hits the optimal rate, with an efficient single-loop form. Experiments confirmed the theory on both fronts.
arxiv-2602-06557:
Graph neural networks filter signals through a shift operator, a matrix encoding the graph's structure, but choosing that operator has been mostly guesswork. Yassine Abbahaddou introduces a principled selection criterion. His alignment gain metric measures the geometric distortion between the input signal space and the label space under a given operator.

Theory ties that alignment to generalization bounds through a spectral proxy for the Lipschitz constant, the sensitivity of the network to input changes. The result is a cheap ranking rule: score each candidate operator before training and pick the best, instead of searching by trial and error. The criterion works whether the operator is fixed in advance or learned, and it applies to any prediction task on graphs.
arxiv-2602-07257:
Making mRNA vaccines starts with in vitro transcription, where yield and quality hinge on a tangle of linked reactions. Keqi Wang and twelve co-authors build a modular model of that process, split into initiation and capping, elongation and truncation, termination and read-through, breakdown, and precipitation steps.

Each module follows biochemical rules and lab data, with mass balances, complex formation, and enzyme action, and the joined model tracks the linked dynamics. Residual and sensitivity checks test it. Bioprocess builders get a predictive model that can guide tuning of yield, capping efficiency, and integrity instead of relying on trial and error alone.
arxiv-2602-07357:
Quantum tuning usually encodes decisions as bits, but penalty terms for constraints then bloat the Hamiltonian and strain near-term devices.  Shashank Sanjay Bhat and three co-authors benchmark the option: coding decisions in high-D qudit spaces through Quadratic Unconstrained D-ary Optimization.

Across traveling salesman, vehicle routing, graph coloring, scheduling, and Max-K-Cut problems, the D-ary form captures structural constraints without extensive penalties. Qudit-level quantum approximate tuning runs the comparison against binary codings.  Quantum tuning teams get thorough evidence on when the coding itself, not just the method, decides scalability.  The comparison spans routing, coloring, scheduling, and cut problems, giving the coding claim broad empirical footing.
arxiv-2602-07457:
Repository-level code editing demands understanding dependencies across many files, and recent benchmark gains lean heavily on elaborate agent scaffolding.  Qinglin Zhu and ten co-authors ask how much of that ability can be trained in , using real pull requests as the signal.

Their Clean-PR pipeline converts noisy GitHub pull request diffs into validated search-and-replace edit blocks, yielding the largest public corpus of its kind: two million pull requests across twelve programming languages.  Mid-training on that corpus, followed by agentless fine-tuning with error-driven augmentation, lifts SWE-bench results.  Code model builders get evidence that training data, not just scaffolding, drives repo-level editing.
arxiv-2602-07557:
Pulsar timing arrays have found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational wave background, opening a new window on gravity theories beyond general relativity.  Mohammadreza Davari and one co-author explore symmetric teleparallel f(Q) gravity, where deviations arise through the non-metricity scalar while tensor modes still travel at light speed.

Their model-independent parameterization yields an analytic approximation for how wave amplitude damps during cosmic evolution. Comparison with NANOGrav 15-year and IPTA data keeps the damping setting consistent with general relativity while allowing small deviations future data could detect.  Gravitational experts get prospective bounds on a modified gravity theory from the newest pulsar timing evidence.
arxiv-2602-07757:
Mid-infrared spectroscopy can fingerprint compounds, but sensitive and broadband readings have long fought each other. Zhaoyu Cai and thirteen co-authors break that trade-off with a microresonator-anchored, rapidly sweeping laser for the fingerprint region.

Their design uses two microresonators: one microcomb calibrates rates while a high-quality resonator resolves the laser's instantaneous shape, correcting sweep nonlinearity and broad linewidth. Converted to the mid-infrared, the system reaches a record product of signal-to-noise ratio and bandwidth. Chemists and spectroscopists gain a tool for fast, sensitive, wide-range molecular detection that earlier swept lasers could not deliver.
arxiv-2602-07857:
Charged particles losing energy as they travel through matter pose a hard transport problem, coupling direction, energy, and scattering. Ben S. Ashby and two co-authors develop a semi-analytic deterministic method that treats directed motion and energy loss by integration along characteristics, the natural paths particles follow.

Scattering enters through source iteration, where the angular gain is lagged so each step solves decoupled directional problems linked only by angular sums. The authors prove coercivity and boundedness of the transport form, contraction of the iteration under a subcriticality condition, and a rigorous error bound that tells users when to stop. An elastic discrete-ordinates approximation is analyzed too, giving users both theory and a computable scheme.
arxiv-2602-08057:
Concealed emotions in video, feelings people try to hide, are hard to label at scale. Yufei Wang and four co-authors build a multimodal weak-supervision framework and test it on the iMiGUE dataset of tennis interviews, reaching state-of-the-art results.

The pipeline detects and crops faces, extracts visual features, and uses a large vision-language model with chain-of-thought and reflection prompting to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning text. Body keypoints, modeled with a simplified network, join image and transcript features in an ultra-long-sequence transformer, with each modality pretrained separately first. Affective-computing researchers gain a practical recipe for learning hidden-emotion recognition without exhaustive manual annotation.
arxiv-2602-08157:
Nuclear magnetic resonance of near-equivalent spin pairs needs double-quantum excitation, but existing schemes are fiddly. Urvashi D. Heramun and seven co-authors describe a family of methods exploiting spinor behavior: a quantum state's sign flips under a full rotation, a quirk that can steer the phases of single-quantum coherences.

One set of methods uses symmetry-based pulse sequences, the other uses spin-lock-induced crossing, matching nutation frequency to spin coupling, including a variant robust to radiofrequency amplitude errors. A precursor state prepared this way converts rapidly to double-quantum coherence with a simple quarter-turn pulse. Demonstrated on fluorine-19 NMR of diastereotopic nuclei, the methods give NMR spectroscopists cleaner, more tolerant tools for studying near-equivalent pairs.
arxiv-2602-08357:
Response functions reveal how a many-particle system reacts to probes, but computing them for general fermion systems is hard. Weijie Du and four co-authors build a hybrid quantum-classical framework that computes those responses and also yields the full bound-state spectrum. Their arXiv paper combines a Lorentz integral transform with a new way of feeding Hamiltonians into circuits.

Three protocols extract responses and structural details from the transformed data. The team tests the method on oxygen-19 with realistic nuclear forces, recovering both its spectrum and its response. The circuit designs are meant to stay practical and scalable for general fermion Hamiltonians. Readers get a bridge between quantum hardware and nuclear structure problems that classical methods struggle to reach.
arxiv-2602-08457:
Judging whether search results are relevant is essential for testing retrieval systems, yet human labeling is slow and costly. David Otero and Javier Parapar ask whether language models can judge better when they first learn what relevance means for a topic. Their arXiv paper introduces Relevance Context Learning, a two-model setup that makes topic criteria explicit.

An instructor model reads judged query-document pairs and writes a narrative of what counts as relevant for that topic. An assessor model then uses that narrative to judge new pairs. In a hybrid pooling test, humans judge a shallow pool while models label the rest. The method beats zero-shot prompting and standard in-context learning consistently. Readers get a smarter way to spend scarce human judgments.
arxiv-2602-08557:
Teaching robots to push and slide objects without grasping them is hard, because reinforcement learning struggles to discover contact-rich strategies. Marc Toussaint and seven co-authors combine learning with a smarter way of choosing where episodes start. Their arXiv paper targets non-prehensile manipulation in settings full of contact.

A new state sampler covers diverse contact modes by respecting contact structure, and resets drawn from it are paired with projected interpolation and curriculum learning. The combination beats plain reinforcement learning and alternative reset schemes, training universal, non-prehensile, and dynamic policies. Readers get a practical boost for robot manipulation that leans on contact rather than gripping.
arxiv-2602-08757:
Vehicle models often ignore transient tire dynamics, treating tires as quasi-static, but that shortcut lacked rigorous justification. Luigi Romano and four co-authors provide it through singular perturbation theory for single-track models with distributed tire friction. Their arXiv paper models the vehicle as coupled ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations.

A perturbation parameter, the ratio of rolling contact length to longitudinal speed, formalizes the time-scale split between body motion and tire dynamics. For small values, standard finite-dimensional tools analyze local stability and design stabilizing controllers. Readers get the first singular-perturbation framework for such ODE-PDE vehicle models, grounding a long-standing modeling practice in theory.
arxiv-2602-08857:
Do trained transformers really run simple rules inside, or only mimic them? Xinting Huang and four co-authors offer a way to find out. They rewrite a trained transformer faithfully as a program in RASP, a small language for describing transformer computations, then use causal interventions to trim it to a small sufficient sub-program.

On tiny transformers taught on rule-based and formal-language jobs, the method often recovers short, readable programs from models that generalize to longer inputs. The authors present this as the most direct evidence yet that such models truly implement simple RASP programs, not just approximations of them. It gives interpretability research a concrete extraction tool.
arxiv-2602-09757:
Grasping the trust of natural language writing is key for deploying base models in security-sharp domains. Mihnea Ghitu and Matthew Wicker note that proven tainting guards give provable toughness bounds for sorting, yet fail for self-feeding writing. They cannot handle stepwise guesses or the hugely large output space of language models. Their 2026 paper builds a frame for proven writing, setting staying power, toughness to any change in writing, and soundness, toughness to aimed harmful changes.

Targeted Partition Aggregation is offered as the first method proving soundness against aimed attacks, finding the minimum tainting budget needed to induce a single harmful class, token, or phrase. Wider with mixed integer linear coding, it gives tighter pledges for multi-turn writings. Tests prove agent tool-calling soundness under set taint up to half a percent and eight-token staying power spans in taste-based tuning, though run-time latency stays open.
arxiv-2602-09957:
Designing a stellarator, a twisted magnetic bottle for fusion plasma, means hunting good shapes in a landscape crowded with local minima. A 2026 paper led by Dario Panici, with five co-authors, brings a tool called deflation to that hunt. Ordinary searches depend heavily on the starting guess and weights, and often fall back into minima already found.

Deflation rewrites the objective to penalize solutions already in hand, pushing the search toward distinct new minima from a single starting setup. The paper first explains the method for nonlinear systems, then applies it to stellarator equilibria and coil design. It reports families of global equilibria, helical-core equilibria found without prescient guesses, and several distinct high-quality designs.
arxiv-2602-10257:
Ion fluids driven far from balance show nonlinear transport that smooth-medium theories struggle to explain. A 2026 paper led by Seokjin Moon, with one co-author, studies ion pairing dynamics in ion fluids using molecule simulations and out-of-balance rate theory. The study focuses on a lithium salt in water and acetonitrile under steady electric fields, computing reactive flows and average first-crossing times of ion pairing.

A moving stand-in for free-ion counts tracks field-driven change closely tied to nonlinear conductivity growth, rising about forty percent at high field strength in acetonitrile versus under ten percent in water. Kinetic analysis shows Onsager's classic theory greatly overstates field-driven split-up growth in molecule fluids, because solvent-shaped paths and field-driven dielectric drop curb split-up in detailed solvents. The results give a molecule-level reading of nonlinear ion-fluid transport beyond smooth-medium theory.
arxiv-2602-10357:
Contrastive learning builds broad pictures, but theory under imbalanced data patterns common in real uses remains limited. A 2026 paper led by Haixu Liao, with four co-authors, builds a theory framework for training dynamics of contrastive learning with Transformer nets under imbalanced data. Neuron weights move through three distinct training stages, with distinct dynamics for majority, minority, and noise features.

Minority features shrink feature room, raise the need for more complex designs, and hinder separation of ground-truth features from noise. Those neuron-level patterns inspire pruning, which restores scores lost to imbalance and boosts feature separation, offering conceptual insights and usable guidance. Key theory findings are checked through number tests.
arxiv-2602-10557:
Nathan Shettell and five co-authors take quantum-grade gravity measurement into the field in a 2026 paper. Absolute gravimeters are drift-free and precise but bulky; relative gravimeters are portable but drift over time. Survey work in remote terrain needs both virtues at once.

Their hybrid approach stations an atomic gravimeter on site. It calibrates two mobile spring gravimeters daily during a survey spanning twenty-four square kilometers of dense tropical terrain. Over seven days, the atomic reference suppresses drift in the relative readings through asynchronous cross-comparison. The deployment captures regional gravity slopes faithfully under harsh settings, showing how field-operable quantum sensors can extend laboratory sharpness to geophysical survey work.
arxiv-2602-10957:
Ying-Jen Yang and Ken A. Dill derive design rules for nonequilibrium flows in a 2026 paper. Molecular motors and enzymes are living machines whose repeating cycles can be mapped as random flows moving across networks. But current random motion describes such flows on fixed networks. Making networks for global dynamical objectives requires varying local transition rates systematically.

Their scalable approach builds on the fluctuation-response duality in Caliber Force Theory, a path-entropy variational formalism for nonequilibrium systems. It scales efficiently with network hardness and reveals new insights, including a transition from timing-dominated to branching-dominated fluctuations in a kinesin motor model. The paper gives mock biology and biophysics a principled route from desired flow conduct to network design.
arxiv-2602-11157:
Safety tuning in English does not automatically travel to other languages. Max Zhang and four co-authors test response-based knowledge distillation for multilingual jailbreak prevention. They distil refusal conduct from a proprietary teacher into three open student models using tens of thousands of multilingual jailbreak prompts.

The result runs counter to hope: standard tuning on safe refusal data raised jailbreak success for all students, by up to a sixth of the scale. Transfer to unseen languages varied by base model. Removing nuanced edge refusals, a key source of harm, mitigated or reversed the decline, though thinking scores still slipped. The study warns that distillation can quietly weaken the safety it aims to spread.
arxiv-2602-11257:
Dim galaxies may owe their dimness to their satellite systems. Silvio Rodriguez and nine co-authors study central low-surface-brightness galaxies and their satellites in the Illustris TNG simulation, within standard cosmology. Low-surface-brightness haloes differ in spin and concentration from bright-galaxy haloes.

Low-surface-brightness centrals host more satellites with larger velocity dispersion, and satellite count tracks surface brightness continuously for massive centrals. At fixed stellar mass, their satellite systems are dominated by spin, and systematically counter-rotate against the primary disc. The authors read this as a sign of few mergers, since mergers favour radial orbits typical of bright systems. Satellite motion thus illuminate how dim galaxies form.
arxiv-2602-11357:
Versatile AI chips waste compute when use sags across workloads. Xiaoling Yi and six co-authors present Voltra, a DNN accelerator chip that uses 3D spatial data reuse with flexible shared memory access. Balanced reuse across three aspects lifts spatial use well above a usual 2D design.

Flexible data streamers enable mixed-grained preload and moving memory sharing, lifting time use severalfold and cutting latency against non-preload and separated-memory designs. Fabricated in sixteen-nanometre technology, the chip reaches competitive peak energy and area speed while holding high use across diverse workloads. Voltra argues that dataflow, not just raw throughput, decides accelerator speed.
arxiv-2602-12057:
Primordial black holes could probe the early universe, and bouncing worlds with long contracting phases might amplify them. Xuan Ye and four co-authors build a unified framework for black hole birth in dust-radiation bouncing cosmologies, focusing on the classical shrinking phase, ignoring bounce details. They compute the curvature power spectrum for a tiny dust equation of state, derive the two-fluid Jeans length, and extend the three-zone collapse model to two fluids.

Two collapse criteria yield the curvature threshold for birth across benchmark masses from tiny to huge scales. The critical threshold is extremely small and nearly mass-independent, shifting only near dust-light balance. Yet the power at formation times is many orders of magnitude smaller still, so mass fractions vanish across benchmarks. Radiation pressure and two-fluid collapse strongly suppress production versus pure dust, implying substantial birth would need extra boost mechanisms.
arxiv-2602-12257:
Stochastic gradient descent in over-parametrised models often behaves as if it had a hidden preference, and symmetry may explain part of that bias. Govind Menon led this work with two co-authors, studying Langevin dynamics with noise projected onto directions at right angles to an isometric group action. The model is built to cast fresh light on symmetry in stochastic gradient descent.

When start and target densities both respect the group, the projected process matches in law a standard isotropic process plus an extra drift. That drift follows the negative log volume of the group orbit, and the proof couples the two processes through a third process on the group itself. The extra drift is identified as the mean curvature of the orbits, a neat geometric form of implicit regularisation.
arxiv-2602-12357:
Quasar clustering offers a route to primordial non-Gaussianity, a faint imprint of the early universe on large-scale structure. E. Fondi led a large team here, using Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument quasars to tackle a stubborn degeneracy. The scale-dependent bias signal for local non-Gaussianity, parameterised by fNL, is fully tangled with a bias parameter tied to assembly bias.

Using IllustrisTNG simulations matched to DESI quasar selection, the team builds a robust prior for the assembly bias parameter, averaging about 1.4 with weak redshift dependence, stable to selection noise and consistent with recent merger histories of quasar hosts. Checks against CAMELS simulations show robustness to astrophysics and cosmic variance. Applying the prior to DESI data release 1 gives fNL equal to minus 3.3 plus or minus 9.2.
arxiv-2602-12757:
Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces promise to steer wireless signals by shaping how waves bounce, but most designs assume flat panels. Real walls, columns, and curved facades break that assumption, and existing curved-surface methods only handle preset shapes. Mohamadreza Delbari and five co-authors propose a learning method for flexible surfaces of any curvature, built on a compact model of surface shape.

A neural network reads a sparse set of received power readings, infers the surface geometry, and picks the best phase settings for each element. Simulations show the method converges fast and beats standard flat-panel beamforming by a wide margin, holding up across varied curvatures. The authors also test how errors in sensor position affect performance, a practical concern for real deployments on curved structures.
arxiv-2602-12857:
Triangulating a manifold symmetrically means respecting a group action, and small covers provide a rich test case. Raju Kumar Gupta and Soumen Sarkar study triangulations of small covers that respect the action of an elementary abelian 2-group. They show that any such equivariant triangulation induces a triangulation of the orbit space, a structural result that organises the whole problem.

They then build the smallest symmetric triangulation of three-dimensional real projective space, with 11 vertices, and prove it is unique at that size. A general construction for connected sums yields a 17-vertex triangulation of the connected sum of two copies, the best known, which also improves a known minimal g-vector result. Finally, they prove that four-dimensional real projective space needs at least 18 vertices under the same symmetry.
arxiv-2602-13057:
Calabi-Yau manifolds are central to string theory and algebra shape, and complete intersections in weighted projective spaces give a rich source of examples. Marco Ghirlanda presents an recipe that classifies Calabi-Yau complete intersections in fake weighted projective spaces, built from nef-partitions, determining all such intersections up to dimension five.

He also computes Hodge pairs for the three-D groups found, discovering twenty new pairs never realised by any toric Calabi-Yau hypersurface. Finally, he characterises explicitly the groups of maximal codimension. For geometers, the recipe turns a sprawling sorting problem into a finite, checkable list, while the new Hodge pairs expand the known landscape of Calabi-Yau threefolds.
arxiv-2602-13157:
Designing an optimal linear-quadratic regulator usually requires knowing the system motion, a luxury rarely available for real aircraft. Sean Bowerfind and two co-authors build a data-driven recipe that synthesises the optimal infinite-horizon LQR feedback controller from a finite sample of input-output data alone. A needed condition links the optimal gain to any arbitrary answer trajectory, and a limited tuning recipe built on that condition guesses the gain matrix.

A feedforward gain for reference tracking can also be found. The paper justifies the method theoretically and shows it on examples, among them a checks test flight using a real scale aircraft whose motion were unknown. For control engineers, the appeal is direct: optimal feedback from data, without first identifying a model.
arxiv-2602-13357:
Diffusion transformers make striking images and video, but each sample needs many iterative denoising steps, and caching tricks that reuse features often drift off course. AdaCorrection keeps cache reuse honest with an adaptive offset correction: at each step it judges cache validity from light spatio-temporal signals, then blends cached and fresh activations to correct drift. The fix runs on the fly, with no extra supervision or retraining.

Tests on image and video benchmarks show generation quality near the original, measured by FID, with moderate speedups and little overhead. The method consistently improved generation performance over cache baselines, and its code is folded into FastCache-xDiT. Dong Liu leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13457:
Planning safe paths past a pursuer means knowing how far and how fast that pursuer can turn, and this paper learns those limits from sacrificial agents. Each sacrificial agent flies a straight line toward an adversary and reports only whether it was intercepted or survived. Those binary outcomes connect to pursuer parameters through a geometric reachable-region model, in boundary-interception and interior-interception forms.

Parameters are recovered by gradient-based multi-start optimization with custom losses per case, and trajectories for the sacrificial agents are chosen by a spread-maximizing heuristic or by Bayesian experimental design. Monte Carlo tests recovered parameters accurately with five to twelve sacrificial agents, enabling safe time-optimal paths for high-value agents. Grant Stagg leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14157:
Ahmed Ghorbel and seven co-authors show in a 2026 arXiv paper that test-time guidance alone can edit images and video well. Text-driven editing can be cast as inpainting: masked regions must fit both the observed content and the prompt. Prior guidance methods for diffusion and flow models leaned on costly vector-Jacobian products.

Building on Moufad and co-authors from 2025, the team explains the theory behind a VJP-free approximation and extends its tests to large image and video editing benchmarks. Results match, and at times beat, training-based methods. The finding matters because it cuts the heavy compute that had limited practical use of principled test-time guidance.
arxiv-2602-14357:
Annalisa Szymanski and three co-authors study a 2026 arXiv question: how do field experts truly shape language-model design? Models more and more serve tricky job fields, yet little is known about how teams design and test them in use. The paper trails a team building a teaching chatbot through a 12-week field study.

Views and talks with builders and experts showed four key habits: workarounds for data gathering, boost when expert input ran short, co-built test rules, and mixed expert-builder-model test plans. Hurdles held expert drive and trust, shaping joint design, and ownership of expert lore. The authors offer design chances that put field lore at the heart of future workflows.
arxiv-2602-14557:
Xudong He and one co-author offers a 2026 arXiv framework called dissipative spectroscopy. It pulls spectral facts from quantum systems via tuned loss, using a broad leaky response theory for both memory-free and memory-full settings. A plan reaches the leaky spectrum through driven swing-loss resonance.

The leaky spectrum can name two-bit soft modes near quantum key points and, on the normal-phase side, foretell broad order with power-law growth after a loss quench. Those marks show up in quasi-bit-ruled regimes once thought trivial. Wider leaky susceptibilities grasp leading memory effects, shown in a leaky fermion model, marking the spectrum as a flexible tool for calm traits and non-calm leaky motion.
arxiv-2602-15057:
Moseley and colleagues describe a new Plotly-Dash query system for the Keck Observatory Archive. The archive grows fast as new instruments arrive and user expectations rise. The team built a Python-based, VO-compliant query system, continuing ADASS 2024 design work.

The build adds real-time ingestion of fresh data and an observer interface for managing data. Chosen tools include Plotly-Dash callbacks and R-tree spatial indexing that speeds spatial search twentyfold. VO-compliant TAP middleware from the NASA Exoplanet Archive and NEID archive joins the mViewer image engine. Two services are now in beta. First, a Data Discovery dashboard answers archive-wide spatial and temporal queries in seconds. It filters by keywords, previews results in an interactive grid, visualizes images, and offers downloads. Second, a notebook visualizes protostar observations in the Rho Oph Dark Cloud with CDS, IRSA, and KOA data.
arxiv-2602-15157:
Burlak and colleagues report photometric, polarimetric, and spectroscopic observations of the eruptive young star IRAS 21204+4913. Its visible brightness has risen markedly since October 2025. The absorption spectrum resembles A to F giants and supergiants, yet it also shows molecular TiO bands. Brightening came with a strong rise in polarization of stellar radiation in the I-band, likely from scattering by dust in an expanding circumstellar shell.

The P Cygni profile of the hydrogen line implies a dusty wind blowing outward. The team attributes the outburst to a rise in the accretion rate of protoplanetary disk matter onto the young star. Unusual features include line width and radial velocity varying with excitation potential, emission in TiO bands, and a comparably bright outburst back in 1948. Several T Tauri stars and a group of Herbig-Haro objects sit nearby.
arxiv-2602-15557:
Neuman and Tuschmann set out a frame for stochastic games played on large sparse graphs. Players sit on graph vertices, and the frame covers games in continuous time and discrete time as well as static games, for finite and countably infinite populations alike. Limits are described through local weak convergence of marked graphs, and players may carry path-dependent payoffs that differ from player to player.

Under a contraction condition, the authors prove that Nash equilibria exist, are unique, and show correlations that decay exponentially with graph distance. Global equilibria can be approximated by truncated local games, and even rebuilt exactly on subgraphs from boundary data. Equilibria also converge along locally weakly convergent graph sequences, including samples from hyperfinite unimodular random graphs.
arxiv-2602-15657:
Anderson and Dean model an active particle that propels itself by self-phoresis in a one-dimensional channel, a setup proposed for symmetric camphor grains. The particle steadily emits a chemical, and gradients in the diffusing chemical field drive its motion. Channel ends reflect the chemical perfectly, so the reflected field confines the particle in effect, turning it back before it reaches either end.

The system switches from a passive state, resting at the channel midpoint, to an active state of highly regular, non-chaotic oscillations. The authors build the phase diagram analytically and derive oscillation frequency and amplitude near the transition. A perturbative analysis captures the motion well even for oscillations as large as half the channel, and a further analysis explains how reflection near the channel edges works when activity is large.
arxiv-2602-15757:
De Grazia and colleagues move sexism detection in social media videos beyond a simple yes-or-no label. Online sexism takes many forms, and tools limited to binary classification miss subtler manifestations for lack of fine-grained, context-sensitive labels. The team contributes three things. First, FineMuSe, a new multimodal Spanish data set with binary and fine-grained annotations. Second, a hierarchical taxonomy covering forms of sexism, non-sexism, and rhetorical devices of irony and humour. Third, an evaluation of a wide range of language models.

Results show multimodal language models competing with human annotators on nuanced sexism. But they struggle to capture co-occurring sexist types when conveyed through visual cues. The work gives researchers a richer data set, a clearer taxonomy, and a realistic picture of where current models succeed and where visual nuance still defeats them.
arxiv-2602-15957:
Adler argues that change called evolutionary is still forced into models with fixed stocks, flows, and rules, where genuine novelty must be written in advance. Such models can swing, oscillate, and depend on their path, yet they cannot grow a new kind of structure on their own. He treats that gap as a core systems problem, not a biological metaphor.

His answer is Stability Driven Assembly, a spare non equilibrium framework in which random interactions plus unequal persistence create selection with no genes, no copying templates, and no imposed fitness function. Longer lived arrangements pile up and join later interactions more often, so persistence shapes what forms next. The scheme reads as a genetic algorithm driven by staying power, and it lets equilibrium count only as a provisional regime that a more persistent arrangement can overturn.
arxiv-2602-16057:
Dawon Ahn leads a team of five researchers using video analysis to map how drivers behave at railway crossings. Traditional studies treat each crossing alone, which hides patterns shared across sites. The team splits behavior into three phases: approach, from warning activation to gate lowering; waiting, while gates stay down; and clearance, from train passage to gate raising. TimeSformer embeddings encode each phase, and a multi-view tensor method finds latent components across sites.

Location emerges as a stronger driver of behavior than time of day, and approach-phase behavior proves especially distinctive. Visual maps of the learned components show location-based clustering, with some crossings forming their own groups. The framework scales pattern discovery across many crossings, giving safety planners a principled way to group sites by behavior and target interventions where they fit.
arxiv-2602-16157:
Xinyue Gui leads a team of twelve researchers testing whether vision-language model personas can aid early field-study preparation. Field studies are irreplaceable yet costly, slow, and error-prone. They demand careful preparation. Borrowing the spirit of rapid prototyping from manufacturing, the team proposes a fast, low-cost method that simulates field outcomes with VLM personas. The key question is whether they can mimic human responses where spatial awareness, empathy, and behavior generation matter.

Two parallel studies anchor the work. A real-world street-crossing study uses twenty participants. A video study uses twenty VLM personas on the same task. Five human-computer interaction researchers were also interviewed. VLM personas mirror average human response patterns, including near-identical average crossing times. Yet they lack behavioral variability and depth. The authors see promise for formative studies, preparation, and augmenting human data, not as a replacement for real fieldwork.
arxiv-2602-16557:
Jarryd Horn and co-authors report surface magnetism in FeSb2, a correlated insulator whose bulk is non-magnetic. Interest in topological Kondo behavior has driven study of surface states in FeSb2 and FeSi. FeSi's surface had a spin-orbit coupled ferromagnetic account. FeSb2's surface magnetism had not been addressed. The team separates surface from bulk signals by using how susceptibility changes with surface area.

From that split they extract the surface magnetic anisotropy of a thin, rough-surfaced single crystal. It agrees well with the anisotropy seen in surface magnetotransport. They close with evidence for an anomalous Hall contribution to low-temperature surface transport. Condensed-matter readers get a first magnetic portrait of a surface that may host topological Kondo physics.
arxiv-2602-16657:
Oleg Andreev examines string breaking through spatial Wilson loops, using gauge-string duality. The paper weighs how light flavors affect the pseudopotential, a key quantity for quark confinement physics. It also brings in the notion of a spatial string breaking distance.

That distance is gauged for SU(3) gauge theory over a temperature span from zero to three times the critical temperature. Readers in lattice gauge theory and holography get a compact, duality-based take on where and how strings break at finite temperature, with a new spatial measure to compare against lattice results.
arxiv-2602-16757:
Simran Arora, Sai Swagat Mishra, and P. K. Sahoo study late-time cosmic expansion in f(Q) gravity, where Q marks the nonmetricity scalar. The matter sector is a bulk viscous fluid with a free equation-of-state parameter, generalizing the standard dust picture of cosmic matter. Background evolution equations are derived and the expansion history is analyzed.

Model values are pinned using cosmic chronometers, baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI DR2, and Type Ia supernova data. With best-fit values, statefinder and Om diagnostics separate the viscous f(Q) case from standard Lambda-CDM. The deceleration parameter shifts from early slowing to current speeding, and the effective equation of state is traced. Bulk viscosity in f(Q) gravity thus offers a viable, data-consistent account of late-time acceleration.
arxiv-2602-16957:
Hasan Can Biyik and co-authors study cross-lingual euphemism transfer between Turkish and English, asking whether semantic overlap suffices for positive transfer. Euphemisms swap in for socially sensitive expressions, softening or reframing meaning. Their reliance on cultural and pragmatic context complicates modeling across languages. Potentially Euphemistic Terms in Turkish and English are sorted into two subsets. One holds shared terms, the other non-shared terms, based on functional, context, and meaning alignment.

Findings reveal a transfer asymmetry. Meaning overlap is insufficient to guarantee positive transfer, above all in the low-resource Turkish-to-English direction. There, scores can degrade even for shared euphemisms, and in some cases improve under non-shared training. Differences in label spread help explain those counterintuitive results. Category-level study suggests transfer may be influenced by domain-specific match, though evidence is thin.
arxiv-2602-17257:
Chongjun Ouyang led a five-author team on spotting broken segments in pinching-antenna systems. These systems use segmented waveguides. A failed segment degrades service. Yet the uplink signal arrives passively combined, hiding which segment failed. The paper proposes a signal processing framework that tags each segment with a known low-rate modulation at its feed, giving every segment a unique signature.

From the tagged-pilot model, the team builds two detectors. For long pilots, a low-complexity per-segment maximum-likelihood detector is developed. For short pilots, a compressive sensing detector that exploits sparsity in the failure pattern is adopted. Numerical tests show the per-segment detector nearly matches joint detection. The compressive sensing detector detects reliably with short pilots. It can beat baselines that need much longer ones.
arxiv-2602-17357:
Pranav Aggarwal led an eleven-author team building an AI safety system grounded in India's realities. Existing global AI safety systems, the paper argues, show contextual blindness toward India's socio-technical landscape. With a population of a billion and a half and a massive informal economy, India's AI uptake faces caste-based bias, linguistic exclusion of vernacular speakers, and infrastructure failures in low-connectivity rural zones. 

The team introduces ASTRA, an empirically grounded AI Safety Risk Database built bottom-up. It defines AI safety risks as hazards from design flaws like skewed training sets or missing guardrails, fixable through technical iteration or architectural change. A tripartite causal taxonomy sorts risks by timing of implementation, responsible party, and intent. A domain-agnostic ontology organizes thirty-seven leaf-level risk classes into Social Risks and Frontier and Socio-Structural Risks, piloted in education and financial lending as a living utility.
arxiv-2602-17457:
Yang Lan led a two-author team building two-bubble blow-up cases for the mass-critical generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation. The paper proves there is a global solution that blows up in infinite time and nears the sum of two decoupled bubbles with reverse signs. The proof draws on techniques built for the 2D mass-critical nonlinear Schrodinger equation in a similar context by Martel and Raphael.

The main difficulty comes from unstable paths tied to scaling, which interactions excite. Beating it requires a refined model involving some spread-out profiles, plus a sharp grasp of links between solitons and such profiles. This gives a strict example of multi-bubble blow-up action in that setting. It shows how two bubbles with reverse signs can evolve apart while the solution as a whole blows up in endless time.
arxiv-2602-17657:
Yi Zeng and team report the experimental realization of fractional Fermi seas in a one-dimensional Bose gas. The Pauli exclusion principle anchors the structure of matter, and extensions such as Haldane's generalized exclusion statistics predict exotic states with momentum distributions of uniform but fractional occupancy.

The team prepared an excited Bose gas through ramping cycles in interaction strength. The resulting states are excited yet stable, and they show Friedel oscillations, the smoking-gun mark of the underlying fractional Fermi sea. Stabilizing such states opens a route to deeper insight into quantum thermodynamics under exotic statistics. It also paves the way for uses in quantum information and sensing, where controlled exotic states may prove valuable.
arxiv-2602-17757:
Ali Fatemiabhari and Carlos Nunez perform a broad holographic study of Krylov complexity for a wide class of confining quantum field theories. A geometric rule ties the time rate of complexity to the proper momentum of a massive probe. They analyze radial paths in several top-down gravity duals showing confinement and a mass gap.

In all shapes with a smooth IR end-of-space, a robust and shared overall trait appears: Krylov complexity swings. The swing rate is set by the confinement scale, while size depends on both the UV cutoff and the IR scale. Extra kept charges shift these patterns without changing their overall shape. The lengthwise nudged Ising model shows an overall match. Swinging complexity thus looks like a shared mark of confinement and a sharp probe of IR rework in tightly coupled theories.
arxiv-2602-17857:
By topology, Rene Garcia-Lara shows that solutions exist for the field equations of a gauged Chern-Simons-O(3)-Sigma model over a compact Riemann surface. A minimal deformation constant is found, so at least one solution exists for every chosen set of vortices and antivortices, provided the size stays below that constant. For small values of the Chern-Simons deformation parameter, multiple solutions are proved when the total numbers of vortices and antivortices differ.

The Maxwell limit is computed for solutions of the field equations. In contrast, when vortex and antivortex numbers are equal, at least one solution is proved for any value of the deformation parameter, and the limit to infinity is proved. Dependence of the fields on the deformation parameter is investigated numerically on the sphere. Readers gain existence and multiplicity results for a gauged sigma model with Chern-Simons deformation, plus a computed Maxwell limit.
arxiv-2602-17957:
T. R. Adams and team investigate the kinematics of Ursa Major III, a potential ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, using Bayesian inference to search for intrinsic rotation. Rotation size matters for estimating total mass, which decides whether Ursa Major III is truly a dwarf galaxy or possibly a star cluster with a large binary share.

The team fits a non-rotating model and a rotational model to the current total member stars, finding the non-rotating model preferred about five to twelve times. A reduced population with stray stars removed gives a similar preference for non-rotation. They calculate a lower-bound rotational mass and a matching lower bound mass-to-light ratio of seven hundred thirty-four. Ursa Major III stays an unclear object with viable cases for both dwarf galaxy and self-bound star cluster scenarios, yet under both it is unlikely to be supported by rotational pressure.
arxiv-2602-18057:
Hongsong Wang and team improve text-to-motion, which makes lifelike human motion clips from natural language prompts. Two-stage systems using discrete motion codes have pushed the field, but they neglect cross-sequence time match: the shared time patterns across cases of the same action. That neglect yields meaning gaps and motions that break physics.

The authors propose TCA-T2M, a system for time-consistency-aware T2M. A spatial VQ-VAE for cross-sequence time matching, coupled with a masked motion model for text-guided motion, handles alignment. A kinematic constraint block softens discretization flaws to keep motions sound. Tests on the HumanML3D and KIT-ML benchmarks show state-of-the-art results, showing why time consistency matters in robust, smooth motion.
arxiv-2602-18157:
Oumar Mbodji studies how to invest and spend wisely when the value placed on the future shifts over time. His 2026 paper takes up the classic Merton problem, where an investor splits wealth between risky assets and spending, but lets the discount rate change rather than stay fixed. A shifting discount rate makes today's best plan clash with tomorrow's.

The fix is a self-consistent plan, one no future self would want to abandon, built by a repeated approximation. Mbodji shows this plan matches the plain best plan once the discount rate is swapped for a wealth-aware version that depends on time and wealth level. Spending and investment shares then follow in feedback form, read straight off the value function. The result gives investors a steady rule for a world where patience itself moves.
arxiv-2602-18257:
Francesco Martinelli and one co-author study how charge quadrupoles couple to magnetism and shape in two twin materials. Their 2026 paper treats the five-d-one double perovskites barium magnesium rhenium oxide and barium sodium osmium oxide, which share structure and electron count. First-principles calculations drive the analysis.

Both materials lean toward quadrupolar order arising on its own in the cubic paramagnetic phase, slightly weaker in the osmium compound. Strong spin-orbit coupling ties local magnetic moments to charge quadrupoles, producing the odd canted moment patterns seen in both. Adding structure splits the twins: strong Jahn-Teller coupling stabilizes antiferroic order in the rhenium compound, matching lab data, while weak coupling in the osmium compound leaves its magnetic ground state still elusive. The work nails one twin's mechanism and sharpens the puzzle of the other.
arxiv-2602-18357:
Wallace Albertini and four co-authors give AI quality assessment a statistical backbone. Their 2026 paper notes that standards like ISO/IEC 25059 offer a quality model but no practical, statistically robust way to judge functional correctness for probabilistic AI systems. The proposed SCFC approach ties business requirements to a confidence statement that weighs both average performance and variability.

Four steps carry the method. First, set quantitative specification limits and sample in a stratified and probabilistic way. Then bootstrap a confidence range for the performance measure and compute a capability index as the final indicator. A case study on two real industrial AI systems, with expert interviews, finds the approach feasible and valuable, with experts positive on utility, ease of use, and intent to adopt. Evaluation moves from a single point estimate to a confidence statement.
arxiv-2602-18557:
Bercel Boldis finds simple structure in strong-coupling expansions. His 2026 paper continues studying certain observables in N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, given by a determinant with a Bessel kernel. By reorganizing the series of the determinant at large 't Hooft coupling, a simple structure emerges.

Each exponentially suppressed correction relates simply to the perturbative series. The new approach quickly generates the full series for observables such as the octagon form factor, multi-gluon amplitudes, and the cusp anomalous dimension. High-precision numerical work verifies the results and gives a full account of the resurgence pattern of the strong coupling expansion.
arxiv-2602-18657:
Tate Rowney and three co-authors link the Lean proof assistant to outside languages. Their 2026 paper presents DSLean, a framework for two-way translation between expressions in Lean and external syntax. Domain-specific languages mediate between proof assistants and outside automation, but moving between the prover's internal form and such languages is tedious engineering.

DSLean needs only a specification of an outside language and its Lean equivalents, hiding meta-level implementation details. The team shows what it can do by building three new automation tactics, opening access to outside solvers for ring ideal membership, interval arithmetic, and ordinary differential equations. The framework cuts the chore of translation so prover users can lean on outside tools without hand-building the bridge each time.
arxiv-2602-18757:
Most self-driving systems learn one average driving style, yet real drivers differ sharply in how they brake, steer, and follow. Xiaoru Dong, with nine co-authors, presents Person2Drive in 2026, a platform and benchmark for personalised end-to-end autonomous driving that treats style as something to measure and to learn.

The platform generates diverse personal driving data in simulation, scores style with vector-based metrics. Adapts a model by fine-tuning only its trajectory prediction head, leaving the pretrained base intact for safety. Experiments show fine-grained personalisation without sacrificing driving performance or success rate, even in hard scenarios, a step toward cars that drive like their owner rather than like everyone at once.
arxiv-2602-18857:
Balancing exploration and exploitation is the central challenge of reinforcement learning. Bayes-optimal agents do it well in theory, but belief tracking and planning are usually intractable. Joery A. de Vries, with five co-authors, proposes VariBASed in 2026. It is a variational frame for Bayes-adaptive Markov decision processes, covering both learning and planning.

The design joins three things. Belief learning uses variational methods. Planning uses sequential Monte-Carlo. Meta-reinforcement learning ties them together. On a single GPU, it scales favourably to larger planning budgets. It improves both sample efficiency and runtime efficiency over prior methods.
