That makes Bayes-adaptive planning more practical, without giving up the principled trade-off that motivates it. The point is speed with care. Good plans should use less data and less time.
arxiv-2602-18957:
Graph streams are too large to store in full, yet analysts still need answers about their structure. Jakub Lemiesz, with two co-authors, introduces EdgeSketch in 2026. It is a compact graph sketch for fast analysis of massive graph streams.

EdgeSketch gives unbiased estimates for key graph properties with controlled variance. Graph algorithms can run directly on the stored summary. Construction needs only a single pass over the edge stream. Offline analysis then relies solely on the sketch. Two applications test the approach, community detection by the Louvain method and graph rebuilding via node similarity estimates. Experiments show substantial memory savings and runtime improvements over lossless representations and prior sketching methods, while maintaining reliable accuracy.
arxiv-2602-19057:
Directional quantum codes promise hardware-friendly error correction. Mohammad Rowshan, writing alone in 2026, analyses them from the word up. Directional codes use ancilla qubits following a fixed direction word on square or hex grids. That route generates the stabilizers.

The author builds a word-first frame for route-generated, translation-invariant CSS codes on rectangular tori. A direction word induces a finite support pattern. From it come a route-to-support map, a lattice classifying compatible layouts, and finite-torus admissibility criteria. A word equivalence theory handles symmetries, reversal, and cyclic shifts. An inverse-problem criterion decides when a pattern comes from a single route. A quasi-cyclic reduction explains why code dimension reacts to boundary conditions. A worked example ends with a sharp dimension rule for thin rectangles.
arxiv-2602-19357:
Spatial visualization means imagining, transforming, and manipulating the spatial traits of objects and actions. Nilay Yilmaz and four co-authors ask whether vision-language models have this ability, building MentalBlackboard, an open-ended benchmark based on paper folding and hole punching tests. It covers two tasks, prediction and planning, probing how models handle folds, holes, and symmetry.

Prediction tests show models struggling with symmetrical transformations, even when they get the unfolding sequence right, and rotations pose a further challenge. In planning, the best score came from Claude Opus 4.1 at just 10 percent accuracy. The top model overall, o3, reached 71.6 percent on a generalization task needing no spatial visualization, but only 25 percent on text-based prediction.
arxiv-2602-19657:
Temporal graphs change snapshot by snapshot over shared vertices. Exploration asks whether agents can visit every vertex, one edge per snapshot. Duncan Adamson and Paul G. Spirakis introduce always S-connected temporal graphs. Each snapshot has at most as many components as S has members, each tied to one member. They use the idea on graphs with an (r, b)-division: a split into disconnected S-connected parts, S at most b in size.

An always S-connected graph with m equal to S size and average degree Δ admits exploration by m agents in O(n^(3/2) m^3 Δ^(3/2) log^(3/2)(n)) snapshots. As a subroutine, it lets one agent explore any always-connected graph of treewidth at most k in O(n^(4/3) k^(11/2) log^(5/2)(n)) snapshots. That beats the prior best for small k. Interval graphs with few large cliques get an O(n^(4/3) log^(5/2)(n)) bound.
arxiv-2602-19757:
A spherical design is a finite set of points on a sphere that integrates polynomials exactly up to a given degree, much as a good quadrature rule does on a line. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ryutaro Misawa, working alone, gives an explicit, implementable way to build such designs.

The construction lifts point sets from tight fusion frames, yielding explicit five-designs in every dimension. A key ingredient is an explicit construction of simplex three-designs as orbits of the symmetric group. Feeding those simplex designs back in, the author also builds seven-designs in every even dimension from six upward, with point counts growing polynomially when a simple number-theoretic condition holds. Readers get concrete designs, not just existence proofs.
arxiv-2602-20157:
Feed-forward reconstruction systems depend on dense geometry and pose supervision. Those labels are costly at scale and scarce for dynamic real-world scenes. A 2026 arXiv paper by Zhongxiao Cong and three co-authors presents Flow3r, a framework that adds 2D matches, or flow, as supervision, allowing large-scale training from unlabeled videos.

The key insight is splitting. Flow between two images should be predicted using geometry latents from one image and pose latents from the other. That splitting guides learning of scene geometry and camera motion, and extends to dynamic scenes. In experiments, factored flow prediction outperforms alternative designs, and performance scales consistently with unlabeled data. The authors integrate factored flow into visual geometry systems and train with eight hundred thousand unlabeled videos. Flow3r leads across eight benchmarks. Its largest gains come on in-the-wild dynamic videos. The benchmarks span static and dynamic scenes.
arxiv-2602-20357:
Muhammad Khan and Yangyang Xu study stochastic minimax problems with a nonconvex-nonconcave shape, a central challenge in modern machine learning. Earlier methods often needed strong concavity on the maximization side or strict geometric assumptions to guarantee convergence. The authors instead assume weak convexity in the primal variable and an extended Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property in the dual variable, with an exponent between zero and one.

That weaker set of assumptions greatly widens the class of problems the method can handle. The authors propose a variance-reduced algorithm that provably reaches a near-stationary solution with state-of-the-art sample complexity, in both smooth finite-sum and online settings and in a structured nonsmooth setting. To their knowledge, theirs is the first unified method to combine weak convexity, the extended property, and variance-reduced stochastic updates. It suits large-scale uses where reliable minimax methods have been scarce.
arxiv-2602-20657:
Sanitizable signatures let an approved party alter set message blocks while leaving the rest firmly bound, but post-quantum designs with strong backing have been scarce. Shahzad Ahmad and two co-authors present a post-quantum scheme built on a chameleon hash function from the McEliece cryptosystem. The chosen editor holds the trapdoor of a Goppa code for controlled clash-finding through Patterson decoding.

The paper gives formal rules and proofs of existential unforgeability and immutability, grounded in the hardness of syndrome puzzles in the random-oracle model. There, a robust random oracle blocks trivial linear hash collisions. A key novelty is a precise account of transparency: by capping the weight of signer-generated random values, the scheme hides edits fully, making edited ones identical to freshly signed ones. The work claims the first clear post-quantum code scheme.
arxiv-2602-20757:
Chetan Singh and three co-authors work with Chew, Goldberger and Low equations, a set of hyperbolic PDEs with non-conservative products used for plasma flows. They apply when local thermodynamic equilibrium fails and the pressure tensor is rotated by the field. That leaves the pressure tensor described by two scalar parts.

As the field evolves, controlling its divergence matters. The team uses the generalized Lagrange multiplier technique for the CGL model, giving the GLM-CGL system. To suit entropy-stable schemes, they recast the GLM-CGL system by treating some terms as non-conservative. The resulting system has a non-conservative part not affecting entropy evolution. Test results for the GLM-CGL system, compared with the CGL system without the GLM diminishing approach, demonstrate that the GLM approach indeed leads to significant improvement in field shrinking.
arxiv-2602-20857:
Signals that change character over time, from speed traces to brain waves, need fitting methods that follow local patterns. Teymur Aghayev proposes Segmented Continuous Optimization in this 2026 arXiv paper. The method fits curves piece by piece across segments, using trigonometric, polynomial, and exponential models, while keeping first-derivative continuity at the joins.

That continuity lets the fit track both local detail and global trend in raw signals with wavy or transcendental behavior, where straight lines and simple polynomials fall short. Tests cover how close the fit runs and how fast it runs across all models used. Cases on speed and EEG data show the method in real use, reading off signal patterns, fitted settings, slopes, and integrals.
arxiv-2602-21057:
Feynman integrals for massless scalar three-point functions hide a symmetry under Fourier transformation. Oliver Schnetz proves that symmetry in this 2026 arXiv paper. Off-shell integrals are self-dual, so a momentum-space integral equals a position-space integral of the same graph with transformed edge weights, given matching vertex labels. Every such integral can therefore be written as a graphical function.

The result follows from a 2015 theorem on parametric representations, but it was only noticed in 2025 in work on four-dimensional supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Schnetz generalizes that observation and draws consequences for graphical functions, including a new identity and a new twist relation for scalar integrals in phi-four theory. Readers get a duality that simplifies a whole class of integrals.
arxiv-2602-21357:
Bayesian inverse problems need after-data means, but Monte Carlo guesses demand many samples when values vary widely under the after-data, a cost that bites for rule-bound problems. Ali Siahkoohi and Hyunwoo Oh cut that cost in this 2026 arXiv paper with case-based neural control helpers, learned spread-out helpers that cut gauge variance.

Stein's rule shapes a design of layered coupling layers with workable Jacobian traces, scaling the method to high sizes. Training needs joint dial-data samples plus the after-data score, workable from physics odds, neural stand-ins, or learned making models. Once trained, helpers carry over across sightings with no re-teaching. Tests on toy and Darcy-flow problems beat classic Stein helpers with big variance cuts, even with a learned stand-in score.
arxiv-2602-21957:
Yuchun Tu and four co-authors rethink how recommendation systems learn across many devices without pooling private user data. Standard federated methods sync full item vectors between server and devices, assuming exact coordinate alignment is what makes collaboration work. The authors argue instead that the relative relationships among items matter more than shared coordinates.

Their framework, CGFedRec, has the server learn item clusters and send only compact cluster labels downstream, so devices need not hold global item vectors at all. Local vectors stay free to vary, capturing personal taste while global structure keeps them consistent. Experiments show much lower communication costs with recommendation accuracy that beats rivals across several data sets.
arxiv-2602-22057:
Quantum tomography rebuilds unknown states and processes from readings, but its theory usually assumes each device output stands alone and matches the rest. Leonardo Zambrano drops that assumption, covering real cases where noise, drift, feedback, or hostile acts make outputs depend on the past. He studies a projected least-squares method under fully adaptive state and channel preparation.

The good news: the number of samples needed still matches the best possible scaling from the separate-output case, for both states and processes with single-copy readings. Dropping that old rule changes only what the rebuilt object means, namely a time average, not how costly it is to learn. Testers thus get the same sample savings under far more honest rules.
arxiv-2602-22357:
Astronomers wrangling large tables rely on STILTS, a powerful toolset whose rich syntax daunts newcomers. R. A. Shaw and three co-authors present STILTS-NLI, a natural-language interface that turns plain prompts into STILTS commands, with agentic support for a friendlier experience. It fine-tunes a compact, open-source language model on a synthetic dataset curated and validated for coverage and syntactic correctness.

The specialized small model generates valid commands that match and sometimes beat larger proprietary models. By leaning on small, open models, STILTS-NLI offers an accessible, low-resource solution for observatories and students alike. The tool lowers the entry barrier to professional-grade table manipulation without demanding expensive models.
arxiv-2602-22657:
Hidetoshi Nishimori presents an Ising spin-glass model with linked disorder that bridges two famous cases. It slides smoothly from the pure Ising model with aligned spins to the Edwards-Anderson model with symmetric disorder. On a special Nishimori line, values become exactly computable from the pure model.

Energy, magnetization, and pairwise measures on that line equal the pure Ising values at a well-set effective temperature, on any lattice in any dimension. Most notably, the model's heat response on the line equals the pure model's energy, not its heat response. The upshot is pure-Ising-like tipping at that special point, unlike the standard symmetric-disorder class, opening a little-studied corner of linked disorder.
arxiv-2602-22757:
Nils Van de Berg and one co-author ask whether sparse graphs are typically pinned down by their spectrum. The giant component of an Erdős-Rényi graph turns out to be cospectral, sharing its adjacency spectrum with a non-isomorphic mate, when average degree is low enough. The proof uses a specific pendant tree plus Schwenk's tree-swapping trick.

Pendant trees may be essentially the only obstruction. Prune them by passing to the 2-core, and the giant may become spectrally determined with high probability. Most of the paper backs that idea with theory and numerics, including a theorem that local switching cannot make the 2-core cospectral. Rational and fixed-level cospectrality variants are also discussed.
arxiv-2602-22857:
Andrea Bardin and two co-authors give an exact quantum verdict on macroscopic self-trapping in bosonic Josephson junctions. In a perfectly symmetric two-mode Bose-Hubbard junction, mean-field theory predicts population imbalance can trap itself. The team asks whether that trapping survives exact quantum dynamics.

For any finite particle count, exact evolution breaks self-trapping after finite time, no matter the starting state. Symmetries of the Hamiltonian yield a mathematical proof, with spectral analysis revealing branching eigenvalue gaps and nontrivial imbalance-amplitude structure. Those features split the dynamics into two clearly distinct regimes and explain a quasi-trapping regime at large particle numbers, bridging mean-field predictions and exact quantum behaviour.
arxiv-2602-22957:
I. B. Cunha and two co-authors construct self-dual lumps in an extra-coupled CP1 Maxwell-Chern-Simons model. Starting from the bent O(3)-sigma model, they map it plainly to the CP1 form, where a local U(1) gauge balance emerges from the Fubini-Study shape of the target space.

In the static regime, Chern-Simons effects plus Pauli-like nonminimal coupling reshape the effective gauge connection, force the electric sector to appear, and yield magnetized, electrically polarized BPS lumps. The Bogomolnyi procedure fixes the self-interaction potential for self-duality and produces the BPS equations. Magnetic flux stays quantized, fixed entirely by the gauge field's asymptotic behaviour, and finite-energy solutions form regular, localized, singularity-free lumps with confined flux and a nontrivial localized electric field.
arxiv-2602-23257:
Jizhou Liu and one co-author develop random tests for switchback trials. In these trials, a unit such as a market or platform switches between treatment and control over back-to-back blocks. Judgment is hard because such trials often have few blocks, while results show links over time, yearly cycles, and treatment effects lingering across periods.

The main result is a conditional random test for the null of no total treatment effect. It is finite-sample sound under standard rules on time spillover and needs no formula-based model. Partner tests check those rules. A carry-over test asks whether past placements still matter past a horizon. A look-ahead test asks whether future placements affect current results. Scaled versions gain large-sample soundness for averages. Rules of thumb clarify design trade-offs. Number tests with toy results and a ride-share model show the real-world lessons.
arxiv-2603-00057: Hou and colleagues study how instructors tailor generative AI chatbots for classroom use. They first sort existing prompt resources into ten customization categories, including persona, guardrails and personalization. Interviews with ten university STEM instructors, who card-sorted the categories by priority, show course materials and teaching strategies rank highest, while persona and tone rank lowest. Priorities vary with course size, subject and teaching style, so the authors argue modular chatbots offer the best path forward.
arxiv-2603-00157: Bible, Hasnaeen and Qi present FujiView, a multimodal system and dataset for predicting scenic visibility around Mount Fuji from webcam images plus weather data. Its late-fusion design joins image-derived class scores with numerical weather features to sort visibility into five categories. The dataset holds over 100,000 webcam images from more than 40 cameras, paired with current and forecast weather. Vision features lead short-term nowcasting, while weather forecasts take over beyond one day; late fusion scores about 0.89 accuracy same-day and up to 84% next-day.
arxiv-2603-00257: Peñarrubia and Nadler run controlled N-body experiments on dwarf spheroidal galaxies in dark-matter haloes full of subhaloes. Stellar orbits shaken by random force fluctuations gain energy for good and expand toward a dynamical attractor, with half-light radius near peak radius and dispersion near half peak circular velocity. This state is reached alone and under tidal stripping, though mass loss speeds evolution greatly. Assuming Milky Way dwarfs have reached this state, halo masses collapse onto narrow sequences, and larger systems deviate as cored dark-matter profiles suggest.
arxiv-2603-00357: Lee and eight colleagues address fault tolerance for language model training on more than one hundred thousand graphics processors. Breakdowns there are routine, and restarts eat training time. Their SPARe scheme stacks spare data shards across parallel groups and reorders work on the fly to hide failed nodes during gradient sync. It matches classic replication for uptime while holding extra compute near steady, and at very large scale it cuts training time sharply against classic replication.
arxiv-2603-00957: Ai, Bei, and Wang prove global strong solutions exist for the three-dimensional inhomogeneous incompressible viscoelastic system with no extra structure assumptions. Swapping earlier inverse-Sobolev conditions on initial data for integrable ones, they develop new transformations and spectral analysis to capture faster decay of the velocity field. That decay is what secures uniform bounds on density and the deformation tensor, closing the global argument.
arxiv-2603-01257: Xu and three colleagues compare four LLM-based patching designs in one controlled test: fixed workflow, single-agent, multi-agent, and general-purpose code agents. Judging patch correctness, failure modes, token use, and run time on real vulnerability tasks, they find clear trade-offs. Fixed workflows run lean but snap, single-agent systems mix flexibility with low cost, and multi-agent designs generalize better at higher overhead and drift risk on complex tasks. Unexpectedly, general-purpose code agents patch best overall, adapting across vulnerability types through general tool interfaces.
arxiv-2603-01557:
Aditya Shukla, Yining Yuan, Ben Tamo, and colleagues test whether AI summaries of home health data can be trusted. Their 2026 work uses dementia monitoring records with body measures and room sensors over time. Fluent summaries may sound right yet miss long spells of abnormal readings that matter for care.

The team scores summaries by events, not by word overlap or style. Daily events come from fixed abnormal thresholds that must persist to count as real. Scores track missed abnormal spells, missed durations, covered measures, and invented events. Plain scoring hides a stark split: some models score well on style but recall almost no abnormal events. A vision-based pipeline that reads plotted charts aligns best with true events, which argues for event-aware checks in care tools.
arxiv-2603-01657:
Abderaouf Bahi, Amel Ourici, Ibtissem Gasmi, and colleagues forecast renewable power at new sites with no labeled data there. Their 2026 work faces a common block: good models need site records that privacy, cost, or logistics may deny. A model must also keep adapting as weather patterns drift over time.

Their frame, FreeGNN, adapts a graph model to unseen sites with no source data and no target labels. A teacher-student setup guides learning, while a memory store replays past cases to block forgetting. Graph-based rules keep spatial links intact, and a drift-aware weight adjusts how fast the model adapts. Tests span three real data sets for solar, wind, and broad energy contests. Ablation checks confirm that each added part earns its place.
arxiv-2603-01857:
Eugenia Gabriela Loera Villeda, Ivo Steinbrecher, and Alexander Popp mesh contact problems in two independent parts. Their 2026 work separates the contact surface mesh from the bulk volume mesh of each body. Contact zones and solid interiors need different element types and resolutions, so one shared mesh serves both poorly.

The contact surface uses a smooth boundary layer mesh built from the CAD model boundary curves. NURBS curves give exact shape and smooth joins between elements on that layer. The bulk instead uses a simple structured Cartesian grid, cheap to build and refine. A mortar-type constraint couples the two non-matching meshes so forces pass correctly across the seam. Several layer-building strategies are detailed, and numeric examples validate the full workflow for contact mechanics.
arxiv-2603-02157:
Kathleen Chang, Zhiyang He, Theodore Yoder, and colleagues speed up quantum error correction in this 2026 paper. Quantum codes spread data across many qubits to guard against noise. Surgery is a flexible way to compute on such codes, but it is slow. Each step can take a number of check rounds that grows with code size.

Their new gadgets perform many logical measures at once in fixed time. Space cost stays near fixed as well, a rare pairing. The trick is sharing cost across many steps: many surgeries finish in time once thought needed for one. The gadgets keep much of surgery's flexibility while matching faster gate methods. They suit near-term tests and open new design paths for fast quantum logic.
arxiv-2603-02257:
M AlMasri studies a classic approximation method in the complex plane in this 2026 mathematics paper. The Rayleigh-Ritz method guesses a wave form, then tunes it to approach the true energy. AlMasri works in the Segal-Bargmann space, a setting where waves are functions of complex numbers. Trial waves are bell-shaped curves stretched by two parameters.

A strict bound on one parameter proves necessary for the guesses to stay valid. For the basic oscillator, the method recovers the exact ground state. For a stiffer oscillator with a quartic term, adaptive bell shapes yield tidy energy formulas. Simpler power guesses give firm upper bounds but cannot adjust their width. Shifted guesses prove vital for lopsided potentials that break symmetry.
arxiv-2603-02357:
Xiaochun Liu and Richard Luger forecast extreme financial losses with a quantile method in this 2026 paper. Banks must estimate Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, two gauges of worst-case losses. Both live in the far left tail of return distributions. Their method models the conditional scale of returns, defined by the gap between two quantiles.

Restricted quantile regression estimates that scale without assuming a distribution shape. Value-at-Risk comes from the left-tail quantile of rescaled returns. Expected Shortfall averages the quantiles below that level. The approach captures skewness, heavy tails, and leverage effects robustly. Simulations and real data show it often beats GARCH and joint quantile rivals. A test on world stock indices through the COVID-19 period highlights its grip on shifting risk.
arxiv-2603-02857:
Adam Pearson, Francesco Mazza, Marcello Caleffi, and Angela Sara Cacciapuoti build a test bed for the quantum internet. Real quantum network gear is costly and scarce, so design work needs good software first. Their 2026 tool, Q2NS, sits on top of ns-3, the standard network test bed.

Quantum links must be run next to the plain messages that control them, a pairing with no past model. The design splits control logic from node and channel parts, so users can rewire pieces fast. A plug-in slot swaps between three ways to store quantum states. Tests show the tool runs faster than leading rivals while keeping its models flexible. A viewer shows both the real links and the links made by shared quantum states.
arxiv-2603-03257:
Sahar Diskin and five colleagues present a proof in percolation theory, the branch of mathematics that studies how random connections spread through a network. Their 2026 paper works with percolation above its critical point, called the supercritical regime. The setting is broad: every infinite transitive graph, where each point looks like every other.

The team proves that the chance the starting point sits in a finite cluster of a given large size falls off exponentially fast. The rate of that fall is governed by the graph's isoperimetric function, which measures how clusters can grow. Results of this kind are known as sharpness results. They pin down exactly how behavior changes once the critical threshold is crossed.
arxiv-2603-03357:
Taiwo O Sangodapo studies products of picture fuzzy subgroups, an abstract algebra topic built for reasoning under uncertainty. Ordinary sets force yes-or-no membership; fuzzy sets allow degrees. Picture fuzzy sets, introduced in 2013, go further by tracking three stances at once, loosely support, opposition, and neutrality, mirroring real votes where people can back, oppose, abstain, or refuse.

The 2026 paper defines how to combine two picture fuzzy subgroups through a direct product, the standard way of pairing structures in algebra. It then establishes several characterizations of that product using cut sets, which slice a fuzzy object at chosen thresholds into ordinary sets. Such characterizations let researchers verify product properties with simpler tools. The work sits in pure fuzzy algebra, extending a theory already applied to voting analysis and medical diagnosis.
arxiv-2603-03757:
Kento Sakai extends a classic map of surface geometry to graphs with several curves at once. Teichmüller space, the space of shapes a surface can wear, is famously hard to navigate directly. Masur and Minsky showed its large-scale geometry matches the curve graph once the space's thin regions are electrified, collapsed for distance purposes, making the whole space weakly relatively hyperbolic. His 2026 paper generalizes that picture to the k-multicurve graph, whose vertices are sets of k curves.

The electrification now runs along regions where k curves simultaneously grow short in extremal length. The key ingredient is a bound on graph distance in terms of intersection number, adapted from an upper bound Lackenby and Yazdi proved for the pants graph. The result widens the dictionary between Teichmüller geometry and combinatorics.
arxiv-2603-03857:
Yangfu Li and colleagues propose DeepScan, a training-free framework that improves visually grounded reasoning in large vision-language models. People locate visual evidence by spotting key cues and then relating them to the wider scene, and DeepScan copies that bottom-up style. Its first stage, Hierarchical Scanning, explores local cues and extracts evidence at several scales instead of attempting one-shot localization of the full evidence, which distracting context often defeats.

A Refocusing stage then improves the localized evidence view by combining the vision-language model with visual experts. Evidence-Enhanced Reasoning then merges views at different levels through a hybrid evidence memory to produce accurate, interpretable answers. DeepScan raises performance across diverse visual tasks and model sizes without extra training, scoring strongly on the fine-grained V-star benchmark with the model tested.
arxiv-2603-04357: Agarwal and colleagues bound error thresholds for Pauli channels with coset weight enumerators. That framework, from DiVincenzo, Shor, and Smolin, probes non-additivity in small stabilizer codes and concatenations. Several new short concatenated codes show strong non-additivity. Closed forms for phase and bit flip repetition enumerators yield long code threshold estimates. Optimizing channels for maximal non-additivity at the hashing point gives mixed positive, negative, and counterintuitive results. The work thus maps both wins and limits for future bounds.
arxiv-2603-04557: Bate and colleagues compare flare runs under force free versus non-force free starts. Flare models usually start from non-linear force free maps of surface fields. Ignoring plasma forces may cap free magnetic energy. Two MHD runs of the X2.1 flare in NOAA Active Region 11283, on 2011 September 06, differ only in initial setup, sharing code. The non-force free case shifts far more and releases about twice the magnetic energy, with brighter, wider model UV glow closer to seen shape and light curves.
arxiv-2603-04657: Furst and Venkateshwaran support thermodynamics teaching with Stan, an LLM-based helper. Education AI centers on student tools, while instructor support is new. Stan serves both sides from transcripts and an index. For students, a retrieval pipeline answers queries by pulling out terms and building grounded responses with page references. For instructors, the same transcripts yield lecture summaries, flag confusion, and catalog anecdotes for hard material. All parts run locally using open-weight models, without cloud, keeping costs predictable. Deployment surfaced failures like context truncation and schema drift.
arxiv-2603-04857: Zhang and colleagues offer FireBench for testing order following in firm and API-driven LLM apps. Existing benchmarks focus on chat-helper making constraints rather than firm needs. FireBench covers six skill sides across pulls, customer support, and coding agents, with over 2,400 samples. Eleven LLMs are tested, showing order-following conduct in firm cases. The benchmark draws on real-world firm and API usage patterns. FireBench is open-sourced to help users assess fit, coders diagnose scores, and the crowd help.
arxiv-2603-05057: Inayat Arshad and colleagues propose MUTEX, combining a multilingual transformer with conditional random fields for Urdu toxic span detection. Urdu toxic span detection lags because most systems use sentence-level classification and miss specific spans, worsened by scarce token annotations, linguistic complexity, code-switching, informal expressions, and rich morphology. MUTEX pairs XLM RoBERTa with a CRF layer for sequence labeling, tested on social media, online news, and YouTube reviews with token-level F1. It reaches 60% token-level F1, the first supervised result for Urdu toxic span detection.
arxiv-2603-05257: D. Silvera-Vega and team combine density functional theory with Raman spectroscopy to study TaTe4, NbTe4, and solid-answer lattice dynamics. Lattice dynamics explain the tiny origin of charge density waves where electron-phonon coupling dominates. For stoichiometric compounds, calculations predict a phonon wobble steady with trimerization, supporting a lattice distortion driver. Calculated Raman modes match room-temperature spectra, letting assignment. Across solid answers most modes evolve smoothly. The highest-rate Eg mode, from shift-metal motion, keeps near-parent rate while intensity redistributes with stoichiometry, showing short-range character.
arxiv-2603-05357: Mohammad Mahdi Moradi and Sudhir Mudur offer DiSCTT, an accord-guided self-course. Test-time change promises better thought without supervision, but uniform objectives adapt inefficiently. DiSCTT allocates plans by doubt from sampled-path agreement. Supervised fine-tuning on pseudo-labels consolidates high-accord inputs; low-accord inputs use reinforcement learning with accord regularization. Across thinking benchmarks, DiSCTT outperforms older models, achieving higher accuracy with lower math and training times. Accounting for difficulty and doubt enables stable and lean test-time change.
arxiv-2603-05557: Biondi and team probe the gravity analogy for shallow water waves on a background flow with constant shear, moving in one direction. Moving beyond the standard spin-free treatment, they show sideways background vorticity fits just right with a working curved spacetime steering lengthwise surface waves. They extract the changed sound metric, whose conformal factor steering wave scattering becomes strongly tied to vorticity. Background shear thus cuts mode scattering a lot across an uneven bathymetry and changes surface gravity of the analogue a bit at the transcritical horizon.
arxiv-2603-05657: Kara and Vien study algebra fixed values of edge ideals under suspensions. Spurred by full suspension keeping order while maxing projective dimension, they refine this to picked suspensions joining the new vertex only to a set subset. Over minimal vertex covers, order stays kept while projective dimension grows by one. In contrast, uniform pattern fails for maximal free set suspensions, so they analyze paths and cycles fully. Projective dimension always grows by one, and order plus the a-value stay kept except for one edge path family.
arxiv-2603-05757: Zhang and team present EmboAlign, lining up video making outputs with limits for zero-shot handling. Video making models produce smooth rollouts holding moves. However, they often produce unreal rollouts, and re-aiming brings errors from flawed depth guessing. It uses a vision-language model to extract task limits. Limit-guided picking keeps the most likely rollout try. Limit-based tuning refines the path under the same limits. On six real-robot tasks, it improves success by 43.3 points over the base without training data.
arxiv-2603-06157: The authors von der Gracht and Lohse give a method to build vector fields whose dynamics follow a chosen hierarchical structure of lower directed graphs under a top digraph. Lower graph realizations are heteroclinic networks, connection patterns over states, while top level edges mark transitions between patterns. Top level connections here are excitable with zero threshold rather than heteroclinic. Every neighborhood of one invariant set holds a start whose limit lies in the second set. Hierarchical networks, excitable above and heteroclinic below, can thus be created systematically.
arxiv-2603-06457: De Vries gives examples of K3 surfaces over the rationals, of degree 10, whose geometric Picard rank is 1. Those surfaces arise as intersections in nine-dimensional projective space of three hyperplanes, one quadric, and the Plücker embedding image of the Grassmannian of 2-planes in 5-space. The paper also gives a degree 6 K3 surface over the rationals with Picard rank 1, extending the rank-1 phenomenon to a second degree.
arxiv-2603-06657: Barkman develops a control-rule frame of aging, splitting burden into regulatable and information-limited damage. Inner repair tunes tuned damage build-up and clearing, while information-limited damage lies beyond control. An enough theorem states that damage stays bounded if and only if inner repair exceeds tuned damage production. Information-limited damage must be bounded or removed by engineered fixes. Phase diagrams separate bounded, drifting, and runaway regimes across a boundary. Testing finds information-limited making dominates the aging rate, while repair power has weak pull beyond saturation.
arxiv-2603-06857: Ding and colleagues measure detective quantum efficiency and noise spectrum of the Timepix4 detector in event-driven electron imaging at two voltages. In raw readout mode, zero-frequency score tops a high mark at both voltages. At Nyquist frequency, efficiency stays solid at the lower voltage but falls close to zero at the higher voltage. Early parallel-beam diffraction data from a gold nanoparticle sample shows the detector can capture weak diffracted spots beyond a wide angle at the higher voltage.
arxiv-2603-07357: Gunn and colleagues make generative priors tunable instead of fixing them at one complexity. A latent size too small misses signal detail, while one too large chases noise, so their design lets the complexity dial move per problem. The approach covers diffusion models, normalizing flows and variational autoencoders. Across sensing, inpainting, denoising and phase retrieval it beats fixed baselines, with a closed-form optimum for the linear case.
arxiv-2603-08057: Vanc and colleagues present See and Switch, a framework for teaching robots by demonstration that handles real-world variability. Programming by demonstration opens robot programming to non-experts, yet choosing the right task variant online from visual input still strains current teaching tools. Their framework represents tasks as graphs of skill parts joined by decision states, allowing conditional branching during replay. A vision-based Switcher reads eye-in-hand images to pick the next skill part and to spot novel situations that call for fresh demonstrations.
arxiv-2603-08157: Blanco and colleagues study the Wiring Diagram Problem, a three-dimensional layout task from cable harness design and pipeline routing in tight spaces. Tree-like systems of supply units, intermediate devices such as valves or junctions, and terminal parts must be placed and linked under strict rules on safety separation, obstacle avoidance, geometric feasibility, and constructibility. The authors cast the problem as a mixed-integer linear programming model and discretize the design space into structured network graphs. The model minimizes total cable or pipeline length.
arxiv-2603-08257: Wang and colleagues improve gradient estimators for machine learning models with discrete latent variables. Such models need gradient estimators to enable backpropagation efficiently. ReinMax, the newest Straight-Through estimator, can be viewed through a numerical ODE lens as using Heun's method to reduce bias, but at the cost of high variance. The authors introduce ReinMax-Rao and ReinMax-CV, which fold Rao-Blackwellisation and control variate techniques into ReinMax to cut its variance. Their estimators perform better when training variational autoencoders with discrete latent spaces.
arxiv-2603-08757: Anna Romanowska and colleagues treat a polytope as a standalone space with an inner geometry of its own. They map the full set of coordinate systems that pin down a point inside it, using barycentric algebra to draw out the convex structure. For convex polygons, they study chordal coordinates from triangulations, give an algorithm for point coordinates, and recover the Catalan count of triangulations from parsing trees.
arxiv-2603-08857: Samata Gokhale and colleagues sense unknown tiny birefringence past the classical limit with hyper-squeezed light. Two pairs of crossed-polarization nonlinear media make and measure two-mode light squeezed in number-phase and polarization. Under realistic gain and loss, the scheme promises sensitivity gains of several decibels, set by loss alone.
arxiv-2603-09157: Tavishi Sharma and colleagues present TrustBench, a framework that checks an agent's planned action before it runs rather than grading output afterward. It pairs a trust benchmark spanning several dimensions with a toolkit agents call at the decision point. Domain plugins encode special safety rules for healthcare, finance, and technical work. In their tests harmful actions fell sharply, domain plugins beat generic checks, and the added delay stayed under 200 ms.
arxiv-2603-09257: MoonJeong Park and colleagues derive new error bounds for transductive learning, where test features are visible during training. Classical complexity measures here are hard to compute and often miss real behavior. Their bounds rest on optimal transport: they compare encoded feature distributions with Wasserstein distance, globally and per class. On graph node classification the bounds are cheap to compute and track real error well. The analysis also shows how network depth trades class tightness against class separation.
arxiv-2603-09357: G. Brochier and colleagues report the controlled creation and splitting of magnetic multi-soliton states in a quasi-one-dimensional two-component Bose gas held uniform. In the Manakov regime the spin dynamics follow an easy-axis Landau-Lifshitz equation, whose gauge link to the attractive nonlinear Schrödinger equation lets them build multi-solitons from known solutions. Two- and three-soliton states breathe robustly as integrable theory predicts. A weak local perturbation then breaks integrability and splits a two-soliton into its basic parts.
arxiv-2603-09557: Yu Li and colleagues formulate cable-towed planar object manipulation where the tether can self-wrap around the object's edges. A cable pulls only when taut and goes force-free when slack, and wrapping shifts the point where force applies, coupling routing geometry with motion and tension. Their routing-aware, tensioning-implicit trajectory optimization joins a taut-slack constraint with transmission maps for length and wrench. A hierarchy of three tractable relaxations follows from a strict reference formulation.
arxiv-2603-09857: Marco Ghimenti, Anna Maria Micheletti and Angela Pistoia study eigenvalues in sloshing problems, where a fluid surface moves in a bounded domain. The setup solves Laplace's equation inside, with one boundary part tied to the eigenvalue and the other held fixed or flux free. Their result is clean: under small changes to the domain shape, every resulting eigenvalue is simple. No two modes share the same value.
arxiv-2603-09957: Ann Yuan and coauthors find that reasoning makes language models more honest, the reverse of the human pattern. Their new data set poses realistic moral trade offs where lying pays at varying cost. Across model sizes and families, giving the model room to reason lifts honesty. The cause lies partly in representation geometry: deceptive answers sit in unstable regions and are easily shaken by small changes.
arxiv-2603-10157: Arjun Berera and coauthors ask whether a thermal starting state for the gauge field during inflation strengthens primordial magnetic fields. Standard treatments assume the Bunch Davies vacuum, which lets magnetic energy dilute steeply as space expands. A thermal state breaks conformal invariance through its temperature scale alone, slowing that dilution to a gentler power. The boost can be huge, though the toy model still misses observed lower bounds on its own.
arxiv-2603-10357: Neta Rozen-Schiff, Liron Schiff, and Stefan Schmid present GenCC, a framework that uses large language models to write congestion control utility functions for networks. Senders cannot coordinate directly, so they tune rates from latency and loss signals guided by such functions, a design task that once took years of analysis. GenCC pairs model code generation with a realistic network testbed. Guided by code evolution or mathematical chain-of-thought, the models produced protocols close to optimal, beating leading congestion control methods by wide margins in several scenarios.
arxiv-2603-10457: Brandon Yee and co-authors build theory and tools to spot group oscillations in intense particle beams at mid-range energies. From Vlasov-Poisson theory they work out how the beam responds, for three kinds of beam spread. Undamped Langmuir modes appear once beam density passes a set point, they prove. The plasma frequency is fixed by a sum rule, whatever the spread's shape. A learning tool called Prometheus, trained on simulation data, found the onset and the odd effects the theory predicts, passing all six checks.
arxiv-2603-10657: Andrew Renninger studies whether Brasília's urban form mixes its people through daily movement, or sorts them apart more efficiently. The planned capital, built around modernist neighborhood units with planned satellites and informal edges, is a rare test case. Combining mobility data with measures of urban form, amenities, and road networks at scales from districts to street cells, he finds segregation sharpens as resolution tightens. Movement softens home segregation for most, though poorer groups travel farther and richer groups stay most selectively exposed.
arxiv-2603-10757: Tongkun Guan and co-authors ask whether weak STEM visual reasoning in multimodal models comes from perception or from reasoning, by scaling each part separately. Scaling perception beat scaling reasoning every time, marking perception as the true bottleneck. Their answer is code as a perceptual medium, since executable code carries precise semantics matching structured STEM visuals. They built ICC-1M, a million image-caption-code triplets, using code as ground truth for captions. A new benchmark tests perception directly through reconstruction code, giving deterministic scores.
arxiv-2603-10957: Ilijas Farah argues that the Gelfand-Naimark duality between compact Hausdorff spaces and unital commutative C*-algebras deserves wider use in topology. Stone duality serves compact zero-dimensional spaces well, and the Wallman duality between spaces and lattices of closed sets covers some general ground. Farah contends the algebra-side view yields real insight into compact Hausdorff spaces, and especially into Čech-Stone remainders and their autohomeomorphisms.
arxiv-2603-11757: Mirzaei and co-authors study social bandit learning, where one agent learns partly by watching others act. The social agent sees others' actions but never their rewards, and no agent aims to teach. Their free energy method works over the policy space. It rates other agents' expertise with no oracle and no social norms to lean on. The agent then mixes its own experience with the policies it estimates from peers. The team proves convergence to the optimal policy.
arxiv-2603-11957: Raikote and co-authors introduce CHiL(L)Grader, a short-answer grading system that knows when to trust itself. Instruction-tuned models grade confidently even when wrong, so full automation is unsafe for high-stakes tests. The system calibrates confidence with temperature scaling, grades only sure cases, and routes the rest to humans. Teacher corrections feed back in as rubrics evolve. Across three data sets it auto-scores 35 to 65% of answers at expert-level quality. A wide quality gap between accepted and rejected answers confirms the routing.
arxiv-2603-12057: Wang, Jiang, Wang, and Chen guide image generation from coarse references with a tool called the h-transform. Training-free methods often need the exact forward operator or struggle to balance guidance and quality. Their method adds a drift term at each sampling step of a pretrained diffusion model. The drift steers output toward the fine sample that the coarse input implies. An adaptive weight schedule then balances guidance against synthesis quality. Tests span varied image and video generation tasks.
arxiv-2603-12157: Afeltra, Pinamonti, and Ho study when solution sets for the CR Yamabe equation stay compact. In dimension five, they prove uniform bounds for positive cases of subcritical equations. Positivity of the CR Yamabe constant and of the p-mass at each point drives the result. The set then sits precompact in Hölder topologies. A second result goes the other way in a symmetric setting. On the three-sphere, a group-invariant structure admits solutions whose maxima diverge, which proves noncompactness there.
arxiv-2603-12457: Lindeman and Nagel map how disordered solids fail as a landscape of instabilities over shear angle. A solid under strain, they argue, is a network of weak spots that can interact along distinct forcing directions. Their simulation tool applies strain at a continuously variable angle under periodic boundaries. Lines of instabilities appear across that angle space in the revealed landscape. Some lines cross, others fade to zero, and paths through phase space can dodge weak points. Hysterons that undo themselves on reversed shear explain how line ends close.
arxiv-2603-12757: Haoyang Liu and Cuihua Du study the chemistry and motion of the GD-1 stellar stream. Data-driven abundances show no clear alpha knee, and the thin stream and its cocoon share the same pattern. That match supports a common origin from a low-mass progenitor. In test-particle simulations, the Sagittarius dwarf does not heat the stream enough to form the cocoon. It does reshape the stream spread and drags more stars toward the Galactic center, as data show.
arxiv-2603-12857: Giulio Barletta and co-authors track perovskite solar cell decay with machine learning on luminescence images. These cells are efficient, yet their working stability blocks wide use. Electrical sweeps give good metrics but are slow and miss local damage. Their LumPerNet reads electroluminescence and photoluminescence images taken as a device ages. It estimates how much efficiency the cell retains. Global brightness change held most of the signal, while spatial detail added robustness.
arxiv-2603-12957: Håkon Hoel and Johannes Vincent Meo present adaptive numerical methods that estimate blow-up times for autonomous ordinary differential equations. Step sizes follow how sensitive an auxiliary hitting time is, all set in advance. That a priori design is the novelty of the work. The authors derive theoretical error rates for the scheme. Tests show a clear saving in computational effort over rival approaches. Numerical experiments back the theory and show how the methods behave in practice.
arxiv-2603-13157: Andres Izquierdo and co-authors use line tomography to hunt embedded planets in protoplanetary discs. Disc substructures could come from planets or from disc instabilities, and centroid maps alone cannot split them. Synthetic tests show a few hours of ALMA time can reveal planet-driven traits. Those traits include Keplerian deviations and local line broadening, plus skewness that flags the cause. In HD 135344B, the data hint at three massive planets in and near dust gaps. MWC 758 instead fits a warped, eccentric disc.
arxiv-2603-14457: Collado-Gonzalez, McConnell and Englot fuse sonar and camera data for safe underwater mapping. Cameras give sharp detail but fail in murky water. Sonar works in poor light yet lacks resolution and height cues. Their system pairs stereo sonar with a single camera. The paired sonar views fix height, so each scan yields full 3D points. Camera regions of interest add more points with confidence scores. Marina field tests show the method maps complex shapes well, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-14957: Shan and co-authors unify image understanding and generation in one autoregressive model, CyCLeGen. Split designs use separate modules for seeing and drawing. CyCLeGen instead loops image to layout to image and back. Cycle consistency acts as the training compass. The model can inspect its own outputs through the loop. Synthetic supervision from cycles lets it improve with less labeled data. A reinforcement objective rewards cycle-consistent behavior. Broad benchmark gains span both understanding and generation tasks, they report.
arxiv-2603-15057: Heiss and co-authors break down the error sources behind global feature effect plots, such as partial dependence and accumulated local effects. These plots are estimates, and their trust level was poorly understood. The team splits mean squared error into model bias, estimation bias, and two variance parts. Simulations across many data processes and learners test training, holdout, and cross-validation strategies. Holdout data is cleanest in theory, but training-data bias proved tiny in practice. Cross-validation cut model variance, notably for overfit models.
arxiv-2603-15157: Reumers and co-authors present a finite element method for computing Newtonian noise in gravitational wave detectors. Seismic waves shake the soil and change its density, which tugs on the interferometer mirrors. Their formulation splits the noise into total, bulk, and surface parts on a finite element mesh. Coupling matrices depend only on geometry and material, so new wave fields reuse them cheaply. Tests on plane waves and a Rayleigh wave case match reference results. The method ships in the ANNA toolbox for MATLAB and Python.
arxiv-2603-15357: Zhang and Liu propose RAPI, a framework that infers user traits from recommendation lists alone. Recommender systems shape choices in many fields, and their output lists are easy to observe. RAPI builds a surrogate model that mimics the target recommender, using BERT content embeddings for items. An augmentation module extends the lists by output similarity. A weighted classifier then assigns dynamic weights to infer each trait. Tests on four collections reached trait inference accuracy up to about 0.76 across scenarios with varied information access.
arxiv-2603-15557: Xiong and co-authors build a diagnostic framework that traces hallucinations inside vision-language models as they unfold. Instead of treating a false caption as a static error, they model generation as a path through a low-dimensional cognitive state space. Probes project that path into a readable form. Their key finding links geometric oddness of the path to high information surprisal. Detection then becomes anomaly spotting in that space. Tests on POPE, MME, and MS-COCO reach state-of-the-art results, even with weak or dirty calibration data.
arxiv-2603-15857: Jajoo and co-authors simplify how behavioral foundation models learn state features. Such models promise agents that adapt to any new reward. Their reach stops at rewards spanned by preset state features. Complex training goals were thought vital for rich features. Plain next-state prediction in latent space forms features too. That plain goal shrinks feature spread and span, though. Their RLDP method adds a simple orthogonality penalty. Feature diversity then holds through training. Low-coverage tests favor RLDP where prior methods falter.
arxiv-2603-15957: Jana and co-authors ground coding self-play with real hard questions as goalposts. Teacher-student self-play can drift toward hard but useless problems. Their GASP method anchors training on real-data goalpost questions. The teacher first builds an easier variant of a goalpost. It then builds a harder variant of that easier form. The ladder slowly closes the gap to the goalpost. Pass-at-20 on LiveCodeBench rose 2.5 percent over unguided play. Some goalpost questions fall that no baseline could solve.
arxiv-2603-16557: Yoon and co-authors test whether AI assistants apply saved user preferences with judgment. Persistent memory helps personalization, but some preferences clash with social norms. BenchPreS checks if models apply or suppress preferences by context. Two metrics score misapplication and apt application. Even frontier models struggled at this selectivity. Stronger preference followers over-applied the most. Reasoning skill and prompt defenses did not fix the flaw. Models treat preferences as global rules, not context signals.
arxiv-2603-16757: Mollaali and co-authors present pADAM, one diffusion model that learns many kinds of physics at once. Most solvers handle a single equation, so they do not transfer well. pADAM learns a shared prior over system states and, where relevant, physical parameters. One trained model then handles forward prediction and inverse inference with no retraining. The authors report accurate results from sparse data, from simple diffusion up to Navier-Stokes flow. With conformal prediction, it also gives uncertainty ranges with coverage guarantees.
arxiv-2603-17157: Zhu and Han study network games where agents act on simplified, wrong models of their world. Agents see noisy aggregate signals from local network effects and read them through simple conjectures. Long run behavior is captured by Berk-Nash equilibrium, which can diverge from the Nash equilibrium of the true game. They quantify this gap with a Value of Misspecification metric. They then introduce cognitive arbitrage: a designer nudges agents' conjectures with tiny distortions to steer outcomes. A two timescale learning scheme converges to the optimum.
arxiv-2603-17357: Zhao builds WebPII, a benchmark for spotting personal data in web screenshots. Computer-use agents raise privacy risks when their training shots hold real user details. The set has 44,865 synthetic e-commerce images with fine labels for many kinds of identifiers. It also tests partly filled forms, where users are mid-entry. A model called WebRedact more than doubled the text-only baseline score, he reports, at real-time speed on a CPU.
arxiv-2603-17857: Bechtel and Theewis prove strong results for a class of quasilinear stochastic evolution equations. Their setting is bounded domains with an Lp frame where p exceeds two. Recent weak existence results supply the first half of the argument. Yamada-Watanabe theory then upgrades weak solutions to strong ones. An L1 contraction step gives pathwise uniqueness of those solutions. The pair of results closes well-posedness for this class of random PDEs.
arxiv-2603-17957: Xu and Signer explore cross-media annotation as a boost for scholarly reading. Scholars already pull video, audio, and web pages into their PDF work by hand. Most PDF tools accept only a narrow range of media inside notes, though. Their design study maps a tool that links PDF passages to outside materials with ease. Richer links could enrich how scholars read a text. Guided tours for later readers open up as well, they suggest.
arxiv-2603-18157: Hebbar and co-authors introduce a model for learning-augmented algorithms based on online learning. Past instances of a problem should inform the solution for a future instance. Performance is the average ratio to the optimal cost across all instances. For k-median clustering, their learner nearly matches the best fixed solution in hindsight. Experiments show near-optimal results, and the method adapts on its own to shifting instance sequences.
arxiv-2603-18257: Liu, Cheng, and Bogdan find what a learning agent can truly control by acting, not just watching. Noise terms driven by the same hidden causes as the true state can fool watch-only picks. Their method makes the agent's own acts random, so each input axis gets a fair test. Two-sample tests with false find control then mark the axes the agent can move. In 12 test worlds with up to 100 noise axes, it matched the true best score in 11.
arxiv-2603-18657: Dao, Matrouf, Rouvier, and Evans tackle spoof detection that must work across many speech corpora. Training on several corpora can hurt rather than help, they find. Corpus-specific bias likely blocks generalization. Their IDFE framework uses multi-task learning with a gradient reversal layer. The layer strips corpus identity from learned embeddings. Features then keep spoof cues while dropping dataset habits. Across four datasets, average equal error rate falls by 20 percent versus the baseline. The result supports domain-invariant features for anti-spoofing models.
arxiv-2603-19157: Lee and co-authors help image models draw rare mixes of traits that they seldom saw in training. Their ADAPT method plans the prompt steps in a fixed way, guided by attention scores. It blends in parts of the prompt that sit at right angles to the main text cues. No new training is needed. On the RareBench test set, ADAPT tops prior methods for rare mixes. The team reports clear gains while image quality stays intact.
arxiv-2603-19257: Shim and Wei let users state routing tasks in plain words and get valid paths back. Real tasks carry extra rules on route count, length caps, and depot spots. Their system first matches a request to a known template in a library. For new task types, the model builds its own formal version from the text. Draft routes are checked, compared, and refined over rounds of self-correction. The design aims to cover many routing forms with one tool.
arxiv-2603-19457: Jose and co-authors compare how turbulence moves through two round pipe expansions with like mean shapes. One expansion is a sharp 90-degree step, the other a gradual 45-degree wedge. Stereo and time-resolved imaging track the flow at two Reynolds numbers. The wedge stirs more energy over a broader shear layer near the split. The step confines that action to a thin zone by the corner. Both cases share a spectral hump in cross-flow swings near separation. Flow speeds match, so the gap lies in structure and persistence.
arxiv-2603-19557: Lee and co-authors report lattice results on scattering in an Sp(4) gauge theory. The theory, with two fundamental Dirac fermions, may underlie dark matter as strongly interacting massive particles. The team uses Lüscher's formalism on finite-volume energy levels. They study two pseudoscalar states scattering in the spin-1 channel. Findings are preliminary and span a broad range of fermion masses. The work tests how dark particles in this theory interact with each other.
arxiv-2603-19657: Liu and Zhang study how to pick the number of parts in a multidimensional Gaussian mixture model. The parts share one known covariance matrix. From characteristic function data, they build matrices whose rank equals the part count. A minimax lower bound shows how many samples telling k parts from k minus one requires. Their spectral thresholding estimator needs more samples but is provably sound. A singular value ratio version suits practice. Means are then fit by gradient descent on a MUSIC-type objective.
arxiv-2603-19857: Li and co-authors present FoleyDirector, a system for steering sound made from video. Current video-to-audio tools lack fine control over when each sound occurs. FoleyDirector guides generation with structured temporal scripts, one caption per short time segment. A fusion module attends to these scripts as the audio forms. A second method makes in-frame and off-screen sounds in parallel. The team also built the DirectorSound dataset and two test sets. Results show stronger timing control with high sound quality.
arxiv-2603-20057: Kovalenko reviews multiscale modelling of hemicellulose and lignin in plant cell walls. The review also covers cellulose nanocrystals and whole lignocellulosic walls in water. A molecular solvation theory, 3D-RISM-KH, sits at the center of the account. It has been used on hemicellulose hydrogels and on forces inside primary cell walls. It also probes how lignin interacts with itself and with hemicellulose. These contacts prove mostly hydrophobic and entropy-driven, through water exclusion. The insights aim to guide biomass use, from plant breeding to pretreatment design.
arxiv-2603-20257: Esclapez and co-authors build a better score function for rare event simulation in ocean climate models. Splitting methods like TAMS need a good score to estimate tiny transition chances with few runs. Their method projects the model dynamics into a reduced state space. Data from the runs then shapes the score function there. A two dimensional model of the Atlantic overturning circulation serves as the testbed. The new score beat existing options and kept variance low, even at small noise levels.
arxiv-2603-20757: Colletta and co-authors build Josephson junctions from stacked superconducting films in a nanobridge form. Their stacks pair niobium with niobium nitride or titanium nitride. A high resistivity nitride layer forms the weak link. The top niobium layer sets the critical temperature and film quality. This design tunes the superconducting gap without ion beam milling. It also avoids oxide tunnel barriers. The junctions ran inside dc SQUIDs with reliable behavior. They offer a scalable path for superconducting electronics.
arxiv-2603-20857: Jiao and co-authors present FRoG, a fast and robust method for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting, which renders new views of static scenes in real time. Dynamic methods often render slowly, need a good starting point cloud, or fail in dim scenes. FRoG embeds time data per Gaussian and fuses it early to speed rendering. A depth and error guided step adds Gaussians where detail is weak. Tests show faster rendering with top level visual quality.
arxiv-2603-20957: Liu and co-authors show that fine tuning can unlock verbatim recall of copyrighted books in large language models. Firms have told courts that models do not store training text, and they rely on filters to block copying. By training models to expand plot summaries into full text, the team got three major models to reproduce most of held out books. The effect spread across authors: training on one novelist unlocked books by over thirty others. Three rival models recalled the same books in the same regions.
arxiv-2603-21257: Wang and co-authors present CALVO, a serving engine for language model inference with heavy network demands. Distributed prefix caching reuses KV cache blocks, but fetching them from remote servers can bottleneck long context requests. CALVO makes cache loading a first class concern. Loading and GPU computation run as separate, asynchronous stages, which uses network, PCIe, and compute resources better. Loading delay also enters the per-request service cost. On a real testbed, SLO attainment rises by up to about sixty two percent.
arxiv-2603-21357: Ding introduces AgentHER, a method that recovers training signal from failed agent runs. Agent training pipelines usually discard failures, though most runs fail. AgentHER adapts hindsight experience replay to language agent runs. A run that fails one goal often succeeds at an alternative goal, so it can be relabeled as a success for that goal. A four stage pipeline sorts failures, extracts outcomes, relabels with model help, and packages data for fine tuning. On WebArena and ToolBench, it beats success-only training.
arxiv-2603-21457: Stewart and Duru examine a stability question for high-order numerical methods that solve nonlinear conservation laws. Entropy stability keeps solutions bounded, but local energy stability stops spurious high-frequency waves from taking over. Whether one method can have both traits was open. They analyze dual-pairing summation-by-parts methods and find that the built-in upwind filter can ensure local energy stability. Tests on the Burgers and shallow water equations, plus a turbulent shear flow, support the analysis.
arxiv-2603-21757: Sakos and co-authors give a global training method for parametrized quantum circuits with few trainable parameters. Finding the best parameters is hard, and standard searches can stall on barren plateaus. Their scheme returns a near-global optimum with high probability, in time polynomial in the accuracy and qubit count. The quantum device is used once, up front, to gather data. A classical phase then optimizes with moment and sum-of-squares methods. A side result places this circuit class inside BQP, which caps the hard problems it can encode.
arxiv-2603-21957: Du and co-authors compress the visual tokens of video language models down to about 2 percent. Two-stage methods break down at such low budgets, dropping key evidence. Their method treats compression as one global allocation over a single pool. Attention weights and semantic similarity jointly pick tokens that add the most and repeat the least. Leftover tokens are merged back in by clustering, and a text-aware pass inside the model trims further. At 2 percent retention, it kept 90 percent of baseline scores.
arxiv-2603-22057: Jeon and co-authors present SpatialBoost, a framework that teaches vision encoders about 3D space. They often miss how objects sit in real 3D scenes. SpatialBoost turns dense 3D spatial facts from an image into plain language. A large language model then feeds that knowledge back into the encoder. Training uses multi-turn chain-of-thought reasoning to build spatial understanding step by step. Applied to DINOv3, the authors report a gain on ADE20K from 55.9 to 59.7 mIoU. That score sets a new state of the art on the benchmark.
arxiv-2603-22257: Messere and co-authors test whether gas around Milky Way-like galaxies sits in an extended disk. They study ion distributions in Milky Way analogs from the IllustrisTNG simulation. For each ion, they measure alignment with the disk and the share of absorption matching rotation. Magnesium II aligns best: 63% of its mass follows the disk's spin axis. Oxygen VI aligns least, at 35%. A mock survey finds corotation shares near 80% for MgII and 60% for OVI. The pattern supports a disk-like, corotating gas structure.
arxiv-2603-22357: Niculescu and co-authors review how AI tools can aid aphasia therapy. Aphasia, often from stroke or brain injury, breaks speech and daily communication. Therapy works, but therapists are scarce and tools rarely fit local language or culture. The authors draw on neurocognitive research and their own field study. They built two digital therapy prototypes shaped by local language diversity. The designs aim to raise patient engagement and match therapist needs. They argue adaptive AI tools can widen access to care.
arxiv-2603-22657: Sabhlok and co-authors observe glowing gas around seven radio-loud quasars at redshift near two. They use the Keck Cosmic Web Imager to map Lyman-alpha, helium, and carbon emission. The Lyman-alpha glow spans 80 to 120 kiloparsecs. The other lines cover smaller regions. Inner gas glows two to ten times brighter than in other samples. The authors infer that quasar light powers the inner lines, escaping along the radio jet. Their two-part model splits inner gas, shaped by the host galaxy, from outer turbulent gas.
arxiv-2603-22757: Li and co-authors present GPAD, a network for spotting defects in factory goods with 3D data. Shape flaws like dents and warped contours are hard to catch in flat images. GPAD first builds a point cloud expert to extract fine geometric features. Surface normal math sharpens those features into a geometric prior. A two-stage fusion then mixes data types and the prior. Attention guided by the prior helps segment defect regions. Tests on MVTec-3D AD and Eyecandies beat prior top methods on accuracy.
arxiv-2603-22857: Teranishi proposes a secure two-party protocol for matrix multiplication. The inputs are fixed-point numbers, and the result is approximate. Security rests on standard lattice-based assumptions, he proves. The whole computation takes a single round of communication. He applies the protocol to run a linear control law in encrypted form. The client does less online work than with the plain controller. Inputs, outputs, and parameters stay private. A numeric example shows control precision holds despite approximation and quantization errors.
arxiv-2603-23557: Barbero builds a physical scheme for sorting exoplanets by what heats them. Starlight bathes every planet, yet tides can outshine it as a heat source. His frame centers on a ratio of absorbed star flux to tidal flux. A value near one marks the border where both matter equally. Applied to about 2,000 exoplanets, most worlds prove star-driven. A real share, though, runs on tides. Orbit size and eccentricity sway the tidal flux most. The scheme gives a clear lens on planet heat regimes.
arxiv-2603-23957: Wang and co-authors present PointRFT, a reinforcement fine-tuning method for point cloud learning. Point clouds carry 3D shape and meaning, but reinforcement methods were little tried there. PointRFT adapts group relative policy optimization with two rewards: one for accuracy and one for dispersion. These rewards steady training and limit distribution shift. In few-shot classification tests on three 3D foundation models, it beats plain supervised fine-tuning. A hybrid pretraining pipeline with PointRFT reaches state-of-the-art results when data are scarce, they report.
arxiv-2603-24157: Ghosh and co-authors present CarePilot, a multi-agent system that automates long healthcare computer tasks. They also build CareFlow, a human-annotated benchmark of long workflows in medical tools. It covers annotation software, DICOM viewers, health record systems, and lab systems. Plain vision-language models do poorly on these long tasks. CarePilot uses an actor-critic design. The actor picks the next step from the screen and memory, while the critic checks each action and corrects it. Scores beat strong baselines by about 15 and 3 percent.
arxiv-2603-24257: Galliena and co-authors present a memory-augmented vision-language agent that captions objects in 3D scenes. Normal models describe the same object differently from each viewpoint, which breaks scene memory for robots. Their agent joins data association, captioning, and exploration in one autoregressive model. It reads the current image, a top-down map, and an episodic memory of past objects. Training uses a disagreement-based policy in photorealistic 3D settings. Caption scores rise by up to 11.86 percent, and self-consistency by 7.39 percent, over baselines.
arxiv-2603-24557: Bittner shows that geometric curvature governs work in open quantum steady states. Classical thermodynamics links work to areas enclosed by cycles in state space, but whether this survives in driven, dissipative quantum systems was unclear. For a driven two-level system, Bittner builds a work one-form whose curvature sets the work of cyclic processes. Strong dephasing kills the work, so coherence is required for the geometry to matter. Yet the work depends on where the cycle sits, not on coherence alone. Reversing the cycle flips its sign.
arxiv-2603-25257: Salmi and Bogucka defend fog computing resource assignment against sneaky model attacks. A k-means system first clusters requested workloads, then sorts new requests into those clusters. An attacker can probe the sorter with queries, learn its shape, and craft requests that overload the chosen machines. Their defense hardens the sorter in advance with adversarial training. Fake attacks join the training mix, so the model learns to shrug them off. Tests show the provisioning system stays stable under the attack.
arxiv-2603-25457: De Paoli and Zhu find exact transport laws for buoyant mixing inside porous rock. Rising warm fluid fingers through pores, and that brief fingering stage boosts transport in aquifers and carbon stores. Old rules for it were mere fits. Their balances tie transport, flow strength, and scalar decay together at each moment, with no slack. The action stays inside the mixing layer, which yields a one-knob model for the mean field. It predicts self-similar profiles and a linear transport law. Giant simulations confirm the claims.
arxiv-2603-25557: Nain and co-authors replace a costly quantum solver with a neural net trained on very few examples. Impurity solvers are the bottleneck in dynamical mean-field studies of correlated electrons. Their net learns from one to two orders fewer samples than past work. Inside the training range it matches Monte Carlo accuracy. Outside it, at colder temperatures, its guesses still seed the exact solver well. That head start cuts total solve time by up to five times. The trick suits fast scans of phase space.
arxiv-2603-25657: Jiang and Pananjady study how to minimize a convex loss when the data oracle is noisy. Standard tools like sample average approximation can do badly at real sample sizes, they show. Their method, called VISOR, uses a variance reduction trick to do much better with the same samples. They prove matching lower bounds that depend on the instance at hand. An accelerated form of VISOR is optimal in both sample and oracle cost. They apply the theory to generalized linear models and linear regression.
arxiv-2603-25757: Wayo and co-authors show that surface-code threshold estimates depend strongly on the decoder used. They compare four decoders under Pauli noise and under native GKP-style digitization. The tools are MWPM, Union-Find, belief propagation, and a neural-guided MWPM. At distance five, MWPM and Union-Find form the accuracy and speed frontier. The neural-guided version is slower and less accurate, and belief propagation trails far behind. Only MWPM gives stable threshold crossings. Threaded runs speed things up while keeping statistics sound.
arxiv-2603-25857: Busch and co-authors test whether language models truly learn molecular properties from context. Models might instead recall memorized answers from training data. The team runs blinding experiments that strip away information step by step. Nine models from the GPT and Gemini families face three MoleculeNet datasets. Shot counts of 0, 60, and 1000 act as a further control. Controls and bootstrap intervals back the analysis. The authors find no sign of verbatim recall on the old benchmarks. Blinding does expose clashes between stored knowledge and context.
arxiv-2603-26257: Batic, Dutykh, and Essa Sukaiti build wormhole models inspired by noncommutative geometry. In these models, point sources are spread out by Gaussian smearing, which keeps the shape smooth. They derive broad relations that show how the redshift function shapes stress and energy near the throat. With tuned redshift, the exotic matter stays in a thin zone near the throat. They then test quasi-de Sitter and Chaplygin-like matter laws, getting flat, horizon-free wormholes with local redshift wells.
arxiv-2603-26357: Dao and Metaxas present MPDiT, a transformer design that cuts the cost of diffusion and flow-matching models. Standard diffusion transformers use the same patch size in every block, which wastes compute. MPDiT starts with large patches to catch broad global context, then shifts to small patches for fine local detail. The design cuts compute by up to 50% in GFLOPs while keeping output quality strong. New time and class embeddings also speed up training, and tests on ImageNet back the choices.
arxiv-2603-26557: Köster and co-authors present MemBoost, a serving framework that cuts language model cost by reusing past answers. Real workloads repeat many near-duplicate queries across users and sessions. MemBoost lets a small model reuse stored answers and pull support from a growing memory. Hard or doubtful queries are escalated to a stronger model. Unlike standard retrieval setups, the design suits live chat with answer reuse and cost-aware routing. Simulated workloads show far fewer costly calls while answer quality stays near the strong baseline.
arxiv-2603-26657: Rahman and co-authors present a way to tune how equivariant a vision model is, with error bounds attached.
