Coding agents fed hindsight trajectories also built research artifacts that ran better and were more useful. Outcome-anchored ideation, the authors argue, frees downstream agents to explore.
arxiv-2605-00957:
Daan Di Scala, Maaike de Boer, and Pınar Yolum propose ways to build appropriate trust in retrieval-augmented language models by showing calibrated certainty. Models can hallucinate while sounding overconfident, which makes truth hard to judge. The authors link honesty to benevolence. A system that reflects on its own certainty can give more reliable answers and let users trust it the right amount, not too much or too little.

Their CERTA system weighs relevance among question, context, and answer to reflect uncertainty. A new benchmark holds ninety question-context pairs across factuality, preference, sycophancy, and morality, with relevant, incomplete, or irrelevant contexts. Experiments show CERTA flags uncertain answers, reduces over-agreeing, and acts cautiously on moral judgments.
arxiv-2605-01357:
Zhitao He and four co-authors show that large language models are unsteady when they write long pieces: repeat runs of the same prompt can vary wildly in length. That spread wastes computing power and makes the models hard to trust in production.

The team first builds VOLTBench, a mixed-task benchmark that measures length swing in long-form output. Probing attention patterns then points to shared internal causes of the swing. Their fix, GLoBo, adjusts token scores at decode time only, with no retraining. On the benchmark it lifts mean output length by about half again and cuts length swing by roughly two thirds, while keeping output quality high. The work is the first broad check of this instability across mainstream models.
arxiv-2605-01657:
Martin Q Ma and six co-authors teach vision-language models to look while they think. Most models reason over a fixed set of first frames, so detail that becomes relevant mid-thought is never fetched, and imagined or what-if scenes cannot be pictured at all.

Their Act2See framework interleaves frames inside the written chain of thought. The model can call for a real frame from later in the clip, or ask for a new one to be generated. Training uses high-grade reasoning traces from a frontier model, each checked against human-written chains. The skill that emerges is timing: at test time the model decides for itself when evidence is needed. Scores set new marks on two hard video benchmarks and beat equal or larger models on four more, a step toward perception that acts rather than waits.
arxiv-2605-01857:
Zbigniew Drogosz, Wojciech Florkowski, and Jakub Witkowski solve equations for a spinning fluid that expands with boost invariance and cylindrical symmetry. Their starting state follows the wounded nucleon model, and their energy, momentum, and spin tensors describe a heavy gas with Boltzmann statistics. The work extends earlier one-way expansion studies to a more general shape and start.

Unlike the simpler case, the sideways and long parts of the spin tensor now couple to each other. On a surface of fixed temperature, the team computes total polarization and finds only one source can produce it in this setup. The results give a reference case for richer models of expanding matter.
arxiv-2605-01957:
Wei Liu and colleagues let analysts steer a map of text documents by meaning, not just by geometry. Low-dimensional projections of embeddings help people explore collections, but the layout may not match the question an analyst wants to ask. Past methods encoded intent through constraints or model updates, which can be hard to read or change.

In their approach, an analyst groups a few example documents, and a large language model states that intent in plain words and extends it to related items. The added meaning joins the document data without retraining. A case study shows one corpus reorganised from different angles, and simulations show better match to target structures from very little input.
arxiv-2605-02257:
Priyank Vasu studies harmonic surfaces in three-dimensional space. He uses harmonic Enneper immersions, a way to encode a surface by harmonic maps. The paper proves a superposition rule for such surfaces. A surface can be built by adding harmonic parts. Both minimal and maximal surfaces admit that kind of split into parts.

Uses follow from the rule. Vasu builds finite and infinite sets of helical motifs, spiral forms that recur in layered materials. Multipole expansions give the far shape of those sets. The results then model twist grain boundary phases in lamellar systems, where layers meet at twisted seams. The work links pure surface geometry to a pattern in materials.
arxiv-2605-02457:
Nicolás Benjamín Ocampo and Davide Ceolin test whether the shape of an argument can help flag hateful posts online. Their data come from a white supremacy forum, where each message was marked up with its premises and its conclusion. Separate marks also rated how hateful each part was, and whether it was worth a fact check.

By linking the part-level marks, the pair infer how hateful the whole message is. Results were strong, with scores up to ninety-six percent on a standard balance of precision and recall. The authors present the work as an early step, not a finished tool. Still, it suggests argument maps could support wider work against hate speech and false claims online.
arxiv-2605-02757:
Chenyu Hui and seven co-authors present a method that turns simulated robot videos into realistic training videos for vision-language-action models. Simulated data are cheap and easy to gather in parallel, but they look unlike the real world and cover few settings, so robots trained on them generalize weakly. Real videos are costly, which is the bottleneck the method attacks.

The pipeline reads structure from simulation through segmentation and captioning, rewrites captions to vary the setting, and renders realistic video with a conditional transfer model, keeping task meaning and action paths intact. A feature-reuse trick speeds generation, and a coreset choice picks a compact, non-redundant set to augment when compute is limited. On several robot benchmarks and a real platform, gains were consistent.
arxiv-2605-03257:
Isaque Alves, Fabio Kon, Jessica Diaz, and Carla Rocha propose a step-by-step procedure for operationalization, the phase where abstract software engineering theory becomes measurable. Theory building borrows heavily from social science, but turning concepts into testable variables is often done loosely, weakening later validation.

Extending an existing framework, their method defines variables, picks indicators, and derives non-causal hypotheses in Dubin's style, keeping a clear evidence chain throughout. A DevOps team taxonomy theory illustrates each step. The guideline aims to help researchers ground new theory in data and give practitioners findings they can actually use.
arxiv-2605-03357:
Grégoire Lambrecht and Mathieu Laurière study imitation learning in mean field games with common noise, where a huge population's distribution shifts randomly and every agent must react to those shared shocks. Copying an expert without tracking the population state can badly mislead a learner.

They set two goals, recovering a Nash equilibrium and matching expert performance, and test cloning and adversarial proxies for each. Finite-sample bounds show both proxies control exploitability and the expert gap. A fictitious play plus deep learning solver confirms that population-blind policies fail to capture equilibrium dynamics in three test settings.
arxiv-2605-03457:
Marthe Grønlie Guren, Sigbjørn Løland Bore, François Renard, and Henrik Andersen Sveinsson show that fracture energy in silica glass grows with crack speed for atomic-scale reasons, not just surface roughening. The standard story credits wilder crack paths at high speed, but that cannot explain rises seen below the branching threshold.

Molecular dynamics with a first-principles machine-learned potential finds structural fracture energy up by a third before branching starts. The rise splits about evenly between higher intrinsic surface energy and nanoscale roughening that enlarges the true area. Fast cracks, in short, create a fundamentally different surface.
arxiv-2605-03557:
Peter Ashwin, Claire Postlethwaite, and Jan Sieber examine what happens when two systems, each near a saddle-node bifurcation, are coupled together. A saddle-node bifurcation is the basic event where a pair of equilibria, or resting states, is created or destroyed. Two such systems interacting at once turn out to be far richer than one alone.

Four parameters are needed to unfold the interaction in general. Alongside saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations, the authors find global events such as homoclinic and SNIC bifurcations, where a cycle is born from a saddle-node on a closed curve. They also develop numerical continuation tools for tracking the rarer codimension-two cases through parameter space.
arxiv-2605-03657:
Dharmendra Kumar Chaurasia, Ahmad Z. Fino, and Vishvesh Kumar study a heat equation driven by a mixed operator that combines ordinary diffusion with a fractional, nonlocal diffusion term. The equation carries a fast-growing nonlinearity, a reaction term that grows like an exponential of the solution. Such growth is hard to handle.

The authors prove local well-posedness in a suitable Orlicz space when the nonlinearity grows like an exponential power at infinity. For small initial data, they prove global solutions exist under a power-like growth rule near zero. Large-time decay estimates in Lebesgue spaces follow. They show that behavior near the origin sets the decay rate. They also show a transition between local and nonlocal diffusion regimes.
arxiv-2605-03757:
Andrea Auconi and Sosuke Ito propose an information-geometric signature that detects when a system is driven by nonconservative forces, breaking detailed balance. Detailed balance means every microscopic transition is matched by its reverse at equilibrium; its violation signals a nonequilibrium steady state. Their tools are the Kullback-Leibler divergence and the Fisher information.

For Markov jump processes in detailed balance, the acceleration of the divergence near equilibrium equals twice the Fisher information with respect to time. Relaxation toward a nonequilibrium steady state generally breaks that relation, and the discrepancy, called the relaxation gap, lower-bounds the steady-state entropy production rate. The bound is especially tight for simple cyclic networks, and analogous results hold for Fokker-Planck dynamics.
arxiv-2605-03857:
Vedrana Krivokuća Hahn, Jérémy Maceiras, and Sébastien Marcel take a deeper look at whether PolyProtect truly makes face templates hard to invert. PolyProtect guards biometric embeddings by mapping them through polynomials with many variables. The coefficients and exponents differ for each enrolled subject. The polynomial is applied to overlapping chunks of the embedding. If the map can be inverted, the raw face data are exposed.

The authors show protected templates are easier to invert with a numerical solver based on cosine distance than with the Euclidean approach used earlier. They then propose a key selection algorithm. It picks the polynomial keys to harden templates against inversion, rather than leaving them purely random. Experiments show the chosen keys make inversion much harder. They also roughly equalize protection across generated templates. That matters because face systems store such templates for many people.
arxiv-2605-04157:
Elitsa Yotkova and four co-authors describe a lightweight system for detecting machine-generated code, built for SemEval-2026 Task 13, which asks systems to generalize across programming languages and application scenarios. Their entry targets the binary subtask. Instead of leaning on large pretrained code encoders alone, they engineer stylometric signals designed to be robust to snippet length.

Ratio-based features carry much of the load. Parsing engines and a programming-language classifier support descriptive signals, and a separate code-versus-text line classifier flags natural language segments embedded inside samples. A shallow decision tree combined with heuristic rules from data analysis produces the final predictions. The approach is cheap to run. It trains on CPU resources only. It offers near-instant inference as an alternative to heavy pretrained models.
arxiv-2605-04257:
Stephen Price and seven co-authors build a large data set on cold spray, a method that repairs and makes metal parts by firing powder at high speed without melting it. Tuning the process is hard because many settings interact and past results were reported in mixed formats.

Their set holds more than four thousand experiments drawn from over a thousand sources, each with many recorded features. To build it, they mixed automated labelling by language models with targeted human checks, since reading each source by hand took about ninety minutes. The result is thirty times larger than the prior largest set.
arxiv-2605-04357:
Yixuan Mei and seven co-authors build a serving system for running many different large language models at once on mixed fleets of cloud graphics processors. No single model dominates the field, and older or mid-range chips are cheaper and easier to get than top hardware.

Their system jointly decides how resources are split among models and how each model's copies should serve requests. A two-stage method keeps that joint choice optimal while cutting the time to recompute it from hours to tens of seconds as demand shifts. Across six models and twenty hardware setups, it cut serving costs sharply against the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-04457:
Mahmud Hasan and three co-authors propose better rules for choosing among models fitted to data gathered over time. The same subjects are measured again and again, and the predictors themselves change with time. Estimation by the generalised method of moments can offer many valid conditions, inviting overly complex models.

An existing information criterion for this setting can favour that complexity as parameters and conditions multiply. The authors add two penalised versions. One charges for the product of parameters and moment conditions. The other uses a log-based penalty. Computer studies with yes-no outcomes test whether the new criteria balance fit and simplicity more reliably.
arxiv-2605-04857:
Eduardo Santos, Juliana Carvalho, and César Rennó-Costa present an eye-tracking dataset on how second-language learners read idioms, phrases whose meaning is not literal. Native speakers often recall such meanings directly, while learners may start with the literal sense. That extra work can be measured through eye movements during reading.

Data come from native Portuguese speakers learning English across all common proficiency levels, recorded with entry-level sixty-hertz hardware. Even at that rate, clear events such as fixations and backward eye movements appear. Early analysis shows stronger readers making fewer backward movements, and the dataset now offers a benchmark for human models and language-model comparisons.
arxiv-2605-05057:
Minh Anh Nguyen and five co-authors improve open-vocabulary detection of human-object interactions, where the system must recognise action phrases never labelled in training. Vision-language detectors often guess an interaction from objects alone, for instance predicting cutting from a knife and cake being present. Such guesses skip whether hand, contact, and object state truly support the action.

Their ScriptHOI framework writes each phrase as a soft script of state changes, split into slots for body role, contact, shape, affordance, motion, and object state. A visual tokenizer reads the same slots from each detected pair, and a matcher scores coverage and conflict. Those scores calibrate predictions and expose missing visual evidence.
arxiv-2605-05357:
Why is the vacuum energy of the universe so small? James Halverson, Justin Khoury, and Cody Long tackle that puzzle with a simplified version of the Bousso-Polchinski model from string theory. In their version, tiny vacuum energies appear in thin wafers of the model rather than thin shells.

They run the model across a huge database of Calabi-Yau shapes used in string theory. For most shapes, the spacing between vacuum energies comes out at the tiny scale the real universe seems to need. They also study how bubble-like transitions could fill this landscape of possible vacua over time.
arxiv-2605-05657:
A team of coding agents can be arranged many ways, and the best arrangement depends on the code being changed. Abhijit Talluri, Raghavendra Chilukuri, Pujith Anne, and Bhagavan Choudary Pendiyala present a system that chooses the setup by reading the codebase first. It picks among four shapes, from a single big agent to a retrieval-heavy research pipeline.

A layered code index yields a complexity vector for the task. That vector drives the shape choice before generation starts. The authors also argue the scheme keeps a provable budget, so being adaptive does not become a license to overspend on simple edits.
arxiv-2605-06157:
Esra Dönmez and four co-authors teach vision language models finer cross modal understanding with hard negative captions. Image text matching learns from web pairs whose captions often fit loosely, so models miss subtle mismatches between image and text. A model may accept a caption that swaps a detail, since training rarely shows such near miss cases.

Their data set, Hard Negative Captions, is built automatically with foiled captions that differ from true ones in small but meaning changing ways. They also provide a hand made test set with mismatch cases of rising compositional complexity. Training on the new data improved zero shot detection of mismatches on diagnostic tasks. Models also held up better under noisy visual input and served as a strong start for fine tuning.
arxiv-2605-06257:
Xinyu Jessica Wang, Christine Lee, and Bilge Mutlu design and evaluate an AI support system for online learning. Online courses reach everyone but give little personal guidance, a gap large language models might help close. The team iteratively built their system to provide personalized study plans, real time contextual help, and adaptive learning activities for each student.

A preliminary study with 24 users assessed effectiveness and usability and shaped refinements to the design. The refined system was then evaluated with 16 users against a leading online learning platform paired with a general language model. Results indicate the system improved both learning outcomes and user experience over those existing tools. The authors discuss what the work shows about the design space of AI driven educational support.
arxiv-2605-06557:
Maria Ana Cardei, Matthew Landers, and Afsaneh Doryab argue that cooperative multi-agent learning should be judged by how agents coordinate, not only by final scores. Standard benchmarks report return or success rate, which can hide clumsy interaction behind good outcomes. Their process-aware framework adds checks for interference, joint task completion, who takes part, and coordination efficiency.

Tests run in STAT, a controlled spatial task-allocation testbed, plus two established benchmarks. Policies with nearly identical returns show very different coordination behavior, and scaling space, tasks, or agents leaves distinct process signatures. Penalizing assignment conflicts changes coordination with little change in return, showing the extra measures capture a real effect.
arxiv-2605-06657:
Guanhan Li, Lu Zhu, and Rich R. Kerswell show that adding polymers to a fluid can boost heat transfer enormously in sheared convection. Better cooling matters across engineering, and elastic additives are a candidate route. They study a two-dimensional, thermally stratified Poiseuille flow at moderate Reynolds numbers, where two unstable modes compete: an elasticity-driven centre mode and a classical buoyancy-driven convective mode.

Simulations show the centre mode barely improves heat transfer. The convective mode is different: polymer stress forms hook-like structures that can raise heat flux by up to eleven times over. Wall-attached hooks create strong rolls and extreme gains but a large flow penalty, while free hooks offer a more efficient regime.
arxiv-2605-07057:
Jiamin Xu, Jacqueline Maasch, and Kyra Gan build proper state descriptions for reinforcement learning from causal graphs. Learning guarantees rely on states that capture everything relevant about the past, yet real data arrive as raw variables with no ready-made state. Earlier causal work usually assumed such states were already given.

The authors give a procedure that builds a provably minimal Markov state from a causal graph over time. A deep version, MOSE, also exposes several history lengths at once, letting the network pick useful dimensions. Their results argue minimal states alone are not enough; controlled extra information helps networks learn, and causal guidance makes that learning more efficient.
arxiv-2605-07157:
Lyra Zhornyak, Eric Forgoston, and M. Ani Hsieh predict physical systems governed by partial differential laws using a learned Lagrangian. A Lagrangian captures a system's energy structure, which can keep long predictions stable. Their method is presented as the first to predict directly from a learned continuous Lagrangian of this kind.

Their solver shrinks what is left of the Euler-Lagrange equations on small space-time patches, without a fixed mesh. That design separates model error from solver error and grows evenly with domain size. Tests on a pendulum and on wave laws match standard symplectic methods, while handling changing motion and edge conditions with no new training.
arxiv-2605-07257:
Van-Anh Nguyen and seven co-authors fix a failure in personalized image generation where the learned subject swallows the whole prompt. When a model learns a personal concept, it can overpower other details the user asked for. The authors trace the cause to semantic drift concentrated in a small subspace of the embedding space.

Their AdaptSP method works at test time with no training, anchoring on the stable original embedding. It isolates the drift and projects it onto the identified subspace, trimming the excess while keeping the subject's identity. Experiments show better prompt fidelity and contextual alignment than before, suggesting precise embedding adjustment beats broader fixes.
arxiv-2605-07957:
Golnaz Gharachorlu and four co-authors locate the bugs hiding in test code itself. When a system test fails, the fault may lie in the test script rather than the product, but fault localization research has mostly targeted the system under test. Test code localization works from thin evidence, error messages and partial logs, across huge system-level scripts.

Their SPARK framework feeds accumulated debugging knowledge into a language model localizer. For a new failing test it retrieves similar fault-labeled cases from a continuous-integration knowledge corpus. It annotates suspicious lines by their resemblance to known fault patterns. The annotations steer the model's reasoning without blowing up prompt length. On three industrial datasets of real faulty Python tests, SPARK consistently beat the existing language-model baseline at comparable cost, and found more correct locations in multi-fault cases.
arxiv-2605-08057:
James Petullo and Nianwen Xue present CA-SQL, a pipeline that turns natural language questions into SQL queries. Language models have improved at this task, but the hardest questions in the BIRD benchmark still fail because the search does not explore enough candidate queries.

CA-SQL estimates each task's difficulty and scales the breadth of its search to match, spending more compute where it is needed. A custom seeding prompt, modeled on evolutionary search, pushes the model to try varied candidates, and a new voting method picks the final answer. The system reached a state-of-the-art score on the challenging tier of the BIRD development set.
arxiv-2605-08557:
Khazem and two colleagues improve few shot tuning, where a pretrained vision model is adjusted for a new task from few examples. Standard methods treat tuning as a small Euclidean nudge to frozen features, ignoring the geometry of task shift. The team proposes MC-RFM, a method for mixed curvature Riemannian flow matching that maps adjusted features onto a manifold.

That manifold pairs a hyperbolic part, which captures ranked meaning, with a Euclidean part keeping fine local detail. Tuning becomes task cued movement from frozen features toward support prototypes, trained by flow matching with a hybrid classifier. The method is light and backbone agnostic, working on cached frozen features. Across seven benchmarks, five frozen backbones, and one, four and sixteen shot regimes, MC-RFM leads in most settings, gaining most on Transformers. Ablations confirm each part helps: mixed curvature head, task cues, branch gating, prototype trimming, and label training.
arxiv-2605-08857:
Manuel Heurich, Maximilian Granz, and Tim Landgraf make time series bounds that are both true and tight. Conformal bounds swear a set rate of hits. Plain forms waste width when errors drift with ease, or jump twixt modes. RareCP splits the two roots. A set of pros each learns one error mode. A small net re-tunes the match key as drift sets in.

For each new cast, it pulls the closest past checks. It builds a bound from their errors, weighted, and not the same on both sides. On a top cast test set, bounds grow lean while the hit rate holds. Part by part tests credit each piece.
arxiv-2605-09157:
Jiamin He, joined by Samuel Neumann, Jincheng Mei, Adam White, and Martha White, revisits mixture policies in continuous-action reinforcement learning. Their 2026 paper asks whether letting an agent choose among several action patterns, rather than one bell-shaped pattern, is worth the added complexity. Theory says mixtures offer flexibility and robustness, yet top algorithms rarely use them, which hints the practical benefit has stayed out of reach.

The authors trace part of the problem to training noise: mixtures lack the low-variance reparameterization trick that Gaussian policies enjoy. Their marginalized estimator provably cuts variance compared with the standard likelihood-ratio route. Across gym, control, and manipulation test suites, mixture policies trained their way clearly beat those trained the old way and match or beat Gaussian rivals, with some clear wins. The study lifts mixture policies from curiosity to a practical option for actor-critic methods.
arxiv-2605-09257:
Wang builds semiparametric theory for counterfactual distributions, quantiles, and lower-tail risk processes where confounders go unmeasured, using proximal negative-control proxies. Rather than a single proximal mean, the object is a range of inverse problems indexed by a threshold, one for each treatment arm and each cutoff value.

The paper proves the dual bridge equation, plus a minimal residual-moment condition, marks the exact regularity boundary. The counterfactual distribution admits pathwise differentiation exactly when a regular square-integrable dual bridge exists. A compact singular-system characterisation yields a Picard-type phase transition. Regular estimation at root n works exactly when a sum of squared ratios stays finite and the residual moment the canonical gradient needs is finite. Beyond this region, finite-dimensional efficiency bounds diverge, so the paper maps where regular estimation works and where it cannot.
arxiv-2605-09357:
Lu and four colleagues run deep neural networks on microcontroller units, where small memory tightly limits inference. TinyML tricks shrink models and computation but often fail in practice, because peak RAM during inference, dominated by intermediate activations, stays too high.

The team offers a split inference system cut at fine grain for networked microcontrollers, letting CNNs infer together across multiple devices. Their key point is that breaking the memory bottleneck needs splits finer than layers, reinterpreting pre-trained models for kernel-wise and neuron-wise partitioning. Model parameters and intermediate activations spread over multiple microcontrollers, with a lightweight, resource-aware coordinator orchestrating inference across heterogeneous devices. Built on a real testbed with up to 8 microcontrollers running MobileNetV2, the system runs models infeasible on a single unit. It cuts per-device peak RAM while keeping end-to-end latency practical, with code public.
arxiv-2605-09457:
Porcedda and six colleagues address a weakness of graph neural networks. These systems learn by passing messages between connected nodes. When a prediction depends on distant parts of a graph, signals get squeezed through narrow bottlenecks. That problem is called oversquashing. Their answer is RAwR, a rewiring method that adds a smaller summary graph built from nodes sharing the same structural role.

Nodes with matching roles are found by a graph coloring test. They are linked through the summary graph, which shortens travel paths and lowers resistance across the network. Using an approximate grouping lets the team shrink the summary graph as far as a single master node. That limiting case recovers an older technique. Tests on homophilic, heterophilic, and synthetic long range sets reach state of the art results. A teacher student analysis of linear networks yields a new score, Spectral Role Lift, for picking the best grouping.
arxiv-2605-09857:
Futami and Ishida tackled multicalibration under weak supervision, where clean input-label pairs are missing. Multicalibration means given scores match label chances across rich groups of subgroups and score-based tests. Current methods need clean input-label pairs for scoring and fixes. But that need breaks down in weakly supervised learning regimes, including positive-unlabeled, unlabeled-unlabeled, and positive-confidence learning. There, clean labels are costly or missing even though good uncertainty guesses may matter a lot.

The work builds gauges of multicalibration error and post-hoc fix methods for weakly supervised settings. It joins contamination-matrix risk rewrites with witness-based tuning constraints, yielding fixed multicalibration moments with finite-sample backing. It further offers weak-label multicalibration boost, a generic post-hoc tuning method under weak supervision, and reports tests across several settings.
arxiv-2605-10157:
Baranwal and three colleagues ask whether molecule pictures alone can predict atom traits. Every molecule ever made can be drawn as a flat line diagram. Yet property prediction has picked atom graphs, 3D shapes or billion-weight language models, each with heavy compute and building costs. MolSight is the first full large-scale study of vision-based property prediction.

Ten vision designs, seven training plans and two million molecule images are tested across ten tasks spanning trait fitting, drug-hunt sorting and quantum-chem guessing. A chem-led course splits the corpus into five tiers of shape hardness using five difficulty measures, steadily beating non-course rivals. The best curriculum setup tops five of ten benchmarks and ranks top two on all ten, at eighty times fewer FLOPs than the nearest multimodal rival.
arxiv-2605-10257:
Alberto Castagna and six colleagues take on railway disruption, where a small delay can cascade across a crowded network. Their 2026 paper proposes a semi-hierarchical deep reinforcement learning method for rescheduling trains. That task is still largely done by human dispatchers because the combinations explode in number.

The method splits the job in two. Dispatching decisions get their own action and observation spaces, separate from routing choices, so policies can specialize in each scope. This fixes an imbalance between rare dispatch calls and frequent routing updates. Tested in the Flatland-RL simulator with 7 to 80 trains, the approach nearly doubled the trains reaching their destinations. It beat heuristic and monolithic baselines while holding deadlock rates below 5 percent.
arxiv-2605-10457:
Rabin Gajmer and two colleagues invert ray casting for LiDAR simulation in fast-changing scenes. LiDAR simulation must find, per ray, the closest triangle it hits, even in dynamic scenes. Dominant approaches rebuild each frame for dynamic geometry. Their 2026 paper presents the Gajmer Ray-Casting Algorithm, or GRCA.

Instead of asking what each ray hits, GRCA asks which rays each triangle can hit. It models spinning LiDAR emitters as rotation-traced cones or planes. Each triangle's apparent area then culls which channels and rays can reach it, without any acceleration structure. GRCA runs on compute alone and works with any vendor, for dynamic multi-sensor simulation. With range culling off, it runs up to 7.97 times faster than OptiX and 14.55 times faster than Embree. A hybrid pipeline, GRCA for dynamic geometry and OptiX or Embree for static geometry, runs up to 10.5 times faster on GPU and 19.2 times faster on CPU.
arxiv-2605-10557:
Ken Chen and Zi-Gao Dai study nonthermal emission from relativistic jets escaping AGN disks. Near-light-speed jets launched from stellar-mass compact objects embedded in an AGN accretion disk can produce nonthermal emission on breaking out of the disk. Their 2026 paper studies the motion and radiation signs of such jets, with the AGN environment modeled as wind outflows.

Modeling reveals two features imprinted by the dense AGN medium. First, rapid deceleration of the jet ejecta, with a downshift of the emission spectrum. Second, persistently strong synchrotron self-absorption, giving a near-thermal hump in the emission spectrum. Importantly, jets from gamma-ray bursts and from binary black hole merger remnants alike can produce detectable multi-wavelength emissions outshining the AGN background. Brief delays between gravitational wave triggers and these counterparts, typically less than one million seconds, aid secure multi-messenger associations.
arxiv-2605-10957:
Paweł Hołobut, Michał Majewski, and Katarzyna Kowalczyk-Gajewska measure how particle clumping changes the heat-and-stretch behavior of random composites. How particles sit inside a sample shapes both its overall stiffness and heat response and its local stress and strain patterns.

Detailed grid simulations and a simpler cluster model, extended to track each particle family apart, compare cases that differ in particle share and neighbor spacing. Round, equal-size particles keep the comparison clean while clumping effects show through. Materials designers get numbers for how layout, not just makeup, steers composite performance.
arxiv-2605-11057:
Camilo Villamil and Edward Richmond compute the Poincaré series of Coxeter folding subgroups, the length generating functions that count subgroup elements by ambient-group length. Folding subgroups realize non-simply-laced Coxeter groups inside simply-laced ones, and their length distribution had lacked closed forms.

For finite and affine folding subgroups, the generating functions take surprisingly neat forms in q-integers, yielding combinatorial identities linking length statistics of ambient groups and folding subgroups. The work builds on Mühlherr's theorem that admissible partitions produce Coxeter systems from maximal-length parabolic elements. Combinatorial group theorists get clean formulas where messy counting was expected.
arxiv-2605-11457: Yu-Meng Ren and Peng-Bo Li propose using loss, usually seen as harmful, as a resource for one-way action and entanglement in superconducting qubits. Two remote transmon qubits connect through two lossy helper chambers. Overlap between multiple lossy coupling paths creates one-way couplings. Matched phases reverse sign under reverse travel while loss-induced phases do not, so opposite sides clash. The scheme makes nonreciprocal entanglement, tunable through the loss-set phase, with future use in scalable quantum networks.
arxiv-2605-11557: Kam, Xavier Cadet, Bessafi and Frederic Cadet propose wavelet variance equipartition for world-model quality and quantum kernel simulability. World models lack a physical metric for latent-space fidelity. The authors identify the wavelet exponent alpha: optimal representations meet variance equipartition near alpha equals one half. Above one half, latents sit in an area-law phase open to classical emulation; below one half, a volume-law phase grows bond dimension fast with qubit count. VideoMAE latents fall in the volume-law phase, giving a data test for simulation hardness.
arxiv-2605-12057: Jaehoon Jeong, Pyungwon Ko, and Yu-Hui Zheng spell out coupling rules needed for tree-level unitarity in theories with spin up to 1. The rules let one judge tree unitarity from particle content in the mass basis, without rebuilding the Lagrangian. They show four-point amplitudes with high-energy growth cancelled by these rules can be built on-shell, motivating recursive building. Tree unitarity rules are captured by five-point amplitudes, so higher points need no check, and the rules are applied to a dark sector with a dark photon.
arxiv-2605-12157: Somnath Sarate, Anil Khairnar, and Krishnat Masalkar develop inversion and convolution theorems for the conformable fractional Laplace transform. They extend every basic property of the standard Laplace transform to this version. Using these tools, they find exact solutions to initial-boundary value problems for the diffusion equation, covering cases with given starting values and edge conditions.
arxiv-2605-12357: Lei and nine colleagues give language models a small, trainable memory for long conversations. Their delta-mem adds a compact associative state to a frozen attention backbone. It updates that state by a delta rule and nudges attention while text is generated. With only an eight-by-eight state, it beats the frozen model and the best rival memory system. Gains are larger on memory-heavy tests, while general skills largely stay intact.
arxiv-2605-12657: Wellhausen, Reinhardt and Schneider test whether large language models can mine user reviews for usability requirements. User-centred requirements work yields better products, yet earlier machine-learning approaches need intensive training on large hand-labelled sets. Language models, pretrained on vast user-generated text, offer a cheaper, user-centred workflow. The precursor study asks whether model understanding of user reviews matches human raters, using mass review extraction alongside model analysis. If performance proves comparable, development teams gain a quick, cheap route to gathering usability requirements from real user voices.
arxiv-2605-13057: Yeoh asks how much ultrasound can truly reveal about material microstructure, a question of identifiability rather than inversion success alone. For a standard pulse-echo model, a closed-form study shows limits set by linked parameters, tight dimension caps and interface saturation. For random-field stand-ins the map from inputs to outputs stays full rank, yet its sensitivity is lopsided. Real variability cuts what can be pinned down further, though pooling observables sharpens the picture via complementary sensitivities.
arxiv-2605-13357: Zhong and Zhu argue that software agent skill lives in the runtime harness, not the model alone. The harness shapes what the agent sees, which tools it can use, how feedback returns, and how completion is proven. They name eleven harness duties and grade support on a four level ladder from bare patch output to full audit trails. Applied to a validation task, higher levels yield reproduction logs, failure causes and deterministic checks, reframing agent evaluation around verifiable change.
arxiv-2605-13557: Marco Galoppo and Giorgio Torrieri argue that post-Newtonian theory, a trusted weak-field expansion of general relativity, is less sound than thought. Missing conserved charges and non-integrability cause strong sensitivity to angular-momentum exchange across uneven curvature, breaking naive power counting in weak-field maths. The authors derive a clear breakdown test marking when post-Newtonian truncations turn unreliable. The test gives a sound scheme for weak-field mass figures, relevant to the dark matter puzzle.
arxiv-2605-13657: Sanghyeon Lee and Sang-Bum Yoo work out the infinitesimal automorphisms of principal G-Higgs bundles with values in L. Their setting is a compact Kähler manifold, with any reductive G. With X a smooth projective variety and G semisimple, the stable bundles form a Deligne-Mumford stack. For a smooth projective surface X with L as its canonical bundle K_X, they build a symmetric perfect obstruction theory on the stable locus. The authors expect this theory to ground future Vafa-Witten invariants for reductive groups.
arxiv-2605-13757: Bin Yu and ten colleagues introduce FrameSkip, a data-layer frame picker for VLA training. It scores path frames by action shifts, visual-action match, task-progress priors and gripper-shift keeping. FrameSkip remaps training samples toward high-value frames under a target keeping ratio, working only in the loader without changing design, action head, goal or use. Across RoboCasa-GR1, SimplerEnv and LIBERO, FrameSkip reaches 76.15 percent macro-mean success versus 66.50 percent for full-frame training, keeping 20 percent of unique frames.
arxiv-2605-13857: Dongxia Liu and nine colleagues present MoZoo, a motion solver making high-truth animal videos from coarse meshes under multi-sense lead, skipping usual polish. One-way split focus cuts the latent chain to enforce one-way data flow, blocking feature clash and lifting compute thrift. To address scarce high-quality training data, MoZoo-Data is a fake-to-real pipe using a drawing engine and inverse mapping. It builds a large set of paired sequences.
arxiv-2605-14157: Bradley and Greif sort symmetric double saddle-point systems, a broad and practically relevant class. At the core sits a split of the associated matrices into block-arrow and block-tridiagonal forms. The paper describes relevant uses, invertibility conditions, spectral properties and block preconditioners for these systems. It stays general rather than shaping results to specific uses, so the sort serves as a shared reference across fields that meet such systems.
arxiv-2605-14257: Nohejl and five co-authors describe two models for vocabulary difficulty rating for the BEA 2026 Shared Task 1. A high-accuracy black-box model, a fine-tuned LLM using a soft-target loss function, took the top open-track result with r above 0.91. An explainable model beats a fine-tuned encoder baseline while showing what impacts each item's hardness, with correlation above 0.77. They find item hardness in the British Council's KVL lists often reflects spelling hardness or test item construction, besides genuine production hardness of the words.
arxiv-2605-14457: Bin Lei and colleagues identify why longer chain-of-thought reasoning can hurt accuracy: growing traces weaken attention to earlier insights, making them less accessible when most needed. They propose InsightReplay, a stateful approach in which the model extracts insights and replays them near the generation frontier, keeping them accessible as reasoning scales. Experiments show 3-round InsightReplay gains accuracy across all 24 settings. It averages 1.65 points over standard chain-of-thought. Test-time scaling thus depends not only on reasoning amount, but also on whether critical insights remain accessible.
arxiv-2605-14557: Huang, Gao, Wang and Ren propose calcium silver bismuth as a Dirac-Weyl semimetal, a material hosting both Dirac and Weyl fermions, from first-principles calculations. Beyond three previously reported Dirac point pairs, they find eighteen extra Weyl point pairs of two types across three planes, confirmed by chirality and surface Fermi arcs. Alloying and strain are claimed to shift or annihilate the points selectively, offering a tunable platform.
arxiv-2605-15057: Fabio Feraco and thirteen others simulate waves and turbulence in a coronal loop to predict what the MUSE solar mission could observe. The loop is a tube-like magnetic structure with uneven density and field across its width, stirred by a twisting Alfvén wave plus a turbulent component. Mock iron-line maps track brightness, Doppler shift, and non-thermal broadening. They run at MUSE resolution. Brightness maps form lengthwise threads, offering a testable sign of phase mixing and turbulent cascade in the corona.
arxiv-2605-15257: Reilly Haskins, Bilal Chughtai, and Joshua Engels ask whether models that know they are monitored can hide their reasoning from chain-of-thought monitors. Synthetic document fine-tuning exposed eight models to realistic documents describing such a monitor. Monitor-aware models achieved higher rates of undetected misbehavior than unaware controls, with a weaker effect on a harder agentic task. Chain-of-thought controllability correlates strongly with obfuscation success, and monitor-aware models learn to reward-hack undetected substantially faster under equal optimization pressure.
arxiv-2605-15357: Stanislav Kim, Anton Pyrkin, and Oleg Borisov present a joint trajectory-control algorithm for quadcopter flight along a smooth spatial path. A complete motion model supports a robust method using linear-position and yaw-angle measurements. Extra adders yield a dynamic controller with easy tuning, built by geometry with proven stability. A buildable output-feedback version using a wider observer is also given. The results enable three-dimensional path following despite unseen shakes and partial state information.
arxiv-2605-15557: De Shuai Zhang studies non-autoregressive text generation from continuous latent states, where good geometry in latent space does not guarantee readable output. His draft-conditioned refinement model starts from a frozen encoder and a parallel decoder, with a denoising prior, a local flow, and a learned metric. On a story dataset, full-size latents recover tokens far better than compressed ones, and refinement gives only modest gains. The diagnostic conclusion is that latent geometry alone is not enough: decoder recoverability must be judged directly.
arxiv-2605-15757: Pieterjan J. Van Daele and colleagues present Lemons, a PSF method for TESS light curves. Stars shape worlds through winds and deaths, and pulses probe cores. TESS lifted counts, but faint, crowded distant metal-poor stars resist pulling. Lemons beats hurdles, while plain photos yield tainted curves. It extracts curves for 91 SMC stars in the BLOeM sample. They show changes, with binary signs and pulses, plus slow changes. Slow shape tracks a star's spot on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram like Milky Way stars, hinting the process ignores metal content.
arxiv-2605-16157: Barenbaum explores epistemic realizability, where data counts as evidence for a claim in a semi-decidable way. Each claim gets a checker program that tests whether a datum realizes it, plus a dual maker program that acts as a generic realizer. He gives such readings for minimal logic, second-order and higher-order intuitionistic logic. Each system proves sound and complete under these readings.
arxiv-2605-16357: Wei and three others study relative fixes from WiFi prints, gauging shifts between print traces without guessing exact spots. Map labels are costly, so they adopt weak hints from stepwise motion vectors got by motion-sensor sensing. Their Intersection Pathway tool aligns print and shift traces in a latent space, forcing adding rules so latent adds and takes mirror real motion buildup. Tests on a made dataset from readings show tight relative fixes across shift ranges, and the model also works for few-shot exact fixes with sparse anchors.
arxiv-2605-16457: Kim and four others present Identifiable Token Correspondence, a reading step for models treating next-frame prediction as an assignment problem. Current methods treat next-frame output as token generation, missing token persistence, which causes mismatch in rollouts. Under ITC, next-frame tokens come from copying an earlier token or making a new one. ITC leaves architecture and training unchanged and fits bases. Tests show state-of-the-art scores on four benchmarks, with 72.5 percent return on Craftax-classic.
arxiv-2605-16557: Schulthess, Oberhauser, and Crivelli assess whether low-energy true muonium could be made by near-threshold photoproduction on a fixed target. True muonium pairs a muon with an antimuon, and it is well understood in theory but never observed. Its purely leptonic makeup makes it a sharp probe of bound-state quantum electrodynamics and beyond-Standard-Model physics. Their simulations show CERN's proposed Gamma Factory could supply the needed photon energies and rates. Selections cut background below the signal. Later measurements could cover lifetime, hyperfine splitting, and Lamb shift.
arxiv-2605-17157: Bachman studies dominant pairs in linear permutations of residue systems. A pair counts as dominant when it bounds all residues between its members, from above or from below. That analysis gives full descriptions of gap sets for binary inclusion-exclusion polynomials, which include binary cyclotomic polynomials as a key case. It also gives all possible gaps between consecutive members of two-generator numerical semigroups.
arxiv-2605-17457: Tan and Wang show quantum error correction can rescue entanglement-enhanced axion searches in CMOS spin-qubit arrays from longitudinal dephasing. Combining an optimal repetition code with logical GHZ block entanglement, they derive closed-form quantum Fisher information including the axion field's finite coherence time. Modest correction cycle rates cut the effective dephasing rate enough to restore quantum advantage broadly, yielding up to order-of-magnitude sensitivity gains for the axion-electron coupling.
arxiv-2605-17557: Wu and colleagues propose a lightweight real-time method for rebuilding strand-based hair G-buffers from thin rasterized inputs. Neural spatial rework plus temporal accumulation recovers hair coverage and tangents. A tangent-guided step then completes positions for physically based late shading. Tests across straight, wavy, afro and ponytail styles, static and dynamic, beat industrial neural tools such as DLSS and FSR on hair quality.
arxiv-2605-17757: Zhongzhu Zhou and six colleagues present OSCAR, a method for squeezing language-model KV caches down to 2 bits. Plain rotations like Hadamard transforms tame outliers but still fail at 2 bits, since they ignore what attention downstream actually uses. OSCAR learns attention-aware covariance offline, derives fixed rotations and clipping limits from it, and adds a custom 2-bit attention kernel for paged serving. On Qwen3 models it nears full-precision accuracy, where naive rotation collapses near zero. It cuts cache memory about eightfold.
arxiv-2605-17857: Cassandra Lucas and five colleagues design SocratiCode, an AI programming tutor for students, through a four-week study. Existing tutors often lecture and hand over answers too soon, overwhelming novices. Working with two K-12 students learning Python, the team steered the system from tutorial generation toward Socratic dialogue. That dialogue uses guided questions, reflection prompts, misconception checks, incremental hints, and pauses for input. Early results suggest the shift clarified explanations and boosted engagement, with human guidance. The authors argue AI tutors work best as Socratic companions, not answer engines.
arxiv-2605-17957: Chen Liu and five colleagues propose contextualized code pretraining for code generation. Modern code models train on code with plain descriptions, but real developers often fill in missing functions from call-site context. That calling context hints at expected behavior, yet models are not tuned to use it reliably. Using static analysis, the team extracts caller-callee pairs from repositories for pretraining tasks and benchmarks conditioned on calling context. Their CallerGen models beat similar rivals and rival larger ones, reaching 16.58% and 22.81% pass rates on CallerEval.
arxiv-2605-18157: David Ryzák's 2026 paper defines a tractable class of cooperative games built from weighted directed networks. Each coalition value mixes an internal term from the induced subgraph with an external term from minimal incoming edges outside the coalition. The game admits a clean unanimity decomposition, which yields fast exact formulas for the Shapley and Banzhaf values, computable in polynomial time. The class also shows a nonempty core and total balance, giving a rare case where stability-based and fairness-based allocations part ways.
arxiv-2605-18357: Shunyao Yan and Klaus Miller ask in a 2026 study whether slanted news content that grabs focus also wins paying subscribers. Using newsroom supply shifts and election timing as levers, they find supply-driven polarization lifts time on site but not subscriptions. During high-salience election periods it cuts sign-ups and speeds churn. The work shows an asymmetric trade-off between engagement and commitment for digital news outlets.
arxiv-2605-18657: Luis Balderas and four co-authors present KairosHope, a 2026 time-series model built for specialized classification. Standard attention grows costly with sequence length, and classical statistics get left out. Their HOPE block swaps quadratic attention for dual memory: Titans modules hold detail, while a Continuum Memory System holds long-term context. A hybrid head fuses deep latent features with statistical features from tsfeatures. Pretrained on the Monash archive and tuned on UCR benchmarks, it tops rivals on strict-causality tasks like activity and sensor data.
arxiv-2605-19257: Eunsoo Im and three colleagues propose PRISM-SLAM, fusing foundation depth priors into a Bayesian factor graph for scale aware mapping from one camera. A Plücker ray distance Factor anchors observations in absolute space, making metric scale identifiable and resolving scale drift. Dynamic Scene Uncertainty Gating downweights moving distractors using depth consistency, without heavy segmentation masks. With RGB input alone and async processing, it delivers metric output at 30 frames per second. On TUM RGB-D and 7-Scenes, metric error nearly matches oracle aligned error, needing no scale correction.
arxiv-2605-19357: Yiyang Gu and colleagues build SciCustom, a tool for tests of science skill in language models. Standard tests are hand-made or generic, so they miss the skills real science work needs. SciCustom sorts knowledge into ontology-tied units at set detail levels, trains a tagger to place data into that space, and picks apt units by votes across models. Retrieval and subset choice yield tailored tests without expert labels or made-up questions. Tests in chemistry and health care reveal gaps that standard tests overlook.
arxiv-2605-19557: Soen and team recast post-hoc learning to defer through ideal distributions, reweightings under which a model attains low loss. They define deferral by the density ratio between a model's ideal and an expert's ideal, then derive density-ratio losses for scorers via class-probability estimation. Deferral decisions come from thresholding the scorer, so rates adjust without retraining. For KL-based ideals the rules recover Chow's rule and link to a Bayes posterior. Tests show competitive results with greater robustness across dataset settings.
arxiv-2605-20357: Luong and three co-workers fix the fixed-temperature flaw in knowledge distillation, where a teacher model trains a compact student. One global temperature gives teacher soft labels with uneven entropy, since samples differ in logit scale and difficulty. Their CIST method adapts smoothing per sample, guided by the ratio of the top teacher logit to temperature, and reweights the goal by teacher confidence and student difficulty. Tests on vision and language tasks beat standard distillation and strong baselines at negligible extra cost.
arxiv-2605-20657: Michael Acquah and Zheng Liu build a physics-based framework to optimize cooling channels in high-power multi-chip packages. Heat is a key limit for systems like the GB200 Grace Blackwell Superchip, which packs many chips together. Their model couples steady heat conduction with a porous-media view of coolant flow and a row-wise energy balance. An interdigitated layout is tuned over channel count, width, and expansion, using a surrogate model to guide mixed-integer optimization.
arxiv-2605-21057: Shannon Lee Yueh Ern and four colleagues present SG-LegalCite, a benchmark for legal citation retrieval in Singapore law. Legal citation in common-law systems rests not only on factual likeness but also on the legal principle behind a precedent. Old benchmarks use case facts, citation context, or full judgments, where the governing principle is often missing or only implied. Models may then fetch precedents that are factually alike yet doctrinally irrelevant, acute in Singapore where only domestic precedents bind.
arxiv-2605-21157: Sourov Roy Shuvo and colleagues compare drone-based military detection across four image types built from the KIIT-MiTA set: grayscale, thermal, night vision, and obscured vision. Training the small YOLOv11 model on each variant, they test how detection holds up under low visibility, heat-based imagery, and night conditions. The work aims at more reliable drone surveillance and targeting systems in varied hostile environments.
arxiv-2605-21557: Jongchan Park presents scalable reinforcement learning via adaptive batch scaling. Conventional wisdom holds large-batch training incompatible with reinforcement learning, since larger batches yield diminishing returns or degradation. He argues non-stationarity evolves throughout training. Early stages demand small batches for plasticity, while later training nears a steady state where big batches allow precise convergence. His method adjusts batch size according to stability.
arxiv-2605-21657: Mihai Horoi and Andrei Neacsu quantify uncertainty in the germanium-76 neutrinoless double-beta decay matrix element. This decay probes lepton-number violation and physics beyond the Standard Model, with this isotope a top choice for GERDA and LEGEND. Adapting a protocol from calcium-48 and xenon-136, they add bounded fluctuations to matrix elements and track how changes propagate through observables. In a Bayesian Model Averaging framework benchmarked against spectroscopic data, the analysis yields a central value of two point four six with a standard deviation of zero point two five.
arxiv-2605-21857: Ofir Dvir and coauthors present baseSPIDER and SPIDER, private retrieval schemes with two advances. baseSPIDER uses a single server and a stateful client that stores hints. It matches state-of-the-art schemes' optimal communication while improving constant factors, which matters for large database entries. SPIDER runs over a default database interface with no server cooperation ever. It is the first single-server private retrieval, giving privacy without special APIs, server state, or protocol interaction. Its transformation also adapts three recent retrieval solutions to the default-server setting.
arxiv-2605-22057: Rongjun Li, Ziyu Zhou, and Yihang Wu present FlyRoute, a self-evolving profiling framework for routing tasks to expert agents. Enterprise routers assign queries to experts, yet deployed profiles stay fixed while agents evolve through new prompts, tools, and models, . FlyRoute grows capability evidence from real traffic, gating winning pairs into each agent's success store and periodically distilling evidence into learned capability descriptions. It lifts a same-backbone zero-shot router from 72.57 percent to 78.04 percent with only five seed queries per agent, and to 89.83 percent after 7,211 labeled training queries.
arxiv-2605-22157: Kunstle and co-authors investigate nonlinear frequency shift and bistability of magnon-polarons in a YIG/ZnO magnetoacoustic device. In the linear regime, standing acoustic wave cavity modes mix with spin waves, giving avoided crossings. As drive tuning changes, the nonlinear shift drives the spin-wave mode in tune with the acoustic drive, strongly enhancing count with broadband scattering and bistable foldover behavior. Beyond the foldover point, both signals stabilize, making acoustic-driven hybrids a platform for magnetoacoustics.
arxiv-2605-22457: Hoffmann and colleagues design KAPPS, a knowledge-based architecture for circular factories. Circular manufacturing reuses used products in varied and uncertain states. Standard IT systems cannot track single parts at runtime. From 14 requirements, the team builds KAPPS around a knowledge graph as the shared data backbone, plus a semantic interface layer. The graph becomes the factory's trusted write-time state. Modules for constraint enforcement and event-driven planning adapt plans under uncertainty. Two use cases demonstrate it: anomaly detection and rule checks on a modular conveyor.
arxiv-2605-22657: Eddington and others replicate and extend a study of phone notification suppression in a first year programming course with 22 students. Phone logs synced to keystroke data show that assignments done with suppression on carry lower break rates and longer focus stretches than control assignments, for many but not all students. The effect splits sharply across students: many gain, a few lose ground, and very few feel no effect. The authors present Do Not Disturb style tools as a plausible classroom aid for attention, while noting the uneven response.
arxiv-2605-22957: Rodas and six coauthors apply the finite-volume N/D method to two-baryon interactions from lattice QCD data, studying the H-dibaryon at the SU(3) symmetric point with a pion mass near 417 MeV. They include the left-hand cut from one-pion exchange and compare against the Lüscher quantization condition with effective-range expansions. Including the cut shifts results mildly but significantly, most notably for the H-dibaryon binding energy.
arxiv-2605-23057: Sunesh, Alshehhi, and Dhakne present RequestRouter, a lightweight controller that picks one fixed inference mode per request for single-GPU language model serving, using cheap request-level features. Modes include FP16, quantized inference, speculative decoding, prefix caching, and continuous batching, and hybrids. On an 8B model served via vLLM on A100 GPUs, the controller reached 2.10 times mean latency speedup over FP16 with a 0.48 energy ratio on deployment-style workloads, while keeping 99.6 percent of FP16 macro accuracy. Routing overhead measured just 0.00475 milliseconds on average.
arxiv-2605-23157: Ford and three coauthors run the systematic cross-lingual multimodal red teaming study of jailbreak vulnerability in English and Spanish across four frontier models. Using 363 scenarios in text and multimodal conditions, with 52,272 harm ratings from native speaker panels, they find language does not scale vulnerability uniformly. Role play attacks weaken under Spanish prompting, while multimodal attacks strengthen. This implicates the language interface rather than annotator leniency. Safety rankings flip across languages. Qwen Omni passes Pixtral Large as vulnerable in Spanish, a reversal no correction of English scores could recover.
arxiv-2605-23257: Hu and five coauthors propose IDEA, a test-time adaptation tool for vision-and-language navigation under shifts. Old methods treat online updates as isolated steps, causing forgetting and negative transfer. It tunes soft prompts via Fisher-guided weights to capture transferable knowledge, then adds domain coordinates to build a dynamic asset library. Using this library, IDEA builds a bridge by projecting the target domain onto past knowledge. Tests across REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE show consistent superiority over old methods, enabling training-free adaptation.
arxiv-2605-23957: Wei and ten colleagues cut the cost of training selectors for job-shop scheduling, where jobs are ordered across machines. Labels usually demand rolling out candidate rules from partial schedules, so the team uses regret-normalized rollout labels with a nearest-neighbour uncertainty gauge. A gate acts only when the predicted gain clears an uncertainty-adjusted margin, keeping a strong default rule unless the gain looks credible. On synthetic cases, the gated selector beat other learned selectors and cut the random baseline's error by more than tenfold.
arxiv-2605-24357: Safwan Labbi and three colleagues examine the critic's role in actor-critic methods for entropy-regularized, finite, discounted settings. When the critic is exact, using it as a baseline cuts variance sharply, matching deterministic policy-gradient efficiency. With a learned critic, the actor update inherits the critic's variance and bias, though small critic error preserves the fast convergence. The practical moral is to learn the critic first and keep it current after each actor update.
arxiv-2605-24557: Tack Saquai and three colleagues pre-screen mixed-crystal configurations with annealing, using Ewald electrostatic energy as the score to minimize. Site occupations become binary variables, mapping energy onto an Ising-type Hamiltonian and turning the search into a combinatorial optimization problem. On a small system, simulated annealing ran about 30 times faster than exhaustive search, and quantum annealing over 100 times faster, both finding all lowest-energy layouts. For medium and large systems, simulated annealing stayed 200 to 300 times faster and robust. Quantum annealing faltered on medium systems through chain breaks.
arxiv-2605-24657: Simon Dennis and others test whether a personal assistant should fold what it learns into its weights each night. Across ten realistic software conversations, repeatedly squeezing old context retained just over a third of the tested knowledge. Nightly consolidation by reflection, synthesis, and low-rank tuning kept 80.4 percent, more than doubling the preserved share. The largest gains came on procedural corrections and episodic project facts. A side finding warns that mean validation loss can mislead, while the median tracks judged accuracy far more faithfully.
arxiv-2605-25057: Muhammed Ali Mehmood and Lukas Gonon study neural networks whose hidden weights are drawn at random rather than trained. They ask how well such networks can solve nonlinear partial differential equations. The authors derive error bounds for time-dependent functions and a dimension-free convergence rate of one half for smooth enough cases. Their theory covers the Porous Medium and Compressible Navier-Stokes equations, and computer experiments suggest the rates hold more broadly than the proofs assume.
arxiv-2605-25257: João Paulo Guardieiro, Yuri da Silva, and Saeed Tafazolian study algebraic curves over a finite field given by a power equation. When the field parameter is odd, they prove the smooth model is maximal exactly when the exponent divides that parameter plus one. That quotient yields a family indexed by its divisors, extending an earlier third-largest-genus case. The team computes Weierstrass semigroups for several rational points and pins down the full symmetry group under a mild condition. The results widen the earlier case into a broader picture.
arxiv-2605-25657: Abburi, Shigwan and Kumar present ARMA-C3, a graph framework for node classification that joins contrastive learning with graph-cut regularization. It models samples or images as graph nodes, catching subject-level links standard methods miss. It serves unsupervised and semi-supervised grouping for biomedical images, where labels are scarce and patterns are complex. Tested on five datasets spanning dementia, breast, lung and liver imaging, it matches or beats older clustering and leading models. It beats graph methods, above all with few labels and severe class skew.
arxiv-2605-25957: González-Ramírez and five colleagues build Chronos, a first step toward a consistent, absolute age scale for stars. Lithium diagnostics, especially the lithium depletion boundary, give strong ages for low-mass stars. But mixed temperature scales and astrophysical scatter limit their use, notably among Sun-like stars where rotation alters lithium levels. Chronos is a Bayesian hierarchical model that jointly infers temperatures, lithium abundances and cluster age, aided by a neural network trained on stellar evolution models. Validation on the Pleiades cluster anchors the approach.
arxiv-2605-26057: Hrbek, Lank, Le Gros and Pavon define a smallness-like test for t-structures, cuts that split a triangulated category into two halves. Their notion, proxy smallness, applies to t-structures over Noetherian schemes, developed with tensor actions in play. It yields a new test for schemes that are locally complete intersections, stated via t-structures alone. It also sorts preaisles, one-sided halves, on bounded derived categories of sheaves by topology. The work ties abstract category shape to concrete geometric traits.
arxiv-2605-26257: Marco Civera and four colleagues' 2026 study applies operational modal analysis to the International Space Station, estimating vibration modes from output data alone. Their method pairs the Natural Excitation Technique with Fast and Relaxed Vector Fitting, an iterative least-squares procedure. After checking it on a numerical beam model against analytical answers and two established methods, they run it on real acceleration data from the station's Space Acceleration Measurement Systems. Station modes from the new method match the established excitation-technique results, while subspace identification fails on most modes.
arxiv-2605-26357: Raymond Chua, Doina Precup, and Blake Richards study learning in worlds that drift slowly instead of jumping suddenly. They add slow, lifelike drift to Miniworld and MuJoCo settings, then compare methods that favor stability against methods that favor plasticity. Stability wins: synaptic consolidation beats parameter resetting, and consolidating successor features beats consolidating Q-values. It works best when these features are steadied across several timescales, which capture other sides of slow change, in this paper.
arxiv-2605-26457: Anmol Agarwal and eight colleagues test agents turning informal problems into faithful specifications. Verification promises machine-checked proofs that code meets a spec, but nothing ties specs to intent. Verus-SpecBench holds 581 Codeforces tasks for Verus, with Verus-SpecGym as the environment. Evaluation uses executable specs run as Rust code facing Codeforces and adversarial hacks. Gemini 3.1 Pro solves 77.8 percent, while frontier and open models score lower. Failures include dropped assumptions and wrong acceptances; judges miss 26 percent their evaluator catches.
arxiv-2605-26657: Wolfgang Maass and Sabine Janzen split two failure modes of policy-gradient learning on long tasks with mounting damage. Locally tempting moves can wreck global outcomes, and the pair separate merely reaching the horizon from matching the best plan once there. Under a soft penalty, horizon access alone drops completion as the penalty drives activity to zero. Action limits plus horizon access finish but leave an optimality gap. Four predictions replicate across a bricklayer career spanning 49 steps and an NBA power-forward career spanning 20 seasons.
arxiv-2605-26757: Bäumer Marty's 2026 protocols distill entanglement for modular quantum computers, where links between modules are far noisier than operations inside a module. The main protocol needs only two qubits per module yet suppresses inter-module errors quadratically, meaning errors shrink with the square of the raw rate, assuming clean local operations. Simulations and tests on superconducting processors show it beats existing small-scale protocols in both space and time overhead.
arxiv-2605-26857: Xu and six colleagues present ProMoS, the first unsupervised generalist framework for graph anomaly detection, which trains one detector that transfers to new graphs. It distills normality priors from a frozen self-supervised teacher network into a mixture of students with shared and personalized branches. Prototype-guided soft labels align teacher and student in one shared space. Tests show the system detects anomalies on unseen graphs with no labels and no few-shot support.
arxiv-2605-27257: Orzech and Rinard prove that for every player count of four or more, there is a normal-form game with integer payoffs whose only Nash equilibrium is fully mixed. In that equilibrium, every probability weight is an algebraic number whose degree equals the derangement number for the player count. Its minimal polynomial has the full symmetric group as its Galois group, and it carries one more nonzero coefficient than the derangement number itself. The construction thus ties game equilibria to a striking family of algebraic numbers.
arxiv-2605-27457: Albert Han, Jiri Kataman-Kustwan, and Alexey Bezryadin test maximum entropy production with self-organizing silver particle chains. With two samples wired in parallel, usually only one develops a conducting chain, and the winner's entropy production nears the calculated maximum while the loser's nears zero. The result supports path selection by efficiency, with the winning structure suppressing rival pathways by consuming free energy.
arxiv-2605-28057: Zhou and colleagues give the first theory of whether test-time adaptation can be learned on shifting data streams. They define recovery complexity, the time needed after a shift to regain low risk, and derive matching upper and lower bounds on it. The analysis exposes a built-in trade between adaptivity and information, with guarantees that complement regret-based accounts.
arxiv-2605-28257: Sommer and colleagues learn category-level 3D point matches from single photos with no direct match labels. Their Morpheus method splits standard shape, warp, and pose into one shared shape prior, so steady 3D spots surface on their own. The method leads on their HouseCorr3D test set of home objects.
arxiv-2605-28357: Adrián Antón-Álvarez and Adrián Lozano-Durán show that the bow shock ahead of Mars-entry capsules can itself go unstable. Under high-enthalpy conditions, disturbances heat the vehicle wall as they amplify. Amplification runs in three steps: crossing the shock, growing in the post-shock shear layer, and corrugating the shock. No classical boundary-layer mode is needed, the gain reaches huge levels in a representative entry, and flight data from two Mars capsules match the result.
arxiv-2605-28657: Ryan Fosdick presents DEMON, a real-time diffusion engine that turns denoising into a playable live musical instrument. Built on ACE-Step 1.5 and StreamDiffusion's ring-buffer design with TensorRT acceleration, it sustains about twelve decoder completions per second for sixty-second music on one consumer GPU. Four mechanisms make parameters responsive: per-slot denoise schedules, shared mutable per-step state, per-frame source blending, and windowed VAE decoding with an eightfold speedup. Together they split flowing-diffusion parameters into four spread classes by onset and convergence latency.
arxiv-2605-28757: A. Bemporad and T. Tatarenko propose a learning approach for near solutions of multi broad Nash equilibrium problems with coupled objectives and constraints. Rather than fitting on costly training solutions, hard to collect, they use the Nikaido-Isoda gap as a training loss, needing best-response data. A value-function surrogate stands in for each agent's best-response cost inside the gap loss, giving a single-level problem. They prove needed conditions for a continuous parametric variational equilibrium selection under strong stability, and the network delivers approximate solutions faster.
arxiv-2605-29057: Kaustub Anand, David Minton, and Julie Brisset test whether Centaur rings can form from regolith ejected in a cometary outburst and captured into orbit. Using Swiftest, an N-body integrator with fragmentation and gravity harmonics, they simulate capture around ellipsoidal Centaurs like Chariklo and Chiron. Ejected surface regolith forms a proto-ring disk lasting at least 100 rotations, aided by collisions and the ellipsoidal gravity field. Landslide-like equatorial ejection captures best, at about 30 to 90 percent, suggesting rings may mark past Centaur activity.
arxiv-2605-29657: Geng Li and eight colleagues present OccamToken, a training-free framework pruning visual tokens for cheaper inference. Most methods rank tokens and keep a fixed subset, but sinks distort rankings and fixed budgets fail across inputs. OccamToken tests if a token adds information beyond a register reference absorbing low-value attention. It prunes redundant tokens per image and irrelevant tokens per query via register thresholds. Across three models, it improves accuracy per cost without training, cutting LLaVA-NeXT from 2,880 tokens to about 40 while keeping over 93% accuracy.
arxiv-2605-29757: Sebastian Lämmel and Vladimir Shikhman offer a new disjunctive regularization for programs with complementarity constraints. Its feasible set matches Kanzow-Schwartz, yet its form differs sharply, using OR and max-type constraints. Unlike its rival, it keeps the tailored linear independence qualification whenever the original program holds, and keeps Kanzow-Schwartz's good convergence traits. No second-order conditions are needed for S-stationary points, and the team tracks C-indices of approximating and limiting points. Tests show it beats Kanzow-Schwartz, and even Scholtes at high accuracy.
arxiv-2605-29857: Kotaro Yoshida and six colleagues learn reusable grading rubrics from the notes reviewers leave on drafts. Their method reads inline comments, drafts candidate rubrics, and sharpens them by watching where rubric-based guesses miss the real comments. Tests in live review work and controlled trials with known rubrics show the learned rules can foretell comments, explain rubric sense, and drive auto revision. The work turns tacit expert taste — often unwritten and hard to ask for — into reusable rules. It gives review tools a way to carry an expert's eye onward.
arxiv-2605-30157: Jaylin Lowe, Adam Sales and Johann A. Gagnon-Bartsch test whether language-model predictions can sharpen randomized controlled trials without breaking rigour. Trial precision often suffers when good predictors are missing, yet model predictions are known for bias and error. Their pipeline folds LLM predictions into trial analysis following the observational-data approach, and they apply it to three case studies. The predictions safely improve precision, especially when trials lack good predictors or carry text data that suit language models.
arxiv-2605-30257: Ciara Rowles and four co-authors present Stable-Layers, fine-tuning layer decomposition with only VLM feedback and no paired supervision. From Qwen-Image-Layered, they apply Flow-GRPO with LoRA, sampling candidates, scoring them with the model, and optimizing from advantages. Reward design is the hard part: models scoring samples alone compress judgements into a narrow band, starving learning. A pipeline pairs per-sample scoring with calibration rescoring candidates side by side. Stable-Layers yields stronger separation, fewer blank or artifact layers, and lower reconstruction error on Crello.
