arxiv-2605-30357: Ghazi Sarwat Syed surveys the move to edge computing, with computation done at the data source. He flags central architectures and performance metrics that may shape the next generation of intelligent sensor systems. Artificial intelligence, connected devices, and high speed mobile networks drive huge computational demands. These demands challenge traditional sensor architectures. The article thus surveys edge architectures and metrics for intelligent sensing under growing demands.
arxiv-2605-30657: Chapouto, Forlano, and Laurens study the periodic intermediate nonlinear Schrödinger equation, asking when its solutions exist and behave well. Using a gauge change, they prove local well-posedness for large data at regularity at least one half. They extend this to global well-posedness under a small norm constraint, using the full integrability of the continuum Calogero-Moser equation. They also prove unconditional well-posedness in the energy space and show solutions converge to Calogero-Moser solutions in the deep limit.
arxiv-2605-31057: Glorian and colleagues tackle dense self-attention, the bottleneck for long-video diffusion. Cost grows with length, and beyond the training horizon models converge to frozen repetitive video. Their training-free LVSA combines a structured window with rotating global anchors, removing fixed-grid bias causing artifacts. With a FlashInfer kernel, LVSA cuts compute several times and enables extended generation otherwise out of memory on one GPU. They introduce VQeval, scoring loopy failures that other evaluators reward. LVSA is quality-neutral at training length, quality-positive beyond it.
arxiv-2605-31557: Forte and team present EGOSTREAM, a diagnostic testbed for streaming episodic memory in egocentric vision. Current streaming video benchmarks offer limited tools for diagnosing what models remember. EGOSTREAM organizes 2,250 questions along seven dimensions: detail, temporal, spatial, event, social, causal, and prospective memory. A new Answer Validity Window states how long an answer stays valid as the scene evolves, expanding questions into 8,528 recall-conditioned evaluations. Baselines show token pruning beats merging on fine details, while offloading rescues ultra-long-term recall, yet top methods ceil at about 45 percent.
arxiv-2606-00257:
Lafuente-Mercado probes how credit for good text acts can go flat in cheap model tuning. In reward-based training, each word should earn its share of praise or blame. Cheap tuning with small add-on blocks is the norm in real pipes. That slant hides a flaw, he argues.

With add-on blocks, the model stays near its base form. Word-level gaps that seed praise cues can then wash out or clump. After scaling in one run, cues may go near flat or heap on bland spots. He sets gauges to spot this clump in plain terms. His fix, ARCA, reads praise from the add-on's own inner shift. A math test sweep shows the sound mid-range spread it calls for.
arxiv-2606-00357:
Sun and co-authors build strong models from weak pick signs through merged add-on blocks. Good teach data for big models is scant and dear. Pairs of a weak model and a weaker one still give rich signs. The gap twixt their replies marks which traits count.

Their frame, PDA, takes one such gap per weak pair. Each gap is taught as a small LoRA add-on through pick-based steps. Add-ons are then merged to stack their gifts in one model. A shape-wise merge, GAM, lines up add-on spaces first to cut clash. Tests span lore tasks and agent hunts. Stacked weak signs beat each lone sign and grow with more signs. Gains top past merge tools by clear marks.
arxiv-2606-00757:
Saber and Salehi-Abari add a training trick for graph neural networks in this 2026 paper. These networks learn from data on linked nodes, but they overfit with ease. They also squash news from far nodes into too small a space. Random edge cuts can curb overfit, yet they can skew what training shows versus real use. Rewiring helps far nodes talk, but it is not built to regularize.

Their method, RADE, both drops and adds edges at random during training. The design keeps training and real use in line, so the random changes add no shift. Added edges also open long-range paths at run time. A small extra algorithm tunes the drop and add rates by gradient norms as training runs. That makes the method near free of hand-set knobs. On node and graph tests, the authors report, RADE curbs overfit and eases over-squashing at once.
arxiv-2606-00957:
Zhao squeezes a giant video model into low-precision numbers in this 2026 paper. The target is Wan2.1-T2V-14B, a 14-billion-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. His format is W8A8 HiFloat8, run on Ascend 910B chips. A block-by-block scan of all 40 attention blocks shows a split: edge blocks act unlike middle ones.

Uniform quantization would bruise those edge blocks. His fix protects the boundary: the first two and last three blocks stay in BF16. The other 35 blocks take the eight-bit format. On five VBench dimensions, the quantized model matches or edges its full-precision base, within a small five-prompt set. A four-way ablation backs the full protection as the best pick. He also tests quantization-aware training as a second stage. On single-card hardware it fails to beat plain post-training quantization, he reports.
arxiv-2606-01057:
Gao and co-authors benchmark AI agents that build 3D models by writing code in this 2026 paper. Procedural modeling through code gives assets that are exact, editable, and ready for engines. Neural 3D generators cannot match that control. But the craft demands deep skill in 3D software APIs and geometric reasoning in code.

Their benchmark, 3DCodeBench, asks 12 top vision language models to act as modelers. Each gets text and image references and must emit procedural code for 3D software. A sister platform, 3DCodeArena, ranks outputs by pairwise human taste. Pure metrics miss how shapes look, so human duels fill the gap. Two lessons lead the results, they report. Failures cluster on API mismatches between model memory and real software. Even good renders suffer loose or floating parts. More thinking budget and multi turn fixes lift scores overall. The call is for better procedural coding data to train on.
arxiv-2606-01257:
Li and Giessing build error bars that hold along a whole fit path. Gradient methods drive much of modern statistics. Most theory checks them at one fixed step or end point. Yet users may stop based on the data itself. They may also need doubt bounds at each stage. The pair study gradient flows from risk minimization over time.

They prove a uniform central limit result for the gap. The gap runs between sample and population flows. It acts like a Gaussian process over all time. Their covariance tool evolves with the flow itself. It needs no matrix inversion, resampling, or sample splits. It yields intervals with valid coverage over time.
arxiv-2606-01557:
Boero and co-authors define everywhere learning, a stricter training paradigm. Standard AI training minimizes average loss over data. Everywhere learning demands loss constraints hold with probability one. Each point in the data distribution must satisfy them. An approximate duality theory supports their generalization analysis. It shows how close empirical and statistical solutions sit. Dual variables reweigh data toward hard-to-satisfy points.

Generalization turns on a mismatch of mass concentration. It compares where data mass sits versus where constraints bind hardest. A sparse L1 penalty on relaxations can control that gap. An experiment in agentic classification illustrates the merits. Language model tasks supply that test case. The paradigm suits settings where average performance is not enough.
arxiv-2606-01857:
Kirchdorfer and co-authors improve how work is handed between staff. Handovers shape cost, wait time, and staff load in firms. Learning-based rules can adapt such allocation choices. But past rules ignore how staff work together. That teamwork pattern shapes real handovers a lot.

Their method tunes a handover rule for each worker. It joins a multi-agent process simulator with search. The search weighs several goals at once. It yields Pareto-best rules tuned per person. Tests use fake and real-world data sets. The authors report cost down 37 percent on average. Wait time falls by 58 percent on average. Heuristic baselines are beaten across the tests.
arxiv-2606-02057:
Sundberg and co-authors build a tool to watch latency inside host machines. Networks now chase sub-millisecond response times. At that scale, the end host itself adds delay. The link between card and CPU can be slow. The kernel network stack adds its own delays. Scheduling of applications adds still more delay.

Past work studied host latency at scattered levels. No tool watched it continuously in production use. Their netstacklat tool fills that gap directly. It captures latency at several points in the host. Points run from early kernel stages to application reads. Tests span 144 variants of HTTP workloads. Both Nginx and Apache servers are covered. The tool shows where host delay truly arises.
arxiv-2606-02457:
Steckloff and co-authors set a size limit for debris around white dwarfs. Dead stars often host compact disks of planetary debris. Models of disk birth use tidal breakup of minor planets. Those bodies are treated as rubble piles with no strength. In truth, Van der Waals forces give them some cohesion.

That small strength sets a cap on fragment size. For typical strengths of 10 to 1000 pascals, the cap runs from 0.1 to 1 kilometer. This is the km-size barrier. Most debris mass sits in fragments near that size. Later disk history must start with dust-making collisions. Only then can Poynting-Robertson drag shape the disk. Internal strength also confines fragments more tightly in radius. The correction adds weight to the role of collisions. It also bounds size spreads for disk models.
arxiv-2606-02657:
Poudel studies learning bounds when the world switches between calm and crisis regimes. Standard generalization bounds assume train and test data match. Regime-switching environments break that assumption. The mix of calm and crisis states can differ at deployment. His framework quantifies the extra risk from that mismatch. Distribution shifts are modeled as Markov-switching.

An exact decomposition splits the risk. Regime mismatch separates from regime sensitivity. The bound extends to beta-mixing data with a spectral-gap correction. A minimax lower bound is shown on synthetic data and on 25 years of global equity indices. The penalty is an ex post realized gap. A training-only estimator shows no significant correlation with it. Crisis geometry can be detected in features. Crisis timing cannot. The framework, Poudel stresses, is not a forecast machine.
arxiv-2606-02757:
Vinogradov and co-authors review past work on air corridors for advanced air mobility. Electric vertical take-off and landing vehicles promise relief for city congestion and emissions. Corridor design, traffic management, and separation rules lag behind the vehicles. Safe high-density flight needs all three. The review follows PRISMA guidelines. IEEE Xplore and Web of Science supply the sources, from 2010 to 2024. A CIMO framework shapes the research questions.

Screening starts from 2,039 papers. Sixty-two articles meet the inclusion criteria. The findings show a lack of unified corridor design approaches. Operational strategies are limited in scope. Standards are borrowed from conventional aviation. The authors propose unified frameworks and category schemes for corridor design and separation. The synthesis informs future work on safe, efficient urban eVTOL rollout. The topic is new, and the rules are still being written. It gives rule makers and designers a shared map of the gaps.
arxiv-2606-02957:
Black, Bogen, Koepke, Barocas, Deng, and Hsu give the first empirical account of how United States banks test for algorithmic discrimination in lending. Fair lending law has shaped bank programs for decades. Yet almost nothing was known about how those programs work in practice.

The study draws on 35 interviews across the fair lending ecosystem. Banks share a floor of fairness practices aimed at preventing lending discrimination, a floor largely absent elsewhere. But the details vary widely. Firms differ in how they test for bias and how they search for less discriminatory models. Regulatory exams emerge as the key driver of compliance work. Still, program impact often turns on navigating business incentives, legal tensions, and regulatory uncertainty. The authors stress the role of supervisory authority. That design feature is distinct in civil rights law and mostly missing from recent proposals on algorithmic discrimination.
arxiv-2606-03057:
Raja, Morris, and Chai test which text forms of molecules work best for language models. Their bench, MolRepBench, tests nine forms across eight tasks. Sixteen models from five families take part. The set holds reasoning models, chemistry-tuned models, and top closed models.

Scores swung with the form used, and no form won all tasks. CML came first, then MolJSON, InChI, and canonical SMILES. Structured forms won the structure tasks. IUPAC names won the sense tasks, and took molecule retrieval for all 16 models. SMILES forms were rarely best, though they fill much of pretraining. Chemistry-tuned models did well with SMILES but fell hard on structured text. A look inside the models, through token splits, probes, and attention maps, showed each form is coded in its own way. The authors urge task-aware form choice for LLM chemistry.
arxiv-2606-03357:
Schwager, Hau, Münker, and Rettinger measure how much of a language model's survey answers come from the prompt's shape, not its content. Psychometric tests on models presume that answers reflect the injected persona and the item's sense. The team tests that premise with a crossed design. Five personas meet five like-worded variants of each of four prompt parts.

The parts are persona wording, task instruction, item wording, and option symbol. Distances between answer distributions are split among the five factors. Thirteen open small models, up to 14 billion parameters, take the Big Five and Short Dark Triad tests. In most models, the task instruction and option symbol move answers more than a reworded persona or item does. For a large share of items, artifact share tops half of the explained change. Non-semantic tweaks beat the personas themselves.
arxiv-2606-03457:
Aigner builds a news sentiment engine that reads markets in real time. It learns from pairs of headlines and price snapshots taken at the same moment. No neural network training and no GPU hardware are needed. The system polls a news feed every three hours. Each item carries 22 price fields.

Three parts form an ensemble. A finance lexicon scores keywords in a FinBERT-like style. A TF-IDF cluster learner groups headlines and tracks how prices moved after each group. A weighting step adjusts each part by its past link to real price moves. All the work runs in under a second on a plain CPU server, at near zero cost per cycle. Comparisons with FinBERT, GPT scoring, VADER, and paid APIs cover cost, speed, and accuracy. The cluster learner adapts to new market regimes without retraining. Aigner presents that trait as the novel core of the design.
arxiv-2606-03557:
Nisiotis and Hadjiliasi build a gateway that routes virtual world requests to the right AI service. Generative AI users in virtual worlds send mixed requests. Each request may need a different backend model and different compute. Embedding every capability in the client hurts extensibility and maintenance. It also complicates coordination across edge and cloud machines.

Their gateway uses a small language model at the edge to classify each prompt's intent. A service registry checks and resolves the routing choice. The chosen backend is then called without changing the client. Tests run in the InterwovenXR virtual museum testbed. Compact models prove reliable as intent routers on edge hardware. Fine-tuning turns sub-billion-parameter models into low-latency routers. Pairing a fine-tuned router with a larger model for replies beats using one model for both jobs. The design lets new AI services join a virtual world cleanly.
arxiv-2606-03657:
Liu and co-authors diagnose how code models learn to use unfamiliar APIs. Libraries change fast, and models must use interfaces they never saw in training. Failed solutions alone reveal little about the missing knowledge. NovelAPIBench builds benchmarks around a target model's API gaps. It finds novel APIs and generates executable coding tasks. Knowledge components vary in a controlled way.

The main benchmark holds 1,670 tasks over 856 APIs and 21 libraries. Failures sort into six categories. Usage examples give the strongest standalone guidance when supplied directly. Adding signature descriptions nears full-knowledge performance. Retrieval from a pool does worse than supplying the target API alone. Fine-tuning on other APIs helps mainly when external knowledge is present. The framework separates knowledge content, delivery, and use. Library maintainers can rerun it as models evolve.
arxiv-2606-03757:
Alekseev, Farah, and Thom study Ulam stability for near maps between C-star algebras. The term asks when near-solutions of an equation sit close to exact ones. Here the maps are near homomorphisms, and the targets are von Neumann algebras. Nuclear cases are the focus.

Stability is proven for the abelian case in this setting. Large classes from the Elliott program also qualify. Stability survives standard constructions, as permanence results show. Cases where it fails are marked by counterexamples. Uses include rigidity results for corona algebras. Operator algebraists get a map of which nuclear classes are stable. The work links approximation to the classification program in a concrete way.
arxiv-2606-03957:
Gedeon and Mihajlik test speech training with conversations that never happened. Real multi-speaker data is scarce in low-resource languages and niche fields. Their pipeline writes scenario-level dialogues with participant details first. Speaker traits are mapped to text-to-speech voice profiles. The made-up speech is then joined into speaker-aware simulated talks.

They trained FastConformer-Large models with five language model families as generators. Tests ran on the Hungarian BEA-Dialogue benchmark. Mixed and scaled data both helped, but generator choice shaped the gains. Their largest run used 67 hours of real talks plus 636 hours of fake ones. It beat a zero-shot model trained on 2,700 hours of Hungarian speech. The method can move to other languages with the right parts.
arxiv-2606-04057:
Narula, Rafique, and Bindschaedler study hidden cues that steer code generation by language models. Models now write much production code. Many tasks allow more than one valid algorithm. Words or metadata outside the task spec can shift that choice. All outputs may still pass the same tests.

They ran 46,535 controlled experiments on 11 tasks. Nineteen cue types and 15 model setups were covered. Shifts in algorithm-family shares were large and systematic, up to 100 points. The shifts tracked cue meaning, even in applied tasks like rate limiting. Naming the algorithm directly was the steadiest fix they tested. Random context thus forms an invisible lottery over speed, safety, and upkeep.
arxiv-2606-04257:
Hunter Monroe connects a famous open problem in proof complexity to exact values of the Busy Beaver function in 2026. The problem asks whether any proof system is length-optimal: shortest proofs for all tautologies, up to a polynomial factor.

The Busy Beaver function marks the frontier of what finite machines can do. Its values grow faster than any computable function. Monroe shows the two questions are linked: settling one would settle the other. He builds the link through short programs that assert hard statements about randomness. The result reframes a logic problem as a computation problem. It also hints that proof optimality may sit beyond current tools, much like Busy Beaver values do.
arxiv-2606-04357:
Jairon Batista and co-authors propose in 2026 a new way to draw samples from a distribution known only up to a constant. They use reverse diffusion, the machinery behind modern image generators. But they avoid its usual error sources.

Their construction embeds the target as the starting marginal of a diffusion built for the purpose. The method needs neither time discretization nor a learned score function. So Monte Carlo randomness is its only error. A key theorem expresses the reverse step's density ratio against a standard reference process in tractable form. Two algorithm families follow. One produces near-independent samples in parallel. The other targets the whole path jointly. Both handled multimodal, strongly dependent targets well.
arxiv-2606-04657:
TeleHunt is a framework and tool for finding crime linked communities, meaning hidden groups, on the Telegram messaging app. Roy Ricaldi and his coauthors described it in a 2026 arXiv paper on cybercrime research and threat tracking. Such groups form and vanish fast, so investigators need a fair way to compare search strategies.

Their system follows pointers from known groups to new ones, filters off topic finds, and labels each market segment. Starting seeds came from open web and dark web sources, and each route was scored three ways. Those scores covered speed of discovery, how open groups were, and how often known groups reappeared. Link based routes beat routes based on names or forwarded posts, and open web seeds beat dark web seeds. Their shared data set holds over 172 million messages drawn from 6,022 communities, many of them crime linked.
arxiv-2606-04857:
Liu and colleagues expose a hidden flaw in how incomplete multi-view data is evaluated, in a 2026 arXiv machine learning paper. Multi-view clustering learns from several views of each sample, some of which go missing. The standard evaluation retrains a model per missing-data configuration, and the authors show this hides a vulnerability: the missing rate alone does not characterize incompleteness. Protocols with identical rates can differ fifty-fold in their share of fully observed samples.

They formalize this as incompleteness divergence and prove that learning becomes ill-posed once complete samples fall below a critical threshold. Their model, CRAFT, moves robustness into the architecture: per-sample independence removes reliance on co-occurrence. One model, trained once on complete data, generalizes across missing patterns without retraining. On seven benchmarks it matches or beats per-configuration baselines while cutting training overhead by 8.8 times.
arxiv-2606-05057:
Junho Choi and colleagues report magneto-optical studies of the layered magnet CrSBr in fields up to 55 tesla in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recent work on thin layers of this two-dimensional magnetic semiconductor found two distinct band-edge light resonances. These are thought to come from excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, living in the bulk and in the surface layers. Because the material is highly anisotropic, excitons stay confined within single layers and surface layers feel a different local environment.

Measuring optical absorption in magnetic fields, the team found the main exciton resonance near 1.36 electron volts and a second resonance about 20 milli-electron volts lower. In small fields that induce ferromagnetic order, the lower resonance shifted only half as much. At high fields it showed a smaller diamagnetic shift. Both behaviors support the picture of separate bulk and surface exciton populations.
arxiv-2606-05257:
Rickard Brüel Gabrielsson measures scaling laws for behavioral foundation models in this 2026 arXiv paper. These are models trained on sequences of actions for recommendation, payments, fraud detection, and commerce. Language models enjoy compute calibration from scaling laws; these largely lack it. The study covers a common two-part architecture: an event embedder that turns items into vectors, and a decoder-only transformer that predicts the next event.

Across 600 runs on interaction data, Gabrielsson varied the parameter split, the critical batch size, the model-to-data allocation, and the number of sampled negatives. An embedder of about two percent of parameters proved compute-optimal at every budget, because embedder parameters cost more per step and see more repeated items. Training was data-heavy at low budgets but drifted toward the Chinchilla heuristic as budgets grew. The training objective disagreed with ranking metrics in ways that scale with compute.
arxiv-2606-05457:
Markus Uehlein and colleagues separate two competing processes that shape how laser-heated metals relax, in this 2026 arXiv paper. What follows an ultrafast laser pulse is a contest between two processes. In one, hot electrons physically move and carry energy away. In the other, electrons collide and settle where they are. Detailed descriptions of both were sparse.

The authors recast the Boltzmann transport equation in energy space. It then describes spatial equilibration and scattering through full collision integrals. Their results hold a twist: transport accelerates the apparent thermalization seen at the irradiated surface, because it removes the most out-of-equilibrium carriers. Yet the same spatial redistribution delays the electron system's settling as a whole. Analyzing the energy-dependent dynamics at the front and back surfaces, they find the dominant process varies with both position and energy window. These are the kind of signals experiments can measure.
arxiv-2606-05557:
Yang Li and colleagues teach software agents to hear the question behind the question in a 2026 arXiv paper. A user who asks where a coworker is may really want to know if she is free. Standard tool-using agents answer the literal query and stop. The team adds a step that guesses the hidden need before any tool runs. A gap score then decides how much probing each query deserves.

The system, AURA, was tested on one hundred queries across four scenes. It covered hidden needs better than a probing baseline built on the ReAct style. Three of the four scenes improved on their own, and the gain repeated on a second model. Tests that stripped parts away credit the gap score, not memorized answers. On plain fact lookup the agent made eighty-two percent fewer probes. It also broke no privacy rules on a guarded test slice.
arxiv-2606-05857:
Arghya Pal and colleagues detoxify audio search results without wrecking their relevance in a 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-audio systems can surface hateful recordings hidden in big collections. Rewriting the query risks changing what the user meant. Their post-hoc framework works after retrieval instead, using a sentiment-controlled mediator in a causal debiasing step. Two variants split the strategy by how hard they push.

Forgive re-ranks and filters toxic hits by adjusting scores. Forget generates counterfactual toxic prompts to steer retrieval away from harmful matches. Both variants plug into existing pipelines without retraining the underlying models. Experiments showed steady toxicity reduction across settings. Retrieval accuracy paid only a minimal price for the cleanup. Safety and reliability rose together, a pairing that blunt filters rarely manage. Context, the authors stress, decides whether edgy audio is hate or art; their mediator tries to keep that context in view.
arxiv-2606-05957:
Shirodkar names the blind spots of oversized models and gauges them in the model's own coordinates in a 2026 arXiv paper. Singular learning theory finds Bayesian complexity through coordinate changes. Information geometry assumes a healthy Fisher metric that big models often violate. A dead direction is a heading along which the metric degenerates. Along it, prediction error fades at a set rate.

That rate, the KL order, can be read from how Fisher curvature decays near the singular point. No Hironaka blow-up is needed. A picking rule converts the rate into Watanabe's complexity share for that direction. Coverage extends to multi-part crossings, prior shifts, and tempered posteriors. Networks follow through a factored Fisher approach with building blocks. One upshot stands out: gradient descent respects the geometry, Adam does not. A fixed Adam variant restores it. The bridge links two fields that described the same mountains in different tongues.
arxiv-2606-06157:
Xinying Tang and Wenqian Zhang prove a sharp spectral condition in this 2026 arXiv paper. A graph is a network of vertices joined by edges. A matching pairs vertices with edges that share no endpoint. A graph is maximum matching covered when every edge belongs to at least one largest matching. The spectral radius, the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix, summarizes how densely the network is connected.

For graphs whose matching number, the size of a largest matching, is bounded in advance, they give a spectral radius threshold that guarantees maximum matching covered status. They also show this bound cannot be improved. The proof also pins down the exact extremal graphs, those with the largest spectral radius in this class. It treats two size regimes, split by how the vertex count compares with the matching bound. Sharpness matters because weaker thresholds would miss some covered graphs.
arxiv-2606-06257:
Bimal Chhushyabaga and Behrooz Ferdowsi simulate how fluid pressure can trigger failure in granular layers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Faults, slopes, and injection wells all involve water pressing through packed grains. Raising pore pressure weakens the grain skeleton, because the fluid carries load that friction needs. When and how the layer lets go depends on feedbacks that field data rarely resolve.

The authors couple a fluid solver with a discrete element model that tracks individual grains in three dimensions. After calibrating the layer's strength envelope, they raised basal pore pressure under drained and undrained conditions. Undrained layers kept the excess pressure, weakened abruptly, and slipped dynamically. Drained layers shed pressure and resisted longer. Failure came only when pressure rise coincided with dilation, broken contact networks, and localized strain bands. Layers already near their strength limit needed far smaller pressure increases to fail.
arxiv-2606-06357:
Dinghao Zhou and co-authors build one audio tokenizer that serves two masters in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tokenizer turns sound into compact latent codes that other models can use. Autoencoder codes rebuild waveforms beautifully but carry weak meaning, so understanding tasks struggle with them. Self supervised encoders capture meaning well yet cannot be decoded back into sound. A single tokenizer for speech systems needs both talents at once.

Their F3 Tokenizer adapts autoencoder latents with two additions. A noise regularized bottleneck uses channel normalization and random perturbation, instead of a variational KL term, to keep code scales controlled for reconstruction and generation. A separate representation encoder then reads the frozen latents and builds rich features for understanding, trained with random quantized prediction and guidance from a frozen language model. The split design keeps the codes decodable while sharpening their structure, and it sped up downstream text to speech training.
arxiv-2606-06457:
Sergio Sánchez Sanjuán and co-authors forecast the fates of young star clusters in Orion in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Orion complex is the nearest large stellar nursery, crowded with clusters a few million years old. Whether each survives as a long lived open cluster or dissolves into the galactic field depends on its dynamical state. Using Gaia astrometry plus radial velocities from spectroscopic surveys, the team measured thirteen clusters in three dimensional motion and structure.

Every cluster came out supervirial, expanding faster than its own gravity can hold. Simulations following them for three hundred million years split the family in two. Seven clusters with milder expansion keep a bound core for at least one hundred seventy million years. Six hotter ones dissolve within one hundred twenty million, seeding the field. Cluster interactions proved negligible.
arxiv-2606-06557:
Mohsen Fathi tests whether a tumbling lump of matter near a black hole can clock the dark matter around it in this 2026 arXiv paper. A rigid body spinning about its middle axis is unstable: the tennis racket effect. Near a rotating black hole, this instability makes a non symmetric matter element flip periodically. His earlier DARK FLIP work modeled that flip. Here he asks how the flip frequency responds when the dark matter halo changes.

Using a controlled effective response model, he scans halo normalization, profile size, and the element's own inertia. The trend is clean: more enclosed dark matter lowers the flip frequency relative to a bare Kerr black hole. Compact profiles strengthen the effect; extended ones weaken it. Einasto, cored NFW, and Hernquist profiles all behave alike, though amplitudes differ. The flip thus acts as a genuine, if subtle, dark matter sensitive clock.
arxiv-2606-06657:
The sine-Gordon model is a classic field theory where waves interact through a cosine shaped force. Vihko rebuilds that model on rougher ground in this 2026 arXiv paper. His background field is logarithmically correlated, meaning its roughness grows slowly with distance. It matches the Gaussian free field in two dimensions. He allows any dimension from one upward.

He treats both the massive and massless versions, stressing the massless one. The field is built without fixing boundary conditions. He also computes how charges and gradients correlate across space. The central result is that the partition function can be renormalized. In plain terms, its infinities can be tamed by a systematic procedure. The results hold without small parameter approximations. They cover the full subcritical range in one dimension. The analysis works directly in the continuum, using scale decomposition and a classic expansion method.
arxiv-2606-06857:
Which features of language does the human brain actually track? Lepori, Kay, and Tuckute use language models as a lens in this 2026 arXiv paper. Critics call such studies black box against black box. The team answers by opening the model's side of the box.

They replace dense model states with sparse autoencoder features. These features are few, named, and easier to interpret. Surprisal, how unexpected each word is, enters as its own predictor. Brain data came from eight people hearing two hundred sentences in a strong scanner. The method recovered known tuning for difficulty and abstractness. It also found a reliable voxel group tuned to people related content. Across the language network, regions shared one feature basis. Frontal areas leaned mostly on surprisal alone. Best fits came from the model's most general features, not random ones.
arxiv-2606-07057:
Automatic keyphrase systems are graded by metrics that miss what readers actually value. Venturini and Kinkel propose a fairer yardstick in this 2026 arXiv paper. Exact word matching ignores meaning, while pure similarity scores ignore ranking. Humans care about both: good phrases, surfaced early.

Their metric, Semantic R-Precision, merges the two concerns. It builds on the rank aware R-Precision framework from information retrieval. Exact stem matches earn full credit. Embedding similarity grants partial credit to phrases that mean the right thing in different words. The authors probe the metric from several angles. Sensitivity, ranking awareness, and discrimination across models all check out. Factor analysis shows it tracks general effectiveness while staying semantically sensitive. Case studies illustrate where older metrics misjudge output. The metric is offered as a complement to, not a replacement for, existing scores.
arxiv-2606-07157:
AI safety monitoring often relies on reading a model's visible chain of thought, its step-by-step written reasoning. Gould and a large team ask how much reasoning frontier models can do silently, without that visible trace, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They measure a time horizon: how long a human needs for tasks the model solves half the time. Longer horizons mean models can internally handle work that once required explicit reasoning steps.

The team assembled over thirty thousand questions across forty-three benchmarks covering mathematics, coding, puzzles, causality, and strategic reasoning. Models answered with no reasoning tokens allowed before the final answer. The silent-reasoning time horizon has roughly doubled every year for six years, they estimate. The strongest model tested passed three minutes of human-equivalent task time, with projections exceeding seven minutes by twenty twenty-eight under their median forecast, though uncertainty is wide.
arxiv-2606-07657:
Qu and co-authors recognize traffic signs with a brain-inspired, quantum-assisted network, in this 2026 arXiv paper on QDS-SNN. Spiking neural networks communicate in pulses, promising energy savings for real-time driving perception, but they lose information and suffer vanishing gradients. Their design adds supervision, corrective signals at intermediate layers, delivered by quantum network modules that exploit superposition and entanglement for parallel computation. A neuron model adapts its pulse timing and behavior, and a quantum-assisted classifier steadies training.

On a quantum simulation platform, the system reached accuracy near 99.7 percent on a German traffic sign benchmark within 6 time steps. That beat a residual-network baseline by over 1 percentage point while cutting consumption by more than half. Results on a second sign dataset are reported. The authors present the hybrid as evidence that quantum assistance can fix spiking networks' training pathologies without surrendering their efficiency advantage.
arxiv-2606-07757:
Francesco Concetti and Simone Franchini prove a universality result for a disordered model in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system assigns energies to configurations through random fields, then keeps only an exponentially large thinned subset. The question is whether the lowest energies behave like Derrida's Random Energy Model, the classic solvable picture of a frozen, glass-like system.

They show that, after a centring that depends on the random fields, the energy levels converge to a Poisson point process with exponential intensity, the Random Energy Model pattern. That extends earlier results, which covered only thinner selections of configurations. The team also identifies the Gibbs weights, the probabilities the system assigns to each state, as a Poisson-Dirichlet law. The free energy they compute shows a freezing transition, where the system locks onto its lowest states, at an inverse temperature set by the model's parameters. Full proofs appear in a companion preprint.
arxiv-2606-07857:
Behfar and Mortier defend distributed language-model training against poisoned participants by keeping several models instead of one, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Edge devices now fine-tune small models collaboratively, but a compromised device can inject poisoned updates that quietly steer the shared model. Classic defences watch a single global model, so coordinated poisoning can hide inside it.

Their idea, model multiplicity, trains multiple small models concurrently, each updated by independently sampled subsets of nodes. Following distinct training paths, the models form independent views of the same population. Divergence between them, measured through gradient similarity, loss evolution, or parameter spread, becomes an alarm. When one model strays far from the ensemble average, its contributing nodes are flagged for isolation or down-weighting. Tests in edge-scale simulations show a system-level signal that single-model defences cannot see.
arxiv-2606-08057:
Yichen Niu and co-authors at Harbin Institute of Technology teach a robot hand from a single first-person video, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Egocentric videos of human manipulation are plentiful, but robot learning from them usually needs pre-scanned models of the objects, since pose, geometry, and contacts are not recorded. Their framework, EgoAERO, is the first to learn dexterous manipulation from one egocentric RGB-D demonstration with no object assets at all.

The system reconstructs contact-consistent hand-object trajectories by tracking and rebuilding the object from the video itself, compensating for head motion and optimising contact plausibility. Two-stage residual learning converts the reconstruction into a robot policy. The team also built EgoDex-R, a dataset of about four point three million RGB-D frames, and an online quality check for demonstrations. In simulation and real-world tests, single-demonstration policies performed close to CAD-based ones.
arxiv-2606-08257:
Karl Brustad settles a long-standing question about a class of partial differential equations in this 2026 arXiv paper. The equations define infinity-harmonic functions in the plane, solutions of the infinity-Laplace equation, tied to maps that stretch distances as evenly as possible. It was conjectured that the gradient of such a function is one-third-Hölder continuous, a precise statement about how rough the slope can be. A classic example shows no better general regularity is possible.

Brustad exploits a known link between this equation and the one-dimensional heat equation. Under an injectivity condition on the gradient, requiring the slope map never to repeat a value, that link becomes usable. The heat equation's smoothing structure then proves the claimed continuity of the gradient. The author notes that injective gradients are not necessary, since smooth solutions such as planes and cones violate the condition while remaining regular.
arxiv-2606-08357:
Haotian Sun and co-authors remove a hand-designed ingredient from diffusion language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion language models generate text by iterative denoising, refining a corrupted draft step by step, as an alternative to writing one token at a time. For images, corruption is natural. But discrete text has no neighborhood structure for good perturbations, so models prescribe artificial corruption schemes. Those states are handy yet misaligned with the drafts and errors that come up in use.

Their model, FReDA, is forward-free: it needs no built corruption process at all. The method recasts diffusion as recursive refinement. The model's own drafts serve as intermediate states, and a learned refinement model moves the draft toward the target text. FReDA proposes candidate drafts and refines them directly or selects among them, so training matches what generation encounters.
arxiv-2606-08457:
Xiaoyang Wang and Yang show that when medical artificial intelligence agents debate, their agreement can be an illusion, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-agent systems for medical question answering treat consensus as a reliability signal: if several agents agree, the answer is presumed trustworthy. But answer-level consensus does not entail reasoning-level alignment, since agents can reach the same answer through incompatible reasoning. The authors introduce CARA, a family of automated metrics measuring whether agents who agree on an answer also agree on the reasoning behind it.

Applying these metrics to a standard debate system, they identify the consistency illusion. Debate reduces detectable contradictions between agents while decreasing the semantic similarity of their reasoning chains. Agents appear to agree more but reason less consistently. To repair this, the authors propose the Grounded Debate Protocol, requiring agents to commit to named medical facts.
arxiv-2606-08757:
Ersoy Şaşıoğlu and colleagues show that rolling a magnetic sheet into a tube turns its spin properties into a tunable dial, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Altermagnets split electron spins by momentum direction despite zero net magnetization, a combination prized for spintronics. Rolling a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet into a nanotube transforms its momentum-dependent spin splitting into one-dimensional splitting. The splitting is controlled by the tube's chiral angle, the angle at which the sheet wraps.

Using a minimal tight-binding model and first-principles calculations, they show the nanotube splitting follows a characteristic twice-angle cosine dependence. It vanishes for nodal orientations and reaches extrema for antinodal ones. The mechanism remains robust across a broad class of such nanotubes.
arxiv-2606-08857:
Liu and colleagues build PaperMentor, a multi-agent writing tutor that coaches researchers inside their own drafts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Junior scholars rarely get detailed feedback from experienced mentors, and existing AI tools either fix grammar or imitate peer review with a final verdict. PaperMentor instead leaves comments directly in Overleaf, the collaborative writing platform, while the author keeps full control of the text. Twelve specialized agents check different aspects of a paper, from formatting compliance to terminology consistency.

The agents draw on a skill library of expert writing advice. In a user study with fourteen participants, 90.6 percent of the generated comments were rated actionable and 67.5 percent were rated valid. Both figures beat a GPT-5.2 baseline run without the skill library. The authors argue the library turns generic advice into concrete, specific guidance. PaperMentor is released as open source so other groups can adopt or extend the tutor.
arxiv-2606-09057:
Gadjev pins down exactly how fast the best possible constant in a weighted Hardy inequality settles as the sequence length grows, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hardy's inequality bounds the energy of a sequence's running averages by the energy of the sequence itself. In the weighted version here, both sides carry power weights in the space of square-summable sequences. For each length n and weight exponent, a smallest constant makes the inequality true; the question is how it converges.

Gadjev establishes the exact convergence rate, not just an upper or lower bound. He also identifies the almost extremal sequence, the near-worst-case input that almost saturates the inequality and thereby proves the rate cannot be improved. Sharp constants matter beyond pure theory: they certify how much averaging can amplify a signal. The paper completes the asymptotic picture for this weighted l2 Hardy inequality.
arxiv-2606-09157:
Abi Akl, Gandon, Faron, and Monnin test whether formal notation helps small language models reason, rather than parrot content, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, SEF-CLGC, entered SemEval-2026 Task 11, which asks whether a syllogism is valid, separating formal reasoning from content bias, the pull of believable statements. Training data mixes natural language with a common-logic grammar, formal notations from knowledge representation.

Using only small models, against the trend toward larger ones, the team trained on natural and symbolic language mixes. Their best model reached a content score of 27.80 percent on the subtask. Notation-based training significantly lowered content bias: models judged arguments by logical form, not plausibility. Structure in the training representation, the neuro-symbolic bet, can substitute for raw scale. For a benchmark built to expose shallow pattern matching, bias reduction matters more than the headline score.
arxiv-2606-09257:
Habib, Ahamed, Gyawali, Doretto, and Adjeroh generate synthetic data for the hardest tabular regime: thousands of columns, dozens of rows, in this 2026 arXiv paper. High-dimensional, low-sample-size domains like genomics have far more features than samples. The data show local correlation groups, sparse cross-group links, heavy tails, feature-varying noise, and structured missingness.

BSTabDiff partitions features into few latent blocks. Each block comes from a shared low-dimensional subunit variable, concentrating dependence learning in the compact block-latent space. Decoding uses copula-driven dependence, per-feature marginals, and explicit missingness. Diffusion or flow priors can drive the block latents. It produced more realistic, stable synthetic data than unstructured generators. The design mirrors the data: correlation inside blocks, near-independence between, so samples are spent learning what matters. For omics, where data are scarce and sensitive, such synthesis enables work raw data cannot.
arxiv-2606-09957:
Meijer and colleagues propose catching machine learning bugs while code is being written, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software analysis. Semantic faults are mistakes tied to how a model uses data, such as training a scale-sensitive model on unscaled inputs. Developers usually find these only after training, by inspecting poor results by hand. That delay wastes time and computing resources on flawed runs.

Their approach is data-aware static analysis, which examines code without running it while also reasoning about the data flowing through it. It combines data and control flow analysis with API contracts, the stated rules for how library functions expect their inputs. Testing on real-world machine learning notebooks, the method detected faults that plain code analysis would miss. The authors frame the work as an early proof of potential rather than a finished tool, pointing toward checks that flag data misuse inside the editor.
arxiv-2606-10157:
Zarina and her team design an observer that infers the hidden state of a magnetic bearing from electrical readings alone, in a 2026 arXiv paper on control theory. Active magnetic bearings levitate rotating shafts without contact, and self-sensing versions estimate position from the currents and voltages already present, avoiding extra sensors. The challenge is building a globally stable observer, a system that reconstructs unmeasured amounts, using only those electrical signals.

Their approach first derives a direct relation linking the unmeasurable part of the state to filtered versions of the inputs and outputs, valid for all times. Building on that relation, they propose a robust asymptotic observer whose estimates converge to the true state. Simulation results illustrate the observer's results, supporting self-sensing bearings that cut hardware cost and failure points in high-speed rotating machines.
arxiv-2606-10357:
Jiang and colleagues bring language model reasoning to industrial recommendation systems without paying its full inference cost, in a 2026 arXiv paper on recommender systems. Cross-domain recommendation uses a person's content interactions to infer purchasing intent on a merchant platform, raising conversion. Real deployments face semantic gaps between domains and massive, noisy cross-domain behavior sequences, while language models that could bridge the semantics are too slow for strict online latency limits.

The framework reasons about user intent at an atomic level, decomposing behavior into fine-grained semantic pieces that transfer across domains. Industrial deployment on a content-to-merchant platform is the paper's proving ground, with the design driven by production constraints on latency and scale. By moving heavy semantic reasoning offline into compact intent representations, the system aims to keep the conversion benefits of language-model understanding while serving recommendations at industrial speed.
arxiv-2606-10457:
Zha and colleagues describe Trace2Policy in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system that learns the unwritten decision rules experts use in audits, compliance checks, and contract review. It keeps a human-readable rule document and improves it in rounds. Each round runs the rules on checked cases, groups errors as missing, wrong, or conflicting rules, patches the document, and keeps only changes passing a regression gate. The finished rules compile into ordinary deterministic Python code.

At a major logistics carrier the system handled 3,349 audit cases over twenty-two days of live operation. Eight refinement rounds lifted accuracy to 79.6 percent on the deployed pool, above the roughly seventy percent plateau of one-shot learning. The compiled pipeline beat the language-model baseline it replaced, which scored 72.7 percent on the same work. An automated variant reproduces the refinement for five to ten dollars per cycle, against about seventy expert-hours by hand.
arxiv-2606-10657:
Janeiro and colleagues ask whether multiple-choice benchmarks measure knowledge or wording in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiple-choice testing is cheap and deterministic, a workhorse benchmark format, but scores are sensitive to phrasing: formatting changes have swung results by up to 76 points in studies. The blind spot is what gets scored, the answer strings: a model may know a fact yet prefer a synonym its training favoured. ParaEval scores each answer option under multiple paraphrases of the question.

To isolate phrasing from knowledge, the team trains English and Spanish models at 1, 3, and 8 billion parameters, plus a back-translation condition that changes wording, not language. Under standard scoring, models with identical knowledge show gaps. Under ParaEval those gaps collapse, in controlled setups and on ARC-Challenge with frontier models. The conclusion is uncomfortable for benchmark culture: a slice of model differences is phrasing familiarity wearing the mask of knowledge.
arxiv-2606-11257:
Cheng and Lai run retrieval-augmented generation entirely on a laptop chip, in a 2026 arXiv paper. RAG combines embedding, retrieval, reranking, and generation; running it on-device helps privacy, latency, and offline use. The energy cost of CPU inference is the barrier. Their system is, to their knowledge, the first RAG pipeline running every neural stage on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of the Snapdragon X Elite.

On a Dell XPS 13, they compare NPU RAG against CPU and integrated GPU baselines. On indexing, the NPU reached 9.1 times higher embedding throughput while using 12.3 times less system energy. On 120 Wikipedia queries, it delivered 18.1 times faster prefilling, 4.0 times lower latency end to end, and 4.0 times less energy than CPU. The GPU was 1.7 times slower than CPU and used 6.5 times more energy than the NPU. A GPT-4.1 judge scored NPU answers on par with both baselines; 86.7 percent of queries scored identically across all three.
arxiv-2606-11357:
Pang, Jun, Liu, and Chen present TileFuse in a 2026 arXiv paper, for running large language models on AMD laptop NPUs. Edge chips increasingly integrate NPUs for on-device inference, but deployment is hard: popular quantization formats like AWQ map poorly onto current NPU stacks, which are proprietary with limited low-level control. TileFuse is a close-to-metal library for AMD XDNA2 NPUs.

TileFuse co-designs weight layout, metadata placement, microkernels, and dataflow. It fuses unpacking, dequantization, and matrix execution into a single kernel flow. It brings AWQ-style formats such as W4A16 and W8A16 directly onto XDNA2, instead of reshaping models around an NPU-specific scheme. In kernel evaluations, it beat full-precision baselines by up to 121.6 percent for GEMM and 281 percent for GEMV. End-to-end on Ryzen AI laptops, it achieved up to 2.0 times lower prefilling latency with 64.6 percent lower energy use.
arxiv-2606-11657:
Katherine Rosenfeld and Maike Sonnewald probe the inner workings of a scientific AI emulator in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model, Walrus, imitates continuum dynamics such as fluid flow across domains. The question is whether its internal activity matches known physics, and whether mismatches explain where its output goes wrong.

The authors train a sparse autoencoder, a tool that rewrites internal activity as a short list of features, on one layer of the model. It yields over twenty thousand candidate features, far too many to inspect. They rank features by enstrophy, a measure of swirling intensity in a flow, and study simple shear flow cases. Some feature groups recur in similar roles across setups, but the pattern is intermittent and does not align neatly with standard physical decompositions. About ten percent of features pass their significance threshold, too many for one metric to isolate what matters, they conclude.
arxiv-2606-11957:
Jinmin Wang and Bo Zhu prove a rigidity theorem in this 2026 arXiv paper. A classical estimate bounds the bottom of the Laplacian's spectrum in terms of curvature. Hyperbolic space, the perfectly negatively curved model space, attains the bound exactly; the question is whether anything else can. Earlier work used a Ricci curvature assumption.

Wang and Zhu work under the weaker scalar curvature lower bound, together with the same shape conditions as their previous paper. They prove the equality case is rigid: a closed manifold whose scalar curvature stays above the negative threshold, and whose universal cover attains the sharp value, must be hyperbolic. Corollaries cover closed hyperbolic manifolds and ones carrying a metric of nonpositive sectional curvature. The proof forces a certain tensor measuring deviation from that model to vanish everywhere.
arxiv-2606-12157:
Pavlou presents an open-source Python tool for a tricky materials measurement, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy, or PALS, times how long positrons, electron-like particles with reversed charge, survive inside a material before vanishing. Those lifetimes reveal tiny defects and empty spaces in metals and other solids. Reading a spectrum means fitting several overlapping decay curves blurred by the detector, a task easily skewed by starting guesses and linked settings.

The tool, fitPALSpectra, wraps the whole job in one workflow covering simulation, fitting, plotting, and reporting. It uses an analytic model that folds the decay curves into the detector response, handles source and sample parts separately, and refines fits with bounded least squares. On synthetic spectra with known true values, it recovered the lifetimes, strengths, detector width, prompt shift, and background accurately. It also exports fit results and correlation matrices in structured files for checking.
arxiv-2606-12557:
Girish and co-authors price privacy in a minimal secure-computation game, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In private simultaneous messages, players each hold private input bits and send one message to a referee. The referee must learn a function of all inputs, and nothing else. Adding quantum communication and shared entanglement changes the costs, but how privacy drives them was poorly understood.

The team proves the first lower bounds that use the privacy condition. One shows a complexity measure of the function, Neciporuk's measure, lower-bounds the entanglement quantum protocols need, yielding quadratic lower bounds for some functions. Another shows the communication matrix's rank lower-bounds two-player quantum protocols that stay private while erring. That result also implies a lower bound for classical protocols. On the upper side, they bound quantum costs by circuit size and depth, and classical costs by the square of the function's Fourier norm.
arxiv-2606-13157:
Bodini and Durand introduce random bit recycling, a paradigm for generating uniform random binary words of fixed Hamming weight while consuming as few random bits as possible, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Choosing a uniform k-subset of an n-element set is a primitive, but random bits come from hardware random generators and are an expensive resource. Information theory sets the target: a generator must consume on average at least the entropy, the binary logarithm of the binomial coefficient.

Existing generators are typically far from that Shannon lower bound. The recycling paradigm salvages randomness that algorithms discard: when a random choice does not use all the entropy of the bits consumed, the surplus is reused rather than thrown away. The authors generate fixed-weight binary words in linear time while consuming a number of random bits close to the entropic lower bound, making the algorithm optimal in bit consumption.
arxiv-2606-13357:
Kressner and colleagues analyse a family of algorithms for nonlinear eigenvalue problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such problems ask for special values where a system resonates; in the nonlinear case the system also depends on the value searched for. Contour integral methods reliably find all eigenvalues inside a chosen region of the complex plane. Their weakness is cost: without iterative refinement, high accuracy demands expensive numerical integration around the contour. One earlier algorithm, NLFEAST, does refine in rounds by adding a nonlinear extraction step.

The authors build a general framework of iterative contour integral methods that includes NLFEAST as a special case. Within it they prove linear convergence of NLFEAST under mild assumptions: the error shrinks by a fixed factor each round. It also explains why some other eigensolvers resist pairing with iterative refinement. Experiments confirm the theory.
arxiv-2606-13457:
Lăcătuş, Möller, and Succi propose a quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum computers evolve states linearly, so nonlinear equations, central to fluid dynamics and reaction modelling, are an obstacle. Methods use state copies that can grow without bound, mean-field shortcuts whose errors depend on copy number, or linearised forms with tight stability demands. The authors' reduced basis algorithm handles polynomial nonlinearities in ODEs and discretised PDEs. After stepping in time, it builds the update map over many steps and finds the reduced monomial basis that appears.

From that basis they construct a linear operator whose action reproduces the exact multi-step dynamics of the discrete scheme. The nonlinearity is absorbed into the basis selection rather than fought at every step. By avoiding runaway copy growth, the method removes one of the obstructions to simulating such physics on quantum machines.
arxiv-2606-14057:
Hahn, He, Liao, and Zhou make granular instruments practical when hidden common factors cannot be observed. These exploit big units: idiosyncratic shocks to large firms or investors survive aggregation and can identify elasticities. But building valid ones seemed to require knowing the latent factor structure. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows valid instruments are exactly the orthogonal complement of the factor-loading space, directions untouched by common shocks.

It is estimable directly from the data covariance, without estimating the factors, and without a large cross-section: the entity count may stay fixed. They add feasible procedures for estimation and testing. In Monte Carlo tests the feasible estimator matched an oracle knowing the true factor space. Applied to the aggregate equity market multiplier, it found large heterogeneity in equity demand responses across investor sectors, and evidence of highly inelastic aggregate demand, supporting the inelastic-markets hypothesis.
arxiv-2606-14157:
Martinez asks how many kilometers of travel a school subsidy is worth, recovering the answer from enrollment flows alone.  Her 2026 arXiv paper treats Philippine school-to-school flows as an entropic optimal transport plan. A national subsidy there steers learners from crowded public schools to private ones. Inverse optimal transport recovers the latent costs making those flows plausible, via two models: a distance-banded model with a subsidy term, and a neural cost model.

The data cover 283,016 learner trips across 23,820 flows in the most populated region. The headline metric, a subsidy-equivalent distance, counts kilometers of travel cost the subsidy offsets. Its values ranged from zero point zero eight zero to zero point six one two, largest at short distances, flattening over longer ranges. The neural model missed the piecewise model's sharp long-range rise, hinting at band aggregation artifacts. A subsidy, she concludes, has a spatial footprint.
arxiv-2606-14357:
Taylor sets out a 2026 arXiv proposal about how software should be written for AI coding agents. Human code repositories carry accidental entropy, meaning clutter that is not real program behavior, such as naming drift, framework churn, and weak proof routes. Taylor argues that frontier models waste much of their capacity learning this clutter.

The proposal rewrites routine software into canonical code, a single governed form for each behavior, carrying proofs, typed change rules, and records of past failures. Early training tests used over sixty-four thousand canonical examples with a mid-size coding model and suppressed banned language markers in its output. Taylor stresses that cost savings of thirty to five hundred times remain hypotheses, not measured results, and frames the plan as a testable research program.
arxiv-2606-14557:
Gökberk Erdoğan and co-authors adapt private information retrieval to DNA-based data storage in a 2026 arXiv paper. Private retrieval lets a user fetch a database item in secret. The user never reveals which item was taken. DNA storage encodes data in synthetic DNA molecules. It is a dense and durable medium. But querying it runs through biochemical steps with their own costs.

The team proposes two ways to adapt two-server protocols. In those, privacy rests on split queries to servers that do not collude. Each approach balances privacy, efficiency, and feasibility in its own way. Their analysis shows how privacy trade-offs shift in this medium. The trade-offs are familiar from digital databases. But here the storage medium is molecular. Queries must be realized as laboratory procedures. It is an early step toward private archives stored in DNA.
arxiv-2606-14757:
Candogan and co-authors give vision transformers a sense of place in a 2026 arXiv paper. Transformer attention is permutation equivariant, treating image patches as an unordered set, so vision transformers lack explicit spatial bias. That gap bites hardest when models are small or training data are limited, exactly the settings where structure must substitute for scale.

Their mechanism, VIOLIN, scans the image along several space-filling curves, paths that snake through every patch, and builds curve-specific decay masks multiplied into the attention matrix. The addition costs a negligible fraction of extra parameters and compute. In limited-data fine-tuning it raised accuracy across all task groups, with gains near nine percent where spatial information is essential, and it stacks with parameter-efficient tuning. It also improved small transformer pretraining and pixel-level classification substantially.
arxiv-2606-14957:
Huang and coauthors introduce Neuro-JEPA, a foundation model for brain MRI, in a 2026 study. Brain scans come in several contrast types, such as T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR, each highlighting different tissue traits. Clinicians read them together, yet few models learn one representation across all three. The team also studies which design choices make multimodal learning robust.

Neuro-JEPA pairs a latent predictive objective, in the JEPA family, with a sparse mixture-of-experts design. It was pretrained on over one and a half million scans. Evaluation covers dozens of tasks from three health systems and twelve public datasets. Rival foundation models beat a simple convolutional baseline only inconsistently across those tests. Neuro-JEPA instead improves on the baseline across unimodal, multimodal, and cross-domain settings alike. The authors argue that data curation and honest baselines are essential for medical foundation models.
arxiv-2606-15057:
Ma and coauthors stress-test defenses against indirect prompt injection with an adaptive attack tool in a 2026 study. Injected instructions hidden in tool outputs can hijack language model agents mid-task. Defenses are usually graded against fixed, hand-written attack strings in static benchmarks. A defense can ace such tests by keying on surface traits of those strings.

Their framework, AutoDojo, extends the AgentDojo benchmark by optimizing attacks against each live defense. A frontier model rewrites injections using only success or failure signals, with a small query budget. Across three task suites and five target models, adaptive attacks beat static ones against nearly every defense. One filter that stopped all static attacks still fell to a sizable share of adaptive ones. Success also climbs when user tasks leave actions open to outside content. The authors release the tool and pre-optimized injections for future defense testing.
arxiv-2606-15157:
Fei and Kalnis compress the key-value cache of language models differently in each layer in a 2026 study. Long contexts swell the cache, eating memory and slowing generation. Standard eviction applies one rule and one budget to every layer alike. Layers differ in role and sensitivity, so uniform treatment wastes cache space.

Their framework, PolyKV, routes each layer to a fitting eviction policy based on layer-level signals. It also hands out uneven budgets while holding the total cache. Offline calibration estimates each layer's preferred pattern and its sensitivity to cuts. Tests use LLaMA and Qwen models on the LongBench suite under budgets. PolyKV recovers over half the quality gap to a full cache on one model, and about a quarter on the other. Gains grow under tighter budgets, where choices matter most. Exact-retrieval tasks remain a weak spot, since decisive tokens can look unimportant during calibration.
arxiv-2606-15357:
Li and coauthor present minibwa in a 2026 bioinformatics paper, a faster program for aligning DNA sequencing reads to a reference genome. Alignment, placing each short read at its matching location, is the bottleneck of variant calling pipelines. The long-standard tool BWA-MEM is hard to speed up without changing its output, so the authors rebuilt the approach with breaking changes.

Minibwa mixes BWA-MEM's variable-length seeding with the chaining method from minimap2, then adds prefetching and shortcuts that skip wasted work in repetitive regions. It runs about four times faster than BWA-MEM and more than twice as fast as BWA-MEM2 at comparable accuracy. It also aligns bisulfite sequencing data, used to map chemical marks on DNA, with high accuracy. Faster alignment cuts the cost of whole-genome analysis, and the authors position minibwa as BWA-MEM's full replacement.
arxiv-2606-15457:
Zhang and coauthors present Lesion-DDPM in a 2026 medical imaging paper, a diffusion model that synthesizes brain MRI scans of multiple sclerosis patients. MS lesions are small bright spots on FLAIR scans, and public datasets are tiny, starving learning systems. Generic generators tend to smooth the lesions away. Lesion-DDPM counters this by injecting anatomical masks at several levels and weighting its reconstruction loss toward lesion voxels.

In tests it achieves the lowest lesion-region error among GAN and diffusion competitors, and neurologists often judged its synthetic scans to be real. The practical payoff shows downstream: a segmentation network trained only on Lesion-DDPM scans, then tested on real ones, outlines lesions clearly better than one trained on the best rival's synthetic data. Mixing the synthetic scans into real training data lifts the score further. Such synthesis offers bigger training sets without sharing scarce patient scans.
arxiv-2606-16057:
Levy and Beheshti study how often a robot should run its expensive global correction step in a 2026 estimation paper. State estimation tracks where a robot is and how its surroundings map out. The Extended Kalman Filter updates quickly at every step but drifts over time because it linearizes curved motion. Factor graph optimization fixes drift by re-solving many steps together, at much higher computing cost.

Their hybrid runs the filter at every step and invokes batch optimization only periodically, with solver settings fixed. Planar SLAM simulations, where an agent maps landmarks while localizing itself, isolate the schedule effect. Drift grows gradually as the gap between optimizations lengthens in the simulations. Computing cost falls rapidly over the same range, an asymmetric trade-off the authors map carefully. Some schedules keep most of the accuracy gain at far less cost, a useful guide for robots with limited power.
arxiv-2606-16257:
Sahin and co-authors bring variance reduction to sampling in 2026, attacking distributions whose shapes defeat the standard Langevin sampler. Sampling from high-dimensional, non-log-concave distributions with unnormalized densities is a core task. When exact gradients are unavailable, stochastic gradients inflate the cost, because the classic sampler needs batch sizes that grow with dimension and noise. Optimization tricks like momentum, STORM, and PAGE cut variance there, but their sampling behavior was uncharted.

The team gives the first analysis of these estimators for non-log-concave sampling, packaged as two samplers, ML-VRLD and SL-VRLD, for different regularity conditions. Both reach a target accuracy in relative Fisher information with a constant number of gradient computations per step, under fixed memory. Convergence in total variation follows under a Poincaré inequality, and weak convergence to the target is proved. The analysis extends to inverse problems with score-based generative priors.
arxiv-2606-16557:
Maity and co-authors reveal in 2026 the atomic-scale shape of quadrupolar excitons trapped in a three-layer moiré crystal, finding two distinct species where models expected one blur. Quadrupolar excitons, superpositions of anti-aligned dipolar excitons, are candidates for exotic many-body physics, quantum sensing, and photonic devices. The team studies twisted WSe2/WS2/WSe2 trilayers by solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation in a large-scale atomistic framework.

The surprise is how much atomic relaxation matters. At small twist angles, large relaxations create two distinct quadrupolar excitons pinned at moiré lattice sites. One is azimuthally symmetric, its electron density maximal at the hole. The other is threefold symmetric, with a node at the hole. Moiré trapping, neglected in common models, proves critical to the many-exciton phases: without it the excitons would collapse into anti-parallel dipoles on a square lattice, while trapping keeps the quadrupolar order.
arxiv-2606-16757:
Fu and colleagues study black hole entropy away from equilibrium in a 2026 general relativity paper. A quiet black hole obeys an area law: its entropy equals the area of its horizon. When matter falls in, the horizon moves, and whether the area law survives at second order in the disturbance was not fully settled.

Working in Gaussian null coordinates on a general stationary background, the team builds the apparent horizon step by step up to second order. Within covariant phase space methods they define a modified canonical energy that includes the matter fields' share. A balance law then ties the second-order entropy change to the energy flux crossing the horizon. When infalling matter obeys the null energy condition, entropy is exactly the apparent horizon area at second order, and the change obeys the second law. The paper also probes what survives when that energy condition fails.
arxiv-2606-16957:
Gaißer, Klumpp and Ribeiro study belief contraction in temporal logic in a 2026 paper. Agents must sometimes give up beliefs, and formal operators describe how to drop one while keeping choices among alternatives coherent. The preference orders behind those operators are usually assumed easy to construct.

In linear temporal logic, where claims concern sequences over time and relations are encoded by Büchi automata, building them turns treacherous. The authors prove the core condition guaranteeing successful contraction is undecidable: no algorithm can always check it. That kills hopes for a general representation theorem for effective contraction in this logic. As a constructive response, they design families of preference orders that meet the conditions by design. The families extend classical distance-based choices and allow layered stacking of several orders. The results also enrich the classical toolbox beyond the standard Dalal construction.
arxiv-2606-17257:
Kundu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on making open-weight video diffusion models safer without retraining them. Such models can produce realistic unsafe content, from violence to misinformation. Existing defences either fine-tune at high cost and risk general skill, or filter prompts and outputs in ways that adversarial prompts can bypass, so the authors steer the model's internal representations instead.

Their method, REINS, finds that safety-relevant structure is encoded linearly in the hidden states of video diffusion transformers. A single direction, found by supervised principal component analysis on safety labels, separates safe from unsafe generation paths. Adding that direction at an intermediate layer during inference redirects harmful requests toward related safe outputs, with no weight updates. Steering worked best near half the model's depth, and the method was tested across nine models.
arxiv-2606-17357:
Gothen and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on speeding up quantum chemistry calculations on near-term quantum processors by replacing gate sequences with engineered pulses. Hybrid quantum eigensolvers are usually built from primitive gates, yet their circuits assemble from recurring elements that mimic an electron hopping between two or four spin orbitals. Tuning one pulse for a whole circuit is hopeless at scale, but tuning pulses for those small elements is feasible on real hardware.

Gradient-ascent pulse design tailors each element's control fields directly to the processor at hand. Numerical tests on a silicon spin-qubit device run single and double excitations in a few hundred nanoseconds each. Compared with gate-based versions, the pulse versions cut runtimes by up to a factor of about fifteen in the reported cases. Shorter runs mean less exposure to noise, a practical route to larger chemistry problems.
arxiv-2606-17557:
Guo and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on restoring images hit by several degradations at once, where unified models tend to fade as the damage grows more complex. Chain-of-thought style restorers work in rounds with specialised modules, but that raises cost and models the interplay between damage types weakly. Their framework, CoTIR, folds the reasoning inside a single model instead, treating restoration as a branch of image editing to start from a strong pretrained editor.

Fine-tuning adapts that editor to restoration, while a differentiable objective inspired by Lagrangian optimisation encodes the structured reasoning into training. A companion benchmark supplies millions of samples with reasoning traces for training and evaluation. On that benchmark and on real composite damage scenes, CoTIR beat both all-in-one models and multi-round rivals. Perceptual quality and fidelity both came out ahead in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-17657:
Cheng and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on making language models imitate specific kinds of human decision-makers, drawn from cognitive science, inside persuasion games.
