Simulated people are used to test and train models, but a single average persona misses how differently real people update beliefs: some follow Bayes, others show motivated reasoning or distorted weighting. The authors turn classic equations of these styles into prompts, asking models to behave as each equation dictates in legal-style persuasion settings between a persuader and a judge.

Large models approximated the equation-defined behaviours well from prompts alone, while small models could not. Training the small models with reinforcement learning to follow the rules cut belief error sharply on unseen parameter settings. Mixing decision-maker types in training improved average belief change even against a strong outside model. Better human simulation promises safer testing of persuasive systems before deployment.
arxiv-2606-17957:
Ramokapane and colleagues argue that keeping children safe online should not mean treating them as intruders, in a 2026 paper. Digital tools now sit at the center of children's learning, play, and friendships. Yet the standard safety playbook leans on bans, age gates, parental controls, monitoring, and screen-time limits, framing protection as keeping children out of systems built for adults.

The authors propose child-fit security as an alternative design stance. Any technology children are likely to use should treat them as legitimate users, and should be accountable for the kind of childhood it makes possible. Protection and participation are designed together rather than traded off. The paper works out what this stance demands of designers and platforms, offering a paradigm meant to replace containment as the default response to children's digital lives.
arxiv-2606-18257:
Wang and colleagues grade the questions that language models write for students, asking whether the questions make students think, in a 2026 paper for the KDD conference. Automated question generation is easy to scale, but a flood of recall-level prompts adds little learning. The team evaluates six widely used models through Bloom's taxonomy, the classic ladder from memorization up to creation, across computer science, school mathematics, and social science.

A hybrid human and AI protocol assessed over twenty thousand generated questions for level alignment, knowledge coverage, and how far each question shifts thinking upward. A fine-grained prompting strategy cut repetitiveness sharply for one model and raised the share of higher-order questions. Yet a bias surfaced: most models drift toward higher-order questions even when constrained, which can overload learners. Structured prompting, the authors conclude, gives teachers real control over cognitive depth.
arxiv-2606-18457:
Dräger investigates how much of a recurrent neural network's weight matrix can be changed or removed without altering what the network actually does on its task, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Exact symmetries of weight space are well studied, but trained networks may also tolerate large changes.

Working with one-layer tanh recurrent networks, he rewrites the recurrent matrix in ordered real Schur coordinates, which separate spectral blocks from directed nonnormal couplings, then deletes selected couplings. On a copy task, some trained solutions survived removing chosen couplings almost unscathed, while others needed those same kinds of couplings for accurate replay. Across flip-flop, sine generation, and context-dependent integration tasks, the pattern of safe deletions varied by task and by individual trained solution. He offers the method as a diagnostic, not as proof that nonnormal structure can usually be ignored.
arxiv-2606-18957:
Pernecker and colleagues report in 2026 on small robots that place optical fibers for a planned large survey telescope. The telescope needs tens of thousands of these robots across a wide field of view. Each robot must set its fiber in place with an error of just a few micrometres. That scale is far larger than in current survey tools, so the build itself is a major risk.

Four rival designs are now being built and tested by teams in several countries. Tests check how exact and how fast each design is, and how well it can be made in huge numbers. One design already shows repeat results well inside the needed limit, which supports the plan. A choice among the designs is due in the next phase of study. The work helps pave the way toward first light for the new telescope in the early twenty forties.
arxiv-2606-19157:
Sakshi and colleagues introduce IndicContextEval in 2026, a benchmark testing whether audio language models truly use supplied context. Such models transcribe speech conditioned on text prompts like domain notes or entity lists. It is unclear whether they use that context or just lean on knowledge baked in during training. Past benchmarks test transcription under fixed prompts and rarely give explicit context, so they cannot settle the question.

The bench holds fifty six hours of natural speech from hundreds of speakers across eight Indian languages and many professional domains. A seven-level prompting scheme adds context step by step, from metadata and descriptions to entity lists in English and native script. It even adds adversarial prompts with wrong entities to test blind trust. Five models show large differences in context use. The results argue that contextual grounding in audio models needs direct evaluation, not assumption from transcription scores alone.
arxiv-2606-19357:
Javed and colleagues built Physical Atari in 2026, a platform for real-time reinforcement learning on a physical robot. The system pairs a robot called the Robotroller, which actuates a real Atari joystick, with an Atari Devbox that renders the game frame and reward signal on a screen. An off-the-shelf camera and desktop computer complete the setup. Learning happens in the physical world, with real latency and wear.

Robustness drove the design. All Robotroller movement runs through bearings to reduce wear, and software monitors servo state at high frequency to limit stress. Accessibility drove the cost. Parts are affordable and can be made on consumer 3D printers, bringing the build in under a thousand dollars. The system ran weeks of non-stop experiments with no mechanical failures. It validated that algorithms can learn directly on robots. It also showed small shifts between learning and deployment can badly degrade policies.
arxiv-2606-19657:
Mattie Ji and Bowen Yang build obstruction theory for quantum cellular automata representations in 2026. Quantum cellular automata update quantum states under strict locality rules on a metric space. Their representations echo projective representations, where lifting to honest linear ones is a classic problem.

Over an arbitrary field, Ji and Yang ask when a QCA representation can be linearised. The machinery is the algebraic K-theory spectrum of QCA from their earlier work. Obstructions turn out to be governed by the homotopy type of the QCA spaces. Universal obstruction classes to linearisation drop out of that structure. In the complex algebraic and unitary case, homotopy types are computed fully. Point, line, and plane geometries all get complete answers. Locality constraints thus leave fingerprints in pure algebra, tying quantum dynamics to K-theory.
arxiv-2606-19857:
Jiayi Zhu and five colleagues test whether language models can talk in unreadable shorthand in 2026. Models are usually fed human-readable text even when another model is the reader. BabelTele names their probe: compact textual forms that drop readability but keep meaning recoverable.

Readability diagnostics, likelihood measures, human surveys, and task tests all probe the forms. Instruction-tuned models recover the core semantics despite heavy departures from natural language. Semantic fidelity holds near ninety-nine percent while text shrinks to about a quarter of its length. Cross-model transfer, agent memory, and multi-agent messaging trials follow. Context overhead falls while downstream performance mostly holds. Success depends on which model compresses and which one reads. Readability, typicality, and recoverability can thus come apart, opening space for model-native codes.
arxiv-2606-19957:
Laura Marks, Jess MacCormack, and Kehui Li survey modest, artistic, and radical answers to the environmental cost of image-generating machine learning in 2026. Efficiency gains from machine learning are dwarfed by the carbon, water, and land footprints of data centres and AI-ready devices. An engineer, a media scholar, and an artist review electricity use in training and image generation, then assess lighter technical paths.

Options include inexact computing, tiny language models, low-precision hardware, and deliberately limited machines. The team also sketches a small image generator trained on non-scraped data, aiming at ethical and artistic quality at once. A true-cost accounting of machine learning's footprint is proposed, alongside a challenge to the efficiency-first framing of computing. The piece gives the sustainability debate concrete design options.
arxiv-2606-20257:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures how charged particles are produced in oxygen-oxygen and neon-neon collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Their 2026 paper reports momentum spectra, particle counts, and mean momentum as functions of pseudorapidity and collision centrality, at a nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.36 TeV. These light-ion runs bridge the gap between proton collisions and heavy lead-lead systems, probing where collective, fluid-like behavior switches on.

Centrality is characterized by total transverse energy in the forward detectors. Particle tracks come from the inner detector over the angular range within 2.5 and momenta from 0.27 to 5 GeV. Results are reported in fine centrality intervals, with yields fitted to extrapolate densities over the full momentum range. A parallel measurement using rapidity instead of pseudorapidity gauges the bias that choice introduces. Light-ion data like these calibrate how particle production scales with system size.
arxiv-2606-20357:
Hsiao-Ru Pan and Bernhard Schölkopf analyze why temporal difference learning, a cornerstone of reinforcement learning, has lower variance than Monte Carlo estimation. Their 2026 paper works in the phased, tabular setting. TD learning bootstraps: it updates value estimates from other estimates instead of waiting for complete trajectories. Bootstrapping, they show, effectively aggregates over more independent trajectories than the raw sample count suggests.

Two consequences follow. The variance of TD is asymptotically bounded above by that of Monte Carlo estimators, and shorter-horizon updates carry less variance for a fixed number of samples. The team then reframes Direct Advantage Estimation as a regression-adjusted control variate, proving it achieves a tighter variance bound than TD in the large-sample limit. Carefully designed numerical environments illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2606-20657:
Zhan Shi and four colleagues report A-Evolve-Training in 2026, an autonomous system that post-trains a 30-billion-parameter Nemotron model with no human in the loop. Post-training normally takes a research team weeks of proposing data mixes, launching runs, reading scores, and deciding what to keep. Their system runs that full cycle itself across four rounds on graphics processor clusters over several weeks.

The resulting model scores 0.86 on a held-out test, close to the top human score of 0.87, and places eighth among about 4,000 entries in the NVIDIA Nemotron Reasoning Challenge. The loop also caught a warning sign: its own development metric rose while external performance stalled on the weakest reasoning area. That self-detection matters because it shows both the power and the risk of automated training, where a flawed internal measure can mislead the system it guides.
arxiv-2606-20757:
Yucheng Xing and four colleagues propose EMMS in 2026, a model for predicting patient survival when some data types are missing. Multimodal models use complementary sources, such as scans and clinical records. They often assume all sources are present. Real clinics often lack one or more. EMMS fuses evidence without a generative step to invent the missing data, keeping the method simple and fast.

The model uses Dempster-Shafer theory and Gaussian random fuzzy numbers for fusion. It weighs two kinds of uncertainty and the reliability of each modality. A missing modality is treated as vacuous evidence. It therefore does not distort available inputs, while uncertainty rises in a natural way. Tests on four cancer datasets show state-of-the-art results with calibrated predictions. Handling missing data honestly matters for clinical tools, because a confident guess built on absent scans can mislead care.
arxiv-2606-20857:
Ningwei Bai and eight colleagues at University College London present SignVLA in 2026, a real-time system that lets sign language guide a robot arm. Vision-language-action models take instructions from speech or text. That limits access for deaf, hard-of-hearing, and speech-impaired users. SignVLA adds a modular sign-to-text interface. Visual gestures become semantic instructions that standard robot policies can already use.

Hand landmark features are extracted from video streams. An attention-enhanced recurrent network reads gesture dynamics over time. It recognizes alphabet signs and command-level signs. A stabilization module smooths predictions for consistent real-time output. The instruction sequence then passes to a robot policy for manipulation. Experiments show stable recognition and successful task execution. Accessible interfaces matter because robot helpers will enter homes and clinics, where spoken commands cannot be the only way to be understood.
arxiv-2606-21257:
Tong Shi and six colleagues tested how far the OpenPangu language models can be compressed in 2026, running them on Huawei Ascend 910B1 processors. Quantization shrinks model weights to fewer bits, saving memory, but aggressive settings can wreck accuracy. The team compared weight-only and weight-plus-activation methods, including GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant, on the 1B and 7B models under one shared protocol.

Across eighteen tasks, 8-bit weight-only quantization proved effectively lossless for both models. At 4 bits, the 7B model stayed practical while the 1B model lost ground on reasoning, math, and code. Most 2-bit and binary settings collapsed to near-random answers, and one 4-bit activation setup produced non-finite perplexity scores. The result is a practical accuracy map for deploying OpenPangu on Ascend hardware.
arxiv-2606-21557:
Murong Yue and six colleagues release PeerMathDial in 2026, the first dataset of middle school students solving math problems together, captured in real classrooms. Most education dialogue data record teachers tutoring students, leaving peer collaboration, a core skill, largely unrecorded. The dataset holds fifty-five dialogues from twenty-seven students across 6,406 conversational turns. The team also built a dialogue act taxonomy, grounded in the corpus with language model help, to label what each turn does.

Three demonstrations show the dataset at work. Dialogue tracking reveals how conversations evolve and how teacher interventions land. Aligning dialogue acts with student surveys links traits such as confidence and leadership to actual behavior. Testing language models on act prediction probes their promise as student simulators for education research.
arxiv-2606-21957:
Shamba, Bach, and Taylor propose ShiFT in 2026, a simpler way to teach time series models from unlabelled data. Contrastive learning trains a model by pulling matching views of a series together and pushing others apart, but the usual views come from hand-crafted augmentations and masking tricks. Those tricks bake in domain assumptions and can create false correlations, limiting how well the learned features travel.

ShiFT instead builds its views by shifting the series in time, a deterministic construction that directly encodes shift invariance. Despite its simplicity, the method reached state-of-the-art results on six diverse real-world benchmark datasets plus the UCR and UEA archives, while cutting training time. The authors also analyze how batch size and the number of negative examples shape downstream performance in time series contrastive learning. Their findings offer practical design guidance for efficient self-supervised learning on temporal data.
arxiv-2606-22357:
Ghasemi and colleagues introduce ORBIT in 2026, a training-free method for steering several behaviours of a language model at once. Activation steering shifts hidden states at inference time to change traits like caution or verbosity. Steering one trait is well studied, but summing per-attribute vectors for several attributes suffers norm imbalance and directional cancellation. Classifier approaches, meanwhile, need retraining whenever the set changes.

ORBIT builds a joint subspace from the per-attribute steering planes by singular value decomposition. It then applies one norm-preserving rotation within that subspace, aimed at a combined target direction. Per-token gating then adapts, deciding which ones need correcting at each position. An optional boost strengthens weak ones. On the new TraitFactory benchmark and ToneBank, across three models, ORBIT steers multiple traits more strongly and evenly than training-free baselines, with better output coherence.
arxiv-2606-23557:
Choi and colleagues train multimodal models to reason about three-dimensional scenes from several photos, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Answering questions about a room from multiple views demands a coherent mental map. Models trained only on final answers often build inconsistent maps and pick poor viewpoints. Their reasoning then sounds plausible while resting on the wrong view of the scene.

The framework, DR-MV3D, splits the job into three supervised steps. First the model builds an allocentric global map, a map from a neutral overhead frame. Then it plans a trajectory of viewpoints suited to the question. Finally it grounds the answer in an egocentric view, the scene as seen from a position inside it. Two dense rewards grade the map and the viewpoint order against geometry from frozen vision models. Tests on MindCube, VSI-Bench, and BLINK show steady gains over strong multi-image baselines.
arxiv-2606-23657:
Chen, Fan, Yan, Wu, and Xiang fix a sampling flaw that freezes quantum dynamics simulations at their first step, in a 2026 paper on computational physics. Variational Monte Carlo follows a quantum system's evolution by sampling configurations of a trial wave function. A local quench, a sudden kick from a charged operator, forces exponentially many configurations to carry zero weight. Some of those configurations still matter for the dynamics, so samplers that never visit them produce biased, frozen evolution.

The authors show the missing support problem is itself local, an artifact of the chosen sampling basis. A local rotation of that basis restores the missing configurations without changing the underlying variational dynamics. Benchmarks show it capturing long time dynamics accurately, including structure factors for dynamics in one dimension and unbiased quench dynamics in two dimensions. The fix may also help ground state calculations.
arxiv-2606-23757:
Liu, Wang, Yang, and Tao combine two Bayesian tools to recover chemical reaction networks from noisy time series data, in a 2026 paper on scientific machine learning. A reaction network states which reactions occur and how fast. Structure and rate constants are tightly coupled, so fitting one without the other invites physically impossible mechanisms that still match the data.

Their workflow, PC MCMC CIGP, samples candidate topologies with a spike and slab Markov chain method screened by hard conservation and thermodynamic rules. A chemical informed Gaussian process, which embeds the candidate mechanism as its prior mean, then calibrates parameters and guides which experiments to run next. On a hydrogen bromine benchmark the sampler separates true radical pathways from deceptive fits. On styrene epoxidation the optimization loop improves final yield by about twelve percent over a reported baseline.
arxiv-2606-23957:
Nagdi and colleagues bolt a short memory and a self correction trigger onto a Koopman autoencoder. The goal is to stop its long range forecasts of nonlinear dynamics from drifting, in a 2026 paper on machine learning for dynamical systems. The Koopman approach lifts a nonlinear system into a space where its evolution is linear, and an autoencoder can learn that lifting. Single steps look accurate. But long rollouts slide off the learned surface. Phases slip, and amplitudes decay or explode.

An attention free memory block averages a short window of recent latent states to correct each step, running in linear time with few added parameters. Dynamic re-encoding adds change point detectors that notice drift and project the state back onto the learned surface. On three benchmark systems, the combined model cuts long horizon error against the plain autoencoder and attention based rivals, over horizons up to one thousand steps.
arxiv-2606-24357:
Filippozzi, Urteaga, and Agostinelli build a Bayesian method that chooses which covariates belong in a generalised linear model, while estimating its settings. Including wrong predictors invites overfitting; omitting needed ones biases everything. Existing Bayesian selection tools compromise somewhere: spike and slab and shrinkage priors often lack full conjugacy, stick to plain linear models, or never assure the selection settles on the truth.

A binary inclusion flag for each input sits directly inside the linear predictor, so picking and fitting proceed at once, and both doubts flow into the posterior. The layered framework is fully conjugate. It applies to any response spread in the exponential family, the class behind most generalised linear models. Theory guarantees cover both selection and the settings. The authors present it as a valid post model selection Bayesian procedure, usable from logistic regression to count models without bespoke tooling.
arxiv-2606-24457:
Jing and colleagues challenge the assumption that fast stereo vision must be weak at generalising. Stereo matching estimates depth by comparing two camera views. Accurate modern models tend to be large, slow, or dependent on foundation model priors. Efficient models are presumed to fail on unseen scenes. Their Lite Any Stereo V2, from Imperial College London in 2026, is an ultra fast series for zero shot stereo on constrained hardware.

The team revisits efficient stereo design under real use conditions. A cost aggregation framework uses only two-dimensional operations. It is optimised for actual inference latency, rather than paper operation counts. Training follows a three stage strategy, combining synthetic supervision with self distillation stages that build robustness. The result aims to deliver strong zero shot depth on scenes the model never trained on, at speeds embedded platforms can afford. Efficiency and generalisation, Jing argues, are a design choice.
arxiv-2606-24757:
Harrison Nicholls leads the CHILI project, a comparison of codes that simulate young rocky planets. Earth and Venus both began as molten worlds covered by magma oceans. Coupled interior atmosphere models are the main tool for reconstructing those histories. Different codes, though, make different approximations, and results can drift apart. CHILI benchmarks the codes against each other to find where the sensitivities lie.

The first results cover evolutionary modelling of the early magma ocean stage. Nominal Earth models agree on solidification times within four million years. They also match empirical constraints on Earth's early history. Venus cases behave far more diversely. There, magma oceans can persist for fifty million years under the right conditions. Cooling times track the starting budgets of hydrogen and carbon. Treatments of volatile partitioning and vertical energy transport still differ between codes. Those choices drive much of the spread between models, the comparison shows.
arxiv-2606-24957:
WenHung Lee and eight colleagues present Dustin, a sparse verification framework that speeds up long context generation with speculative decoding. Speculative decoding raises throughput, but verification becomes the bottleneck: loading the key value cache dominates latency. Static eviction loses accuracy as saliency shifts; dynamic selection costs too much on the verification path. Dustin fuses two signals to find critical tokens: lookahead from the draft model and past attention from the target model.

A sparse estimation scheme limits importance scoring to a small subset of attention heads. On PG-19 and LongBench with the Qwen2.5-72B model, Dustin reaches nearly twenty eight fold speedup in self attention. End to end decoding speeds up over nine fold at a 32k sequence length. Accuracy degradation is negligible in these evaluations. Lee and colleagues target the regime where long contexts and multi batch serving collide, where verification cost bites hardest.
arxiv-2606-25257:
Coding agents follow standing instruction files, and those files change as projects grow. Gianmario Voria and colleagues set out in 2026 to study how developers maintain these agent context files over time. Their planned empirical study mines software repositories that contain such files together with agent generated commits. Changes to the files are classified with a taxonomy borrowed from software maintenance theory, then linked to code quality measures.

Reconstructing each file's history commit by commit lets the team ask when edits happen across a project's life and which kinds of edits track with better or worse code outcomes. Statistical tests compare the maintenance categories against each other. Findings are meant to guide how instruction files should be designed when they govern autonomous coding agents.
arxiv-2606-25557:
Zeolite RHO works like a molecular valve: pressure flips its framework between two shapes, opening or closing the windows into its cages. Salvador Balestra, Antonio Rivas-Blanco, Said Hamad, and Rabdel Ruíz-Salvador ask in 2026 whether that trick belongs to RHO alone or to its whole expanded family. Eight frameworks share the same window motif at growing sizes. Computer models combining lattice dynamics, full elasticity, and finite temperature free energies map each member's switching pressure, checked against high level quantum calculations for the smallest two.

Switching proved generic across the family, and the critical pressure falls exponentially as the framework grows. The parent switches near one gigapascal, while the largest member is predicted to respond below a tenth of that, making these the softest frameworks of the set. A simple Landau picture captures the whole trend.
arxiv-2606-25857:
Michel Benaïm, Tresnia Berah, and Pierre Germain study killed Markov chains, random processes that wander among states until they are absorbed and stop. A quasi-stationary distribution describes how such a chain behaves in the long run when attention is restricted to runs that have survived. The team couples the chain to a reinforced process that, each time it dies, restarts at a spot sampled from its own weighted history.

When the chain can reach every state from every other, the occupation measure settles on the single quasi-stationary distribution. Benaïm and colleagues handle the harder case where that reachability fails and several such distributions exist. Selection then hinges on the weights: if the inverse cumulative weights sum to infinity, the distribution tied to the largest Perron value wins almost surely. When the sum is finite, every candidate keeps a positive chance of being selected.
arxiv-2606-25957:
Samuel Tovey, Stefan Prestel, and Hiroshi Yamauchi propose a new tool for finding survivors after building collapses, when the first days matter most. Their idea sends drones carrying quantum magnetometers over the rubble. Steel inside reinforced concrete distorts the magnetic field, so a fine magnetic map could reveal the hidden structure below and hint at voids where people might shelter.

A full simulation pipeline backs the proposal. Unreal Engine generates a collapsed parking garage, and a per-triangle dipole calculation gives the field it induces, with usable structure in the sub-picotesla to sub-nanotesla range about a metre above the roofline. Sparse readings feed a Gaussian process model steered by Bayesian active sampling. A three-sensor array balances map sharpness against drone payload, and active sampling hits peak structural correlation within roughly one hundred samples across repeated collapse scenarios.
arxiv-2606-26057:
Seth Dobrin and Łukasz Chmiel argue that AI agent safety controls fail when they live inside the agent. System prompts, output filters, and guardrail libraries all sit in the agent's own runtime. Inputs that steer the agent can reach those controls too. The pair call any system with that reach into itself escapable. Real control, they argue, must be architectural, not a polite request.

Four properties define their standard. Process separation keeps the checker outside the agent. Enforcement happens before action, on a path with structural access only. Failure closes the system at both request and system level. Signed evidence can be checked from outside the controlled system's trust boundary. Their Unfireable Safety Kernel implements all four in Rust. Formal checks back the fail-closed claim at two levels. Migrating from Python to Rust was gated on byte-identical outputs across a thousand test fixtures, plus adversarial cross-language cases.
arxiv-2606-26257:
Wojciech Łapacz and colleagues answer a question haunting generative AI: how much of my dataset trained your model? Dataset usage inference estimates that fraction for a candidate dataset. Older methods demand shadow models, costly lookalikes trained to mimic the target. They also demand confirmed non-member data from the same distribution. Both demands collapse in real ownership disputes. Their framework drops both requirements at once.

Synthetic stand-ins replace the held-out data. The method generates its own non-member samples, then extracts varied membership signals from the model. Usage becomes a mixture proportion problem: what share of the candidate set behaves like training data? Experiments on large image generative models show the estimates track the truth reliably. Data owners gain a practical audit tool that works on today's giant models. Copyright and consent disputes, like the lawsuits now moving through courts, are the intended courtroom for such evidence.
arxiv-2606-26357:
Daniel Vainshtein works in holography, the idea that a theory of gravity in one space can match a quantum theory living on its boundary. He studies rotating BTZ black holes, a three-dimensional black hole model, after a deformation, meaning a controlled change to the underlying theory known as a single-trace deformation. The question is how such black holes radiate particles and long strings.

Vainshtein extends an earlier emission mechanism to the rotating, deformed case and tracks probe particles and winding strings, which are strings wrapped around a compact direction. He shows that emission chances for both signs of the deformation track how the black hole's entropy changes, a measure tied to its information content. Consistency then fixes one background field value exactly, and that value matches what the dual boundary theory's spectrum requires.
arxiv-2606-26457:
Daniel Corrales and David Ríos Insua present a probabilistic framework for online test-time adaptation. A trained model meets new data whose pattern has shifted from its training data. That shift is called distributional shift. The model must adapt while in use, without labels for the new data. Recommender systems, hospital monitors, and self-driving systems all face this problem.

Their framework rests on state-space modelling. A state-space model tracks hidden quantities that evolve over time. From that single structure, the authors derive how to learn parameters. They also derive how parameters evolve, how prior settings are tuned, and how predictions are made. The setup aims to give adaptation a principled Bayesian footing. Bayesian methods weigh new evidence against prior beliefs using probability rules. The framework is meant to replace ad hoc fixes with one coherent method.
arxiv-2606-26757:
Majharulislam Babor and four colleagues present a network for checking edible insect species from light spectra. Insects are an efficient alternative protein, but food supply chains need sound species checks. Such checks control allergen exposure, stop cheating, and satisfy regulators. Near-infrared light scans read a sample's chemical fingerprint quickly. Batch-to-batch variation, though, degrades accuracy on unseen production batches.

Their Batch-Invariant Spectral Network learns features that ignore batch identity. A learnable first stage starts from a classic smoothing filter. An entropy-based training goal pushes batch predictions toward uniform guessing, erasing batch clues from the features. Unlike domain-adversarial networks, which adjust only after feature extraction, this design suppresses batch effects before species classification. The goal is a classifier that travels across production batches without retraining.
arxiv-2606-26857: This paper does LCAi: life cycle assessment with big data fusion and retrieval-augmented generation-assisted interpretation. The doing does. Their doing is LCAi. The assessing assesses life cycle. It is sustainability AI. The doing is big data RAG interpretation.
arxiv-2606-27057:
Martel and colleagues take a close look at Arp 143, a pair of colliding galaxies caught mid-interaction. One member is a ring galaxy and the other a lens-shaped companion, and a long tidal plume stretches northward. Spectral data cubes from the SITELLE instrument in Hawaii record light at every point and wavelength at once. Star birth glows almost only in the ring and centre of the ring galaxy, with a few faint spots at the plume's base.

Hydrogen velocity maps show strong non-circular flows, and the ring itself is expanding outward. Its centre sits off-centre relative to the ring, a clue to a past head-on hit. Oxygen levels run slightly below solar in the ring and near solar at the nucleus. Simulations favour a story of an earlier flyby that raised the plume, then a direct collision between a lens galaxy and a spiral.
arxiv-2606-27157:
Xiao and Slock locate indoor devices using a single base station and the echo pattern of its radio signals. The relative power-delay profile lists how strong each echo is at each delay. That pattern works as a location fingerprint even with no direct path, angle reading, or absolute timing. Real receivers, though, see only finitely many noisy samples, blurred and folded in delay, in this study published in 2026.

Expectation-maximisation sparse Bayesian learning rebuilds a sharper posterior power profile from those samples. Doubling the resolution this way lifts top-one accuracy sharply in spatially consistent simulations. Mean position error drops below forty centimetres in the reported runs. The method beats both raw profiles and simple zero-padding, a naive way to fake finer delay grids. Treating messy echoes as information, not noise, lets one access point do work that usually needs several.
arxiv-2606-27257:
Nematollahi, Khorasani, and Meskin design control that keeps robot teams corralled even under cyber attack. In containment, follower agents must herd their outputs inside the moving hull spanned by several leaders. Two twists harden the problem: leader dynamics stay secret from followers, and actuators suffer false-data attacks tied to state, input, or outside signals. In the 2026 control paper, a two-layer adaptive design answers both twists, using only partial state readings at the first layer.

A virtual-actuator layer reconfigures control to cancel attack effects in local tracking error. A network layer then issues task commands through an adaptive protocol fed by neighbour exchanges alone. No global graph knowledge is needed to tune it. Under a leader-rooted spanning-tree condition, nonsmooth Lyapunov analysis gives containment at the command level. Quadrotors carrying damped swinging loads simulate the full system. Attack recovery and containment tracking both hold up.
arxiv-2606-27457:
Moslem leads a team serving language models in production without paying frontier prices for easy questions. A single deployed model is either wastefully strong for simple queries or too weak for hard ones. Their cascaded framework works in two stages. First, incoming queries are clustered, and each cluster is routed to its most cost-effective model under an explicit budget dial. Then a quality estimation cascade inspects outputs, escalating only low-quality answers to stronger models in this systems paper from 2026.

The cascade retains between ninety-seven and ninety-nine percent of the strongest model's accuracy on the test datasets while cutting time per output token in the reported evaluation. Only ordinary task-correctness labels are needed to train the routing. When the model pool changes, the system adapts without manual reconfiguration. Hard or low-confidence cases alone reach the expensive models.
arxiv-2606-27857:
Thorne's hoop conjecture says a black hole forms when mass is compressed within its own circumference in every direction. K K Nandi and five colleagues test the conjecture in 2026 on a new class of spacetimes. The class holds regular, static, spherically symmetric black holes. They are coupled to nonlinear electrodynamics and carry arbitrary exponents. With only the asymptotic mass, the conjecture could appear violated there.

Hod's earlier fix uses a dedicated mass function, the Hod function. Stated through it, the conjecture is protected in this class. That supports reading these spacetimes as black holes. The authors still urge caution. Other factors, including possible violations, argue against the new solutions qualifying as black holes. A final identification clarifies the mass function's meaning. The Hod mass equals the matter counterpart of the Misner–Sharp quasilocal mass in general relativity. Conclusions drawn from the Hod function are thus strictly conclusions of general relativity.
arxiv-2606-27957:
Basketball intuitions can now be tested with play-by-play data. Malvina Bozhidarova and nine colleagues analyse NBA performance and scoring in 2026 at multiple scales. The dataset covers 7054 regular-season games and 504 playoff games, from the 2019/20 to 2024/25 seasons. Methods come from statistics, network science, and complexity science. Individual players, teams, and scoring patterns are all examined.

Findings are presented as quantitative insights into scoring patterns. Both in-season and in-game performance are covered. Looking at several scales separates effects that single-level studies blur. A hot streak for one player need not mean the same thing for the team. Network methods capture how players combine, not just how each one performs. Complexity methods address the timing structure of scoring. The authors aim the results at coaching strategies, player evaluation, and tactical decisions. The work offers an evidence-based view where the sport long relied on intuition.
arxiv-2606-28057:
Language models store a vector for every token in the vocabulary. That matrix grows linearly with vocabulary size. Hashing many tokens into one vector saves parameters but causes collisions that break causal language modelling. Huiyin Xue, Atsuki Yamaguchi, and Nikolaos Aletras propose MultiHashFormer in 2026 to make hashing work for generation. Each token gets a unique hash signature. Several independent hash functions produce its short sequence of hash IDs.

A hash encoder compresses the signature into one latent vector for the decoder. A hash decoder generates the next token's signature, which maps back to text. Models were evaluated at three scales, one hundred million, one billion, and three billion parameters. MultiHashFormer consistently outperformed standard transformer language models across benchmarks. Multilingual expansion works with a constant parameter footprint and no modifications. Rare word representation also improves, the conclusion reports.
arxiv-2606-28257:
Swetha Sankar and thirteen colleagues observed eight rare galaxies that break a standard story. Low-excitation radio galaxies usually have quiet, gas-poor hosts where jets keep gas hot and star formation low. These blue ones are gas-rich and actively forming stars.

Sankar's team used near-infrared spectroscopy to detect warm molecular hydrogen glowing at a few thousand degrees. The strength of that glow varied widely and did not rise with radio power, arguing against the jets as the main heater. The strongest emission appeared in disturbed, merging galaxies, suggesting tidal shocks and inflowing gas do the heating. Compact radio sources might still heat gas locally, making these galaxies a short-lived phase before feedback takes over.
arxiv-2606-28357:
Yihua Zhang and thirteen colleagues built ReasonRec, a recommender that thinks out loud. Multimodal recommenders fuse images and text well but decide opaquely and waste computation on easy cases. ReasonRec wraps recommendation in an explicit three-stage pipeline: observe the user and items, deliberate in writing, then act.

Zhang's team turns varied recommendation tasks into chain-of-thought prompts so the model states its intermediate steps, and trains it with a curriculum that grows reasoning difficulty to handle new and long-tail users. When the agent's own uncertainty runs high, it hands the query to a small classical model instead. Across four task types and five datasets, ranking quality rose by over thirty percent relative to strong rivals, while delegating about a third of queries cut latency sharply.
arxiv-2606-28657:
Olivia Beckwith and Tushar Karmakar average class numbers, the invariants that count how many essentially distinct quadratic forms or ideal classes a number field carries. Averaging smooths their erratic behavior, and Riesz means, which weight the average with a power kernel, are a refined way to do it. The real quadratic and Hurwitz class numbers are the targets here.

To get their asymptotic formula, Beckwith and Karmakar first build the theory they need: L-functions attached to weight one-half sesquiharmonic Maass forms of moderate growth. They prove a formula for Riesz means of the generalized mock modular forms those L-functions encode, extending a recent result of Beckwith and coauthors for ordinary mock modular forms. Feeding in a particular form introduced by Duke, Imamoglu, and Tóth then delivers the class number asymptotics.
arxiv-2606-29157:
Arenas, Schild and Subercaseaux settle the computational complexity of several problems that count orderings of a graph's vertices or edges under adjacency constraints. Counting such orderings exactly is typically hard, and they prove each problem complete for the counting class #P, the standard benchmark of counting hardness. All the proofs run through one new common technique.

They build a family of instances controlled by a parameter that amplifies a simple gadget. After multiplying by a stated factor, the values agree with a rational function of the parameter, whose numerator and denominator can be recovered in polynomial time. Evaluating that function in symbols at a limiting value recovers a known hard function. The technique proves hardness for vertex orderings of bipartite graphs, st-numberings, shellings of bipartite graphs, and linear extensions of two families of posets. One result settles a 2015 conjecture of Felsner and Manneville about height-three posets.
arxiv-2606-29457:
Researchers at Sparq ask how much due diligence, the checking a buyer does before bidding, a takeover bidder should pay for. Each round of diligence gives a noisy private signal about a target whose true value nobody observes. More signals improve bidding but multiply the strategy space, so the game quickly outgrows exact solvers.

The team builds two-player auction games from the takeover literature, including common-value games with a winner's curse and a toehold variant. They benchmark nine solvers, from exact methods to deep learning ones. Learning methods PPO and PPG prove strongest among learners on ordinary hardware. Where games stay small enough to tabulate, exact solvers such as CFR reach lower exploitability, how beatable a strategy is, and run faster. Solving the equilibrium exactly shows the best amount of diligence is finite. It falls as the per-signal cost rises, and competition makes bidders more conservative still.
arxiv-2606-29557:
Guo proves propagation of chaos for quantum mean-field systems governed by Belavkin equations, which describe quantum particles under ongoing measurement. The term means a large system behaves as if its particles were separate copies of one limiting process. Here the particles are density matrices, the objects that describe quantum states.

The limiting dynamics takes the form of a nonlinear matrix-valued McKean-Vlasov diffusion, driven randomly through its local record. Guo's main result covers all one-particle density matrices, mixed states included, across both perfect and imperfect measurement regimes. Under strong assumptions on the starting data, every fixed marginal converges to the tensor product of the limit filters, with an explicit bound. The proof combines purification, dilation, and entropy tools. A second result weakens the starting assumptions.
arxiv-2606-29957:
Wu and ten colleagues introduce SWE-Together, a benchmark that judges coding agents as collaborators rather than one-shot code writers. Real assistance is interactive: users clarify goals, add constraints, and correct mistakes over several turns.

The benchmark rebuilds 109 repository-level tasks from 11,260 recorded real user-agent sessions, keeping sessions with recoverable repository states, clear goals, and observable outcomes. A reactive language-model user simulator replays each session, preserving the original user's intent and giving feedback when the agent's progress calls for it. Scoring covers both final repository correctness and how many corrective turns the agent needed. Stronger frontier agents generally finish more tasks while needing fewer interventions.
arxiv-2606-30157:
Alfie Robinson, James Owen, and Richard Booth ask whether the carbon monoxide snow line in planet forming discs is stable. Below a threshold temperature, carbon monoxide freezes onto dust grains. The boundary between ice and vapor is called the snow line. Earlier one-dimensional models suggested the boundary might oscillate unstably. The team tests that idea with vertical structure included.

Their disc evolution code gains a new ice-vapor chemistry solver. Including vertical structure does produce two stable equilibrium solutions. The snow surface can sit in either of two steady states. Yet evolving simulations never enter the predicted limit cycle. The two-dimensional snow surface shape prevents the oscillation. Vertical transport of volatiles also stabilizes the boundary. Snow line motion from this instability should be transient and random. Steady thermal evolution still reshapes the surface over time.
arxiv-2606-30257:
Xiaoge Lu, Zeke Yao, and Xi Zhang classify the homogeneous hypersurfaces of three four-dimensional Thurston geometries. Thurston's geometries are model spaces, lifted here to four dimensions. The three spaces studied have four-dimensional isometry groups. They are two Sol geometries and the Nil geometry. These surfaces are the basic models of isoparametric theory.

A hypersurface is homogeneous when a group of symmetries sweeps it out. Classifying them matches classifying cohomogeneity one actions up to orbit equivalence. Space forms and symmetric spaces have seen such classifications already. This paper completes the picture for the three named spaces. Every such surface in them is listed and described. The classification supplies canonical examples for isoparametric theory in these spaces. It also closes a gap left by earlier space-form results. The work is purely theoretical, resting on the isometry group structure.
arxiv-2606-30457:
Austin Patel, Ben Pekarek, Joel Enrique Castro Hernandez, and Shuran Song teach robots new tasks from a single demonstration given at test time. Retraining a robot for every new skill is expensive. A demonstration can serve as a prompt instead, they argue. It shows both what the task is and one way to do it. Their Behavior Prompting Policy turns that idea into an architecture.

The policy reads the demonstration alongside the current observation. It translates both into robot actions in context. Temporal matches and spatial differences between prompt and scene must be understood. Data matters as much as the algorithm here. Task diversity drives the prompting capability, they find. A handheld interface, iPhUMI, collects diverse training demonstrations cheaply. Two new benchmarks test adaptation to unseen tasks. Drawing tasks and tabletop manipulation tasks are covered. The handheld device also specifies prompts directly at test time.
arxiv-2606-30557:
EcoVideo, a system for faster video generation released in 2026, comes from Jiayu Chen and seven colleagues. Video models built on diffusion transformers, which clean up noisy frames step by step, are slow because every frame gets full treatment. Earlier cloud-edge splits divided denoising steps between a big cloud model and a small edge model, yet ignored how alike neighbouring frames are.

Chen's group instead splits by frames. Early attention patterns, measured through entropy, a gauge of information density, show which frames carry most detail and need full cloud processing. The light edge model rebuilds the rest by motion-aware interpolation, tracking movement between frames. The system also adjusts its keyframe count and edge refinement depth to live bandwidth and computing power. Tests showed speedups up to nearly three times in low-bandwidth, compute-limited settings, with better quality trade-offs.
arxiv-2606-30857:
Aaron Bundi Anampiu describes a competition system for spotting polarising content online in many languages. The SemEval-2026 shared task covers three subtasks: detecting polarisation, classifying its type, and identifying how it shows itself, across 22 languages. Anampiu entered for English and Swahili, using transformer models matched to each language, RoBERTa-base for English and AfroXLMR-base for Swahili.

Class-weighted losses countered the severe label imbalance, and tuning a threshold per label sharpened the multi-label decisions. Test F1 macro scores reached 0.7901 for English and 0.7910 for Swahili on detection, with type and manifestation scores between 0.4615 and 0.5830 across the two languages. Error analysis showed the models struggle most with dehumanisation and lack of empathy.
arxiv-2606-31357:
Reichert and three colleagues give a service robot a way to settle clashing user requests on ethical grounds. Robots in airports and hospitals get interrupted when several people want help at once, and serving one can disadvantage another. Fixed rules or a central arbiter cannot judge each case, and outside coordination may not exist.

Their self-negotiation framework stores an ethical profile for each user, holding stated values and conditions. When an interruption hits, the robot negotiates internally among those profiles and picks an outcome that fits them. A modular ROS build tested in simulation gave preference-aligned results each time, handled many-sided talks, and answered within 1.5 seconds. Runtime grew near-linearly as more users joined, which suits real public settings.
arxiv-2606-31557:
Agarwal and colleagues build a knowledge graph that links software vulnerabilities to the attack behaviours they enable. CVE and NVD records describe flaws in technical depth but rarely say which tactics and techniques from the MITRE ATT&CK framework an attacker would use. Without that link, defenders struggle to read a flaw's real threat.

Transformer models classify each CVE by behaviour and extract the entities and relations that fill the graph. CySecBERT leads on behaviour labels, with strong macro scores on both techniques and tactics, and the team release an annotated dataset of tens of thousands of entities and relations. A pipeline extractor beats a joint span-based model on both tasks. The graph lives in Neo4j, giving analysts a structured, visual map from flaw to behaviour.
arxiv-2606-31657:
Yoshida and Zhang connect two tools from theoretical computer science: locally testable codes and the sensitivity of algorithms. Sensitivity measures how far an output can move, counted in Hamming distance, when a single input element changes. Locally testable codes are error-correcting codes whose validity can be checked by probing only a few positions.

Their scheme turns any such code into a sensitivity lower bound for the constraint problem it encodes. With one strong code they show that near-optimal approximation for satisfiable Max E3LIN2 needs linear sensitivity, matching the trivial upper bound. Reductions extend the bounds to maximum clique and maximum coverage, and a simpler code handles Max Cut on bipartite graphs. Further results cover randomized algorithms and locality limits in distributed models.
arxiv-2606-31857:
Miller and Wu present an open-source tool that extracts freeway networks from OpenStreetMap for traffic simulation. Preparing such inputs is usually manual, corridor-specific work that resists reproduction. Existing converters target arterial streets or general networks, leaving freeway needs like ramps, lane drops and corridor continuity poorly served.

Their workflow converts map data into a compact, station-referenced form and supports validation against both the source data and aerial imagery. A local frontend lets analysts define corridor queries and inspect segments visually. Two prototype corridors took about one-third of the manual effort. Deployment then covered 359.6 miles of Orange County freeway, averaging roughly 41 seconds of processing and validation per mile.
arxiv-2608-00257:
Lucas and co-authors introduce MDWD, a street-level data set for municipal waste detection. Automated visual monitoring of cities is a growing research area. Waste detection lacks dedicated benchmark resources, though. Past sets target single litter items, aerial views, or whole-image labels. None join street-level images, instance locations, and waste categories in a municipal frame.

The Maltese Domestic Waste Dataset holds 3,697 high-resolution images. It carries 11,461 hand-annotated instances across five domestic waste classes. Those classes mirror Malta's municipal collection system. Images vary in location, lighting, scale, occlusion, and urban context. Benchmarks span YOLO generations and a transformer detector. RF-DETR-M led with 94.49 percent mAP50 on the test set. Smaller variants stayed competitive at far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2608-00457:
Wang and Zheng test an old conjecture in non-Kähler geometry on balanced Bismut torsion-parallel fourfolds. The conjecture links constant holomorphic sectional curvature to special metric types. Nonzero constant should force a Kähler metric; zero should force Chern flatness. Dimension two was settled by 1996. Higher dimensions were known only in special cases.

Balanced BTP threefolds were settled in prior work by Chen and Zheng. Classification tools from Zhao and Zheng powered that step. Here the conjecture is proven for all balanced BTP manifolds in complex dimension four. Classification is still lacking in dimension four and up, they note. Balanced BTP manifolds are highly restrictive despite that gap. The study may shed light on their four-dimensional structure.
baudelaire-fleurs-du-mal-1857:
Charles Baudelaire published Les Fleurs du mal in Paris in 1857, and the book remade French poetry. Its poems move between two poles he called Spleen and Ideal. Spleen is boredom, decay, and the weight of city life. The Ideal is a hunger for beauty, love, and escape. Baudelaire finds his subjects in crowds, wine, lovers, cats, and the Paris streets.

Readers meet famous pieces here, among them Hymn to Beauty, Exotic Perfume, La Chevelure, and Invitation to a Journey. Six poems were banned after an obscenity trial, and the full book stayed under a cloud for decades. Later poets, above all the Symbolists, treated Baudelaire as a founder of modern verse.
baudelaire-flowers-of-evil-1857:
Charles Baudelaire published The Flowers of Evil in 1857, his condemned masterpiece of spleen and ideal in verse. Many call the book the birth certificate of modern poetry in the judgment of poets since its trial. Baudelaire was fined and six poems banned for offenses against public morals in the Paris of 1857.

The poems move between Spleen, the city's rot and ennui, and Ideal, the reach for beauty beyond it. Lesbos, carrion, wine, and the voyage fill sections that map a soul at war with time and flesh. Baudelaire's form is classical and strict while his matter is modern, urban, and deliberately shocking to bourgeois taste. The banned poems and the trial made the book a banner for art's freedom ever since in France. Every modern poet, from Rimbaud to Eliot, works in a world this book remade.
boucher-antiquites-tome-2-1857:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes was a French customs man and a keen digger. His Antiquities celtiques et antediluviennes, Book Two, came out in French in 1857. The work deals with Celtic and pre-flood finds from the Somme gravel beds. Book One stands just past in the set.

Stone tools found with the bones of lost beasts fill his proof. Boucher held that men lived far past the age the books then gave them. Most sages of his day scoffed, then came round to his side. The set is a root work in the tale of man's deep past.
bronte-the-professor-1857:
Charlotte Brontë wrote The Professor first, and it saw print only in 1857, after her death. The posthumous novel is the seedbed of both Villette and Jane Eyre in her work. Publishers had turned it down nine times while she lived and sought a better fate.

William Crimsworth, a mill owner's son, quits trade and teaches at a Brussels boys' school. He loves Frances Henri, a lace mender and pupil-teacher of Swiss and English blood in Brussels. Jealous heads and a spying director test their modest courtship of work and study there. The pair wed, teach, and prosper in a close, unsentimental close of quiet industry. The plain style shows Brontë before the fire of Jane Eyre lit her prose.
brown-estimate-manners-principles-1757:
Brown's Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times, published in 1757, was the most talked-of book of its year in England. Britain had just suffered shocks in the war with France, and readers were ready for a harsh diagnosis. Brown, already known as a controversial clergyman-writer, gave them one.

He charged that England had sunk into luxury, selfishness, and fading religion, and that its ruling class had grown soft. Against that decay he set discipline, public spirit, and a return to serious principle. The book sold by the thousand and provoked answers, sequels, and parodies. It stands as the classic jeremiad of its century, an insider's scolding that tells historians exactly what anxious Britons feared about themselves in the 1750s.
buckle-civilization-england-vol-1-1857:
Henry Thomas Buckle published History of Civilization in England, Volume 1, in 1857. Buckle aimed to make history a science governed by laws. Climate, food, soil, and scenery, he argues, shape the character of nations. Statistics, he claims, show regular patterns even in crime and marriage.

The volume surveys France, Spain, Germany, and Scotland before turning to England. Buckle praises intellect and doubts the power of rulers and churches to drive progress. The book was a sensation and drew fierce attacks. Its positivist program now looks overbold. Yet it changed how Victorians thought history could be written. Volume 2 never matched the first's impact.
cia-0000009857:
A cave on the Houei Vong, where American pilots were held, is located relative to Ban Kang Muong in an April 1967 item. Ban Kang Muong sits in the Laotian panhandle, near trail country. Caves in the limestone hills served the war as depots, shelters, and cells.

Locating a prison cave by its nearest village gave airmen and planners a usable point. Such sites were nearly invisible from the air and hard to reach on foot. The men inside lived cut off in a way few camp prisoners were. This item fixes one cave prison on the map of Laos's hidden war.
cia-0000012257:
Some files hold secrets; others hold the paperwork that organized them day by day. An undated CIA document, its publication year estimated as 1960, lists titles of articles together with the report numbers of a numbered series of issues. Nothing in the sheet explains the pieces it names.

The list names pieces rather than printing them, so its value lies in what it maps. It shows how the agency catalogued its own reporting, issue by issue and title by title. For readers, the fragment is a reminder that intelligence files contain the plain indexes and inventories of a working bureaucracy.
cia-0000015257: Argentine authorities reported a satellite down in Bolivia, in a CIA file dated April 1, 1978. A fallen object near a border set off checks on both sides. Space junk and lost craft fell often in those years. The file holds the first word on a fall that later reports would sort out.
cia-0000022157: Survivors of a C-46 crash were in apparent good condition, and Pathet Lao plans for them are covered in a CIA record dated in 1963. The C-46 was a large transport plane of older design. A crash in Laos left its crew in the hands of the Pathet Lao. Good condition was rare good news in a file full of loss.
cia-0000022357: TASS said Powers could face death, and his case was referred to the Russian Supreme Court, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. TASS was the Soviet state news agency, speaking with official weight. A death threat raised the stakes before the trial even opened. The referral note shows the case moving through the highest Soviet court channels that summer.
cia-0000036557: Photo comparisons for MIA and POW cases 10,147 through 10,158 are the subject of a CIA record dated February 3, 1969, and the case names are blank in the released copy. Analysts compared photographs side by side, hunting for a match that could name a prisoner. A numbered batch like this one shows how large the caseload had grown, and each case stood for a family waiting on an answer.
cia-0000037157:
The burial site of an American military officer near Hong Ho, in Binh Tri Thien province, fills a CIA record dated June 1, 1963. The date is early: American advisers, not armies, were then serving in Vietnam. An officer's grave in 1963 belongs to the war's small and quiet beginning.

The record marks where the officer was said to be buried. Early losses like this one were few enough that each grave was noted on its own. The file shows that the careful accounting of American dead in Vietnam began long before the big battles, with single names and single graves in far provinces.
cia-0000045257:
A prisoner tied to the Duarte kidnapping was pardoned, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A pardon is a formal act of mercy by the state. In a kidnapping case, mercy is rarely separate from bargaining.

Inside, the clemency granted to the prisoner is placed on record. Pardons in such cases are usually part of a larger quiet deal. They free one person as the price of freeing another person. The law's clean language of pardon hid a trade that everyone involved understood at once. The file holds that price in its official form, a legal act on paper that carried, behind it, the whole weight of the crisis.
cia-0000049057: An allegation by the chief of ARENA, El Salvador's hard-right party, fills a CIA item from 1983. The charge touches the paramilitary world that surrounded the party in the war years. ARENA's words and the death squads' deeds were the two halves of the right that Washington had to judge.
cia-0000049257:
The FMLN after its November 1989 offensive is sized up in a CIA paper from 1990, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. The offensive had carried guerrilla fighters into the capital's wealthiest neighborhoods and proved the war could not be won by either side. The paper asks what the front looked like after its greatest effort.

Inside, the movement is weighed after battle: its strength spent or saved, its politics hardened or softened, its appetite for talks. The answers mattered because the war's endgame began with that offensive, at the negotiating table it forced into being. The paper catches the rebels at the turn from war toward peace.
cia-0000049357: Investigations into the murders of six U.S. citizens and a disappearance are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049357, dated September 5, 1982. The heading, cut short in the catalog, frames the file around official inquiries. Readers find a dated agency item about those investigations, kept as a brief record rather than a full account of the cases themselves.
cia-0000075857: Monitoring the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075857, dated February 1, 1991, subtitled Looking for a Needle in a Haystack. The paper frames treaty monitoring as a hard search problem. Its vivid subtitle is the record's most memorable feature, preserved in a short declassified item on weapons treaty oversight.
cia-0000096657: Current Developments in Chinese Communist Agriculture, with Chinese misspelled in the heading, is declassified CIA document 0000096657, dated July 4, 1968. The title promises a farm-sector update from China. Readers find a short declassified agriculture paper whose spelling flaw is preserved in the catalog, a companion in subject to the earlier rice crop report.
cia-0000108157: National Intelligence Estimate Probable Developments in Indonesia is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108157, dated May 3, 1958. The title marks a formal estimate on where Indonesia was likely heading. Probable developments is the estimate phrase in the heading itself. The brief record is a country outlook item, filed in the spring of 1958 as released in the files.
cia-0000109057: Cuban Subversive Activities in Latin America: 1959-1968 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109057, dated January 5, 1968. The heading sets its own span, nine years of Cuban activity across Latin America. Subversive is the title's own word for the activity it tracks. The brief record is a decade survey item, filed at the start of 1968 as released.
cia-0000126957: A November 1965 CIA report gives the short-term political prospects in Panama. The canal made every turn in Panamanian politics Washington's business, and the country's affairs ran through the Canal Zone. The paper forecasts the political weather ahead for that small, watched state. Canal politics gave every Panamanian election an American echo, and short-term forecasts like this one served officials who managed the zone and its treaty questions.
cia-0000132757: Plans by the Cuban government to draw President Eisenhower further in fill a CIA item dated May 5, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the name Eisenho, short for the president. Havana was pulling the American leader into its public campaign that spring. Each clash gave Castro fresh material for speeches at home. The short item reports the plans as analysts heard them.
cia-0000135857: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 6 January 1954, long since declassified, on cable traffic for PBSUCCESS being compromised. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136157: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 5 April 1954, covers team themes for KUGOWN, the talking points handed to the propaganda teams in the field. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136257: The record dated 6 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a possible need for bomb support to swing the army, bombing meant to break its loyalty. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136857: Headquarters does not concur with a LINCOLN recommendation in this 1954 cable, because of the Caracas conference. If the source called LIONIZER goes out on a limb and the conference flops, he will be completely discredited hemisphere-wide as a trustworthy source and become only a joke. Instead, headquarters suggests he denounce current Guatemalan-Moscow status, plead for positive action by delegates, and send letters to former Latin American contacts. The cable protects a propaganda voice by keeping his predictions safe.
cia-0000136957: The Secretary of State's morning statement is relayed in this May 1954 cable. It went to the Guatemala City station, with orders to exploit it. He said most Guatemalans want the communists cleaned out. But they face intense communist terrorism, he said. He noted reports of an army ultimatum to Arbenz. He named no sources for those reports. He neither confirmed nor denied a foreign ministers' conference. The station should invite attention to the statement. It would validate the station's own guidance.
cia-0000137457: Filed in Spanish in 1961, document 0000137457 is one of the papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force trained by the CIA for the Bay of Pigs landing that April. The record gives no subject line beyond the brigade file it sits in, so its contents should not be guessed at. It survives as a declassified page of that operation's archive, released through the CIA Reading Room, in the language most of the brigade's own paperwork used.
cia-03000957:
Egypt dominates the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 23 September 1955. The lead item reports a five-year open agreement, signed on 21 September, for Soviet military equipment. The first order listed is large: 200 jet aircraft, 100 heavy tanks, torpedo boats, and two submarines. The price is put at about 85 million dollars, payable in Egyptian exports. Soviet technicians would stay three months to help assemble aircraft.

The comment judges that Egyptians would need far longer to learn to fly and maintain the planes. It also flags a break in Soviet practice, since arms had gone only to bloc countries before. Other items cover Tokyo dropping a bar to recognising the USSR. A crisis in Greek-American relations, Yugoslav pledges to Greece, and Icelandic opinion on bases follow.
cia-03179157:
Poland opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 23 October 1956. Rallies across the country back Gomulka after his reported defiance of the Kremlin. Youth groups lead them, demanding the ouster of pro-Soviet officials. A Warsaw military academy rally stresses unity of soldiers, workers, and nation. Yet the party paper reaffirms the Soviet alliance as policy's cornerstone, and a Krakow rally's anti-Soviet turn was defeated.

Communist reaction to the Polish developments follows. East Germany stands ready to meet resistance with force. French forces seize five Algerian rebel leaders, flown out after their aircraft was diverted. The arrests, the bulletin notes, leave the internal resistance leadership untouched. Jordan's lower house elections are reported. A new military junta is possible in Honduras. Philippine courts release forty-three Huks. The Arab-Israeli situation closes the issue.
cia-06218657:
Statement of work with addendum, again titled for the Pyramid support contract, is dated 15 May 2007. This version runs to 97 pages, against 84 in the plainer copy held nearby. Contract and request numbers are both shown as 2007*G0063. The work covers professional administrative support services for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Contents match the shorter version at the front, with purpose, scope, security, and program rules. Added material deepens the service descriptions in the later pages. A training support section near the middle lists orientation for new customers at new employee orientation, and product familiarization training. It also lists seminars and workshops, computer-based and web-based training modules, quick reference guides, and a duty to carry a pager at all times.
cia-06626857:
Confidential cable number 7157 from the American embassy in Buenos Aires, dated 12 September 1978, reports a setback expected in the Timerman case. The subject line states the motion was expected to be turned down by the lower court. The embassy cites its earlier cable 7042 on the same matter.

Hector Timerman, son of the former La Opinion editor, told the embassy that day that his father's lawyer had learned the Court of First Instance would reject the request. The request asked for release under the Argentine Supreme Court decision of July 20. Hector said the case would go at once to the Court of Appeals, and to the Supreme Court if needed. An attached Spanish court filing follows, presenting a habeas corpus case for Jacobo Timerman before a federal judge.
cia-06954157:
Portuguese Guinea Handbook, number 0627 and marked Secret with No Foreign Dissem, surveys the territory in sections dated November 1972. Its contents open with geography, then an economic background covering government policy, labor, and the structure of the economy. Transport, telecommunications, and foreign aid follow in the same part.

The geography section states Portuguese Guinea, also known as Guinea-Bissau, was a Portuguese overseas province wedged between Senegal and the Republic of Guinea. Its area was about 14,000 square miles, almost twice the size of New Jersey, the handbook states. Much of it is low coastal plain with swamps, cut by rivers. A later passage states final authority rested with the governor, who answered to Lisbon. General Spinola had allowed yearly peoples' congresses, an expanded form of the village council, to sound out African views, it reports.
copyright-renewals-1957: Copyright Renewals 1957, issued by the Library of Congress Copyright Office, survives in this copy only as a placeholder note. The file states plainly that it is an unused, empty reservation, kept for an ebook in the United States Copyright Renewals series. The renewal records for 1957 were placed instead in two companion files, one covering January to June and one covering July to December. No entries, names, or listings appear here at all. A reader seeking the actual 1957 renewals must use those two companion volumes.
davis-magic-staff-1857:
Andrew Jackson Davis tells his own strange life in The Magic Staff, his life tale of 1857. Davis rose from a poor youth with scant school to the chief seer of his land. Sickly and keen, he fell in trance states as a boy. In them he claimed to learn the lore that made his famed books of creed and worlds.

Ward tales, trek tales, and the birth of his gifts fill the prose. He writes with zeal and a touch of pride. The book is the chief source on the man back of the faith's first texts. It grips as tale as well.
der-chymischen-wahrsagers-vertheidigung-:
A German defence of a chemical soothsayer fills this book of 1757 by D. D. Becker, a doctor of medicine. Its target is a review in the Erfurt learned news, which Becker calls partisan. He goes through that review word by word and answers it at length.

Many weighty alchemical claims are set out and explained along the way. One passage tells how the tender red parts of the earth cling to salts in a solution. When such a liquor is dried down, he says, it gives a reddish saltpetre. The scan is rough and the type is old, yet the fight can be followed. The book shows how sharp, and how public, chemical quarrels in print could be.
dumas-companions-of-jehu-1857:
Alexandre Dumas published The Companions of Jehu in 1857, a romance of the French Directory years. The tale follows the royalist Companions of Jehu, highwaymen who robbed state gold for their cause. Secret societies, duels, and Napoleon's rise frame this late and vigorous Dumas historical romance in France.

Roland de Montrevel, a dashing aide to Bonaparte, hunts the Companions across the wild Bresse country. Their chief, Morgan, proves to be Roland's own friend and his sister's secret husband in hiding. Stagecoach raids fund a royalist rising while Bonaparte crushes foes in Italy and Egypt abroad then. The guillotine and the battlefield thin both camps as the Consulate dawns on France victorious. Dumas keeps sympathy divided, a mark of his mature and fairer historical art.
dumas-the-wolf-leader-1857:
Alexandre Dumas gives the wolf tale his grand sweep in The Wolf-Leader, in English from 1904, first told in 1857. Thibault, a poor shoe hand, makes a pact with a great black wolf in the woods. Each wish he spends costs a hair of his head and a step of his soul. Wealth and rank come, and so does the hunt that must end his wild run at last.

Dumas spins the lore of the loup-garou with his famed zest. The tale is part folk yarn, part doom tract. It shows a master at play with dark stuff. Its pace still grips.
europmc-pmc10131557:
Solier and a large team identify a copper-based signaling pathway that drives inflammation and can be targeted by drugs, in a 2023 study. Inflammation defends the body against harm, but in excess it fuels diseases from sepsis to cancer. The team searched for fresh control points in this ancient system.

They found that copper inside certain immune cells helps switch on inflammatory programs. Blocking that copper signal calmed inflammation in their tests. The work names a new drug target in a pathway doctors have long wanted to control more precisely.
europmc-pmc10132957:
Ebrahimi and Samanta review how protein-based drugs are engineered through structural and chemical design, in a 2023 paper. Protein drugs have changed the treatment of cancer, diabetes, and immune disease. The authors note that proteins were set to make up half of the top-selling drugs of the year.

The review explains how scientists reshape proteins to bind better, last longer, and cause fewer side effects. It covers design guided by three-dimensional structure and by chemical tweaks. The paper shows how careful engineering turns natural proteins into precise medicines. It closes with open challenges in the field.
europmc-pmc10287557:
Okuzumi and a large team report that seeds of alpha-synuclein protein in blood serum can serve as markers for a family of brain diseases, in a 2023 study. These diseases, called synucleinopathies, include Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. In each, alpha-synuclein folds wrongly and spreads through the brain in a seed-like way.
