In patients with severe kidney failure, a link to a scarring disease, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, forced tighter practice near a decade before. Newer reports then found gadolinium stored in bone, brain, and kidney even without kidney failure.

What that storage does stays largely unknown, since clinical data on harm routes are thin. The review gathers known and proposed harm mechanisms and calls for cohort studies and lab work. Wide use plus stored metal adds up to a safety question that deserves a firm answer.
europmc-pmc4908757:
Jonathan Cairns and co-authors released CHiCAGO in Genome Biology in 2016, a tool for finding true DNA loops in Capture Hi-C data. Capture Hi-C maps which DNA regions touch each other, focusing on spots such as gene promoters, at high detail. Spotting real loops in the noisy data poses statistical traps unlike plain Hi-C.

CHiCAGO models the background noise of the method and adjusts scaling and repeated testing to match. On test data it recovers known promoter loops with fewer false calls. The open package gives genome labs a sturdy caller for contact maps, which trace how folding brings far genes and their switches together inside the nucleus.
europmc-pmc4914657:
Patrick McGann and co-authors reported in 2016 the first find of the mcr-1 colistin resistance gene in the United States, in a letter in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. Colistin is a last-line drug, and mcr-1 rides on plasmids that jump between bacteria, first seen in China. From May 2016, a Walter Reed military lab tested resistant E. coli isolates for it.

One isolate from a Pennsylvania clinic patient, who reported no recent travel, carried mcr-1 on a novel large plasmid of about 226,000 letters. The same plasmid held seven more resistance genes, including a broad beta-lactam breaker. Twenty further isolates tested negative. Plasmids of this family spread resistance widely, so the team urges steady national watch.
europmc-pmc4979357:
Sarah L. Stevens and six co-authors review whether blood pressure variability, beyond average pressure, predicts cardiovascular disease and death. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in The BMJ in 2016. High average pressure is a proven risk. Whether swings around that average add risk was less clear. The team searched four databases to February 2016 for cohort studies and trials in adults that tied variability to later events.

Forty-one papers, covering dozens of cohort and trial analyses, qualified. Long term variability, measured across clinic visits, linked to cardiovascular events and death even after average pressure was counted. Home and ambulatory variability also linked to all cause mortality. Their link to cardiovascular events was less settled. The authors say variability deserves a place in risk thinking. They call for fresh cohorts to firm up the shorter term measures.
europmc-pmc4992257:
Brian W. Rotenberg, Dorian Murariu, and Kenny P. Pang ask whether CPAP adherence has improved over twenty years. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery in 2016. CPAP, a bedside air pressure mask, is the gold standard therapy for obstructive sleep apnea. Many patients abandon it, though, and many fixes have been proposed. The team searched major databases for adherence data from 1994 to 2015.

Eighty-two papers qualified. The pooled non-adherence rate, judged against seven hours of sleep a night, was just over a third of patients. The rate did not improve significantly across the two decades. Coaching and behavioral support helped somewhat, but machine and mask redesigns did not move the total. The authors call the flat curve sobering. They question whether CPAP still deserves gold standard status and offer their dataset for guideline writers.
europmc-pmc5005757:
Hideo Masuki and nine co-authors compare blood-based healing materials in the International Journal of Implant Dentistry in 2016. Dentists and surgeons use platelet-rich plasma and related products to aid wound healing and tissue regrowth. The study tested four products made from the same donor blood: the plasma itself, two fibrin forms, and concentrated growth factors.

The team counted platelets and white cells and measured three growth factors and two swelling signals in each product. The two newer fibrin forms held platelet and growth factor levels as high as, or higher than, the plasma product. Their extracts also made human periosteal cells, taken from the membrane around bone, grow faster in a dish, even at high doses. The results support these fibrin forms as both a scaffold and a store of healing signals for implant work.
europmc-pmc5031557:
Natalie R. Johnston and a broad team of co-authors report in Cell Metabolism in 2016 that a few special beta cells lead the insulin response. Beta cells sit in pancreatic islets and release insulin in rhythm when sugar rises. A leading role for a few cells was long suspected but never directly shown. The team mapped activity across whole islets and then used light-based tools to silence or trigger chosen cells.

The maps revealed hub cells with pacemaker traits that stayed in place for hours. Silencing hubs broke the islet's coordinated answer to glucose, while waking them restored the shared pattern. Hubs were tuned by their metabolism, and both inflammation and a fat-and-sugar assault hit them first, spreading failure across the islet. The finding recasts the islet as a network run by a few leaders, whose loss may help set off type 2 diabetes.
europmc-pmc5064957:
Charles L. Francoeur and Stephan A. Mayer review delayed cerebral ischemia after a burst brain aneurysm, in Critical Care in 2016. Patients who survive the first bleed face a second threat days later, when brain tissue starves from poor blood flow. It is a top cause of death and lasting harm in this group. Care once blamed wide artery spasm alone, and the review explains the wider picture now accepted.

Early brain injury, failing microcirculation, lost pressure control, and waves of abnormal cell activity all contribute. Prevention rests on the drug nimodipine plus careful blood volume and heart support. Watching for the complication combines repeated exams with ultrasound and CT scans in alert patients, and adds continuous brain monitoring in those in coma. First treatment raises blood pressure and volume, reversing the deficit in about seventy percent of patients; stubborn cases escalate to balloon widening of arteries and output support.
europmc-pmc5097157:
Taylor W. Schmitz and R. Nathan Spreng, working with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, published a brain imaging study in Nature Communications in 2016. They asked where Alzheimer's disease begins: in the basal forebrain, a small region that supplies the rest of the brain, or in the entorhinal cortex, the more widely favored starting point.

Tracking brain volume over time in older adults, from healthy to ill, they found that shrinkage in the basal forebrain predicted later shrinkage in the entorhinal cortex, not the reverse. In healthy adults whose scans showed an amyloid marker of early disease, only the basal forebrain was already shrinking. Both regions were affected once mild memory loss appeared, which places the basal forebrain first in line.
europmc-pmc5153657:
Hannah Gruner, Mariela Cortés-López, Daphne A. Cooper, Matthew Bauer, and Pedro Miura tracked circular RNAs in aging mouse brains in Scientific Reports in 2016. Cortés-López leads with her first surname, as Spanish naming prints two. Circular RNAs are stable RNA loops, plentiful in nerve tissue, whose jobs are still mysterious.

Profiling RNA from young and old mouse cortex, hippocampus, and heart, they confidently found 6,791 distinct circular RNAs, including 675 new ones. In brain samples the loops strongly piled up with age, a trend confirmed for individual loops by two further methods, while hearts showed no such pattern. The build-up ran largely independent of the parent genes' ordinary RNA levels. The authors suggest these accumulating loops may take part in how the nervous system ages.
europmc-pmc5197557:
B. M. Das Gupta, at the Calcutta School of Tropical Medicine, identifies the parasite behind "dermal leishmanoid." The condition, first described by Brahmachari in 1922, follows treated kala-azar. Months or years after recovery, pale spots spread over the face, forearms, and trunk, then soft non-ulcerating lumps form. Three or four such cases arrived at the school's skin clinic each month. Smears from the lesions teemed with leishmania, and cultures grew the flagellate form.

Yet blood cultures stayed negative, and spleen samples, when the organ could be reached, showed nothing. The infection seemed confined to the skin. Das Gupta weighs whether the parasite is Leishmania donovani or Leishmania tropica. The tie to kala-azar, the spread of the lesions, and their non-ulcerating character all point, he argues, to L. donovani. His note is an early attempt to place post-kala-azar dermal disease on firm parasitological ground.
europmc-pmc5210557:
Anna Gaulton and colleagues updated the ChEMBL database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. ChEMBL is an open, large-scale store of bioactivity data: records of how chemical compounds act on biological targets, drawn mainly from the medicinal chemistry literature. Such data help researchers find tool compounds, read structure-activity patterns, and spot possible off-target effects.

New sources added since the earlier reports include screening sets for neglected diseases, crop protection data, drug metabolism and disposition data, and bioactivity drawn from patents. Assays and targets are now labeled with standard vocabularies, and targets and uses for clinical candidates are included. The records also carry metabolic pathways for drugs and warnings about risky chemical features. Access runs through a web interface, downloads, and web services, keeping the whole collection open to working chemists.
europmc-pmc5273857:
Maarten van Iterson, Erik W. van Zwet, and Bastiaan T. Heijmans, with the BIOS Consortium, tackled hidden bias in genome-scale association studies in Genome Biology in 2017. Studies that test hundreds of thousands of DNA methylation marks, or tens of thousands of gene activity levels, against a trait can produce swollen test statistics, so false hits slip in. Tools borrowed from gene-variant studies, and even the best confounder adjustments, do not fully clear the distortion.

The team proposes a Bayesian method that estimates the true no-effect distribution of the statistics straight from the data, then judges each result against it. In simulations and real data the method kept false positives at the promised rate while holding on to more real findings than the standard genomic control approach, which overcorrects and wastes power. The authors demonstrate it on large combined analyses of aging and smoking.
europmc-pmc5302657:
David M. Greig, conservator of the Royal College of Surgeons' Museum in Edinburgh, described oxycephaly in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1926, in a paper continued from an earlier page. The condition fuses the skull's sutures too soon, forcing the growing brain to push the vault upward into a tower shape. This installment turns to the face, where fusion is universal.

The forehead stands flat and vertical, the eye sockets are shallow because the growing brain presses the thin orbital bones outward, and the upper jaw is underdeveloped and lacks air sinuses. The palate, fused early and unable to widen, stays narrow and deep, squeezing the nasal cavity so the septum bends sideways. Oxycephalic children breathe through the mouth, which further starves the sinuses. Greig stresses that these facial faults follow mechanically from the premature fusion, and closes by resisting loose claims linking such skulls to a supposed criminal type.
europmc-pmc5367557:
Roland R. Griffiths and co-authors ran a twin trial of psilocybin in cancer patients, in the Journal of Psychopharmacology in 2016. The question matched a sister study: can one strong dose lift the depression and anxiety that shadow a life-threatening diagnosis? Their design set a high dose against a dose so low it acted like a dummy pill, with the order swapped between two sittings.

Fifty-one patients took part, with five weeks between sittings and checks for half a year. The high dose brought large drops in both doctor-scored and self-scored depression and anxiety. Life quality, sense of meaning, and hope rose, while dread of death fell. At six months, about four in five patients still showed clear gains. Most tied their brighter view of life, self, ties, and spirit to the high-dose day.
europmc-pmc5379057:
Shuo Xiao led a large team that built a chip model of the female cycle in Nature Communications in 2017. Hormone loops run the female reproductive tract on a twenty-eight day beat, but no lab culture had yet kept that beat live. Their chip links tiny organ units by a shared flow, like blood in the body. Mouse ovary tissue sits as the hormone source at its heart.

The ovary units made the full human hormone wave of a month-long cycle. That wave then drove human tissue units for the fallopian tube, womb, cervix, and liver, singly or in sets of two and five. The full set, named EVATAR, held the hormone loops of the cycle and of a pregnancy-like state in tune. The team sees the rig as a fresh stage for drug finds and safety tests, free of live animal trials.
europmc-pmc5388857:
The GBD 2015 DALYs and HALE Collaborators report world health totals in a 2016 paper in The Lancet. They use two summary measures. One counts years of life lost plus years lived with disability, giving a single burden score per disease. The other counts the years a person can expect to live in full health. Scores were built for 315 diseases and injuries across 195 countries from 1990 to 2015.

Total burden barely moved across those years. Falls in infections, newborn and mother deaths, and poor nutrition were offset by rises in long-term diseases of aging populations. Age-adjusted rates fell for most causes, though rates rose or held flat for ills such as joint wear, depression, and diabetes. The team ties the shift to growth and development levels.
europmc-pmc5399157:
Claire N. Harrison leads a large author group in a 2016 paper in Leukemia with the final long-term results of the COMFORT-II trial. The trial tested ruxolitinib, a drug that blocks the JAK signals, against the best care then on hand for myelofibrosis. That disease scars the bone marrow and swells the spleen. Patients on standard care could switch to the drug once their disease grew worse.

By the trial's main check, more than a quarter of drug patients had large spleen shrinkage, against none on standard care. Over half of drug patients reached that mark at some point, and shrinkage often held for years. Death risk ran about a third lower on the drug, with no new safety worries over long use. The authors say gains held with continued treatment.
europmc-pmc5405057:
Leib Litman, Jonathan Robinson, and Tzvi Abberbock describe an online research platform called TurkPrime in a 2017 paper in Behavior Research Methods. Amazon's Mechanical Turk lets scientists gather behavior data fast from paid online workers, but it was built for business tasks, not research. Many study needs, such as barring past takers or running studies over time, are slow or hard to set up there.

TurkPrime sits on top of that worker pool and adds the missing research tools. It can screen out past takers, track dropouts, send group emails and bonuses, change a running study, and speed approvals. The authors say these tools save time, lift data quality, and allow study designs that were near impossible before. The platform is free for researchers to use.
europmc-pmc5415757:
Liu and co-authors review how the protein p62 links two cell cleanup systems. Their review appeared in Cellular and Molecular Biology Letters. Cells must clear old, damaged, and misfolded proteins to stay alive. One system, the proteasome, breaks down tagged proteins one by one. The other, autophagy, removes larger loads in bulk.

The review explains how p62 shuttles tagged proteins to both systems. It also covers p62 links to stress signals and to HDAC6, an enzyme that aids bulk cleanup. When p62 levels rise or fall, tagged proteins build up or shift place. The authors note that such faults can harm cells and feed disease.
europmc-pmc5435757:
Zhang and co-authors review a cancer therapy built from a ready-made killer cell line. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Natural killer cells attack stressed and cancerous cells fast. A lab line called NK-92 can be grown without donors. Early trials showed that irradiated NK-92 infusions are safe. Some patients responded. The cells can also be fitted with chimeric antigen receptors. Those receptors steer them to chosen tumor targets.

The receptor bypasses signals that normally hold NK cells back. It also beats tumor resistance to natural killing. Unlike donor cells, engineered lines come from single tested clones. They can be made under strict drug-grade rules. In lab and animal tests, targeted NK-92 cells killed blood cancers and solid tumors. In mouse models, treatment sparked the animals' own immunity. Cured mice resisted later tumor challenges. The authors highlight HER2-targeted cells nearing clinical use.
europmc-pmc5454457:
Antaris and co-authors build a record-bright molecular dye for imaging in the second near-infrared window. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. That window spans 1,000 to 1,700 nanometers. Light there scatters less inside tissue. Deep anatomy shows with striking clarity. Organic dyes for the window glow too dimly, though. Low quantum yield forces long exposures. Video-rate imaging stayed out of reach.

The team paired a sulfonated dye with protein complexes. The dye is called CH-4T. Assembly boosted fluorescence about 110-fold. The result set a quantum yield record for molecular fluorophores. Exposure times fell roughly fiftyfold. Imaging ran at 50 frames per second. That speed resolved mouse cardiac cycles. The complex also beat a clinical standard. It outperformed approved ICG dye for lymph node imaging. The nodes sat deep within the mouse body.
europmc-pmc5472757:
Vanpouille-Box and co-authors report a cancer study in Nature Communications. They ask how radiation helps the immune system attack tumors. Radiation can free DNA inside cancer cells and trigger an alarm signal. That signal may prime T cells against the tumor. But the right dose and schedule were unclear.

The authors find that high single doses switch on an enzyme called Trex1. Trex1 breaks down the loose DNA and mutes the alarm. Smaller repeated doses stay below that switch point, they report. Those doses boost interferon signals and draw in dendritic cells. In mice, that pairing helped immune drugs reject tumors. Dose choice may shape patient care.
europmc-pmc5541357:
Franke and co-authors describe version 2.8 of the ATSAS software suite in the Journal of Applied Crystallography. Small-angle scattering reveals the shapes of proteins and particles in solution. The raw curves need heavy processing before they mean anything. ATSAS is the field's long-running analysis package.

The article sums up changes across versions 2.5 to 2.8. The suite displays, processes, and models both X-ray and neutron scattering data. It can blend scattering results with structures from crystallography or electron microscopy. First released in 2003, it keeps pace with robotic sample changers and coupled chromatography setups. Better reporting and validation tools answer rising quality demands. Readers get a guided tour of what the updated suite can do.
europmc-pmc5543157:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. Their subject is flat optical devices called metasurfaces. Such devices bend and focus light, but colors usually focus at different points. That color blur is called chromatic aberration.

The team offers a design rule to remove that blur over a wide band. Their test devices work from 1200 to 1680 nanometers. One metalens focused each wavelength on the same plane. Another surface bent wide-band light by the same angle. Efficiency was near 12 percent for the lens. Readers see how full-color flat lenses and imagers could become practical.
europmc-pmc5570257:
Bertelli and co-authors present a software update in Nucleic Acids Research. IslandViewer predicts genomic islands in bacterial and archaeal genomes. Those islands are gene clusters gained from other microbes. They often carry traits for virulence, drug resistance, or survival in a niche.

Version 4 is built for larger-scale work. A new account system and an HTTP interface allow batch submissions. Prediction methods were updated and expanded. Ready-made results now cover 6,193 complete strains, with virulence and resistance notes included. The visual display also grew more flexible. Readers get a guide to a key tool for tracking how microbes evolve and adapt.
europmc-pmc5572357:
Yang and co-authors review oxidative stress in atherosclerosis in Frontiers in Physiology. Atherosclerosis builds fatty plaques in artery walls. Plaque rupture can cause heart attack and stroke. Oxidative stress is widely seen as a core driver of plaque growth.

That stress arises when reactive oxygen species outrun the body's defenses. It can damage proteins, fats, and DNA in vessel cells. It can also trigger cell death signals. The review traces five routes that feed it: inflammation, mitochondria, autophagy, cell death, and epigenetic change. Treatments that fight oxidative stress are also covered. Readers get a broad map of one major theory of artery disease.
europmc-pmc5683757:
Shin and co-authors report a brain study in eLife. It rethinks beta rhythms as brief events, not steady waves. Beta activity is a strong signature of brain function. Averaged beta power predicts perception, attention, and movement. In raw signals, beta appears as short high-power bursts. The team asked what drives the averaged differences. Human brain scans came from detection and attention tasks. Mouse field recordings came from a similar touch task.

Averaged power gaps traced back to event counts. Trials differed in how many beta events occurred. Events landing near a stimulus made detection worse. Fewer pre-stimulus events predicted better touch detection. Attention lowered event rates in the attended region. More beta events meant weaker signal flow, they argue.
europmc-pmc5687757:
Xu and co-authors review the worldwide spread of scrub typhus. Their review covers a mite-borne disease found mostly in the Asia-Pacific region. The disease is caused by a bacterium called Orientia tsutsugamushi. It puts one billion people at risk and sickens about one million each year.

Without proper treatment, the disease can cause organ failure and death. The review pulls together scattered data on where the disease occurs. It also covers prevention and control in old endemic areas and new ones. Wide strain variety blocks lasting immunity, so people can catch it again. The authors stress how much about this neglected disease is still unknown.
europmc-pmc5698557:
Nguyen and co-authors report a cell study in mBio. It shows how bacterial viruses cross into the body. Bacteriophages are the most numerous entities inside us. They turn up in blood, lymph, and organs too. How they pass epithelial layers was unknown until now. The team grew cell layers from gut, lung, and liver. Kidney and brain cell layers were also tested. Diverse phages were applied to one side.

Phages crossed the layers fast and directionally. Movement favored the apical-to-basolateral direction strongly. Crossing began within ten minutes of contact. Only a small share of applied phages made it over. Microscopy placed phages inside cell compartments en route. Traffic seemed to pass through the Golgi apparatus.
europmc-pmc5742157:
Liu and co-authors review bacteria that live inside plant tissue without causing disease. Such endophytes are screened by roots from the soil around them. Root communities end up heavy in Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria. The review sums up which traits help bacteria settle inside a plant.

Movement, cell wall breaking tools, and defense against reactive oxygen all help entry. Once inside, the bacteria can fetch nutrients and fix nitrogen for the host. Some prime the plant to fight later attacks faster. The authors see these microbes as a route to better crops with less chemical input.
europmc-pmc5788257:
Guna and co-authors show that a cell complex, the EMC, inserts tail anchored proteins into membranes. Known insertion paths fail on such proteins when their anchor is only mildly water hating. Those proteins wait in the cytosol, shielded by calmodulin. Release lets them sample the endoplasmic reticulum surface.

There, the EMC proves essential for fast, clean insertion in cells and test tubes, they report. Purified EMC in fake membranes inserted its substrates alone. The work names the EMC a true insertase. That role may explain its wide effects on membrane linked traits across species.
europmc-pmc5852357:
Zhao and co-authors trace a three-link RNA chain that drives breast cancer growth. Their study appeared in Cancer Medicine. The long noncoding RNA HOTAIR runs high in breast tumors. Silencing it slowed cell growth and invasion in the lab.

HOTAIR works by sponging up a microRNA, miR-20a-5p. Freed from that brake, the gene HMGA2 pushes cells to multiply and spread. Restoring the microRNA reversed the cancer cells' behavior. Mouse xenografts confirmed the chain operates in living tumors. Breaking any link of the axis could become a therapy.
europmc-pmc5855557:
Liu and co-authors review lignin, a key polymer in plant cell walls. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lignin gives walls strength and helps plants move water. It also helps plants resist pests, disease, and lodging. The review sets out how plants build lignin step by step. Monomers form in the cell, move outward, and then join into chains.

The authors cover how gene changes alter lignin content and makeup. They sum up lignin's roles in growth and stress defence. They also note uses in energy and drug fields. Changing lignin can help crops and energy plants perform better. Readers get both the chemistry and the plant biology in one survey.
europmc-pmc5879757:
Okumura and Takeda review how mucosal barriers keep the gut in balance. Their article appeared in Inflammation and Regeneration. Trillions of microbes live in the human intestine. They aid nutrition, metabolism, and immunity. A barrier of gut lining cells keeps them at a safe distance. The review explains how that barrier holds homeostasis. It sorts barriers into chemical and physical kinds.

Chemical barriers include antimicrobial peptides that attack invaders. Physical barriers include mucus and tight cell junctions. Microbes and immune cells tune both layers with care. When the barrier fails, bacteria breach the gut wall. Excess immune response and inflammation can follow. Such failure feeds inflammatory bowel disease, they note.
europmc-pmc5885957:
Netsi and co-authors link persistent postnatal depression to child outcomes. Their study appeared in JAMA Psychiatry. The team followed 9,848 women with varied depression levels. Their 8,287 children were tracked into adolescence. Postnatal depression that stayed severe stood out sharply. Children of those mothers faced more behavioural problems by age 3.5. They also earned lower mathematics grades as teens. Depression in adolescence was more common in that group.

Women with persistent depression kept symptoms for years. Many still struggled eleven years after childbirth. The authors urge priority treatment for this group. Lasting maternal illness and child risk travel together here.
europmc-pmc5891557:
Terwee and co-authors present COSMIN methods for judging content validity. Their article appeared in Quality of Life Research. Content validity asks whether a questionnaire truly fits its target. It is the key property of patient-reported outcome measures. It is also the hardest property to assess well. The team set out to build shared standards for the task. An online Delphi study ran over four rounds.

Some 159 experts from 21 countries took part. They rated draft standards on five-point scales. Consensus of 67 percent was reached on all items. Ten criteria define good content validity in the final set. They cover relevance, coverage, and how well patients grasp items. A rating system sums up evidence for reviews.
europmc-pmc5897357:
Gräf and co-authors hunt rare variants behind heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. This rare lung vessel disease carries a poor outlook. Most family cases trace to faults in the BMPR2 pathway. Much heritability stayed missing, though. The team sequenced whole genomes of 1,038 index cases. They compared them with 6,385 controls without the disease.

Rare variants clustered in three genes more often in cases. Those genes were ATP13A3, AQP1, and SOX17. A key role for GDF2 was confirmed independently. Mutations in SOX17 and AQP1 tracked with disease in families. GDF2 faults cut protein release from test cells. The findings open fresh paths for therapy research.
europmc-pmc5897557:
Rosenblum and co-authors review progress and challenges in targeted cancer drug delivery. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Interest in targeted delivery has risen steeply for decades. Yet only 15 passive nanocarriers have won clinical approval. No actively targeted carrier has passed clinical trials. The review asks why translation keeps failing. Body barriers clear most carriers before they reach tumours.

Under one percent of passive carriers reach even leaky tumours. The liver's defence cells seize a large share en route. The authors propose criteria for new active targeting designs. Barriers at vessel walls and inside cells get close review. They close with directions for workable tumour targeting.
europmc-pmc5910057:
The GlobalSurg Collaborative tracked wound infections after gut operations across the world. Their cohort study appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. Data came from 12,539 patients at 343 hospitals in 66 countries. Each country was classed as high, middle, or low income. Cases covered both planned and urgent gut resections. The team counted infections within thirty days of surgery.

About one patient in eight developed such an infection, they report. Low-income countries bore far more cases than rich ones. Contaminated operations posed the greatest danger everywhere. Germs that resisted the preventive antibiotic were also commoner in poorer settings. Adjusted risk stayed highest for low-income patients. The authors call for prevention work aimed where need is greatest.
europmc-pmc5964457:
Freeman and co-authors review virtual reality in the assessment, understanding, and treatment of mental health disorders. Their systematic review appeared in Psychological Medicine. Virtual reality lets people face problem situations again and again. Therapists can then teach them how to cope. The authors surveyed the first twenty years of such work. They found 285 empirical studies in all.

Most studies treated anxiety, with 192 papers on it. Schizophrenia, substance use, and eating disorders followed. Study quality was generally low, the authors report. The firmest finding is that VR exposure treatments reduce anxiety. The term VR was often misused for flat, non-interactive tools.
europmc-pmc5979957:
Al Bkhetan and Plewczynski build a statistical model to predict chromatin looping across the genome. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports. The genome folds in three dimensions inside the nucleus. Those folds link distant promoters and enhancers. Lab methods to map loops are costly and noisy. Their 3DEpiLoop algorithm learns from one-dimensional data instead. It uses epigenomic and transcription factor profiles.

Predictions matched reported experimental interactions well, they report. Anchor signatures looked similar across scales and cell types. CTCF anchors were rich in transcription factors but poor in histone marks. RNA polymerase II anchors showed the reverse pattern. The code is shared in a public repository.
europmc-pmc5987357:
Malinauskas and co-authors review ultrafast laser processing of materials, from science toward industry. Their review appeared in Light: Science & Applications. Tightly focused femtosecond or picosecond pulses deliver optical energy with fine precision. Two-photon excitation places changes deep inside bulk material. Local edits can be smaller than 100 nanometres. Three-dimensional structuring is almost unrestricted with this method.

Pulse length, chirp, and polarization give wide control over changes. Processing speeds now approach metres per second. That pace speeds the move from lab to factory floor. The authors stress the trade-off between resolution and throughput. Biomedical scaffolds and photonic wire bonding show the reach.
europmc-pmc5995457:
Soares Martins and co-authors compare methods for isolating exosomes from distinct body fluids. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. Exosomes hold promise as sources of diagnostic markers. No agreed best isolation method exists yet. Standard centrifugation is slow and needs large samples. The team tested two precipitation kits and one column kit. Fluids were serum, plasma, and cerebrospinal fluid. Particle counts, shape, stability, and purity were all checked.

All three kits isolated exosomes from each fluid, they report. One kit, ExoS, gave the best yield and purity. Small sample volumes worked with these methods. That matters for clinical and translational research.
europmc-pmc6017557:
Manyi-Loh and co-authors review antibiotic use in farming. Their article appeared in Molecules in 2018. Heavy farm use leaves residues in meat and milk. Resistant bacteria can then reach people through food. Animal waste also spreads resistance into soil and water.

The review draws on published findings from many countries. It stresses weak rules in much of the developing world. Drugs are often sold without prescriptions there. Poor sanitation and weak testing make the problem worse. The authors call for tighter rules on making and selling antibiotics. They also urge better tracking of use and resistance. Global teamwork, they argue, is needed to protect public health.
europmc-pmc6087757:
Konishi and Kiyama review TREM2/DAP12 signaling in microglia. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. Their activation can protect neurons or harm them. The TREM2 receptor and its partner DAP12 sit at a control point.

Both genes cause Nasu-Hakola disease when broken. TREM2 variants also raise Alzheimer's risk. The complex governs survival, debris clearance, and cytokine release. It shifts microglia into a disease-linked state. In some illnesses that shift helps. In others, like nerve injury, it hurts. The review weighs evidence across disease models. Readers get a balanced view of a double-edged pathway.
europmc-pmc6134757:
Liao and co-authors wrote a review in Cell Communication and Signaling on the cancer regulator FOXM1. FOXM1 is a protein that switches genes on during cell growth. It is found at high levels in most human cancers. High levels point to a poor outlook for patients. How it goes off track was not fully clear.

The review sums up the three layers that control FOXM1. Gene activity sets how much is made. Small RNAs trim its message after that. Chemical tags then alter the finished protein. The authors say mapping these controls can guide new cancer drugs. FOXM1 was named Molecule of the Year back in 2010.
europmc-pmc6152157:
Eyre and co-authors report a case in Eurosurveillance of gonorrhoea that resisted standard treatment in England in February 2018. A man was diagnosed after sex in Thailand with a woman living there. His infection carried resistance to ceftriaxone and high-level resistance to azithromycin, the two main drugs.

First-line treatment with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline failed. A second drug, spectinomycin, also failed. Genome sequencing showed two resistance mechanisms combined in one strain. Its background resembled a commonly circulating strain. The authors warn that urgent action is needed to stop further spread. The case is an early alarm for hard-to-treat gonorrhoea.
europmc-pmc6200857:
Le Heron and co-authors wrote a review on apathy and the brain. Apathy means a loss of drive for self-led, goal-based acts. It appears in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke. The review appeared in Neuropsychologia. It draws on brain imaging work from many disorders.

The authors report that apathy links most to harm in two core areas. One is the dorsal front cingulate area. The other is the ventral striatum. They build a frame with three parts of drive. A person must be willing to work, keep working, and learn what is worth work. Harm to any part can cause apathy. The frame gives clear tests for later work and care.
europmc-pmc6224657:
Hsu and co-authors studied how one gene change helps blood stem cell clones grow after chemotherapy. Their study appeared in Cell Stem Cell. The gene is PPM1D, which helps cells respond to DNA damage. Changes in blood forming clones become common with age. Such growth is called clonal hematopoiesis. It can come before blood cancers.

The team found PPM1D changes in one fifth of patients with blood cancers that followed prior treatment. Those changes matched past exposure to the drug cisplatin. Cells with overactive PPM1D outgrew normal cells after DNA damaging drugs. The gain came mostly from resisting cell death. In mice, mutant blood cells also won out after cisplatin. The work shows that treatment itself can select which clones expand.
europmc-pmc6257357:
O'Neill, Barton, and Ward review the long debate over how artemisinin kills malaria parasites. Their review appeared in Molecules. Artemisinin comes from a plant used in Chinese medicine. Its drug family now leads malaria treatment worldwide. Combined forms are standard, to slow drug resistance. Warning signs of weaker response had appeared at the Thai-Cambodian border.

How the drug works inside the parasite is still unsettled. Several target molecules have been proposed over the years. The review weighs the proof for how the drug is switched on in the body. It also covers the main candidate targets. Artemisinin compounds also show effects against cancer cells and other parasites. Those wider uses make the mechanism question more pressing. Clear answers could guide safer, stronger follow up drugs.
europmc-pmc6293057:
McAllister and co-authors estimate the global burden of pneumonia in young children. Their systematic analysis appeared in The Lancet Global Health. It covers children under five in developing countries. The years run from 2000 to 2015. The team drew on a large review, health survey data, and death records.

They report that illness episodes fell by about a fifth over the period. Cases dropped from 178 million to 138 million. Deaths fell from 1.7 million to 0.9 million. Hospital stays rose sharply at the same time. Five countries carried over half of all cases in 2015. Most key risk factors also fell, low birthweight aside. The work gives planners a clear baseline for child health goals.
europmc-pmc6324057:
Braschi and co-authors detail the HGNC and VGNC gene naming resources in 2019. Their report appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The HGNC gives each human gene a unique symbol and name. Clear names keep gene research from confusion. The VGNC does the same job for other vertebrates. It covers species that lack their own naming bodies.

The database held over 40,000 approved human gene symbols. More than 19,000 of them mark protein-coding genes. The VGNC named over 15,000 chimpanzee protein-coding genes. It added over 14,000 each for cow and dog. Horse genes passed 13,000 as well. The Genenames website got a major redesign. It is simpler, works better on phones, and groups genes into over 1,200 families.
europmc-pmc6327557:
Leask and co-authors set out principles for co-creating public health programs. Their paper appeared in Research Involvement and Engagement. One-size programs often fail to change health habits. People differ in needs, means, and daily life. Co-creation designs programs with the people affected. The team drew lessons from several case studies.

The cases targeted sitting time and strength and balance. Groups ranged from schoolgirls to older adults at home. The principles fall into four stages. Planning asks what the aim is and who should join. Conducting covers the shared activities themselves. Later stages cover checking results and spreading what worked. The authors give practical recommendations for each stage. Their framework helps teams involve the public well, not just in name.
europmc-pmc6397457:
Ma and co-authors review the gut-brain axis in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Gut microbes and the brain affect each other in both directions. That cross-talk shapes brain growth and may shape brain disease as well.

When the gut-brain link breaks down, harm can follow, the review argues. Links are discussed for degenerative brain diseases and for brain tumors. The authors also cover ways to reset gut microbes, from diet to transplants. Much proof still comes from animal work, they note. Human tests are the clear next need.
europmc-pmc6411957:
Lu and co-authors report a genome study in Nature Communications on Brassica napus, the oilseed rape crop. This crop formed when two Brassica species crossed, doubling its genome. No truly wild form is known, so its origin stayed unclear.

The team resequenced 588 plant samples from many regions. One half of the genome traces to a European turnip ancestor. The other half traces to kin of kohlrabi and broccoli. Winter oilseed types look like the earliest form, they report. Selection on defense genes helped the crop adapt after it formed.
europmc-pmc6425557:
Jenni Sidey-Gibbons and Chris Sidey-Gibbons give doctors and medical researchers a hands-on intro to machine learning, building three working prediction models as the lesson. Interest in these methods has surged after visible successes, yet many medical readers lack a path from theory to practice. Open-source R software and a public dataset keep the barrier low.

Their models sort breast mass cell samples drawn from a set of 683 cases, split into training and validation groups. Regularized regression, support vector machines, and a small neural network each scored 94 to 96 percent accuracy. A voting mix of the three pushed accuracy to 97 percent. Readers can follow each step and reuse the approach on other tasks.
europmc-pmc6441157:
Maacha and co-authors review how extracellular vesicles mediate the conversations inside the tumor microenvironment and help cancers resist drugs. Tumor cells, stromal cells, and immune cells exchange vesicles loaded with proteins and RNA alongside the older routes of direct contact and secreted signals. Those parcels can switch recipient cells into tumor-friendly behavior.

Vesicle traffic is tied to growth, new blood vessels, spread, and treatment failure; fibroblasts, for instance, ship vesicles that hand chemoresistance to pancreatic cancer cells. Blocking vesicle secretion would cut the transfer of oncogenic cargo at its source. Sections weigh that strategy's promise and the practical difficulty of stopping a system healthy cells also use.
europmc-pmc6480557:
Kieliszek profiles selenium, the trace element Berzelius found in 1818 and named for the moon. It sits inside guard enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase, making it a frontline cleaner of free radicals. Too little of it raises the risk of many chronic diseases.

Food carries it mainly in organic forms, selenomethionine and selenocysteine, which the body absorbs better than the selenite and selenate used in supplements. Content swings with soil, and cooking can lose tens of percent as compounds escape into air. Because deep shortage is widespread, the review weighs selenium-rich foods and yeast biomass as routes for people whose diets fall short.
europmc-pmc6524357:
Aryal and co-authors measure antioxidant content in wild vegetables from western Nepal. Their study appeared in Plants. They tested eight wild leafy plants used in local diets. Methods included DPPH and hydrogen peroxide scavenging tests. FRAP and ferric thiocyanate assays were also used.

Cassia tora showed the strongest DPPH activity, with an IC50 of 9.898 μg/mL. Alternanthera sessilis led on hydrogen peroxide scavenging. Its value nearly matched ascorbic acid. That species also held the most phenolic content, at 292.65 mg GAE/g. Portulaca oleracea held the most flavonoid content. Activity tracked phenolic and flavonoid levels closely. The authors present these plants as sources of natural antioxidants.
europmc-pmc6536957:
Wu, Lu and Bai review the two faces of Nrf2, a master switch for cellular defense, writing in Cancer Medicine. Held in check by its partner Keap1, Nrf2 wakes under oxidative stress and turns on a battery of protective genes. That shield prevents cancer, fights inflammation and keeps redox balance — in healthy cells.

Established tumors hijack the same switch. Many cancers lock Nrf2 permanently on, and the shield becomes armor: metabolism rewires, cell death is repressed, stem-like cells renew themselves, and chemotherapy and radiation lose their bite. Patients fare worse for it. The review weighs this double edge and surveys Nrf2 inhibitors in development, arguing that disarming the shield could become a real cancer strategy.
europmc-pmc6540057:
Casares, Escribá and Rosselló review the lipids that build cell membranes, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. A membrane is not a plain wall. Its mix of fats forms domains that position proteins and start signals. Inside the cell, each organelle wears a membrane with its own recipe, and that recipe helps set the organelle's identity.

The authors survey the lipid toolkit, then walk organelle by organelle — endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes, nucleus — showing how composition keeps each one working. Cells guard the mix with sensing and repair systems. When the balance slips, diseases follow, from cancer to brain and metabolic disorders. The review closes on membrane lipid therapy, which aims to fix cell function by re-tuning the membrane itself.
europmc-pmc6600457:
Przybyłek, Karpiński, and Majtan review the antibacterial power of propolis. Their article appears in the journal Molecules. Propolis is the resinous glue bees use to seal and guard the hive. Its makeup shifts with local plants and climate. Yet samples from many regions can kill bacteria.

The authors analyzed studies on more than 600 bacterial strains. Propolis worked better on Gram-positive than Gram-negative bacteria. Samples from the Middle East showed the strongest action. They hit both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli hard. Samples from Germany, Ireland, and Korea were weakest. The review also covers extraction methods and active compounds such as flavonoids.
europmc-pmc6691157:
Shannon-Lowe and Rickinson survey the global landscape of Epstein-Barr virus associated tumours. Their review appears in Frontiers in Oncology. Most humans carry EBV lifelong without symptoms. Yet the virus is linked to many cancers. Some 200,000 new cases arise yearly worldwide. B-cell tumours dominate the list. Hodgkin and Burkitt lymphomas feature prominently. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma also appears. Immunocompromised hosts develop further lymphoproliferative diseases. Non-B-cell tumours surprise by contrast.

Nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinomas are epithelial cases. T and NK cell lymphomas occur too. Leiomyosarcoma strikes the profoundly immunosuppressed. Latency programmes differ across tumour types. Host genetics and environment shape risk. Cancer genomics reveals complementary somatic changes.
europmc-pmc6695957:
Marquardt and co-authors review progesterone and estrogen signalling in the endometrium and endometriosis. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Healthy endometrium keeps both hormones in tight step. Estrogen builds tissue during the growth phase. Progesterone then prepares the receptive window. Their receptors switch on large gene sets. In endometriosis that balance breaks down. Progesterone resistance meets estrogen dominance. Inflammation heightens as a result. Pelvic pain and infertility follow the imbalance. About ten percent of women of childbearing age suffer it.

Core pathways occupy the review's centre. Their paths in epithelium and stroma differ. Faulty control in ectopic tissue gets full treatment. Hormone treatments attempt to correct the signals. Targeted drugs are the hoped-for outcome.
europmc-pmc6769257:
Almagro Armenteros and co-authors used deep learning to find signals in protein targeting peptides. Proteins carry address tags that send them to the right cell compartment. While building TargetP 2.0, a leading predictor of these tags, the team noticed a biological signal earlier work had missed. The deep learning output exposed it.

Targeting peptides differ by destination. Some route proteins into the secretion path, others into mitochondria or chloroplasts. The paper explains the regions these tags are built from. It also reports predictions for nearly 289,000 proteins across 13 species, from yeast to humans. All predictions sit on a companion website. Better tag reading sharpens maps of where proteins do their work.
europmc-pmc6842957:
Nader and co-authors review blood rheology in Frontiers in Physiology. Rheology is the study of how blood flows. Blood thins as it moves faster, a trait set by the share of red cells, the plasma, and how red cells clump and bend. In the smallest vessels, that bending matters most. Small changes can alter flow to tissues.

The review sets out the key measures and what shifts them. It then turns to sickle cell disease, where stiff, misshapen red cells disturb flow and drive crises. Walking tests link poor red cell flexibility to worse exercise capacity in patients. A final section weighs what exercise does to these measures, and what forms may be safe.
europmc-pmc6882857:
Delaneau and co-authors present SHAPEIT4, a tool for haplotype estimation, in Nature Communications. Each person carries two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent. Knowing which variants sit together on the same copy, called phasing, underpins disease and population genetics. Genome counts are exploding, and older tools strain under the load.

SHAPEIT4 runs in less than linear time as sample size grows, a rare property. It returns highly accurate haplotypes on the two standard test sets, UK Biobank and Genome in a Bottle. It can also fold in outside help, from large reference panels to long sequencing reads. The software is open source.
europmc-pmc6890857:
Ng and Lee review traumatic brain injury in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Blows to the head remain a leading cause of death and disability among civilians and soldiers alike. The first impact tears tissue outright, and that damage is done at once. A slower second wave then unfolds over months to years. That delay is the opening for treatment.

The review maps the delayed processes: axons degenerating along their length, mitochondria failing, and excitotoxic chemistry burning neurons. Oxidative stress and programmed cell death add to the toll. Each process offers drug targets, and the authors catalogue the candidates aimed at them. Delivery across the blood-brain barrier remains a shared obstacle.
europmc-pmc6984357:
Darriba and co-authors present ModelTest-NG, a fast tool for picking the right model of evolution. Their article appeared in Molecular Biology and Evolution. Family trees of species depend on the model used to describe how DNA or protein sequences change. The wrong model can bend the tree.

Earlier tools from the same group, jModelTest and ProtTest, were popular but slow. ModelTest-NG is a rewrite from scratch. It runs one to two orders of magnitude faster at equal accuracy, the authors report. New features include correction for biased sampling, mixture and free-rate models, and automatic handling of data partitions. The tool is free software, built for modern high-performance computers. It targets the huge sequence alignments that current sequencing projects produce.
europmc-pmc7000657:
Zatterale and co-authors review how long-lasting inflammation in body fat links obesity to diabetes. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Obesity is a major health burden of this century. Overeating appears to spark a slow, low-grade inflammation, and fat tissue is where it takes hold.

As fat expands, its own cells die, starve of oxygen, and strain mechanically, each a trigger for immune attack. Macrophages flood in until they form up to 40 percent of fat tissue cells. They settle into an inflammatory mode and release signals that blunt insulin action. Other immune cells, from dendritic cells to T cells, join in. The authors map the molecular steps and survey current treatment strategies aimed at this pathway.
europmc-pmc7017057:
Jin reviews the JAK/STAT3 signalling pathway in the journal Cells, writing as sole author. When switched on, this pathway helps cancers grow, spread, and resist chemotherapy. Much of that effect runs through the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. That shift lets settled tumour cells become mobile and invasive.

The review explains how signals such as interleukin-6 turn the pathway on. It then traces how active STAT3 raises spread and helps form cancer stem cells. Those stem-like cells are blamed for many treatment failures. Jin also covers the tumour surroundings, the role of small RNAs called miRNAs, and new regulators of the pathway. The survey links basic signalling to the traits that make cancers hard to cure.
europmc-pmc7021657:
Oliveros and co-authors review high blood pressure in older adults for Clinical Cardiology. Hypertension in later life raises the risk of heart failure, stroke, heart attack, and death. An aging population and rising obesity are swelling its global burden. Age also stiffens arteries and weakens kidney function, which complicates care.

The review gathers current evidence and recent guideline advice on assessing and treating older patients. Care must be tailored to each person, weighing frailty, other illnesses, and social factors. Lifestyle measures come first and also support drug treatment. Diuretics, renin-angiotensin system blockers, and calcium channel blockers have each shown benefit on heart outcomes in this age group. The authors close by urging prevention earlier in life.
europmc-pmc7025157:
Arbyn and co-authors estimate the worldwide burden of cervical cancer in The Lancet Global Health. Persistent human papillomavirus infection is the main cause of this cancer, and vaccines plus virus testing now make prevention realistic. The World Health Organization aims to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem during the 21st century. A firm baseline is needed to judge that push.

The team drew estimates for 185 countries from the Global Cancer Observatory 2018 database and the WHO mortality database. They calculated new cases and deaths for 2018, with rates adjusted for age and grouped by region and by development level. Burden varied sharply across the world, falling hardest on lower-resource countries. The figures give the elimination campaign its starting line.
europmc-pmc7033057:
Rayman reviews selenium and health in the journal Hormones, writing as sole author. Selenium is a trace element that the body needs only in small amounts. Both shortage and excess occur naturally in different parts of the world, and excess can also come from supplements. Health effects often follow a U-shaped pattern, with harm at both low and high status.

Why people differ in tolerance takes up much of the review. Gene variants can help some handle very low or high intakes. Exposure to toxic elements that bind selenium can blunt its harm. Dose and chemical form matter too: at high doses one form, selenomethionine, produces toxic breakdown products. Early-life exposure may even reshape gut microbes so that excess selenium leaves the body faster. The picture is a balance, not a simple more-is-better rule.
europmc-pmc7136157:
Melmed and co-authors present the consensus statement on treatment outcomes for acromegaly from the 11th Acromegaly Consensus Conference, in Nature Reviews Endocrinology. Acromegaly is caused by excess growth hormone, usually from a pituitary tumor, and distorts the face and hands while raising diabetes and heart risk. Thirty-seven experts reviewed the literature in April 2017.

Since the previous 2014 guidelines, new drugs and new treatment sequences had appeared. The panel weighed current and emerging medicines, including somatostatin receptor ligands, growth hormone receptor blockers, and dopamine agonists. They judged effects on hormone levels, symptoms, tumor size, and surgical outcomes. The statement sets outcome goals and advises how to order treatments in practice.
europmc-pmc7145657:
Kumar and co-authors present the 2020 update of the ELM resource, a catalogue of short linear motifs in proteins, in Nucleic Acids Research. These tiny stretches of amino acids act as docking sites and signals inside cells. They often sit in loose, disordered protein regions. Every entry is hand-curated from experiments reported in papers.

The team added 21 new motif classes and revised 12 more. They also logged over 400 new cases. The new cases stress DNA damage responses and the cell skeleton. Many show motifs copied by bacterial proteins that hijack host cells. The database now holds 289 motif classes and 3,523 cases drawn from 3,467 papers. It has served cell biologists for almost 20 years.
europmc-pmc7161957:
Li and co-authors check where the SARS-CoV-2 doorway protein ACE2 appears at the interface between mother and fetus and in fetal organs, in PLoS ONE. Whether the virus can pass from mother to unborn child was disputed. Using public single-cell RNA data, they mapped ACE2 activity cell by cell.

ACE2 was highly expressed in placental cell types, including cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast cells, and in support cells of the decidua. It also appeared in specific cells of fetal heart, liver, and lung, though not kidney. Mouse data showed lung ACE2 peaking in the first days after birth. The authors say vertical transmission and placenta damage both need careful clinical investigation.
europmc-pmc7195857:
Williams and co-authors test whether a soft, fatty type of plaque in heart arteries predicts heart attacks. Their study appeared in Circulation. It draws on the SCOT-HEART trial of CT scans in patients with stable chest pain. Usual risk tools rely on scores, calcium levels, or artery narrowing. The team asked whether plaque character does better.

They measured low-attenuation noncalcified plaque as a share of vessel volume. This soft plaque is the kind most likely to rupture. Patients carrying more of it faced higher risk of later heart attack. The measure beat the standard tools in their analysis. Calcium scores, by contrast, mark stable hardened plaque. The findings argue for reading scans by plaque type, not just blockages.
europmc-pmc7224457:
Liu and co-authors ask whether pangolins served as the intermediate host for SARS-CoV-2. Their study appeared in PLoS Pathogens. The virus likely began in bats, but the bridge to humans was unclear. The team assembled the full genome of a coronavirus found in 3 sick Malayan pangolins. They compared it with the human virus and with bat coronaviruses.

The pangolin virus proved to be a close relative of both. Yet the analysis does not support the human virus emerging directly from it. Pangolins look more like natural hosts of their own betacoronaviruses. The sick animals had severe respiratory disease when found. Smuggled pangolins may carry such viruses unnoticed. The study narrows, but does not close, the search for the pandemic's animal path.
europmc-pmc7299157:
Barandouzi and co-authors review studies that ask if the gut microbes of people with depression differ from those of healthy people. Their review follows the brain-gut axis, the two-way talk between gut and brain. They searched for human studies from January 2000 to June 2019.

Nine papers fit the rules. Tests of microbe diversity did differ between the two groups, though not in one steady way. For the big microbe groups, results clashed from study to study. Two groups, Actinobacteria and Fusobacteria, did show up at higher levels in depression more than once. Many smaller groups also shifted, some up and some down. The team calls the proof mixed, but real enough to keep chasing.
europmc-pmc7301057:
Ren and co-authors show that a small accessory protein of SARS-CoV-2, ORF3a, can push infected cells to kill themselves. Their study appeared in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. Apoptosis, orderly cell suicide, is one of the host's antiviral defenses and shapes inflammation. The related SARS virus's ORF3a protein was already known to trigger it.

In three cultured cell lines, cells making the SARS-CoV-2 ORF3a protein showed significantly more staining for apoptosis markers than control cells. Measured death rates confirmed the effect. The team compared the two viruses' proteins in the same system to judge relative strength. Accessory proteins help decide how damaging a coronavirus is, so mapping what ORF3a does adds a piece to understanding why this virus causes the disease it does.
europmc-pmc7319457:
Ianevski, Giri and Aittokallio release SynergyFinder 2.0, a web tool for the study of drug pairs and how they interact. Their paper notes that paired drugs are standard care for ills from tuberculosis to late-stage cancer. Pairs can beat one drug alone and can block resistance. But screens of pairs make data that are hard to read at a glance.

First out in 2017, the tool had won wide use in lab work on cell lines and on cells taken from patients. The new build adds tools for sets of three or more drugs. It adds richer views of synergy, spots odd data points on its own, and gives stats across repeat runs. The team expects the build to widen its use in drug screens and in care matched to one patient.
europmc-pmc7320157:
Wei and co-authors engineer lipid nanoparticles that deliver CRISPR gene-editing machinery into specific organs through the bloodstream. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. CRISPR-Cas9 edits DNA as a protein-RNA complex, but most disease targets were unreachable for lack of carriers able to deliver it systemically.

Their tunable particles edited muscle, brain, liver, and lung tissue. A single intravenous injection edited six genes at once in mouse lungs. High potency let them build organ-specific cancer models by knocking out several genes in liver or lung, restore dystrophin in mice with muscular dystrophy, and sharply lower blood PCSK9, a cholesterol-related protein. The general strategy could extend protein delivery and precise gene correction to many more diseases.
europmc-pmc7345657:
Bhattacharya and co-authors review candidiasis and antifungal resistance in Antibiotics. Candidiasis is infection by Candida yeasts, which normally live harmlessly in the body. More than 20 Candida types can cause it, with Candida albicans the most common, and people with HIV, transplants, or diabetes face the highest risk.

Infections range from white patches in the mouth to deep organ disease. The review explains how the yeasts stick to tissues, invade, and form hardy growths. It then sorts the main drug families by target: cell wall, the membrane fat ergosterol, or DNA building. Azole drugs are widely used, but their growth-slowing rather than killing action helps resistance evolve. Readers get a compact tour of a common infection and its shrinking drug options.
europmc-pmc7347557:
Pastorello and co-authors present the FLUXNET2015 dataset in Scientific Data, a global record of how land and air trade carbon dioxide, water, and energy. Tower instruments at 212 sites around the world measured these exchanges directly. The collection covers more than 1,500 site-years, running through 2014.

Sites run independently, so the team reprocessed every record with uniform methods and quality checks. The release adds filled gaps in the time series, estimates of plant uptake and ecosystem breathing, and uncertainty values. For 206 sites the data carry an open Creative Commons license for the first time. A shared processing pipeline, ONEFlux, is published as open code. Climate and ecosystem modelers get a common yardstick.
europmc-pmc7350257:
Shorning and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on prostate cancer signaling. It centers on the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, which is switched on in many prostate tumors. The review traces how this pathway talks with three other key pathways. Those are the androgen receptor, MAPK, and WNT pathways.

The authors outline the gene changes that turn the pathway on. They then show how cross-talk can speed tumor growth and help cancer resist drugs. That resistance affects both pathway-targeted drugs and standard hormone-blocking therapy. Better maps of this network could help sort patients for the right treatment. They could also point to new drug approaches. Readers get a guide to why single-pathway drugs often fail in this cancer.
europmc-pmc7364557:
Guo and co-authors review the molecular roots of Alzheimer's disease in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of age-related dementia, and no effective treatment exists. The authors blame that gap partly on an unclear mechanism, and gather what decades of work have shown.

Two proteins anchor the story: amyloid-beta, which clumps outside cells, and tau, which tangles inside them. Support cells called glia add their own failures, and certain receptors pass amyloid's toxic effects to neurons. Genetics, aging, infections, sleep, gut microbes, and the risk gene APOE all enter the account. Readers get a broad map of a devastating disease and the many fronts on which researchers are attacking it.
europmc-pmc7378357:
Matejuk and Ransohoff overview the conversation between two brain cell types in Frontiers in Immunology. Astrocytes and microglia are non-neuronal cells that support and defend the brain. Neuron-to-glia talk has been studied for years, while glia-to-glia talk remained murkier.

New imaging and computing tools let neuroscience picture the brain as dense networks of exchange rather than lone cell types. The authors review how astrocytes and microglia signal each other in development and in neurodegenerative disease. Signals between them can protect neurons or drive damage, depending on context. The stated goal is practical: understand the crosstalk well enough to fight incurable brain disorders. Readers get a readable map of a busy, underappreciated channel.
europmc-pmc7463657:
Czarnecka and co-authors review the molecular biology of osteosarcoma, a bone cancer of the young. It is the most common primary bone cancer in children and teens. Inherited syndromes can raise its risk.

The gene TP53 is the most often altered gene in this cancer. The RB gene also shows frequent changes, above all in children. Other driver changes hit genes such as NOTCH1, FOS, NF2, and BRCA2. Small RNAs tune key growth pathways in the tumor cells. Some tumor cells act like stem cells and may seed spread and drug resistance. Care still rests on chemotherapy and surgery. New targeted drugs, such as cabozantinib and sorafenib, are in study. The review maps genes, pathways, and treatment leads.
europmc-pmc7523057:
Smith, Li and Rafferty present the Implementation Research Logic Model, called the IRLM. Health research often uses many models for parts of a project. Projects still struggle to link those parts in a clear way.

The model gives a shared structure for that link. It connects determinants, strategies, mechanisms and outcomes. Teams can use it to plan, run and report projects. The authors built it with input from varied research teams. They also tested its use in training for over 130 researchers and partners. Readers get guiding principles and variants for common study designs.
europmc-pmc7542157:
Ju and co-authors review NADPH balance in cancer cells. NADPH supplies reducing power for building molecules. It also helps cells keep redox balance under stress.

Cancer cells rewire NADPH pathways as they adapt. That rewiring makes them rely on the network for defense. It also leaves them open to oxidative harm. The review covers how signals and enzymes control NADPH levels. It then covers treatments that target this system. Aiming at NADPH may help kill cancer cells. Readers get functions, controls and drug ideas in one place. The work links basic metabolism to cancer therapy choices.
europmc-pmc7586657:
Koboldt reviews best practices for variant calling in clinical sequencing. Next-generation sequencing has expanded clinical genetic testing widely. It serves inherited disease and cancer care alike.

Accurate variant calling underpins all later analysis steps. Tools and methods have changed fast over ten years. The review stresses trio sequencing for inherited disorders. It also covers somatic mutation calls in cancer patients. Panel, exome and genome methods are compared for detection. Strengths and limits of each are set out. Recommended tools for variant classes are provided. Guidance covers review, validation and benchmarking of calls. Core principles should hold as new sequencing methods emerge.
europmc-pmc7745957:
Oliver and co-authors set out a US advisory panel's first advice on the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. The Food and Drug Administration cleared the vaccine for emergency use on December 11, 2020. The vaccine is an mRNA type given in 2 doses, 3 weeks apart. The panel met the next day to advise.

The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices backed use in people aged 16 years or more. It weighed gains and harms with a formal evidence framework. This was an interim call, to be updated as data grow. It pairs with prior advice on who should get scarce first supplies. The report records the basis for a fast public decision.
europmc-pmc7791157:
Wang and co-authors identify AXL as a candidate second receptor for SARS-CoV-2. The virus is known to enter cells through ACE2. Yet ACE2 levels are very low in the airways. Other entry helpers may exist.

AXL bound directly to the front part of the viral spike protein. Adding AXL to lab cells let the virus in as well as ACE2 did. Removing AXL cut infection in lung cell lines sharply. It also cut infection in primary human lung cells. A soluble form of AXL blocked infection. In fluid from COVID-19 patient lungs, AXL levels matched viral spike levels. The authors argue AXL helps the virus infect the human airway.
europmc-pmc7873057:
Rodriguez-Garcia and co-authors use CAR T cells to clear suppressive macrophages from tumors. The tumor setting blocks immunotherapy for many patients. Tumor macrophages are a major part of that block. Some push tumors forward, and others fight them.

A macrophage subset wearing folate receptor β acts suppressive. The team built CAR T cells to kill just that subset. In mouse tumors, clearing them changed the scene. Fresh inflammatory cells moved in. The body's own tumor-specific killer T cells followed. Tumors grew slower and mice lived longer. Pre-clearing also boosted a second CAR T therapy. Giving both at once did not help, though.
europmc-pmc7919457:
Uhrig and co-authors present a research study on finding gene fusions in RNA sequencing data. Fusions arise when two genes join into one abnormal message. They drive many cancers and can be hit by targeted drugs. Finding them in sequence data is a routine task, yet existing tools are often slow or inaccurate.

The team built a new algorithm called Arriba. It pairs high sensitivity with a short runtime. On 803 published pancreatic cancer samples, Arriba found many driver fusions. Several hit proteins that drugs can target, such as ALK and FGFR2. The fusions clustered in tumours without KRAS mutations, as if standing in for them. Two new fusions changed cells in lab tests, proving they can drive growth. The authors offer the tool for both research and clinical use.
europmc-pmc7939257:
Morrison presents a biographical essay on Carl Weigert, a pathfinder in medicine. The essay was read before the Boston Medical History Club in November 1923. Weigert made his mark young. Between 1871 and 1875, still in his twenties, he studied smallpox in a way that changed laboratory practice. Morrison argues his true rank is still not grasped.

The smallpox work opened the staining of bacteria and tissues in distinct colours. It also began the study of diseased tissue in serial sections. Weigert first described coagulation necrosis in the skin lesions. From that came his core idea: tissue injury is the body's first answer to outside attack. He pressed the view against Virchow himself. The idea drove a lifetime of research across pathology. Morrison closes by noting the methods Weigert left behind, which shaped daily medical science.
europmc-pmc7957857:
Prentice and co-authors report a laboratory study on how a coronavirus builds its copying sites. The mouse hepatitis virus copies its RNA on double-membrane vesicles inside the host cell. How those vesicles form was unknown. The team tested whether autophagy, the cell's recycling system, plays a part. They used gene knockouts, chemistry, and imaging to probe the link.

The copying sites sat alongside two hallmark autophagy proteins. Infection switched autophagy on by a path that a standard blocker could not stop. In cells missing a key autophagy gene, the virus copied poorly and no vesicles formed. Restoring the gene restored both. The rough endoplasmic reticulum swelled oddly in the mutant cells. The authors conclude that autophagy parts are needed to build the copying sites. Those sites in turn make copying far more efficient.
europmc-pmc8106557:
Wu and co-authors survey how gut microbes and their products feed metabolic disease. Obesity, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and heart disease keep climbing worldwide. Lifestyle drives much of that rise, but not all of it. The gut hosts dense microbial crowds at the body's main energy gateway. They turn food into bioactive compounds that reach every organ.

Host genes, immune tone, and diet together shape that inner crowd. In turn, its chemicals steer fat storage and sugar control. The review maps the metabolite cast in detail. Short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, and other products each get a role. Where the links to each disease stand, the authors judge the evidence. Fixes that retune the microbiome close the survey. Diet shifts, live microbes, and pathway drugs all appear. The gut, they argue, is a drug target in itself.
europmc-pmc8113357:
Scala and co-authors link gene profiles to shape and firing in mouse motor cortex neurons. Cell types were long defined by one trait at a time. Patch-seq measures three traits in the same cell. The team patched, stained, and sequenced over 1,300 neurons. Nearly every gene-defined type in the region got a physical portrait. Families told a clean story; types within them did not.

Broad families, marked by genes like Vip, Pvalb, and Sst, stood apart. Their forms and firing patterns barely overlapped at all. Single types inside a family blurred into each other. Shape and firing shifted along smooth gradients between neighbors. Sharp borders between close types could not be drawn. The cortex, the authors argue, mixes both logics. Families branch like a tree, types shade like a landscape. Any parts list of the brain must hold both truths. Pure gene labels alone will mislead.
europmc-pmc8234057:
Chen, Xu, and Chen summarise how gut microbes steer neurotransmitters and cognition. Gut microbes talk to the brain through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. That talk shapes brain activity and mental function.

The review sets out how microbes guide the making of neurotransmitters. It covers their transport and their action in the nervous system. It then links microbe imbalance to failing cognition. Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases get close attention. The routes include immune and metabolic paths as well. Knowing them may open diet or microbe-based ways to protect the mind. The stakes rise as these diseases grow more common worldwide.
europmc-pmc8265157:
Letunic and Bork present version 5 of the Interactive Tree Of Life, an online tree tool. It displays, edits, and annotates phylogenetic and other trees. Anyone can use it free of charge.

Version 5 brings a wholly new tree display engine. A MEME motif dataset type joins the set. Annotation options widened for several existing types. Node labels now take category and multiple values. Users can also draw and label by hand on the tree. The update serves the huge trees that modern sequence data produce. New annotation drawn by hand joins the feature list.
europmc-pmc8329257:
Elmusrati, Wang, and Wang review immune evasion in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. This cancer kills often and responds poorly to most drugs. Surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation remain the main tools.

The tumour microenvironment helps the cancer advance. Immune surveillance should catch such tumours early. Cancer cells evolve ways around that watch. They can mute their own visibility or release suppressive signals. The review sorts those escape routes. It shows how the setting and the cancer conspire. Better immune therapies rest on that map, the authors argue. Advanced therapies grow from that foundation, they argue.
europmc-pmc8556157:
Laursen and co-authors show that breastmilk-linked gut bacteria make aromatic lactic acids in the infant gut. Breastfeeding shapes the baby's gut microbes deeply. Those microbes guide early immune growth. Few milk-dependent microbe products that talk to the host were known, though.

The team found that Bifidobacterium species turn aromatic amino acids into lactic acid forms. A new enzyme, an aromatic lactate dehydrogenase, does the work. Tests in specially colonized mice confirmed the conversion. In 25 Danish infants tracked to 6 months of age, the acids tracked with milk-sugar-eating Bifidobacterium species. The work names a fresh channel of host-microbe talk.
europmc-pmc8593957:
Davenport and co-authors report a rapid survey of maternal mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic. Depression and anxiety affect one in seven women around birth. The team asked how lockdown and distance rules changed mood and activity for pregnant and new mothers. The online survey ran in spring 2020.

Of 900 women, 520 were pregnant and 380 had given birth in the past year. Signs of depression rose from 15 percent before the pandemic to 40.7 percent at survey time. High anxiety rose from 29 percent to 72 percent. Women who met activity goals of 150 minutes a week had lower scores for both. The authors call for more screening and care.
europmc-pmc8842557:
