Deng and co-authors update progress on m6A, a chemical mark placed on RNA. This mark is the most common edit in messenger RNA. It shapes how RNA is processed, moved, and read. When the marking system goes wrong, cancers can grow and spread. Its regulator proteins have become drug targets. The review asks what drug hunters have found so far.

The authors describe the writers, erasers, and readers of the mark. They trace how faulty marking drives tumor progress. They then survey drug discovery from two sources. Traditional medicines supplied natural candidate compounds. Modern chemistry supplied designed and synthesized ones. The authors make a case for artificial intelligence in the hunt. They argue it can speed the search for m6A-targeting drugs.
europmc-pmc8868457:
Murugaiyan and co-authors gather alternative strategies against antimicrobial resistance. Resistant infections grow harder or impossible to treat. Deaths and illness climb as standard drugs fail. No new antibiotic class has arrived in two decades. The review looks beyond the traditional single-drug model. It focuses on antibiotics and their reinforcements. Many routes are on the table.

The authors cover combination therapy first. They then treat attacks on the enzymes that create resistance. Drug delivery systems that shield antibiotics follow. Physical and chemical methods get their own section. Vaccines earn a chapter as prevention against resistant pathogens. Unconventional ideas, including the CRISPR-Cas system, close the survey. The authors argue these strategies could change care. Multi-drug-resistant infections are the test case.
europmc-pmc9259657:
Gerasimavicius and co-authors compare how loss-of-function, gain-of-function, and dominant-negative mutations affect protein structure. Most known disease mutations change protein-coding regions. Much work has focused on mutations that break structure and cause loss of function. The other two mechanisms are far less understood.

The team studied pathogenic missense mutations by their mechanism. Dominant, non-loss mutations had much milder effects on structure than expected. Dominant-negative mutations clustered strongly at protein interfaces. Nearly all prediction tools performed poorly on non-loss mutations, even sequence-based ones. Yet such mutations tend to cluster in three-dimensional space, which could flag them. The authors warn that current pipelines likely miss many of these disease variants.
europmc-pmc9268357:
Pinto and co-authors describe a human antibody that blocks a wide range of betacoronaviruses. Three such viruses have crossed into humans in the past 20 years, including SARS-CoV-2. Most antibodies target the variable S1 part of the spike protein. This team instead found antibodies that bind a helix in the steadier S2 part.

Five monoclonal antibodies bound spikes from all betacoronavirus subgenera tested. The strongest, S2P6, blocked viruses across three subgenera. It also cut viral burden in hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2. The S2 target changes far less than S1 across strains. That makes it a strong candidate site for broad vaccines and drugs. The approach aims at future spillovers as well as current variants.
europmc-pmc9868457:
Tan and Wong look ahead to how diabetic retinopathy care may change by 2030. Diabetic retinopathy is the main eye complication of diabetes and a major global health problem. Imaging with optical coherence tomography and anti-VEGF treatment already changed care in recent decades.

The authors expect disease burden to grow and shift toward middle- and low-income regions. They foresee more focus on nerve damage and non-vascular parts of the disease. New imaging, such as widefield systems and OCT angiography, should add richer data. Artificial intelligence should aid screening, diagnosis, and prognosis. New drugs, gene therapy, and updated classification systems round out the outlook.
fowler-self-instructor-phrenology-1857:
O. S. Fowler and L. N. Fowler ran the great phrenology trade in the States. Their Illustrated Self-Instructor came out in 1857. The book taught any buyer to read heads at home, his own and those of kin. Cuts show each bump and trait in clear form.

Steps tell how to feel the skull and score each trait on a chart. Advice then links the scores to jobs, mates, and the care of self. The book put a white bust with marked zones in parlors all over the land. It is a prime text of the field at its peak.
frus-1861-d157:
A round of letters on 21 October 1861 included one from William H. Seward to William Dayton. The letter is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Paris and to Berlin in the same late October round. The letters kept each post aware that it formed part of one front. Dayton's copy shows the Secretary's hand at work across the map in a single week. The round of late October letters spans the map of the Union's foreign front. One week, one hand, a whole front: the round shows the office at its peak load.
frus-1861-d257:
Washington's orders went out to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands in a dispatch dated 4 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 257 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d57:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 June 1861. It is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As June closed, both American armies moved toward their first great clash. Adams could only report London's talk and wait, like Seward, for news. His letter shows an envoy holding his post steady while events at home rushed toward battle. From London, even the clash of armies came first as rumor, then as dread fact. Rumor in London ran fast, and Adams learned to sift it with a cold eye.
frus-1862-d157:
Secretary of State William H. Seward directed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London on 4 October 1862, printed as Document 157 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister to Britain, acted on these orders in his talks with British officials.

Orders from Washington had to cover events the Secretary could not foresee, since replies took weeks. Seward therefore mixed firm lines with room for his envoy's judgment. A letter from this week belongs to the stretch when Britain, after Antietam. Chose to wait rather than step into the war, a choice Adams worked to make permanent.
frus-1862-d257:
Dated 8 March 1862, Document 257 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The day after Seward wrote, the ironclad Virginia attacked Union ships at Hampton Roads, and the Monitor fought it to a draw. Naval news like that echoed loudly in France, a great sea power with its own ironclad plans. Seward's letters to Paris in March belonged to a season when each battle reset foreign guesses about the war. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d357:
On 10 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Henri Mercier another letter, printed as Document 357 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was the French minister in Washington throughout this period.

Two letters in four days show the French channel carrying steady traffic in the winter of 1862. Much of that traffic was case work: ships, trade, and the rights of French citizens caught by the war. Such business rarely made headlines, but it filled the envoys' days and kept the larger relationship in repair. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English.
frus-1862-d457:
John Lothrop Motley wrote from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1862. His report is Document 457 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

February 1862 brought a run of Union victories, and Motley's reports could carry that improving story into Austrian ears. Still, Vienna moved slowly and spoke carefully, and its press often echoed Confederate hopes. A minister's dispatch in such a place was part news, part weather report on opinion. Seward gathered these readings from every capital before deciding where the dangers lay. Motley's February letter is one gauge in that wider instrument panel.
frus-1862-d557:
A Mr. Goodrich received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1862. It is Document 557 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed among the Belgian papers of that summer.

The letter sits in the file between Seward's orders to Minister Sanford in Brussels, part of the same run of Belgian business. Instructions of this kind carried Washington's directions to the officers who served the mission and its work. July 1862 was a month of strain, with the Virginia campaign gone wrong, and every post abroad needed steady direction. The document is a reminder that a legation was a small team. The State Department's paper reached beyond the minister whose name heads the file.
frus-1862-d57:
A dispatch dated 2 May 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 57 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d657:
On 9 December 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Robert H. Pruyn, who was set to lead the American legation in Japan. The letter is document 657 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Townsend Harris, the first minister to Japan, was on his way out of the post.

Before an envoy sailed, the State Department loaded him with written orders. Seward's letters to Pruyn that winter formed the base of the new man's charge. This letter is one of them. It shows how much care Washington took with a post that guarded trade and the flag in a land still new to American ships.
frus-1863p1-d157:
On 16 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 157 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Adams's pair took the next head of the London news in line. That April, the news ran from the shipyards to Parliament, and the legation sorted it all for home. This letter is the mate to document 156. With it, the pair shows the post's mid-April pace: steady, split by topic, and aimed at a reader who used every page.
frus-1863p1-d257:
An instruction dated 7 August 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 257 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Union victories in July 1863 let Washington speak with more confidence. Orders sent after Gettysburg and Vicksburg carry a firmer note than those of the spring. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d357:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 10 January 1863. It appears as document 357 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d457:
A letter of 11 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 457 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d557:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 8 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d57: A Mr. St. John wrote this letter to a Mr. Smith on 28 October 1862. It is document 57 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the last of the Confederate group printed there. The evidence names the two men and the date, but not their posts or the letter's subject. This note stays within those bounds.
frus-1863p1-d657:
Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 6 November 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d157: Kirk wrote on November 21, 1943 to Nahas, Egypt's prime minister and foreign minister, and the letter is Document 157 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired with his note to the royal cabinet chief the same day, it shows the American minister working both doors of the host government on the conference's eve. The record gives the names and the date. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d257:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 23 November 1943, met at half past two in the afternoon. They take up China's role in the defeat of Japan under paper C.C.S. 405. General Stilwell opens with word from Chiang Kai-shek that no Chinese proposals should be laid before the chiefs until he has talked again with Roosevelt and Marshall.

Sir Alan Brooke and Admiral Leahy judge the first four proposals in the paper workable, and the rest unrealistic for now. Formosa is singled out: it could not be attacked from the Chinese mainland without landing craft. General Marshall urges care and sympathy anyway, noting that Chiang, long reluctant to build ground forces, now shows real interest in them for the first time. Admiral King agrees the Generalissimo should not be discouraged if that can be avoided.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d357:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 28 November 1943 record a morning session at half past eleven. The American chiefs weighed British wishes against Overlord. The first plenary session with Stalin was only hours away. President Roosevelt opens the discussion himself.

Roosevelt understands the British think Allied forces in Italy can reach the Pisa-Rimini line. General Marshall lays out the costs of the rival path. Advancing to Ancona and taking Rhodes in February would push Overlord back to about 15 June, perhaps July. Rhodes would suck in considerable means. The British want Rhodes in place of the Andaman operation, and Turkey's entry above all, claiming Bulgaria and Romania would then fall. Marshall doubts the Straits could open for six to eight months even so, and argues for backing Eisenhower without unduly delaying Overlord.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d457:
Closing day at Cairo also brought a further session of the Combined Chiefs of Staff on December 6, 1943, with minutes printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, top American and British officers, had spent the conference turning the Tehran agreements into a workable common strategy. Their meetings ran alongside those of Roosevelt and Churchill.

The session record follows the standard form: who was present, what was raised, and what was decided. Its interest lies in timing as much as content, since a final session shows which questions were still open when the conference broke up. Paired with the day's agreed minutes, it completes the official picture.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d557:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on March 4, 1944, continuing a run of messages across the first days of March. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, in the follow-up correspondence to the conferences.

Churchill's March letters pressed the business of a coalition approaching its greatest operation: the cross-Channel invasion fixed at Tehran for the late spring. Around that fixed point circled arguments about Italy, the Balkans, and relations with France and Russia. For readers, the message is one more turn of the handle by a prime minister who believed that writing itself was a form of command.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d57: General George Marshall, Chief of Staff of the Army, wrote to Admiral William Leahy, the President's Chief of Staff, on October 25, 1943. The letter is Document 57 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Staff chiefs writing to each other carried the military side of summit planning while the diplomats met in Moscow. The record names the two soldiers and the date. Its subject rests in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1944-quebec-d157:
Roosevelt settled the French Indochina question for the moment with a short memorandum to Hull on August 28, 1944. The British ambassador's proposals, and the French Committee's aide-mémoire behind them, would wait. The president planned to meet Churchill at Quebec, and he intended the matter to be deferred until after that meeting.

One reason for caution appears in his final line. French participation in planning political warfare in the Far East, Roosevelt noted, involved one of the principal partners: China. Indochina lay in the China theater, and Chiang Kai-shek's views could not be bypassed. Hull was also told orally that the president would raise the French proposals with Churchill directly.
frus-1944-quebec-d257:
On September 13, 1944, the United States Chiefs recommended the Combined Chiefs send General Wilson their own draft message rather than the British one. The approved text, dispatched as Fan 415, gave Wilson two decisions for his future planning in Italy. Both responded directly to his requests for guidance in Naf 774.

First, there would be no withdrawals of major units from the Fifth Army until the outcome of Alexander's present offensive was known. Second, for the capture of the Istrian Peninsula, Wilson could count on the amphibious lift then in the Mediterranean. He was to prepare the operation as soon as possible and submit his plan to the Combined Chiefs by October 10 at the latest.
frus-1944-quebec-d57:
September 6, 1944 found Churchill writing to Roosevelt once more. He was on the last stage of his Atlantic crossing. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill reached North America that week. He then traveled on to Quebec. The conference there would open on September 12. His letters ahead of arrival staked out Britain's needs. Britain wanted a voice in the Pacific war. It wanted fair terms for continued American aid. It also wanted agreement on Germany. For readers, the message shows him arriving in writing first. He reached Quebec in person days later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d157:
A memorandum dated 21 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was C. H. Carson of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The reader was the Assistant Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Ladd). It is document 157 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d257:
On 17 December 1947, the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 257 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The ink on the National Security Act was barely dry, and both the CIA and the Council were finding their feet.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d357:
The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a letter to Mathias F. Correa on 18 December 1948. Readers meet it as document 357 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d57:
Admiral Chester Nimitz, now chief of naval operations, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 15 December 1945. Nimitz had taken over the Navy's top uniformed post the month before. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Nimitz brought the prestige of the Pacific victory to every paper he signed. His views on intelligence, formed in a theater where code-breaking had won battles, carried weight beyond their words. Readers should note the change of hand: King had guarded the Navy's claims through the autumn; Nimitz now held them as the settlement neared. The Navy's thread in the volume thus passes from one great wartime admiral to another without losing its force.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d157:
Poland's western frontier kept growing on Soviet maps, Harriman warned on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, tracks how Moscow's offer to Poland had widened in a few months. He writes that he is somewhat concerned by the expanding concept.

At first the Soviets spoke of East Prussia, less Königsberg, and a frontier perhaps as far as the Oder, with Stettin and Breslau thrown in. Then the Oder line hardened into the settled intention. Talking with de Gaulle, Stalin pushed further: the Oder to the lower Neisse, then south along the Neisse to the Czech border near Görlitz. A Pravda article had confirmed the new line in print.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d257:
General Deane sent the Joint Chiefs Stalin's shopping list on 17 October 1944. His cable from the American military mission in Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, records the night's meeting with Stalin, Molotov, and General Antonov. The list prices Soviet entry into the Pacific war.

Stalin first handed over the supplies America must furnish for a two months' stock in the Far East. Fuel leads: 120,000 tons of high-octane gasoline, 70,000 of motor gasoline, and collapsible storage tanks. Foodstuffs run to some 180,000 tons. Then come 30,000 trucks, 500 amphibious jeeps, 400 C-47 and 100 C-54 aircraft, and naval craft from frigates to sub-chasers. Railroad needs close the list: 500 locomotives, thousands of cars, and some 800 kilometers of rail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d357:
Exact words matter in this American paper of February 6, 1945, which prints the proposed voting formula for the Security Council. The formula had gone to Stalin and Churchill on December 5, 1944. Each member of the council would have one vote. Routine decisions would need seven affirmative votes.

All other decisions would also need seven votes, including the concurring votes of the permanent members. A study of the formula's effects follows the text. This was the heart of the Yalta bargain on the United Nations: great powers kept a veto on action, but not on debate. The paper preserves the wording that made the San Francisco conference possible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d457:
Stalin's dinner on February 10, 1945, ranged from reparations to Jewish problems, and Bohlen's minutes record the talk. Churchill opened with a toast to the King of England, the President of the United States, and Mr. Kalinin of the Supreme Soviet. He asked Roosevelt, the only head of state present, to reply.

Roosevelt answered with a memory from the summer of 1933, his first year as President. His wife had gone to open a school in the country. On its wall hung a map with a great blank space, a place the teacher said it was forbidden to name. The anecdote — about the unrecognized Soviet Union — set the evening's warm tone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d57:
Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 15 January 1945. The cable lists who would travel with him to the conference the Americans code-named Argonaut. It was sent by Navy channels and is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta.

Along with Charles Bohlen, Stettinius names H. Freeman Matthews and Alger Hiss, who would handle Dumbarton Oaks matters. Four secretaries and a military aide chosen by General Marshall complete the party. He also asks Harriman to bring stenographer Nelson Newton to help Bohlen write the minutes. Harriman instead brought Edward Page Jr., as the editors' note explains.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d157:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded another extract of his June 16, 1945 talk with President Truman. The extract is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, drawn from the same White House meeting that produced document 70. This passage turns to China and the Yalta Far East agreement.

Ambassador Hurley had passed on questions from Chiang Kai-shek about how points in the Yalta agreement would be carried out. Grew told the President he saw no way to answer until the matter had been discussed with Stalin, so replies must wait for the Big Three meeting. Nor could China's Dr. Soong well take the questions up with Stalin alone. The President definitely concurred. The passage shows the Yalta Far East bargain hanging over relations with China.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d257:
A briefing paper documented the shut-out of American reporters in Eastern Europe, dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 257 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It supports the agenda item on freedom of communication and information in Europe.

American correspondents have found it practically impossible even to enter the lands freed by the Soviet armies, the paper says. Soviet military authorities and the Soviet-run control commissions have followed a steady policy of exclusion, and applications since December have been refused or ignored. In Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia the picture is only a little better, with strict censorship. Meanwhile Soviet newsmen enjoy the same freedom in the West that American and British reporters do. The paper lays out the record Washington meant to lay before Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d357:
France's exclusion from the reparations talks fills an extract of Grew's memorandum of a June 25, 1945 conversation with Ambassador Bonnet. The French ambassador came to ask a favor. His government wanted the American ambassador in Moscow told to keep the French ambassador there informed of the three-power Reparations Commission's work.

Bonnet stressed France's deep interest in reparations, and its feeling that a French member should have sat on the Commission. France, he said, had suffered greatly in the war. Grew replied that he would give the request prompt consideration. The extract catches France pressing at the door of a club of three.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d457:
Numbers for the Soviet buildup in Bulgaria follow in Kirk's cable of June 30, 1945, again reporting General Oxley. A Russian division, Oxley was informed, had completed crossing the Danube at Ruse about three days earlier. It moved south toward Trnovo and Shumen. His tentative estimate placed ten Soviet divisions across the country.

Two divisions stood near Varna and Burgas, two near Sliven and Kotel, and others toward the Turkish frontier, at Plovdiv, and north of the Balkan mountains. General opinion put Soviet troops in Bulgaria at 200,000 men. Oxley cautioned that many sources were of doubtful truth, but called the picture probably fair, and the best obtainable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d557:
Belgrade charge Harold Shantz wired Washington again on July 14, 1945. His secret report is document 557 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It records a talk that day with Ivan Subasic, Yugoslavia's deputy premier.

Subasic said he would not join the steering group of the new popular front congress. Tito had told him the front would control all political life, and government men must belong to it. Subasic meant to stay in office, since outside it he could sway nothing. Shantz closes with a bleak verdict of his own. There is no hope of free democracy in Yugoslavia, he writes, and new laws will be window dressing for a one-party regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d57:
Field Marshal H. Maitland Wilson, head of the British Joint Staff Mission in Washington, wrote to Admiral William Leahy on June 12, 1945. The letter is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Wilson picks up Leahy's suggestion that the two sides swap ideas on an agenda for their military chiefs.

The British Chiefs of Staff, Wilson reports, agree and go further. They want a formal meeting of the Combined Chiefs of Staff tied to the Big Three gathering, held in London beforehand, with three or four clear days for work. The British chiefs will attend the Berlin meeting with small staffs. The main topic, Wilson says, will be the war against Japan, including whether Russia joins it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d657:
A two-line secret wire from Ambassador Winant in London forms document 657 in the Potsdam papers. Dated June 25, 1945, it settles the venue fight over the Tangier talks. The French government was being told of the outcome through the British Embassy in Paris.

Winant reports that the British government had agreed to a Paris meeting on Tangier. That met France's refusal to send its team to London. Details of the message to the Soviet government were expected to be concerted in Paris at once. Washington would be promptly told when that message was sent. The brief wire closes one small contest and sets up the next. The talks could now open in Paris on July 2, with Moscow informed in parallel.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1057: Assistant Secretary James Dunn answered Nikolai Novikov's note from Berlin on July 27, 1945. The Soviet note had enclosed an aide-mémoire about German troops in Norway. Moscow claimed those troops were not being disarmed under the surrender terms. Dunn's reply is only a few lines. Norway, he points out, is an area of primary British military responsibility. He therefore assumes the British government will supply the information the Soviets seek. The letter closes without offering any American findings of its own.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1157:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson set down this memorandum on 19 July 1945, inside the Potsdam weeks. Stimson was the cabinet's elder statesman. When he put his thinking on paper, the War Department's counsel gained a fixed form the president and the team could use.

His memoranda across the summit gave Truman the military house's view in writing. This one dates from the first week, when stands were forming on Germany and the Pacific war. It is the war secretary's considered word, mid-talks. Readers get the judgment of the man who had run the army's civilian side since 1940.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1257:
Togo wrote to Sato on 27 July 1945, the day after the Potsdam Declaration reached Tokyo. The Allied terms demanded surrender and left the throne's fate unclear. Japan's leaders split over the answer, and Togo, who sought an end, kept his Moscow channel alive.

His instruction to Sato shows the foreign minister still working the Soviet door as the crisis peaked. If Moscow would mediate, Tokyo might gain terms the declaration denied it. That hope, thin as Sato's reports had shown it to be, drove this cable. It is Tokyo's hand on its last lever, pulled on the declaration's morrow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1357:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to the acting secretary of state on 23 July 1945, reporting from the Potsdam side of the Atlantic. The channel between Byrnes and Grew ran in both directions all through the conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Most papers in this run flow from Washington toward the summit, so a message from Byrnes homeward stands out. The secretary abroad still had to steer his own department: staff, budgets, and other talks all needed his hand. Readers get a sense of the two-way strain of summit diplomacy. The man at the table must also run the office he left behind in Washington.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-157:
State Department minutes record a meeting on August 1, 1945, the closing day of the Potsdam Conference. The leaders adopted the final protocol that day. Formal minutes from the close anchor the end of the second Potsdam volume's session records. They were kept by Department staff as the official American account.

Closing-day minutes have a summing-up quality. Readers find the last points cleared and the results stated. The record also marks the handoff: work now passed to foreign ministers and occupation staffs. These pages give the conference a documented end to match its documented start.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-57:
No record has been found of the substance of the conversation at this meeting. That single sentence is the whole of an editorial note in volume two. It is the fifty-seventh unnumbered item following document 710, in the run of conference records for July 1945.

Nothing is added about who met, or where, or what was at stake. The reader who needs the context must reconstruct it from the documents around the note. Such entries recur throughout this volume wherever the editors' searches came up empty. They serve as markers of the archive's limits. A meeting important enough to note took place, and its content is simply gone from the files the editors could search.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d757:
Document 757 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 25, 1945. Staff prepared it during the conference's second week. Working papers carried the detailed load: options, figures, and draft lines. This one stayed in the delegation's files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

The workshop papers of July 25 came after a week of contact. Drafters knew which lines the other sides resisted. Readers can look for that knowledge in the text's shape. The document shows drafting as a response, not a monologue. It forms part of the broad staff record that makes Potsdam so fully knowable.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d857:
Document 857 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 19, 1945. It comes from the conference's first weekend. Staff used the early days to turn positions into draft language. The paper remained in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

First-week working papers show a team still exploring. Options sit side by side, not yet ranked by pain. Readers can enjoy the openness of that stage. Every later text in the volume narrows what papers like this one left wide. The document is a snapshot of possibility, taken before the bargaining began to bite.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d957:
J. Howard Marshall, general counsel to the American reparations delegation, wrote this memorandum on July 30, 1945. He states what the United States should want out of Germany. Two things rank first: German technical knowledge and know-how, and relief from the huge import burden of supporting western Europe.

Knowledge can be gathered in the western zones, Marshall notes. Food, fuel, and potash, though, can come only from the east. Russia wants capital equipment from the west. Marshall's advice is to refuse any such delivery until Russia agrees to ship food, fuel, and fertilizer east to west. Without that trade, American taxpayers pay, and rationing at home tightens.
frus-1961-63v10-d257:
Richard Goodwin's memorandum to President Kennedy reports his 2 a.m. talk with Ernesto Guevara on August 17, 1961, at a Montevideo party. Che arrived in green fatigues, at ease, and spoke with care. Cuba's turn to a socialist, one-party state, he said, cannot be reversed.

Guevara warns against three false hopes: rescue by pressure, a moderate Fidel, or revolt from within. Cuba's case, he argues, fires left thought across the continent. Plane thefts and the Alliance for Progress also come up. Goodwin had no power to bargain. His report gave the White House a rare direct read of Havana's mind.
gao-gaoreports-b-298757:
Hamilton Sundstrand Power Systems protested its removal from an Air Force competition. The buy covered production of large aircraft start system units. Those towable units feed air to start jet engines on the ground. GAO ruled in B-298757 on December 8, 2006.

The agency found the proposal short on key design facts. Talks gave the firm a chance to fill those gaps. The gaps stayed open after that round. GAO found the removal fair on that record. A proposal with many holes in core design points can be cut. The firm had its chance to cure them. It did not. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298957:
3SG Corporation protested a Veterans Affairs order to Xerox Corporation. The buy covered a scanning and archival fix in Anchorage, Alaska. The job would scan an estimated 75,000 pages of records. GAO decided B-298957 on January 5, 2007.

The agency had cast the firm's bid out. It read the bid as a refusal to work at the agency site. GAO read the bid text with care. The bid said in plain terms that work would occur at that site. The agency's gloss on side terms was strained. A bid that states fit terms cannot be cast out on a misread. The rejection was flawed. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299457:
Apptis protested a Defense Information Systems Agency award to ViON Corporation. The contract covered enterprise storage services for defense users. The firm also attacked the use of a contractor as an evaluator. GAO ruled in the B-299457 series on May 23, 2007, with a split result.

The conflict claim came too late, since the plan was known before closing. On the merits, though, key flaws stood. Trial run scores lacked sound papers to back them. Past-record facts were weighed under a risk head where they did not fit. Talks also skipped real flaws in the firm's bid. GAO sustained the protest in part and denied it in part.
gao-gaoreports-b-299557:
A-TEK protested the rejection of its proposal under a General Services Administration buy. The contest sought many awards for information technology services. Some task orders would pay on a cost basis. GAO ruled in B-299557 on May 3, 2007.

The terms asked for proof of a sound accounting system. That proof had to come from a federal audit check. The firm's papers did not supply that check. GAO found the rejection fair on that gap. Cost-based work needs a books system the government can trust. The firm blamed the agency for the gap. That claim did not cure the missing proof. The bid could be cast out. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310357:
Essan Metallix Corporation lost its protest in GAO decision B-310357, dated December 7, 2007. The Army sought British stainless steel tubes. Essan had held the past deal for the tubes. That deal was cut for default in January 2007. The firm had failed four tries to pass first tests of its tubes. The Army then shopped the left work to known tube makers.

GAO denied the protest. An agency may shut a failed firm out of the re-buy of its own left work. The shut-out was fair here. Four failed tests and a default cut give firm ground. A firm that fails its deal cannot claim a right to bid its cure.
gao-gaoreports-b-400157:
Logistics Health, Inc. lost its protest (GAO decision B-400157, dated August 13, 2008). The Army sought a web of tooth care firms for its troops. The call ran as a set-aside for small firms in full. This firm is a large firm that held the past deal. It said the set-aside shut it out with no fair base. The web would serve up to 14 sites for troop checks.

GAO denied the protest. Market scans found eight small firms in the field. Two of them looked fit and sound for the work. Two fit small firms are the bar for a set-aside. That bar was met on this file.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-257:
Telecommunications, GAO-05-257 of April 6, 2005, charts the fast rise of dish TV as a rival to cable. Direct broadcast satellite service began in 1994. It first fit farm and far-off homes best. A 1999 law let it carry local channels, which made it a true rival in towns and cities too. It is now cable's chief foe.

GAO tracks how dish use changed since 2001. It sets town, suburb, and farm rates side by side. It weighs how the kind and strength of cable foes shift those rates. The study rests on federal price survey data and a dish trade group's counts, shaped in a math model.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-457:
Training and testing of airport screeners are updated in GAO report GAO-05-457, released on May 2, 2005. The Transportation Security Administration had revised its basic course and set a rule for ongoing training. GAO drew on six past products and a survey of 155 Federal Security Directors. It asked what training had improved, whether required training was being finished, and how well screeners were checked at finding threat items.

A new online learning center put courses within reach of screeners. But short staffing and slow Internet links at some sites made the weekly training goal hard to meet. GAO also found weak controls over required training. Duties for checking that training was done were not clear, and records of remedial training were missing. Tools to test screener performance had grown stronger, yet key targets were still not final. The report shows an improving system with loose follow-through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-557:
Screening cargo containers at foreign ports is the work of a program reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-557, released on April 26, 2005. Customs and Border Protection began the Container Security Initiative in January 2002. Its staff target high-risk shipments overseas and have them inspected before sailing. GAO had flagged management problems in 2003.

Sharing with foreign customs staff has grown stronger, and teamwork across borders has improved. Yet staffing gaps mean the program cannot target every U.S.-bound shipment from its ports. As a result, 35 percent of shipments were not targeted, and so not inspected overseas. The staffing model also ties staff to ports even when some work could be done from home. A second gap concerns gear. The agency has set no minimum standard for the detection power of the scanning and radiation tools used. That leaves little proof that inspections can in fact find hidden weapons.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-757:
Coast Guard deepwater ships and aircraft are reviewed in GAO-05-757, issued July 22, 2005. The old fleet was failing at a rate the service called unsustainable. A repair and replace program began in 2002. Its cost was put at $19 to $24 billion. GAO tracked fleet condition from fiscal years 2000 to 2004. It also checked care steps and buying risks.

GAO found that the condition of most old aircraft and cutters fell over that span. The service's own measures do not capture the full decline. Crews now do heavier repairs between trips, yet ships still lose mission ability. The service has begun new plans to rank repairs and to measure condition better. Buying new assets on a faster path holds added risk, GAO warned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-957:
A metals waiver for Air Force planes is faulted in GAO-05-957, dated September 23, 2005. A law called the Berry Amendment requires defense buys of U.S.-grown or made goods, including specialty metals. In April 2004, the Air Force chief waived it for good for 23 aircraft types. They cover over 1,200 planes. GAO judged the evidence and analysis behind the waiver. It ran no legal analysis of the move.

GAO found the Air Force skipped its own policy steps. It did not study compliance options plane by plane. Its case rested on visits to one maker, two subcontractors, and an engine maker in early 2003. From that base, it assumed others would also fail to comply. A temporary waiver for 19 types came in September 2003. The permanent one added 4 more. Policy called for market research and an alternatives study first, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-57:
Late rent aid payments can leave building owners short on mortgage and repair money. Report GAO-06-57, issued November 15, 2005, reviews project-based rental assistance. The Department of Housing and Urban Development pays subsidies under contracts with private multifamily projects. The payments keep homes affordable for low-income households. Owners said the department had chronically paid late in recent years. Late payments could strain operating costs and upkeep funds.

GAO was asked to discuss how timely the monthly payments are. It identifies factors that affect payment timing. It also describes effects of delays on project owners. The department should streamline its processes, GAO said. The goal is timely assistance payments.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-757:
False anthrax alarms at military mail sites are investigated in GAO-06-757. The report is dated September 15, 2006. In March 2005, two nearly simultaneous scares hit Defense Department mail facilities in the Washington area. One was at the Pentagon, and the other at a commercial office complex. Both proved to be false alarms, but agencies responded for days. The Postal Service suspended some operations while tests ran.

GAO found that the two incidents unfolded in different ways. Problems reflected both a failure to follow existing contract rules and procedures, and a lack of plans for some situations. The department took many actions after the scares. Yet GAO said those actions did not fully resolve the problems found. Further steps were required to ready mail sites for the next alarm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-157:
Private firms can inspect medical device plants in place of the Food and Drug Administration. GAO reported on that program's slow start in GAO-07-157, issued January 5, 2007. A 2002 law told the agency to accredit outside inspection firms. The firms check plants that sell devices in the U.S. and abroad. GAO counted applicants, accreditations, and inspections through October 31, 2006. It also asked what might draw makers to pay for such checks.

The agency accredited 17 of 23 organizations that applied, GAO found. Two were refused for weak technical skill. Two more sent in faulty applications. Yet almost no inspections had taken place under the program. Accredited firms ran just two inspections on their own in over two years. They ran 36 more in the United States and one abroad jointly with agency staff as training. Only 7 of 16 firms had finished training to work alone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-357:
Tsunami rebuilding in Indonesia and Sri Lanka is costing more and taking longer than planned. GAO reviewed the aid program in GAO-07-357, a report dated February 28, 2007. Congress gave $908 million after the December 2004 disaster. The aid agency runs $482 million of the work. GAO examined its showcase projects in both countries. Site visits took place in August and October 2006.

Costs rose and scope shrank in Indonesia, GAO found. The agency had spent $58 million of its $351 million country budget by December 2006. Its showcase road dropped from 150 miles to 91 miles. Cost per mile jumped 68 percent, to about $2.7 million. The main road contract was still unawarded in February 2007. Land purchase snags slowed several projects. Both countries faced possible deadline extensions. GAO pressed for updated cost and schedule reporting to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-457:
Aid work in Burma runs into walls set by its military rulers, as GAO-07-457, a GAO report from April 6, 2007, records. Burma is among the poorest and most cut-off states on earth. United Nations (UN) groups and other global bodies form a key source of outside help. Their funding had grown in recent years. The regime had answered with fresh limits on their work.

GAO listed the main aid efforts aimed at Burma's health, food, and social needs. It then traced how new curbs, such as travel bans and red tape, shrank those efforts. Staff spoke with UN, U.S., and Burmese officials and saw project sites in person. The report shows a hard trade: aid reaches people in need, but each rule from the regime trims what helpers can do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-557:
Most drugs given to children were never tested on children, and GAO-07-557, a GAO report dated March 22, 2007, judges a law meant to change that. About two-thirds of drugs prescribed for children lack studies and labels for child use. That gap risks wrong doses and weak results. The Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act of 2002 pays drug makers to run child studies. The prize is 6 extra months with no generic rivals.

GAO studied the requests the Food and Drug Administration sent from 2002 through 2005. It counted how many studies firms ran and how many they refused. It tracked how labels changed once results came in. The diseases covered range widely, from infections to rare ills. The verdict is mixed: the prize does pull studies into being, but refusals and slow label updates leave gaps that Congress may want to close.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-657:
When government laptops vanish with private data, word must move fast, and GAO-07-657, dated April 30, 2007, draws lessons from real breaches. A May 2006 breach at the Department of Veterans Affairs put millions of records at risk. Like cases at other agencies since then sharpened the point. GAO studied the VA case plus five others. Each involved lost or stolen gear and at least 10,000 people affected.

The lessons are plain. Top officials must hear of a breach at once. A named team must stand ready to rule on whom to tell and how. Address lists are often stale, slowing the letters. Staff drills matter before the crisis, not during it. Contractor duties must be spelled out in advance. The budget office has issued guidance since, GAO notes. One gap stays: no rule says when to offer credit monitoring to victims. GAO told the budget chief to write one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-857:
Who counts as a college under federal law is weighed in GAO-07-857, dated July 31, 2007. The Higher Education Act holds two definitions of an institution of higher education. The broad one covers public, nonprofit, and for-profit schools. Their students can reach $83.1 billion in aid. A narrow one bars for-profit schools from nearly $1.96 billion in other funds. GAO searched the U.S. Code for programs the change would touch.

No mandatory spending programs rest on the narrow definition, GAO found. A single definition would thus not lift federal spending at once. More schools could compete for grant funds, though. Few for-profit schools run the science programs many grants target. Long-term effects on spending stay unclear. The Education Department argued the change could raise costs via postal rates and tax breaks. GAO doubted the postal claim and said tax law does not use these definitions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-157:
Enforcement against faked goods is reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-157 (March 11, 2008). Counterfeit and pirated goods cheat rights holders and can endanger buyers. Five federal agencies share the fight. Customs seizes goods at the border. Other bodies probe crimes, and justice officials prosecute them. A joint center coordinates the work.

GAO found that such enforcement has broadly grown in recent years. Still, it ranks low among agency priorities, and few staff work on it alone. Gains are hard to prove without better use of data. GAO set out four actions, led by sharper analysis of enforcement figures across the agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-57:
Drug-Free Communities grants are audited in GAO report GAO-08-57, dated July 31, 2008. The program funds local coalitions that fight youth drug use; 25 percent of students ages 13 to 17 reported illicit drug use in 2007. The drug control policy office runs the program and picked a health agency to operate grants in fiscal year 2005.

Grant making in fiscal years 2005 and 2006 broke rules and controls, GAO found. The policy office did not monitor its operator as standards require. Proof of eligibility screening was missing from 47 of 66 grantee files checked. One side screening track let about 86 percent of 2005 renewal grantees be funded without a full eligibility check. Roles in the joint agreement were vague. The office described fixes it has made since.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-657:
Farm benefit programs stalled when the Agriculture Department's computers froze in January 2007 and stayed down for 1 month. GAO-08-657, dated May 16, 2008, reviews the fix-it plan and the long-term rebuild, called MIDAS. Reviewers asked whether the plans fix management flaws, not just machines.

The short-term plan added capacity and backup tools. But it skipped key flaws: user problem reports were tracked in uneven ways, no staff owned performance data, and roles were unclear. That left leaders unsure the systems would hold up. GAO told the department to write clear plans for those gaps and to build cost and time guesses it can trust.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-757:
Fake papers got undercover testers into the country again and again. GAO-08-757, dated May 16, 2008, sums up secret tests and site checks from January 2003 to September 2007. Testers tried land, sea, and air entry points, plus open border stretches between them.

Testers crossed 42 times with a 93 percent success rate. Inspectors often took fake IDs or mere spoken claims as proof of citizenship. At some spots no ID was asked at all. Open border areas with no staff or sensors drew concern too. The report gathers the proof behind calls to harden entry checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-857:
The auditors who check defense contractors were themselves accused of sloppy work. The Defense Contract Audit Agency follows national audit standards by choice. GAO-08-857, dated July 22, 2008, probes hotline claims about 14 audits at three offices.

GAO upheld the claims. In three audits, contractor staff and buyers swayed the scope and verdicts, a grave breach of independence. At two offices, papers did not back the verdicts, bosses dropped findings without proof, and too little work was done. A third office had weak supervision. Case tables show how verdicts were softened. The findings strike at trust in contract audits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-957:
Do companies owned from abroad pay less U.S. tax than U.S.-owned ones? GAO-08-957, a July 2008 report, compares the tax bills of foreign-controlled and U.S.-controlled corporations from 1998 through 2005. Worry about transfer pricing, the prices sister companies charge each other, drives the question. GAO updated three earlier reports with the newest data available.

By most measures, the foreign-controlled firms reported lower tax. A larger share of big foreign-controlled firms reported no tax at all in a given year, and they were more likely to report none over several years. For all firms, the no-tax gap was clear through 2001 but not statistically firm after that. Most big firms owing nothing in 2005 also reported no income that year. The two groups also differ in age, size, and industry mix.
gaskell-life-of-charlotte-bronte-1857:
Elizabeth Gaskell published The Life of Charlotte Brontë in 1857, two years after Brontë's death. Charlotte's father and husband asked Gaskell, her friend, to write the authorized life of her. The book fixed the Brontë myth of the lonely moorland parsonage for the next century.

Gaskell traces Haworth's graves, the sisters' childhood worlds, and their secret writing lives in detail. She tells of Brussels, the Bell books, fame, and the deaths that emptied the house. Some portraits of living people drew threats of lawsuits and forced cuts in later editions printed. Her warm, novelistic hand made the life read like one of Brontë's own tales of Yorkshire. It remains the source all later Brontë lives must start from and argue with.
gosse-omphalos-1857:
Philip Henry Gosse tries to untie the knot of Genesis and geology in Omphalos, from 1857. God, he argues, created the world with the look of age upon it. Fossils lie in the rocks as Adam bore a navel, signs of a past that never truly happened in his bold and strange solution.

Geologists and clergy alike rejected the clever argument at once. The book appeared just as Darwin's Origin loomed over the age. Ingenious yet untestable, it convinced almost no one on either side. It stands as the most famous failed peace treaty between Genesis and geology, a landmark of creationist thought in the Victorian age.
hegel-philosophy-history-sibree-1857:
G. W. F. Hegel gave his Lectures on the Philosophy of History in Berlin in the 1820s. The English text here is J. Sibree's translation of 1857. Hegel argues that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Each great people, from China to the German world, plays its part and passes.

He divides history into Oriental, Greek, Roman, and German worlds. Reason, he claims, governs the whole process despite war and suffering. The state is the main carrier of freedom in his account. These lectures seeded Marxism and all later philosophy of history. They remain grand, bold, and hotly debated.
hitchcock-remarks-upon-alchemy-1857:
Ethan Allen Hitchcock made the first case in the United States for a soul first read of the great art. His Remarks upon Alchemy and the Alchemists came out in 1857. Hitchcock was a chief of troops who read old adepts at night in camp. He held their gold was a code for man's soul.

He walks through the chief names and their dark signs with care. His claim was fresh in his land and day. The book set the great art down in that land's thought. Waite and his peers later hailed its worth. Hitchcock served in wars on the far shore of his land. He brought a camp man's plain sense to a theme prone to sheer fog.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-josep: Aaron ben Joseph of Buda was a Judaeo-German poet of the seventeenth century. He was captured in Ofen, the capital of Hungary, on September 2, 1686. Imperial troops under Duke Charles of Lorraine took the city from the Turks that day. His poem "Ein Schoen Neu Lied von Ofen" was printed at Prague in 1686. It describes the fate of the Jews of Buda. The poem is dedicated to Sender ben Joseph Tausk, whom it praises warmly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-moses:
Aaron ben Moses ben Asher, commonly called Ben Asher, was a distinguished Masorite of Tiberias. He flourished in the first half of the tenth century. His family of Masorites reaches back six generations to Asher the Elder, of the last half of the eighth century.

Aaron wrote a manuscript of the Old Testament with vowel signs and accents. He revised it several times over many years of study. That codex became the standard for later generations, and the present Masoretic text rests largely on his work. He also wrote short treatises on Masoretic and grammatical subjects, and a list of eighty homonyms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abi-and-ab-in-p: Abi and Ab are parts found in Hebrew proper names, the entry explains. They can stand first, as in Abijah, Abishur, Abinoam, and Abner. They can also stand second, as in Eliab, Joab, and Ahab. Their exact sense is still argued over. Each such name may be a whole sentence, or only a phrase. The vowel in Abi may be a link sound, or a suffix meaning my. Most scholars lean to the sentence form, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-b-moses:
Abraham b. Moses Cohen was a learned rabbi, likely of Spanish origin, who lived in Italy in the first half of the sixteenth century. He died about 1550. Early writers mixed him up with Abraham of Pisa, and some facts about him stay in doubt.

His known work was as editor of Judah he-Hasid's Sefer Hasidim. He added a contents list of one hundred columns, a long preface, and an epilogue. He also wrote a supercommentary on Rashi and one on the Sheiltot, plus sermons and responsa. None of those works was ever published, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adalberg-samuel: Samuel Adalberg was a Polish author born at Warsaw in 1868. His great work holds forty thousand Polish proverbs. It came out at Warsaw from 1889 to 1894. The entry calls it the largest set of its kind. He also gave strong work to the study of proverbs in Polish and in Jewish use. His Jewish proverb work ran in the journal "Wisla" in 1890. It then came out as a book of 985 pages. No facts beyond the work and its size are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahabah-rabbah-g:
Ahabah Rabbah, "Great Love," and Ahabat 'Olam, "Everlasting Love," are the opening words of two benedictions. Both stand just before the Shema' in the service. The first is used in the morning service of the German ritual. The second is used in the evening service of both rituals, and in Sephardic mornings.

The entry traces the split back to Rab and Samuel. They arranged the prayers for the Babylonian schools. The blessing itself gives thanks for God's love for Israel, shown in the Torah. Over time, words were added by later hands. A text Zunz held to be sixty-two words grew to one hundred and two in the German form. The entry prints full translations of both the morning and evening versions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alaish-1057:
Alaish is the name of a Spanish-Jewish family, found in several forms. It usually comes with "abu" before it. Abu-al-'aish means "Father of Life" in Arabic, or "Father of Bread." As Bolaix, the name stands in a Barcelona list of Jews from 1391.

An Isaac ibn al-Aish served as tax officer to Queen Maria. A Solomon ibn Aish is probably the physician of that name who died at Seville in 1345. Joseph ibn Alaish was a rabbi at Alcala who died in 1349. His pupil Menahem ben Aaron tells how they read the Tosafot of R. Perez together. An Abolays is named as the supposed Arabic translator of a Chaldean book on the magic powers of stones. The modern forms of the name are Belais and Balaiss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-suuml: Alexander Süsskind ben Moses Kantshiger was a Biblical scholar of the eighteenth century. His work is "Miznefet Bad," which means The Linen Miter. It came out at Zolkiev in 1747. It is a set of studies on how the Pentateuch is arranged. The book follows the order of the weekly sections. The entry warns against mixing him up with Alexander Süsskind ben Moses of Grodno. Fürst and Benjacob both give Moses as this author's father's name. No dates for his own life are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allegory-in-the:
Allegory in the Old Testament is a tale with a second sense. The tale speaks of one thing on its face. It points to a higher truth by a clear likeness. Hebrew wisdom grouped such forms under two terms. One term meant a likeness or wise saying. The other meant a riddle or veiled speech.

Fable, parable, and allegory stand close yet differ. A fable uses beasts or plants that speak. Its lesson stays in the world of daily life. The entry gives the tale of the trees picking a king. The bramble takes the crown that good trees refuse. That tale is then read against Abimelech and Shechem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amariah-1357: Amariah is a name borne by ten men in the Bible. The entry lists each man with his verse. One was the great-grandfather of Zephaniah the prophet. One was high priest in the Temple of Solomon. One signed the pact in the days of Nehemiah. One came back from exile with Zerubbabel. One had charge of sacred affairs under Jehoshaphat. One helped at the Temple gate under Hezekiah. The list runs from priestly lines to a man who had wed a foreign wife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anan-1457:
Anan was a Babylonian teacher of the third century. He learned under Mar Samuel. He was a peer of Rab Huna. His fame rests on his care as a judge. He was known for an utmost sense of right. Tales link him to the prophet Elijah. Two books are said to have come from Elijah's visits.

Nahman once mocked a point of law by Anan. He said Anan must have played at draughts in class. Still Nahman held him high and called him Master. Huna took a note from Anan as a slight. That note brought Anan deep shame in the clash. His school kept his name in its own title. Much of his thought may live in that school's words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apostol-daniil-:
Daniil Pavlovich Apostol was hetman of the Cossacks on both sides of the Dnieper. Born in South Russia in 1658, he died on December 15, 1734. His place in this encyclopedia rests on one act: he was the first to ask that a harsh law against Jews be softened.

When Catherine I expelled the Jews from the Ukraine on May 7, 1727, Apostol applied to the senate for relief. Cossacks, who eighty years earlier had massacred Jews in huge numbers, had learned they could not trade without Jewish merchants. His plea won an edict of September 2, 1728, letting Jews attend Little Russian fairs as wholesale traders only. Later edicts widened the right, even to retail trade at fairs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arianism-1757:
Arianism was a heresy of the Christian Church begun by Arius, bishop of Alexandria, who died in 336. He taught that the Son is not of one substance with the Father. His teaching split the Church badly, and that split in turn touched the fortunes of Jews in many lands, the entry says.

Most Germanic peoples, Goths, Franks, Lombards, Suevi, and Vandals, were baptized as Arians and settled across the old Roman empire. Jews in those lands thus fell under Arian rule. The entry contrasts that rule with the orthodox Church's: Arian rule was marked by wise tolerance and mild treatment of other faiths. Part of the reason, it argues, is a plain sense of justice; part is that Arian teaching on the Son stands nearer the Jewish view of the Messiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-baeru:
Baerush Dob Ashkenazi was rabbi at Slonim in Lithuania and later at Lublin in Poland. Born about 1801, he died at Lublin on March 6, 1852. His brother Abraham Aryeh published his works after his death. The first, Noda ba-Shearim, Known in the Gates, came out at Warsaw in 1849.

That book holds legal answers on the Eben he-Ezer, new readings on tractate Gittin, and rules on majority and possession, with sermons at the end. The second, Shaare Yerushalaim, The Gates of Jerusalem, followed at Warsaw in 1866. It comments on the Seder Zeraim of the Jerusalem Talmud and adds notes on treatises of both Talmuds and on the work of Isaac Alfasi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astruc-des-gabb: Astruc des Gabbai, also called Abba Mari ben Abraham, was a Provençal scholar. He lived at Béziers at the end of the thirteenth century and the start of the fourteenth. The entry is frank about how little survives of him. Nothing is known of his life, and nothing is known of his scholarly work. His name comes down through a relative, perhaps his grandson, the poet Abraham Bedersi. In an elegy for Don Bonafos Roguet, Bedersi also mourns Astruc, who had died several years before.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ave-lallement-f: Frederick Christian Benedict Avé-Lallement was a noted writer on crime. He was born in Lübeck on May 23, 1809, and died there on July 20, 1892. His standard work on German rogues and thieves came out at Leipsic in 1858-62. One chapter of it treats the Jews, in terms hostile to their morals. In the long fight of Lübeck's Jews for equal rights, he stood with their foes. He held that the Jew had harmed the world's trade since the days of the Patriarchs. Gabriel Riesser answered his newspaper attacks in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baal-zephon-225:
Baal-zephon was an Egyptian place near the Red Sea. For all the attempts made to place it, its site was still unknown when the entry was written. Egyptian sources name a goddess whose name echoes the place. The Phoenician tongue has a matching name for both a god and a city on Mount Lebanon. Whether the Egyptian city, the Egyptian goddess, and the Phoenician name truly connect is not certain, the entry says.

Rabbinic tale adds a point of its own. This idol alone stood unharmed when the tenth plague struck Egypt and broke the idols. God spared it on purpose, the tale says, to deepen Pharaoh's folly as he chased Israel to the sea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahamonte-benit: Benito Lopez Bahamonte was a Spanish Christian who wrote a Hebrew grammar. The hosted entry is a bare two-line notice, and it states only that much about him. His book was made for school use and bears a Spanish title meaning a grammar of the Hebrew language, written in Castilian. It was printed at Madrid in 1818. No dates for his life, no post he held, and no word on his other work appear in the text given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baptista-giovan:
Giovanni Giona Galileo Baptista was a baptized Jew who taught Hebrew and served as a Vatican librarian. He was born in Safed on Oct. 28, 1588, and died May 26, 1668. His Jewish name was Judah Jonah ben Isaac. He studied Talmud, traveled as a rabbi through Italy and Poland, and was elected dayyan in Hamburg. In 1625 he went back to Poland and turned Christian at Warsaw.

Driven from Poland, Baptista settled in Italy. He taught Hebrew first at Pisa, then at the Neophyte College of Rome, and later joined the Vatican library staff. The entry lists his works. Chief among them are a Hebrew version of Bellarmin's catechism in 1658 and "Berit Ḥadashah," a Hebrew New Testament with a preface by Clement IX. A study of the differences among the three Targumim was left unfinished, its manuscript kept in the Vatican Library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bartholdy-jacob:
Jacob Salomon Bartholdy, Prussian diplomat and art patron, was born in Berlin on May 13, 1779 and died in Rome on July 27, 1825. He was the uncle of Felix Mendelssohn-Bartholdy. Of a prosperous Jewish family, he studied at Halle and toured Greece with the artist Gropius. His book on modern Greece appeared in 1805. In Dresden the pastor Reinhard converted him to Protestantism that same year. He later died in that faith.

Bartholdy fought against Napoleon in 1809 and was severely wounded at Ebersberg. In 1815 he became Prussian consul-general to Italy and settled in Rome. He engaged Cornelius, Overbeck, Schadow, and Veit to fresco his house, the Casa Bartholdy. The Joseph frescoes were later bought by the Prussian government for the National Gallery in Berlin. Berlin's museum also bought his collection of Etruscan vases, bronzes, and ivories. The entry credits him with a fresh impulse to the revival of fresco-painting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beeroth-wells-2: Beeroth was one of the cities of the Gibeonites, which fell to the tribe of Benjamin after the conquest. That hold seems to have been brief. Second Samuel reports that its people fled to Gittaim in time. The name returns in the lists of exiles who came back with Zerubbabel, in both Ezra and Nehemiah. The entry matches the town to the modern El-Bireh and points readers to two works on the geography of ancient Palestine for its grounds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-of-can: Benjamin of Canterbury was an English rabbi and a pupil of Rabbi Tam. He died at the start of the thirteenth century. Only one ruling of his is known. It bars buying milk from a Gentile unless a Jew is present when the milk is drawn. Notes on a work by Joseph Ḳimḥi have also been tied to his name. The entry weighs whether he came from Canterbury or from Cambridge instead, and notes a Magister Benjamin of Cambridge in the records of 1204.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bereza-cartuska: Bereza, called Kartuskaya, is a town in the government of Grodno, in Russia, on the river Jazelda. In 1890 its Jewish population was 850 out of a total of 2,625 people. Jews first settled there in 1629. A charter from Grand Duke Sapieha let them build a house of prayer and hold services without disturbance. It also let them build homes as they wished and share the rights of Jews on his other estates. His son confirmed the grant in his own hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berr-george-315:
George Berr, born at Paris on July 31, 1867, was a French actor and dramatist, brother of the journalist Emile Berr. He left classical studies at sixteen for the Conservatoire, won its first prize for comedy in 1886, and joined the Comédie Française, becoming a sociétaire in 1892.

The entry praises his range, from Rostand's "Romanesques" to Banville's "Gringoire," where he was judged equal to Coquelin, and notes his appointment in 1901 as professor of declamation at the Conservatoire. Writing as "Colias," he produced comedies, a pantomime, and a comic opera, several of them with collaborators such as Paul Gavault.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bibel-sche-orie: "Der Bibel'sche Orient" was a short-lived magazine. Only two numbers ever appeared. They came out at Munich in 1821. Isaac Bernays is supposed to have edited it. Its stated aim was to show the sacred books' spirit. It promised purity without learned verbosity. The entry calls its style dark and mystical. Schelling's philosophy shaped it strongly. It read mythology into the Scriptures. It favored Reform more boldly than Mendelssohn's circle. The magazine drew notice at first. Then it was soon forgotten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blau-ludwig-335: Ludwig Blau was a Hungarian scholar and publicist. He was born at Putnok on April 29, 1861. He trained at three yeshibot, including Presburg's. He studied at Budapest's rabbinical school and university. He took his doctorate in 1887. His rabbinical diploma followed in 1888. In 1889 he became professor at the school. He taught Bible, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Talmud. Since 1891 he edited the "Magyar Zsido Szemle." His writings treat Talmudic-era Jewish life. One book studies ancient Jewish magic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bodek-herman-34:
Herman Bodek was a Galician Hebraist born in Brody on Sept. 27, 1820. He died at Leipsic on Aug. 19, 1880. He lived long in Leipsic as a court translator of Hebrew and a man of business.

Bodek wrote for Jewish journals in several lands. His book Eleh Dibre ha-Berit, printed in 1880, explains the signs and objects of Freemasonry. It drew on German works on the subject. He wrote it mainly for Jewish Masons in the Orient. Bodek himself belonged to a Masonic lodge in Leipsic. His learning covered both rabbinical books and newer Hebrew writing. Readers in several lands knew his name from those journal pieces over many years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bravo-abraham-3: Abraham Bravo was a financier living in London in 1710. He came from a Spanish-Portuguese family. The entry counts him among the earliest Anglo-Jewish poets. In English verse he praised a work by his friend Daniel Israel Lopez Laguna. Laguna had translated the psalms from Spanish. Another Abraham Bravo, surely a kinsman, lived in Jamaica in 1773. Benjamin and David Bravo went from London to Jamaica and were naturalized there in 1740, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bruck-max-miksa: Max Bruck, called Miksa, was a Hungarian painter born at Budapest in 1863. A brother of Lajos Bruck, he showed a gift for drawing while still at school. He studied at the National Academy of Design and worked at wood carving. In 1880 he went with his brother to Paris and stayed several years, then spent three years in Munich. Back home he entered Benczúr's School of Arts. The entry calls him a professor at the Academy of Painting. It lists pictures held at the imperial castles in Vienna and Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-butrymowicz-mat:
Matheus Butrymowicz was a Polish statesman and landlord of the eighteenth century, from an old Lithuanian family. He sat in the Warsaw Diet from 1788 to 1792 and ranked among its most enlightened members. He cared deeply about Polish trade and industry. To build both, he argued, Poland had to use the energy of its Jewish inhabitants.

In 1789 he published a plan to turn Polish Jews into useful citizens and laid it before the king. He showed that Polish law shut Jews out of the realm's three estates. Jews paid special taxes yet held no citizen rights, and land law barred them from farming. When the Diet formed a reform committee in June 1790, he served as an active member. He defended Jewish faith and pushed for shared civic life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carnival-4057:
Carnival, in Rome, was a season of games in the weeks before Lent. Jews were forced to take a degrading part in it. Pope Paul II widened the Roman games with footraces.
