pmc-11597857:
Shahinur Acter, Lindokuhle Ngema, Michele Moreau, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It introduces PRIMERS, a nanoparticle system that combines cancer treatment with imaging, so doctors can watch the therapy as it works.

Standard cancer treatments often harm healthy tissue. The system starts with tiny bowls made of polydopamine, a sticky polymer, then coats them with gadolinium, a metal that lights up on MRI scans. The bowls showed a strong MRI signal in lab dishes and in animals. They can also carry drugs, including an immune therapy antibody, and release them faster in the acidic setting found in tumors. The authors present the bowls as markers that could anchor combination therapy, pairing radiation, immune drugs, and imaging in one platform.
pmc-11605357:
Doudou Yang and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-four bibliometric analysis of research on Codonopsis pilosula, a traditional Asian herb. The plant is gaining official recognition as both medicine and food. No overview of its research landscape existed.

Thousands of papers from many countries and institutions were mapped with three analysis tools. Output grew in three stages, from slow beginnings to an explosive recent phase. Leading countries, authors, journals, and funders were identified. Highly cited works and emerging frontiers were charted. The map helps new researchers see where this herb's science is heading.
pmc-11608357:
Renzheng Wang and four colleagues tune the switching of a seven-level inverter with an enhanced particle swarm method, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Selective harmonic elimination gives excellent harmonic quality. Its bent equation system, though, is hard to solve, and that blocks real use. Their stronger swarm method aims to converge fast to the global optimum.

The method lifts the spread of its swarm in two phases. Opposition-based learning upgrades the first swarm. In each round, self-tuning swarm search combines with several other tricks to escape local optima. Tests on nineteen benchmark functions put the method ahead of rival tools. On the inverter problem it solved about three times faster than standard particle swarm optimization. Its picks stayed sharp, with small output error. The work targets cleaner power for inverters with many levels.
pmc-11611157:
Samuel Hylander and six co-authors track vitamin B1 as it climbs the sea food web. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The vitamin, thiamin, is made by bacteria and plankton, while every eater above them must take it in with food.

Shortage of thiamin harms reproduction in fish and birds worldwide. The team used outdoor sea bags of about two cubic meters, adding thiamin, nutrients, or both, and measured uptake through the plankton chain. Phytoplankton grabbed the vitamin fast in both plain and fed bags. Their numbers were then set against published levels across feeding levels. No general rule yet governs how such vitamins pass upward. The study supplies rare measured rates for one key vitamin.
pmc-11611657:
Sunghwan Kim and colleagues studied repeated suicide attempts in Korean adolescents in two thousand twenty-four. Research on teen suicide in South Korea remains scarce. The team used ten years of hospital repository data. Teenagers arrived at one emergency department after attempts. Psychiatric interviews assessed each young person. First-time and repeat attempters were compared directly.

Repeat attempters were mostly female. They showed more severe mental health problems overall. Family psychiatric history appeared more often in this group. Hopelessness and helplessness feelings ran higher. Their suicidal thinking was more repetitive and severe. Regret after the attempt was lower. Clinicians gain markers flagging repeat risk early. Follow-up care can focus there.
pmc-11612357:
Gaston van Hassel and ten colleagues track kidney decline in patients born with a heart fixed by the Fontan operation, in a twenty twenty-four study. This surgery reroutes blood flow for children with one working heart chamber. Kidney harm is common in heart disease but was little mapped in this group. The team followed eighty-two patients over eleven years with repeated kidney blood tests.

Kidney scores fell about twice as fast as in healthy peers. Twelve percent met the bar for kidney dysfunction on one test, and twice that share on a second test. The authors link the decline rate to death risk using joint models. They urge routine kidney checks in Fontan follow-up.
pmc-11621457:
JunHwa Kwon and his team set out a paired-charge way to add hydrogen into metal oxides in a set, checked way. Their 2024 study is at base level. It uses molybdenum trioxide as the test case and checks what the change does to the work of lithium cells.

Moves of protons twixt stuff were worked on in fine grain in plain air. When the oxide took in protons, its frame of parts shifted. That shift let lithium move fast on picked sheets of the frame. The new path made high-rate work and life through charge rounds more firm in cell tests. Charge tests and first-rule math checks backed the same read. The team says set hydrogen steps give a sound route to good swap-charge acts in sheet oxides. Such stuff is used for stored charge and for more fields.
pmc-11622657:
Arthur Ling, Eng Wah Teo, and Ngien Siong Chin build a questionnaire to measure commitment to recreational sport. A lack of physical activity is a global problem. Recreational sport is a key outlet for healthy lifestyles. Yet no tool graded the commitment of recreational and leisure sport users. Their Recreational Sport Commitment Questionnaire was built in four stages: item generation, content and face validation, data collection, and psychometric assessment.

A first pool of sixty items was cut by expert review to forty-two. A first factor study on one sample suggested thirty-one items across seven factors. A confirming study on a second sample set the final twenty-six-item instrument, with fit indices in the good range. It also showed proof that it measures what it should, sets groups apart, and holds together well. A validated measure lets providers distinguish casual participation from durable commitment.
pmc-11624757:
Cihan Önen, Ahmet Göktaş, and Şerafettin Okutan published a case-control study in twenty twenty-four on anxiety and sleep among family caregivers of psychiatric patients in Bitlis, Turkey. Some of these caregivers had been injured by sharp objects during the patient's illness. The team asked whether that history deepened the anxiety and poor sleep link.

One hundred eleven caregivers were interviewed at a community mental health center and a state hospital. Over half slept poorly, and more than half had moderate or severe anxiety. Each extra anxiety point raised the odds of bad sleep, and the connection ran stronger in caregivers who had been injured. The authors highlight a hidden burden on families.
pmc-11638457:
Tianying Zheng and his team build a self-run brain-like net to find a scarred liver from MRI scans joined with blood marks. Their 2024 study is based at lots of sites. It tests the tool next to stage of the ill made firm by flesh tests, in more than thirteen hundred sick folk.

The pic model was taught on stock scan kinds, then joined with age and eight blood marks. Sixty-five in each hundred of sick folk had a scarred liver made firm. On outside tests, the joined model scored grades for right calls much more high than two stock blood-based scores. It beat two scan docs on that count. Checks by subgroup showed like work through groups. The self-run plan needs no hand marks on scans and gives a find path that does not cut into the body, which beat plain picks here.
pmc-11642657:
Chen and five co-authors studied adding aluminum to gear steel in twenty twenty-four. Gears of 20MnCr5 steel are carburized and quenched, hardening the surface for long contact fatigue life. The team asked how aluminum changes the tooth surface under different heat treatments.

They measured retained austenite, a softer phase left after quenching, and compressive residual stress locked into the surface. Microscopy and X-ray tools tracked grain size and phases at fine scales. Aluminum plus tuned carburizing raised surface compressive stress at depth and reduced harmful inclusions. A deeper hardened layer also improved wear resistance. Together these changes eased fatigue crack growth, and experiments showed significantly longer gear life. The authors present the recipe as a route to more durable gears.
pmc-11643657:
Dan Zhu and co-workers tested a new stuff that uses shake force to break down dye waste. Such stuff, called piezocatalytic, turns force from motion straight into chemical acts for water care. The team made gamma-AlON bits through heat steps with carbon and nitrogen. They put 40 milligrams of bits in dye baths and shook them with sound waves for two hours. Four plain dyes were put to the test.

Break down hit near 78 percent for rhodamine B. The rest broke down at near 65 to 74 percent. Tests with trap agents probed how it works. They pointed to hydroxyl and superoxide bits as key parts of the act. The 2024 study is the first told use of this stuff in this role. It hints that shake driven clean up could treat dye waste water with no added drugs.
pmc-11643857:
Giuseppe Castaldo and six colleagues test whether a gentler diet can maintain the gains of a ketogenic diet in fibromyalgia, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Their earlier work put twenty-two women on a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic therapy. Scores for symptoms, mind strain, and gut imbalance all improved. Metabolic markers shifted across pathways tied to fibromyalgia.

After forty-five days, the women moved to a low-glycemic, low-insulinemic diet for forty-five more days. The question was whether the ketogenic gains would survive the switch. The first diet fixed metabolic flaws and eased symptoms well. The follow-on diet then preserved the clinical gains. It also offers a practical plan that lasts and helps patients stick with it. The authors stress adaptable nutrition for chronic disease care.
pmc-11644457:
Senila and coauthors assess life cycle costs of bioplastics from orchard waste. Bioplastics can replace oil-based plastics since they rot and are non-toxic. Orchard waste offers a farm source for such plastics. The team compared two bioplastics by full life cycle.

One plastic was made from orchard waste in staged steps. Those steps held extraction, fermentation, and polymerization. The next plastic is made by microbes through fermentation. Impacts were counted from raw source to final product. Energy, emissions, and waste were all tallied. Results show which route burdens nature less.
pmc-11644757:
Siqi Li and colleagues test coal mine waste as a cover for poor soils in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Saline-alkaline land suffers from high alkalinity, few nutrients, and weak water holding. Covering such soil is a known remedy. Coal gangue, the rock waste of coal mining, holds soil-like nutrients and trace elements. The team spread it over problem soil and grew ryegrass on top.

They varied the waste's particle size and the cover depth. Mid-size grains at a good depth raised the soil's water content and organic matter. Total nitrogen also rose. Enzyme activity and grass growth improved along with the soil. The study turns a mining waste pile into a land repair tool. Soil scientists and land managers in mining regions are the readers.
pmc-11644857:
Parveen Bajaj leads a team that builds a sensor to blockchain frame. Their work from twenty twenty-four uses free space optical links. Fast, safe data flow is a growing need in tech.

Fiber links are fast but capped by electronics, they note. Their frame joins light links, sensors, and blockchain in one. Light link quality was tested at many speeds and ranges. A boost part was tried with and sans it for compare. Smart contracts and shared storage guard the data flow. Fit to weather change is also part of the frame.
pmc-11645257:
Tesfaye Gebrye and four colleagues pool world studies on how common carpal tunnel syndrome is, in a twenty twenty-four review. The condition, a pinched wrist nerve, burdens health and work. The team searched five databases for studies from twenty twelve to twenty twenty-four and kept thirty-one papers from fifteen countries. Together they covered more than five million people.

Rates ranged widely, from near zero to three quarters of a group in small samples. The pooled estimate was about fourteen percent, though with a wide band of doubt. Studies came most often from the United States and Saudi Arabia. The authors call the overall burden high and urge better prevention and care planning.
pmc-11647357:
Jeffers, Pilnick, and Armstrong study women who decline breast screening or treatment, in work from twenty twenty-four. Some women refuse screening or cancer treatment because of overdiagnosis and overtreatment harms: finding or treating cancers that would never have caused trouble.

Participants were recruited through social media, forums, and word of mouth after invitations from the national screening program. Semi structured interviews were analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis. Their reasoning is often careful and informed, not ignorant, the design implies. Services that dismiss these women may miss a chance for honest discussion of benefits and harms.
pmc-11651957:
Xiaole Li and eight colleagues build a machine learning predictor for atrial fibrillation coming back after catheter ablation, the keyhole procedure that treats the rhythm disorder. Among 325 patients treated a first time, seventy-nine saw their fibrillation return. The team paired a blood-based insulin resistance index with CT measures of fat around the atrium and the coronary arteries.

Four factors on their own predicted recurrence: the volume and density of fat on the atrium, fat inflammation around one coronary branch, and the metabolic index. A support vector machine built on them predicted recurrence well, whatever the diabetes status. The model offers a practical way to flag patients who need closer follow-up after ablation.
pmc-11654057:
JianLi Wang, Cindy Feng, Mohammad Hajizadeh, and Alain Lesage publish the protocol for a trial testing whether telling high-risk Canadians their personal depression risk, with coaching, prevents depression itself. Their tool combines sex-specific risk prediction with evidence-based self-help strategies, delivered with a coach's guidance.

The assessor-blinded trial will recruit five hundred men and five hundred women at elevated predicted risk but without a recent depressive episode. Half receive the communication program; half serve as controls. Interviews at baseline, three months, and twelve months track depressive episodes, symptoms, self-help use, service use, and self-efficacy. If it works, the program could become a selective prevention model inside tiered mental health services.
pmc-11656157:
Rebecca Habisch, Peter Neubauer, Jorge Soza-Ried, and Eva Puschmann show that harvesting virus repeatedly, instead of once, multiplies manufacturing yield. Oncolytic viruses are a growing cancer therapy class, but production slots are scarce and batches are precious. Most clinical processes still grow virus in a single batch and harvest once. The team compared repeated harvest against that classical process head-to-head. Cell density was unaffected by the change.

The cumulative infectious titer after repeated harvests ran over four hundred times higher than the batch yield. Each additional collection skimmed fresh virus while cells kept producing. The result argues for repeated harvest or perfusion formats when producers choose a process design. For patients, higher yield per batch means lower costs and wider availability of viral therapies.
pmc-11656957:
Qin and coauthors adapt a trauma care attitude scale for Chinese nursing interns. Interns often feel ill-equipped to work with trauma survivors. Their attitudes shape how well they care for such patients. A sound scale can gauge those attitudes for training plans.

The team translated the scale with cross-culture steps. A survey of 490 interns at two colleges tested the scale. Surveys ran in two waves in early and mid 2024. Seven experts graded each item for fit and clarity. Test scores checked scale stability and truth. The Chinese form held up well for intern use.
pmc-11658457:
Wu and eight co-authors design dyes to boost radiotherapy for kidney cancer, in work from twenty twenty-four. Renal cell carcinoma resists radiation, so higher doses or sensitizers are needed. A dye that gathers in tumor cell mitochondria could make radiation hit harder where it matters.

Their indocyanine dyes carry polyethylene glycol chains of varied lengths on one side, making them water and fat friendly at once. That balance drives them to mitochondria, the cell power plants. Damage there amplifies radiation effects. The chemistry aims for stronger tumor kill without raising dose to healthy kidney tissue.
pmc-11658957:
Li and coauthors link thyroid hormone to liver fat in a large group. A scan score gives a proxy for fat in the liver. Thyroid hormones steer how the body burns and stores fat. The team asks if hormone levels track that scan score.

The set held 3,461 adults who had the liver scan from 2018 to 2023. Higher free thyroxine tracked with lower liver fat scores. That link held in both men and women in the set. Curve checks showed where the link bends or levels off. The work hints thyroid checks may aid liver fat care. More work must test cause and effect.
pmc-11665657:
Sarah Maman-Haddad and colleagues publish RNA sequencing data from pig placenta and endometrium in late gestation, a resource for work on fetal maturity and piglet survival. Deaths near birth come most of all from low piglet maturity at the end of gestation. Maturity rests on a fine balance at the feto-maternal interface, between what the fetus needs in food and what the mother can give, where placenta and uterus meet.

The data come from a project linking that interface to how the fetus matures and to survival at birth. Tissues came from purebred and reciprocal crossbred fetuses of two breeds at far ends for fetal maturity: Large White, with high deaths of the newborn, and Meishan, with low deaths. About 224 samples of each tissue were picked, with rich data on breed, gestation day, sex, genotype, and maturity. Reads ran to over one hundred million per sample on average.
pmc-11665857:
Julien Lie-Panis, Léo Fitouchi, Nicolas Baumard, and Jean-Baptiste André model how groups set by folk turn weak name effects into strong drives to work as one. Name sole often fails when joint work costs much or watch is poor. Their model nests two binds. One is the first joint work bind. The next is a joint act to build a group that shifts its pay offs.

The nest form makes a lift effect. Name is too weak to hold joint work straight, but strong to drive gifts to the group. The group then lifts drives in the first bind till joint work holds. The team sets groups next to tools that lift loads with wheels and ropes. They hint folk built groups, by plan or not, to use this lift through name in groups.
pmc-11673757:
Zhifeng Zhou and six colleagues analyze muscle coordination in people whose ankles keep giving way, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Chronic ankle instability follows sprains and alters how muscles fire together. Landing, especially when unexpected, exposes the problem.

Twenty patients performed anticipated and surprise landings. Muscle synergy patterns were extracted with matrix factorization and clustering. During surprise landings, hip and thigh muscles, gluteus maximus and vastus lateralis, carried more weight. The calf muscle dominated expected landings instead. Patients thus lean on proximal muscles when caught off guard. The adaptation protects the ankle but may load the knee and hip differently. Rehabilitation could target the pattern directly.
pmc-11676757:
Bethany Armentrout and a team of co-authors link emotional distress to heart health in young adults with type one diabetes, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Their survey reached 165 people aged eighteen to thirty-one. It scored both general distress and diabetes-specific distress.

Higher scores on either distress type tied to lower cardiovascular health scores. The links held after accounting for age, illness length, sex, race, and pump use. The authors argue that easing both kinds of distress may guard young hearts. They call for longer studies to test cause and trial talk therapy.
pmc-11677557:
Alba Cantón-Suárez and colleagues review how physical exercise acts at the molecular level in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is one of the most common diseases that break down the brain. It often begins with personality changes and psychiatric symptoms. It then moves to mild cognitive impairment and at last to dementia. Exercise is part of the non-drug care used for the disease.

Studies show exercise can delay the process that breaks down the brain. It improves the redox state in brain tissue and has anti-inflammatory effects. The review gathers what is known about these molecular effects. It asks how movement changes the chemistry of the diseased brain, and what that means for care.
pmc-11679657: Muhammad Butt introduces a research topic on fiber-optic sensors, in this editorial from twenty twenty-four. Such sensors read the world through light in glass threads. They can sense strain, temperature, pressure, chemicals, and more, from how the light changes along the fiber. They work where electronics struggle: immune to electrical noise, small, and able to run over long distances. The editorial opens a collection on the field, framing why these sensors matter, from engineering and medicine to environmental monitoring, and what the gathered papers set out to advance.
pmc-11679857:
Marijana Kasalović and eight co-authors synthesize tin-based compounds and show that the organic decoration on the tin atom decides how cancer cells die. Two new tributyltin complexes carry quinolone-derived carboxylate ligands differing in a short linker. Spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography mapped their structures in solution and in the solid state.

In solution the tin center binds four partners; in crystals it takes five, linking into chains. Quantum chemical calculations examined the bonding in detail. Against breast, colorectal, and melanoma cell lines, the compounds' killing profiles differed with the ligand. In melanoma cells they triggered an anoikis-like death, the fate of cells torn from their anchors. The title's claim is the lesson: the organic moiety matters.
pmc-11683657:
Uihlein and co-authors ask surgical staff what they expect from an AI-backed decision aid for older patients. Joint geriatric care improves outcomes for older surgical patients. Where a patient goes after surgery also shapes recovery strongly. A project called SURGE-Ahead is building an AI aid for these choices. The team ran qualitative interviews with surgical staff. They probed current pain points in geriatric care first.

Staff then shared views on bringing AI support into that care. Questions covered tech needs and workflow fit. Trust and control featured in what staff asked for. The findings will shape the aid's design before it meets real wards. Early staff input, the authors argue, decides adoption.
pmc-11690357:
Katherine Miller and Megan Shepherd-Banigan study veterans newly diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. They ask how pre-existing mental illness affects emergency department use, and whether living in a nursing home changes the picture. Mental illness can complicate dementia care and may drive more intensive health service use and higher costs.

In their cohort, ninety-six percent of veterans with a new dementia diagnosis lived in the community and four percent in nursing homes. Mental illness was more common among nursing home residents than community dwellers, at nineteen versus twelve percent. Veterans with pre-existing mental illness were younger at diagnosis in both settings. In the year after diagnosis, community dwellers with mental illness used emergency departments far more often than those without. The authors argue that dementia care must plan for mental illness from the start.
pmc-11696757:
Boča, Štofko, Ladická, and Rajnák computed the quantum chemistry of two anti-blood-cancer drugs in water in twenty twenty-four. The drugs, bendamustine and melphalan, are mustard-type agents. Understanding their electron behavior in water helps explain how they act and react in the body.

Using density functional theory, refined by a high-level coupled cluster method, they optimized each molecule's shape and computed many properties. These included dipole moments, vibration patterns, and measures tied to gaining or losing electrons. Both drugs showed very low ionization energy, implying strong antioxidant capacity. One drug's charged form was more stable in water, while the other's was less so. They also mapped two rival paths for electron-proton transfer and found one proceeds over lower energy barriers.
pmc-11697557:
Mahmoud Ardeshir leads a team that coats steel with a mixed metal layer. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses a five metal high entropy alloy. The coat was laid on plain carbon steel by arc welding.

Three power levels were tried for the welding step. At the mid level, the coat held two crystal phases. Hardness rose a lot over plain steel at that level. Tests in acid showed the coat fought rust far better. Best rust proof was also found at the mid power level. Such coats could guard steel in harsh use.
pmc-11726757:
Menezes and four co-authors review gut microbes in brain aging, in work from twenty twenty-four. Age linked brain change can lead to memory loss and diseases such as Alzheimer disease. The gut and brain talk through a two way link that shapes swelling in the brain.

With age, gut microbe diversity falls and pro swelling species grow, the authors note. Those shifts link to Alzheimer development. Therapies such as stool transfer, probiotics, and prebiotics may restore gut health and aid thinking. Human proof is still thin, so the review calls for more trials that account for personal differences.
pmc-11727757:
Lingyun Zhang and ten co-authors review cascaded metasurfaces, optical devices made by stacking thin patterned layers that steer light. One layer can do much, but stacks open far more acts through coupling between layers. The review came out in twenty twenty-four.

Near field stacks breed new resonance modes that tune phase, polarization, and wave spread. Far field stacks, with wider gaps, suit classic optical design and serve in lens fixes, spectrometers, and retro reflectors. Tunable stacks shift by motion, which aids beam steering, zoom lenses, and holograms. The authors close with the promise of compact, multi role optics.
pmc-11728757:
Ian Cameron, Louise Ada, Maria Crotty, and a wider team wrote this short report, published in 2024, from a national stroke trial. It delivers a blunt verdict: botulinum toxin injections do not restore arm activity in chronic stroke survivors whose arms barely move.

The analysis covered seventy-one survivors, each injected in wrist-crossing muscles for spasticity more than three months after stroke. Three months later, the team re-measured hand activity, stiffness, joint range, grip, pain, and general health. The median change was zero on the main activity test, and near zero nearly everywhere else. Care burden even ticked the wrong way. The authors say that in patients with severe activity limits, the injection is not effective on any measured outcome and does not appear clinically justified. The report aims to stop a costly habit.
pmc-11852257:
Isaac George, Paulo Neves, Martijn Cox, and Adrian Ebner report one year of follow-up on a seventy-year-old man who received an experimental artificial bypass graft. Vein grafts, the workhorse of coronary bypass surgery, fail in up to thirty percent of cases within a year, so an off-the-shelf conduit is a long-standing need. The implanted device is a biorestorative polymer tube reinforced with a fine nitinol skeleton.

The graft treated one vessel in his three-vessel disease. Angiography at six months showed it open with normal flow, and cardiac CT confirmed patency at twelve months. The case is offered as early evidence of safety and feasibility for the conduit.
pmc-11917457:
Yang Dong, Dandan Liu, Ya Yu, Ziyu Xiong, and Hongying Rao map a decade of research on falls among older hospitalized patients using bibliometric visualization. Falls in this population cause injuries, prolong stays, and burden staff, making the field's hotspots worth charting. The team searched the Web of Science for articles from twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-three, excluding conference papers, reviews, and editorials.

Using CiteSpace software, they visualized the literature's structure: publication patterns, collaborations, and keyword evolution over the decade. Duplicate and off-topic records, such as falls in other age groups or non-hospital settings, were screened out. The analysis examines the progression and shifting focal points of the research domain. Its aim is to give healthcare professionals and researchers a reference foundation for advancing fall prevention and management strategies in hospitals.
pmc-12008357:
Dirakwaranon and five colleagues compare sexual function in cervical cancer survivors and healthy women in twenty twenty-four. Sexual problems can follow cervical cancer and its treatment. The study ran at a university hospital in Thailand over about ten months. A standard questionnaire measured sexual function in both groups.

One hundred sixteen women took part, split evenly between survivors and controls. Sexual dysfunction affected about thirty-five percent of survivors. The rate in healthy controls was about ten percent. Survivors scored worse on lubrication, satisfaction, and pain domains of the index. Age and body mass index were alike in the two groups. The authors call for attention to sexual health in survivorship care.
pmc-12664257: A short correction notice from twenty twenty-five fixes the work addresses listed for a study by Jian Zhou and co-authors. The study was about drug resistance in bacteria found in a newborn care unit. The notice says the lead contact author, Chunming Jiang, should have had two addresses, not one. It prints the wrong list and the right list side by side. No results or claims in the study itself are changed by this notice.
pmc-12672157:
Richard Phillips and Jamie Coleman study how British medical students use commercial learning platforms, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. Talks were held with five students and six junior clinical teachers at the University of Birmingham. Students called the platforms near-essential for exams, prizing easy access, game-like features, and practice in familiar formats. Peer habits strongly steered which sites got used. Students valued how the tools exposed knowledge gaps and fit self-paced study. Costs and fair access worried them, and teachers warned that simplified content could blunt deeper clinical thinking.
pmc-12690957:
Paulisi and co-authors track gene pace and gate reach as a herb meets shade. Open strand zones host marks that switch genes on and off. In Arabidopsis, light replies rest much on gene switch work. Shade cuts the red share of light, which the herb reads fast. Sight parts sense that cut and go still in the shade. Still sight frees PIF parts, chiefly PIF7, to reset gene work.

That reset drives the herb's full shade reply in the text. A strong first wave of gene shifts fades with long shade. Gate scans at one hour and 25 hours test the tie. Most first-aim genes had open gates pre shade in the scans. Gene pace tied to a fast PIF rise at the one-hour mark. Reach at the gates rose with that PIF wave in step.
pmc-12691857:
Simon, Gineste, Reiss, Thompson, and Laporte joined many data kinds in twenty twenty-five to map paths in a rare group of muscle ills. These ills waste and weaken muscle from birth, with no cure yet. They pool gene, protein, and chem reads from mouse forms of three gene kinds.

Groups of genes that shift as one were tied to good or grave muscle states. Good groups held shrink, power burn, and gene read acts. Grave groups held defense, nerve, vessel, and fat burn acts. A web walk in a joined map flagged chems tied to the ills that drugs might shift.
pmc-12701257:
Kohei Kamada and colleagues published a sports medicine study in 2025 on the anterior cruciate ligament. The ligament has two bundles that stretch differently as the knee moves. X-ray imaging from two angles tracked the athletes' knee bones in motion. Models built from scans let the team compute each bundle's length. During fast running, one bundle stretched more than the other. During landing, both bundles stretched by similar amounts. Peak stretch also came at different knee angles in landing. The authors suggest graft fixing angles that copy this natural pattern.
pmc-12715257:

All three proved square planar in shape. In the test reaction, run under mild green terms, they made the target fused pyrimidine products fast and well. High turnover rates showed their speed. The team set catalyst type, solvent, and dose against Lewis acids, bases, and ionic liquids. The catalysts held their strength through the runs. That marks them as practical tools for hard ring synthesis.
pmc-12719257:
Baoyu Huang, Zhipeng Yin, Gang Gao, Longhai Li, and Miao Yang name DDX49, a helicase, as a fresh outcome marker in colorectal cancer and trace how it drives cell growth. This cancer ranks third worldwide. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Silencing the gene in two cell lines cut growth and colony forming, and damped a key growth pathway. A pathway booster partly restored growth. Silencing a partner protein copied the effect, while boosting it rescued growth, pinning the chain of action.
pmc-12728057:
Marilyn Frézier and eight co-authors guide pain testing in arthritic animals in this two thousand twenty-five review. Osteoarthritis pain rewires the nervous system in people, cats, and dogs alike. Quantitative sensory testing probes that rewiring with measured stimuli. Used well, it can show whether animal pain matches the human condition. The authors review pain physiology first, then the testing toolkit.

They explain how to standardize tests in rats, cats, and dogs, with practical appendices. Other methods, like electrical diagnostics, get a place too. The guide also covers how current drugs act on sensitization. Consistent testing makes animal results translate better to clinic. Veterinary and pain researchers are the readers.
pmc-12729457:
Zihui Cai and a team including Miguel Ángel Prieto Lage test whether lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, can shield gut cells from a grain toxin. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. The toxin, called DON, often taints wheat and corn and can harm the gut and immune system.

The team exposed pig gut cells to the toxin in dishes. The toxin weakened the cell barrier, raised stress, and boosted signals that drive swelling, ending in the firing of a cell alarm complex. Adding lycopene reversed these changes. A drug that switches on one pathway, named ERK, wiped out the benefit, which pins lycopene's effect to that path. The work names a target for shielding the gut from this common food toxin.
pmc-12731957:
Corina Cinezan and colleagues link tooth loss to heart failure after heart attack. Their cross-sectional study from twenty twenty-five bridges mouth and heart health. Both fields share inflammation as a common thread. Whether missing teeth track post-attack heart failure was underexplored.

Two hundred heart attack patients had teeth, heart function, and conditions recorded. Heart failure meant low pumping fraction or a clinical diagnosis. Patients grouped by how many teeth they had lost. Pumping strength fell steadily across the tooth loss groups. Nearly two in five patients met the heart failure definition. Adjusted models tested tooth loss as an independent predictor. Dentists and cardiologists share more ground than practice suggests.
pmc-12733157:
Desmond Seybold, Gregory Contreras, Jia-Feng Chang, Ting-Yu Yeh, and Michael Stear review fresh knowledge on the parasite behind trichomoniasis, the most common non-viral sexually spread infection. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five, with over two hundred million people affected yearly.

Packets it sheds carry RNA and proteins that signal to host cells. The review covers the grip molecules it uses, the immune answers it provokes, and its side relationships with other microbes and cancers. The authors stress that these interactions drive the disease.
pmc-12735457:
Svetlana Smirnova and her team build two-part kits based on water to draw out and gauge five man-made food dyes. Their 2025 study in chem tests takes in azorubine, Allura Red, sunset yellow, tartrazine, and fast green in food tests.

Two salt pairs formed the green draw-out kits. In the first, just azorubine drew out in full. That split rests on how much the dye shuns water, which the team gauged in a straight way. In the next kit, all five dyes drew out in full no matter what their traits were. The team worked on acid grade, part grades, and time acts for both kits. Least grades that could be found were very low. Straight gauge spans ran through wide grade spans. Both steps were used with good ends on real food tests.
pmc-12736057:
Alexandra Tabaran and colleagues tested traditional pork products for safety in 2025. Artisanal smoking and drying give prized flavors. Those methods can also add chemical and germ risks. The team collected products from markets and small producers. They analyzed well over one hundred samples. Four marker smoke chemicals were measured with precision tools. Standard plate tests counted hygiene-related bacteria. Targeted tests hunted two dangerous germs, with gene confirmation.

Smoke chemical levels varied widely between products. Smoked sausages carried the highest loads. Dry-cured ham and smoked bacon ranked lower. Total sums stayed under the European safety limit overall. Bacterial loads ran higher in goods from unregulated producers. That gap points to weaker hygiene in making and storage. One dangerous germ appeared in ten sausage samples. Another appeared in three traditional products. The authors urge tighter control of smoking and handling.
pmc-12736657:
Branka Mikavica and two co-authors present a smart way to place computing tasks in fog networks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fog computing puts small servers near devices, backed by the cloud. Swarms of connected devices now demand more computing, and energy use is a worry. The system tracks each fog node's energy state as workloads shift. It gives the most urgent tasks first pick of resources. Tests show the approach holds delay limits while cutting energy use. Time-sensitive tasks, like those in health or traffic systems, stand to gain. The paper targets designers of edge computing services.
pmc-12741957:
Semary and six co-authors assess disability and health care access among Sudanese refugees in Egypt, in work from twenty twenty-five. Sudanese refugees have lived in Egypt for decades amid instability at home. The twenty twenty-three crisis brought a new wave of displaced people.

Living conditions, health status, and the effect of disability on access to care were studied. A phone survey reached more than five hundred newly displaced Sudanese. Discriminant analysis sorted which factors best separate those with good access from those without. Disabled refugees face compounded barriers, and the findings can target aid where it changes access most.
pmc-12742057:
Kim, Choi, and Son compare ChatGPT with human doctors on newborn gut surgery emergencies. These cases, from blocked intestines to twisted bowel, need fast choices to prevent harm or death. The team tested if the chatbot could support such high-stakes decisions.

Hard cases covered ileal atresia, midgut volvulus, Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, and pseudo-obstruction. Each case became a short-answer question with history and imaging details. Questions asked for likely diagnoses and next steps. Answers from ChatGPT were then set against those of human clinicians to judge accuracy and safety side by side.
pmc-12747057:
Andreas Posa, Stefan Schob, Walter A. Wohlgemuth, and Malte E. Kornhuber describe three cases of Fahr's syndrome, in an article from twenty twenty-five. The syndrome is a rare, slowly progressive disorder marked by calcium deposits in the brain. All three patients arrived after a first epileptic seizure. Each showed strikingly low blood calcium.

Brain scans showed pronounced bilateral calcifications in various areas. Calcium substitution and anti-seizure treatment restored the patients to their previous condition. All were discharged home seizure-free. The authors stress long-term laboratory and imaging follow-up for high-risk patients. People who have had thyroid surgery are a named example. Timely substitution therapy, they argue, can prevent avoidable neurological and psychiatric complications.
pmc-12748057:
Eunji Park and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five retrospective study comparing air and ground transport for stroke patients in rural South Korea. Fast treatment decides outcomes in acute ischemic stroke. Long transfers to specialist centers remain a major barrier in rural areas.

Records covered adults transferred from hospitals at least thirty kilometres away over several years. Patients were matched by age, sex, and referring hospital. The team compared transport times, clot treatments, and independence at discharge. Readers in emergency medicine get a grounded comparison of helicopter and ambulance transfers for reaching stroke care in time.
pmc-12749157:
Paula Souto and colleagues test insecticides against the invasive yellow-legged hornet by mouth. Their toxicity study from twenty twenty-five targets hornet workers. The hornet spreads fast in Europe and preys on native insects. Its colonies threaten farming, wildlife, and people nearby.

Four commercial products were fed to hornets in the lab. Two compounds stood out as most promising for control. One killed quickly at low doses in feeding tests. The other also disturbed behaviour and colony health at sublethal levels. Oral exposure matches how bait-based control would work. Careful product choice matters to spare bees and other insects. Hornet managers gain evidence for targeted baiting.
pmc-12752857:
Bibi Rafeena Ally-Charles and eleven co-authors test guava leaves as a germ killer against key disease germs, as drug proofing spreads. Rising proof and drug harm push the hunt for add on and swap cures. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Dried ground leaves were soaked in varied solvents and the extracts screened for plant chem-icals. All seven chem-ical classes sought were found. Paper discs soaked in the extracts were tested on germ plates by a standard spread method. One extract showed strong germ kill at the top strength tested. The authors set the leaf extracts against current drugs for effect.
pmc-12756957:
Gemma Postill leads a team that tests a death coding scheme in bowel disease. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with premature mortality in IBD. Death patterns point to where action can cut inequities.

The scheme lists leading causes for global priority setting. Its fit for chronic disease subgroups was unknown. Ontario records linked bowel disease deaths over years. Each case was matched to five non disease decedents. Cause codes were compared between the two schemes. Early death meant death before seventy-five years. Administrative health data formed the base.  Matching used sex plus birth and death years.
pmc-12764957:
Karsten Øvretveit and colleagues published a 2025 genetics study predicting physical fitness from DNA. Fitness strongly predicts heart disease and early death. Part of fitness is inherited. The team built a combined genetic score in Norway. A separate British cohort helped tune it.

Top and bottom score groups differed in measured fitness. High scorers had fewer heart events. They also had lower blood pressure disease rates. Death rates were lower as well. Women showed some extra risk links. A DNA score cannot replace exercise testing. Still, it confirms fitness genetics carry real health weight.
pmc-12780557:
Qiuhui Hu and colleagues identify an enzyme that may slow liver cancer spread. Their study from twenty twenty-five examines glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, called GCDH. Metastasis causes most deaths in hepatocellular carcinoma. Metabolic rewiring is a known hallmark of that spread.

Cancer data showed lysine breakdown activity falling as tumours advanced. GCDH drives a key step in that breakdown pathway. Lower GCDH levels let a powerful inflammation pathway switch on. That switch then promoted tumour spread in lab and animal tests. Low GCDH also tracked with more immune cells entering tumours. Patient outlook worsened when GCDH ran low. The enzyme emerges as both a warning marker and a research target.
pmc-12785257:
Junhyuk Lee, Hyeonji Jang, Boyun Kim, and Jewon Jung review studies on how tiny plastic particles harm living bodies, read through their cell chemistry, in a twenty twenty-five article. Nanoplastics form as larger plastics break down and can cross body barriers. The team compared studies in mammals with those in water species, using metabolomics, the full read of small cell chemicals.

Both sets of studies showed stress from oxygen damage, failing power units, and swelling responses. Shared disturbed paths covered fat handling, energy cycles, and amino acid use. In mammals the liver and gut suffered most; in fish, the gills, liver, and brain. The authors urge joining this method with other full-read tools for a complete risk picture.
pmc-12785957:
Steven Scahill, Kelly Jean Sherman, and Dennis Paul study two sodium-handling proteins in breast cancer that has spread, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. Both proteins, a gated sodium channel and a sodium-potassium pump, run high in many advanced cancers and may drive spread. What turns them up together was unknown.

Using nerve cells as a guide, the team dosed a lab model of spreading breast cancer with an inflammation signal. Short exposure raised the genes for both sodium handlers. Longer treatment lowered channel levels while reshaping the pump's forms and placement. Drugs that block sodium traffic also changed how the cells behaved in spread-like tests. The authors conclude that inflammation jointly tunes both handlers and may feed cancer growth.
pmc-12788157:
Derikov leads a large team controlling quantum dot position with light, in work from twenty twenty-five. Quantum dots are tiny semiconductor crystals that glow, useful for imaging and displays. Placing them exactly, and moving them on demand, is a prized skill.

The dots sat in a liquid crystal that was doped with light sensitive dye molecules. Ultraviolet light through a slit melted the crystal order only in the lit stripe. That local phase change pushed the dots to redistribute in a set pattern. Glow microscopy with a laser tracked the move live. Light driven assembly like this could build switchable optical parts.
pmc-12789457:
Khang Wen Goh and five co-authors design a blockchain that drops lone trust points by mix of quantum and post-quantum guards. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. Old chains face risk from big quantum machines, while pure quantum chains lean on one key source and cost a lot. Their plan spreads key make across many nodes.

Two sign layers let users swap twixt quantum signs and lattice-based classic signs by need and line state. Vote-based picks with score ranks run the chain pact, and bad nodes lose shares. Math models show part of the flow can take quantum signs with no jam. The rest runs near classic speed. Firm clash proof is claimed.
pmc-12800157:
Masood and co-authors match head hit marks cross men's and women's touch sports in one pool. Head hits tie to sharp and long brain harm in sport hosts. Wear tools give hit marks, yet most past work used one sport. Tool ways split a lot, which caps cross-sport reads of marks. Their pool came from mouth guards worn in four sports. Sports were men's grid play, men's ice play, women's rug play, and women's ball play.

All hits were worked one way in the shared pool set. Marks span peak moves, hit spans, and hit aim per blow. Group gaps in all marks proved firm cross the sports. Men's grid play showed the top mid peak marks in the pool. Women's ball play showed the low mid marks in the pool. Aim reads gave shock turns, like high marks for that sport.
pmc-12802257:
Muhammet Fatih Keyif, Sabahattin Destek, and Betül Keyif present a two thousand twenty-five surgical study of abdominal wall endometriosis. The condition grows womb-like tissue in the belly wall, often after cesarean birth. It commonly shows as a painful lump near the scar.

Records covered twenty-one surgically treated patients at one center. Every patient had a prior cesarean, and most lumps hurt in cycles. Deep invasion into the muscle layer appeared in over two fifths of cases. Mesh repaired larger defects, and only one case returned. Surgeons get practical guidance on a rare, often delayed diagnosis.
pmc-12808457:
Shujin Lin, Haining Li, Shiyan Bai, and Xiao Han review mobile RNAs in plants. Their review deals with RNAs that move across the plant body. Small RNAs, messenger RNAs, and other types all can travel.

They act as system wide signals that cross cell and species bounds. That helps plants adapt to drought, salt, and pest attack. Transport paths that let them move are set out in detail. Their jobs go past gene control to marks and resource shares. Uses span RNA based pest sprays and gene editing delivery. Tough crops are the long term aim.
pmc-12815757:
Yanyan Li and five co-workers pooled proof on if felt stress lifts the risk of ischemic stroke. Work more and more blames stress of the mind, but felt stress on its own had dim effects. The 2025 review searched five data banks for work that used known felt stress scales. Eleven papers met the bar for the pooled test. Risk scores, tuned for bias, were joined across the work.

Felt stress on its own was tied to high stroke risk once scores were tuned. Group checks sharpened the view. People with high felt stress showed much more risk. Those with low felt stress showed no clear link. The team calls theirs the first pooled test on this point. The finds back stress checks as part of stroke care that aims to stop the ill, most of all for people who bear heavy loads.
pmc-12819357:
Ahmed Khalaf and four co-authors compare opioid free sleep care with opioid based care for children in day dental surgery. Opioid free care is used more in child surgery to dodge sickness and slow wake up. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records covered over a hundred children aged three to ten who had crowns or fillings, split into two care groups. Pain scores were nil in both groups at both checks after surgery. Wake room time was clearly shorter in the opioid free group. No child in either group felt sick, needed rescue pain drugs, or stayed in hospital by surprise.
pmc-12822057:
Piotr Ogrodowicz and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five barley study linking development timing to stress defence gene activity. Four spring barley types differed in flowering time and leaf hair features. Combined drought and fungal attack tested them together, as fields often deliver both.

Early-heading types behaved as drought escapers, finishing before stress peaked. A key day-length gene mirrored the timing split. Screening measured drought response and infection severity per type. Gene expression for a defence family was tracked across development. The work shows why breeding for timing and surface traits must consider stress arriving in combination.
pmc-12822257:
Six researchers led by Renke He studied how T cells, a core part of the immune system, change their gene activity with age. Old T cells lose range and strength, which weakens defense in later life. The team used gene data from single cells and from bulk samples across healthy age groups.

Young T cells were run by one set of gene switches, and old ones by another. A growth signal path called TGF-beta stood out, with several of its parts turned up in worn-out memory T cells. The authors name these parts as possible markers of immune aging. The work may guide ways to slow that decline.
pmc-12853857:
Ashraf Jehad Abuejheisheh and a large team of co-authors survey smoking and stress among Palestinian nursing faculty, in a two thousand twenty-five nationwide study. Health educators who smoke undermine their own role modeling.

One hundred sixty-four faculty from seventeen institutions answered questionnaires including a standard stress scale. Smoking prevalence was thirty-seven percent, cigarettes the usual form, driven by peers, stress relief, and cultural norms; women and single participants smoked more. Nearly half reported moderate to extremely severe occupational stress, and current smokers were more stressed than others. Stress fell with age. The authors recommend culturally tailored cessation programs and tobacco-free campus policies.
pmc-13070757:
Baowen Shao and five co-authors review how China's new generation of older adults is adopting digital tools, and how that adoption reshapes what they buy. Their review appeared in two thousand twenty-five. China's population is aging fast, and today's retirees differ from past cohorts. Sorting how they learn and use technology matters for policy and business alike.

The review groups buyers by age, place, mindset, health, and wealth, stressing how varied this market is. Technology for this group spans health tracking, home safety, social connection, and support services. Gains include better monitoring, independent living, and smarter use of resources. The authors note the research leans on a few regions and skips non-users. They call for user-centered design, wider digital literacy, and long-term studies. Integrated, AI-backed services are their closing prescription.
pmc-13157757:
Carlos Eduardo Pinzon Florez, Ciro Gómez Ardila, and Myriam Ruiz-Rodriguez examined what happens to the money when a failed health insurer's members are dumped onto surviving insurers. The mass transfers arrived unpaid for, bringing sicker, costlier members without matching funds. The 2026 ecological study warns regulators: closing a bad insurer without funding the transfer can destabilize the solvent ones meant to absorb the shock.
pmc-13171557:
Yanping Cai and others checked thinking problems in older schizophrenia patients in 2026. Elderly patients in hospital were looked back at here. Nearly one hundred and fifty patients joined. A standard thinking test defined the problem. Patient clusters were also explored with stats. Nursing sorting was the real aim.

Thinking problems proved common in the group. Weak social support tracked with the problems. Lower daily freedom also tracked closely. Diabetes added a further link here. Patient types split into distinct clusters. Each cluster mixed thinking and social traits. Tiered nursing care may fit better. Future checking is still needed.
pmc-13176657:

Enzyme replacement therapy followed, with the response tracked. The case urges clinicians to test pancreatic function before settling for a functional label.
pmc-13179557:
Shailendra Yadav and co-authors test extract from the fruit of the Terminalia arjuna tree, in the lab, next to Candida auris that resists many drugs. Their 2026 in vitro study is a response to a rise in infections from this fungal pathogen, which is hard to treat.

Fresh fruits were pulled in near Lucknow. They were distilled and made more strong, into an extract to test at more than one strength. Isolates of the resistant fungus, from clinics, were put to the test with disk diffusion screening. A broth microdilution method then set the minimum inhibitory concentration. The bark of the tree is used, in the old way, for skin ailments. Those take in ringworm and candidiasis. That hints at activity that may fight fungi. Full results on zones where growth was held back, and on concentrations, are in the results part of the piece.
pmc-13190457:
Peng Dai leads a team with a case of a fistula after lung surgery. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a man of fifty-six. He coughed blood clots and loose staples after lobe removal.

Staple line fail is rare but can bring a grave fistula. That leak can cause pus in the chest or lung infection. Guide books back stump cover for clear high risk folks. This man had low level risks that sat below thresholds. Low protein, low blood counts, and a hid infection are named. Such stacked faint risks may be missed.
pmc-13193957:
Fen Lin and four co-authors track Crohn's disease among women of reproductive age in China, India, and the United States, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Global incidence crept upward over three decades. China rose fastest, its rate more than doubling, while India and the United States grew modestly. Peak incidence hit earlier in China than in the other two countries.

Decomposition analysis blamed epidemiological change for China's rise and demographic change for the others'. Projections to twenty forty see China's rate inching higher and the American rate falling. Disability rates are expected to drop in all three, least in China. The authors map distinct regional patterns for a disease of growing concern in young women.
pmc-13194757:
Yating Wan and Chenzi Guo present a 2026 interview profile of Radha Nagarajan, chief technology officer of Marvell's optical engineering group, in a Light People feature. Nagarajan leads development of the company's optical platform products, holds a visiting professorship in Singapore, and was elected to the United States National Academy of Engineering. He holds over two hundred and fifty patents.

Early work targeted long-haul networks; later roles followed silicon photonics into data centers, where artificial intelligence demand exploded. A constant theme, he says, is turning advanced technology into real, manufacturable products at scale.
pmc-13197457:
Adriana Hanulíková and colleagues studied how listeners handle accent shifts within one language in 2026. Speakers alternated between standard German and a regional variety, a tough test of real-time adaptation.

Effort ran higher for the regional accent and for switches from standard to regional speech. As the dialogue went on, the accent gap shrank as listeners adapted. Traits such as openness also played a part.
pmc-13198057:

Seeds grew in three blend ratios for fifteen days. Lab checks showed the shale is rich in iron and other mineral oxides. The leanest blend, one part Djdi to three parts soil, gave the best results. It raised sprouting rates, mineral uptake, and growth. It also boosted health-linked plant compounds and the genes that make them. Stress markers rose too, a point to watch. The blend looks promising for greener farming.
pmc-13198657:
Nehemiah Kweku Essilfie and colleagues review breast cancer biology and therapy response in Ghana in a 2026 article. Breast cancer killed close to half of diagnosed Ghanaian women in 2022. The authors back precision medicine, meaning care matched to each tumor's markers. Immune checkpoint drugs look promising for one aggressive subtype but need local trials. They call for gene testing capacity, staff training, and community teaching to catch disease earlier.
pmc-13201357:

The team studied 307 patients with genomic profiles, including 213 patients who already had brain metastases, and tracked neurologic death against other causes of death. Higher risk scores meant a clearly higher risk of neurologic death in both groups. Splitting patients into three bands separated outcomes sharply, which suggests blood-based testing could help personalize care for high-risk patients.
pmc-13202157:
Kant, Datta, Farrar, and a large team build a learning model to spot viral chest infections in children in hospital. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. They train six learning methods on past cases from two large child hospitals in Canada. A plain logistic model does best, using age, sex, and signs at intake. It works best in infants and in cases of one common virus. Set into hospital records, such a model could speed outbreak spotting and test use.
pmc-13202357:

Sixty-one patients were assigned to the drug or placebo, and the drug was well tolerated with similar adverse event rates in both groups. Sputum markers of neutrophil activation fell with treatment, including a marked drop in neutrophil elastase levels. Sequencing found no detectable effect on the lung microbiome, backing further growth of the resistance-sparing concept.
pmc-13202857:
Fungi that attack insects could offer greener mosquito control, and a 2026 study by Sina M Morsy catalogs local options from Assiut Governorate in Egypt. The research article names fungi found on mosquitoes by shape and DNA, then tests their enzyme output for breaking down insect cuticle.

Eight species were described, including four Fusarium species and the known insect pathogen Purpureocillium lilacinum. Twenty-two isolates produced enzymes such as proteases, lipases, and chitinases at varying strengths in the screening assays. pmc-13205657:
Amanda Silva Santos and colleagues report sixteen years of laser light therapy for numbness and altered feeling in the face and mouth, in this case series from Brazil, published in twenty twenty-six. Records covered one hundred twenty-five patients. Tooth extraction was the cause in sixty percent, and most patients needed about three rounds of twelve sessions. By the end, two thirds reported change in their symptoms, from partial to full recovery. Cases after jaw surgery needed more rounds, though round count did not predict outcome. The authors are plain about the design: with no comparison group, the series can describe practice and outcomes, but cannot prove the laser caused the gains.
pmc-13208157:

The paired group showed ear-ly start of fixation signs and of the full ill. Score depth matched the rest, yet hard life blows were far more often told. Nail bit-ing and hair pull-ing were far more common in that group too. Faith and body fixations also stood out, they find.
pmc-13208957:

Clinic patients came in one after the next, over a span of months in two thousand twenty-three. They had psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis. A standard inventory questionnaire scored sensitization in each case. A score of forty was the threshold for a high likelihood of the state. The team tied the scores to clinical features and to quality of life. This state can push disease activity scores up and mislead treatment escalation. To find it is to argue for pain-directed therapy alongside immune drugs. The team frames the work in personalized medicine for rheumatic disease.
pmc-13211057:
Brainwave patterns could separate two dementias at the bedside, and a 2026 study authored by Muhammad Suffian builds a compact artificial intelligence system for that task. Trained across subjects rather than within them, the model averaged ninety-seven percent accuracy on a thirty-six person hospital cohort in the reported evaluation. It then ran efficiently on a Jetson edge platform, supporting real-time clinical use.
pmc-13215057:

pmc-13215157:

Most appliances improved the jaw relationship through forward lower-jaw positioning plus slight restraint of upper-jaw growth, with tooth movements helping. One trainer device worked mainly on teeth with little skeletal change. Vertical face height barely moved for most devices, though one raised it. Evidence certainty was limited, so selection stays individual.
pmc-13215557:

Drawing on research from Antarctic stations, space analogues, and past missions, the team simulated both a lunar gateway station and a south pole surface base. Tens of thousands of Monte Carlo runs exposed trade-offs between crew productivity and psychological well-being. The authors offer the model as a benchmark planners can use to test team structures, workloads, and resilience before real crews fly.
pmc-13216157:
Sidilene Pereira Alves dos Santos and co-authors present a 2026 review of phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms as helpers for restoring Amazonian forest. Tropical soils lock phosphorus away in forms roots cannot use, and seedlings planted on degraded land often starve for it.

The review gathers what is known about bacteria, fungi, and other microbes that free phosphorus by releasing acids, enzymes, and binding compounds. Nearly all evidence comes from farm crops, where inoculation has raised available phosphorus and plant uptake. Almost nothing has been tested on native Amazonian trees. The authors argue for research on locally adapted strains matched to native species, so microbial biofertilizer can cut chemical fertilizer use in restoration planting.
pmc-13217157:
Isabelle Mekone Nkwele and co-authors present a 2026 case report of skin myiasis, infestation by fly larvae, in a four-month-old boy in Yaoundé, Cameroon. The condition is common in rural tropics but under-recognized in city infants.

The baby arrived after four days of inconsolable crying with multiplying inflamed nodules, each pierced by a tiny opening that wept fluid; in some, a larva could be seen moving. The picture fit the tumbu fly, Cordylobia anthropophaga, whose eggs hatch from clothes dried indoors or left unironed. Treatment was hands-on: gentle extraction of the larvae, antiseptic baths, and antibiotic ointment. Healing was complete within three months, leaving mild pigmentation and small scars. The authors stress prevention through drying and ironing clothes.
pmc-13217857:
Franziska Bischof and co-authors present a 2026 study of how evolution reshaped HCA2, a receptor that tastes microbial and metabolic chemicals and helps govern fat metabolism and inflammation. Across mammals, the same sensor has been tuned very differently.

Most mammals' versions behaved in line, but odd-toed ungulates stood out. Selection tests and faecal metabolite profiles point to gut microbe products, including phenylpropionic and trans-cinnamic acids, as the pressure behind the shift. Pinpointed mutations showed which residues control the change. The authors read the story as host-microbe chemistry sculpting the receptor over deep time.
pmc-13218157:
Inhu Bae and colleagues lay out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of how spin in research reporting sways healthcare decision makers. Spin means presenting results so a study looks more favourable than the data justify, and it can distort what readers take away from a paper. Clinicians and policy makers read abstracts under time pressure, so the size of that distortion matters.

The review will follow PRISMA guidelines and search MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and an education database from their beginnings to January 2026. Only randomized trials will be included: trials that test how spin changes readers' impressions of findings, and trials of strategies meant to help readers spot spin. Reviewers will independently select studies, extract data, and judge bias with the Cochrane RoB2 tool. Where the data allow, results will be pooled in meta-analyses, and findings will be published and presented internationally.
pmc-13218257:
Zhen Yue and co-authors present a 2026 terahertz metadevice that steers waves in distinct channels at once. Metasurfaces are flat sheets of tiny patterned units that can bend and shape electromagnetic waves, but most designs combine channels along only one property, such as wavelength or polarization. Using several properties in one device has been held back by limited design freedom and channels leaking together.

The team built the device from anisotropic meta-atoms, unit cells that respond in unlike ways to each polarization, in a single layer. Their design steers wavefronts on their own across three frequency bands under two crosswise polarizations, giving six distinct transmission channels. Simulations checked three example devices: a metalens whose focus shifts by band and polarization, a vortex-beam generator that stays achromatic, and a six-channel holographic display. The authors propose the design for terahertz communications, high-capacity data encryption, and holographic imaging.
pmc-13219557:
Philipp Reschke and colleagues survey the physicians who order imaging about how radiology appointments are managed in hospitals in a 2026 study. How referrers experience scheduling, and where it breaks down, has rarely been asked, even though delays ripple into delayed treatment. The nationwide survey ran from June 2023 to June 2024 and captured 220 physicians, seventy-nine family doctors and 141 hospital-based doctors.

Family doctors, the more experienced group, rated the harm of imaging delays to patient care above neutral, and both groups scored coordination with radiology as a challenge. Preferences for fixes split by setting: hospital doctors wanted workflow tracking and automatic appointment reminders, while family doctors favored centralized scheduling and priority lanes for urgent cases. Short-notice availability topped the priority list for everyone. pmc-13219957:
Guoyong Xu and colleagues use machine learning on gene expression data to nominate two biomarkers for osteosarcoma in a 2026 study. The team mined eighty-eight tumor samples from a public platform, using four hundred normal samples as the comparison set.

PYGM, a glycogen-breaking enzyme, behaved more subtly: lower in tumors than in normal tissue, yet higher inside the high-risk group. Bench assays on tumor tissue confirmed proteins' presence and location. The authors present the pair as candidate biomarkers for refining osteosarcoma prognosis.
pmc-13220457:
Maheen Ibrahimi and colleagues profile patients who return to hospital with a second injury in a 2026 study of trauma recidivism at a centre. Trauma is the leading killer of people under forty-five, and repeat admissions pile costs onto health systems while signaling risks. The study used a registry from a tertiary centre in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, covering admissions from January 2021 to September 2024.

Among fourteen thousand patients, 245 were recidivists, injured by the same mechanism. They were different from patients: older by more than a decade, majority female, and overwhelmingly injured by falls, mostly at home, in bedrooms and bathrooms. Fewer than half went home, against two thirds of the others. Regression tied recidivism to falls and self-harm injuries, older age, female sex, and discharge against medical advice or to drug and alcohol rehabilitation. They argue prevention must pivot toward fall and frailty programs for older adults.
pmc-13221457:
M. Nageeb Rashed and co-authors build a natural gum and nanomuscovite composite for pulling heavy metals from water, in a 2026 materials study. The two-to-one gum blend performed best. At neutral pH with a small dose, it removed about ninety-five percent of both metals within an hour. Uptake followed the Langmuir model, and the process released heat while proceeding spontaneously. A cheap, largely natural sorbent with that performance could suit small-scale water treatment.
pmc-13221957:
Lee and a large team mine first person accounts of schizophrenia for social difficulties in twenty twenty-six. Published narratives offer rich views of lived social experience. The team used automated language and network tools to find patterns. They screened accounts published in a specialist journal over four decades.

From two hundred seventy-nine articles, they kept one hundred thirty-three first person accounts. A questionnaire based screen found thinking related syndromes in all of them. Fifty-six accounts showed interpersonal difficulties such as social anxiety and few close friends. Those accounts were longer, more negative, and less formal in language. First person accounts used fewer social words and more self references than third person ones. Network analysis linked interpersonal difficulties with hearing voices. pmc-13222557:
Ying Du and co-authors compare overlapping meta-analyses of stem cell treatment for diabetic foot ulcers, in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. Nine meta-analyses comparing stem cells with conventional care were graded for evidence level and methodological quality. A decision algorithm then picked the most robust review for settling the clinical question.

The chosen meta-analysis showed better ulcer healing, longer pain-free walking distance, and fewer amputations with stem cell treatment. Adverse events also ran lower than under conventional care in that review. Quality scores across the nine reviews were generally decent, with a median near the top of the scale. Stem cells look promising for these hard-to-heal wounds, within the limits of the underlying trials.
pmc-13222957:
Chandran and eight co-authors report one case of spinal cord injury rehab, in work from twenty twenty-six. Walking again is a top goal after such injury. Combining skin surface stimulation of the cord with robot aided walking may boost recovery, but proof for ground based robot training is thin.

Their patient was a man aged forty with a long term partial injury. He first did sixteen sessions of robot aided walking with a wearable frame. He then did sixteen more sessions with cord stimulation added. Standard tests tracked nerve function and walking speed. The case layout lets readers compare the two phases in the same person, a useful hint for larger trials.
pmc-13223657:
Jai K Das and co-authors review interventions for mental health after extreme weather events, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Searches across five databases through February 2024 screened over eleven thousand papers, leaving thirty-three studies of randomized, quasi-experimental, and before-after designs. Outcomes covered trauma symptoms, depression, anxiety, stress, and general functioning.

Interventions significantly improved symptoms across the board. Trauma symptoms dropped sharply in controlled comparisons and moderately in before-after studies. Depression and anxiety scores also fell, with before-after designs showing larger shifts than controlled ones. Quality checks used standard bias tools for each design type. As climate disasters multiply, these results support offering structured mental health help early.
pmc-13224257:
Reza Mollahouseini, Abolfazl Rahimizadeh, and Walter Wiliamson report a 2026 case pairing two rare skeletal conditions. The patient, a 29-year-old woman with achondroplasia, a genetic cause of short stature, also had an os odontoideum, a detached bone piece at the top of the spine. pmc-13224757:
The 17th EUNOS Congress collects the abstracts of the European Neuro-Ophthalmology Society meeting, held in Milan, Italy, in June 2026. Talks cover age-related change in the optic nerve sheath, European stroke vision guidelines, and a severe case of Tolosa-Hunt syndrome. Others report pupillography catching a torn carotid artery behind acute Horner syndrome, and a nose-delivered nerve growth factor in mice. Readers get the whole meeting in brief, talk by talk.
pmc-13225557:
Yuanyuan Fan and six co-authors map two decades of work on AI in anatomy teaching with a count-based review. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. AI is now woven into how body build is taught, yet no full map of the field's growth and hot spots had been drawn. The team pulled English papers from a large science base and charted them with count tools.

One hundred eighty-four papers from twenty oh five to twenty twenty-four fit the brief. The United States led in both paper count and cited weight. Focus moved from broad medical teaching to image cuts, deep nets, and surgery guides. Large chat models have drawn fresh focus of late.
pmc-13226857:
Yasemin Atici and co-authors feed a 2026 rat study testing high doses of two common dietary compounds: monosodium glutamate, the flavour enhancer, and taurine, an amino acid familiar from energy drinks. Damage markers climbed in blood, cortex, and hippocampus across all treated groups, while antioxidant defences fell. pmc-13227857:
Yinxian Li and four colleagues build a model to predict loss of both hearing and sight in middle-aged patients with knee osteoarthritis, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Losing both senses is worse than either alone, and joint disease may hasten it. The team trained four time-to-event machine learning models on 605 people from a national aging study. A hospital group served as an outside check.

The models were scored on ranking skill, error, and calibration. A second, wider definition of sense loss was tested for firmness. Explanation tools named the top risk drivers. The authors aim to flag patients early so sight and hearing can be guarded before both fail.
pmc-13232557:

pmc-13232857:
Bandar Alghamdi and colleagues mine in 2026 gene activity data for low-oxygen signals that predict survival in lung adenocarcinoma. pmc-13233657:
Ricardo Salemi Riechelmann and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of spinal fusion surgery for degenerative lower back disease. pmc-13233857:

pmc-13234057:

Pathway analysis connected the raised microRNA to insulin signaling, protein tagging systems, estrogen-driven gene expression, neuron migration, and the cell's internal skeleton. The authors propose it as a candidate molecular marker for this dementia's biology, meriting confirmation in larger groups.
pmc-13234557:
Emily Dunning, Chad Shenk, Zachary Fisher, Steffany Fredman, and John Felt re-check how early maltreatment shapes teen mental health, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Their data came from a long study of 1,354 children at risk, followed from age four to sixteen. The twist is contamination: some children in the comparison group were also mistreated.

Once that hidden exposure was corrected, early maltreatment clearly predicted more teen symptoms. The effect size grew by about two-thirds after the fix. The result held after checks for later mistreatment. The authors warn that uncleaned comparison groups can hide real harm.
pmc-13235157:

Hospital barriers included staff shortages, limited space, and payment rules that reward other care. Tension also arose between guideline advice and what women themselves felt they needed. The authors call for structural and financial reform to make early labour care match women's needs.
pmc-13235657:
Samuel G. Robinson and Alireza Hamidian Jahromi argued in 2026 that medical training leaves surgeons unprepared for gender affirmation surgery. The authors call for a thorough rethink of curricula so quality keeps pace with need. Their viewpoint addresses educators, training programs, and specialty boards directly.
pmc-13236857:
Shiyi Wang and colleagues followed 6,175 older Americans for eight years in a 2026 cohort study linking physical and mental decline to later dementia. pmc-13237057:

pmc-13237857:

pmc-13238557:

pmc-13239457:

pmc-13239657:

pmc-13240957:

pmc-13241457:

pmc-13241557:

pmc-13241657:

pmc-13241757:

pmc-13241957:
