The association concentrated among men, married respondents, and those over 35. It faded among women, the unmarried, and the young. Zhou suggests testing appearance-based appeals in tobacco control.
pmc-13242357:

Gene-era reductionism, they argue, pushed broad thinking aside without solving complex disease. Beta-blockers in heart failure show body logic beating first guesses. Wearables, organ chips, digital twins, and AI tools now offer the field new tools. Public health know-how campaigns could help restore the field's standing.
pmc-13242457:

pmc-13242757:

The caveat is that findings may not extend to symptom-free people.
pmc-13242857:

pmc-13244057:

pmc-13244257:

pmc-13244357:

pmc-13245057:

pmc-13245757:
Islam, Shompa, and Hasnat mined an infamous weed for medicines in this 2026 PLOS One study. pmc-13246457:
Omar B Da'ar and co-authors study how Saudi teens who vape view smoking in a 2026 survey analysis. Teen vaping is rising, and glamour around smoking may pull users toward cigarettes. The team used a national school survey from 2022.

Feeling that smoking is socially comfortable and holding branded goods raised that view. Contact with anti-smoking messages and shop marketing lowered it instead. pmc-13246557:
Vaia, Kim, Jeyasingh, and co-authors report an infant's case that widens the picture of a rare brain disorder, in this 2026 Neurological Sciences brief report. pmc-13246657:

pmc-13247357:
Cooper Kansala and co-authors propose that the feeling of free will is a learned illusion in a 2026 theory paper. Debates on free will usually ask whether acts are determined. The authors shift ground: since the only proof of freedom is the feeling itself, explain the feeling.

Their model starts from brain signals that fire before a person feels an urge to act. When an urge and an act arrive close in time, the brain links them as cause and effect, much like superstitious learning in animals. Reward circuits and body feedback keep reinforcing that link. The frame fits with determinism and suggests how illness or drugs could loosen the feeling.
pmc-13247557:
Jonsson and co-authors measured wood rotting in rivers across a continent, in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Decomposing plant litter feeds river food webs, but climate, landscape, and human pressure all tug at the rate. pmc-13247757:
Kumiko Hashimoto, Hiroyasu Sengoku, and Shunsuke Date describe a one-cut robotic lung surgery method in a 2026 technique paper. Robot lobectomy usually needs several ports, and the common Xi system was built for that style. A single incision crowds the robot arms against each other.

pmc-13248357:
Amaefuna, Morgan, and Bekibele ran a crossover trial on mask-related dry eye in Abuja, Nigeria, published in 2026. Exhaled air leaking upward from a facemask can dry the eyes during long shifts. pmc-13248457:
Freese and colleagues surveyed German family doctors about climate duty, in a 2026 BMC Medical Ethics paper. About two thirds called climate and environment topics relevant to their role, and most accepted doctors as societal examples. The authors recommend clearer guidance in standards, guidelines, and training so doctors know what their role asks of them.
pmc-13249557:
Yan Zhang, Leilei Fu, and Yinu Wang introduce the third volume of a collection on small molecule leads against cancer in a 2026 editorial. Natural products with complex shapes remain rich sources of new drug starts. Fresh targets matter most where tumors resist current drugs.

One study traces how a feverfew compound reshapes amino acid use and stress chemistry in lung cancer cells, naming a new target. pmc-13250257:
Ziyaei and co-authors describe a woman whose fear of a fatal brain disease produced movements that mimicked it. The patient became convinced that she had Huntington's disease, a rare inherited condition.

Brain examinations and laboratory tests found nothing abnormal, yet her conviction about Huntington's disease held firm. The authors note that earlier reports tied such anxiety to other degenerative diseases, making this Huntington's-focused case unusual.
pmc-13250457:
Murshadul Alam Murad and colleagues surveyed stroke risk in Bangladesh for this 2026 study. Stroke is rising there, yet no local work had compared five-year and ten-year risk or pinned down which factors matter most.

Age, blood sugar, and an uneven heartbeat rhythm drove the five-year risk. For ten years, age, high blood pressure, smoking, and the rhythm problem stood out. The authors call for mass awareness to cut these changeable risks.
pmc-13251057:
Takahashi surveys city dental patients who had also received care in rural areas, hunting for discontent that satisfaction scores miss. The 2026 Patient Preference and Adherence pilot ran an anonymous paper questionnaire at one Tokyo dental clinic. Ninety patients compared their urban and rural medical experiences, emotions, and unspoken complaints.

Just over two in five felt a real difference between city and countryside care, while about half felt little or none. Of patients with concerns they could have raised, about two thirds never told the facility. pmc-13251757:
Hao and Jiang review a nose-based nerve block as a gentler option for headaches after spinal anesthesia in new mothers. Their 2026 Journal of Pain Research paper covers postdural puncture headache, a common setback that slows recovery after childbirth procedures. The standard fix, an epidural blood patch, works but carries its own risks.

The review explains the anatomy, proposed mechanisms, and practical techniques behind the block. Evidence so far comes mostly from case reports and small series in obstetric patients. The authors close with the controversies and open questions that larger trials still need to settle.
pmc-13253757:
Junhan Zhou and co-authors examine death risk in a 2026 study of 9,598 United States adults aged 20 and older. Data came from national health surveys in 2003 to 2006 and 2009 to 2014, with deaths tracked to 2019. The team weighed CKM syndrome, a linked heart, kidney, and metabolic state, plus psoriasis, a skin disease.

Adults with both had the highest risk, at 7.09, and heart or brain death risk reached 16.47. The authors say adults with both states form a high-risk group that needs close, long-term heart and metabolic care.
pmc-13254757:
Renata Raptova and a large chemistry team present a one-pot route to a new family of light-activated polymerization starters in a 2026 paper. Photoinitiators decide when and where liquid resins harden into polymers, a control prized in coatings and 3D printing. Curing speed, conversion, and how much initiator could leach out all depended on the initiator's architecture. The authors pitch bis-BAPOs as tuning knobs for advanced photopolymer materials.
pmc-13255057:
Peter Birkeland and co-authors present a 2026 report of two skiers whose sciatic nerves were sliced through by a ski edge. Surgeons explored and repaired each nerve early, then immobilized the leg so the stitch line stayed slack. Over time, both men regained useful movement in most muscles. Ankle dorsiflexion, lifting the front of the foot, was the exception that did not recover. The authors argue that nerve ends pull apart with delay, so prompt repair is the key decision, and buttock-level repairs can end better than often assumed.
pmc-13255757:
Ratima Kumanbut and co-authors report a 2026 study of a natural antibacterial treatment for farmed Nile tilapia. The formulation strongly attacked Streptococcus agalactiae, a major tilapia pathogen, and stayed stable during storage. It worked well under stomach-like acidity but lost some strength under intestinal conditions. In live fish, the encapsulated version proved less toxic than the free compounds. The authors present the carrier system as a promising antibiotic alternative that could protect fish health while reducing the environmental and human-health costs of drug-heavy aquaculture.
pmc-13256057:
Cai, Shang, and Lu measured personal mastery, the sense of control over one's life, in two hundred thirty-four gout patients attending a Shandong gout center in late 2023. Participants completed scales for mastery, mindfulness, and confidence in managing pain, alongside general information. The team then modeled which factors predicted a stronger sense of control.

Mastery scores sat at a moderate level overall. Higher education, higher income, greater mindfulness, and stronger pain self-efficacy all predicted better mastery, while visible tophi and multiple other illnesses predicted worse. The authors advise clinicians to watch patients with fewer resources and more disease burden, and to build mindfulness and pain confidence.
pmc-13256757:
Weihua Qiu and co-authors review in 2026 the Connexin 26 protein and the gene behind it, GJB2, whose mutations are the leading genetic cause of hearing loss worldwide. Twelve copies of the protein assemble into channels that let neighboring cells in the inner ear exchange ions and signals.

Gene therapy and editing are under study, while cochlear implants remain the standard care the review measures new ideas against.
pmc-13257357:
Yu-Jin Lim and co-authors engineer feeder cells to grow natural killer cells for cancer therapy in a 2026 study. Donor killer cells can be given off the shelf without the graft risks of T cell products. Growing enough cells from a small blood sample remains the bottleneck.

Safety and consistency testing must still clear the path to patients.
pmc-13257557:

pmc-13258157:
Yakha A. Vissurkhanova and colleagues build iron-copper catalysts from copper ferrite and carbon materials in a 2026 study. Characterization by microscopy, diffraction, and heat analysis supported each step. pmc-13258557:
Nutchanat Chatchawankanpanich and co-authors test whether capsaicin, chili's burning compound, can keep Epstein-Barr virus dormant. pmc-13259157:
Chandan Sheikder and colleagues give small ground robots ant like scent coordination without satellite positioning in a 2026 study. Robots follow virtual pheromone trails made from light patterns, with a chemical sensor channel as backup. All sensing and learning runs onboard each robot.

pmc-13259457:
Oualid Sbai, Lorena Perrone, and Patrick Poucheret review plant polyphenols, gut germs, and brain health in a 2026 piece. Dementia counts keep rising round the world, and food gives one shield path. Gut germs turn polyphenols into live forms that can reach the brain.

pmc-13259857:

pmc-13263357:

pmc-13263557:

pmc-13263657:

pmc-13264357:

pmc-13264857:

pmc-13264957:

pmc-13265157:

pmc-13265257:

pmc-13265657:

pmc-13265757:

pmc-13265857:

pmc-13266157:

pmc-13266257:

pmc-13266757:

pmc-13267157:

pmc-13267257:

pmc-13267757:

pmc-13268957:

pmc-13271557:

pmc-13271957:

pmc-13272057:
Wenrui Zhang and coauthors describe in 2026 a case of insulin autoimmune syndrome that followed use of a common stomach acid drug. In this syndrome, the immune system makes antibodies against the body's own insulin, causing repeated low blood sugar. Drugs with sulfur groups were the classic trigger, so a proton pump inhibitor link is unusual.

The patient took pantoprazole alongside three other medicines and developed stubborn hypoglycemia with very high insulin and antibody levels. Stopping the acid drug ended the episodes, and antibody levels slowly returned to normal. Gene typing showed an inherited susceptibility pattern, supporting a drug-triggered immune reaction in a primed patient.
pmc-13272457:
Kawooya Abubaker and coauthors pool in 2026 studies of bacterial contamination in ready-to-eat vegetable salads sold across Africa. Salads skip any final cooking step, so field and kitchen germs can reach the plate directly. Evidence on how often pathogens appear was fragmented across many small studies.

Thirty-one studies met the criteria after searches in September 2025, following standard review reporting rules. Pooled prevalence was calculated with random-effects models, and the authors checked how much single studies swayed the results and whether publication bias skewed the picture. The synthesis gives food safety authorities a continental baseline for salad hygiene policy.
pmc-13272657:
Ruolei Gu leads a 2026 paper warning that overly agreeable large language models may change how people treat each other. Chat with AI is instant, compliant, and largely free of consequences. Human talk, by contrast, grew up with give-and-take and social accountability.

The authors name the risk norm leakage: blunt, command-like habits learned with AI carrying into talk with people. Early studies suggest short-term spillover, such as harsher judgments, less cooperation, and seeing others as less human. Models that flatter and comply may strengthen that style, they argue. How long such effects last, and how large they are in daily life, remain unclear.
pmc-13273157:
Cecilia Li leads a 2026 retrospective study of early switching to oral antibiotics for uncomplicated enterococcal bacteremia, a bloodstream infection. The study covered adults treated at two Boston hospitals from 2021 to 2024. It compared patients kept on intravenous therapy alone with those switched early to pills, tracking cure at 90 days.

Of 209 patients, 119 had intravenous therapy alone and 90 switched early to oral treatment. Cure rates were similar, at 73.9 percent and 82.2 percent, with no clear differences in failure, readmission, or death. Hospital stay was much shorter in the switch group, at 9 days against 20 days. The authors call early switching a safe and effective option.
pmc-13273357:
Yi Wang and co-authors replied in 2026 to comments on their work about gut microbes, their metabolites, and therapeutic foods for undernourished children. The food, called MDCF-2, was designed to repair the gut microbiome. Commenters had raised the role of butyrate, a microbial product that feeds gut lining cells.

The authors agree that butyrate is plausible but likely not the only active product. Repair begins when some gut microbes digest parts of the food, and the resulting products may signal the host directly or feed other microbes. Location and cell state in the gut lining shape the effect. They describe two study designs in germ free mice, one using whole communities from trial children and one using defined cultured sets, to test these routes.
pmc-13273657:
Li and colleagues use computer modeling to test implant-supported dentures for the lower jaw. Their 2026 journal article applies finite element analysis, a method that predicts stress inside materials. The team varied the parts that hold the denture clips.

The model tested housings and inserts made from three materials. The materials were titanium, PEEK, and PEKK, two stiff plastics. Each setup was loaded with a force of 100 newtons. A titanium housing with a PEKK insert gave the lowest denture stress. That same pairing gave the highest stress in the implant and bone. Nylon inserts spread stress more gently. The authors say nylon may better protect the implant and jawbone.
pmc-13273757:
Huizi Jin and a large team asked whether curing hyperthyroidism before IVF restores birth rates in a 2026 retrospective study. An overactive thyroid harms female fertility, but whether outcomes recover once hormone levels settle was unclear. The team compared three groups of patients at one center.

They followed 17,621 women through their first egg retrieval between 2014 and 2022. Small groups had active or resolved hyperthyroidism, while the vast majority were controls. Fresh cycle live birth was lower with active disease than in controls. Cumulative live birth also ran lower in both thyroid groups than in controls, and resolved cases did no better than active ones in adjusted models. Longer disease duration tracked with worse outcomes, which suggests lasting harm.
pmc-13273857:
Hirotsugu Aiga and co-authors measured hidden out-of-pocket health spending in Vietnam in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Families there provide much of the hands-on care for relatives in hospital, paying for meals, travel, and insurance themselves. Standard global measures count only direct bills, which may badly understate hardship.

They surveyed 219 households with a patient at one provincial hospital and paired interviews with billing records. Adding indirect spending doubled the share of households facing catastrophic costs at the strictest threshold, from about a sixth to nearly a third. Insurance premiums, food for patients and caregivers, and transport drove the gap. The authors argue that world monitoring rules should count indirect spending, or financial protection will look better than it is.
pmc-13274157:
Tian Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how plants time leaf aging when nitrogen runs short. Aging leaves recycle their nutrients to the rest of the plant, a survival move under starvation. The team studied a plant switch protein called ROP2 and tested a version locked in its active state.

Plants with always-on ROP2 kept growing early in nitrogen starvation, then aged their seed leaves early. The switch turned up three aging-promoting control genes and turned down their brakes. Later, gene activity flipped wholesale from growth programs to aging programs. The authors cast ROP2 as a balancer that trades growth against nutrient recycling as conditions worsen.
pmc-13274257:
Amr Amal Amin and co-authors report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two entry routes for fixing broken shin bones with a metal rod. Front-of-knee pain is common after this surgery, and the entry cut may be to blame. Fifty adults with closed shin shaft fractures were assigned to a side-of-kneecap route or a through-the-tendon route.

The side route gave better knee function scores at both three and six months and less pain at three months, though pain evened out by six months. Operations were also quicker and needed fewer X-ray shots with the side route. Every fracture united in both groups, in similar time, and complications stayed minor throughout the six-month follow-up.
pmc-13274857:
Sadegh Taheri and colleagues present a 2026 journal article comparing the genetics of Baluchi sheep raised in Iran and Afghanistan. Breeding leaves marks in the genome, and spotting them can reveal genes behind meat, milk, and fertility traits. The team genotyped eighty-six Iranian and fifteen Afghan Baluchi sheep with a standard marker chip.

Both flocks held moderate genetic diversity, with the Iranian flock the most uniform and clearly distinct as its own cluster. Scans for selection marks flagged candidate genes tied to body weight, carcass traits, and seasonal breeding in the Iranian flock, and to weight and milk yield in the Afghan flock. The authors note the small Afghan sample and chip bias as limits on their conclusions.
pmc-13275357:
Hamza Khan and co-authors reviewed real world use of rimegepant to prevent migraine in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Rimegepant is a pill that blocks a migraine related receptor and is approved for both attacks and prevention, but everyday evidence was thin. Their hospital in Chongqing examined three months of treatment.

Records covered forty adults, most of them women, split almost evenly between chronic and episodic migraine, all taking the drug every other day. Monthly migraine days collapsed from an average above seventeen to under three, and headache days fell sharply as well. Disability and impact scores improved markedly, and quality of life rose. Gains came mostly in the first month, and by month three the two migraine types looked alike despite different starting points.
pmc-13276157:
Fengning Chen and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a drug-resistant staph bacterium that plagues Chinese hospitals. The strain, called ST59-MRSA, resists standard antibiotics and causes invasive infections. Network analysis of clinical samples singled out a gene named qorA, found mainly in this strain.

The gene helps the bacterium keep its internal chemistry balanced and resist oxidative stress, the damage from reactive oxygen. Deleting it weakened the bacterium's defenses and made immune cells kill it more easily. An antioxidant chemical partly rescued those defects. In mice, the mutant lost ground to normal bacteria in the liver and spleen. Oddly, it gained an edge in the heart, lungs, and kidneys. The authors say the gene trades immune evasion against metabolic cost, organ by organ.
pmc-13276257:
Amr Mounir and co-authors report a 2026 pilot case series on ring implants for severe astigmatism. Astigmatism blurs vision when the cornea, the eye's clear front window, bends light unevenly. The patients here had strong but regular astigmatism and corneas that were not thinning or bulging.

Surgeons used a laser to place small curved ring segments inside the cornea of twenty eyes. Vision without glasses improved at every check over six months. Corrected vision improved early on but not by the final visit. The average astigmatism fell by roughly three fifths. Several measures of image distortion also dropped, while corneal thickness stayed stable. No complications occurred during or after surgery. The authors call for larger studies with longer follow-up to confirm these early results.
pmc-13276457:
Kin Lok Wong and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on an antibody drug that calms overactive B cells in autoimmune disease. In lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, B cells help attack the body's own tissues. Most B cell drugs wipe the cells out; this one, SM03, instead strengthens a natural brake on them, a surface protein called CD22.

In lab tests with cells from healthy donors and patients, the drug cut B cell activation, antibody-producing cell formation, and inflammatory signals, all without killing B cells. In a lupus-like mouse model it shrank the spleen, lowered self-attacking antibodies, and reduced kidney damage signs. In monkeys with induced arthritis it eased joint scores and cartilage damage dose by dose. The authors call it a disease-modifying candidate for lupus, arthritis, and related conditions.
pmc-13276757:
Maite Ramírez and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on whether emotional intelligence shields children growing up in dysfunctional homes. Household dysfunction is among the most common harmful childhood experiences and raises risks of substance use and psychiatric illness. A protective inner factor could soften that path.

The study included one hundred eighty-seven children and adolescents aged seven to seventeen from a multicenter Spanish project. Statistical mediation models tested emotional intelligence as the middle link. It carried a real share of the effect on age at first substance use and on severity of use. It also mediated roughly half the link to lifetime psychiatric diagnoses and prescribed psychiatric drugs. For behavior problems and overall functioning, it acted as a complementary pathway. The authors urge building emotional skills in exposed youth.
pmc-13276957:
Mai A Abdelmawla leads a 2026 review of body clocks and small RNA molecules that do not code for proteins. Circadian rhythms are the roughly twenty-four-hour cycles that shape sleep, hormones, and metabolism. Non-coding RNAs help tune the clock genes that keep those cycles on time.

Different RNA types adjust clock genes by acting as scaffolds, sponges, or switches, in the review's account. When rhythms slip out of sync, RNA patterns change too, with links to cancer, heart disease, and brain disorders. The authors discuss blood RNA tests for clock disruption and treatments aimed at RNA targets. Personal care that fits each person's rhythm is the longer goal they outline.
pmc-13277757:
Lydia Harris leads a 2026 case report of a patient found to have two rare histiocytic diseases over seven years. Histiocytic diseases arise when a type of immune cell builds up in tissues, often in many organs at once. A 69-year-old woman first received a diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis in 2017 after a biopsy of a bone behind her ear.

Two years later, imaging found fluid around her heart and a tissue mass near its upper chamber. Seven years after her first presentation, a biopsy of the heart lining diagnosed Erdheim-Chester disease as well. Heart features that are unusual for the first disease should raise suspicion of mixed disease, the authors warn.
pmc-13279657:
Cesare Cavalera and colleagues give a 2026 review of generative AI in mental health care. Generative AI, which writes text and talk, now aids checks, care plans and talk therapy tasks. The review weighs clinical promise against risks to the human bond in therapy. The authors frame AI as an add on tool, not a stand in for human therapists.

Studies show AI can aid diagnosis steps, find brain wave marks and forecast symptom paths from session notes. Trials of AI chatbots cut anxiety and low mood in the short term, most where clinician access is scarce. Human led care still wins on deep emotional bond and impact. Risks hold dependence, echo back that feeds bad views or false beliefs, and hard legal and moral knots. The mirror can flatter as it helps, so guard rails matter.
pmc-13279757:
Pengfei Shi and Alan Bairner published a 2026 analysis of how China's national youth sport policies shifted across a decade. Drawing on incrementalism theory, which expects policy to change in steps, the authors applied bibliometric, content, and network analysis to 105 policy documents. The documents came from the central government between 2013 and 2023.

Three phases emerged. Policy attention began with cultivating competitive talent during the 2012 to 2016 political period. It then moved to integrating sport with education from 2017 to 2021, and adopted a health-first principle from 2022 onward. The turns align closely with party congress cycles and national Five-Year Plans. Small early measures sometimes served as anchors that later, larger reforms built upon. The authors also flag coordination friction between the sports and education bureaucracies. They suggest the lessons travel best to countries with strong central coordination and a developmental view of youth wellbeing.
pmc-13279957:
Nagendra P Luitel and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of why people with depression in Nepal struggle to reach care. The study examines both the demand side of help-seeking and the supply side of services. Nepal has worked to fold mental health into primary care, yet the treatment gap remains wide. The authors map how system weaknesses intersect with community beliefs, money problems, and geography.

On the supply side they found limited resources, thin staffing, patchy infrastructure, and medication supplies that come and go. On the demand side, stigma, cultural beliefs, and uncertainty about where or when to seek support kept people away. Long travel distances and costs added friction. Providers reported heavy workloads and little backing for this work. The authors argue that expanding clinics alone will not close the gap. Coordinated action on stigma, communication, supply chains, and workforce capacity must move together.
pmc-13280257:
Carlos Alberto Rodriguez-Aceves and colleagues give a 2026 review of surgical care for traumatic peripheral nerve injuries. Such injuries come from cuts, crush or stretch of nerves outside the brain and cord. They can cause nerve pain, numbness, weak muscles or all three, with deep life impact. Sound clinical checks and the right scans are key to spot injury type and pick care. The review covers the surgical toolkit and its timing.

Techniques span nerve freeing, direct stitch repair, nerve grafts and nerve transfers, used alone or joined. Among all factors that shape prognosis, surgical timing stands as the most critical. Degenerative change marches on after trauma no matter the cause, so delay shrinks gains. Repair choice turns on gap length, nerve type and wound state. Early expert referral gives patients the best shot at function return.
pmc-13280457:
Andrea de Abreu e Gouvea and colleagues report a 2026 case of three rare birth defects found together in surgery in a young infant. Type II choledochal cysts are true pouches on the bile duct and make less than two percent of bile duct cyst cases. Their patient was a forty five day old term born girl. Imaging first flagged bowel malrotation with concern for volvulus, a twisted gut emergency.

Exploratory surgery revealed the full set: a Type II choledochal cyst, a partial annular pancreas, where pancreas tissue rings the gut, and duodenal stenosis, a narrowed small gut. Management held cyst excision, a diamond shaped gut to gut join and a Ladd procedure for the malrotation. Recovery was uneventful after the combined repair. Broad thinking in infants with upper gut block can catch linked defects that scans miss.
pmc-13280957:
Diego Paredes-Burneo and colleagues traced the family tree of an Andes plant group in a 2026 study. Brachyotum shrubs spread fast and wide in the high tropics, and their past is hard to untangle. The team read gene code from about two thirds of the group's species. They used two kinds of gene data and several ways to build the tree. The methods often clashed with each other.

Some methods grouped all Brachyotum as one family line, and others split it. One method found four past events where genes flowed in from kin groups, a process called introgression. Data from leaf power cells clashed with data from cell cores, which backs the flow idea. The authors say fast plant spreads may be too tangled for simple tree methods to capture.
pmc-13281157:
Takashi Matsunaga and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a man whose lymphoma drained protein from his blood. He was fifty-one and had a slow-growing lymphoma. His gut leaked blood proteins, which left him swollen with fluid in his belly. His platelets, the blood bits that form clots, were also low. Two rounds of standard antibody care helped only briefly each time.

A scan with a tagged blood protein proved the gut leak. Doctors then gave a newer antibody drug that links immune cells to cancer cells. His blood protein rose steeply, and the swelling and belly fluid eased. His platelets climbed back to normal and beyond. The cancer went into full remission, held for more than four months when the report was written. The authors credit the drug's deep sweep of the faulty cells.
pmc-13281757:
Yuanping Chen and colleagues published a 2026 case report on cervical cancer that spread to the brain. Spread to the brain is rare in this cancer and the outlook is grim. The woman had an advanced cancer of mixed cell type. After drug and radiation care, a single lump appeared in her brain. Surgeons removed it, and tests showed the tumor was rich in a growth switch called HER2. That switch can be targeted by drugs.

After surgery she got focused radiation plus two drugs. One drug blocks the HER2 switch, and the other is a chemo pill. The cancer vanished on scans, a full response. Side effects stayed manageable. She stayed free of new growth for close to twenty-nine months from the brain surgery. The authors say the case hints HER2 drugs deserve study in this rare spread pattern.
pmc-13281857:
Ahmed Barakat and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a baby girl with a rare birth defect set. She was one year old and had a soft swelling on her lower back. What looked like a simple hernia, a bulge through a weak wall, proved wider. The same flaw set touched her spine, ribs, and belly wall. Checks also found defects in her limbs, genitals, eyes, and heart. Sound and CT scans confirmed a left lower back hernia and mapped the rest.

Surgeons repaired the hernia and covered the gap with a natural tissue mesh. The syndrome at play is thought to stem from a very early fetal change. It strikes several body systems at once. The authors stress that a back hernia in a baby should trigger a full body check. Care from many specialties, they say, gives such children the best start.
pmc-13282257:
David Dingli and co-authors present a 2026 mixed methods study on the time burden of infused treatments for a rare blood disorder. The disorder, shortened to PNH, destroys red blood cells and can be life threatening. Its main drugs block part of the immune system and are given by infusion, either by vein in a clinic or under the skin at home. Schedules range from twice weekly to every eight weeks.

Sixty-one United States patients completed a survey on time spent on treatment tasks, and twenty-five also gave interviews. All had used their current drug for at least six months. Across drug types, patients spent a median of about three hours and fifteen minutes on treatment activities each session. The authors frame such hidden time costs as part of the treatment decision, alongside how well a drug works. Interviews let patients describe that burden in their own words.
pmc-13282357:
Valentina Vinelli and co-authors present a 2026 pilot trial testing a sustainable, plant-rich diet pattern in healthy young adults. The pattern, called EAT-IT, adapts a global reference diet meant to feed people within planetary limits. Nine subjects, with a mean age of twenty-six, took part in a six-week cross-over trial. Each person followed both the test diet and a control diet based on Italian guidelines, in random order.

The test diet raised fibre intake clearly and slightly raised one class of fats. Fasting insulin and an insulin resistance score fell during the test period. Gut microbe mixes shifted, with one major group rising and one family falling. Participants generally accepted the diet but found it more effort, above all preparing legumes. Food records, body measures, and blood tests tracked the changes. Given the tiny sample, the authors frame the results as exploratory.
pmc-13282457:
Edwin Mendoza and co-authors describe a 2026 case of delayed liver injury in a woman exposed to two possible liver toxins at once. Nitrofurantoin is a first-line antibiotic for urinary infections that rarely causes severe liver damage. Their patient was a fifty-seven-year-old woman with fatty liver disease who developed sudden yellowing of the skin after a short antibiotic course, while also taking a commercial weight-loss supplement.

Blood tests showed strong liver cell damage, and autoimmune markers were positive, muddying the diagnosis. A liver biopsy showed non-specific inflammation favouring drug injury over autoimmune hepatitis. All suspect substances were stopped, and she received an intravenous antidote-style drug, N-acetylcysteine, urgently, though its benefit in this setting is unproven. The authors argue clinicians should weigh combined exposures when several liver-damaging substances are in play.
pmc-13282857:
Veronika Matschke and co-authors present a 2026 study tracking whether lab-grown glioblastoma cultures keep their energy and movement traits over time outside the body. Glioblastoma is a highly varied, invasive brain tumour. Cultures grown from patients' tumours are key test models, but their traits may drift. The team profiled breathing, fuel use, and migration in primary cultures at one and five weeks, alongside routine clinical markers.

Two energy subgroups appeared early, split by spare breathing capacity, and most cultures kept their initial profile, though some shifted from low to high breathing, showing adaptation. Fuel preferences changed with time in patient-specific ways, including greater glutamine reliance. Migration varied widely between samples; cultures from male patients closed test gaps two to six times faster than those from female patients. Movement did not track the energy grouping, marking it as a separate trait axis.
pmc-13282957:
Yulin Zeng and Ping Han report a 2026 survey study of pressure to compromise care among doctors in China. Such pressure means acting against sound clinical judgment due to system limits. The study links that pressure to burnout, job satisfaction, and patient ratings.

A survey ran from January to March 2025 in a large hospital in Zhejiang Province. A total of 120 doctors in 10 departments took part, with a response rate near four fifths. Half reported frequent compromise on a five-point scale. Scores rose with burnout and fell with job satisfaction in the data. Obstetrics and emergency care showed the highest rates in the hospital.
pmc-13283157:
Arctic char parasites get their most complete North American inventory yet in a 2026 review-plus-fieldwork effort headed by Les N Harris. The fish is a key food species for northern peoples. Fast Arctic warming makes a baseline record of its parasites urgent for future checks.

A review of 30 studies from 1956 to 2024 listed 67 parasite types. Field work added samples from 378 fish across five Nunavut areas from 2020 to 2024. Field tests found 35 types, some new for char in this region. Worm groups ruled both the review and field lists. Sea-going fish carried more types than lake fish, and patterns varied by place and season.
pmc-13283457:
Kamal A Abouzaid and a large team examined in 2026 a groove on the thigh bone linked to walking on two legs. The groove forms where a hip muscle tendon crosses the neck of the femur. Some researchers read it as a sign of habitual upright walking, a defining human trait. The team checked dry bones and dissected bodies to see how often the groove truly appears.

Eighteen bones from fourteen people and twenty-eight preserved bodies were studied. The groove showed in about a quarter of all subjects, usually on one side only, and its depth varied. New details included a small notch and a soft tissue bed under the tendon. The authors suggest strong hip movements, not upright walking alone, may carve the groove.
pmc-13283857:
Three statistical worries form a 2026 letter by Dan Xu, Hui Ma, and Dongnan Hou about a pain drug trial in older lung surgery patients. Cai and colleagues had compared two opioids in 247 patients after chest surgery. The letter praises the topic while urging more careful reading of results.

First, the main analysis used a per-protocol set rather than all randomized patients. Dropping patients after randomization can bias results when exits link to side effects. One lost patient and pump stoppages for nausea could tilt the effect upward. An all-patients analysis would guard the benefit of randomization in the trial. The writers ask for added checks before wide clinical adoption.
pmc-13284457:
Shang-Hui Ye and colleagues report a 2026 drug delivery study for hypochondroplasia, a cartilage disorder that causes short stature. Gain-of-function changes in FGFR3 overdrive growth plate signals, yet the plate lacks blood vessels, so drugs reach it poorly. The team coated nanoparticles with chondrocyte membranes and added a collagen II binding peptide to target cartilage.

In a mouse model, the particles carried a Hedgehog pathway drug to the growth plate. Treated mice showed stronger Hedgehog signals, better cilia repair, healthier cartilage cell traits, and longer bones and bodies. The authors present the platform as a promising way to deliver drugs to hard-to-reach growth plate tissue.
pmc-13284557:
Jihwan Park and Mi Jung Rho modelled in 2026 which psychological traits drive problematic smartphone use, aiming to guide app design against it. Data came from an online survey of 691 Korean smartphone users aged from their twenties to their fifties, collected across late 2019 and early 2020. Two structural models were built around anxiety, depression, self-control, and ADHD traits.

Anxiety and depression scores were strongly correlated, yet anxiety did not touch problematic use directly. Its influence ran through depression instead. Lower self-control made smartphone dependence more likely, and higher ADHD traits went with more problematic use. Simple single-score versions of standard anxiety and depression scales still fit the models well. The authors name those four factors as the ones app builders should design around.
pmc-13284757:
Esaúl Marroquín León and a large team synthesised recent guidelines in 2026 on rebuilding the breast after mastectomy. Two main routes exist: using the patient's own tissue, called autologous reconstruction, or using implants. Choice depends on cancer needs, surgical risk, and patient preference. The team searched for current practice guidelines and strong clinical studies, comparing complication rates, radiotherapy effects, and patient-reported outcomes measured with the BREAST-Q questionnaire.

Implants placed in front of the chest muscle caused less pain and less movement deformity but more fluid collections, and they can fail after radiotherapy. Own-tissue rebuilding gave better long-term psychosocial and sexual quality of life scores. Obesity and smoking stood out as the two main drivers of reconstruction failure. The authors frame the decision as a three-way balance, not a default.
pmc-13285657:
Gut fungi and viruses, not just bacteria, steer lung health from afar, Jiang Yu and co-authors argue in a 2026 review. Along the gut-lung axis, mixed germ kingdoms form one web that shapes mucus immunity and fuel use. The review sorts that web for asthma, chronic lung blockage, acute lung failure, and lung cancer.

Three shared circuits carry most traffic: germ-pattern alarms, a fatty acid path that calms defender cells, and a food-derived path through indole signals. Each illness bends those circuits in its own way. Fixes may mix diet tweaks, live and dead microbe products, and virus-of-bacteria tools. The authors urge whole-web thinking over bacteria-only plans.
pmc-13285757:
Subash Thapa leads a 2026 population survey of hard childhood experiences and mental health among young people in Nepal. Abuse, neglect, and family trouble in childhood are known risks for later illness, yet large data from South Asia stay scarce. The survey covered residents aged 16 to 29 across three provinces chosen at random.

Weighted results stand for a sample of 6,055 young people, and close to two in three reported at least one hard childhood experience. Anxiety touched about one in four, while depression and deep distress were less common but still marked. Those with four or more such experiences faced far higher odds of every outcome, including suicide attempts. Felt social support softened part of each link, which supports screening plus help that builds support and resilience.
pmc-13286157:
Muhammad Afaq Tahir and co-authors model cancer drug candidates that block a cell-cycle switch in a 2026 computer study. The switch, called CDK1, pushes cells into division, and tumors that lean on it may stall when it is jammed. Their compounds rest on a pyrazolo-pyrimidine frame, and three kinds of simulation probed which shapes grip the switch hardest.

Field models that map shape to strength scored well enough to trust for ranking new variants. Docking runs showed the best pairs locking onto a few key pockets inside the protein. Two compounds from a home library of one hundred stood out for grip strength, and motion simulations held their complexes steady over time. Body-handling forecasts also looked kind for both picks, which earns them a place at the front of the queue for lab making and testing.
pmc-13286857:
Carina Sjöberg and colleagues interview parents whose babies and toddlers were monitored around surgery for congenital heart disease. The 2026 Swedish study spoke with ten parents of children aged three to thirty-six months. Being present while machines track a child's vital signs is stressful, and parents' sense of involvement shapes their whole experience of care.

One overarching theme emerged: parents strive for connection and control through participation and staff support. Clear information laid the groundwork for taking part. Parents balanced wanting closeness against needing breaks, and they valued help that let them stay near and share responsibility while trusting staff with technical care. Tailored information and individual adjustments, the authors conclude, make participation real.
pmc-13286957:
Carlos O Schild and co-authors document a rare bacterial invasion of a racehorse's leg in a 2026 veterinary case report. A 5-year-old Thoroughbred mare developed worsening lameness and swelling around the left hock that broke into a deep, non-healing ulcer. The tendon beneath lay exposed through the skin, and nodules studded the surrounding tissue. Multiple antibiotics failed to turn the course, and the mare was euthanized on welfare grounds.

Autopsy and microscopy showed chronic ulcerating inflammation chewing through skin, tendon sheaths, and ligaments, with collagen breaking down around clusters of bacteria. Cultures from the ulcer, tendon, ligament, and joint fluid all grew Serratia odorifera in pure form. The team notes this germ, an opportunist known from human hospital infections, had never before been reported causing soft-tissue disease in horses.
pmc-13288357:
Abdelrahman Salman and Yasar Sakarya compared cornea scans in 2026 across three groups: eyes with keratoconus, eyes that bulged after laser vision correction, and healthy control eyes. All cases of the second group followed surgery for short sight. Fifty-six eyes were measured on one imaging system.

Keratoconus eyes showed the steepest front curves. Post-laser bulging eyes sat between them and controls on curve values. Both bulging groups had thinner corneas than controls, with no clear gap between them. Back-surface measures were raised in both disease groups. The authors stress full depth scanning, since the two bulging conditions look alike yet differ in cause and care.
pmc-13289157:
Sam Sherratt-Mayhew and colleagues review sight-saving therapies for a fading eye disease in 2026. The disease is retinitis pigmentosa. It slowly kills light-sensing cells. The review asks if protective drugs keep sight sharp. Four databases were searched with no date bars.

Ten trials with 1,364 people were kept. Drugs ranged from antioxidants to omega-3 fats. One herb showed a modest gain in one small trial. Proof for that gain was rated very low. Vitamin A and two other agents moved lab measures only. Overall proof ran from moderate to very low. The authors want larger, standard trials.
pmc-13289257:
Ahmad A Tarhini led a 2026 genetics study on thyroid inflammation after immune therapy for advanced melanoma. Immune checkpoint drugs can trigger the immune system to attack the thyroid gland. The team searched the whole genome for inherited variants that predict this side effect and tested polygenic risk scores, which sum many small genetic effects.

Germline DNA came from 744 people in a phase 3 adjuvant trial who received ipilimumab. A custom score built from 10 variants linked strongly to thyroiditis risk and severity, with good separation between risk groups. Several published thyroid disease scores also linked to the side effect, but the custom score performed best. The findings support genetic screening to guide closer thyroid checks during treatment.
pmc-13289357:
Ezgi B Ulas and colleagues describe a 2026 phase II trial plan, called RECLAIM, for metastatic lung cancer that stopped responding to anti-PD-1 therapy. Tumors with low or no PD-L1 often gain little from such therapy, and later options work poorly. The trial tests whether radiation plus two immune drugs can rescue response in this group.

The single-arm study aims for 30 evaluable patients whose tumors show low or negative PD-L1 and grew after first-line anti-PD-1 care. Treatment pairs ipilimumab and nivolumab with focused radiation to one to four lesions, then continues the drug pair. Main checks are safety plus disease control and shrinkage in lesions that got no radiation, at six and twelve weeks. Shrinkage away from radiated spots would signal a body-wide immune lift.
pmc-13289857:
Md. Abdur Rafi led a 2026 national survey study on wealth gaps in high blood pressure care in Bangladesh. High blood pressure drives much non-communicable disease burden, yet how diagnosis, treatment, and control split by wealth was poorly quantified. Data came from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey 2022, covering 14,178 adults aged 18 or older with measured pressures.

Overall, 22 percent had hypertension, totaling 3,142 people in the survey. Among them, 59 percent had been diagnosed before, 72.5 percent of those diagnosed got treatment, and 44 percent of those treated reached control targets as defined. Older age sharply raised odds of hypertension in adjusted models. Inequality indexes then mapped how each care step favors richer groups.
pmc-13290457:
Predicting how long patients with colorectal cancer spread to the liver will live is the aim of a 2026 machine-learning study by Nan Li and colleagues. Standard statistics struggle with the tangled, nonlinear links among clinical variables, so the team built and checked six algorithms.

From a retrospective cohort of 861 patients, the models learned to forecast survival at 36 and 60 months, with traditional Chinese medicine exposure among the inputs. An optimized XGBoost model performed best and held up on a later, temporal validation set. Explanation analysis ranked TNM stage, liver metastasis burden, and the intensity of Chinese medicine treatment as the strongest factors, with heavier treatment linked to better survival in a dose-like pattern. The group deployed the model as a web tool that returns personal risk estimates with visible reasoning.
pmc-13290557:
Boston's hospitals sit inside the city's map of racial and economic inequality, Eralp Kaan Karduz shows in a 2026 brief research report. The study asks how segregation patterns cluster around the hospitals that serve each neighborhood.

Karduz merged survey, health, and hospital data (CDC PLACES, state hospital records, and the 2018–2022 American Community Survey) for Boston's general acute-care hospitals and mapped census tracts. Race, poverty, and poor health each clustered significantly, and bivariate maps showed the three clustering together around hospital sites. Safety-net hospitals turned out to serve the areas with the deepest health and economic vulnerability, while wealthier hospitals sit in healthier zones. Patterns near the recently closed Carney Hospital underlined the burden of shifted care. The author calls for collaboration across hospitals and policies that face this spatial legacy directly.
pmc-13290657:
A man treated as worsening sarcoidosis turned out to have T-cell lymphoma wearing sarcoidosis's clothes, Renee Morecroft and colleagues report in a case report and literature review from 2026. The 57-year-old had known systemic sarcoidosis, then developed repeated high calcium and a new need for blood transfusions.

His marrow showed fibrosis with noncaseating granulomas, which fit sarcoid-driven secondary myelofibrosis. A repeat biopsy changed the story: T-cell lymphoma with a sarcoid-like reaction, and no sign of a primary marrow disease. Sarcoid-like reactions occur in a small share of lymphomas and mimic sarcoidosis closely in symptoms and tissue. The patient is now on BV-CHP chemotherapy with close blood monitoring. Morecroft and colleagues warn that atypical courses and falling blood counts in sarcoidosis patients demand a fresh look for lymphoma.
pmc-13290757:
Prescribing art works better when a database tracks who actually shows up, Kristen Krause and colleagues show in a 2026 analysis of the ArtsRx program in New Jersey. Arts prescribing, where clinicians refer patients to cultural activities, is spreading in the United States but rarely tracks engagement well.

The retrospective study pulled customer-relationship records for 498 people referred between 2023 and 2025. Only 21.9% completed the program and 45.7% withdrew, yet among completers, attendance averaged 78.2% of scheduled activities, against 8.7% for those who dropped out. Engagement tracked program year and who referred the participant, while race, ethnicity, and gender showed no link. Krause and colleagues argue the tracking platform itself is the finding: it makes quality improvement and fair scaling possible.
pmc-13291057:
Chatbots for mental health are judged through a trauma lens by Xintong Lu and colleagues in 2026. Such bots promise easy, scalable support. People with trauma histories need extra safety and control. How users read those traits was unmapped before.

A web survey drew 606 chatbot users. Their views split into five domains. Trust and data safety were two of them. Empowerment, peer support, and cultural fit made up the rest. Most users rated their bot highly. Trust, empowerment, and peer support predicted a trauma-informed view. People using bots for convenience saw them less that way.
pmc-13291157:
Uneven screening of lab-made DNA orders is a global safety gap, argue Sana Zakaria and colleagues in a 2026 essay. Screening helps block misuse of synthetic genes. Rules exist in the United States, Europe, Britain, and New Zealand. Many other regions have no such mandate.

Data on more than 700 known providers show few public screening systems. Poor and middle-income regions often lack both rules and tools. Cost, skill gaps, and weak oversight build on each other. New design tools powered by artificial intelligence raise the stakes. The authors propose stepwise paths that lower entry costs. Broad, layered checks, even if imperfect, would cut shared risk.
pmc-13291657:
Hemophilia care in Mexico lays a heavy load on families. Jaime García Chávez leads a 2026 expert consensus study on that burden. Daily preventive care is complex and time-consuming. Poor adherence then cuts how well treatment works.

Blood experts rated 32 statements in a first survey round. Topics spanned drug effect, dosing work, and daily life strain. Weak-agreement items were debated in round two. Consensus passed half the statements in the end. Experts agreed current drugs have limited effect. Prep and dosing steps were judged complex. Emotional strain was also a shared concern. Simpler care could lift adherence and results.
pmc-13291757:
Liebetrau and co-authors publish the protocol for testing olanzapine to prevent delirium after cardiac arrest in this 2026 paper. Delirium, sudden confusion and agitation, often strikes comatose survivors during intensive care recovery. It is linked to more deaths and longer hospital stays. No drug strategy for preventing it in these patients is established. This comparison forms one arm of the Danish DANOHCA trial.

Comatose adults revived from cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause will receive 10 milligrams of olanzapine or a placebo. Three evening doses are given in total. The main measure is days alive and out of hospital within 30 days of admission. Enrolment began in June 2023 and aims for 1000 patients at five sites. Liebetrau expects the trial to show whether prevention is worth adopting.
pmc-13291957:
Ziyue Xie and co-authors plant glowing nanosensors inside leaves to watch pesticides travel, in a 2026 study. Knowing where a spray ends up in a plant would help farmers waste less. Older tracking methods kill the plant and cannot follow movement live. The team built gold nanorods with a tiny gap holding a reference molecule. Delivered into leaf air spaces, the rods report pesticide levels through Raman light scattering, using the reference for calibration.

With sensor plants in place, the group compared watering roots against spraying leaves. Root-fed tricyclazole climbed upward in step with dose and time. Sprayed pesticide barely crossed the leaf's waxy skin barrier. Commercial forms of the same compound entered and moved better than the pure chemical. The authors offer the platform for tuning delivery methods. Real-time maps could cut the share of pesticide that never reaches its target.
pmc-13292157:
Karim El-Kersh and co-authors surveyed a 2026 patient group on palliative care in pulmonary arterial hypertension, a serious lung vessel disease. Palliative care can run alongside disease treatment to ease symptoms, yet it is rarely offered and often misunderstood. The web survey, shaped by patients and clinicians, reached 200 adults across 42 states in autumn 2023.

Most respondents were women, with a mean age of 58.5 years among them. A quarter described palliative care simply as end-of-life care, and over half linked it with needing extra support. Fully 85.5 percent had never discussed palliative services with their provider, and most of those were never offered a consultation. Still, 88.5 percent felt comfortable raising the topic, so the authors urge clinicians to start the conversation.
pmc-13292257: Lakshmi Sarvani Videla and Babu Reddy Mukamalla published a 2026 correction to their article on an explainable ensemble method for recognizing facial expressions. The notice restores a missing citation to Lyons and colleagues for the JAFFE database inside the dataset section, thanking the database's creators for the resource. The JAFFE set holds 213 grayscale images of ten Japanese women posing seven basic emotions. Two Lyons references, from 1998 and 2021, were added to the reference list, and The journal has updated the source article. Only this citation fix is available here.
pmc-13292357:
Pan Zhang's team tests a 2026 plant remedy for sepsis-driven kidney injury: exosome-like nanovesicles squeezed from dandelion. Sepsis often wrecks the kidneys, and the iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis seems to help drive that damage. The team isolated the vesicles, named PGY-Exo, and tried them in a living sepsis kidney model plus human vein cells inflamed with bacterial toxin.

Labeled vesicles entered both the cultured cells and kidney tissue. Treatment calmed reactive oxygen buildup and lowered TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6 levels in their experiments. Proteomics fingered the transporter SLC7A11 as the key downstream target. Knocking that protein down erased the vesicles' protection, and the authors conclude the vesicles lift SLC7A11 to hold back ferroptosis and spare the kidney.
pmc-13292557:
Melanie Brunner's team presents a 2026 protocol for catching kinases and phosphatases in the act across the whole proteome. Their on-bead assays, OBIKA and OBIPhA, let active enzyme complexes work on a cell's proteins under near-native conditions, then use mass spectrometry to name direct substrates and the exact sites changed. Preserving natural protein interactions is the design's selling point.

The workflow extracts the proteome gently, couples it to NHS-activated Sepharose beads through amino groups, and runs the enzyme reactions on that solid support. Traditional test-tube assays strip away the partnerships and modifications that steer real signaling, the authors note. They position the method as a high-throughput answer to a persistent problem: global phosphoproteomics shows which sites change, but rarely which enzyme did it.
pmc-13292657:
Tomislav Katanec and colleagues test a 2026 dental pilot idea: adding the cholesterol drug simvastatin to a bovine bone graft might help extraction sockets heal with more new bone. Nine patients needing teeth out on both sides received the graft alone in one socket and graft plus locally applied simvastatin, 1 milligram in saline, in the other. Core biopsies at three months were measured under the microscope.

Tissue makeup barely differed between sides. Connective tissue dominated both, at 59.1 percent in control sockets and 64.3 percent in statin sockets on average. New bone made up 31.0 percent against 26.2 percent, and leftover graft about 10 percent either way, all statistically insignificant. The authors conclude that at this dose and delivery, simvastatin adds nothing to early socket preservation.
pmc-13292757:
Mammar Khames and colleagues offer a critical review, published in 2026, of how brucellosis is diagnosed in camels. Brucellosis causes abortion and infertility in livestock and can also infect people who drink raw milk or handle birth material.

Across culture, blood tests, and DNA tests, the review finds weak methods and little proof that any test works well in camels. No blood test has been properly checked for camels, and the role of their unusual heavy-chain antibodies is still unknown. DNA studies also lack shared standards. Because test results are unreliable, current counts of sick camels and risk studies rest on shaky ground, which hampers joint human and animal health action.
pmc-13293657:
Yun Yu and co-authors link, in a 2026 study, the gene HMGA2 to fear behavior in dogs, separate from its known effect on body size. Small dogs tend to be more fearful, which has long blurred whether fear genes act on their own.

Genome scans across breeds tied HMGA2 to fear traits. In mice, boosting the gene in a fear hub of the brain weakened fear memory without changing weight, while deleting it strengthened fear memory. Gene activity pointed to roles in nerve signaling, synapse flexibility, and early brain growth. A human cell test also found a switch region that controls the gene, supporting a direct fear role.
pmc-13293757:
Samuel Olson and co-authors present, in a 2026 hardware paper, a programmable benchtop chamber that uses ultraviolet light to link biological molecules under controlled conditions. Light linking maps how proteins and RNA interact, yet samples overheat or burn easily in standard gear.

The portable system is built to give set light doses at safe, cool temperatures for tubes used in daily lab work. Full build files are shared under an open license, and hardware cost is listed at $250 in the specifications the authors give. Controlled dose and cooling protect delicate samples, which should make linking results easier to repeat across labs.
pmc-13294157:
Leandro Bosch and coauthors survey patient views on laser hair removal for hidradenitis suppurativa in a 2026 exploratory study. The chronic skin disease often needs layered therapy, and laser treatment is gaining use with little patient-centered data. An anonymous online survey ran from July to December 2024 among United States adults, drawing 110 completions from 132 starts.

Only 24 respondents had tried laser removal, with a median of 8 sessions. Cutting inflammation drove 92% to try it, and lumps, swelling, and flare frequency showed the strongest reported gains. Half kept benefits past 12 months. Cost blocked many: 63% paid over $1,000, and 38% stopped early.
pmc-13294257:
Pupu Li, Xia Xue, and Zisen Zhang review why CAR T therapy loses ground in B-cell blood cancers for 2026. The treatment reshaped care for relapsed lymphoma and leukemia, yet early and late resistance still cap lasting success. Causes sort into three buckets: traits inside the tumor, fading function of the engineered cells, and a suppressive tumor neighborhood.

Countermeasures are advancing on all three fronts, from multi-target receptors to metabolic and epigenetic tuning and neighborhood remodeling. The review maps each failure route to its matching fix and looks ahead to designs that hold activity longer. Better durability, not just stronger first hits, is the goal.
pmc-13294357:
Hailong Zhang and coauthors hunt a gene signature for cervical cancer diagnosis in a 2026 combined data and bench study. Public tumor datasets were mined with differential expression, network analysis, and three machine learning filters, then checked in paired patient tissues and two cancer cell lines. Four genes survived: CCND1, TRIP13, MYBL2, and GNB4.

Together the four beat any single gene, reaching an area of 0.989 in the reported model. A drug that blocks autophagy shifted all four genes, hinting at PI3K and AKT pathway ties. Silencing GNB4 slowed cell growth and cut pathway activation marks, giving the signature a functional anchor beyond pattern matching.
pmc-13294457:
Ailsa K Orr, Alex Bateman, and Dmitrij Frishman test whether folding software can spot fake proteins in a 2026 study. Spurious entries arise from gene prediction errors and should not fold, yet earlier AlphaFold work gave short fakes high confidence scores. Three predictors, ESMFold, AlphaFold2, and AlphaFold3, were run on fake and real sets split by length.

All three still scored short fakes suspiciously high, but sorting improved past 100 amino acids. Score mismatches flagged two likely fake shadow entries in a trusted database and one wrongly flagged real entry. A Gaussian process model scanning the big AlphaFold database found more suspects, best used with other checks.
pmc-13294957:
Xingwang Wang and colleagues pair two light-activated materials into one stronger cleaner for antibiotic-laced water, in a 2026 study. Tetracycline residues slip through wastewater treatment and linger in rivers, so the team joined a titanium-based metal-organic framework, MIL-125, with bismuth oxycarbonate in a heated solvent process. The junction between them, arranged as a Z-scheme, is meant to keep useful charges apart long enough to attack pollutants.

A suite of imaging and spectroscopy checks confirmed the two parts had integrated cleanly, with larger surface area and better light absorption than the bismuth compound alone. Against a typical tetracycline solution the composite destroyed up to ninety-five percent of the drug, clearly beating the single material. Trapping experiments named superoxide radicals and positive holes as the main attackers. The authors see the design as a template for visible-light catalysts aimed at varied organic pollutants.
pmc-13295057:
Jathziri Avalos-Grajales and colleagues show that the recipe ratio, not fancy after-treatment, can decide how well gold nanoparticles amplify a sensing signal, in a 2026 study. The technique is surface-enhanced Raman scattering, which reads molecular fingerprints from hot spots where light concentrates near sharp metal features. The team grew gold particles from seeds while varying the balance between gold precursor and the reducing agent sodium borohydride, watching growth live through light absorption.

Scarce reductant gave small, even particles under slow, diffusion-limited growth. Equal parts flipped the system to delayed nucleation and fast growth, yielding larger triangular plates with wide size spread. Under the microscope those triangles packed sharp edges and junctions where fields concentrate, and the equal-ratio batch amplified Raman signals up to nine times more than dispersed particles. Controlling growth kinetics, the authors argue, is a clean bottom-up dial for plasmonic performance.
pmc-13295557:
Alan Ho and co-authors systematically review whether plant polyphenols can blunt the oxidative stress that damages cells in type 1 diabetes, in a 2026 paper. Type 1 diabetes care still centers on insulin and glucose control, leaving the underlying redox imbalance largely unaddressed, even though it leaves the insulin-making beta cells exposed and feeds complications. The review gathered preclinical studies testing polyphenols, the broad family of plant compounds, against oxidative stress and blood sugar outcomes.

Across the animal and cell studies, polyphenols consistently eased oxidative stress: fat damage products and reactive species fell, while the body's own defenses, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione, recovered. Many effects ran through the Nrf2 pathway, a master redox switch. Blood sugar results, by contrast, swung with the compound and the experiment, and often moved independently of the redox gains. The authors advise future trials to measure oxidative endpoints first.
pmc-13295757:
Xiaole Han and colleagues build a DNA switch that answers only inside a narrow acidity window in a 2026 study. Most acidity sensors flip simply from off to on, blurring the slight sourness of tumours against healthy tissue and very acidic cell compartments. Their three-strand design adds two opposing off modules to carve a working band.

One module shuts the system at low acidity and the other at high acidity, leaving the middle band active. Tuning by sequence design moved that band as intended in tests. The system lit up faint surface gradients on cancer cells and also gated glowing aptamers and a gene-editing enzyme by acidity alone.
pmc-13295957:
Thilo Pfau and co-authors measure stride patterns in 2026 among chuckwagon racehorses at the Calgary Stampede. Teams of four thoroughbreds pull a heavy wagon in two rows, with front lead horses picked for agility and rear wheel horses for pulling power.

Satellite trackers on sixty horses recorded speed and stride across each race stretch. At racing speed, lead horses took quicker, shorter strides than wheel horses behind them. Gaps between the rows were widest at the start and finish and narrowed mid-race. The authors say body type and speed changes deserve further study.
pmc-13296657:
Attila Nemes and colleagues measure the left atrium in healthy mid-pregnancy using advanced ultrasound in a 2026 study. Pregnancy expands blood volume and raises cardiac output, yet detailed atrial measurements in healthy women are scarce. Nineteen pregnant women were compared with forty-three non-pregnant women using three-dimensional speckle-tracking scans.

The pregnant group showed a larger maximum atrial volume and stronger emptying during parts of the cycle. Once volumes were adjusted for body size, though, the group difference disappeared. Some measures of atrial stretch rose, while the late pumping phase stayed unchanged. The authors read the larger volume mainly as an adaptation to increased body weight rather than a sign of strain.
pmc-13297457:
Trust in robots and other embodied agents shifts with context, yet most computer models treat it as fixed. Yang Li and Yao Song tackle that mismatch in a 2026 study using quantum natural language processing, a compositional method for reading open-ended survey answers about trusting embodied agents.

Their quantum-inspired pipeline grouped responses into ten clusters and surfaced eight dimensions of trust, two of them new, among them calibrated trust and predictive reliability. Set against classical clustering, the approach separated meanings more cleanly and kept context intact when the wording was reprocessed. The authors frame trust as built from looking back at past performance and looking ahead to expected behavior, and offer their method for trust-sensitive text analysis.
pmc-13297657:
Hidden tuberculosis is more common in patients whose immune systems are suppressed for rheumatic disease, shows a 2026 study led by Anna Starshinova. The group compared 44 such patients, none with known tuberculosis contact, against 51 healthy controls using modern immune-based blood and skin tests.

Positive results appeared in 20.5% of the patients versus 5.8% of controls, a significant gap. Rheumatoid arthritis accounted for 29.6% of the patient group, and over half were receiving biologic therapy, the setting where dormant infection can wake into active disease. Anyone testing positive went on to chest CT scanning. The findings argue for careful screening before and during immunosuppressive treatment.
pmc-13297757:
Changgeng Shang and colleagues catalogue the GRAS gene family in the eastern cottonwood tree and track its drought response, in a 2026 study. GRAS genes steer plant growth and stress coping, yet the family was unmapped in this poplar. Ninety-two members were found and sorted into twelve subfamilies.

The family grew mainly through large segment duplications, and its control regions bristle with stress and hormone response switches. Under drought, members woke on staggered schedules: one within the first hours, two DELLA members peaking mid-way, and two holding steady across a full day. Five drought-linked DELLA genes were confirmed by a second method. Breeders gain candidate genes for drought-hardy poplars.
pmc-13297857:
Busaba Chuatrakoon and colleagues test whether a simple walking test can flag artery disease in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study. Blocked leg arteries are common in diabetes and cause much disability, while the standard ankle pressure test is not always handy. Two hundred twenty-three clinic patients took a shuttle walk test and had artery checks at ankle and toe.

Patients who walked 215 metres or less on the shuttle test had about double the odds of artery disease. A risk equation built from the results sorted patients fairly, though far from perfectly. The authors offer it as a first-pass screen where pressure testing is hard, and call for outside checks before any clinic adopts it.
pmc-13297957:
Most mouth cancer patients at the main referral center in Indonesia arrive late in the disease, Faradiba N R Iskandar and her team show in a 2026 chart study. They read the files of 404 treated cases from 2021 to 2025, noting tumor site, stage, care given, and habits.

The tongue was the top site, hit in 76.0% of cases. Late-stage disease showed in 64.1% of all cases. Surgery was the most used care path. Yet 21.5% of patients had no firm cancer care on record at all. The team urges faster spotting of the disease, smoother referral paths, and tighter records so fewer patients slip through the cracks.
pmc-13298157:
One patient's two sinuses offered a rare head-to-head test of dental grafting methods, described by Cristian Scognamiglio and colleagues in a 2026 case report. A healthy 68-year-old woman needed sinus lifts on both sides of her upper jaw before implants could be placed.

The right side received the standard approach, animal-derived bone graft under a collagen membrane. The left side used only a resorbable magnesium membrane, with no graft at all. Six months later, biopsies showed 56.4% newly formed bone on the graft-free side against 22.5% on the grafted side. Two-year imaging confirmed mature bone and stable implants on both sides, and the authors urge larger trials.
pmc-13298257:
A pagoda tree variety's chloroplast genome shows weak preferences in how it spells its genes, report Zhi-Qiang Mu and co-authors in a 2026 genomics study. They sequenced and assembled the genome of Styphnolobium japonicum f. oligophyllum and analyzed codon usage across its 52 protein-coding sequences.

The genome spans 158,739 base pairs in the typical four-part structure and holds 129 functional genes. Preferred codons overwhelmingly ended in A or U: 29 of 31 favored codons did so. Statistical plots pointed to natural selection, rather than mutation pressure, as the main force shaping the bias, and the team catalogued 19 optimal codons. The data are offered as groundwork for future genetic engineering in this tree.
pmc-13298957:
Ultrasound before surgery can spot breast cancer patients whose armpit nodes are clear, suggests a 2026 Indian retrospective study by Sanika Limaye and colleagues. They checked preoperative axillary ultrasound against sentinel node biopsy results in 165 women with early-stage breast cancer.

Of 86 patients called node-negative on ultrasound, the call proved right with 90.69% accuracy, and the negative predictive value across the cohort was 90.47%. Node shape, fatty hilum, and margins carried the diagnostic weight. The authors argue the scan could let some women skip sentinel node biopsy altogether, trimming surgery where resources and staging needs allow, though they recommend prospective validation first.
pmc-13299257:
Hae Sung Lee and others review how muscle-released signals from exercise might ease both muscle loss and chronic musculoskeletal pain in older adults, in a 2026 systematic review. The two states co-occur more often than chance predicts. Thirty-two human studies spanning trials, cohorts, and mechanism work met their rules.

Persistent activation of an inflammatory pathway appeared in both conditions, driven by ageing cell secretions, bacterial signals, and mitochondrial stress. Exercise-related muscle signals frequently coincided with calming that pathway and better pain inhibition. Multicomponent training showed the most consistent dual benefit. The authors propose education followed by progressive resistance training, while stressing direct proof is still missing.
pmc-13299457:
Christine Supina Pavić and co-authors review the many protein forms of p53, a central tumour suppressor, as possible cancer biomarkers, in a 2026 survey. Two promoters, varied splicing at both ends, and alternative translation starts generate numerous isoforms. These forms can partner with the full-length protein or compete at target genes, reshaping its activity.

Isoform expression differs between tumour types and normal tissue, influencing cell death, cycle control, migration, ageing, and stemness. The review gathers recent work on expression profiles and functions across common cancers. Shifting isoform ratios directly, or targeting pathways one isoform controls, could improve therapy, the authors suggest.
pmc-13299757:
R Kato and colleagues measure how pacing thresholds relate to scar depth in pig heart ventricles, in a 2026 experimental study. Wide box-shaped ablation lesions removed sideways effects, so pacing from the lesion centre tested depth alone. Fourteen animals contributed twenty-eight lesions of varying depth, measured after heart removal.

Threshold rose steadily with depth, with each added millimetre of scar multiplying the needed current by a consistent factor. Inverse calculations linked specific threshold values to estimated depths with fairly tight ranges. Earlier atrial work had found no capture beyond a set distance from living tissue. The authors offer the ventricular model as a practical guide for reading pacing responses after ablation.
pmc-13300457:
Melissa Lamar and co-authors study how personal views of a neighborhood shape census-based vulnerability scores in a 2026 paper on cognition in older Latinos. Official indices mark some districts as highly vulnerable, yet residents may see those same streets in a better light. The study enrolled 224 self-identified Latino adults without dementia, averaging about seventy years old. They rated their neighborhoods and took yearly cognitive tests, while their addresses were mapped to a federal vulnerability index.

More positive views of the neighborhood tracked with stronger scores in global cognition and working memory, driven mainly by feelings of community cohesiveness. Seeing more health opportunities nearby went with slower global decline. Views also changed the link between census vulnerability and cognition, most of all for memory scores. The authors urge researchers to pair official measures with resident views, and planners to build engaging environments, not only physical repairs.
pmc-13300857:
Fungal threads double as highways for bacteria, and Roberto Regalado with colleagues mapped the traffic rules in a 2026 microfluidics study. Bacteria grown alone were compared with bacteria sharing channels with Aspergillus flavus, a mold whose hyphae form ready-made networks. Most species traveled farther with the fungus present.

Two human pathogens, Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, spread well only in fungal company, but by opposite means. Listeria needed working flagella, while S. aureus surfed in waves driven by its quorum-sensing soaps. Grown together, Listeria curbed S. aureus movement, an effect lost when its quorum system broke. Movement on fungal roads, the authors show, is species-specific machinery.
pmc-13301157:
Siyuan Yue and co-authors engineer a fungus that turns straw sugars into lactic acid in one vessel, in a 2026 study. Enzyme cost is the choke point for plant residue biorefineries, so consolidated processing, where one organism both digests fiber and ferments, is the goal. Starting from a Talaromyces strain, the team applied two rounds of mutagenesis to raise enzyme output, then inserted a lactate making gene borrowed from another fungus.
