The mutant out secreted its parent and a benchmark industrial strain, chewing through over seventy percent of a heavy corncob load. Fitted with the borrowed gene, it produced about fourteen grams of lactic acid per liter, well above both comparison strains. That still trails bacterial factories on speed and yield, which the authors concede openly. They present the strain as a working platform for further engineering toward industrial straw to plastic feedstock conversion.
pmc-13301857:
M Vitolo and co-authors follow a 2026 prospective cohort of atrial fibrillation patients to measure harm from combined heart, kidney, and metabolic conditions. Single conditions in this cluster are each known to worsen outcomes, yet their combined weight had been unclear. The team also asked whether carrying more of these conditions reshapes the heart's upper chamber.

The cohort held 1,236 patients, grouped by whether they had zero, one, two, or three of the conditions. Upper-chamber enlargement became more common as the count rose, reaching about forty percent in the heaviest groups. Risk of death, heart attack, stroke, or heart failure admission climbed in steps with each added condition. The authors argue for joined-up care that treats the cluster rather than each disease alone.
pmc-13302057:
B Bocz and co-authors compare four laboratory workflows for vein isolation ablation in a 2026 prospective study aiming to eliminate X-ray guidance. Fluoroscopy helps guide catheters but exposes patients and staff to radiation. Newer tools, including steerable sheaths the operator can see on the mapping screen, promise a radiation-free route.

Procedural data covered 557 patients treated over three years under four different setups. Fluoroscopy time fell from about three minutes in the conventional setup to a few seconds in the newest one. Procedure and ablation times also shrank steeply, with the very-high-power short-burn workflow finishing fastest. All four complications in the whole cohort occurred under the conventional workflow, supporting the streamlined approach.
pmc-13302157:
Zhihao Wang and co-authors introduce, in a 2026 imaging paper, a compact neural network that clears haze from a single photograph. Haze varies across a scene, thinning detail near the camera while hiding distant objects, so restoration needs both wide context and fine local repair. Large models do this well but cost heavy computation.

Their network, called ADPCNet, splits the job into context estimation, geometry-aware sampling, detail compensation, and adaptive fusion of parallel branches. It holds only about seven million parameters, far fewer than many rivals. Benchmark tests on three standard hazy-image collections showed scores rivalling much larger systems, indoors and outdoors alike. The design targets real-time uses such as traffic cameras and outdoor inspection.
pmc-13302557:
Castello-Abietar and co-authors track candidemia over ten years at a large hospital in Spain. Candidemia is a bloodstream infection by Candida fungi, and it carries high death rates. Steady tracking helps hospitals guide treatment and prevention as patterns shift over time.

The study covers 2015 to 2024, spanning the COVID-19 years and the period after. It charts how cases, patient traits, and fungal types changed across the decade. It also weighs faster diagnosis and an antifungal stewardship program. The aim is to show what sped up care and where infection control still lags.
pmc-13303557:
Kamal Ali and co-authors describe a 2026 cohort study of breathing support for very preterm infants. Babies born before 30 weeks often receive high-frequency oscillatory ventilation with a set tidal volume, and clinicians need clear signs of how well carbon dioxide is cleared.

Minute-by-minute ventilator readings were paired with blood gas results from 60 infants during their first 72 hours. Blood carbon dioxide stayed steady despite wide swings in the ventilator clearance measure. A derived efficiency score varied by baby and by hour, rose with faster oscillation rates, and linked to death or serious lung disease. Efficiency plus oxygen and pressure measures sorted risk somewhat better.
pmc-13303957:
Daniela Bermudez-Aguirre, Joseph Uknalis, and Katrina L. Counihan measure, in a 2026 food safety study, the glue-like substances Salmonella bacteria secrete while building biofilms on stainless steel. These films shield the pathogen on food plant surfaces and resist cleaning. Two temperatures, fridge-like cold and body warmth, were compared over fifty hours.

Warmth produced a fast surge of free and film cells within five hours, yet the formal biofilm index ran higher in the cold. Sugars in the slime peaked at fifteen hours in warmth, proteins peaked at a day under both conditions, and loose DNA stayed flat throughout. Microscopy showed three-dimensional warm films laced with fibres and secreted material. The authors say such detail helps design sanitation that actually breaks films down.
pmc-13305257:
Jing Yang and co-authors link a simple body ratio to bone strength in United States adults in a 2026 survey study. Weight divided by waist size may carry bone information beyond standard weight charts.

Data came from 7,005 adults in a national health survey spanning 2011 to 2018, with bone density read by X-ray scanning. Higher weight-to-waist values tied to higher total bone density in every model tested, and the trend rose in a straight line. The link ran stronger in men than in women. Time-followed studies must confirm whether the ratio truly protects bone or merely tracks it.
pmc-13306357:
Haijun Lin proposed a neural system for spotting depression from just three forehead brain-wave channels in a 2026 study. Portable screening needs methods that work when only a few sensors can be worn at rest.

The DEP-TFDualNet design mixes multi-scale filtering, attention across time and frequency views, and sequence modelling to recover information lost with few channels. In the tested cohort it gave the best subject-level results and the lowest Brier score among compared models in reported figures. The authors frame the work as early evidence for low-sensor screening, not a finished clinical tool.
pmc-13306557:
Tian Wang engineered a porous framework that makes hydrogen peroxide in light and keeps working in darkness in a 2026 study. The quinoline-linked material, named Py-1Q, stores part of the light energy as free electrons for later release.

Under visible light the material produced peroxide at 1535 µmol g−1 h−1 in reported figures, a rate 8.5 times its simpler counterpart. In darkness, stored charge still yielded 95 µmol g−1 h−1 in the given measures. Computer analysis tied storage power to spread of the lowest empty energy level, guiding solar storage design. The work may also cut cold chain costs for shots sent to far off clinics.
pmc-13306657:
Anna Shao simplified making vaccine nanoemulsion with jet mixing and freeze-drying in a 2026 study. Standard production stacks high-shear mixing and microfluid steps, adding cost and contamination risk, while wet storage invites microbe growth and droplet merging.

Jet mixing settings were tuned to match standard product traits in droplet size and structure checks. Freeze-drying with protective sugars then allowed storage without a cold chain and later re-wetting for use. Light scattering and microscopy tracked how drying and revival changed droplets, supporting a single-vial format for future products.
pmc-13307057:
Shiquan Ling segmented outdoor terrain for self-driving vehicles by joining a foundation vision model with pyramid detail in a 2026 study. Wild ground scenes shift light fast, blur class borders and cost too much to label pixel by pixel.

The LapDINO design takes broad meaning from the self-taught DINOv3 model as a semantic map and fine edges from Laplacian pyramid layers as structural contours. Two-way attention lets each stream refine the other during encoding. Added attention branches sharpen the mix, aiming for safe navigation beyond paved city roads.
pmc-13308657:
Luciana Melo Campos and her team report a 2026 case of belly beriberi from thiamine lack in a boy aged eight years, first read as pancreas swelling. The boy had five months of belly pain, food refusal, gagging, and weight loss before a scope test sent his state downhill fast.

He spent 15 days on vein feeding with no thiamine in the mix, while blood lactate kept climbing each day. At a university hospital, staff guessed the true cause and gave vein thiamine, and his signs cleared within 24 hours of that dose. A check of the feed mix, which lacked the vitamin, sealed the call. Gut beriberi belongs on lists for sick children.
pmc-13308857:
Gabalape Arnold Sejie and co-authors model in 2026 what blocks HIV testing among teens and young adults at a private college in Botswana, where uptake stays low. Their survey drew 353 students by random picks, and 229 told of a test in the past 12 months for this study.

Casual ties, homes more than five kilometres from a test site, and living with a partner all tracked with missed tests. Faith group also shaped the odds in the model, with each named group showing higher missed test odds than non believers. Oddly, poor views of testing tracked with less missed testing in the data. Tailored fixes for reach and culture could lift uptake toward 2030 goals.
pmc-13310657:
Di Li and co-authors report a fishbone injury infection first blamed on an autoimmune disease in a 2026 case article. Mycobacterium marinum is a water germ that infects skin through cuts, often in people handling fish. Its slow sores can mimic many skin diseases and evade standard cultures.

A 39-year-old man with Sjögren syndrome history cut his fingers on a fishbone at work, then developed redness, swelling, ulceration, and nodules spreading up the hand and arm. Cleaning, stitching, and biopsy failed to heal the wound over four months of drainage. Three weeks on two oral antibiotics, clarithromycin plus rifampicin, settled the swelling and crusted the wound shut. The authors rest the diagnosis on history, lesion pattern, tissue findings, and drug response.
pmc-13311757:
Áine Teahan and co-authors present the 2026 systematic review on whether pharmacist prescribing works as well and as safely as prescribing by other clinicians. Pharmacists now prescribe in a growing set of health systems.

Six databases were searched from their start to January 2025, with grey searches and citation chasing added. Thirty-nine quantitative studies met the rules, which demanded a clear statement of pharmacist prescribing rights. Standard bias tools graded trials and non-randomized studies, and a structured narrative method joined the results. Of the included studies, 32 reported on effectiveness. The review weighs the proof base behind wider pharmacist prescribing.
pmc-13311957:
Anuradha Kaistha and co-authors present the 2026 study on a new antibody pair that can show whether T cells in tissue are clonal, a hallmark of T-cell lymphoma. Standard clonality tests are slow, costly, and lose tissue context.

The pair targets the two constant regions of the T-cell receptor beta chain, TCR beta 1 and TCR beta 2, which healthy T cells mix but a clone uses singly. Staining results cover 13 lymphomas and 8 benign T-cell samples, with double staining examples. Automated counting can compute the ratio between the two forms. The assay mirrors the kappa-lambda test used for B-cell tumors.
pmc-13312157:
Nina A. Ran and a large multicenter team set out, in a 2026 research letter, to compare two operations for skin cancer that has come back after earlier treatment. Recurrent cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma carries higher risks of spreading and of death from the disease than a first tumor. Mohs micrographic surgery, which checks margins layer by layer during the operation, had already shown advantages for primary high-stage tumors, but no comparison existed for recurrent ones against wide local excision.

The investigators assembled records from 12 centers in Spain, Brazil, and the United States, including only recurrent tumors removed with clear margins and no added therapy. Because patients steered toward one operation differ systematically from the other group, the analysis used propensity score weighting, with any leftover imbalance handled as covariates, in competing-risk models. The letter tracks local recurrence, regional spread, and disease-specific death as its three outcomes.
pmc-13312457:
Dainn Woo and David A. Kulber present a 2026 case report and surgical technique for a rare finger injury nicknamed the 'baby Stener' lesion. In this injury, the radial collateral ligament of the small finger's knuckle joint tears and slips through the neighboring sagittal band. The band blocks it from healing, much as the classic Stener lesion does in the thumb.

Left unrecognized, the trapped ligament can leave chronic pain, instability, and weak function, so the authors argue for early surgery rather than the conservative care finger ligament injuries usually receive. Their repair uses an internal brace to support the reattached ligament. The report walks through the diagnosis and the operative steps in detail, aiming to help hand surgeons spot this uncommon pattern and treat it before lasting impairment sets in.
pmc-13312657:
Xinyan Chen, Chenzhi Lai, Tian He, Zong Chen, and Xiaolei Jin map stem cells in skull seams to learn why some babies' skull bones fuse too early. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The condition, called craniosynostosis, warps skull growth.

The team worked with mice carrying a gene fault that mimics a human form of the condition. They read gene activity cell by cell and also mapped it in place, at very fine scale, across three stages of early growth. A tool they built, SpatialCell, sorted cells by shape and learned patterns to reach near single-cell detail. The atlas shows the stem cell niches reshaping by stage. In sick mice the stem cells sat closer to bone-forming cells and turned on bone programs too soon, while the next cell type in line ran out early.
pmc-13313157: A 2026 correction notice fixes the title of an article in Translational Animal Science about growth performance, carcass merit, and nitrogen status in long-fed feedlot steers fed industry-average or reduced protein diets. When first published, the article's title carried a wrongly prepended phrase about crude protein concentration. The publisher apologizes for the error, and the published article now carries the corrected title. Nothing in the study's content, data, or conclusions is altered.
pmc-13315157:
Wenyan Ma and colleagues track, in a 2026 study, how the heart health of Hispanic and Latino adults in the United States changed between 2008 and 2024. They compare with survey peers. Using five of the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 metrics inside a Latino cohort study with three visits, the team measured the share meeting favorable levels. The metrics covered nicotine exposure, body mass, blood lipids, blood sugar, and blood pressure among adults free of disease. The nutrition survey supplemented the analysis.

The trend lines split. Favorable blood lipid status climbed from 29.4 percent to 45.3 percent in the cohort, and favorable nicotine exposure rose from 56.3 percent to 63.4 percent over the period. Favorable blood glucose slid from 44.6 percent to 37.5 percent in the figures. Against White adults, the pattern was better nicotine metrics but worse weight and glucose. The authors call the mixed ledger a case for tailored prevention rather than campaigns.
pmc-13315257:
Niko Gioacchino Zeni and a large team tested bakery leftovers as hen feed in a 2026 trial with laying hens. From 21 to 35 weeks of age, 180 Lohmann Brown hens got a standard diet or a swapped diet. The swap replaced 20 or 40 percent with a mix of bakery, pasta, chocolate, and sweet-making by-products.

Egg counts and laying rate did not change with the swap. Egg mass fell at the 40 percent level, and hens on both swapped diets ate more, which raised feed conversion ratios, though output stayed acceptable. Egg quality and fat makeup were also measured. The work tests a circular use for food-industry leftovers.
pmc-13315457:
Disha Upadhyay and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how machine learning is paired with multi-criteria decision methods to pick sites. Choosing a plant, facility, or service location means weighing cost, logistics, customer access, environmental care, social acceptance, infrastructure, and rules all at once.

Following standard review steps, the team covered 189 articles from 2015 to 2025 across seven fields, from energy and public services to retail, water, waste, and emergency planning. They propose a combined framework that adds benchmarking, clear explanations, and validation steps. The aim is more open methods and stronger decision support when tools such as analytic hierarchy process or neural networks are used. Good site choices save money and serve people well for many years.
pmc-13315757:
Bianca Panis and colleagues present a case series in 2026 on fertility in classical galactosemia, a metabolic disease where a missing enzyme often causes early ovarian failure. Counseling has shifted lately, stressing reduced fertility rather than total infertility, since natural pregnancy can still happen.

Two women, one aged 26 and one aged 30, with gene-confirmed disease and ovarian insufficiency conceived naturally. Both kept a lifelong galactose-free diet and regular hormone monitoring, and each had an uncomplicated pregnancy with a healthy baby at term. The authors advise a two-year trying window and warn that AMH levels do not reliably predict who can conceive.
pmc-13315857:
Yong Yang and co-authors report in 2026 that R788, a blocker of spleen tyrosine kinase, protects brain tissue in experimental ischemic stroke. Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability, and oxidative damage plus regulated cell death are key injury paths that treatment might target.

The team tested R788 in mice with a blocked middle cerebral artery and in nerve-like cells hurt by hydrogen peroxide, using 24 mice in four groups. Treated groups kept more living cells, with lower iron buildup and fat oxidation, and changes along the STAT1, Nrf2, and GPX4 axis. The results offer a new mechanism for stroke care ideas.
pmc-13316157:
Yuping Lei and colleagues screened older men with coronary disease in 2026 for abdominal aortic aneurysm during routine heart ultrasound, a first such study in China. Men aged at least 65 who had coronary angiography at Liaocheng People's Hospital in early 2024 were enrolled prospectively.

All 384 patients completed aorta measurement during their heart scan, taking on average 2.1 minutes with a spread of 1.7 minutes around that mean. Aneurysm was found in 23 patients, or 6.0 percent of those screened, and four of those cases measured at least 50 millimeters and needed referral. Risk factor analysis aimed to sharpen who should be screened.
pmc-13316557:
Masato Nakadai and colleagues present a 2026 exploratory study of the lunate, a small wrist bone that can collapse in older women in a pattern unlike classic Kienböck disease in young men. Because the bone is tiny and oddly shaped, its density and strength had never been measured this way.

Using detailed CT scans plus computer stress modeling, the team studied 21 young women and 57 women aged 65 or more. Older women showed lower density and predicted strength in nearly every bone region and in both wrists, with the steepest age links in spongy and surface layers. Young women's stronger hand side scored higher. The pattern hints at fragility breaks, and the method may suit other small bones.
pmc-13316757:
Behnam Alaei, Reza Amiri Chayjan, and Mohammad Ali Zolfigol optimized, in a 2026 engineering study, a filter process that concentrates tomato serum while saving its lycopene and vitamin C. Filters clog fast, so they added periodic washing in two stages to keep flow alive.

Tuning settled on a wash cycle of 120.9 seconds at 22.3 degrees Celsius as the sweet spot in their trials. The setup concentrated lycopene over threefold and vitamin C similarly, holding back 98.3 percent and 96.4 percent of them in the reported runs. Without washing, flow died after about four minutes; with washing, runs reached the target strength. The method gives juice makers a way to bottle tomato goodness without cooking it away.
pmc-13316957:
Sandra Kwarteng Owusu leads a 2026 study of what predicts death among children admitted with pneumonia to a large hospital in Ghana, where lung infection remains a top killer of the young. The team reviewed records to find warning signs present at arrival.

Of 630 eligible children, 394 had records complete enough to use, and 19 percent of them died, many within the first two days. Most patients were under two years old. Low blood oxygen at arrival and diarrhea each roughly doubled the risk of death in adjusted models, with hazard ratios of 2.08 and 2.19 in the reported figures. Chest indrawing was common in both outcomes. Fast oxygen checks and support, the authors urge, deserve priority.
pmc-13318057:
Martin Lardy and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, the calcium sparks inside oligodendrocyte precursor cells, the young cells that grow into the brain's insulation makers. Calcium signals steer activity-guided insulation, and they come in spontaneous flickers plus responses to ATP and glutamate.

Their random, space-aware model packs in every major calcium flow, membrane voltage, and a self-amplifying release loop, tuned to real fluorescence recordings. It reproduced both flicker types without any chemical receptors and matched three distinct response patterns to long chemical pulses, sorted by a machine classifier. Fast self-amplification proved the key engine, and voltage channels nudged flicker rates. The model gives experimenters a test bed for insulation biology.
pmc-13318257:
Le Chang heads a 2026 analysis of stomach cancer that tests whether mitochondrial genes stay evenly expressed, as often assumed, or drift apart by cell type. Data came from a public single-cell set covering 24 patients and 48 samples.

Grouping cells one by one gave 43 clusters across 15 subtypes, and scores for conserved mitochondrial genes were calculated several ways. When profiles were pooled to mimic bulk sequencing, cancer and control samples looked alike, hiding the pattern. Single-cell views instead showed tumour-linked epithelial cells scoring higher while other cells scored lower. Survival checks also flagged KRT7 and KLRC1 as markers tied to outlook in early disease, pointing to cell-specific treatment ideas.
pmc-13318557:
Sabyasachi Bandyopadhyay and colleagues report a 2026 proteomics study of COVID-19. They used nose and throat swabs from patients and healthy controls. The goal was to find protein markers for diagnosis. The markers might also explain how the illness develops.

Swab proteins were broken down and read by mass spectrometry. Changes were mapped through interaction and pathway tools. Accuracy was checked by standard curve analysis. The team found 26 human proteins differing between groups. Of those, 11 stood out as candidate markers. They also found 29 viral peptides from SARS-CoV-2 proteins, six of them mutated. Candidate markers linked to altered energy pathways and disturbed immunity. Their accuracy ranged from 70 percent up to full marks in these tests.
pmc-13318657:
Jiayi Zhang and co-authors review, in 2026, how liver cancer cells rewire amino acid use. Such rewiring helps hepatocellular carcinoma grow and resist drugs. The review asks how different amino acids interact inside these tumours. It also asks which points in the network might serve as drug targets.

Attention centres on glutamine, arginine, and tryptophan pathways. Each feeds growth, spread, and treatment resistance in distinct ways. The pathways also cross-talk, so blocking one may shift the others. Limiting certain amino acids can improve how well existing treatments work. The authors map recent clinical advances and list open questions. Their aim is a base for new therapies aimed at tumour metabolism.
pmc-13318757:
Xu-Long Lu and Li-Min Yin report a 2026 retrospective study of survival after chemoembolization for primary liver cancer. Outcomes after this artery-based treatment vary widely. Consecutive adults treated between January 2022 and December 2023 were followed. The team built a model to predict overall survival.

The sample held 185 patients, with a median follow-up of 30.6 months. Deaths numbered 85, and median survival reached 28.0 months in the cohort. Response rates were 48.1 percent, with disease control at 73.5 percent by their criteria. Larger tumours, vein invasion, spread outside the liver, and weaker liver function each predicted worse survival. Blood clotting and tumour marker levels mattered too. Their score discriminated well, with a C-index of 0.812 in training.
pmc-13318857:
Pamela Schuetze reviews, in 2026, how mental health and substance use intertwine during pregnancy. Mood and anxiety disorders are common in this period. They frequently occur together with substance use. Combined exposure raises risks for mother and child, including altered fetal brain development.

The review covers how common the pairing is and the pathways linking the two. It traces effects that can continue after birth through the home environment. Barriers to proper treatment are substantial, the author notes. Effective practice favours universal screening and trauma-informed, non-punitive care. Mental health and substance services should be integrated into perinatal settings. Future work needs long-term designs, diverse samples, and culturally responsive, scalable care models.
pmc-13318957:
Ruihua Wang and colleagues review, in 2026, genistein, a soy compound, as a multi-target defence against ischaemia-reperfusion injury. That injury follows restored blood flow and involves oxidative stress, inflammation, and several forms of cell death. Proven drug treatments remain scarce. The team searched three databases for studies from 2010 to 2024.

Genistein switches on protective pathways across organs, with evidence strength varying by organ. Strong causal proof exists for some pathways in brain and kidney injury models. Liver and gut evidence is still only correlative. One enzyme, SIRT1, links reduced cell death with reduced inflammation in their account. The review flags big translation gaps: effective dish doses far exceed body levels, and most animal work pre-treats only. A salt form with better solubility shows promise.
pmc-13320257:
Huan Liang and co-authors design iron particles that swell inside cell waste sacs to kill cancer in a 2026 study. A rust driven cell death path needs iron plus acid to work well, yet tumor cell fluid is barely acid, so plain iron particles lose punch. Their shape shifting particles are built to end up in the far more acid waste sacs and grow there into lasting iron stores.

An enzyme coat helps the particles shed their shell and push deep into tumors, then sac acid swells them so they cannot be pumped back out. Trapped iron keeps making death signals, bursts the sac wall, and tips the cell into death. The death style also alerts the immune system, which adds a second attack on the tumor.
pmc-13320357:
Marzieh Saei Ghare Naz and co-authors pool studies on a common virus and womb lining illness in a 2026 review. The illness, where womb lining tissue grows outside the womb, causes pain and fertility loss for many women. Scattered reports had linked it to a sexually passed virus that also drives neck of womb cancer, so a pooled check weighed both directions of the claim.

Twelve studies with 38265 women in total entered the pool from three databases up to August 2025. Virus carriage looked common among women with the lining illness, near three in ten in the pooled share, though studies clashed widely. Pooled odds in both directions sat near flat, with no clear proof that either state raises the other. More careful work is needed, the team notes.
pmc-13320557:
Ida Olesrud and colleagues test a new viewing tool for pituitary tumour surgery in a 2026 safety study. Telling tumour from normal gland during nose route surgery is a central challenge. A dye called indocyanine green can make tissue glow, and the new scope overlays that glow on a normal colour view without switching modes.

Over 28 months, 130 patients had surgery with the overlay scope, and it worked in every case with no dye harm or technical failure. Among hormone active tumours, 75 percent reached early chemical remission. At follow-up, 17 percent still had visible tumour on scans, while an overall removal estimate reached 77 percent when remission cases without scans were counted.
pmc-13321457:
Xiaoyan Dong proposes a computer framework to estimate mental load in translation students in a 2026 study. Cognitive load is a hidden state that cannot be read off single words, so the method builds proxy scores from human measures. Those inputs include workload ratings, eye tracking, pupil size, keystroke logs, timing, and translation quality.

Three modules handle limits, time segments, and output uncertainty, letting the model follow word, segment, and whole text levels at once. The task is framed as continuous prediction rather than fixed classes. Tests span English to Chinese, Japanese, and Spanish data sets, with checks across new learners and new languages against several rival model types.
pmc-13323057:
Eduardo Gushiken-Ibanez and co-authors show that a common skin yeast helps keep mouse skin healthy, in a 2026 study of Malassezia furfur. This fungus lives on mammalian skin and can act as partner or as pathogen, depending on context.

Compounds the yeast makes from tryptophan switch on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a regulator of skin cell growth and inflammation. In human skin models and mouse skin, those compounds raised proteins that support structure and barrier function. Colonised mice given tryptophan had calmer dermatitis and a restored barrier, while a yeast mutant unable to make indoles gave no such benefit. Mice lacking the receptor in skin cells also gained nothing.
pmc-13324257:
Ch Santoshi, Suresh Kumar Mandala, and Raghavendar Raju built a deep learning tool to spot leaf disease early. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, aims at precision farming. Leaf disease can cut food supply at scale, so early finds matter. Many smart tools fail in real fields due to clutter, light shifts, blocked views, or faint early signs. Plain image nets also miss the exact spot of harm and are hard to read.

Their tool, LDDHybridNet, pairs image and sequence nets and homes in on the region of harm. It is built to show its grounds, so farm staff can trust its calls. Readers in farm tech get a design that aims for early, sharp, and clear disease finds in the field.
pmc-13325157:
Priyanka Das, Satyajit Saha, and Amit Kumar Bhunia build light sensors from cadmium and zinc sulfide nanostructures in a 2026 study. The devices rest on Schottky barriers formed against silver contacts.

Cadmium sulfide nanorods, zinc sulfide nanoparticles, and a half-and-half mix were grown by simple precipitation and coated by spin coating. All three sensors rectified current strongly, up to a million-fold within one volt in the dark. The nanorod device proved most sensitive, with detectivity near 2.75 × 10^5 jones and rise and fall times near 187 and 194 ms. Each device also showed switchable photocurrent. The zinc sulfide version trailed on most measures.
pmc-13325857:
Alberto S. Luviano and colleagues study light-switchable wormlike micelles built with azobenzene guests in a 2026 paper. Long tubular micelles thicken solutions, and light offers a clean remote switch for their shape.

At pH 11, CTAB and sodium salicylate solutions with the trans forms of two azobenzenes grew tidy wormlike tubes. Ultraviolet light at 360 nm flipped the guests to their cis forms and broke the network into fragments. Yet the overall tangle scale barely moved, and the fluid stayed in the semidilute regime with slightly lower thickness. Heat flipped the guests back at a steady single-rate pace. Local shape and bulk flow thus part ways under light.
pmc-13328257:
Maria Dobrushina and co-authors share early lessons from a 7-tesla MRI drug study in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 perspective. Pairing medicines with ultra-high-field imaging promises sharp data, but the practical hurdles of the early phases are seldom reported. Their pool began with 1,001 patients at their site.

Only 476 carried the needed diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia from Alzheimer's, and just 48 people, 10 percent of that group, passed every screen. Beta-blocker use alone excluded 27.5 percent at one stage, lack of interest took 20 percent, and metal or tattoos barred 8 percent in the tallies given. The authors offer fixes for recruiting, screening, and scheduling that balance strict science with real-world feasibility.
pmc-13330657:
Rodrigo Morchón and colleagues map monthly heartworm risk in pets in Chile in a 2026 study. Heartworm, spread by mosquitoes, can kill dogs and cats by harming heart and lung vessels. The team modelled habitat fit from vector records and climate data, then checked the model with blood tests from north-central Chile.

Tests covered 323 pets, with 178 cats and 145 dogs. Prevalence came to 12.9 percent in cats and 5.5 percent in dogs in the reported results, and all positive pets sat in high-risk zones. Risk peaked in the southern summer and fell near zero in winter. Forecasts to 2100 warn of large southward growth in fit habitat. Monthly risk maps could time preventive care.
pmc-13331157:
Alp Temiz and colleagues track real-world use of anifrolumab in lupus over 12 months in a 2026 study. Twenty adults with active disease received the drug every 4 weeks across centres, with checks at baseline and every 3 months. People with active kidney or brain involvement were excluded.

Disease activity scores fell steeply by month 12 in the reported values, and most patients reached low activity state while half reached remission marks. Steroid doses dropped, with most baseline users reaching low daily doses and three stopping fully. Drug persistence at 12 months was 65 percent in the cohort summary. Fifty-five side events arose, four of them serious. Immune markers also calmed.
pmc-13331457:
Sudipta Mondal and colleagues report a 2026 case of a frail patient in their nineties with a nonstop wide-complex fast heart rhythm showing a left bundle branch block pattern. Adenosine stopped the rhythm only briefly, and electric shocks failed because it restarted at once.

Recordings from inside the heart narrowed down how the rhythm was driven and, after it stopped, revealed alternating bundle conduction during slow rhythm. The measured H-V interval of 306 ms ranks among the longest ever reported and points to a badly diseased conduction system below the His bundle. The patient received a pacemaker plus beta blockers and amiodarone. The authors stress how very slow conduction can still persist in such damaged tissue.
pmc-13331957:
Yiou Fu and co-authors developed a questionnaire in 2026 to measure marital anxiety in married breast cancer patients who are still of childbearing age. Treatment effects such as breast loss, sexual problems, and fertility risk can strain a marriage, yet no dedicated scale existed for this worry.

Working from social ecological theory, the team drafted items through a literature review, patient interviews, and expert advice, then tested the scale on 509 patients split between two analysis samples. The final tool has 25 items across three main dimensions and nine sub-dimensions. Reliability scores were solid, with an overall alpha of 0.865 and a test-retest value of 0.902, and content validity indices were high. Some fit measures were only marginal, so the authors call the scale a useful starting tool that still needs wider checking.
pmc-13332357:
Michael Kostares and colleagues map 2026 variation in selected cranial emissary foramina in adult Greek skulls. These variable bone channels can carry veins between networks outside the skull and venous sinuses inside it. Their surgical relevance turns not only on presence, but on side, size, shape, and nearness to landmarks. The team used a mixed design pairing direct study of dry skulls with CT scans.

The retrospective set held 200 adult specimens: 50 dry skulls and 150 CT examinations. Four channel types were assessed for presence, side, shape, size, and topographic relations: parietal, sphenoidal, mastoid, and the posterior condylar canal. Side-to-side variation and co-occurrence patterns were also explored. Surgeons and radiologists gain a Greek population reference for planning skull-base work and for reading scans without mistaking normal channels for disease.
pmc-13332457:
Qinqin Shu and Yan Li tracked how nursing workload rises and falls across an intensive care stay in a 2026 retrospective study. Their records came from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2008 and 2019. Earlier work measured nursing intensity once, missing how the pattern itself might signal a patient's course.

Among 7,334 adults who stayed at least seven days, a daily score built from sedation handling, charting frequency, and organ support needs sorted patients into four paths. The rapid improvement group, 9.6 percent of patients, saw intensity fall from 56.2 points to 29.8 points and had the lowest death rate at 9.6 percent, plus the shortest stays. The late escalation group, 4.9 percent of patients, climbed from 38.5 points to 61.7 points, and 39.3 percent of them died. After adjustment for age, sex, and severity, rapid improvement carried 74 percent lower death odds while late escalation carried 86 percent higher odds than the persistent high group.
pmc-13333357:
Wei Mi and colleagues review 2026 control of the committed step in LPS building. LPS is a key outer membrane component of most Gram-negative bacteria, maintaining wall integrity and forming a barrier against environmental stress, host defenses, and many drugs. Its synthesis must be tightly run to assemble the outer membrane properly while preventing toxic buildup of middle products. Central to control is LpxC, a deacetylase driving the committed step and directing metabolic flux into the pathway.

In Escherichia coli, LpxC amount is mainly run by proteolysis through the membrane-bound AAA protease FtsH. Two key membrane proteins regulate that process: LapB acts as an adaptor promoting LpxC breakdown, while YejM acts as an anti-adaptor blocking that activity. Through this network, signals from multiple stages of LPS building plus inputs from other cell wall pathways tune LpxC levels. The review maps a control circuit that drug makers could use.
pmc-13334057:
Jonadab Dos Santos Silva and colleagues discuss a 2026 trial of cannabinoids for Alzheimer-type dementia, calling it promising but not yet script-ready. Cury and colleagues present the first random placebo-controlled trial of a low-dose balanced THC-CBD extract targeting thinking in Alzheimer-type dementia. The study is a first in a field long ruled by stories and weak evidence. It showed modest thinking improvement on the Mini-Mental State Examination, yet lacked daily-life and behavior outcomes, raising questions about real-world benefit.

Method limits, including small sample size and limited power, temper reading yet point to a need for bigger studies. For clinicians, the trial turns guesswork into evidence-based counseling, backing informed talks while warning against early use of unregulated cannabis products in Alzheimer's care. A real signal, measured with a narrow thinking test, is not yet a treatment ready for the script pad.
pmc-13335657:
Hui Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 three-part kinetic control strategy for low-defect single crystals for X-ray detection. All-mineral 0D material shows strong stability and great potential in X-ray detection. Practical performance is limited by built-in point defects and solvent mixing.

The authors propose a three-part kinetic control strategy using iodoacetic acid as an additive to regulate crystal growth. The COOH group coordinates with under-linked lead ions to suppress deep-level traps. Released iodide ions fill potential iodine gaps, while the bulky CH2I group provides steric blocking against solvent mixing. This engineering approach yields Cs4PbI6 single crystals at 1.95 times 10 to the power 10 ohm cm and an enhanced carrier mobility-lifetime product. X-ray devices based on these crystals achieve a high response of 897.4 microcoulombs per gray-air per square centimeter.
pmc-13336357:
Yeqiang Zhou and co-authors built a protein-mimicking polymer that changes shape to sense iron with extreme sensitivity in a 2026 materials study. Synthetic water-soluble polymers usually cannot hold defined folds because their charges repel, yet this peptidomimetic polyelectrolyte keeps helical and sheet forms across the physiological pH range.

Its ordered folds create clustered carbonyl groups that fluoresce in the near-infrared with a large Stokes shift. In sheet form the polymer chelates ferric iron cooperatively at several sites, snapping into a helix and quenching fluorescence nonlinearly. The team calls this conformational transduction amplification. They used it to visualize and track iron distribution and metabolism inside cells and whole organisms in real time, a capability relevant to anemia and overload disorders.
pmc-13336457:
Xiaoyan Meng and co-authors identified a nerve cell subpopulation that tumors recruit to build a protective niche in head and neck cancer in a 2026 study. Nerves thread densely through the mouth and face, and their role in squamous cell carcinoma growth is gaining attention.

The team traced Schwann cells through cancer development and found an HLA-DR positive subset that cancer cells induce and that accumulates as tumors progress. Cancer educates these cells through the NRG1/ERBB3 axis and JAK/STAT signaling, giving them immune-shaping, tumor-friendly traits. The converted Schwann cells release CCL2, summoning a macrophage subset that in turn draws CD4 T cells via CXCL10, completing a cancer-neuron-immune niche. Blocking CCL2 with pirfenidone or CXCR3 with AMG487 suppressed tumors in an orthotopic model.
pmc-13336757:
Bincy Lathakumary Vijayan leads a large 2026 team building sodium-ion batteries that dissolve safely inside the body. Such power sources could spare patients a second surgery to remove implants. The team tried thin molybdenum or magnesium films as current collectors inside quasi-solid batteries.

Molybdenum versions clearly won, giving a discharge capacity of 6.8 mAh per square centimeter at a C/2 rate, about twice the magnesium result in the study tests. They kept 86% of capacity after 100 cycles at 2C in lab cycling. Cell tests passed the 70% viability safety threshold, and implants in animals degraded safely over three months. Changing the coating thickness tuned working life from days to months.
pmc-13336857:
Yuefan Bai and co-authors test a plant compound against drug-resistant stomach bacteria in a 2026 study. Helicobacter pylori drives gastritis, ulcers, and stomach cancer, and standard antibiotics increasingly fail while also disturbing gut microbes. Carnosic acid, drawn from traditional Chinese medicine, killed the germ strongly and narrowly in lab tests.

No resistance appeared after long repeated exposure in the lab runs. The compound blocked urease, curbed biofilms, slowed swimming, and damaged cell membranes, working even better in stomach-like acid. Paired with omeprazole in mice, it cleared resistant infection better than standard triple therapy, with little harm to tissues or gut microbe diversity. A multi-target natural lead could spare broader antibiotics.
pmc-13336957: A 2026 correction notice repairs Figure 1 of a 2024 Advanced Science paper by Yue Dong and co-authors on core-shell gel nanofiber scaffolds made by microfluidic spinning for wound repair. Overlapping scanning electron microscope images appeared in panels c–e because one image, cropped and enlarged to show fiber detail, was mistakenly reused during figure assembly. The notice supplies corrected Figure 1 and Figure S2 and states plainly that the error was an oversight in figure preparation. It does not change any results, discussion, or conclusions of the original paper.
pmc-13337057:
Biwen Zhu and colleagues show how stiff liver tissue invites pancreatic cancer to settle in a 2026 study. Scar-making stellate cells lay down collagen that stiffens the liver, but the settling mechanism was unclear. On gels of tuned stiffness, stiff settings switched stellate cells on and started a self-reinforcing stiffening loop.

Stiffness opens a calcium channel, Piezo1, stressing cell internals and raising output of a factor called GMFG. Shipped into cancer cells, GMFG binds TNS4 and boosts grip on matrix plus fat making, two growth programs. In mice, blocking the channel or the GMFG-TNS4 axis cut liver spread and early seeding. Softening the welcome mat could slow a deadly metastasis.
pmc-13337457:
Seri Jeong and colleagues track immune signals around a stitch that holds the cervix closed in pregnancy in a 2026 study. Cervical insufficiency, painless opening in mid-pregnancy, is a major cause of preterm birth. The team collected 128 neck-of-womb swabs from 64 women, before and after cerclage, and measured 17 checkpoint regulators plus 17 inflammatory signals.

Several checkpoint levels fell after the stitch while others, including TIM-3 and PD-L2, rose alongside many inflammatory markers. Before stitching, women with bulging membranes carried higher levels broadly. Seven named signals, including CCL2, IL-6, and IL-17A, ran higher before cerclage in women who later delivered preterm. Such profiles could help predict which patients the stitch will save.
pmc-13337657:
Keshav L. Ramachandra and co-authors model how ghost knifefish sense nearby fish of their own kind in a 2026 study. These fish use a spread of electric sensors across the body to pick up faint, wide signals. Dense sensors near the head help with small prey, but their value for broad signals was unclear.

Computer models that copy real body layout tested detection and direction sensing at different distances. Denser sensors improved detection most at middle distances of 35 to 50 cm, in front of the fish. Surprisingly, the dense front array added little to judging direction for broad signals. The authors argue that pooling many sensors mainly helps when signals are spread out.
pmc-13337757:
Christina E. Freibott and colleagues sort college students by opioid knowledge and campus ties in a 2026 study. Data came from 7,087 students aged 18 to 25 at 17 colleges in the 2021 to 2022 Healthy Minds Study. The aim was to find groups that campus programs could target more precisely.

Four profiles emerged, from highly knowledgeable students ready to act in an overdose to students cut off from campus resources. The largest group, at 60 percent, knew little yet said they would intervene in an overdose as reported. Profiles differed in misuse, naloxone knowledge, Good Samaritan policies, and mental health. Tailored education and wider naloxone access follow from the pattern.
pmc-13337957:
Estefania Gonzales and colleagues tested in 2026 whether gonadal vein width tracks pelvic vein symptoms in women with pelvic varices. The study weighed symptom links against vein blockage near the pelvis and surface varicose veins, since overlap muddies diagnosis. Files and scans from 2013 to 2024 found patients with pelvic varices wider than 5 millimetres.

Of 200 patients, mean age 52.4 years, 84 had symptoms and 116 did not, and vein width was read by two readers on CT, MRI, or ultrasound. Models then tested which traits best matched symptoms. The work helps doctors tell true pelvic vein disease from other vein troubles when weighing treatment.
pmc-13338757: Frontiers Production Office issued a 2026 correction. It covers only the AI use note of a study on youth work against gambling harms in Springfield. The note was wrong as printed. No generative AI was used to create the work. Figure alt text wording is also now stated correctly. The rest of the study stands unchanged.
pmc-13340857:
Karan Prasad and colleagues looked at four odd eating disorder cases in 2026 where diagnosis was missed at first contact. Odd forms strain standard diagnosis rules, which leads to missed cases and delay. Each patient had met doctors before, yet eating problems went unseen, masked by worry, drink use, attention problems, or life stress.

Risks in the cases were top level sport, past trauma, drug use, gender dysphoria, and harsh life events. Sport stars in weight class sports may eat very little while keeping a high body weight, which hides the problem. The cases urge doctors to screen for eating problems even when first complaints point elsewhere.
pmc-13341857:
Metabolism as the missing middle layer of cognition is proposed by Bianca Bonato and Umberto Castiello in a 2026 review. Brain imaging and electrodes mostly catch side echoes of neural activity, while the chemistry powering signaling stays out of view.

Mass spectrometry now detects metabolites, transmitters, lipids, and volatile compounds in tiny amounts, and breath testing can sample some of them without entering the body. The authors weave energy research with metabolic profiling to argue these signals track cognitive states. Reading the results is tricky: body-wide physiology, gut microbes, and the surroundings all leak into the same measures. Designs pairing chemistry with neural data are the way forward.
pmc-13342157:
Chamaida Plasencia-Rodríguez and colleagues mapped next drug choices in 2026 after biologic or targeted synthetic drugs fail in rheumatoid arthritis. Biologic and targeted synthetic drugs widened treatment choice, yet proof on drug order after failure stays mixed and hard to use. The review searched PubMed and Cochrane Library from 2010 to June 2025.

Reviews, pooled trials, randomised trials, and real world studies in adults after at least one failed targeted drug were grouped into preset clinical scenes by count and type of prior drugs. The scene based map gives doctors a hands on guide for next drug choice after targeted drug failure.
pmc-13342957:
Mohammed Kattan, Swailma Shaikh, and Abdulhamid Elyousfi report two 2026 cases of glomus tumors hidden in the fingertip pulp. Such tumors usually sit under the nail, but these two women had four years of sharp pinpoint pain and cold sensitivity with normal X-rays and no nail changes at all.

Ultrasound aimed exactly at the sorest spot found small, blood-rich nodules in both patients. MRI described one lesion clearly yet missed the other. Surgery removed both tumors fully, pain stopped at once, and relief held at six months. The authors argue that a blank MRI should not rule out the diagnosis when targeted ultrasound can pinpoint the spot.
pmc-13343157:
Mustafa Obeid and co-authors design a gene therapy for WWOX-related epileptic encephalopathy in a 2026 mouse study. Children missing working WWOX copies face severe developmental and seizure disorders with no effective treatment, so the team tuned a replacement therapy in mice that lack the gene entirely.

Neuron-only gene expression, driven by the human synapsin promoter in an AAV9 virus, beat broader or glia-targeted designs. Dropping an extra control element allowed careful dosing, and the best dose restored survival, growth, behavior, and fertility close to normal. Treated brains gained myelin and calmed inflammation, and early treatment in the first five days of life gave lasting rescue, setting design rules for patient trials.
pmc-13343257:
Shuxuan Qin and colleagues report a rare heart case in 2026. A 13-year-old girl with tetralogy of Fallot had her left common carotid artery growing from the main pulmonary artery instead of the aorta. She arrived with a bulging chest wall but no blue spells, fainting, or growth delay.

Ultrasound confirmed the classic Fallot defects plus a right-sided aortic arch and an odd vessel, and CT angiography traced the carotid's strange origin and twisted start. Brain vessel imaging showed strong backup circulation, so surgeons repaired the heart and tied off the stray carotid in one operation. Oxygen saturation rose from 92 percent to full, and recovery stayed good at six months.
pmc-13343857:
Aroa Silgado and co-authors evaluate a new blood test for chronic Chagas disease in 2026. Diagnosis of Trypanosoma cruzi infection demands two agreeing antibody tests, and cured patients can stay positive for years, so the team checked a chemiluminescence assay built on antigens the parasite itself sheds.

Using 227 stored serum samples judged by two reference tests, the new assay agreed 93.8 percent of the time, with 92 percent sensitivity and full specificity. Cross-reaction appeared only in some Leishmania-positive samples, never in viral ones. Uniquely, its antibody index fell steadily after treatment, making it a strong confirmatory test and a rare tool that can track recovery over time.
pmc-13343957:
Peter J. Brechting and Chad A. Rappleye mapped the peroxisome protein set in 2026 in disease phase Histoplasma yeasts during infection. Inside host phagocytes, Histoplasma beats defences and grows within phagosomes, a process needing peroxisome function for many poorly mapped roles. Early disease depends on proper trafficking of peroxisome matrix proteins carrying a type 1 targeting signal.

Proximity labelling with a peroxisome targeted TurboID biotin ligase named peroxisome proteins, with comparative proteomics against cytosol controls. The protein map shows which peroxisome proteins back growth inside cells. The findings point to fungal peroxisome biology as a possible weak spot in histoplasmosis.
pmc-13344057:
Jordan Marchak and co-authors surveyed clinics on two digital tools that support care for childhood cancer survivors, in twenty twenty-six. Survivors need guideline-based follow-up for life, but many face gaps in care. The two tools, Passport for Care and Cancer SurvivorLink, help build, update, store, and share tailored care plans. Eighteen clinics that use one or both were asked what they know of the tools and how news of features should reach users.

Awareness of the core features of each tool was high. Knowledge of the teaching and clinician-focused extras was thinner. Clinics picked distinct ways to spread word to clinics, clinicians, survivors, and the wider public. The survey was part of a joint push to link the two tools, so that survivor-centered care plans can follow patients more smoothly across settings.
pmc-13344857:
Akira Otani and co-authors write up a 2026 case where fixing one heart valve eased leaks in two others. An 87-year-old woman with stubborn heart failure had tight, low-flow aortic stenosis plus moderate-to-severe mitral leakage and severe tricuspid leakage, and her age and frailty ruled out open surgery.

The team chose a 23-millimeter Navitor Vision valve delivered through the leg, picked for her small aortic ring and to spare the mitral valve nearby. Implantation left no meaningful gradient or leak, pressure unloading let both leaky valves improve, and drip drugs were stopped. Follow-up scans showed lower right-side pressures and lighter leakage all around, rewarding careful valve selection.
pmc-13345857:
Sifan Fei and co-authors review medicine-food homology substances for heart and vessel disease in 2026. In traditional Chinese medicine, certain natural products count as both food and remedy, and the review gathers how items such as astragalus, codonopsis, hawthorn, and ginseng act on cardiovascular pathways.

Four core routes organize the evidence: defending vessel walls, protecting heart muscle, tuning the gut-heart axis, and controlling risk factors. Trials show these substances boost standard therapy as add-ons with mild side effects. Gaps remain in trial size and product standardization. Large multi-center trials, omics integration, and strict quality control, the authors argue, would carry these remedies toward precision use.
pmc-13346757:
Rony and coauthors track why surgical births rose sharply in Bangladesh. The rate rose from about 4 percent in 2004 to near 45 percent in 2022. Surgical birth saves lives when care needs it. A surge past need points to overuse, the team argues.

They used national survey data for close to 27,000 married women. Records span three waves from 2004 to 2022. Wealth, school, place, and clinic type all shaped the rate. Private clinics drove much of the rise in late years. The shift widened gaps between rich and poor mothers, the team finds. The team weighed each factor on its own while holding the other factors in place.
pmc-13347357:
Xiaosheng Chuai, Longyong Shu, and Zhonggang Huo rebuild past tectonic stress in the Pingdingshan mining area, in a geology study from 2026. Rock damage was read at three scales, from quarry-wide cracks down to crystal-level slips in tectonite, to split the area history into Indosinian, Yanshanian. Himalayan stress phases and to date the main rock-forming stage.

Sandstone cracks fell into tensile and shear families, and crystal damage was led by dislocation glide and climb in the microscopic checks. The greatest stress direction swung from north-south through northwest and northeast toward north-northeast across the phases in the reported sequence. Late Yanshanian stress sizes were then calculated for mine planning context.
pmc-13347657:
Mohammad Istiaque Hossain and colleagues coat silica films with thin metal layers to shed desert dust, in a study from 2026. Solar panels and optics lose power when dust sticks and light bounces off, so sputtered films of plain silica, titanium over silica. A conductive oxide over silica were exposed outdoors for two months and probed for roughness, wetting, and hardness.

Titanium-topped films drew the least dust, a gain tied to surface shape, wetting, energy, and likely charge drainage in the reported analysis. Hardness held up well after outdoor ageing for that stack. Modelling put panel efficiency near 27.28 percent for the titanium build, linking dust control to real power gains in harsh sites.
pmc-13348057:
Bianca Laker and colleagues report the complete genome of a soil bacterium that can eat xanthan gum, in an announcement from 2026. Microbacterium strain UB-LE1 was fished from Teutoburger Forest topsoil near Bielefeld, Germany, by feeding cultures only xanthan, picking the flask that thinned the gum most. Isolating an orange colony for storage and DNA work.

The closed circular genome spans 3,410,522 base pairs with a G plus C share of 70.46 percent in the reported assembly, a firm base for finding the enzymes that cut this common thickener. Such degraders interest food, waste, and drilling fields where xanthan buildup needs controlled breakdown.
pmc-13349757:
Keren Michael, Nick Farajev, and Orit Karnieli-Miller map what builds moral courage confidence in medical students, in a survey study from 2026. A total of 178 clinical students answered online scales on workplace professionalism climate, empathy attitudes, talk confidence. Belief in their power to act against wrongdoing by others or themselves despite personal risk.

A supportive professionalism climate tied directly to courage confidence on both fronts, with path values of 0.40 and 0.44 in the reported model. Empathy reached courage only through talk confidence, a two-step path, so the authors urge training that fixes ward climate while also building empathy and speaking skill together.
pmc-13350257:
Zhao Wu and co-authors built a sepsis-specific inflammation grading system in a 2026 study using a large intensive care database. They first tested 18 existing nutrition and inflammation scores in 11,577 sepsis patients for how well each forecast death in hospital or in intensive care.

Seven scores predicted death but only weakly. Two simple ratios based on inflammation, one comparing neutrophils to lymphocytes and one glucose to lymphocytes, performed best. Joining them into a new system sharpened prediction, and the result was checked in a separate hospital cohort. A score built from routine admission blood tests could help intensive care teams spot the sickest patients sooner.
pmc-13350357:
Xiaobin Zhang and co-authors weighed in 2026 two plans to stop leakage after rectal cancer surgery. One was a transanal drainage tube. One was a diverting stoma. Leakage after anterior resection remains a top post-surgery worry. It lengthens hospital stays and at times needs reoperation.

Seven studies covering 1,347 people were hunted through December 2025. No marked overall gap in leakage risk was found between tube and stoma groups. The odds ratio was 0.73. Subgroup results favoured the tube on some outcomes. The synthesis helps surgeons weigh a less invasive tube against a stoma that alters bowel function and quality of life.
pmc-13351157:
Ida Bromell Kindberg and co-authors followed teenagers operated for scoliosis in a 2026 case series with unusually long follow-up. The 120 patients, aged 11 to 21 at surgery with segmental screw constructs, were tracked for a median of nine years, between five and fifteen.

Complications occurred in 12.5 percent. The spinal curve was corrected by 78 percent on average, drifting only slightly by the final check. Quality of life and self-image scores improved significantly, and 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied, with work and education status recorded. Durable results like these help families weigh major spine surgery during adolescence.
pmc-13351857:
Yu Ning, FuQiang Zhao, and Qian Liu describe TouchWGNN in 2026, a touch-based system for skilful robot hand control. Robot hands struggle to judge object pose when sight is blocked and contact changes fast. Their hand carries a low-cost sensor array with 113 force points spread across key contact areas of five fingers.

Touch readings form a graph over space and time, where nodes hold force and position and edges link nearby points. A graph encoder reads contact shape, a time module tracks its change, and the result merges with camera and joint data for learning by trial. Tests on cube turning and Baoding ball swapping beat single-sense baselines, showing raw touch adds clear value.
pmc-13351957:
Hammad A. Khan and colleagues review endoscopic surgery for chest-level disc herniation in 2026. Such herniations are rare, sit in complex anatomy, and open surgery carries notable harm. Three databases were searched to February 2026 for studies of at least 5 adults with reported outcomes.

In total, 23 articles covered 695 patients, with 586 treated by endoscopy and 109 by open surgery. Nerve pain was the top reason for endoscopic surgery at 44.2 percent, followed by cord pressure at 43.7 percent. Many hardened discs were treated by both routes. The review weighs safety, benefit, and where the margin over open surgery truly lies.
pmc-13352057:
Silia Ayadi and colleagues propose a 2026 framework linking dairy processing to varied breast cancer findings. Studies of dairy and breast cancer disagree, and results differ by product type and how much processing it undergoes. Nutrition alone may not explain the split, so the authors turn to chemistry created during processing.

Heating and storage can form cholesterol oxidation products and other active lipid compounds. In lab models, some of these compounds sway inflammation, oxidative stress, and hormone signals, while others may protect. Direct human evidence tying intake of such compounds to breast cancer is still thin. The review maps what to measure next so the processing idea can be tested properly.
pmc-13352157:
Abdikadir Ahmed Hassan and colleagues write a 2026 letter on stubbornly high cervical cancer deaths in India. Their letter responds to work by Singh, Grover, and Dhanasekaran using GLOBOCAN 2022 and other global datasets. Screening coverage stays very low, and deaths have not fallen since India's 2016 screening policy began.

The writers caution against blaming the screening test alone. Trend data cannot separate one policy part from shifts in treatment, referral, and case mix over time. Poor follow-up after screening in a South India programme shows the whole chain from test to treatment matters. They argue the full care path, not one test swap, needs repair.
pmc-13354957:
Deepash Kothiwal and co-authors studied yeast in 2026 to learn how cohesin, a protein that holds sister DNA copies together, also keeps genes near chromosome ends switched off. They made a form of cohesin that cannot gain a small tag called SUMO. Then they checked gene activity, DNA packing, and how chromosome ends sit in the cell.

Without the tag, genes near the ends turned on, even though the usual silencing proteins stayed in place. Chromosome ends also failed to grip the cell edge and packed less tightly, while cohesion itself stayed normal. The work shows the tag has a distinct job in shaping and silencing the ends of chromosomes.
pmc-13355357:
Donghong Yin and others tested two education strategies to cut routine cephalosporin skin testing after China's 2021 policy ended the practice, ran the interrupted time series study in 2026. Many prescribers kept ordering skin tests from habit and liability fears, and in one nephrology department rates stayed high three months after the policy change. A useful rollout push was needed.

Point education and rotation talk were brought in to prescribers, and skin test rates were tracked before and after the step. The time series shows whether aimed education, rather than the policy alone, shifted conduct. Clinic leaders gain a tested approach for closing the gap between national guidance and ward practice.
pmc-13356557:
Heidy Cos and co-authors analyzed in 2026 hospital readmissions after surgery to remove colorectal cancer spread to the liver. Readmission is a key quality measure, but its drivers after this surgery were unclear. Using a global database of 935 patients treated from 2000 to 2018, they matched readmitted patients with similar patients who stayed home.

The overall readmission rate was eight percent, at a median of two weeks. Readmitted patients had far more deep infections, bile leaks, and liver failure. Yet survival and receipt of follow-up chemotherapy did not differ from matched peers. The authors say patients readmitted for mid-to-late problems can recover fully and stay on their treatment path.
pmc-13358757:
Yi-Fan Zou and co-authors test a faster recovery plan for a deadly heart emergency in a 2026 study. A tear in the aorta, called a type A dissection, needs urgent surgery with the heart stopped and the body cooled. Standard anesthesia keeps patients on machines long afterward. The team tried an ultra fast track plan that wakes patients much sooner.

They reviewed 90 patients treated at one Nanjing hospital in 2023 and 2024: 30 on the fast plan and 60 on standard care. The fast plan group had lower hospital costs and was checked for safety and recovery speed. If waking sooner proves safe even here, it could reshape care for this high-risk surgery.
pmc-13358857:
Xiaohan Jin and co-authors review the state of lung transplantation in a 2026 paper. Transplant remains the only firm cure for end-stage lung disease, and 2025 brought progress on several fronts. The authors gathered the year's key studies and sorted them into four areas: how organs are shared, care around surgery, how grafts get injured, and new frontiers.

They also drew on society guidelines and early 2026 work. Gains ranged from fairer allocation rules to deeper insight into why donated lungs fail over time. The review serves as a map of where the field stands and which problems, from organ shortage to chronic rejection, still block the road.
pmc-13360257:
Raimonda Tamulionytė-Skėrė led a 2026 study of breeding readiness in warmblood mares. Vets judge a mare mainly by ultrasound scans of her womb and ovaries, the standard tool in practice. But getting pregnant also depends on fine body processes a scan cannot show. The team measured blood and body markers around the time of insemination, among them the hormone estradiol and an inflammation marker called IL-6.

Mares that became pregnant had higher estradiol levels than those that did not. The team also tracked follicle size, womb swelling, age, and past foaling history as part of the picture. Their aim was to see which added markers tell vets more than scans alone. Such markers could help breeders time insemination better and raise the odds of a foal.
pmc-13360557:
Anqi Li and co-authors report a 2026 series of six cases where breast cancer spread to the ovaries. The breast cancer was invasive lobular carcinoma, a type known for spreading to the belly, gut, and pelvic organs. Its spread to the ovaries is rare and can look just like a fresh ovarian cancer. The six women were 33 to 65 years old and had a history of this breast cancer.

Ovarian masses showed up during follow-up visits or at first diagnosis. The team studied the scans of the ovaries, belly lining, and fluid to learn why these cases get misread. Mistakes can lead to big surgery the patient does not need. The authors stress the value of a biopsy before surgery, so treatment matches the true source of the tumor.
pmc-13360757:
Wenda Hu and others showed that water inhibition of alkanol dehydration on titanium dioxide depends on crystal facet, in 2026. Water is ubiquitous in biomass-derived feeds, yet its tiny impact on oxygen-removal reactions was poorly known, mainly for drivers exposing other facets. Facet-given conduct could explain inconsistent catalyst work.

Using well-defined titanium dioxide nanocrystals with dominant (101) and (001) facets, the team found water inhibition of isopropanol dehydration about four times more severe on the (001) surface. In situ NMR, infrared light tests, kinetics, and theory traced the difference to distinct water-alkanol complexes. Catalyst designers gain facet-level guidance for biomass conversion in wet feeds.
pmc-13361257:
Yuzhen Ge and co-authors built a catalyst that turns polypropylene waste into liquid fuels in a 2026 study. Breaking this common plastic down with hydrogen can make fuels and chemicals, but the reaction often goes too far and wastes product as gas. Ruthenium catalysts are the best known, yet their tight atom clusters drive that over-cutting. The team seeded single cobalt atoms into the ruthenium surface on a titania support.

The mixed sites kept ruthenium's cutting power but raised the barrier against late over-cutting. Tests ran on both virgin polypropylene and waste plastic. Careful in-process analysis showed how the mixed atom sites behave while working. A catalyst that stops at long liquid chains could make plastic recycling pay, turning trash into fuels and feedstocks instead of low-value gas.
pmc-13362657:
Giovanni Maizza and colleagues report a 2026 study of a pulsed laser weld in IN792, a nickel alloy used in hot engine parts. They probed the weld with a fine grid of tiny indents to map hardness spot by spot. The team also introduced a new hardness measure that strips out a known size effect, so results can be compared fairly across welds and labs.

Their math split the fused zone into its main phases: the soft matrix took just over half the volume, and fine hard grains most of the rest. Hardness values shifted between the top, neck, and bottom of the seam as cooling speed changed the grain mix. The method also offers a way to size the heat-affected zone when microscopes cannot.
pmc-13363057:
Bo Wu and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on a sunlight-driven catalyst that breaks down dye pollution in water. They paired carbon-doped graphitic carbon nitride with a bismuth compound rich in oxygen gaps, forming a two-part junction that keeps light-made charges apart longer. Glucose served as the carbon source in a two-step build. Standard tools confirmed the crystal shape, surface traits, and chemistry of the blend.

The best blend cleared nearly all of two test dyes within 90 minutes under light, far better than either part alone or an undoped pairing. Superoxide radicals did most of the attacking work. Computer modeling backed the test results. The team offers the recipe as a model for designing strong, cheap catalysts for dirty water cleanup.
pmc-13364257:
Zhengyan Zhang and Quan Feng present a 2026 study on a new way to train a large vision and language model to spot plant disease. Their method adds small trainable parts to both the image side and the text side of the Qwen model. Text answers then guide how the image side learns.

The team trained the model on one crop disease set and tested it on a second set from a new source. Scores stayed high in both tests, with only a small drop on the new set. The work shows a path to farm tools that can name a disease and also explain the call in plain words.
pmc-13365457:
Handika, Suraedi, Sjah, Hamdany, and Sentosa test two sensing methods on eco concrete beams in twenty twenty-six. The beams use palm oil boiler ash and nano silica in place of some cement. Four point bending tests load the beams until failure. The team tracked strain and cracking with fibre optic and camera based methods.

Distributed strain from the fibre system rose at the beam bottom as cracks grew. Camera based imaging mapped crack openings from tiny to several millimetres wide. Deflection derived from the fibre data matched direct sensors within seven percent. The fibre method gives continuous strain over the whole beam for global behaviour. The camera method captures local deformation and cracks with high precision. The authors present the pair as complementary tools for structural assessment.
pmc-13366357:
Luke McGeoch and co-workers track in 2026 lung germ RSV bursts in care homes in England in the first cold span after a new shot roll out. The shot went to folks age 75 to 79, but most home folks run old than that. The team pulls burst reports from Oct to March.

pmc-13400657:

pmc-13402257:

pmc-13402357:

pmc-13403157:

pmc-13403357:

pmc-13403557:

pmc-13403657:

pmc-13404957:

pmc-13405557:

pmc-13405657:

pmc-13407857:

pmc-13407957:

pmc-13408157:

pmc-13410357:

pmc-13410557:

pmc-13411057:

pmc-13411157:

pmc-13412057:

pmc-13414057:

pmc-13414557:

pmc-13415257:

pmc-13416457:

pmc-13416757:

pmc-13417857:

pmc-13418057:

pmc-13418757:

pmc-13419057:

pmc-13421257:

pmc-13421357:

pmc-13423457:

pmc-13425657:

pmc-13426257:

pmc-13426357:

pmc-13427057:

pmc-13427557:

pmc-13430857:

pmc-13432157:

pmc-13433657:

pmc-13434457:

pmc-13435357:

pmc-13436557:

pmc-13436657:

pmc-13437157:

pmc-13437257:

pmc-13437757:

pmc-13450557:

pmc-13450957:
