pmc-13452357:
Mariotti and colleagues test rapid gene sequencing in this 2026 study of a deadly transplant complication, thrombotic microangiopathy, in which small blood vessels clog and shred red cells after stem cell transplantation. Among 195 adult transplant recipients screened early with harmonized diagnostic criteria, ten met the threshold for confirmed disease.

Those ten patients suffered 60 percent one-year non-relapse mortality and showed strong complement activation, with blood levels of the marker sC5b-9 significantly above both unconfirmed patients and healthy controls. Their DNA carried seven rare variants in complement-related genes. A rapid nanopore sequencing workflow identified every variant with complete agreement against conventional testing, delivering answers within 72 hours in the study's design. The authors argue early genomic results could trigger timely complement-blocking therapy and might one day extend to screening donors.
pmc-13452557:
Bence Balázs Mészáros and eight co-authors find a way to turn esters straight into ethers, skipping the alcohol stage that normal reduction gives. Ethers are common building blocks in drugs and materials, but making them this direct way has long been hard. Their 2026 method pairs a shop bought silane reagent with small doses of custom borane catalysts, compounds built around boron.

The reaction runs with high selectivity, meaning it hits the target bond and leaves other groups alone. By swapping the catalyst, the team could steer the same starting ester toward different ether products. They even pulled off a rare swap of an enol ester into an enol ether, a change long seen as out of reach. Computer models point to a closeness effect inside the catalyst as the force that drives the unusual path.
pmc-13453457:
Ezgi Senoglu and colleagues present a step-by-step protocol for reading chemical marks on DNA-packaging proteins in single cells from lab-grown brain tissue. These marks, called epigenetic marks, switch genes on or off without changing the DNA code itself.

The method, named Epi-CyTOF, uses a machine that tags proteins with metal labels and weighs them cell by cell. Steps cover designing the antibody panel on a computer, attaching labels, preparing and staining samples, and reading the complex results. The team built the protocol on cortical organoids, tiny brain-like clusters grown from stem cells, as their model system. They also give tips for using the method on tumour organoids grown from gut and food-pipe cancers.
pmc-13453857:
Akiyoshi Takami and Ichiro Hanamura argue for clearer talk about food in blood diseases, in a commentary dated twenty twenty-six. New patients often ask what to eat to get better. The question mixes hope, habit, and a wish for control.

For most blood cancers, proof that a diet or supplement changes the disease itself is thin, they note. Social media and ads amplify diet tales and risk misleading the sick. The authors urge doctors to split supportive nutrition from true disease-changing care. Stronger public medical literacy is their shield against false claims.
pmc-13454057:
Jun Li and four co-authors test whether large language model embeddings, the number lists that encode text, can shrink tabular data for unsupervised analysis. The trick is tempting for medical tables, since turning each row into text fills gaps left by missing values. Their 2026 study compares the embedding route against working straight from the original variables, judging each by stability under small shakes.

Across several datasets and settings, the embedding route wobbled more every time. A little extra missing data, or a shuffle of column order, reshaped the low dimensional picture far more than in the direct route. With no ground truth map to check against, stability is the fair test, the authors argue. Their verdict: plain LLM embeddings are not a reliable base for unsupervised shrinking of tables, at least in this straight form.
pmc-13454657:
Itaru Hosaka and four colleagues show, in a 2026 study, how language software can mine a giant cardiology meeting program for research trends. Reading years of session listings by hand is slow and patchy. The team fed programs from the Japanese Circulation Society meetings of 2023 through 2026 into a Japanese language tool paired with topic modeling.

The software pulled 42,400 text blocks from the program files. Eight main research themes emerged from the wording. Coronary artery disease and heart failure held steady interest across the years. Team-based care involving many professions grew more visible. Fresh clusters formed around rhythm disorders and valve interventions. The authors present the workflow as a sturdy way for attendees and planners to spot rising topics without reading every page themselves.
pmc-13454857:
Radici and colleagues model how climate change may spread the Asian tiger mosquito and dengue fever risk across France through the year 2085. The mosquito, Aedes albopictus, already lives in much of Europe and can carry dengue, a virus spread by mosquito bites. Their work uses a process based model, tuned against recent local dengue cases in France, and runs it under high and mid level paths for emissions and population growth.

By 2085, under the high pressure path, most of France apart from mountain areas suits the mosquito, and local dengue spread is possible in most settled areas. Under the mid level path, results vary far more by region and climate model. Sparsely peopled areas show only fair odds for the mosquito but the highest odds for dengue spread, and mild coasts may let the mosquito stay active all year.
pmc-13455457:
Joanna Louise James and colleagues ask New Zealand parents how they received news that their baby was growing slowly in a 2026 interview study. Slow fetal growth affects up to 10 percent of pregnancies and raises risks, yet parents often lack clear, trustworthy information once a problem is named. Twenty-four participants across Aotearoa New Zealand joined focus groups or interviews by Zoom, describing what they were told, what they sought online and what would have helped.

Most parents expected a normal pregnancy and felt distress at diagnosis, valuing clinical information most when it was carefully chosen and given with empathy. Many still searched online for causes, medical terms and other families' stories, and timing mattered, since news given at a hard moment was harder to absorb. Parents wanted varied formats at varied times, gathered in one credible place, so understanding could build layer by layer rather than arrive all at once.
pmc-13455757:
Jeffrey A. Lam and six colleagues ask, in a 2026 pilot study, what recovery actually means to young adults living with major depression. Standard scorecards prize symptom cuts, yet patients may prize feeling whole again. The team surveyed 43 outpatients aged 18 to 35 at an urban safety-net psychiatry clinic, pairing personal rankings with standard scales.

About 62 percent still carried heavy depressive symptoms, while only about 17 percent counted as flourishing. Roughly 42 percent scored high on personal recovery. Asked what mattered most, participants put coping well with stress first, then functioning well, then holding hopes and dreams. Even among those with mild symptoms, most reported low flourishing. The authors argue that tracking patient-chosen outcomes alongside symptoms would give a fuller picture of mental health care's value.
pmc-13457857:
Guohao Kong and colleagues build a controllable AI image system for design work in a 2026 study. AI image tools often miss briefs and wobble on style, limiting their use in posters, logos and app screens. The team combined diffusion models, CLIP cross-modal alignment and ControlNet spatial controls into one workflow covering brief analysis, controlled generation and multi-option exploration, with metrics for quality, signal fidelity and brief matching.

Tests on posters, brand logos and mobile interfaces, using DesignBench-20K and a custom commercial set, found mobile interfaces strongest and design cycles cut by over 91 percent. Outputs held up under textual noise up to 10 percent and data shifts up to 40 percent, while ablation tests showed each component mattered differently for layout and brief matching. Designers gain a faster drafting aid with stated limits, not a replacement for judgement on abstract meaning or rights.
pmc-13457957:
Maryam Nayeri and colleagues build a sensitive label-free sensor for a breast cancer marker in a 2026 study. CA 15-3 in blood helps track breast cancer spread and recurrence, yet standard immunoassays are costly and slow. The team coated a glassy carbon electrode with carbon nanofibres, deposited palladium nanoparticles, and attached aptamers that bind CA 15-3, reading binding as a change in charge transfer resistance by impedance spectroscopy.

The sensor responded linearly from 0.01 to 200.0 units per mL with a detection limit of 0.0078 units per mL, and results on human serum samples matched the standard ELISA method well. Clinics gain a cheaper, faster candidate for CA 15-3 monitoring, though larger validation across disease stages and interfering conditions must come before routine diagnostic use.
pmc-13458757:
Randi Chen and colleagues ask whether a longevity gene decides how much quitting smoking protects a man from lung cancer. FOXO3 variants linked to long life govern stress-response pathways that might govern repair of smoke damage. Their 2026 prospective study follows 4,339 ever-smoking American men of Japanese ancestry in the Kuakini Japan-Hawaii cohort, enrolled in the early 1970s and genotyped for rs2802292, through 28 years of follow-up.

One hundred eighty lung cancers occurred. Among former smokers, carriers of the longevity G allele had far lower risk than TT homozygotes (hazard ratios 0.42 for lung cancer, 0.23 for the non-small cell type). Among men still smoking, genotype made no difference. Each year quit compounded the benefit for G carriers, cutting risk about 28 percent yearly for non-small cell cancer; TT carriers gained almost nothing per year. The authors float genotype-informed prevention, pending replication in bigger, varied cohorts.
pmc-13459257:
Yuanping Liao and co-authors compared two blood thinning strategies for preventing vein clots after hip or knee replacement surgery, using records from 26 large teaching hospitals. Their 2026 study covered 11,686 patients operated on between 2014 and 2017, of whom 4,591 received the oral drug rivaroxaban and 7,095 received injections of low molecular weight heparin. The team compared symptomatic deep vein thrombosis and lung embolism rates in hospital, alongside bleeding events, blood loss, and transfusion needs.

Deep vein thrombosis was uncommon overall, at 0.40 percent of patients, but it struck the rivaroxaban group more often. The rate was 0.74 percent with rivaroxaban against 0.18 percent with heparin injections, an odds ratio of 4.07 as reported. The same gap appeared separately in hip patients and knee patients. Only one symptomatic lung embolism occurred, in the heparin group after knee surgery.
pmc-13459357:
Valverde and colleagues tested in 2026 blocking the IL-17 receptor to calm periodontitis, the gum disease that destroys tissue and jaw bone. IL-17 is an immune signal family tied to this inflammation, and the receptor is a shared node for several family members, so blocking it could damp the whole pathway. The team profiled gum and saliva from healthy, diseased, and treated people, then gave the blocker brodalumab to mice with induced gum disease.

Valverde found IL-17-making T cells were raised in disease and fell after therapy, and gum biopsies confirmed the signal dropped with treatment. In mice, local injections of the blocker cut inflammatory gene messages in the gums. The main IL-17 signal was suppressed by day four and held down to day eight, and a second family signal fell too. Bone scans tracked jaw loss. The authors present receptor blockade as a candidate host-directed therapy.
pmc-13459457:
Ismail Macha and co-authors report a baby saved by caesarean delivery performed after her mother's death at a regional hospital in Rukwa, Tanzania. The mother, a 34 year old woman at thirty six weeks of pregnancy, arrived with a severe dental abscess. It had caused a month of jaw swelling, fever, and discharge. In their 2026 case report, the team describes her deterioration and the emergency decision to operate after she died. The procedure is rarely documented from resource limited settings in Africa.

The operation delivered a girl weighing 2,600 grams, with Apgar scores of 6 at one minute and 8 at five minutes, respectable for the circumstances. She was admitted to the neonatal unit for further care. At publication the child was one year and nine months old, meeting developmental milestones with no apparent neurological impairment. Timely surgery with skilled staff and basic neonatal support can succeed even without advanced critical care.
pmc-13459757:
Ilaria De Martino and co-authors engineered immune cells that treat a cancer shield signal as a trigger instead of a barrier. The signal is PD-L1, a protein tumors use to switch off immune attack. Their 2026 study built a synthetic Notch style receptor, called a SNIPR, into monocytic cells so that touching the signal protein activates an internal program. One programmed output makes the cell secrete CV1-Fc, a decoy that blocks the CD47 do not eat signal, licensing the cell to engulf cancer cells.

Circuit activation scaled with how much of the signal the target displayed, letting the cells gauge their target before firing. The receptor also partly blunted normal PD-1 signaling. When the circuit switched on, macrophage like cells derived from the THP-1 line engulfed SKOV-3 ovarian cancer cells more effectively in culture. The signal is a programmable input for cell therapies, the authors argue.
pmc-13461457:
Li and colleagues reported a 2026 case report of spinal cord damage after chemotherapy delivered into the spinal fluid of a fifty-eight-year-old woman. She had B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia with relapse in the central nervous system, treated with seven cycles of intrathecal chemotherapy. About a month after finishing, weakness spread through both legs.

She also lost sensation below the upper chest and could not pass urine, and MRI showed bright signals in the cord's dorsal columns without enhancement. Li's team excluded infection, autoimmune, metabolic, vascular, and leukemic causes before settling on chemotherapy induced myelopathy. Stopping the spinal treatment and giving supportive care left deficits partly permanent at three months. The authors urge close neurological monitoring during such therapy.
pmc-13461557:
Ming Ma leads a 2026 review of paper mulberry as animal feed. Paper mulberry is a fast-growing woody plant with protein-rich leaves, grown in many areas. The review asks how the plant part, the harvest stage, and the way the feed is processed change its value. It follows feed makeup through animal responses to milk and meat quality.

Evidence is strongest for cattle and sheep, where silage or fermented paper mulberry partly replaced roughage while output held steady. Changes were reported in stomach fermentation, use of nitrogen, milk fats, and meat traits. Results in pigs, poultry, geese, fish, and rabbits were mixed, pointing to lower amounts in the diet and tighter control of fiber and bitter plant compounds. The authors list gaps: standard raw material, clear rules for good fermentation, dose studies, and proof of how the plant acts in the body.
pmc-13461857:
Kosuke Suzuki leads a 2026 study of how liver health shapes the action of lenvatinib, a drug for liver cancer. Dose is set by an older liver score and body weight. Since the drug clings to the blood protein albumin, low albumin could leave more free drug in blood and change both benefit and harm. The team used a newer liver grade, called ALBI, built from albumin and bilirubin levels.

Forty-one Japanese patients who received the drug joined between 2020 and 2024. Free drug exposure, adjusted for dose, rose as ALBI scores worsened, while total exposure showed no such link. Patients at grade 2b or worse had higher free exposure, shorter time before the cancer grew, and more side effects. The older liver score did not split side effects as clearly. The authors suggest ALBI grade at treatment start could predict exposure, benefit, and harm.
pmc-13462557:
Meng-Fan Jia leads a 2026 study of an enzyme called SRD5A2 in colorectal cancer. The enzyme converts testosterone into a stronger form, dihydrotestosterone, and plays roles in sex development. Its profile in bowel cancer was poorly known. The team studied samples from 180 patients, sorting them by enzyme level, and silenced the gene in cancer cells to test growth.

Enzyme levels ran higher in tumors than in normal tissue nearby. High levels went with worse traits and shorter survival, standing as an independent risk factor after adjustment. The link held across most stage subgroups. In dishes, silencing the enzyme slowed growth, movement, and invasion while raising cell death. Protein tests showed shifts in the shape-changing program that frees cancer cells, in growth pathways, and in the cells' energy balance. The authors name SRD5A2 a driver and marker in colorectal cancer.
pmc-13463857:
Yuji Uehara and five co-authors review twenty years of care for lung cancers driven by classic EGFR mutations. Drugs that block the EGFR switch reshaped treatment for this cancer type across early and late stages. The review runs from the first blocker pills to the current standard, osimertinib, and paired regimens.

Brain spread, drug resistance, and treatment order after paired regimens each get close review. Open questions include care after the FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA trials, tumor type shifts under pressure, and fourth-round blocker drugs. New delivery routes for gene-based drugs and data-led care close the survey. Clinicians gain one map of a fast-moving field and its unsettled choices.
pmc-13463957:
Bhandari and colleagues evaluated Nepal's Primary Emergency Care training in 2026. The six-day course teaches frontline health workers to handle urgent cases and injuries. A four-level model structured the study. The team drew on records of 295 graduates. They retested 48 of them at 11 health facilities with knowledge checks and observed simulations. Interviews and group discussions with staff and hospital leaders added context.

Knowledge jumped by about 36 percentage points right after training. That gain was statistically firm. At follow-up testing, the average had slipped back by about seven points. Scores still held well above the starting line. Paramedics lost the most ground of any staff group. Trainees reported greater confidence. Observers found graduates teaching untrained colleagues, spreading skills beyond the classroom. Leaders described emergency departments that worked better when trained staff had supportive conditions. The authors recommend refreshers to hold the gains.
pmc-13464257:
Michael Z.L. Zhu and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 62-year-old woman whose routine scan found a tumour in the right upper heart chamber. Primary heart tumours are rare, and right atrial myxomas make up only 8 to 15% of them. Imaging showed a mobile, round mass measuring 23 by 25 by 25 millimetres, raising risks of blockage, clot travel, or sudden collapse.

Surgeons removed the mass fully, and tissue study confirmed myxoma, a benign jelly-like tumour. Recovery ran smoothly with no return at twelve months on follow-up scans. The case stresses urgent referral for chance heart masses, full removal, and planned surveillance, since even silent tumours can turn dangerous without warning.
pmc-13464657:
İrem Toprakçı and four co-authors build a two-layer delivery powder for curcuminoids, the active compounds in turmeric. Fat-loving curcuminoids extract well into green solvents, yet turning them into a stable, usable powder is another matter. The team first screened thirty solvent blends built on thymol or menthol.

A thymol and lactic acid blend pulled the richest extract, and tuned settings raised the yield further. The extract was wrapped in a double-layer emulsion, then spray-dried into powder with high capture of the active load. Digestion tests freed about a third of the load in both stomach and gut settings. The powder also cut cancer cell activity in dishes in a dose-linked way, which invites deeper study.
pmc-13464957:
Simone N. Visser and five co-authors review FLASH radiotherapy for lung cancer, a method that delivers the full dose in a blink-fast burst. Standard radiation scars healthy lung around the tumor, while proton beams already tighten the aim. Animal studies hint that FLASH speed spares healthy tissue at equal tumor kill.

Early human work shows proton FLASH is technically workable, with dose patterns matching or beating standard plans. Why the burst protects healthy tissue stays unsettled, with several biology accounts in play. Two hard problems stand out: keeping the dose shape tight at FLASH speeds and handling breathing motion in the chest. The authors map the device upgrades still needed before clinic trials can widen.
pmc-13465357:
Montero Carrillo and co-authors reported in 2026 a 19-year-old man in metropolitan Caracas, Venezuela, with a neck abscess caused by Brucella abortus. Brucellosis usually spreads from farm animals or unpasteurized dairy. The young man had no farm contact and no travel history. He did eat cheese regularly. His illness began in July 2024 with undulating fever and malaise.

A month later the fever intensified with chills. A painful, red, warm swelling grew on the front of his neck and formed an abscess needing drainage. Genetic testing of the pus confirmed Brucella abortus biovar 1. Treatment with rifampicin and doxycycline brought full recovery. Skin and soft-tissue involvement is uncommon in brucellosis, and neck abscesses are rarer still. The authors say this is the first recorded case of this presentation in Venezuela. They urge tighter hygiene control across the dairy chain.
pmc-13465457:
Kakimoto and colleagues compared two kinds of practical training for Japanese radiological technologist students in 2026. Cold-run training uses harmless stand-ins for radioactive material. Hot-run training uses the real thing under supervision. In total, 143 students rated their learning on five-point scales. Open-ended answers were analyzed for themes about the experience.

Both formats earned positive ratings. The hot run scored significantly higher on safety awareness and learning satisfaction. It also won on safety-related secondary outcomes. Students described tension and clinical realism in the hot sessions. Those feelings came with a sharper sense of risk. One pattern cut the other way. Fourth-year students rated themselves lower than third-years on every item, despite more experience. The authors suggest pairing both formats while adding support that keeps confidence from eroding as training advances.
pmc-13465657:
Li and co-authors searched ten eukaryote genomes in 2026 for genes acquired sideways, by horizontal transfer rather than inheritance. The species ran from human, mouse, and cow to frog, zebrafish, fruit fly, and yeast. Each genome was compared against thousands of eukaryote, bacterial, and virus genomes. Long-read sequencing and targeted lab checks guarded against false alarms from contamination.

Every species carried sideways-acquired regions. Counts ran from 10 to 237 separate transfers per species. The affected genes clustered in membrane transport jobs. Some transfers had copied themselves widely inside their host genome. A few touched hundreds or even thousands of genes that way. Transfers into complex organisms were long assumed rare and marginal. The authors argue the flow is universal across the eukaryotes they tested. It counts as a real, if modest, engine of genome change.
pmc-13465857:
De Silva and colleagues tallied fifteen years of natural hazards in Sri Lanka in 2026, drawing on the international EM-DAT disaster database. Events from 2010 to 2025 were checked against each other to avoid double counting. The team summarized hazard types, timing, and human impact across the island nation.

Fifty-nine recorded events affected about 14.5 million people in total. Roughly 1.5 million were displaced, and 2,218 died. Floods, often paired with landslides, were the most frequent and damaging events. They affected more than six million people and killed 479. Cyclones came less often but killed the most, 823 people. Droughts touched even more people than floods, over 6.5 million, yet rarely forced anyone from home. Bad years clustered in 2011, 2014, 2016, and 2025, underlining the case for flood-focused prevention.
pmc-13466657:
Jae Bum Kwon and colleagues use interpretable machine learning to explain how much hemoglobin patients lose after knee replacement surgery, in a 2026 cohort study. The group held 866 patients treated under one standardized protocol over ten years, none of whom received transfusions. Earlier work leaned on transfusion as a rough yes-no outcome, which varies by hospital habit.

Four learning methods, from plain regression to stacked ensembles, were trained on patient traits and surgical details. A clot-stabilizing drug given into the joint for some patients entered as one predictor among many. Because the models stay readable, surgeons can see which factors drive blood loss and plan prevention for the patients who need it most.
pmc-13466957:
De Kroon and co-authors measure, rather than estimate, how hormone therapy changes hair growth in transgender people. Their 2026 longitudinal study followed 36 participants, 20 transgender men and 16 transgender women, starting gender-affirming hormone therapy. Digital microscopy counted terminal hairs at several body sites at the start, three months, and twelve months, alongside body image questionnaires.

After a year, transgender women had significantly less hair on the upper lip, chin, and upper abdomen. Laser treatment made no meaningful difference to that reduction. Transgender men gained hair at every measured site, including the thighs. Both groups reported better body appreciation, more satisfaction with their hair pattern, and stronger gender congruence. The authors recommend microscopy as an objective tool for comparing hormone regimens in future work.
pmc-13468357:
Tansheet Jawad and colleagues survey in 2026 what teenagers in a rural district of Sindh, Pakistan, actually eat, and how far it falls short. Adolescents in poorer countries carry a heavy burden of dietary inadequacy, yet overall diet quality is rarely quantified. A cross-sectional survey using staged cluster sampling collected a 24-hour dietary recall from each participant and scored intake against age- and sex-specific reference standards for fourteen nutrients.

Adequacy for each nutrient was averaged into a mean adequacy ratio scaled from zero to 100, giving one diet quality number per teenager. Regression analysis then hunted for the household and personal factors tied to better or worse scores. Numbers of this kind let nutrition programs in rural Pakistan target the scarcest nutrients and the most affected groups instead of spreading supplements blindly.
pmc-13468557:
Jiali Wang and colleagues fabricate in 2026 diamond transistors with unusually high output current, aiming at power electronics that can shrug off heat and radiation. Diamond conducts heat superbly and withstands huge voltages, but building a good transistor channel in it is hard. Their devices use a thin boron-doped diamond layer, about 500 nanometers thick, grown on a single-crystal diamond substrate. A pure buffer sits beneath, and a silica layer serves as both gate insulator and protection.

The transistors showed clean p-channel behavior, the on-off current ratio staying near one hundred thousand across the temperature range. At room temperature the maximum output current was 0.18 milliamps per millimeter, rising to 1.05 at 150 degrees Celsius as resistance collapsed. Breakdown held at 347 volts for the tested gate-drain spacing. Simulations located the peak electric field near the drain-side gate edge, guiding the next design round.
pmc-13469157:
Lei Tian and co-authors review in 2026 how to measure the tiny, high-frequency magnetic fields that micro-coils produce for micro-magnetic stimulation. The technique nudges neurons with submillimeter coils. The dose of stimulation depends on those fields, yet they are weak, hug the coil closely, and shift with frequency and coupling, making honest readings genuinely hard. Probe parasitics, impedance mismatch, phase distortion, and spatial averaging all spoil readings.

The review sorts existing methods into four families: direct field measurement, resonance-boosted detection and calibration, spatial field mapping with reconstruction, and adaptive compensation. Each family is compared on frequency range, sensitivity, spatial sharpness, complexity, and whether it can run online during stimulation. Without a traceable chain from detector output to local field to dose, micro-magnetic stimulation cannot be dosed like a drug, which is the standard this review pushes toward.
pmc-13469457:
Hew-Butler and colleagues follow American college football players' bodies across four years. Their 2026 paper scans 27 players, thirteen linemen and fourteen others. Scans used dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry at August training camps. Sessions ran in 2019, 2021, and 2022, the pandemic wiping out 2020. Total, lean, and fat mass and bone density were tracked against position.

Linemen were far heavier throughout, carrying about 90 kilograms of lean mass and 31 of fat against roughly 72 and 15 in non-linemen. Across the span, the whole squad gained about 3.3 kilograms of lean mass and slightly denser bones. The positions diverged in composition of gain: above a total-mass breakpoint of about 104 kilograms, linemen added fat at nearly twice the rate of lean tissue. The authors suggest realistic yearly gain targets of one to two percent to avoid excessive fat accumulation.
pmc-13470557:
Arthur Villordon and colleagues present a data set, published in 2026. It records where lead accumulates inside sweetpotato plants. The plants were grown under controlled exposure. Two orange-fleshed cultivars were used. They were Bayou Belle and Beauregard. Both were raised in a greenhouse. They received no lead or one of two lead doses in their water.

The team measured lead in four tissues. These were the storage root people eat, other roots, stems, and leaves. Three pooled replicates covered every combination. Cultivar, dose, and tissue defined each one. This gave 72 observations in total. Lead levels were measured by mass spectrometry after acid digestion. The data support food-safety and breeding work. They show how this toxic metal partitions through the plant.
pmc-13471257:
Hatice Şeyma Yücel tests in 2026 whether machine learning can predict tomato root shape from measurements taken above ground, sparing young plants from destruction. Root architecture drives how well a rootstock feeds and waters the plant grafted onto it, but digging roots up kills the specimen. Nineteen hybrid rootstock candidates, bred from cultivated tomato crossed with a wild relative, were grown alongside two commercial rootstocks and one scion variety.

Plants were measured at four points across their first month, with roots imaged at each stage. Simple inputs such as genotype, plant height, and stem thickness fed several predictive models. A gradient boosting model and plain linear regression performed best, explaining up to ninety five percent of variation in root length, surface, and volume. Root thickness proved harder to forecast.
pmc-13471757:
Salem Ghribi and colleagues synthesize in 2026 a nanofertilizer designed to feed crops nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium while leaking far less into waterways. Their particles pair an amorphous calcium phosphate core, doped with potassium, with a urea coating that releases slowly. Standard fertilizers lose much of their nutrient load to runoff, so a controlled release design addresses both cost and pollution.

Soil columns blasted with simulated heavy rain showed the particles cutting phosphorus, calcium, and potassium losses by more than tenfold against conventional products, with urea emerging gradually. Greenhouse corn trials kept the advantage: phosphorus and calcium leaching fell by about a third, urea leaching by about three quarters. Shoot growth matched the control while root mass rose by nearly half. Soil acidity stayed near untreated levels.
pmc-13471957:
Lauren Herrera and colleagues map in 2026 the geographic mismatch between Americans who have myasthenia gravis and the specialists trained to treat it. The disease, which weakens muscles through immune attack, is growing more common past age sixty five, while neuromuscular physicians make up only about four percent of neurologists. Medicare claims supplied case counts, and board records supplied specialist counts, compared state by state for two periods.

National cases rose from about twenty nine thousand to nearly thirty six thousand between the two windows. Specialists also grew, so the national ratio improved from about fifty cases per specialist to forty four. The South carried the heaviest ratios and the Northeast the lightest. Six states had no certified neuromuscular physician in either period. The authors warn that averages hide real access deserts.
pmc-13472957:
Amitava Banerjee and a large team report a 2026 phase 3 trial of joined-up care for Long COVID in England. Six National Health Service clinics took part, and care was grouped by local primary care networks. Adults with lasting symptoms after COVID were assigned to usual care or to added support. The added options were a whole-body scan, a phone-based rehab program, or both together.

Fatigue was the main measure, checked at 12 weeks and again at 24 weeks. More than eleven hundred people joined, and fatigue scores fell in every group by a similar amount. The scan and the app did not beat usual care on the main measure. Readers get a clear test of whether extra tools add value beyond good team-based care.
pmc-13473457:
Jin and co-authors present IR-WSANet, a lightweight neural network that spots tiny infrared targets, such as distant drones, against noisy backgrounds. Their 2026 paper rebuilds the YOLOv10 detector with wavelet-based convolution that separates fine detail from broad scene structure, plus a single-head attention module that weighs local and global cues together.

Detection accuracy jumped on all three test sets: mean average precision reached 97.2% on the SIDD-City set, 82.6% on SIDD-Mountain, and 82.8% on the HIT-UAV aerial set, beating the YOLOv10 baseline by 2.8 to 14.1% across the benchmarks. The single-head design also cut the attention parameter count by 27% against multi-head attention, keeping the model light enough for field hardware. The authors target early-warning and surveillance uses.
pmc-13473657:
Chiu-Mei Lin and four colleagues studied in 2026 whether chrysin can protect arteries in diabetes by tuning recycling. In diabetic artery disease, inflammation and autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning process, interact harmfully. A small RNA called miR-204-5p was suspected of controlling a key autophagy marker, LC3B, in macrophages under high sugar. The team exposed macrophage cultures to 25 millimolar glucose and built a diabetic rat model of carotid artery balloon injury.

In cell cultures, chrysin raised LC3B while lowering miR-204-5p. Combining chrysin with a mutant form of that RNA reduced LC3B binding under sugar stress. In diabetic rats, chrysin and the wild-type RNA each shrank artery wall growth after injury, by 46.3 percent and 36.3 percent at fourteen days, alongside calmer macrophage polarisation. The authors present chrysin as useful against sugar-related artery disease, while noting cell and animal results point in different directions.
pmc-13474557:
Saeideh Izadi-Yazdi and co-authors use deep learning in 2026 to predict radiation dose maps for a cancer scan tracer. The tracer lights up tissue that supports tumors, aiding both scans and later targeted radiation care. Dose maps were first built with heavy physics tools from scans of twenty-two cancer patients. Two tracers were compared on uptake and dose to healthy organs.

The newer tracer gave sharper tumor contrast and lower dose to organs at risk than the standard tracer. A transformer model learned to predict dose maps fast, beating a simpler network on accuracy scores. Its error stayed low and nearly all checks passed a strict match test. Fast dose prediction could make personal treatment planning routine.
pmc-13474657:
Xiaoyu Ji and eleven colleagues tested in 2026 whether fermented corn germ meal improves gut health in broiler chickens. They fed 180 day-old broilers for 42 days on a basal diet, the same diet plus unfermented meal, or the diet plus fermented meal at 7 percent.

Fermentation raised protein and several acids while cutting fibre, but did not change growth. It did raise a gut acid at days 21 and 42, shifted gut signalling pathways, lowered two stress-linked signals by day 42, and raised an anti-inflammatory signal by day 21. Fermented meal also steadied gut microbe succession over time. The findings support fermented meal as a feed option for antibiotic-free poultry.
pmc-13474757:
Tianwen He and co-authors measure heart fat in 2026 in adults whose bodies combine low muscle with obesity. That mix, called sarcopenic obesity, carries heart and metabolic risk beyond either trait alone. Chest scans of 1,678 adults gave fat area around the heart and its density. Body makeup and grip strength sorted people into four groups, from normal to the combined state.

Only forty-five people met the combined state, yet their heart fat stood out sharply. Both fat area and density ran higher there than in the normal group, even after full adjustment. The combined effect beat what either trait gave alone. Heart fat scans may flag the highest-risk bodies early.
pmc-13475057:
Ding and colleagues report a 2026 study of what predicts success in group cognitive behavioral therapy for orphaned adolescents in Malaysian sheltered homes. Seventeen homes were identified and nine took part; homes were assigned to the eight-session SAHABAT therapy program or a waitlist. Depression, anxiety, self-esteem, and automatic thoughts were measured before, during, and right after the program.

Being in the therapy group, rather than the waitlist, predicted better depression and anxiety outcomes at once and across the program. Starting scores mattered too: adolescents with lower starting depression and anxiety, and higher self-esteem, ended better. Negative automatic thoughts predicted depression outcomes only. The pattern helps shelter staff triage: group therapy works broadly, but youths who start worst may need extra support layered on top to close the gap.
pmc-13477057:
Akhil Anil and co-authors compare two keyhole methods in 2026 for mitral valve repair at two United Kingdom centers. One method works fully through scopes with three-dimensional views and no rib spreading. The other uses a small chest cut with direct sight. A total of 114 matched patients with degenerative leakage were compared one to one.

Clinically notable leak return ran far lower after the fully scoped method. Bypass and clamp times ran a touch longer there, without clear significance. Both groups left repair with at most mild leak and no deaths in thirty days. Intensive care and hospital stays trended shorter after scoped repair.
pmc-13478057:
Tang and colleagues compared microscopic silica fossils inside rice leaves in 2026, asking whether chromosome count changes their shape. These fossils, called phytoliths, form in a fan shape in rice bulliform cells, and archaeologists use their size and surface facets to judge whether ancient rice was wild or farmed. The team grew haploid rice, carrying one chromosome set instead of the usual two, beside normal diploid rice and measured the fans.

Haploid fans shrank by about 18 percent overall, with fan width near 34.8 micrometers in the haploid plants measured. They also carried fewer of the fish-scale facets used in archaeological keys, averaging about 6.7 facets, and only about 7 percent reached nine or more facets. pmc-13479357:
Yong He and colleagues report a single-cell study, published in 2026. It maps the cell landscape of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. This is a common skin cancer. It arises from surface skin cells. The team sequenced RNA from individual cells. More than eighty thousand cells were used. They came from tumours, nearby normal skin, and patient blood. The aim was to see how cell types interact inside the tumour.

The team traced immune cell development. Blood monocytes progress toward a specialised macrophage state. That state promotes blood vessel growth. It also promotes tissue remodelling. A regulator called NR1H3 was linked to the macrophage programme. Its signature correlated with poorer survival. This held in several squamous cancer cohorts. NR1H3 is now a candidate treatment target.
pmc-13480257:
Giorgio Montesi and colleagues present a 2026 software tool that hunts gene markers by committee rather than by a single method. Gene signatures built by one algorithm often fail on new patient groups. Their open-source package, named TENTACLES, runs up to fifteen learning methods plus clustering tools and keeps the genes that many methods rank highly.

Crohn disease served as the test case, with 689 samples from four public gene datasets. The committee settled on a 28-gene panel that held up across groups better than single-method lists, while using far fewer genes than standard screens. A trimmed five-gene core kept strong sorting power in a fully blind check. The team offers the tool for any disease where noisy gene data have frustrated marker hunts.
pmc-13482757:
Zhenhua Li and Dingbiao Li reviewed in 2026 how fine particle pollution drives lung cancer through the GPER receptor. PM2.5 is a class I human carcinogen, and GPER, a membrane estrogen receptor, runs high in lung tumours.

Estrogen-like parts of PM2.5, plus metal ions, switch on GPER, which then fires MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways to stir inflammation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis. These shifts spur tumour growth, spread, and shape change while remodeling the tumour microenvironment. GPER thus links particle exposure to malignant progress, making GPER blockers a promising prevention and treatment avenue.
pmc-13483157:
Ya Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of a natural compound that helps rice seedlings ride out heat. Heat waves now hit the world's top staple crop harder each decade. Spraying seedlings with GABA, a signalling compound plants make anyway, eased heat harm in step with dose, with a low dose working best in their tests.

Treated seedlings kept growing, leaked less from damaged membranes, and showed fewer dead cells as reactive oxygen fell. Defence enzymes ramped up and a protective antioxidant pool rose. Gene and chemical profiles showed amino acid and sugar stores rebalanced toward calm. Heat alarm genes also switched on harder, driving stronger waves of protective proteins. A cheap spray that primes several defence lines at once may suit field trials as summers warm.
pmc-13483857:
Honglin Zhu fuses image-derived features with clinical information to stage rectal cancer before surgery more precisely. Published in 2026, the multicenter study enrolls 968 patients with rectal adenocarcinoma, split into training and internal validation groups, plus 82 patients from another center for outside testing. Over twelve hundred features are extracted from each magnetic resonance scan.

A radiomics-only model and a clinical-only model each staged early versus deeper tumors moderately well on internal testing. The weighted fusion of both beat either alone internally and held up respectably on the outside center data. Calibration and decision analyses complete the evaluation in the full report. Accurate staging before surgery shapes choices about added chemoradiation, so a validated combined model has direct planning value.
pmc-13485157:
Mara Villar-Arenzana traces a chain from chemical stress in blood to thinking problems after first-episode psychosis in teenagers. Published in 2026, the study revisits a cohort where low levels of the antioxidant glutathione predicted loss of left frontal gray matter and weaker working memory over two years. Mediation modeling tests whether brain shrinkage carries the chemical effect.

Lower starting glutathione was confirmed to predict greater frontal volume loss, and greater loss predicted steeper working memory decline. Statistical mediation supported an indirect path, with volume loss sitting between the blood marker and the memory outcome. Healthy controls showed no such chain. Targeting oxidative stress very early might therefore protect both brain structure and cognition, though intervention proof still lies ahead.
pmc-13486757:
Shiode and colleagues validated a scan-based way to measure the bone plate that caps the ends of bones inside joints, using cadaver wrists. That plate, the subchondral bone plate, matters in joint degeneration, but CT brightness values drift between scanners, blocking comparisons. Their 2026 study profiled relative brightness changes instead of absolute values in eighteen wrists from nine donors, then checked the estimates against mechanical indentation tests at the same spots.

Scan-based thickness estimates tracked the indentation measurements strongly, with negligible average bias between the two methods. Two independent readers produced consistent results, supporting the method's reproducibility. Locating where the plate starts proved less reliable than measuring its thickness, and the authors flag that step for refinement. Shiode says relative profiling could let ordinary clinical scans feed joint research without specialized equipment.
pmc-13487257:
A K M Baki and co-authors fabricate a palm-sized metasurface that twists microwave polarization across an exceptionally wide band. Published in 2026, the reflector uses a half-octagon copper pattern on a circuit board substrate backed by a ground plane, arranged in a 60 by 60 cell array. A rectangular notch triggers a special asymmetry that stretches the working bandwidth.

Measurements covered 12.68 to 38.79 gigahertz, spanning three radar and satellite bands, with fractional bandwidth above 104 percent. Conversion efficiency stayed above 91 percent, and performance held steady for signals arriving at angles up to thirty degrees. Theory, simulation, and bench results agree closely. One flat panel delivering linear, elliptical, and circular conversions on demand suits compact antennas that must serve several systems at once.
pmc-13487957:
Israel Kayode Kolawole leads a large Nigerian team evaluating care for cardiac arrest outside hospitals in a 2026 multicenter survey. Data came from six teaching hospitals, one in each geopolitical zone, covering 387 adults whose hearts had stopped before arrival. The team checked each link in the chain of survival, from recognition and calls for help to resuscitation attempts and hospital outcomes.

Most arrests happened at home, and most were witnessed, yet ambulances arrived in only about a third of cases where they were called. Resuscitation before hospital was attempted rarely, and fewer than two percent of patients survived to discharge. The authors call for a coordinated, deliberate effort to rebuild emergency response across the country.
pmc-13488157:
Huan Yang, Hong Wang, and Lei Yang study heatwaves and kidney disease in older Chinese adults in a 2026 analysis of a national aging survey. Data covered 6,718 people aged forty-five or older between 2011 and 2015, with kidney function estimated from blood tests at the start and end. Heatwaves were defined many ways, combining temperature cutoffs with spells lasting two to four days.

Stronger and longer heatwaves were linked with higher odds of developing chronic kidney disease across nearly all definitions used. Risk clustered in some regions, and people with hypertension, diabetes, or heart disease looked more vulnerable during the most intense heat definitions. The authors urge kidney prevention plans that account for a warming climate.
pmc-13488257:
Vikram Vikhe and colleagues report a 2026 case of life-threatening ammonia buildup revealing a hidden urea cycle disorder in a 32-year-old man. The urea cycle clears ammonia, a toxic waste product, from the blood, and partial enzyme defects can stay silent until illness strikes. The patient sank into coma within hours after vomiting and a recent feverish gut illness, yet liver and kidney tests and brain scans were normal.

Blood ammonia climbed to many times the safe level despite first treatments. Chemical patterns pointed to a defect early in the cycle, and a family history of parental relatedness and an unexplained newborn death fit an inherited cause. Dialysis, protein restriction, sugar fluids, and ammonia-lowering drugs restored him, and he stayed stable on supplements.
pmc-13489557:
Jessica E. Knobbe and Jennifer R. Bermick review how fetal sex shapes outcomes after chorioamnionitis in a 2026 synthesis of human and animal evidence. The condition is infection or inflammation of the membranes and placenta around the baby, common in early births, and it can injure the developing brain and lungs. Male babies suffer more from many inflammation-related problems, yet sex is often ignored in this literature, which the review sets out to correct.

Across species, males showed stronger acute inflammation, more brain inflammation, and greater structural brain vulnerability after exposure in the studies gathered. Human data linked male patterns with higher cerebral palsy and developmental risk. Females showed their own weak points, including lung function and later metabolic paths. Sex-aware risk checks are urged.
pmc-13489957:
Christopher Koch and a very large team present the Pakistan Genome Resource in a 2026 report on 173,303 sequenced participants. People who naturally carry two broken copies of a gene reveal what blocking that gene's protein might do, which helps drug developers pick safe targets. Pakistan's high rates of marriage within families make such double knockouts more common, and South Asian genomes have been underrepresented in global catalogs until now.

Participants collectively carried homozygous loss-of-function variants, meaning both copies switched off, in 6,476 genes. The resource maps how variants distribute across pathways, links genes with blood biomarkers, and supports recall studies where carriers of a gene of interest are invited back for deep testing. The authors frame it as a reference for the population.
pmc-13491357:
Shuo Tian and six colleagues published this 2026 case report of a single patient, a 70-year-old man whose star-shaped bladder stone, a jackstone calculus, sat beside prostate cancer. The spiky stones signal urinary stasis from outlet obstruction. After a year of worsening urination despite medication, imaging showed the stone and an enlarged prostate of 125 millilitres, his PSA was elevated at 16.2, and biopsy confirmed low-grade adenocarcinoma in two of twelve cores.

After discussion he underwent laparoscopic prostatectomy with the 3.1-centimetre stone removed in the same operation. Pathology upgraded the cancer to Gleason 3+4, Grade Group 2, with clear margins, showing the biopsy had understated it. Follow-up at one, three and twelve months found his symptoms improved with no more infections. The authors warn that a bladder stone must not end the workup in men with abnormal PSA, and that combined single-stage surgery is practical when treatment is chosen.
pmc-13491657:
Xuelian Song and four colleagues tell in 2026 how a leadless pacemaker that slipped into a lung artery was fished out and reused in an eighty-two-year-old woman. Leadless devices avoid the wires and chest pockets of older pacemakers, yet one can detach during placement. The woman had severe valve disease, heart failure, and pauses in her heartbeat shown on monitoring.

Soon after the Aveir device was positioned low in her right ventricle, it dislodged into the right pulmonary artery. The team caught it with a gooseneck snare together with the triple-loop snare of the retrieval catheter. The same device was then re-implanted successfully. The authors offer the rescue as a practical lesson for teams learning this newer technology.
pmc-13491957:
Nicky Van Broeck and five colleagues lay out in 2026 a three-year study protocol on keeping values-driven innovations alive in primary healthcare. Clinics drown in short-lived projects while facing fragmentation and staff fatigue, so the Belgian team wants to learn what helps a good idea become permanent. The protocol first defines what counts as values-driven, then follows selected innovations from birth to long-term embedding.

Four theories, covering realist evaluation, sustainability, implementation context, and normalization, are woven into one guiding framework. Case studies will mix document review, repeated interviews, and questionnaires across the three phases. Stakeholders will co-create a sustainability model and a set of monitoring indicators in the final phase. No results are reported yet; the value lies in the design and its participatory machinery.
pmc-13493657:
Stephen Weidinger leads a ten-author team re-analyzing in 2026 three phase 3 trials to ask how fast and how completely the eczema drug abrocitinib can deliver near-clear, itch-free skin. The bar was strict: at least ninety percent improvement in a standard eczema score plus an itch rating of zero or one. Data came from two head-to-head trials against dupilumab and one extension study of patients dupilumab had failed.

The higher abrocitinib dose beat dupilumab on the strict target as early as week two in one trial. By week sixteen in the other, about twenty-seven percent on the high dose hit the target, ahead of the low dose, dupilumab, and placebo in that order. Baseline itch severity did not change the picture much. Even prior dupilumab non-responders reached the target at meaningful rates after switching.
pmc-13493757:
Jensen Yeung and four colleagues test in 2026 whether Canadian treat-to-target goals for eczema match what dermatologists actually do in practice. The goals set measurable thresholds for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and advise changing treatment when patients miss them, yet they rest mostly on expert opinion. Chart reviews covered 297 adults on advanced systemic therapy, assessed five hundred three times over up to a year.

When patients met the target, doctors changed treatment in under one assessment in ten. When patients missed it, doctors acted more than half the time, most often by switching the systemic drug altogether. That alignment suggests the thresholds capture real clinical judgment rather than arbitrary numbers. The authors present the result as a first validation step and ask for prospective confirmation.
pmc-13493857:
Brzezińska and co-authors tested whether three weeks of ischaemic preconditioning changes how runners' bodies react to hard exercise. The method repeatedly squeezes a limb cuff to briefly cut blood flow. Forty male long-distance runners joined the 2026 double-blind trial, half receiving real preconditioning and half a sham version, with 35 finishing. Each man ran twenty 400-metre repeats before and after the programme, giving blood samples around the runs.

Before the programme, the run raised every inflammation and growth marker measured. Afterwards, the preconditioned group showed stronger responses in two immune signals, with peak gaps over the sham group reaching roughly a quarter to a third higher. One brain-related growth factor rose only in the sham group, while another nerve marker climbed more with preconditioning. The authors warn the findings do not yet prove faster recovery.
pmc-13493957:
Yan and colleagues sequenced the complete chloroplast genomes, the small DNA circles that run photosynthesis, of four Triumfetta species, a mallow genus with several medicinal members. DNA came from pressed herbarium specimens, proving old collections can still yield full genomes. The 2026 analysis compared the four newcomers with the ten previously published genomes for the genus, hunting for structural quirks and variable spots useful as identification barcodes.

Each genome kept the standard four-part layout and held 112 distinct genes, with lengths around 160 thousand DNA letters. Three species shared a distinctive six-gene inversion, a flipped stretch of DNA found in no other branch, marking them as close relatives. Seven highly variable locations emerged as candidate barcodes for telling species apart. Family trees built from the genomes split the genus into two major groups with strong geographic patterning, aiding naming disputes and conservation work.
pmc-13494157:

Mediterranean eating has strong proof from Europe, but its standing against low-fat eating and the American Heart Association 2020 goals in US adults was less clear. They focused on 12,197 adults aged 55 to 80 who had diabetes or several risk factors, and modeled 20 years of sustained adherence to each diet. Estimated risk was lowest under the Mediterranean pattern, next under the heart association goals, and highest under the low-fat diet. Gaps narrowed in a broader, lower-risk group. The authors read the results as support for Mediterranean-style eating in US prevention advice.
pmc-13495157:
Sergio Consoli and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether large language models can forecast breast cancer survival as well as classic statistics. Survival models often miss tangled patterns in rich health data, while real patient records stay locked by privacy rules. The team tuned several language models on a synthetic registry of 60,000 patients built to mimic European cancer registry data.

They compared the models with Cox regression and gradient boosting, two standard tools, using scores that handle patients whose outcomes are still unknown. The language models proved competitive, with clear gaps between model designs. The best were then run on real Dutch registry data covering more than 180,000 patients, where they held up well in backward-looking tests and less well in live-style use. The authors say synthetic data can train sound models without exposing real records.
pmc-13495257:
Leandro Raider and colleagues follow, in a 2026 study, one class of Brazilian medical students through all six years of training under a well-being support program. Each year students were checked for anxiety, depression, quality of life, activity, and resilience, then sat with a researcher to discuss results and get guidance.

Eighty-four students completed the run. Anxiety and depression scores stayed low throughout, and activity levels stayed high. Resilience grew markedly, with the share of students scoring high or very high more than doubling by the end. Closing interviews credited the program with shaping professional values and habits of self-care. The authors argue medical schools should build full care programs for their students, for the students' sake and their future patients' alike.
pmc-13500457:
Robert-Csaba Begy and colleagues warn in 2026 that escaping radon gas can quietly corrupt a widely used method for dating lake sediments. The method times deposits up to about 150 years old by tracking a lead isotope, yet its maths assumes the gas intermediate in the decay chain stays trapped. Three lakes were studied, Balaton in Hungary plus St. Anna and Red Lake in Romania, which differ in sedimentation speed, porosity, and organic content.

Balaton showed heavy radon loss in its upper layers and matching lead deficits large enough to skew ages severely in the reported ranges. St. Anna, slow and organic-rich, showed the largest discrepancies despite lower gas levels, while faster sandy Red Lake deviated least. The authors conclude that pore water must be analysed and radon diffusion corrected, above all in slow, porous sediments, before such chronologies can be trusted.
pmc-13501557:
Abdulkadir Kantar and İsmail Altintop report a 2026 retrospective review of forensic cases involving very elderly patients at Kayseri State Hospital in Turkey. The study covered 160 patients aged 75 or older who came to the emergency department between June 2018 and August 2025 with non-traffic forensic cases. They were drawn from more than three million department visits in that span. Records supplied demographics, existing illnesses, incident type, injury details, and outcomes. Mean age was about 80 years, and 55 percent were women.

Assault caused about four in five of the presentations, with injuries concentrated on the head, neck, and upper limbs. Abrasions made up about 42 percent of findings and bruises about 24 percent. Nearly four in five patients tried to conceal what had happened, and repeat department visits appeared in about 14 percent of cases, hinting at ongoing abuse. Most patients went home, and the death rate was 2.5 percent. The authors urge systematic screening for elder abuse.
pmc-13503657:
Muhammad Nadeem leads a 2026 math study of predator and prey numbers when prey can hide and also fear predators. The model uses fractional calculus, which lets past states keep some weight, and a switch rule that turns terms on or off. The aim is a more true-to-life view than plain models give.

The authors prove that a solution exists, stays at or above zero, and stays within bounds. They test when balance points hold steady, both near the point and from far off. A lower fractional order slows the return to balance and stretches out short-term swings. Test runs show that refuge for prey steadies the system, while fear can unsettle it.
pmc-13503757:
Salvatore Castelbuono leads a team that measured heart rhythm signals in people with severe heart failure, in a 2026 study. The nerve control of the heart is badly off in this illness, yet rest tests show little of how it copes under strain. The team watched rhythm change as patients pedaled harder.

Seventy-seven patients with weak hearts did rest and bike tests with heart tracing throughout. Standard rhythm measures fell as work rose, as expected. Measures of signal complexity rose instead, and hearts grew less predictable. Early in exercise, patients who later died or needed a transplant or pump showed a distinct complexity pattern. One such measure stayed tied to bad outcomes after other facts were weighed in.
pmc-13503957:
Shahrzad Bastani Alahabadi presents a two-part system to track drugs through supply chains and mine patient reviews, in this 2026 paper. Fake drugs slip into weakly tracked chains, causing deaths and vast losses. A shared tamper-proof ledger can log each step a drug takes.

One part records drug movement on a custom blockchain inside a simulated smart supply setting. The other part reads patient reviews with two learning agents tuned by a trust-region method. One agent labels unlabeled reviews it is sure of, widening the training pool. The second ranks which words drive each call and gets rewards for fair calls on rare classes. Tests on two large review sites gave accuracy above 93 percent, with fast ledger speeds.
pmc-13504757:
Lennart Seizer, Keisuke Takano, and Johanna Löchner ask whether evening stress hormone levels shape how bad moods carry across the night, in a 2026 pilot study. Emotional inertia, the tendency of a mood to persist, links to mental health when the mood is negative. Sleep sits between evening and morning states, yet its role was unclear.

Twenty-six women who care for family members logged moods and gave saliva samples each morning and evening for two weeks. Higher evening cortisol, the main stress hormone, went with stronger carry-over of negative feelings to the next morning. The authors read this as early evidence that the stress system helps set overnight mood persistence. They call for bigger, more varied samples to test the finding.
pmc-13505057:
Alharamlah and colleagues surveyed dentists in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province about dental tourism, patients crossing borders for cheaper or faster treatment, from the receiving end. The 2026 questionnaire reached 326 dentists across four cities, from general practitioners to consultants in public and private practice. Almost every respondent had treated dental tourists, making the phenomenon a routine part of local practice rather than an exception.

Affordability was the reason dentists heard most often, and veneers, crowns, and bridges were the treatments most commonly done abroad. Specialists and consultants met tourists significantly more than general practitioners did. Most dentists believed treatment abroad can compromise oral health, pointing at follow-up gaps and uneven quality when problems surface back home. The authors frame the findings as a prompt for local services to compete on price transparency and continuity, rather than simply criticising patients who travel.
pmc-13507057:
Shuai Wang and colleagues study, in 2026 work, roof stability in a coal mine roadway at Guqiao Coal Mine in the Huainan area of China. Fast digging leaves a stretch of roof briefly without supports, and the team asked how wide that stretch can safely be. They combined computer models, plate theory, and response surface methods.

Unsupported distance proved the strongest factor for roof sag and failure. Past two meters, sinking sped up sharply and control grew much harder. The team set one meter as the best distance for this roadway. Paired with a dig-and-support cycle and strong bolt and cable support, digging speed rose from 6 meters per day to 15 to 18, with a stable roof.
pmc-13507157:
Yixuan Du, Keyi Wang, Long Chen, and Yan Zhou assess, in 2026 work, how well intangible cultural heritage and rural development move together across China. Panel data cover 31 provinces from 2013 to 2022, drawn from official yearbooks and statistics. Methods include a coupling coordination model, spatial clustering checks, and a random forest forecast, a machine learning method using many decision trees.

Coordination between heritage strength and rural growth rated high overall. The map showed an east-high, west-low pattern, with central and northeast areas in between. Gaps between provinces narrowed after a 2022 peak in spread measures. Heritage inheritors ranked as the top density factor in forecasts. Both systems are expected to keep growing, though at slower margins.
pmc-13507357:
Bo Keun Park leads a 2026 team that builds a hybrid polymer binder, blending spandex with poly(acrylic acid), for extra-thick lithium battery electrodes. Packing more active material per electrode raises energy density toward 450 watt-hours per kilogram, yet the standard binder migrates during drying and cracks thick coatings. Their two polymers split the labor.

Spandex adds stretch and grip on nickel-rich cathode material, while the acid polymer converts at the surface into a lithium-carrying form that speeds ion traffic. Electrodes loaded at 70 milligrams per square centimeter cycled stably with only two percent binder. Pouch cells outlasted conventional-binder counterparts. Factories could adopt the water-friendly process without new equipment lines.
pmc-13508057:
Md. Mohi Uddin and colleagues critically review how to make silicene, a one-atom-thick silicon sheet tipped as a successor material for electronics. They compare four making routes against three yardsticks: scale, stability in air, and keeping the sheet's prized electronic behaviour.

No route passes all three tests, the review finds, since silicon has no layered parent crystal to peel and silicene rusts fast in air. Growth on silver gives the sharpest crystals but kills the key electronic feature, while a newer fast route makes flakes in minutes, not days. A gold base kept that feature in simulations, and one route yields air-resistant hydrogen-covered sheets needing a cap layer. Uddin proposes pairing the fast growth route with that cap as the most promising near-term path.
pmc-13508257:
Jianfan Ping and six co-authors test three chatbots on anesthesia planning for heart patients facing non-heart surgery, in 2026 work. Such pre-surgery reviews are high stakes, and large language models are entering clinical use fast. The team turned records for 41 patients with severe heart disease into standard case summaries. DeepSeek led on one major risk class, while Grok led on heart function and risk scores and matched a lung risk task best. ChatGPT trailed on most tasks. Agreement between models and with experts ranged from slight to strong depending on the task. All three systems leaned hard toward general anesthesia and heavy monitoring, and none raised one common brain monitor. The authors see promise but warn these tools are not ready to plan alone.
pmc-13508357:
Yalçın Yaman leads an eleven-author team running the first national survey of a chronic gut infection in native Turkish goat breeds, in 2026 work. A commercial blood test flagged past exposure, and careful statistical models turned rates into breed risk comparisons.

About one in seven goats tested positive overall, and nearly every herd had at least one positive animal, showing the infection circulates widely. Breed rates varied almost threefold. Four breeds carried clearly higher risk, and two breeds accounted for the largest shares of the national burden. One striking contrast paired a white Angora group with no positives against a colored Angora group with the highest rate. The survey gives veterinary planners a breed-aware base for control programs.
pmc-13508457:
Maxwell Seward and six co-authors run a small pilot scan study asking whether the drug clozapine lowers a brain chemical in treatment-resistant schizophrenia, in 2026 work. About thirty percent of patients fail standard dopamine-blocking drugs, and high glutamate in one brain region has been tied to that poor response. Clozapine is the standard rescue drug and may work partly through glutamate, though proof is thin. Seven patients in early psychosis who met resistance criteria had the chemical measured in that region before starting clozapine and again after six months.

Glutamate dipped after six months, in line with the team's guess, but the change was far from statistically firm. The effect size was small, and the confidence range spanned zero widely. The authors present it as pilot groundwork: the direction fits the theory that clozapine cools glutamate, and a larger study is now justified to test the signal properly.
pmc-13509857:
Sara Manganelli, Giulia Raimondi, Fabio Alivernini, James Dawe, and Elisa Cavicchiolo study whether a classroom climate that supports student choice links to math results, in 2026 work. Their data cover a representative group of 26,564 Italian tenth-grade students. The team treated the climate in two ways at once: as a shared property of each classroom and as each student's own sense of support.

Careful modeling confirmed the climate measure worked the same way at both levels, and classrooms differed from each other a good deal. A supportive shared climate went with higher math achievement at the classroom level, even after student background factors were counted. The same link did not appear for a student's personal sense of support alone. The authors say choice support works mainly as a whole-class condition, not just as a private feeling.
pmc-13510257:
Valappil and Kim wrote a 2026 review of acupuncture for autism spectrum disorder, a condition present from early life that affects how people connect with others and act.
