The studies Valappil gathered suggest acupuncture shifts several brain systems at once, including glutamate, GABA, dopamine, serotonin, and noradrenaline signals. Work in autism models also reports a steadier balance between signals that excite and signals that calm brain cells, plus changes in growth factors and calmer inflammation. Direct proof of how it works in autistic people is still thin, the authors warn. Treatment plans and outcome scores vary widely, so standard trials with brain measures are needed.
pmc-13510357:
Figueiredo and colleagues sequenced in 2026 an E. coli strain from shop-bought mussels in Portugal that resembled a disease-causing type. Shellfish filter water and can gather faecal bacteria and resistance genes, yet routine checks count only E. coli numbers. The strain, from cleaned mussels out of a Class B harvesting area, underwent drug testing and full genome sequencing with long reads. Analysis covered resistance and disease genes, plasmids, and family-tree placement.

The genome carried 116 disease-linked loci and a mobile plasmid bearing beta-lactamase-linked hits. Family-tree analysis placed it in a harmless-type background, not among classic disease lineages, suggesting it picked up disease modules in the environment. The authors argue whole-genome sequencing adds value beyond simple counts for shellfish safety. They warn that cleaned, retail shellfish can still carry bacteria with disease-causing potential worth monitoring.
pmc-13510657:
Logan T. Trujillo examines why brain signals read at the scalp tell a different story from signals at the cortex itself, in 2026 work. Theory predicts a curved link between how integrated brain activity is and how complex its network pattern looks. Studies of cortical sources support that curve, yet scalp readings show a straight inverse link instead, a mismatch this study set out to explain for resting alpha rhythms.

Three source factors were tested as possible causes of the gap. The split appeared for irregular, noisy cortical signals but not for regular rhythmic ones, and it did not stem from how sources were grouped into modules. The author traces the mismatch to volume conduction, where signals spread through the head and mix at the scalp, smoothing scalp irregularity. Future work on brain organization, the study warns, must weigh this mixing when reading scalp data.
pmc-13511057:
Maria Koutra and seven co-authors compare RNA sequencing methods for studying acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer with wide genetic variety, in a 2026 review. Reading RNA shows which genes are active in cancer cells, and newer methods have sharpened how this leukemia is classified and treated. The review weighs four approaches side by side.

Bulk sequencing reads the whole message pool at population level, giving a broad activity map. Targeted sequencing zooms in with greater sensitivity on changes that matter for care. Single-cell sequencing resolves activity cell by cell, exposing variety and family trees inside the cancer. Spatial methods add location, showing cell types inside their tissue setting. The authors argue that blending these tools with other data layers can shift care from broad chemotherapy toward precise medicine matched to each patient's cancer.
pmc-13512457:
Safari and colleagues present a 2026 mathematical framework for diagnostic urgency, the question of which possible diagnoses doctors should check first in an emergency. They model urgency with four inputs: how bad outcomes may be, how irreversible the harm is, how much treatment can prevent, and how fast treatment benefit decays with delay.

From six stated axioms, or rules, they prove that any fair urgency score must add one component for each input. Their score matched established disease burden weights across 42 emergency conditions with a very strong correlation. It also tracked hospital death and intensive care admission in a large records database, and it separated high-risk from low-risk conditions well. The authors stress the score is a formal foundation, not yet a tested bedside rule.
pmc-13516457:
Haojie Xu and four colleagues pool global evidence on asthma among adults with atopic dermatitis in a 2026 meta-analysis. The two diseases share type 2 inflammation and often travel together along the so-called atopic march. How common asthma is in adults with the skin disease, though, had stayed fuzzy. The team gathered seventy-five observational studies from three databases through January 2026 and combined their results with random-effects models.

About twenty-six percent of adults with dermatitis had asthma, and dermatitis came with nearly fourfold odds of asthma overall. The spread was wide: under ten percent in Asia against over sixty percent in South America. Modern targeted drugs treat both diseases, and scattered reports of asthma appearing during skin treatment likely reflect the disease's natural course rather than drug harm, the authors argue. They urge screening that respects region and ethnicity.
pmc-13516557:
Hend Emad and seven colleagues trace drug-resistance genes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa across food and hospital sources in a 2026 study. This germ haunts hospitals, and its spread through food could seed untreatable infections. The team screened 116 samples, sixty-one from patients and fifty-five from retail food, testing the recovered germs against sixteen drugs. They also built a fast gene test to track integrons, the DNA cassettes that shuttle resistance between bacteria.

The germ appeared in about thirty-six percent of samples, at similar rates in food and clinics. Every isolate landed in the extreme tiers: most were extensively drug resistant and over a quarter resisted everything. Resistance patterns in food and human isolates matched almost perfectly. One integron type was universal, while a second marked the fully resistant strains without exception. Emad's team offers the test as an early-warning tool for surveillance.
pmc-13516657:
Ana Pérez-Perdomo, Sara Pedregosa-Fauste, Carlos Martínez-Gaitero, and Adelaida Zabalegui validate a Spanish version of a nursing student competency inventory in a 2026 study. The inventory rates the knowledge, reasoning, and clinical skills students need for practice. The team translated it into Spanish and back, then surveyed students at three universities, in Barcelona, Lleida, and the Tecnocampus.

Most respondents were women in their twenties, and nearly half were third-year students. The average self-rating sat at a solid level on the scale. Ethics and accountability scored highest, while clinical biomedical science scored lowest, a useful map of where teaching lands and where it lags. Expert review rated the content highly valid, and the scale's internal consistency was excellent. The authors conclude the Spanish inventory is a sound tool for judging student competence in Spanish settings.
pmc-13516757:
Xi-Rui Zhou leads a nine-author review of nose-to-brain drug delivery in a 2026 article. The blood-brain barrier blocks nearly all small drugs, leaving brain diseases undertreated. Spraying or dropping medicine into the nose offers a side door along the smell and trigeminal nerves. The authors map those routes, then survey design strategies, formula tuning, and device engineering meant to make the trip reliable.

Their main contribution is a five-part test for clinical readiness. A candidate must aim precisely, behave predictably in the body, prove safe across organs, fit its device in real use, and translate honestly from animal noses to human ones. Scoring today's research against those pillars exposes where translation stalls. Zhou's team offers the framework as a bench-to-bedside checklist for a field rich in clever formulas and poor in finished products.
pmc-13516957:
Jonathan Henzel and six colleagues published a solar cell study in two thousand twenty-six on imaging shaded perovskite cells. When part of a solar panel is shaded, those cells run in reverse and can degrade. A light-emission imaging trick used on other cell types may reveal the damage paths.

The team showed the glow signal truly comes from the light-absorbing layer itself. Their images matched heat-based current maps while showing finer detail and sharper sensitivity. The glow pattern changed between small and large reverse currents. That split hints at two different breakdown routes. The authors say the method could help explain reverse bias damage, though open questions remain.
pmc-13518457:
Yoon Jung Hwang and eight colleagues map gene activity inside liver tumours that grow wrapped in their own blood vessels in a 2026 study. This vessel-wrapped pattern, called VETC, marks hepatocellular cancers with worse outlooks yet better responses to vessel-targeted drugs. Using spatial gene profiling on tissue from twenty-four patients, the team compared wrapped zones, unwrapped zones, and healthy liver.

Thirty-nine genes ran hot in the wrapped regions, clustered around vessel growth, fat burning, and cell-shape change, while immune pathways went quiet. Four stood out, and one, LAMTOR2, proved tumour-specific across large datasets. Protein staining echoed the RNA signal and hugged the tumour edges. Single-cell data placed LAMTOR2 highest in malignant liver cells of the wrapped type, busy with fat breakdown and detox work. Hwang's team offers it as a candidate flag for sorting patients toward vessel-targeted treatment.
pmc-13518857:
Falk L Wiegmann and Nancy L Ford examine in 2026 how a common image-blending trick quietly distorts quality scores in micro-CT scanning. Algorithms that fill missing scan data work in overlapping tiles, and Gaussian feathering smooths the seams between tiles. Nobody had checked what that smoothing does to diagnostic measures.

Using phantom scans rebuilt from half-sampled data, the pair derived the math and measured five quality metrics. Feathering cut variance by up to 19.6 percent at overlap centers, shrank noise measures, and inflated one quality index by up to 38.5 percent. Ordinary fidelity scores barely noticed. Nearest-priority blending, they suggest, may suit studies that validate filling methods by diagnostic metrics.
pmc-13518957:
Fabiana San Martin and a large team solve the full atomic structure in 2026 of the internal flagellar filament of Leptospira, the corkscrew bacterium behind leptospirosis. These spiral cells swim by waving inner threads hidden inside the cell, sheathed in proteins found nowhere else. How the thread's build lets it invade tissue was unclear.

The core flagellin variant dictates which 9 to 12 sheath proteins wrap around it, tuning thread curvature across a wide range. Leptospira interrogans uses the lower-curvature design, which proved vital for swimming through thick fluids and during infection. San Martin's team calls the setup modular core-sheath coupling, likely shared across spirochetes.
pmc-13519857:
Adam Daou and colleagues present this 2026 case of a rare jaw tumor, a calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor also called a Pindborg tumor. It grows slowly from tooth-forming tissue and accounts for under one percent of specimens sent to oral pathology labs.

Their patient was a twenty-three year old man with a firm, painless swelling stretching from his lower lip to his chin. Scans showed a well-defined mixed lesion in the front of the lower jaw, pushing nearby tooth roots aside and carrying specks of calcification. Surgeons scooped out the tumor while preserving as much bone as possible. The authors stress that careful clinical, imaging, and tissue checks together secure the right diagnosis for such uncommon lesions.
pmc-13520157:
Tingyue Lu leads a twelve-author team naming SMC4 in 2026 as a low-oxygen-driven promoter of pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease where lung artery walls thicken until the heart fails. Patient gene data showed SMC4, a chromosome-organizing protein, sharply raised. Mouse models and human artery muscle cells under low oxygen showed the same rise, concentrated in the vessel muscle layer.

Experiments traced a chain: the oxygen sensor HIF-1 alpha switches SMC4 on, SMC4 recruits the enzyme HDAC6, and together they silence the cell-cycle brake p21, letting muscle cells multiply. Mice born with partial SMC4 deficiency resisted vessel remodeling and heart strain under low oxygen. Lu and colleagues propose the axis as a drug target.
pmc-13520257:
Hannah L Riley leads a six-author pharmacology study in 2026 measuring how amantadine behaves in horses, a first step toward using it against hard-to-treat chronic pain. The drug blocks NMDA receptors involved in pain amplification, yet equine dosing data were missing. Eight horses received one intravenous dose and three oral doses in a randomized crossover schedule, with blood sampled for up to 96 hours.

Peak blood levels rose with dose size, and the drug cleared with a half-life near four hours. Only about 23 percent of an oral dose reached the circulation. Five horses showed brief wobbliness after the intravenous dose, with no other major effects. Riley and colleagues judge the drug well tolerated and ready for pain-effect trials.
pmc-13520357:
Mali Zhang and colleagues adapt in 2026 a questionnaire on nurses' ethical awareness of artificial intelligence for use in Chinese hospitals. No well-tested Chinese version existed, so translation, cultural adjustment and statistical checking were all required.

Responses came from 455 nurses at one large hospital in Shenzhen between December 2025 and January 2026. Analysis trimmed the scale from 21 items to 15, grouped into three linked domains. Fit checks favoured models that allow those domains to correlate. Reliability results follow in the full text. Nurse educators gain a candidate tool for spotting training needs as AI spreads into wards.
pmc-13520457:
Yuki Shimada and colleagues ask in 2026 whether being active in late afternoon or early evening predicts lower depression and anxiety symptoms the next day among workers in Japan. Timing of activity, not only total amount, might matter for next-day mood.

Phone tracking plus daily evening surveys ran for two weeks, yielding 1,400 observation days from 116 full-time daytime workers. High symptoms appeared on about one day in five. Late afternoon activity showed a weak, non-significant link with fewer next-day symptoms in the opening results. Evening activity findings follow in the full analysis, adjusted for prior-day symptoms.
pmc-13521157:
Yuzo Honda and colleagues tackle in 2026 fixation of the most severe elbow coronal shear fractures, where the joint surface shatters and loses rear support. Screws alone can fail when rear bone stock crumbles, while standard plates fit the irregular fragments poorly.

Their fragment-specific plan pairs headless compression screws with tiny 2.0-millimetre locking plates shaped to each fragment group. Rationale draws on how shear forces shift once the rear buttress is lost, raising risks of displacement, hardware failure and stiffness. Surgeons facing Dubberley type 3B injuries gain a tailored construct logic rather than a one-plate-fits-all approach.
pmc-13521457:
Park and colleagues solve a manufacturing bottleneck in gene therapy: purifying lentiviruses, the delivery vehicles that carry corrective genes into patients' cells. Depth filters trap cells but swallow much of the virus harvest too. Their 2026 microfluidic system instead spins the harvest through tiny curved channels where inertia sorts cells from virus without any filter to clog. They call the process microfluidic cell clarification, tuned by controlling flow rate and diluting the recirculating cells with buffer.

Under tuned conditions the device recovered more than nineteen twentieths of the virus while removing the same share of cells, matching a theoretical model with almost no product loss. Across three batches it beat the benchmark filter process, finishing with recovery a quarter to a third higher in the reported comparison. Performance held at flow rates up to one and a half litres per hour, which points toward production scale.
pmc-13522057:
Stefan Weidauer and Randolf Klingebiel reviewed granulomatous diseases of the brain and spinal cord, where chronic inflammation forms nodules called granulomas. Published in 2026, the review spans causes from self-directed immunity and infection to tumors, foreign material, immune deficiency, and drugs. Such diseases vary widely, yet early treatment often helps, so narrowing the diagnosis quickly matters.

Brain imaging plays the central role, since distinct scan patterns can point toward one cause among many, even though imaging cannot replace tissue biopsy. The review walks through representative diseases in each cause group, pairing scan features with symptoms and look-alike conditions. Many of these diseases answer to immune-suppressing or anti-infective drugs once identified. Readers get a map for reading scans that guide urgent treatment decisions.
pmc-13522757:
Wenbo Zhang and a large team develop an in situ cancer vaccine to overcome resistance to immunotherapy in a 2026 study. The mixture combines two immune stimulants and is injected directly into tumors, turning the tumor site itself into a source of antigens. One component helps deliver the other into cells, activating interferon pathways that drive a form of tumor cell death the immune system notices.

Treated tumors showed stronger dendritic cell maturation and better display of tumor antigens, producing targeted T cell responses and immune memory that prevented recurrence. The vaccine also sensitized tumors to PD-1 blockade, a standard immune therapy, and improved results when paired with microwave ablation. The authors present the pairing as a promising route against tumors that resist current immune therapy.
pmc-13522857:
Sarah O'Donovan and colleagues explored why nutrition care struggles to take root in Irish health care. Published in 2026, the interview-based study talked with 37 health workers and students across five Irish health fields, from medicine and nursing to pharmacy, physiotherapy, and occupational therapy. Nutrition shapes chronic disease risk, yet its daily care by other staff remains poorly mapped.

Three themes emerged: fuzzy role lines and shaky self-belief, system and day-to-day barriers, and patchy care across settings. Everyone valued nutrition, but thin training, unclear hand-off routes, thin staffing, and worry about loading colleagues blocked action. Self-belief rested more on personal drive than on formal teaching, producing uneven care. The authors call for stronger training, clearer hand-offs, teamwork, and better access to dietitians.
pmc-13523257:
Salimi and colleagues measure two immune messengers in the blood of inpatients to see whether immune signals track with obsessive-compulsive symptoms and suicidal thinking. IL-17A and CCL20 are both linked to brain inflammation in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Their 2026 cross-sectional study drew patients in episodes at a Mashhad hospital, excluding anyone with infections, immune disease, or substance problems that could distort the readings.

The two disorders looked alike in immune terms: neither messenger differed significantly between the schizophrenia and bipolar groups. They diverged clinically, with bipolar patients reporting markedly more suicidal thoughts and holding jobs more often in the sample. Within the bipolar group, higher IL-17A came with lower odds of suicidal thoughts, an inverse link the regression singled out, while compulsive features showed complex interactions with sex, background, and treatment. The authors argue immune profiling could refine risk assessment.
pmc-13523857:
Karl Pillemer and others present a 2026 research agenda on aging and climate change, drawn from a consensus workshop linking research to practice. Older adults face outsized health risks from climate change, yet studies remain scarce and scattered. Funders and researchers needed shared priorities.

Forty-four people, including researchers, care workers, and policymakers, used structured small-group discussion and a known priority-setting process. Consensus produced fourteen research priorities. Examples include measuring money impacts on older people, building climate messages grounded in data, and removing barriers to program access. Health care integration, emergency protocols, and fairness research also featured. The authors frame the agenda as rooted in practice, favoring usable knowledge over description, and offer it to guide program work and funding choices.
pmc-13525657:
Rong Jiang and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 study, what drives the valuation of healthcare big data assets in China, where policy pushes hospitals to treat data as a strategic asset. Value realization is hampered by variable data quality, uncertain uses, privacy risks, and unclear benefit sharing. Their framework joins a technology-organization-environment model with information ecosystem theory.

Expert and practitioner surveys identified six conditions, from data quality and sharing interfaces to benefit-sharing rules, collaboration mechanisms, market demand, and privacy governance. A fuzzy-set comparative method then traced combinations leading to high value. Three pathways emerged, driven by quality and security, by demand-led collaboration, and by market transactions. Data quality and standardization appeared in every pathway, marking them as foundational, while other conditions mattered differently across routes.
pmc-13526057:
Valentina Lancellotta leads a large team in a 2026 retrospective study of image-guided brachytherapy boosts for vaginal cancer recurrences. Brachytherapy places radiation sources close to the tumor for a concentrated dose. Patients first received external beam radiation, with chemotherapy in some cases, then a high-dose-rate internal boost guided by imaging.

Thirty-two patients with a median age of fifty-four were analyzed. Two-year local control reached one hundred percent, while metastasis-free survival was 77.8 percent and overall and cancer-specific survival were both ninety-three percent. Chemotherapy was linked with lower metastasis risk in simple analysis, and cisplatin-based treatment showed the lowest rate. Older age predicted mortality and was the only independent factor in adjusted analysis. Toxicity was mostly mild, with one late severe vaginal narrowing.
pmc-13527057:
Huey and colleagues published a 2026 trial on iron-rich millet and toddlers' gut microbes in Mumbai. Iron pills can disturb young gut microbes, raising worry about side effects. The trial fed children millet bred to carry extra iron and zinc. It compared that grain with normal millet over nine months of meals.

Paired samples from 81 children showed no harmful gut shifts from the rich grain. Endpoint checks covered 108 children and agreed with the paired result. Hints emerged that the grain may aid helpful microbe chemistry instead. The enriched millet carried nearly triple the iron of the control grain. Crop-based iron may thus protect both blood and gut health. All children entered the trial without severe anemia at the start.
pmc-13527157:
Ke Cao and six co-authors use artificial intelligence to read body makeup from scans of colorectal cancer patients, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Weight alone says little about how muscle and fat change as cancer advances. The team measured the whole lower back region in three dimensions.

The study covered more than eleven hundred patients treated in Melbourne over a decade. A trained program split muscle, deep belly fat, and fat under the skin on each staging scan. Values were adjusted for age, sex, and height, then compared across four disease stages. Belly fat fell early and fell further in the most advanced stage. Muscle and surface fat dropped only at that late stage. The results map how the body wastes as the cancer grows.
pmc-13527857:
Andrew Turner and others explore, in a 2026 study, how Australian adults experience direct-to-consumer telemedicine services that sell medical visits through online platforms. Such services surged after the pandemic. Talks with thirteen users covered skin care, women's health, men's health, and fertility services.

Four themes emerged. Ease of use, flexible timing, short waits, and easier access for rural people and people with limited mobility were the headline gains. Privacy mattered for problems carrying shame, such as obesity and erectile dysfunction, prompting care people might not seek on their own. People worried that easy access could lead to poor prescribing, notably of medications. Telemedicine was seen as an add-on to general practice rather than a stand-in, although poor care from regular doctors had pushed some people toward it.
pmc-13527957:
Matt Percival and ten colleagues report a 2026 feasibility study of a pharmacist-led program to improve how medication information travels with older patients leaving hospital in southeast Queensland, Australia. The package combined digital risk screening, recorded reasons for drug changes in the electronic record, patient information in web and paper forms, and pharmacist involvement at discharge.

On three medical wards, 36 patients were approached and 17 consented; all twenty doctors and three pharmacists invited took part. Most surveyed patients felt included in medication decisions, and clinicians praised smoother workflow and learning value, though uptake varied between teams. The authors judge the program practical and acceptable, with communication and training the main fixes needed.
pmc-13528057:
Agathe Auer and seven colleagues compare three PCR machines for two major animal diseases in a 2026 study. The diseases are African swine fever and avian influenza. Two machines are lab systems. The third, called Franklin, is portable for farm-side use. The team tested 72 swine fever samples from eleven countries. Fifty flu samples from seven countries were added.

Both lab machines agreed closely. The portable unit at first missed many swine fever positives under the standard protocol. Adjusted settings fixed that and gave the best detection limits of all. For flu, the portable unit and one lab machine missed some cases the reference machine caught. The authors say field testing is viable with care. Protocols written for labs may need tuning for portable gear.
pmc-13528157:
Bin Zhang and four colleagues ask how much of the fatty liver to diabetes link runs through a blood fat ratio in a 2026 study. The cohort, called NAGALA, held 15,453 adults without diabetes. Ultrasound spotted fatty liver at the start. People were followed for a median of about five years. In that time 373 developed diabetes.

Fatty liver nearly tripled the risk of diabetes after adjustment. The fat ratio, triglycerides over HDL cholesterol, also predicted diabetes. Its top quarter carried about double the risk of its bottom quarter. Math that splits direct and indirect paths credited the ratio with about twelve percent of the link. That share held in men but not women. The ratio alone sorted future cases moderately well. The authors offer it as a cheap risk flag.
pmc-13530457:
Motalebi, Varshoee Tabrizi, and Khalili-Hezarjaribi profile breast cancer patients in northeastern Iran, in work from twenty twenty-six. Breast cancer traits vary by region, in age, stage, and tumor biology. Regional patterns guide prevention and early detection planning.

More than four thousand women treated at a radiotherapy and oncology center were included in the retrospective cohort. Demographic and clinicopathological factors were described and their interrelationships explored. Complete case analysis meant some analyses used smaller subsets. A large local profile gives health planners real numbers for screening age and service capacity in that region.
pmc-13531057:
Shinya Minami and colleagues describe in 2026 a staged workaround for valve replacement when leg arteries are too narrow and diseased for the catheter route. A 71-year-old woman with severe aortic narrowing first received overlapping covered stents that lined her iliac and leg arteries into a smooth internal channel.

Two weeks later the valve traveled through that prepared channel and seated successfully. Practice on a bench model beforehand shaped the plan. Closure used suture devices plus one extra stent graft. The report presents the channel-building approach as an option for hostile anatomy, with timing questions left open.
pmc-13531557:
Maria Pou and colleagues report a cohort study, published in 2026. It covers long-term gout control in Catalan primary care. The team used records for 94,759 people. All were newly diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They examined treatment patterns. They asked which factors predicted keeping blood urate below target. Urate is the chemical that triggers gout attacks. The target had to hold for most of the follow-up.

Long-term control remained poor. It had not improved over the decade. Good control linked to earlier treatment start. Higher doses of standard urate-lowering drugs helped. Febuxostat use and better adherence also helped. Poor control was predicted by delayed treatment, male sex, and obesity. Kidney disease, abnormal blood fats, and high blood pressure also predicted it. Early treatment is a fixable target.
pmc-13531957:
Michał Sekuła, Maciej Dubaj, and Rafał Patryn review in 2026 five years of court-substituted medical consent at a Polish teaching hospital. When adults cannot decide and no representative exists, a guardianship court must authorize treatment. The team analyzed 240 petitions filed between mid-2019 and mid-2024.

Patients were typically older, with a median age of 73. Broken speech and reasoning from brain problems caused most incapacity, then unconsciousness and dementia. Blood transfusions and feeding tube placements dominated requests. Courts approved about 97 percent, with a median wait of five days, which can still matter in urgent care.
pmc-13532757:
Kervancı and Adebiyi built in 2026 a prediction pipeline that reads bacterial genomes to forecast meropenem resistance. Their target was Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital bacterium often resistant to this last-line antibiotic. Many machine learning models flatter themselves by leaking family links between training and test bacteria, and flat gene lists miss gene-to-gene interplay. Their pipeline splits data by bacterial lineage to block that leak, and uses a transformer encoder, an attention-based model, to turn gene presence patterns into rich features.

Kervancı found the hybrid system beat standard methods such as logistic regression and random forests. The best setup reached accuracy above nine in ten on internal tests, and checks showed most of the gain came from the learned gene features rather than the final classifier. On an outside set of 305 samples from several countries, the model still held up well, which supports use across settings.
pmc-13534457:
Vivian Soetikno and colleagues test in 2026 whether 6-gingerol, a natural compound from ginger, can ease kidney scarring in rats with a blocked ureter. Scarring is a main path to kidney failure, driven by oxidative stress and a growth signalling pathway. Rats with a tied ureter for 14 days received the compound or no treatment.

Treated rats showed less scarring and less collagen build-up in the blocked kidney. Activity of the growth pathway fell, scarring genes quieted, and antioxidant defence rose while a damage marker fell. Readers see a natural candidate worth testing further for kidney protection.
pmc-13536257:
Cameron I Wells and colleagues study in 2026 deaths after colorectal surgery in Australia and New Zealand that might have been prevented. Audit data covered 1,058 deaths after planned or emergency bowel resection from 2010 to 2023. Reviewers judged whether care issues that were preventable played a part in each death.

Nearly one third of deaths were classed as potentially preventable, with a higher share after planned surgery than emergency surgery. Sepsis, organ failure, and lung infection led causes, and join leaks were the most common complication. Weak patient selection, preparation, and late rescue stood out.
pmc-13536557:
Magnus Sundberg and colleagues test in 2026 seismocardiography, a chest vibration method, to estimate fitness in older adults without exercise. The gold standard exercise test is hard for many older people, and other estimates are often inaccurate. Thirty-six healthy adults aged 65 to 75 had resting sensor measures plus a cycling test.

Resting estimates correlated moderately with measured peak oxygen use overall and strongly in the subgroup with validated peak values. The sensor method still overestimated fitness on average across the group. Further tuning for older adults is needed before use in large cohort studies.
pmc-13536757:
Lixia Lan and co-authors evaluate a structured support program for eye injection therapy in age-related macular disease in a 2026 comparison of 350 patients treated from 2022 to 2024. Half received standard care alone, while half added personal teaching, adherence counseling, reminders, and proactive follow-up contact. Missed visits, delays, treatment persistence, vision scores, satisfaction, and disease understanding were compared.

Patients in the support program missed far fewer visits and had far fewer long delays than standard care patients. Good adherence and continued treatment were both much more common with support. Final vision was also better, and more patients gained vision. Satisfaction and understanding scored higher as well, while safety results were similar. The authors recommend building such support into routine retinal care.
pmc-13538057:
Jessica Trowbridge and co-authors gather reviews on how chemical exposures and social stressors combine to harm health in a 2026 overview. Factors such as income, care access, and discrimination can change what a chemical dose does to a body. Eighteen systematic and scoping reviews met set criteria and were rated for quality with a standard tool. Findings from the stronger reviews were then summarized.

Air pollution was the most studied exposure, while social stressors were defined in widely varied ways across reviews. Two reviews with certainty grading found worse outcomes when chemical and social stressors were counted together than alone. Most included reviews rated low or critically low in quality. The authors argue that current risk methods miss joint effects and need updating to include social conditions.
pmc-13538257:
Federica Davanzo and colleagues test simple blood count ratios as activity markers in vessel inflammation disease in a 2026 single-center study. Ratios of neutrophils, platelets, and monocytes to lymphocytes come from routine blood counts. Ninety-nine patients with two disease forms were sampled during active disease or during strict steroid-free remission, alongside 258 healthy controls. Ratios were compared across groups and checked against activity scores.

All three ratios ran higher in active disease than in remission and tracked activity scores and inflammation levels moderately. Neutrophil and platelet ratios separated active disease from remission best, lifting accuracy well beyond age and sex alone. Ratios stayed higher in remission than in healthy controls, suggesting lingering immune shift. Treatment type within remission shifted some counts. The authors propose the cheap ratios as helpful add-ons needing prospective checks.
pmc-13539657:
Megan M Hare and colleagues study early reward circuit wiring in one-month-old infants as a marker of later temperament. Resting brain scans during natural sleep measured connection strength between two core reward regions in 94 infants, about eleven minutes of clean data each. Caregivers later reported temperament at six months, rating pleasure from intense and from gentle stimulation.

The two reward regions already showed positive connection in the first weeks of life. Infants with weaker connection showed greater high-intensity pleasure at six months, enjoying energetic, stimulating play more. Connection strength showed no link to gentle pleasure. The authors propose early reward circuit variation as a marker of emerging differences in how babies respond to reward, with lessons for affective development.
pmc-13540257:
Ricardo Lopes and seven colleagues report a 2026 nationwide survey of dog exposure to two tick-borne infections in Portugal, Ehrlichia canis and Babesia species. Dogs act as sentinels whose blood shows where ticks are passing germs that also matter for wider One Health surveillance.

Nearly three thousand serum samples collected between 2015 and 2025 were tested for antibodies. Exposure was higher for Babesia, at twelve percent, than for Ehrlichia, at four percent. Ehrlichia clustered in the warm south, notably the Algarve, and rose in older dogs. Dogs positive for Babesia were also likelier to carry Ehrlichia antibodies, suggesting shared tick exposure.
pmc-13540857:
Weihao Wang, Long Diao, and Jingting Yu ask, in a 2026 meta-analysis, whether artificial intelligence tools in education actually calm academic anxiety. Studies point both ways, so a pooled estimate was overdue.

Twenty-two studies giving thirty effect sizes were combined with careful statistical methods. The overall effect was moderate and favourable, meaning AI interventions cut anxiety noticeably on average. Test anxiety and general academic anxiety responded, while mathematics and language anxiety did not. Intelligent tutoring systems and robots worked; chatbots and virtual tools did not clearly. Most subgroup contrasts were not statistically firm, the authors caution, and benefits persisted at delayed retesting.
pmc-13543357:
Angela Sibanda-Makuvise and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of whether insect-specific viruses, which infect only insects, can blunt the mosquito-borne viruses that sicken people. As insecticides lose power and mosquito ranges expand, these harmless-to-humans viruses have attracted interest as biological control allies. The reviewers searched four databases and kept only live-mosquito studies where an insect-specific virus and a disease virus infected the same insect.

pmc-13543457:

pmc-13543557:

pmc-13546357:

pmc-13546857:

pmc-13547457:

pmc-13547957:

pmc-13548557:

pmc-13548657:

pmc-13550457:

pmc-13551757:

pmc-13551957:

pmc-13552457:

pmc-13553557:

pmc-13553957:

pmc-13554057:

pmc-13554557:

pmc-13555857:

pmc-13558057:

pmc-13559357:

pmc-13559657:

pmc-13560157:

pmc-13560757:

pmc-13562357:

pmc-13562457:

pmc-13562557:

pmc-13562657:

pmc-13562957:

pmc-13563457:

pmc-13563757:

pmc-13563857:

pmc-13563957:

pmc-13564357:

pmc-13565457:

pmc-13566457:

pmc-13567957:

pmc-13569557:

pmc-13570857:
