pmc-13571157:
Xialin Wang and four colleagues published an environmental study in two thousand twenty-six on the Irtysh River Basin in Central Asia. The river crosses borders, so its water is shared by upstream and downstream lands. Climate change is tightening water supply and raising tensions over its use.

The team joined river flow records and climate forecasts with a water-food-energy framework. They traced how shifts in heat and rain change runoff, farm water needs, power output, and crop yields. Upstream and downstream areas felt the changes differently. Farm demand rose while water power potential fell. The authors argue each region needs its own adaptation plan, agreed across borders. They offer their framework for other shared river basins.
pmc-13571757:
Jing Qi and colleagues package stem cell messages in a heart-tissue gel to keep them at the scene of a heart attack, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Vesicles shed by fat-derived stem cells aid cardiac repair but wash away in hours. Pre-treating the stem cells with metformin boosted vesicle yield, and embedding the vesicles in a gel made from pig heart and aorta tissue promised a slow local release.

In rats with induced heart attacks, the loaded gel outperformed: better heart function, more surviving heart muscle cells, less programmed death, and more new blood vessels. One cargo protein, CTRP1, was traced as a contributor, working through a known survival pathway. The authors present the composite as a delivery answer to the vesicle field's retention problem.
pmc-13572157:
Chong Yao and eight colleagues test how growing millet protects sloping farmland from soil wash-off, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Crop growth changes the soil surface through the season: leaves, roots, and soil traits all shift. The team ran fake rain storms on bare plots and millet plots at four slope angles and at several growth stages. They measured many surface traits, from soil crust to root density.

Millet delayed the start of runoff as it grew, while steeper slopes sped it up. Runoff and soil loss fell by wide margins in planted plots. The authors trace the gains to surface traits near the soil, giving farmers a science base for erosion control.
pmc-13572357:
Chia-Yu Liang and colleagues engineer, in a 2026 mouse study, a triple-repeat peptide vaccine against monkeypox virus. The vaccine is built from the first thirty-four building blocks of A29L, a surface protein the virus uses to attach and enter cells. That short stretch carries the patch neutralizing antibodies target, and repeating it three times was meant to strengthen the immune signal.

Vaccinated mice made antibody levels matching those from the full protein. Their serum recognized the target patch and neutralized live virus in cell tests, while immune cell responses leaned toward the virus-fighting type with strong interferon output. A safe subunit fragment that performs like the whole protein gives vaccine designers a compact blueprint.
pmc-13572457:
Zhanshuo Chang, with two colleagues, reviews 2026 work on fat cells that shed their fat and turn back toward a stem-like state. Mature fat cells were long seen as fixed in their role. Under lab cues or body events such as milk production, they can empty their fat drop and gain the power to form other cell types.

The review tracks what changes inside the cell stage by stage. Fat stores break down, energy carriers shift, key proteins turn over, and cell parts are rebuilt. Marks on the DNA that guide gene use also change. New tools, such as cell lineage tracing and single-cell gene reads, let researchers watch the shift as it happens. Open questions remain on the exact signals in charge and on safe ways to trigger the shift in the body for healing uses.
pmc-13572557:
Daksh Singla, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 robot control system that learns the physics of its own motion while it works. Fixed models age fast when loads shift or parts wear, and hand tuning takes experts. The system aims to keep learning, check itself, and recover from faults with no human in the loop.

A physics-informed network carries the robot's known constraints and hunts unknown ones, such as changing friction, by symbolic regression. A digital twin, a full software copy, lets the system test ideas safely first. Process automation handles data intake, fault spotting, retraining, and rollout. On a robot arm that tracked paths and dodged obstacles under shifting loads, accuracy hit 98.4 percent. Energy use fell by 22.7 percent, and fault recovery ran 41.3 percent faster than standard methods.
pmc-13572657:
Silva and coauthors build a spin-free workflow for bacterial vesicles. The vesicles are tiny membrane sacs shed by bacteria. They serve in vaccine, delivery, and host-germ studies. Standard prep needs a high-speed spin step that many labs lack.

Their flow uses a typhoid germ as the test case. Growth tuning came first to lift vesicle yield. A flow filter then pooled and washed the vesicles. Freeze-drying gave a form that stores for long spans. Each step was checked for yield and vesicle shape. Cell tests showed the vesicles still bind host cells well.
pmc-13574257:
Gonzalo Hernandez-Hernandez, with six colleagues, presents a 2026 modelling method that tailors cell signal predictions to each cell type. The signals run on membrane lipids called phosphoinositides, and the same gene fault or drug can hit one cell type hard and spare another. Precision care needs models that capture that split.

The core model tracks four lipid forms and the signals they spawn, tuned on data from rat nerve cells. A reserve pool of one lipid, PI(4)P, set how sturdy the whole signal chain proved. Twin inverse methods, one based on sensitivity fingerprints and one a neural net trained on fake data, rebuilt the model for three other cell types. Large-pool neurons kept signalling when a key enzyme was blocked, while small-pool cells failed. Mutation runs showed the same split under repeat stress.
pmc-13574557:
Yiyoung Kwon and sixteen co-authors test whether a stool marker can stand in for endoscopy scores in Korean children with Crohn's disease of the colon. Fecal calprotectin is a non-invasive inflammation marker, but its match to the endoscopic SES-CD score needed local validation. Fifteen centers contributed one hundred fifty-four patients under nineteen, studied at diagnosis and follow-up.

Calprotectin tracked the endoscopic score more strongly than other markers, with a solid correlation at both time points. Median values fell sharply from diagnosis to follow-up as half the patients reached remission. Receiver operating analysis gave acceptable accuracy, and the authors derive cutoff values tied to severity and remission. Reliable cutoffs could spare children some invasive procedures.
pmc-13575257:
M M Krebber leads a 2026 animal study of dissolvable blood vessel grafts and whether kidney disease changes how they heal. The grafts, spun from a polycarbonate-bisurea polymer, are meant to be replaced by the body's own tissue over time. A version coated with a cell-attracting peptide was also tested.

Grafts went into healthy rats and rats with induced kidney disease. After two weeks every graft stayed open and grew a lining with vessel and immune cells. Kidney disease animals worsened so fast that their arm of the study was stopped. In healthy rats followed for three months, some grafts widened, and four animals died after graft rupture linked to material breakdown. The peptide coating changed nothing measurable. The authors conclude the grafts grow tissue fast yet fail in ways not yet predictable.
pmc-13576257:
Viviane Richard leads a 2026 longitudinal study of children's mental health in Geneva up to five years after the COVID-19 pandemic began. Effects of the pandemic years varied widely by child, and some difficulties lingered after restrictions lifted. The cohort followed 1,907 children and teens aged 2 to 17.

Parents rated the pandemic's impact in 2022: 9.3 percent called it negative, 7.9 percent positive, and most reported little effect. Children in the negative group had clearly more difficulties in 2022, yet their scores improved toward peers' levels by 2025. One surprise was that tighter family finances softened the 2022 response to a negative impact. A positive impact linked to slightly more difficulties in 7 to 12 year olds. The authors call the overall picture reassuring, with lessons for future crises.
pmc-13576457:
Giorgia Albonetti and seven colleagues anchored an industrial enzyme onto charred bamboo to make catalysis greener. Immobilizing lipase on a solid support lets it be recovered and reused. Their supports came from bamboo heated without oxygen, by fast and slow pyrolysis. A widely used lipase, Candida antarctica lipase B, was adsorbed onto both chars. The loaded materials were tested in ester-making and hydrolysis reactions, in flasks and in continuous flow.

Immobilization yields were high in all cases, but fast-pyrolysis char performed consistently better. It reached ninety-seven percent conversion under optimized batch conditions and held up over four reuse cycles. Industrial fatty acid mixtures were also processed successfully. The twenty twenty-six study shows farm-waste bamboo can replace synthetic supports in enzyme technology.
pmc-13576857:
Ali Mertcan Köse and three colleagues work on cutting the off-target cuts made by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, in a 2026 paper focused on the TP53 gene region. The editing tool follows a guide RNA to a DNA address, yet near-matching addresses can be cut by mistake. Scoring those risky spots well is key to safe design.

The team used latent class analysis to sort off-target sites into three levels: low, middle, and high. Machine learning classifiers then measured how mismatches at each spot within those levels changed outcomes. Their framework also identifies the short PAM anchor sequences that the editor needs beside its target. The authors present the level system as a way to design guides that hit the intended variant while sparing look-alike sites, and they frame it for future editing work on other genes.
pmc-13578757:
Güneş Topçu and colleagues follow women who gave birth in water or on land to see which path links to lower depression scores after birth, in a 2026 study. Eighty seven women were tracked from late pregnancy to three months after delivery. Mood was scored on a standard postnatal scale, and each woman rated the support she felt from her partner.

Scores fell over time in both groups, with the water birth group sitting modestly lower after adjustments. Partner support told the stronger story, tying to lower scores at every point by a wide margin. Group paths over time also diverged. The authors read any water birth gain as hinging on the support around the mother, not on the water itself.
pmc-13579757:
Mohamed Salah Alhaj and Farai Nyabadza model how war, funding, and prevention steer malaria spread in Sudan, in a 2026 study. Their compartment model sorts people and mosquitoes into health states and lets conflict degrade the health system inside the math. Real case data were used to fit the model, and a sensitivity scan ranked which levers move the spread number most.

The analysis found a threshold pattern with a twist: under some conditions the disease can linger even when the headline number looks safe. Simulations agreed on the direction of each force. More funding and stronger prevention pushed spread down, while war pushed it up by breaking programs and care. The authors close with playbooks for holding malaria down during armed conflict, from guarding supply chains to keeping field teams funded.
pmc-13580257:
Nemcovsky Amar and colleagues published a 2026 study on red blood cells as smart drug couriers. Red cells carry loads well and roam the blood for a long time. Their design lets squeezed cells spill cargo only where arteries narrow. That squeezing happens where flow speeds up through a tight spot.

Loaded cells released their cargo when pumped through narrowed artery models. Open vessels triggered no release from the same loaded cells. The sheared cells kept their skins intact and still slipped through tiny channels. Computer flow models tied release to how much cell skins stretched. Such carriers could aim clot-busting drugs at dangerous narrowings someday. Healthy cells nearby would be spared the drug's side effects.
pmc-13580757:
Aziz, Ng, and Rajan report real-world outcomes for a salvage drug mix in germ cell tumors. The mix showed promise in a phase II trial for relapsed tumors. Those tumors had grown despite platinum drug care. One London hospital then adopted the mix in practice.

Records covered patients treated from late 2012 to late 2023. The study is the largest real-world check of the mix so far. Tumor traits, care details, and risk scores were logged. Survival without growth and overall survival were tracked. Risk classes came from two global scoring systems. Results may guide salvage care choices in practice.
pmc-13581557:
Xu and five co-authors studied where to place a defibrillator when one rescuer performs CPR in twenty twenty-six. A lone rescuer must keep pressing the chest while operating the automated external defibrillator, or AED. Placing the device above the patient's head might ease that juggling act.

A manikin trial with thirty-two providers compared four positions in random order. The head position cut time to first shock by fifteen to twenty-six seconds, reduced hands-off time, raised compression share, and lowered felt workload, with no rise in serious errors. A review of two hundred thirteen real arrests pointed the same way but not conclusively. Patient outcomes did not differ. The authors call the clinical signal hypothesis-generating and ask for prospective trials before practice changes.
pmc-13582157:
Kazuki Aihara and co-authors test in this 2026 study how well three imaging tools identify tissue growing inside leg artery stents in pigs. When stents fail, treatment depends on whether the new tissue is clot-like or fibrous, so reading it correctly matters.

One month after stenting, the team imaged twenty-two swine arteries with ultrasound from inside the vessel, a light-based imaging method, and a tiny camera scope. They checked each reading against tissue examined under a microscope. Ultrasound rarely missed fibrous tissue but often missed clot, while the light method caught more clot yet overcalled it. Using both together gave the best balance, and the camera scope missed too much to guide care alone.
pmc-13583757:
Cagman Seker and colleagues reviewed how fractures of the upper arm bone near the shoulder can injure nearby nerves and blood vessels. These injuries are rare but can threaten the arm itself when they are missed or treated late.

The review explains the injury routes: broken bone fragments, stretching or squeezing, and harm done during surgery itself. Most nerve injuries, above all to the axillary nerve, heal well without an operation when watched closely. Vessel injuries are the emergency, needing fast team care to restore blood flow before tissue dies. Since no standard treatment plan exists, Seker proposes a practical pathway built on careful examination, targeted scans, and joint decisions across specialties.
pmc-13584257:
Yali Fan and colleagues report a 2026 study of hidden drug resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that often infects hospital patients. In heteroresistance, most of a strain falls to an antibiotic while a small hardy share survives, which can sink treatment without warning. The team tested 380 clinical strains from one large hospital, collected between 2011 and 2024, against two widely used drugs.

Careful follow-up tests confirmed the hidden pattern in about half the strains for at least one of the two drugs. Rates for both drugs peaked in the years 2017 to 2019, then fell back during the pandemic years. Past use of one antibiotic family raised the odds of the pattern, while being male or having prior antiviral treatment lowered them. The authors suggest routine screening for high-risk patients.
pmc-13584957:
Miao Yu, Shi-Min Chen, and Chen-Ying Yu run a pilot trial of group therapy built on an emotion regulation model for college students who injure themselves without suicidal intent. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Difficulty managing emotions is a core driver of such self-injury. Group formats add peer support to skills training.

Fifty-six students were split evenly between intervention and no-treatment groups. The program ran eight sessions teaching distraction, expression, reframing, and problem solving. Afterward the treated students showed clear drops in anxiety, depression, and self-injury. The control group barely moved over the same span. Gains were still visible at a two-month follow-up. Participants rated the program highly and described internal and external changes. As a pilot, the trial's job is to justify a bigger one. On its own terms it succeeds.
pmc-13585057:
Kristen Bidas and nine colleagues published a soil study in two thousand twenty-six comparing how two minerals hold carbon. Iron oxides are well known for locking carbon into soil. Manganese oxides are less studied, so the team buried coated sands in a forest soil to compare them head to head.

Sand grains coated with manganese oxide, iron oxide, or nothing stayed in acidic forest soil for up to a year. After that year, manganese coatings held about eleven times more carbon per area than iron coatings. The carbon on manganese was rich in certain acid and sugar-like forms. Calcium gathered on the manganese surfaces may have helped the carbon stick. The manganese itself changed state over time, while the iron stayed the same.
pmc-13586557:
Samanta Corsetti and five colleagues flavor plain oils with food industry leftovers and test consumer reactions, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Basil and chili pepper by-products carry valuable antioxidants. Ultrasound-assisted extraction can move those compounds into refined olive and grape seed oils.

The flavored oils doubled in phenolic content compared with plain ones. Grape seed oils with chili or basil showed the highest antioxidant activity. Carotenoids and quality parameters were also measured. Consumers then tasted the oils twice: blind, and informed about their origin. Perception shifted with knowledge, the design reveals. The study pairs process chemistry with marketing reality. Waste valorization only works if shoppers actually want the result.
pmc-13588857:
Niharika Hiremath and colleagues studied how culture shapes peer work in mind-health and drug-use care. Peer staff draw on lived know-how to back recovery, yet staff from shunned race and culture groups are few and face more blocks in old-style care sites. With a ground-up method, the team read talks with peer staff at five mixed care groups in the United States.

Four themes came out: helps for shunned staff, care run by white norms, shunned staff with no voice in the peer cause, and blocks in taking and holding peer jobs. Each theme split into aids and bars to care that fits each culture. Change must come from whole care systems, not just from lone staff, if peer teams are to mirror the people they serve.
pmc-13589357:
Osung Kwon and Tae-Hyun Kim published a health economics study in twenty twenty-six on fine particulate pollution in South Korea. Breathing PM2.5 damages lungs and can kill, so measuring its true effect matters for policy. The authors used pollution blown in from upwind monitors in China as an instrument to isolate cause from local confounding.

They linked mortality records from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two and hospital data from twenty sixteen to twenty nineteen. A small rise in local particles raised deaths among adults over sixty-five and sharply increased respiratory hospitalizations. The paper also values the life years that cleaner air would save, giving policymakers a benefit estimate for reductions.
pmc-13590657:
Pierre-Ewen Lecoq and colleagues showed that gravity changes alter brain-cell activity in levitating neural spheroids. Studying 3D brain models in microgravity is hard, since handling floating cell assemblies is tricky, yet spaceflight research demands it. Their 2026 study used an acoustic bioreactor, a bulk acoustic wave resonator, to trap levitating neuronal spheroids in liquid medium, countering gravity with acoustic force even in weightlessness.

A custom setup enabled live calcium imaging during parabolic flights, which cycle through hypergravity, microgravity, and normal gravity. Calcium activity in the trapped 3D neural networks clearly tracked gravity changes across parabolas. The authors present acoustic trapping as a practical way to study gravity's effects on brain networks, with relevance for astronaut health.
pmc-13591457:
Madison N Irwin and four colleagues count, in 2026, how many older adults carry diagnoses of centralized pain, a kind where the nervous system itself amplifies pain without clear tissue damage. Such pain answers poorly to opioids, which carry extra risk in old age. The team scanned records of more than 320,000 patients aged 65 and up at one large academic center, with and without cancer.

About one in six carried at least one of these overlapping pain diagnoses, such as fibromyalgia or chronic back pain. Holders skewed female and younger within the older group, and carried more other ills. Black patients were less likely to hold such a diagnosis. Cancer patients showed a slightly higher rate than peers without cancer, Irwin and the team report.
pmc-13591757:
Yanqin Chen and five colleagues review, in 2026, models that try to predict which stroke patients will worsen soon after clot busting treatment. Early worsening strikes a sizable share of patients given intravenous thrombolysis for ischemic stroke. Their search across seven databases kept 18 studies and 18 models. A standard tool then graded each study for bias and fitness for clinic use.

Starting stroke severity score was the most used predictor across models. The five models tested on fresh data sorted patients fairly well on average. Every study, though, earned a high bias rating, thanks to shifting outcome definitions and thin reporting. Chen and the team call for tighter standards and nurse led watch for high risk patients.
pmc-13592357:
Tahajud and Ahmed reported a hard case in twenty twenty-six: massive bleeding from swollen veins in the food pipe and stomach of a young man without liver cirrhosis. A chronic clot in the portal vein, which carries blood to the liver, had raised pressure and grown these fragile veins.

The thirty-one-year-old arrived vomiting blood, passing black stools, and in shock, with very low hemoglobin. Fluids, transfusions, and drugs steadied him. Endoscopy found large esophageal veins plus a large stomach vein that had recently bled. Definitive treatment for the stomach vein was not available locally, so the team deferred banding the other veins and arranged urgent referral. Scans confirmed the old clot with bypass vessels and an enlarged spleen. He left hospital on day five without new bleeding.
pmc-13592657:
Zhiguang Huang leads a team tracing how talk inside a Reddit hemorrhoid community changed over a decade. Such forums matter because embarrassment keeps many sufferers from clinics, making peer posts a rare window on real concerns. From 9,954 collected posts, cleaning left 3,746 quality ones spanning 2013 to 2022. Topic modeling mapped themes in the mature years, an emotion classifier sorted feelings, and trend analysis linked feelings to replies and scores.

Neutral posts formed the largest share, with fear and disgust heavy among the rest. Nineteen topics grouped into four domains, from spotting symptoms to surgery and daily life impact. Fearful and sad posts drew the most comments by a clear margin. Huang and the team argue the forum doubles as support space and a guide for digital health design.
pmc-13593557:
Zachary T. Hollis, Eunice Yang, and Brett D. Atwater compare two ways of pacing Bachmann's bundle, the main bridge carrying signals from the right atrium to the left, within one and the same patient. Their 2026 report covers both a conventional wired lead and a leadless device placed in that bundle area.

Pacing at this site can correct the slow signal travel between the atria that raises left atrial pressure and feeds atrial fibrillation and heart failure. The leadless approach matched the wired one in effectiveness for this patient. Ultrasound imaging from inside the heart, together with the timing of left atrial activation, helped the team confirm that the devices truly sat in the bundle area.
pmc-13593657:
Dan Song and colleagues investigated parthenolide, a natural compound from the feverfew plant, as a treatment to speed healing of diabetic wounds. Their 2026 study combined computer-based target prediction with experiments in diabetic mice and in cultured macrophages, the immune cells that shape inflammation at a wound.

The prediction pointed to two signaling hubs, TNF-α and STAT3, as likely targets. In mice, the two higher doses clearly sped wound closure while the lowest dose gave no stable benefit. Tissue staining showed more skin cell growth, more new blood vessels, and more macrophages switched to the calming M2 type. Cell experiments supported the idea that parthenolide works by tuning those two pathways and nudging macrophages toward their healing form, making it a candidate worth further testing for stubborn diabetic wounds.
pmc-13593757:
Ruihong Yu and colleagues pooled everything known about how dexamethasone, a powerful anti-inflammatory steroid, moves through a horse's body and affects its hormones. Their 2026 meta-analysis combined data from twelve studies covering blood, urine, and joint fluid, then fitted a body-based mathematical model to the combined results.

The model showed the drug is cleared mainly by the liver. It lingers at trace levels for nearly three days after a standard injected dose. Tissues bind it in a nonlinear way, which helps explain the long tail. Availability ranged widely by route and formulation, from just over a third absorbed to complete absorption. A single dose suppressed the adrenal glands and raised blood sugar for two to four days. The authors offer the model as support for sensible dosing in equine practice and for regulators setting withdrawal rules.
pmc-13594757:
Bui Nguyen and colleagues report a hidden hepatitis B infection found during kidney transplant checks. Their case report from twenty twenty-six concerns a woman on dialysis. Standard screening suggested her past infection had fully resolved. Her antibody levels looked strongly protective on routine tests.

Deeper testing told a different story before transplant. Core antibody tests came back positive on recheck. Viral DNA was also detectable in her blood at real levels. Missing such occult infection risks viral flare under immune suppression. Transplant drugs deliberately weaken immunity after surgery. The authors urge DNA testing for dialysis patients before transplant, even when surface tests look reassuring.
pmc-13597657:
Baptiste Bonnet leads a fifteen-author prospective pilot study of a robotic platform guiding needles into bone under CT imaging, for procedures that consolidate fragile bone or ablate tumors. Thirty-four patients at three academic centers underwent ninety needle insertions between September 2024 and January 2025, most in the spine and the rest in the pelvis, in their 2026 report.

The robot succeeded in all but one insertion, which was finished by hand. Final needle tips landed on average two millimeters from the planned point, with an angular miss of about three degrees. Seven adverse events occurred in six patients, four of them serious, yet none was blamed on the device or the procedure itself. Procedure times ran long, around three hours. The authors judge feasibility and accuracy satisfactory and call for larger comparative trials.
pmc-13598157:
Matthew K. Brachmann leads a twelve-author study of threespine stickleback fish that independently colonized geothermally warmed waters, using them as a living preview of climate warming. Pairs of warm-adapted and ordinary populations were compared for body traits and genomes in their 2026 analysis.

The warm fish converged in behavior and body: similar appetite, fat stores, and fat loss during starvation. Their genomes, though, diverged at mostly different loci, a non-parallel pattern, except for one shared chromosome inversion tied to metabolic genes. At the functional level the same signaling pathway, the mapk cascade, shifted across pairs, and its genes responded to temperature and to cross-breeding. The authors conclude that selection finds similar outcomes through different genetic routes, so conservation planning should protect functional pathways rather than betting on particular alleles.
pmc-13599357:
Chen and five co-authors reviewed an enzyme's role in bone marrow swelling for this paper from twenty twenty-six. Bone marrow edema shows on MRI as extra fluid and tracks with pain and joint damage. SIRT1 is an enzyme that guards bone health by favoring bone building over bone loss. The review asks whether its failure helps explain the swelling.

Low SIRT1 activity could loosen blood vessel walls and prolong inflammation. It could also raise oxidative stress and add fat inside the marrow. Direct proof tying SIRT1 to the swelling is still thin, the authors admit. Activator compounds such as resveratrol make the idea testable. They call for lesion-level studies before treatment claims can stand.
pmc-13599757:
Marcelo Chávez-Díaz and six co-authors report the first use in Peru of a flap method for partial breast rebuilding, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. The flaps use tissue fed by small arteries between the ribs. They let surgeons rebuild the breast right away while sparing muscle and limiting harm at the donor site.

The team reviewed twenty patients treated over two years at their center. Most had invasive ductal cancer, and most tumors sat in the upper outer part of the breast. Surgeons used single, double-lobed, and combined flap designs. Operations took a little over two hours on average. The authors judge the method safe and flexible for women with small breasts, where shifting the breast's own tissue is hard.
pmc-13600057:
C. Dominik Güss and Jaden Powell ask whether the many vocabularies for dual-process thinking describe different ideas or the same idea under new labels. Dual-process theory divides thinking into a fast, intuitive, effortless mode and a slow, deliberate, effortful mode, yet researchers have coined numerous term pairs for the two modes. The authors reviewed the literature, ran a thought experiment, and compared terms with a BERT-based model called SCEPTER.

Despite lexical differences, the terms proved very similar at their core, a case of old wine in a new bottle. The authors trace the proliferation to the jangle fallacy, in which different labels are mistaken for different constructs. They urge careful deliberation before coining new terms, since fresh jargon can obscure rather than advance understanding.
pmc-13601057:
Pereira leads a large team giving a protocol to grow bat cells in the lab, in work from twenty twenty-six. Some bat species host dangerous viruses and serve as models for antiviral immunity. Studying those viruses needs bat cells that can be grown reliably.

Steps cover collecting tissue from wild bats, digesting it with enzymes, isolating cells, and expanding them in culture. Tests for immune competence of the cultures are detailed. The protocol builds in vitro models for understudied non model species, so virus work does not depend only on live animal studies or on cells from unrelated species.
pmc-13603157:
Sarah Nathel Douglas and her team tell of the build of a plan that trains speech staff and clans to back kids who talk with no speech. Their 2026 work sets out how the FamTAM plan was made step by step.

Near a third of kids with autism use tools that add to speech, such as hand signs, pic marks, and screen kits. Clan training is a must for these tools to work, yet few step plans are there. The plan teaches a way to model talk with aids, with coach work for care givers, and gets school speech staff set to coach clans. Build work took in fine work on what goes in and how it is sent, wise folk checks, and talks with folk who took part. Users found the plan fun, of use in real life, and in line with proof-based work, and put forth more steps.
pmc-13603357:
Abdulkhamid Fayzullaev, Alisher Dedahanov, Soo Young Shin, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It examines the dark side of performance contests at work for women managers in South Korea, tracing how competition erodes their attachment to the organization.

Data came from a national panel survey, covering 1,325 women across 413 organizations. Competition raised two kinds of strain: friction with colleagues and simple overload. Both strains, in turn, lowered the women's emotional commitment to their firm, with the friction path the stronger of the two. Job autonomy, often a buffer, failed to soften the friction path. Strangely, it strengthened the link between competition and overload. The authors say performance systems carry hidden costs for the very managers firms promote them to motivate, and urge care in designing competitive climates.
pmc-13606257:
Ruoshu Li leads an eleven-author team tracking how frozen storage changes mussels by sex. Thick-shell mussels were held at minus 18 degrees and sampled fresh, at 90 days, and at 150 days. The team measured water loss, spoilage markers, fat oxidation, amino acids, flavor nucleotides, fatty acids, and aroma compounds in females and males separately.

Quality slid in both sexes, but along different paths. By day 150, drip loss had risen to 1.2 times fresh levels in females and 1.5 times in males, while spoilage nitrogen reached 2.7 and 2.4 times fresh values. A fat oxidation marker rose about 3.3-fold in both and ended 1.7 times higher in females. Males carried more free amino acids; females showed higher umami concentration at some stages. Aroma profiling found aldehydes enriched in females after 90 days, while males kept stronger ketone and ester notes; fourteen compounds distinguished the groups. The authors offer a basis for sex-aware quality grading and storage.
pmc-13609657:
Huilin Yan and others put out a soil survey in 2026. They sampled faba bean fields on the Qinghai Plateau. Root-zone bacteria help crops take up nutrients. Altitude may reshape those germ communities strongly. Fifteen fields across three areas were sampled with care. Heights spanned a wide high range there. Soil chemistry and germ DNA were checked side by side. Each field gave several sub-samples so results could be trusted. Distance between sites was also studied with stats.

Variety scores varied, but not by much, across elevation groups. Community makeup did differ between area groups overall. Large overlap between sites stayed despite the gaps. Distance on the map foretold makeup gaps quite well. Soil factors added a further account for patterns. A cautious local check did not reach note. Elevation alone is a weak guide here. Place and soil together shape root germs better.
pmc-13611757:
Yue Zhu and Chao Qian test how well repair resin sticks to 3D-printed zirconia crowns. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, compares two printing methods with milling. Bonding resin to zirconia is a known weak point in dentistry. Printed versions, made layer by layer, might grip differently.

Blocks were printed by two light-based methods or milled by machine. After sand blasting, printed blocks came out rougher than milled ones. Tiny resin posts were then sheared off to measure bond strength. Both printed groups matched each other and beat the milled group. Break patterns under a microscope add detail. Printed zirconia may accept repairs and cement at least as well as milled.
pmc-13612257:
Echu Liu, Yiu Wing Kam, and Huilin Cheng open a research collection on helping vulnerable patients through care joining biology with social reality. Vulnerability, the editors argue, becomes actionable at three linked points: recognizing complex needs, turning recognition into responsive care, and building response capacity. The editorial walks the studies as illustrations of each point.

Recognition studies include global gaps in newborn brain injury, and symptom networks in older adults with diabetes. A third covers resistance training in possibly sarcopenic elders, where gut microbes and inflammation shifted with physical gains. Translation studies cover a transitional care program stitching hospital and primary care together, and mental-health assessment in general hospital wards. The editors' through-line is that disease-by-disease medicine misses how needs accumulate in real lives. Integrated biosocial care, they contend, helps systems see the whole patient early enough to help.
pmc-13612457:
Mohammed Badrul Amin leads an eight-author team testing a popular suspicion in Dhaka in 2026: that drug-resistant urinary infections come from poultry. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase E. coli, which shrug off antibiotics, were presumed to flow from chickens to people. The team sampled 2,297 foods from twenty-four wet markets during 2016 to 2018, collected urinary isolates from nearby patients, and sequenced strains from both.

Contamination was rampant: 87 percent of foods carried E. coli, 30 percent the resistant kind, poultry most of all at 43 percent. The genetics, though, acquitted the chickens. Urinary isolates were dominated by phylogroup B2 and the pandemic clone ST131, both absent from food. Four sequence types appeared in both sources, but genomes showed no close relatedness, differing by over twenty-two core mutations. Dietary interviews showed no link either. The authors conclude the urinary strains circulate by another route, and poultry-focused panic would miss the real reservoir.
pmc-13612857:
Joel St-Aubin and colleagues wrote a fictional teaching case for the Medical Physics Leadership Academy about a cancer center that needs new quality-check gear for precise radiation therapy. In the story, junior physicist Dr. Angel Allende has just started at a center with two treatment machines, one newly upgraded for image-guided stereotactic treatment. The chief physicist asks for a new quality assurance program, and the team must build a business case for the software and equipment it needs.

The case is openly a work of fiction, made to spark class discussion about the management and leadership problems medical physicists can face. Learners work through basic finance ideas and practice gathering and weighing money figures for a large purchase choice. Complications the young physicist expects along the way give the exercise its tension and its teaching value.
pmc-13612957:
Ririna Shiba and colleagues compare two store-bought blood tests for cats in a 2026 study using 80 leftover plasma samples from pet cats. Both tests measure serum amyloid A, a protein that rises fast when a cat has inflammation or tissue injury and falls as the cat recovers. Vets rely on the value to judge how sick a cat is, so it matters whether the two kits give the same answer.

The two systems, a Fuji fluorescence test and an Eiken turbidity test, moved together closely, with a rank correlation of 0.948. Yet their actual values differed a lot, showing a mean gap of minus 86.2 percent. The authors warn that results from one kit cannot be swapped for the other, and each test needs its own range for what counts as normal.
pmc-13618957:
Virgilio Blandon and seven colleagues scope published work on non-ablative dermal remodeling lasers in acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation, a stubborn group of pigment disorders. These lasers target water rather than pigment. They may help by stimulating new collagen. The review searched six sources plus trial registries, mapping designs, laser settings, outcomes, and safety.

From one hundred ninety-three records, seven studies qualified: two randomized trials, three retrospective series, and two case reports, totaling thirty-one patients. The fifteen-fifty nanometer fractional erbium laser was studied most. The two trials found no clinical or tissue-level improvement, while the observational reports claimed favorable results despite weak methods and other treatments alongside. Laser-triggered darkening appeared in nearly a quarter of patients in one trial. The authors conclude the findings are too thin and mixed to establish benefit. They call for standardized prospective studies with tissue, molecular, and imaging endpoints.
pmc-13619257:
Noreen Bux wrote a letter commenting on a quality improvement study about team debriefs after cardiac arrests and tube placements in a children's emergency department. Bux praises the original team for raising debrief completion with a structured, technology-based routine. The letter then asks what that success actually proves for patients and staff.

Completion in the study meant a form was submitted, so nobody measured how well each debrief ran or whether care improved. Survival, resuscitation quality, and preventable harm all went untested, as did staff well-being and burnout. Bux calls for multicenter work using checked tools for debrief quality, patient outcomes, and worker health. Cost studies and tests of which parts of the program matter most would help other hospitals decide whether to copy it.
pmc-13619357:
Mahamad Sayab Miya, Elise Valkanas, and T Keith Philips studied the family history of a cave beetle found only in central Kentucky. They collected beetles from sixty-two caves and sequenced part of a standard gene to test whether four named subspecies were real. Cave animals make good subjects for such work because their dark, isolated homes can split populations apart over time.

Every analysis pointed to two large groups, one north and one south, divided by the Barren River. The authors argue the four subspecies should be scrapped: the three northern forms merge into one species, while the southern form deserves full species rank under a new status. Beetles within each group were genetically very similar, which suggests caves in the region connect underground more than expected. The team also found twenty-six populations nobody had recorded before.
pmc-13619457:
Ahmed S Aljohani, Michael B Bonsall, and Robert A Montgomery analyzed population records for two hoofed animals reintroduced across the Middle East. The Arabian oryx and the sand gazelle are both listed as Vulnerable after declines from hunting and habitat loss. The team gathered eighty-four yearly oryx records and forty-three gazelle records, then modeled how growth rates respond to population size and past conditions.

Both species grew more slowly as their numbers rose, a pattern called negative density dependence. Small populations showed no sign of an Allee effect, the trap where tiny groups struggle to recover at all. Oryx growth also carried a lag, with the previous year's conditions shaping the current year's trend. Short head counts can mislead managers, the authors warn, so recovery programs need many years of steady monitoring to read progress correctly.
pmc-13619757:
He and co-authors model second fracture risk after hip fracture surgery in older adults. The study held 4,418 patients aged 65 and over. All had surgery for a first low-energy hip fracture. Follow-up ran three years for a new fragility fracture. A total of 594 patients, or 13.4 percent, broke again.

Risk rose with age, osteoporosis, low body mass, and female sex. Heart disease, poor vision, fainting, and weak rehab added risk. A hip score under 80 after surgery also flagged risk. The XGBoost model beat rival models on test data. The authors built the tool to be readable by clinicians.
pmc-13621457:
Natalya Vo Van-Zivkovic and five co-authors study breeding strategy in sugarcane in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Sugarcane supplies most of the world's sugar, yet its genetic gains have stalled for decades. Its genome is complex and breeding cycles are long. Genomic selection can speed gains by picking parents from DNA alone. But chasing short-term gain can drain the diversity that future gains need.

The risk is worse in cloned, outcrossing crops like sugarcane. Inbreeding then saps vigor and yield. The authors apply optimal contribution selection, a method that balances gain against diversity loss. Their work shows how to set parent shares so progress stays sustainable. Sugarcane breeders and quantitative geneticists are the audience.
pmc-13624457:
Shatha Alharazy and five co-authors find a fresh splice flaw in the KCTD7 gene in a Saudi girl with a grave seizure ill. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such ills bring early jerks and mind fall and spring from many genes. The girl, aged three, was born to kin parents and had full gene reads at a genome hub.

A five-base cut sat in both copies of the gene, while each parent held one copy. Checks backed the split. The flaw is new in print, and the girl's signs match known KCTD7 ills. The team reads it as a like cause and adds it to the Saudi map for this ill class.
pmc-13624857: Hope Freshwater, Pablo Chialvo, and Clare Scott Chialvo build a gene model for the fruit fly Drosophila dunni, targeting its version of a gene called yellow-f2. Their annotation note was published in twenty twenty-six. The model rests on the species' published genome assembly. It forms part of a growing data set comparing how a detoxification gene family evolved in one branch of the fly genus. The work used an undergraduate research protocol for gene annotation from the Genomics Education Partnership.
pmc-13625057:
Hassan Ait Yachou and co-authors give one plant material two jobs in making a biodegradable plastic. They treated microcrystalline cellulose, a fine powder from plant fiber, with phosphorus so its surface groups could start the chain-building reaction that forms PCL, a compostable polyester. The same treated powder then stayed inside the plastic as a reinforcing filler, all without solvents or metal catalysts.

Lab checks with several scanning and spectroscopy tools confirmed the plastic chains had grafted onto the cellulose grains. The filled plastic held up to heat better than plain PCL, resisting breakdown to notably higher temperatures, and it crystallized more fully. A single green additive acting as both starter and strengthener could simplify how such composites are made.
pmc-13626357:
Izabela Marcelina Sowińska and colleagues audit pressure injuries reported as safety events at a specialist hospital in Kraków, Poland. These wounds, earned by lying or sitting too long in one position, are treated as largely preventable and as a mirror of care quality. The team reviewed all 1,272 adverse event reports filed from 2013 to 2020 and set the injury cases against a comparison group of other patients.

Pressure injuries made up nearly a quarter of reports, 305 events in all. Affected patients stayed about six days longer and took far more medicines than the comparison group. In adjusted models, older age, longer stays, more prescriptions, and heavier illness burden each raised the odds. The internal medicine ward filed the most reports, which helps target prevention where the frailest patients gather.
pmc-13626857:
Xiaoqing Gao, Yuxin Li, Ting Fang, and Wenjie Jiang compare the scented waters left over when two mugwort species are distilled for oil. Hydrosols from Artemisia argyi and Artemisia lavandulifolia were gathered across regions and seasons in Shandong Province, China, and profiled by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. The lavandulifolia water carried more of two prized alcohols, terpinen-4-ol and alpha-terpineol, and its overall chemical signature stood apart from its cousin's.

Both waters slowed five test bacteria, and both stopped Escherichia coli and Proteus vulgaris, with lavandulifolia the stronger. Season and origin nudged the recipes, and statistical maps separated the species with some overlap. For makers of natural antimicrobial sprays and cosmetics, species choice and harvest timing are levers worth controlling.
pmc-13627157:
K Vagaytseva and six co-authors build base gene marks for kin calls in two Nenets folk packs of Siberia. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. X-part marks help when plain panels run weak, like sis to sis or gran to grand kid calls. Five hundred four Nenets men were typed on sixteen marks, split by pack, clan, and camp ground.

No true splits showed tween packs. Two marks bore the most kinds, and most marks were rich in tells. The joint shut-out force near maxed. Link pulls tween marks were weak in whole. The base counts are set for court gene use.
pmc-13628657:
Rui Liu and colleagues published a food materials study in 2026. They built a pad to keep blueberries fresh longer. The pad uses a plastic matrix filled with microspheres. Those spheres carry a plant compound called carvacrol. Carvacrol fights bacteria but escapes too quickly alone. A porous mineral cage helps hold it back. Slow release is the central design goal here. Lab checks confirmed the parts combined as intended.

The new pad released carvacrol longer than comparison pads. Antioxidant and antibacterial action lasted through long storage. Blueberries kept fifteen days with the pad fared better. They lost less water and stayed firmer overall. Nutrients and fresh taste were better preserved too. Breathing rate of the fruit also slowed. Such pads could cut spoilage in berry supply chains.
pmc-13629057:
Anna Palma leads a team that builds microneedles to sense a swelling mark. Their work from twenty twenty-six targets TNF-alpha in skin fluid. That fluid can hold more of the mark than blood does.

Microneedles give a blood free, low pain way to sample. Their sensor uses a synthetic peptide in place of antibodies. The peptide is fixed firm on strong plastic needles. That set up forms a three D glow based test. Antibody limits in past tools are a key bar they address. Early local swelling could be caught this way.
pmc-13629257:
Miia Kauppinen and six colleagues reviewed trials of social robots used to calm children and teenagers around surgery. Their 2026 systematic review searched widely across medical and engineering sources and found seven studies with 663 young participants, covering robots used as friendly, interactive distractions during perioperative care.

Pooling the two studies that allowed it showed a significant drop in anxiety after surgery, and several other studies pointed the same way for anxiety around the operation. Effects on pain, fear, and stress, by contrast, were small or absent. Because the robot programmes varied a great deal, the authors call for better-designed trials to pin down which features help and where robots genuinely belong in children's surgical care.
pmc-13629457:
Søren Grove led a 2026 study of whether two commercial vaccines cut the shedding of salmonid alphavirus subtype 3, the virus behind pancreas disease in Atlantic salmon. Infected fish release virus into the water. Shedding rate and duration drive spread between farms. A vaccine that only protects individuals while letting shedding continue can still fail at the population level. The team infected vaccinated post-smolt salmon and tracked shedding in individually housed fish and in tanks of sixty.

Alone in tanks, the inactivated vaccine cut the share of shedding fish, shedding duration, and total shedding. The DNA vaccine cut duration and the share of shedders. In group tanks, where an unintended bacterial co-infection was present, results shifted. The inactivated vaccine cut total shedding but lengthened duration, while the DNA vaccine's cuts were not significant.
pmc-13629557:
Michael S. Ryan and four colleagues examine how the idea of validity in testing must change under competency-based training. They write with a global group of partners. Training judged by shown skill strains older habits of thought. Those habits prize standard tests and fixed pass marks.

The authors work through three points of tension. One is the base model of testing itself. One asks whether validity claims should treat performance whole or in pieces. One asks whether skill should be judged against peers, set standards, or growth over time. For each tension they weigh the classic measurement view. They set it against newer, more practical views. They close with balanced stances. Those keep rigour while fitting modern programme-level testing.
pmc-13629657:
Tristan T. Demmert and ten colleagues tested a new algorithm for cleaning up CT scans around metal implants, where streak artifacts often hide the very bone doctors need to inspect. Their experimental study scanned three cow femur bones fitted with titanium hip nails on a photon-counting scanner.

Images were rebuilt three ways: untouched, with the current artifact-reduction software, and with a prototype that exploits the scanner's built-in spectral data. Artifact severity next to the implant fell at each step, and three radiologists rated the prototype best on every quality measure. The older software also introduced fresh artifacts near the metal, which the prototype avoided. The authors see promise for judging implant complications such as loosening.
pmc-13631557:
Yupeng Zhao and seven colleagues wrote this review of how cancer spreads from its first site to distant organs. Spread, called metastasis, is the main reason cancer treatment fails and patients die. The authors treat it as a moving process shaped over time by changes inside tumor cells and by pressure from the tissues around them.

The review follows metastatic cells from early growth through travel in blood, lymph vessels, or along nerves, then into new organ homes. It covers genetic and non-genetic changes, the niches that form in target organs before cells arrive, and the ways cells settle and grow there. It also weighs current tests and treatments aimed at spread itself. The authors argue that future therapy should match timing, travel route, and markers rather than chase single targets.
pmc-13632057:
Alexandra N Johansen and colleagues review the search for medicines to treat methamphetamine use disorder, a 2026 survey of a field with no approved drug therapy. Use remains high and deaths have risen sharply. Few trials have tested candidate medicines. Development has rarely followed the full path from animal work to human lab studies to clinical trials. The authors mapped that path, asking which candidates were tested at each stage and whether results agreed across stages.

Thirty-six randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials covered twenty-five candidate drugs. Only five had also been tested in human lab and animal settings: aripiprazole, bupropion, d-amphetamine, modafinil, and naltrexone. Most studies at every stage showed no change in methamphetamine use. The review urges a more disciplined pipeline, clearer therapeutic targets, and attention to newer regulatory guidance on non-abstinence outcomes.
pmc-13632457:
Thomas Kaufmann and eight colleagues studied the protein machines that build the actin shell under a cell's surface. That shell, called the cortex, helps cells move and divide. One family of builders, the formins, makes long straight actin cables that resist squeezing forces. The team screened formin types in mouse melanoma cells to find which ones work at the cortex and which switch signals control them.

Two formin groups, Daam and FMNL, gathered at the rear cortex of moving cells and answered to several known switch proteins. Daam proteins proved to be strong cable builders once switched on. Cells missing both Daam copies grew extra leading edges, wandered poorly, and retracted their rears badly. Removing Daam together with the mDia formins softened the cortex, caused excess bubbling, and slowed division. The families clearly share the job of keeping the cortex sound.
pmc-13635057:

The therapy, a lutetium-labeled molecule that seeks a prostate cancer protein, works unevenly. Patients whose scans show weak protein levels across their tumors fare worse on the standard schedule. This multicenter trial enrolls forty-five such patients whose disease kept growing after hormone-blocking treatment.

The main measure is how long the cancer marker PSA stays from rising, with safety tracked closely throughout. A standing rule stops the trial early if serious blood side effects pass a preset line. The protocol also collects pain and quality-of-life reports, radiation dose estimates, and blood markers. Strong responders may pause treatment under close watching.
pmc-13641957:
Dong Hyun Sinn and three colleagues present a 2026 cohort study on whether insulin resistance predicts liver cancer in people with chronic hepatitis B who already take antiviral drugs. Cancer still develops in some patients even when the virus is fully suppressed.

The multicenter study followed 334 patients with hepatitis B cirrhosis for a median of about seven years, during which sixty-two developed liver cancer. Higher insulin resistance scores predicted cancer independently of other factors, and patients above a chosen cutoff faced roughly double the five-year incidence. The authors propose the score as a practical flag for closer monitoring.
pmc-13642057:

Both antimony and boron produced shifts in either direction, toward longer or shorter wavelengths, while narrowing the spread of emission across dots and suppressing unwanted wetting-layer light. Ion dose controlled how much the light output fell, and simulations matched the defect and mixing profiles. Photonic engineers get a scalable, mask-free way to engineer dots on chips, useful for quantum memories, single-photon emitters, and integrated circuits.
pmc-13642257:
Zhi-Guo Wu and nine colleagues present a 2026 review of immunosenescence, the aging of the immune system, as a driver and mirror of decline across many organs at once. Aging increasingly looks like a whole-body process rather than separate organ failures.

It weighs biomarker panels for measuring immune age and discusses senolytic and senomorphic drugs that clear or calm worn-out cells. Limits include mixed contexts and unsettled cause-and-effect. The authors frame the immune system as a lever for extending healthy years.
pmc-13643157:

The discussed study gathered 1,450 confirmed T cell targets and predicted how virus mutations changed HLA binding. Binding-weakening changes were common among important lineage mutations, and they clustered where the matching HLA type is frequent in the population. Ghafari reads this as evidence that population HLA makeup quietly steers which virus variants succeed.
pmc-13643257:
Adnan Agha and five colleagues present a 2026 study protocol for judging the reasoning process of medical language models, not just their final answers. Most tests score multiple-choice accuracy and say little about how a model thinks, even as extended-thinking modes spread.

Six flagship models will answer urgent care cases in standard and extended modes, scored blind by human experts and by a guarded model-judge pipeline. Later, the validated pipeline will grade 3,600 outputs. Student responses were already collected under seal by mid 2026.
pmc-13643457:
Radwan Alkhatib and nine colleagues report a 2026 case of a sunken chest wall causing years of racing heart in a sixty-five-year-old woman. Her palpitations persisted despite high-dose beta-blocker treatment, and scans showed severe pectus excavatum pressing on the front of her heart.

Catheter tests found very low filling pressures with preserved output, meaning the squeezed heart could not fill properly and sped up to compensate. Surgeons corrected the deformity with a modified Ravitch repair. Her palpitations vanished completely and her heart rate normalized. The authors present severe chest deformity as a reversible cause worth remembering in unexplained tachycardia.
pmc-13645757:
Ann-Kathrin Schwientek and sixteen colleagues compare patterns of mental and physical distress in young adults across three groups: Swiss residents, Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland, and Ukrainians still living in Ukraine. Participants were aged eighteen to twenty-four and were drawn at random for a population study. Standard screening scales covered low mood, anxiety, trauma stress, and body symptoms. The team grouped people into clusters with similar symptom profiles.

Complete scores were available for 1,181 participants, most of them in the Ukraine group. Symptom domains moved together across all three settings, and clustering showed shared patterns rather than one unique war profile. The authors argue that care for young adults should expect mixed mental and body complaints, whether or not a person lives near fighting. Their baseline data set up later rounds of the study to track how these profiles change over time.
pmc-13646057:

Staff speech tended to shrink the program's novelty and defend existing routines as a way of coping with change. Talk also guarded the line between insiders and outsiders, which strained teamwork and ownership. Vague leadership blurred who was accountable for making the program work. The authors argue the barriers were not staff stubbornness but framing and structure. Their reading offers managers a lens for why good programs stall inside organizations.
pmc-13646757:
Ryo Nakanishi and five colleagues report a case of wound myiasis, infestation by fly larvae, in a cancerous lip wound of a man in his eighties. His tumor was a Merkel cell carcinoma of the upper lip, an aggressive skin cancer that had returned after radiation and drug therapy. Five days after a chemotherapy cycle, he came in because the tumor smelled foul. Examination found roughly twenty larvae living in the ulcerated, dead tissue.

Washing with saline and physically removing larvae and dead tissue cleared the infestation, and daily wound care kept it from returning. Steady pain control, unbroken wound management, and support involving family and caregivers form their prescription for elderly patients with open cancer wounds.
pmc-13647257:

Resilience fully carried the benefit of both support types and partly carried the dazi benefit as well. Inside the dazi group, safety and trust worries tracked with higher anxiety, and partners chosen for emotional reasons showed weaker resilience than task-based ones. The authors suggest the quality and motive of these light partnerships matter, not just having one.
pmc-13647457:

That blur is not a flaw in the court's model but one of its defining features. The authors offer the case to justice designers elsewhere who must fit restorative ideas to mass, collective harm.
pmc-13648557:
Michael P. Marciel and eight colleagues examine an enzyme called ST6GAL1, which attaches sialic acids to proteins, during pancreatitis, a painful inflammation of the pancreas. Mice engineered to express it healed faster after induced pancreatitis, with restored tissue, less cell death, and fewer immune cells. The authors frame the enzyme as an adaptive mediator of pancreatic regeneration.
pmc-13649557:

The two hormones pulled in opposed ways across most particle types. Higher levels of adiponectin, the hormone tied to good health, matched fewer of the small, dense particles that clog arteries. Higher chemerin matched more of them. The pattern held in a steady way across the data. Since the study took one snapshot in time, the authors cannot say the hormones cause the fat patterns.
pmc-13649657:
Yan Zheng and eight colleagues ran a small trial of Tai Chi for women past menopause who have mild thinking problems. This group faces higher risk of decline, and blood flow problems in the brain may add to it. Forty women in Fuzhou, China, were split by chance into a 12-week Tai Chi class or a health teaching group.

The Tai Chi group gained far more on a standard thinking test, with clear gains in recall, planning, and focus. Brain blood flow rose across key areas, blood vessel signals shifted in a healthy way, and blood markers tied to Alzheimer's disease fell. No harms from the classes were seen. The authors call the gentle exercise a workable, well-liked option.
pmc-13649757:
Cut Putri Hazlianda and seven colleagues rubbed a cream made from bilimbi leaf extract on mice with eczema-like skin disease, testing two skin signals. One signal, IL-22, fuels skin swelling and blocks cell growth into a sound barrier. The other, filaggrin, is a brick protein of that barrier. Thirty mice were split into six groups.

Skin disease was raised with two triggers over four weeks, then creams were applied twice a day for two weeks. Mid and high extract doses cut IL-22 as much as the steroid cream did. Yet the plain cream base cut it just as much, so no extract-specific effect could be shown. Filaggrin did not shift in any group. The authors report the result with that caveat plain.
pmc-13650157:
Logan A Williams and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, search a mother's blood during pregnancy for chemical marks linked to autism in her child. They read methylation, a tagging pattern on DNA, in fragments of free DNA drawn from blood in the third trimester. The pregnancies were already considered likely to result in an autism diagnosis.

Regions tagged differently in autism-linked pregnancies clustered around genes for synapses, the connections between brain cells, and around genes earlier studies had tied to autism. The same tagged regions appeared in autism placenta tissue and in postmortem brain samples, and they overlapped substantially with regions tied to maternal obesity. The authors argue that a blood draw could open a low-burden window onto fetal brain development, setting up later work on how prenatal exposures and genetics interact.
pmc-13650557:

In isolated severe hepatitis, killer T cells attack infected B cells inside the liver and damage nearby liver cells as bystanders; inflammation stays local, and supportive care usually suffices. In the second pattern, infected T or natural killer cells trigger a body-wide cytokine storm with runaway immune activation, which needs immediate immune suppression. Very high viral loads in blood marked far higher mortality in one children's cohort, though no universal cutoff exists. Blood purification remains an experimental extra for stubborn cases. Prompt recognition of the storm pattern, the authors stress, saves lives.
pmc-13650957:
Jhonathan Renner Nunes dos Santos and six co-authors dissect how the solvent steers a multicomponent reaction that builds amino-cyano pyran rings, a scaffold common in medicinal chemistry. Their catalyst is a water-soluble polymer decorated with imidazolium groups, built to behave like a synthetic enzyme, and the study looks past yields to mechanism on purpose.

A solvent model splitting hydrogen-bond acidity, basicity, and polarity showed each property pulling at a different reaction stage, sometimes in opposite ways. Control experiments traced the main pathway: an aldehyde and malononitrile first join reversibly, then an enol form forges the next carbon bond. The method still delivered a series of products in good to excellent yields, and the catalyst recycled without fading.
pmc-13660757:
Leah Poole-Selters and ten colleagues survey how households in northern Namibia cope when drought cuts off food. Coping steps ranged from drawing on relatives and savings to cutting meals and selling assets. Their use varied with household characteristics and with how risky families judged the future to be. Knowing which households reach for the most damaging strategies, such as selling the tools of their livelihood, helps agencies target support before coping turns into lasting loss. The study grounds drought policy in reported household behavior.
pmc-13668957:
Haolin Li, Haibo Zhou, and Jianwen Cai adapted gradient boosting to predict survival in studies that deliberately oversample patients with the outcome.
