Their machine learning approach adds weights that correct the sampling bias. A weighted error measure, based on the integrated Brier score, tunes the model.

The authors prove the tuning criterion converges to the true risk. Simulations tested the method broadly. It was then applied to a study of cancer and mortality in uranium miners. Prediction improved over unweighted alternatives. Better survival models from cheaper study designs could sharpen personalized medicine where full cohorts are unaffordable.
pmc-13669357:
Xiaofeng Zhang leads a team of thirteen authors using light-activated molecular partnerships to bolt a prized fluorine group and a sulfur group onto alkenes in one step. The pentafluorosulfanyl group can transform a drug candidate's properties, but installing it on electron-poor alkenes by three-component reactions had resisted general methods. Their trick is an electron donor-acceptor complex that activates under green LEDs.

The reaction covered electron-deficient alkenes, alkynes, enynes, and even acetylene gas, yielding a diverse set of pentafluorosulfanyl thioethers. Complex molecules including drugs, natural products, and amino acid derivatives were functionalized late-stage. Mechanism studies support the complex-mediated pathway and identify a sulfur chloride as the key intermediate after thiyl radical formation. Mild, atom-economical conditions are the selling point.
pmc-13688957:
Xiuyun Li and nine co-authors show that a plant alkaloid can revive a failing antifungal drug against resistant Candida infections. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Candida albicans increasingly shrugs off fluconazole, the standard treatment. Pairing drugs is a promising way to break that resistance.

The alkaloid, dehydronuciferine, was tested with fluconazole on six resistant clinical isolates. Checkerboard tests confirmed strong synergy across the set. For one strain, the drug dose needed collapsed by more than two thousand fold. In infected wax moth larvae, the pair saved far more lives than either drug alone. The combo also suppressed the fungus's filaments, biofilms, and grip on tissue. Gene readouts tied those effects to silenced growth and adhesion genes. The alkaloid emerges as a strong drug sensitizer.
pmc-2803857:
Camacho, Coulouris, Avagyan, and co-authors introduce BLAST+, a rebuilt version of the classic sequence search tool. Searching for similar sequences is a central task in bioinformatics. BLAST uses smart shortcuts to beat exact methods, but the older software was too slow for very long queries or huge databases.

The new architecture speeds searches and splits the suite into focused programs that are easier to run at scale. Faster search matters because sequence databases grow relentlessly. BLAST+ kept a trusted method usable in the era of whole-genome queries and massive public archives.
pmc-3000457:
Gold, Ayers, Bertino, and co-authors present an aptamer-based technology for measuring many proteins at once in biomarker discovery. Studying whole sets of proteins in a multiplexed, efficient way remained a coveted but hard goal in biology and medicine. Aptamers are short molecules built to bind specific proteins.

Their technology uses such binders to measure thousands of proteins in a single sample. Wide measurement from small samples could reveal disease signatures earlier than single tests allow. The work helped open large-scale protein screening for studies of disease risk, drug response, and ageing.
pmc-3041657:
Chen and Boutros introduce VennDiagram, an R package for drawing highly customisable Venn and Euler diagrams. Biologists often need pictures of disjoint or overlapping datasets side by side. Few tools in the R environment could automate polished, high-resolution diagrams with extensive control.

Their package fills that gap, letting users tune colours, labels, and layout for publication. Overlapping sets appear in everything from gene lists to patient groups. A dependable drawing tool saves hours of manual work and reduces misleading figures in papers and presentations.  Publication-ready output removed the need to redraw diagrams in separate graphics programs.
pmc-4401657:
De Leeuw, Mooij, Heskes, and their colleagues introduced MAGMA in 2015. Gene and gene-set analysis add value to genome-wide studies by grouping marker data in a biologically sensible way. Existing methods for this task, the authors note, suffered from several issues.

MAGMA offers a generalized approach that handles genes and whole sets in one frame. It aims to be fast, flexible, and sound where older tools had gaps. Grouping signals by gene can reveal effects too weak to see marker by marker. That helps researchers connect statistical hits to real biology in traits such as brain and metabolic disorders.
pmc-5210557:
Gaulton, Hersey, Nowotka, and their team updated the ChEMBL database in 2017. ChEMBL is a large open store of bioactivity data: tests of how compounds act on living targets. First reports on it came out in 2012 and 2014, and it has grown since then.

The team kept mining the drug chemistry literature for new test results. They also added new sources of data on how compounds bind and act. A user can look up a compound or a target and see all its known test values in one place. Drug teams use that pooled data to pick leads and train models that predict new drugs.
pmc-5367557:
Griffiths, Johnson, Carducci, and their team ran a trial in 2016 of psilocybin for patients with life-threatening cancer. Such patients often face deep, lasting depression and anxiety. Early small studies had hinted that psilocybin, a psychedelic drug, might ease that distress.

The trial was randomized and double-blind, so neither patients nor staff knew who got the drug or the control at the time. The title reports large and lasting drops in depression and anxiety after the drug. Proof of this grade was rare in psychedelic research at the time. The results helped reopen medical study of psychedelics for distress at the end of life.
pmc-5472757:
Vanpouille-Box, Alard, Aryankalayil, and their colleagues reported in 2017 on radiotherapy and tumor immunity. Researchers are testing whether radiotherapy can make immunotherapy work better. The mechanisms by which radiation induces anti-tumor T cells, though, remained unclear.

The team shows that an enzyme called Trex1, a DNA exonuclease, is induced by radiation doses above a certain threshold in different cancer types. Trex1 chews up the DNA debris that would otherwise alert the immune system. That finding explains why dose per treatment matters for immune effects. It guides how radiation schedules should be designed when the goal is to partner with immunotherapy.
pmc-5891557:
Caroline Terwee and colleagues set out COSMIN methods for judging content validity in 2018. Content validity asks whether a patient questionnaire covers what matters to patients. The authors call it the most important trait of such a measure, and the hardest to judge.

Built through a Delphi process with experts, the standards rate how well a questionnaire was designed. They also rate studies that test whether items are relevant, complete, and clear. Poor content cannot be fixed by good statistics later. The guidance helps reviewers and developers build measures that patients find meaningful.
pmc-5897557:
Daniel Rosenblum, Nitin Joshi, Wei Tao, and coauthors reviewed targeted delivery of cancer drugs in 2018. Tiny carriers can ferry drugs toward tumors and spare healthy tissue. Lab studies of such carriers have multiplied over recent decades.

Yet very few carriers have reached approved clinical use, and none using active targeting had done so at the time. The authors examine why success in animals so often fails in patients. Tumor diversity and weak delivery into tumor tissue are key barriers. Their sober account helps researchers design carriers with a real chance in the clinic.
pmc-6984357:
Diego Darriba, David Posada, Alexey Kozlov, and coauthors presented ModelTest-NG in 2019. Choosing the right evolutionary model is a required step before building trees from DNA or protein data. Older tools for that choice were slow on big alignments.

ModelTest-NG rebuilds two popular predecessors from scratch. It runs one to two orders of magnitude faster while matching their accuracy. Parallel processing lets it handle genome-scale data on clusters. Phylogenetics teams folded it into standard pipelines, where model choice no longer eats the project's time budget. The tool supports both cluster machines and single workstations through the same command line.
pmc-7025157:
Marc Arbyn, Elisabet Weiderpass, Laia Bruni, and coauthors estimated cervical cancer worldwide for 2018 in this 2019 analysis. Lasting infection with human papillomavirus is the main cause of this cancer. Vaccines and virus-based screening now exist to prevent it.

The World Health Organization had just launched a global push for elimination. The authors give case and death estimates for countries around the world. Burden falls heaviest on low income countries with weak screening. Their baseline shows exactly where vaccine and screening scale-up would save the most lives. Regional tables expose deep gaps between high-burden and low-burden countries on every measure.
pmc-7619357:
Ziyun Zhang and six colleagues show that the sugary surface coat of lung macrophages, called the glycocalyx, depends on where in the airway the cells live. The coat surrounds every cell and shapes how it senses and handles its surroundings, and its shedding into blood is used as a marker of inflammation. Still, almost nothing was known about what builds the coat on macrophages or how it differs between their subsets.

In mouse lungs, macrophages carried coats set by their anatomical location and by the signals that turned them from blood monocytes into resident cells. Viral infection then remodeled the coat during inflammation. Knowing that the same cell type wears different coats in different niches changes how researchers should read shedding markers. It opens a new angle on how airway defenses are organized before infection even starts.
pmc-8265157:
Ivica Letunic and Peer Bork presented version five of the Interactive Tree Of Life in 2021, an online tool for drawing and annotating evolutionary trees. Phylogenetic trees show how species or genes are related, and researchers need to display them with layers of extra data attached. The tool is free and open to anyone through a web browser.

The new version introduces a completely rebuilt tree display engine, along with many added features for styling and annotation. The authors walk through what the engine makes possible, from huge trees to richly labeled figures for publication. Tools like this one turn the abstract output of evolutionary analysis into pictures that scientists can reason with.
saturnia-regna-1657: Saturnia regna, 1657. The Saturnian realms. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. History keeps its place secure. Readers can find it here.
steinmann-das-haus-rothschild-1857:
Friedrich Arnold Steinmann wrote this German work on the house of Rothschild in Prague in 1857. Its title means the house of Rothschild, its history and its deals. The book has two parts, and both stand in this text.

Steinmann tells of the rise of the Frankfurt house and its loans to the states of Europe. He writes as a near man of the age, with the facts of the deals set out in full. The Jewish Encyclopedia cites his book as the first sound German work on the house. Both parts stand here in full, just as Prague read them.
tauler-sermons-winkworth-1857:
John Tauler was a Dominican preacher in Strasbourg in the fourteenth century, when plague and church strife shook his city. His sermons, in Winkworth's 1857 translation, carry his mystical preaching to English readers. Tauler belonged to the circle later called the Friends of God.

He urges hearers to sink into the ground of the soul, where God speaks beneath all noise and self-will. His sermons treat birthdays of Christ within the heart, patient suffering, and the prayer that needs no words. Luther admired Tauler, and his voice shaped German devotion long after his death. Winkworth's graceful English helped the sermons find that second life.
the-broad-highway-pg5257:
The Broad Highway, by Jeffery Farnol, opens with a dedication to Shirley Byron Jevons, friend of the author's boyish ambitions, and a note called the Ante Scriptum. The note is word for word the start of the other copy of the book in this set. It tells of an early summer morning spent in a tree's shade, eating fried bacon with a tinker. There the thought of writing a book first came.

The book in mind would treat of roads, trees, and wind in lonely places, of brooks, inns, and country folk. The tinker scoffs that a tree is only a tree. So the author adds folk and feats, counted on his fingers: a highwayman, Tom Cragg the pugilist, a one-legged soldier of the Peninsula, and a midnight flight from desperate villains. Best of all, a most extraordinary tinker. The tinker cries out at finding himself in the book.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: Volume III of The Diary and Letters of Madame d'Arblay (Frances Burney), printed by Frederick Warne and Company in 1892, with notes by W. C. Ward and Macaulay's essay at the front, presents the front matter of its sibling record. The contents open on the French emigrants at Juniper Hall, the charm of Talleyrand, Dr. Burney's objections to the match, and the marriage to M. d'Arblay, then move to a section headed Love in a Cottage for 1793-6. Only the title page and contents synopsis are present here.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
No. 57 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated December 9, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item is news from Germany. Germany, the paper says, has done something that seems like a plain, every-day case of robbery. Some German missionaries have been killed in China. Germany has taken a Chinese port in revenge. The paper tells the story so its readers can judge for themselves.

The German Catholic Church had a mission in Shantung Province, China. Word of an attack on the mission at Yen Chu Fu reached Berlin. Two missionaries were killed. The deed was first blamed on pirates. Later the deed was traced to a plot of the province's governor. He acted in revenge for some old grievance. The paper first defends missionaries at length. It then gives the facts of the seizure.
the-last-of-the-mohicans-a-narrative-of-: James Fenimore Cooper wrote his frontier novel as a narrative of 1757, during the French and Indian War. Only the contents and the first line of his introduction are present here, listing thirty-three chapters plus an introduction. The introduction begins by locating the tale scene and its sources, then stops. The story of Hawkeye, Chingachgook, and Uncas does not appear in this record beyond that opening line and the chapter list.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Venice, the second part of To Paris and Prison in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, uses the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's English version, with chapters found by Arthur Symons. Despite the part's title, Chapter Ten opens in Vienna, covering Casanova's stay and his departure for Venice. He arrives at twenty-eight, well dressed but short of money. His one letter of recommendation, from the poet Migliavacca, introduces him to the Abbe Metastasio.

Within an hour's talk, Casanova finds Metastasio more learned than his works suggest, and genuinely modest. The poet recites unpublished verses on his tutor Gravina's death, tears in his eyes. He shows pages covered with erasures, explaining he never composed more than fourteen perfected lines in a day. Asked his favorite among his operas, he names Attilio Regolo, without claiming it is his best. Readers sit in on a young adventurer's audience with Europe's most famous librettist.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
A supplementary number of the Mirror, No. 402, draws on The Landscape Annual for 1830 to present the leaning towers of Bologna. The annual, subtitled The Tourist in Italy and Switzerland, carries twenty-five plates from drawings by Mr. Prout. Subjects run from Geneva and Chillon through Milan Cathedral and Lake Como to Venice's Rialto and Bridge of Sighs. Thomas Roscoe wrote the descriptions, and the magazine selects one plate and part of its text by the proprietor's permission.

Roscoe's Bologna is celebrated alike in arts and in letters, the mother of studies, the extract begins. The towers plate promises the city's most famous oddity after this introduction. Parisians in the Galerie Vivienne and Londoners in Cheapside are both predicted to cry out in admiration at the plates. Readers receive an annual's Italian tour secondhand, one engraving borrowed for a twopenny sheet.
tob-0157:
Oxford's Sacred Books of the East carried the Zoroastrian canon in volumes four through nine of the series. James Darmesteter and L. H. Mills divided the labor of translation between them. Together their Avesta volumes formed the most complete English rendering of the scriptures in the Victorian age.

Hymns of the Yasna, the purity laws of the Vendidad, and hymns to the yazatas all stand in place. Max Muller's series aimed to give every great Eastern faith a standard English form, and Persia's ancient faith received full honors. Verified from pre-1930 editions, the set remains a working library for students of Zoroastrianism.
tob-10057:
Samuel Marinus Zwemer, a missionary and scholar, presented al-Ghazali to English readers as a Muslim seeker after God. Al-Ghazali was the eleventh-century theologian whose crisis of doubt led him away from a famous teaching career and into Sufi mysticism. Zwemer treats that search as Islam at its spiritual best.

Drawing on al-Ghazali's own writings, Zwemer traces his life, his arguments, and his turn toward direct experience of God. He argues the search for certainty speaks across religions. The portrait is respectful and admiring, notable because it comes from a Christian missionary writing about a Muslim thinker for a largely Christian audience.
tob-10257:
Unknown compilers in the sixteenth century gathered the Rosarium Philosophorum, the Rosary of the Philosophers, from older alchemical writings. It pairs short texts with a famous series of woodcuts. Few alchemy books became as widely copied or as often quoted.

The pictures show a king and queen who meet, unite, die, and rise again in new form. For alchemists, the images pictured the making of the philosophers' stone, step by step. Later readers, including Carl Jung, treated the series as a picture of inner change as well. The work sits at the heart of the alchemical picture tradition.
tob-10457:
Miguel de Molinos, a Spanish priest working in Rome, taught a path of prayer called Quietism in the 1670s. His writings drew crowds of followers across Europe. Church authorities later turned on him, and the Inquisition jailed him for life.

Molinos tells the soul to stop striving, rest passive before God, and pass through dry, empty prayer into deep union. Critics charged that such passivity killed effort, duty, and even morality. The fight over his teaching shaped Catholic spiritual life for decades, and his short, calm prose still draws readers who study prayer and stillness.
tob-10957:
Proclus, the last great systematizer of ancient Platonism in the fifth century, argued in his Platonic Theology that Plato's dialogues contain a complete theology. Volume one, in Thomas Taylor's early English translation, begins the case. A hierarchy of gods unfolds, in Proclus's reading, from the One beyond being.

Taylor was the great English champion of Neoplatonism, and his version brought dense fifth-century metaphysics to English readers when almost none was available. The argument proceeds by careful divisions: gods, intellect, soul, and the orders between them. Readers get Neoplatonism at its most elaborate, the final flowering of pagan Greek theology before the Christian empire closed its schools.
tob-4057:
Volume four concludes the Gutenberg four-volume edition of The Secret Doctrine, rounding out Blavatsky's Theosophical edifice with supplementary material on the system's key ideas. Indexes, glossarial help, and remaining commentary support the vast structure raised in the earlier volumes. The capstone presumes readers have the cosmology and anthropology of volumes one and two in hand.

Best approached after the first three volumes have laid the groundwork, the closing volume serves study rather than discovery. Together the four volumes form the most ambitious occult work of the nineteenth century in its fullest Gutenberg presentation. Committees of readers have mined it for a century; few have finished it quickly.
tob-4157:
Andrew Lang defended a bold thesis in The Making of Religion: the high gods of tribal peoples came before animism, not after it. Against anthropologists who derived religion from ghost worship and fear, Lang argued that so-called primitive peoples already knew a moral creator, a Father in heaven, without missionary teaching. Religion, he proposed, began partly in wonder.

Lang ranged over Australian, African, and American evidence, quoting field reports against the theorists of his day. His contemporaries fought the book; later anthropology partly revived its questions. Controversial then and now, The Making of Religion remains a literate, combative challenge to any simple story of religion evolving upward from savagery.
trollope-barchester-towers-1857:
Anthony Trollope published Barchester Towers in 1857, the battle for Barchester's soul in comic form supreme. Mrs. Proudie and Archdeacon Grantly fight for the diocese in a tale many call Victorian comedy's peak. The sequel to The Warden outsold it at once and fixed Trollope's name with the reading public of England.

A new bishop, Dr. Proudie, arrives ruled by his wife and her chaplain, the oily Mr. Slope. Slope schemes for power and for the widowed Eleanor Bold, Harding's daughter, as preferment and love intertwine in Barchester. The Thornes' fête, the Stanhope family's Italian ease, and a score of clerical feuds fill the bustling canvas here. Eleanor finds happiness with the shy Arabin, and Slope is sent packing to London in disgrace at last. Trollope's ease with fools, knaves, and saints makes the cathedral town feel entirely real.
un-ga-res-a-69-57:
Arms tipped with depleted uranium leave a residue that worries states where such rounds were fired. Resolution A/69/57, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, takes up the question. It recalls votes on the point since 2007. Views of states and of world bodies on the use of such arms and rounds are noted, as sent to the Secretary-General over the years.

The text gives weight to the counsel of three agencies: the atomic energy body, the UN environment arm, and the World Health Organization. Their shared line is to cut the risk to people and to the land from ground fouled by uranium dust. The vote asks that such counsel be put to work where it fits.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/57 of the General Assembly deals with the health and environmental effects of weapons containing depleted uranium. Studies so far have not settled the long-term risks. The United Nations Environment Programme urges a precautionary approach because of uncertainties such as groundwater contamination. Noting both points, the Assembly asks the relevant agencies to update their research. States that used such munitions in conflicts are invited to share detailed information on where and how much was used. That way affected states can assess contaminated areas.
un-sc-res-1357:
Bosnia's peace forces were renewed for another year on 21 June 2001. The Council restated its support for the Dayton Peace Agreement and for the High Representative's work. It thanked the stabilization force, the United Nations mission, and the international police for their service. The Bosnian authorities bore the first duty to make the peace work.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the member states to keep the multinational stabilization force going for a planned twelve months. The force could take all measures needed to defend itself and carry out its mission. The United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, police task force included, was extended to 21 June 2002. The parties were reminded that they had pledged to cooperate fully with all bodies applying the agreement, the war crimes tribunal among them. The Council kept the Bosnian file under close review.
un-sc-res-1457:
Looting of natural wealth in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is taken up in Resolution 1457 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 24 January 2003. A panel of experts had reported that armed groups and foreign actors were stripping the country of resources. That trade, the panel found, helped keep the war going.

The text strongly condemns the illegal taking of Congo's resources and demands that states end it. It gives the expert panel six more months to check its findings and update its lists. People and firms named in the reports may reply, and their answers would be published. States are urged to run their own probes through their courts.
un-sc-res-1557: Security Council Resolution 1557, from 2004, is preserved here in the record wording supplied by English Wikisource. A reader meets the Council's usual order of business: what came before, what the members found, and what they then decided. Keeping the whole text, rather than a digest, is what makes the entry useful for checking claims.
un-sc-res-157:
The Congo crisis split the Council in September 1960. Its permanent members could not agree. That deadlock, the text says, stopped the Council from doing its chief job. On 17 September 1960 the Council chose a different route. It called an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The Uniting for Peace procedure allowed that move. The Assembly would make fitting recommendations on the Congo.

The session met within days as the crisis deepened. Congolese leaders were fighting for control of the new state. Foreign troops and advisers were already involved. The resolution is a twin of the Hungary step of 1956. Both show the Council handing a blocked crisis to the wider membership.
un-sc-res-1657:
A company of peacekeepers was shifted from Liberia to Côte d'Ivoire by the Security Council on 6 February 2006. Côte d'Ivoire's crisis and the blocks on its peace process persisted from all sides. The Secretary-General had written on 1 February 2006 about the need. The United Nations Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, was due for renewal by 31 March 2006.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the Secretary-General to move up to one infantry company from UNMIL to the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire at once. The company would serve until 31 March 2006, adding security for United Nations staff and property. The move was without prejudice to later decisions on UNMIL's renewal or troop levels. The Council said it would review the arrangement within thirty days and by the March deadline. It also kept open the option of further transfers between the two missions.
un-sc-res-1757:
When the Council met on 30 May 2007, it adopted Resolution 1757 on Lebanon. A huge bomb had killed the former prime minister, Rafiq Hariri, in February 2005. Lebanon and the United Nations had signed a deal to create a special court. Beirut's parliament could not ratify it, so the process stalled.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council puts the tribunal agreement into force on 10 June 2007. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon will try those behind the Hariri attack. It can also take linked attacks from the same period. The court mixes Lebanese and foreign judges and sits outside Lebanon. Voluntary gifts may cover any funding gap Beirut cannot pay.
un-sc-res-1857:
With Resolution 1857, adopted on 22 December 2008, the Council turned to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Armed groups in the east lived off the illegal trade in minerals and timber. That trade paid for guns and kept the war going. Experts had traced how buyers abroad fed the chain without checking their sources.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the sanctions regime and its Group of Experts until 30 November 2009. It widens the travel bans and asset freezes to a new target class. Anyone backing illegal armed groups through the stolen resource trade can now be listed. So can those who block aid work. States should make sure firms handling Congolese minerals check their suppliers with care.
un-sc-res-2057:
South Sudan stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 2057 on South Sudan in July 2012. The country had marked one year of independence from Sudan. Cross-border clashes with Sudan had eased but not ended. Fighting between communities in Jonglei state had killed hundreds and driven many from home.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the peacekeeping mission, called UNMISS, through 15 July 2013. Guarding civilians stays the mission's first task. It may use all necessary means within its reach to do so. The text presses Juba to fight corruption, end long detentions, and run disarmament well. It also asks the mission to watch the Sudan border and to report on Lord's Resistance Army attacks.
un-sc-res-357: Numbered 357 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1974 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-457:
American diplomats were held hostage in Tehran when the Council acted in 1979. Embassy staff had been seized that November. On 4 December 1979 the Council voiced deep concern at the dangerous tension. It recalled its president's appeals of 9 and 27 November. Iran's foreign minister had set out his country's grievances in a letter. The Council said disputes must be settled by peaceful means under the Charter.

Iran had to release the embassy personnel at once. It had to protect them and let them leave the country. Iran and the United States had to work out their remaining issues peacefully. Both governments had to show the utmost restraint. The Secretary-General was asked to lend his good offices. The hostages in fact stayed captive for over a year.
un-sc-res-57: Murder in Jerusalem shocked the Security Council into Resolution 57, passed on 18 September 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte, the UN mediator in Palestine, had been shot dead the day before. A band of gunmen in the city killed him, while he was on his peace work in the Holy Land. The text calls the act cowardly, and the work of a criminal group of terror. The UN flag must fly at half-mast for three days. All costs of the death and burial fall to the UN's funds.
un-sc-res-757: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 757, catalogued for 1992 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Bosnia's peace work is renewed in Resolution 1357. It passed by a full vote on 21 June 2001. The Council restated its faith in the Dayton peace pact of 1995. It thanked the many hands at work: the High Envoy, the NATO-led force, the UN team, and its police arm. States near Bosnia, it said, must play a fair part in the peace.

The UN team's term ran for twelve more months. The police task force went on with it. The world force that kept the truce won the same fresh span. The Council kept its yearly watch on the tests of peace: fair votes, the return of those who fled, and court action for war crimes.

Plunder of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's natural wealth is condemned in Resolution 1457, adopted on 24 January 2003. A Panel of Experts had reported on the illegal taking of resources and other riches during the war. The Council said this theft was a main force keeping the conflict alive, deepening the people's suffering, and holding back the country's growth.

The Council strongly condemns the illegal exploitation and demands that the states involved stop it at once. It says Congo's resources must be used openly, lawfully, and on fair terms for the Congolese people. It gives the panel a fresh six-month mandate to check its past findings, hear replies from those named, and advise on laws a transitional government could use to control the trade. States are urged to run their own inquiries, and Congo's move to suspend named officials is welcomed.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve months on 12 August 2004. The mission, created a year earlier, leads United Nations support for Iraqi institutions and representative government. It works through advice, training, and help with elections and law reform across the country. The Council said it would review the mandate in twelve months, or sooner if Iraq's government asked.

The Congo crisis split the Council in September 1960. The new state's army had mutinied. Belgium sent troops back in. The Soviet Union and the West backed rival camps. At the 906th meeting, the big powers could not agree. Resolution 157 passed on 17 September 1960 by eight votes to two. Poland and the Soviet Union said no. France held back.

Blocked at home, the Council passed the file upward. It called a rare special session of the General Assembly. The tool came from the 1950 Uniting for Peace plan. That plan lets the Assembly act when vetoes freeze the Council. The session gave the wider membership its say on the Congo's fate.

Resolution 1657, adopted on 6 February 2006, moves soldiers between two West African missions. The UN mission in Liberia, UNMIL, still had months left on its mandate. Next door, the operation in Côte d'Ivoire needed extra protection for UN personnel and property after attacks and unrest tied to the stalled peace process there.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the Secretary-General to redeploy at once up to one infantry company from Liberia to the Côte d'Ivoire operation, until 31 March 2006. The transfer was meant to give extra security coverage without prejudging later decisions about renewing the Ivorian operation. Inter-mission cooperation of this kind became a standard tool for UN commanders facing sudden local crises.

Resolution 1757 is the Security Council decision of 30 May 2007. It brought the Special Tribunal for Lebanon into being. The tribunal was created to try those responsible for the 14 February 2005 bombing in Beirut. That bombing killed Lebanon's former prime minister and others. The tribunal was also to try connected attacks in Lebanon in the same period.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ordered that the agreement between the United Nations and Lebanon take effect on 10 June 2007. Approval inside Lebanon had stalled. The long annex sets out the tribunal's makeup and its statute. The tribunal has Lebanese and international judges, a prosecutor, and a defence office.

Congo's sanctions criteria are widened in Resolution 1857, adopted on 22 December 2008. The Group of Experts' 2008 reports traced embargo violations and the resource trade behind the eastern armed groups. The Council built on Resolution 1807 (2008) and on listing procedures from its other sanctions regimes. Those procedures include public reasons for listing and a delisting Focal Point.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms, transport, financial, and travel measures until 30 November 2009. It confirms the travel ban and asset freeze reach seven classes of designees: embargo violators, foreign armed-group leaders blocking disarmament, and externally backed militia leaders. They reach those recruiting or using children, those committing grave violations against children or women, those obstructing humanitarian aid, and those funding armed groups through illicit resource trade. The Group of Experts is extended to 30 November 2009, and the Committee must publish narrative summaries of listing reasons.

Resolution 1957, adopted on 15 December 2010, lifts a layer of the sanctions era from Iraq. Iraq's foreign minister had written that January confirming support for the non-proliferation regime and compliance with disarmament treaties. The UN atomic agency reported excellent cooperation from Baghdad on safeguards, and Iraq had begun applying the tougher Additional Protocol inspection rules in February 2010.

Rewarding that record, and acting under Chapter VII, the Council ended the weapons-related restrictions first imposed after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The step aimed to restore Iraq to the international standing it held before 1990. It closed the legal chapter opened by the disarmament demands that had dominated Iraq's relations with the UN for twenty years.

South Sudan's mission is extended through its first independence anniversary period in Resolution 2057, adopted in 2012. Intercommunal violence in Jonglei State had killed hundreds, cross-border clashes with Sudan had eased after Resolution 2046 (2012), and the new government was building institutions under an austerity budget.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, UNMISS, on its Resolution 1996 (2011) mandate through 15 July 2013. Protection of civilians and an improved security environment are the stated priorities, and UNMISS is authorized to use all necessary means for its protection tasks. Until the Joint Border Verification and Monitoring Mechanism starts, UNMISS must observe and report any flow of personnel or arms across the Sudan border. The Council welcomes the March 2012 action plan to end SPLA child recruitment and release all children in its ranks, and presses the government to end impunity and arbitrary detention.

Swaziland was among the last British lands in Africa to go free. King Sobhuza II took the throne of a free state on 6 September 1968. The small land, now called Eswatini, sat between South Africa and Mozambique. Its bid for a UN seat was filed as S/8808. Resolution 257 passed with no dissent on 11 September 1968.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Swaziland. The Assembly did so that month. The king would rule till 1982, one of the long reigns of the age. Landlocked and small, the state leaned hard on its big next-door state for trade. Still, its seat gave it a voice of its own. The text is the plain legal step that put one more African flag in the hall that fall.

Fighting in Cyprus resumed in August 1974, in spite of the cease-fire the Council had demanded the month before. A second round of Turkish military action had opened on the island. Resolution 357 was adopted unanimously on 14 August 1974.

The Council deeply deplored the return to fighting. It reaffirmed Resolution 353 of July in all its parts. The parties were told to carry out those parts without delay. Everyone involved in the fighting had to stop all firing and military action at once. Talks had to restart without delay as well. Their aim was to restore peace in the area and constitutional government in Cyprus. The Council said it would stay ready to meet at once if the cease-fire broke down.

Resolution 457 was adopted unanimously on 4 December 1979, a month after militants seized the United States embassy in Tehran. American diplomatic staff were being held hostage in Iran, and tension between the two countries was rising fast. The Council opened by voicing deep concern that the standoff could endanger wider peace and security.

Its central demand was direct: Iran must free the embassy personnel at once, protect them, and let them leave the country. The text also reminded all states of their duty to respect the safety of diplomats and embassy grounds under the Vienna Conventions. When Iran did not comply, the Council returned to the crisis within the month.

The United Nations mediator in Palestine was shot dead in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte, named in the text, died on his peace mission. The Council said the act seemed to be the work of a group of terrorists. Resolution 57, adopted the next day, records the response. The United Nations flag was to fly at half-mast for three days. The costs of the burial could be paid from the Working Capital Fund. Its president, or a deputy, would attend the burial.

Sweeping sanctions fell on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made up of Serbia and Montenegro, on 30 May 1992. Its authorities, including the Yugoslav People's Army, had ignored the demands of Resolution 752. That text had ordered a stop to the fighting and to outside interference in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Resolution 757 is the Council's answer.

All states had to block imports from the republic and stop exports to it. Its access to funds and other financial resources had to be cut off. The measures would last until Belgrade met the Council's demands. The sanctions built on the arms embargo first imposed in 1991. The text also deplored the forced expulsions aimed at changing the ethnic makeup of parts of Bosnia. The blocking of aid deliveries to Sarajevo and other towns was condemned as well.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
A fifth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/4857, reviews the force around 1960 and 1961. UNEF patrolled the Egypt-Israel frontier from its base in Gaza and Sinai posts. Its task was to keep a truce that neither side fully trusted.

The report covers the force's size, its daily patrol work, and minor incidents along the line. It also deals with funding, a sore point among member states from the start. These yearly reports form the paper trail of the first great peacekeeping force, in its steady middle years.
uslaw-usc-t2-s157:
Section 157 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the funds of the Library of Congress Trust Fund Board. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. The moneys and securities that make up the trust funds given to the board are to be receipted for by the Secretary of the Treasury. That officer is to invest, reinvest, or hold them as the board directs from time to time.

The income, as and when it is gathered in, is to be deposited with the Treasurer of the United States. The Treasurer is to enter it in a special account to the credit of the Library of Congress. That account is subject to payment out as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
